sentence.0: title: Vice Society leverages PrintNightmare in ransomware attacks url: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/2021/08/vice-society-ransomware-printnightmare.html By Edmund Brumaghin, Joe Marshall, and Arnaud Zobec.
sentence.1: Executive SummaryAnother threat actor is actively exploiting the so-called PrintNightmare vulnerability (CVE-2021-1675 / CVE-2021-34527) in Windows' print spooler service to spread laterally across a victim's network as part of a recent ransomware attack, according to Cisco Talos Incident Response research.
sentence.2: While previous research found that other threat actors had been exploiting this vulnerability, this appears to be new for the threat actor Vice Society.
sentence.3: Talos Incident Response's research demonstrates that multiple, distinct threat actors view this vulnerability as attractive to use during their attacks and may indicate that this vulnerability will continue to see more widespread adoption and incorporation by various adversaries moving forward.
sentence.4: For defenders, it is important to understand the attack lifecycle leading up to the deployment of ransomware.
sentence.5: If users have not already, they should download the latest patch for PrintNightmare from Microsoft.
sentence.6: In this post, we'll analyze the various TTPs used in a recent ransomware attack from Vice Society that leveraged this vulnerability.
sentence.7: Many of these same TTPs are commonly observed in other ransomware attacks, such as a previously published analysis of a WastedLocker attack.
sentence.8: Who is Vice Society?Vice Society is a relatively new player in the ransomware space.
sentence.9: They emerged in mid-2021 and have been observed launching big-game hunting and double-extortion attacks, primarily targeting small or midsize victims.
sentence.10: This group also has notably targeted public school districts and other educational institutions.
sentence.11: As they are a new actor in this space, Vice Society's TTPs are difficult to quantify.
sentence.12: However, based on incident response observations, they are quick to leverage new vulnerabilities for lateral movement and persistence on a victim's network.
sentence.13: They also attempt to be innovative on end-point detection response bypasses.
sentence.14: As with other threat actors operating in the big-game hunting space, Vice Society operates a data leak site, which they use to publish data exfiltrated from victims who do not choose to pay their extortion demands.
sentence.15: Below is an example screenshot of this site.
sentence.16: Recent attack methodologyThroughout the course of our analysis of a recent human-operated ransomware attack associated with Vice Society, we observed several notable tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used throughout each stage of the attack lifecycle.
sentence.17: Some of the most interesting characteristics of this attack were:The use of utilities such as proxychains and impacket during the post-compromise phases of the attack lifecycle.
sentence.18: The targeting of backups to prevent recovery following ransomware deployment.
sentence.19: The degradation of ESXi servers used for virtualization in victim environments.
sentence.20: The use of a DLL that takes advantage of the recently discovered PrintNightmare vulnerability for which Microsoft has previously released a security update.
sentence.21: Attempts to bypass native Windows protections for credential theft and privilege escalation.
sentence.22: Below are some key examples of the TTPs used in this attack as they relate to the Mitre ATT&CK Framework.
sentence.23: DiscoveryATT&CK Technique: System Owner/User Discovery (T1033)ATT&CK Technique: Account Discovery (T1087)ATT&CK Technique: Domain Trust Discovery (T1482)Once initial access was achieved, several techniques were observed being leveraged to conduct post-compromise discovery and reconnaissance within the environment.
sentence.24: We observed attempts to access the backup solution employed in the environment, likely to prevent the organization from successfully recovering without paying the demanded ransom.
sentence.25: The "sudo" command was used to obtain credentials associated with a commercial backup solution, likely trying to gain access to backups present within the environment.sudo -s
sentence.27: [Backup Prompt] whoamiWe also observed the use of impacket, a common network protocol manipulation tool to enumerate the environment and obtain additional information about the Active Directory configuration in place.
sentence.28: This is typically done to identify high-value targets that may be attractive, as attacks attempt to maximize their sphere of influence over as much of the environment as possible prior, eventually deploying ransomware and making their presence known.
sentence.29: Below are some examples of the command line syntax used for the performance of this activity.cmd.exe /q

sentence.41: The attacker also used the "proxychains" utility, which is often employed to redirect network traffic during penetration testing, red teaming, and other offensive operations.

sentence.54: A DLL associated with PrintNightmare was observed on systems within the environment as described in the section "Credential Access.

sentence.67: By implementing this persistence, the attacker can regain access to the environment if the targeted organization destroys their initial means of access.
sentence.68: Lateral movementATT&CK Technique: Remote Services (T1021)ATT&CK Technique: Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570)Once operational within the target environment, attackers will typically perform reconnaissance, identifying additional target systems, and then move laterally from system to system as they attempt to escalate privileges and then, ultimately, deploy ransomware on many systems in the environment.
sentence.69: During the investigation, we observed the attacker leveraging Windows Remote Desktop Connections to pivot to additional systems in the environment.
sentence.70: This was typically performed via the following command-line syntax:C:\Windows\system32\mstsc.exe /v

sentence.72: Bypass -file \[IPADDRESS]\share$\p.ps1 During the attack, adversaries copied and executed the aforementioned PowerShell script on multiple systems across the environment.
sentence.74: Technique: OS Credential Dumping (T1003)ATT&CK Technique: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory (T1003.001)The actor attempted to extract credentials from the victim in two ways: Accessing the active directory global catalog file ntds.dit and utilizing comsvcs.dll. Comsvcs.dll is a well-known way to extract LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service) data.
sentence.75: By invoking comsvcs.dll with rundll32.exe, an adversary can create a dump of any process.
sentence.76: This is a classic and clever living-off-the-land binary (LoLBin) tactic that avoids popular credential extraction tools like Mimikatz, which may alert defenders.
sentence.77: We also observed attempts to dump the NTDS.dit, which is a database of Active Directory information.
sentence.78: Examples of the command-line syntax used in these cases are below.cmd.exe /q /c

sentence.82: ac i ntds' 'ifm' 'create full c:\temp_logs' q q 1> \\127.0.0.1\admin$\__[STRING]5 2>&1The actor also utilized PrintNightmare, a recently published series of vulnerabilities by Microsoft that would allow remote code execution when an improper print spooler performs privileged file operations.
sentence.83: This attack vector is notable in the ubiquitous nature of print services in all modern corporate enterprises.
sentence.84: Microsoft has recently released a security patch for PrintNightmare — we encourage all enterprises to patch immediately to avoid exploitation.

sentence.86: We also observed the attacker attempting to clear the contents of security logs on compromised systems.

sentence.90: Disabling this security control allows attackers to leverage pass-the-hash attacks and hinder RDP's security on systems.cmd.exe /q /c

sentence.99: 1 /f We also observed the threat actor attempting to evade detection while enumerating the environment using an AMSI bypass, which is often used as a way to evade detection by endpoint security solutions that may be present on compromised systems.
sentence.100: In this case, the Windows Command Processor was used to invoke PowerShell, which then leveraged Invoke-Expression (IEX) for this purpose.cmd.exe /Q /c powershell.exe -exec bypass -noni -nop

sentence.106: In these attacks, adversaries attempt to exfiltrate large quantities of sensitive information for the purposes of further extortion against victims.
sentence.107: This data, once exfiltrated, is published to attacker-controlled websites that are commonly referred to as "data leak sites" in situations where the victim chooses not to pay the ransom demand.
sentence.108: In this attack, we observed the adversary attempting to exfiltrate sensitive information over SMB (TCP/445) directly from a compromised domain controller.
sentence.109: This was likely chosen as a way to bypass egress filtering that may have been in place at the perimeter of the victim environment.
sentence.110: Defender takeawaysIt can be difficult to account for the myriad ways an attacker can compromise and inflict malware on a network.
sentence.111: Given the techniques demonstrated here, it can feel overwhelming as a defender to account for every avenue of attack.
sentence.112: The good news is that there are several lessons we can learn about this incident: Logging is critical for forensics — ensure there is reliable and secure logging infrastructure in place.
sentence.113: Utilize multi-factor authentication to make credential theft more difficult to exploit.
sentence.114: Look at egress filtering for firewalls and ensure malicious traffic cannot call out to adversary infrastructure.
sentence.115: Utilize an endpoint detection response platform that detects LoLBin abuse and malware implants.
sentence.116: Keep up-to-date and offline backups that cannot be targeted by adversaries.
sentence.117: ConclusionAs demonstrated throughout this post, attackers often make use of a variety of tactics, techniques, and procedures as they work to accomplish their mission objectives.
sentence.118: In some instances, there is significant overlap and similarities between the approaches taken by distinct threat actors.
sentence.119: They often leverage dual-use tools for various purposes to minimize their footprint and evade detection.
sentence.120: Likewise, adversaries are constantly refining their approach to the ransomware attack lifecycle as they strive to operate more effectively, efficiently, and evasively.
sentence.121: The use of the vulnerability known as PrintNightmare shows that adversaries are paying close attention and will quickly incorporate new tools that they find useful for various purposes during their attacks.
sentence.122: Multiple distinct threat actors are now taking advantage of PrintNightmare, and this adoption will likely continue to increase as long as it is effective.
sentence.123: It is important that defenders be aware of the various TTPs being used throughout the attack lifecycle so that they are prepared to prevent, detect, and respond to nefarious activity that may be indicative of a successful compromise of their environment.
sentence.124: Failure to do so could result in widespread operational disruption, reputational damage, and the loss of confidentiality of sensitive information.

sentence.137: title: UNC215: Spotlight on a Chinese Espionage Campaign in Israel url: https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2021/08/unc215-chinese-espionage-campaign-in-israel.html
sentence.138: This blog post details the post-compromise tradecraft and operational tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) of a Chinese espionage group we track as UNC215.
sentence.139: While UNC215’s targets are located throughout the Middle East, Europe, Asia, and North America, this report focuses on intrusion activity primarily observed at Israeli entities.
sentence.140: This report comes on the heels of the July 19, 2021, announcements by governments in North America, Europe, and Asia and intragovernmental organizations, such as the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO), and the European Union, condemning widespread cyber espionage conducted on behalf of the Chinese Government.
sentence.141: These coordinated statements attributing sustained cyber espionage activities to the Chinese Government corroborate our long-standing reporting on Chinese threat actor targeting of private companies, governments, and various organizations around the world, and this blog post shows yet another region where Chinese cyber espionage is active.
sentence.143: In early 2019, Mandiant began identifying and responding to intrusions in the Middle East by Chinese espionage group UNC215.
sentence.144: These intrusions exploited the Microsoft SharePoint vulnerability CVE-2019-0604 to install web shells and FOCUSFJORD payloads at targets in the Middle East and Central Asia.
sentence.145: There are targeting and high level technique overlaps with between UNC215 and APT27, but we do not have sufficient evidence to say that the same actor is responsible for both sets of activity.
sentence.146: APT27 has not been seen since 2015, and UNC215 is targeting many of the regions that APT27 previously focused on; however, we have not seen direct connection or shared tools, so we are only able to assess this link with low confidence.
sentence.147: In addition to data from Mandiant Incident Response and FireEye telemetry, we worked with Israeli defense agencies to review data from additional compromises of Israeli entities.
sentence.148: This analysis showed multiple, concurrent operations against Israeli government institutions, IT providers and telecommunications entities beginning in January 2019.
sentence.149: During this time, UNC215 used new TTPs to hinder attribution and detection, maintain operational security, employ false flags, and leverage trusted relationships for lateral movement.
sentence.150: We believe this adversary is still active in the region.
sentence.151: Attack Lifecycle Between 2019 and 2020, Mandiant responded to several incidents where Microsoft SharePoint vulnerability CVE-2019-0604 was used to deliver web shells, and then FOCUSFJORD payloads to select government and academic targets in the Middle East and Central Asia.
sentence.152: After gaining initial access, the operators conduct credential harvesting and extensive internal network reconnaissance.
sentence.153: This includes running native Windows commands on compromised servers, executing ADFind on the Active Directory, and scanning the internal network with numerous publicly available tools and a non-public scanner we named WHEATSCAN.
sentence.154: The operators made a consistent effort to delete these tools and remove any residual forensic artifacts from compromised systems.
sentence.155: In another incident response investigation, UNC215 pivoted to multiple OWA servers and installed web shells.
sentence.156: In the following days, the operators interacted with these web shells from internal IP addresses, attempting to harvest credentials.
sentence.157: After identifying key systems within the target network, such as domain controllers and Exchange servers, UNC215 moved laterally and deployed their signature malware FOCUSFJORD.
sentence.158: UNC215 often uses FOCUSFJORD for the initial stages of an intrusion, and then later deploys HYPERBRO, which has more information collection capabilities such as screen capture and keylogging.
sentence.159: While UNC215 heavily relies on the custom tools FOCUSFJORD and HYPERBRO, Chinese espionage groups often have resource sharing relationships with other groups, and we do not have enough information to determine if these tools are developed and used exclusively by UNC215. Figure 1: Attack Lifecycle Tradecraft and Operational Security We identified numerous examples of efforts by UNC215 to foil network defenders by minimizing forensic evidence left on compromised hosts, exploiting relationships with trusted third parties, continuously improving the FOCUSFJORD backdoor, concealing command and control (C2) infrastructure, and incorporating false flags.
sentence.160: Reducing Forensic Evidence on Disk UNC215 consistently cleaned up evidence of their intrusion after gaining access to a system.
sentence.161: This type of action can make it more difficult for incident responders to reconstruct what happened during a compromise.
sentence.162: The operators deleted tools used for credential harvesting and internal reconnaissance including a custom scanner dubbed WHEATSCAN after use.
sentence.163: The first FOCUSFJORD payload delivered to a system contains a blob that includes C2 and other configuration data.
sentence.164: On initial execution, FOCUSFJORD writes its encrypted C2 configuration into the system’s registry, sets up a persistence mechanism and then rewrites itself on disk without the embedded configuration and with limited functionality to only read configuration data.
sentence.165: This process enables the operators to obfuscate the configured C2 servers from automated sandbox runs or disclosure in public file scanning services.
sentence.166: A newly identified utility dubbed FJORDOHELPER can update FOCUSFJORD configurations and completely remove FOCUSFJORD from the system.
sentence.167: The tool can be deployed and executed remotely to delete any remaining FOCUSFJORD forensic evidence, including files on disk, configuration data encrypted in the registry, and related services and registry keys used for persistence.
sentence.168: Exploiting Trust Relationships UNC215 leveraged trusted third parties in a 2019 operation targeting an Israeli government network.
sentence.169: As illustrated in Figure 2, the operators were able to access their primary target via RDP connections from a trusted third party using stolen credentials and used this access to deploy and remotely execute FOCUSFJORD on their primary target.
sentence.170: Figure 2: Two FOCUSFJORD samples configured to proxy C2 traffic Concealing C2 Infrastructure UNC215 made technical modifications to their tools to limit outbound network traffic and used other victim networks to proxy their C2 instructions, likely to minimize the risk of detection and blend in with normal network traffic.
sentence.171: The following are examples of HYPERBRO and FOCUSFJORD samples capable of acting as proxies to relay communications to their C2 servers.
sentence.172: We do not have enough context about the following samples to attribute all of them to UNC215, though they are representative of activity we have seen from the group.
sentence.174: 0ec4d0a477ba21bda9a96d8f360a6848 and MD5: 04dece2662f648f619d9c0377a7ba7c0 have embedded configurations of internal IP addresses (192.168.1.237 and 192.168.4.26 respectively) as C2 servers.
sentence.175: If they receive a command with an IP address and port, they will connect and relay the command.
sentence.176: FOCUSFJORD sample MD5: e3e1b386cdc5f4bb2ba419eb69b1b921 has an internal IP address, 192.168.4.197, configured as its C2.
sentence.177: This sample was extracted from MD5: c25e8e4a2d5314ea55afd09845b3e886, which was submitted to a public malware repository in December 2017.
sentence.178: While hunting for FOCUSFJORD samples, we found a sample of a new malware (MD5: 625dd9048e3289f19670896cf5bca7d8) that shares code with FOCUSFJORD, but is distinct.
sentence.179: However, analysis indicates that it only contains functions to relay communications between another FOCUSFJORD instance and a C2 server (Figure 2, Network A).
sentence.180: We suspect this type of malware was used in the aforementioned operation.
sentence.181: The actors stripped out unnecessary FOCUSFJORD capabilities, possibly to reduce the likelihood it would be detected by security controls.
sentence.182: Figure 3 contains the data structure as it is being sent from a FOCUSFJORD sample configured to communicate with another FOCUSFJORD victim.
sentence.183: Figure 3: Two FOCUSFJORD samples configured to proxy C2 traffic FOCUSFJORD Changes We have observed numerous variants of the FOCUSFJORD malware family since 2017.
sentence.184: The authors have added new communications protocols, an updated loading mechanism, and expanded the number of supported configurations in newer versions.
sentence.185: Version numbers indicate that the malware undergoes frequent changes and maybe supported by a team of developers.
sentence.186: Many of these variants contain or remove functionality depending on the operator’s unique requirements at the time, which may suggest that multiple operators have access to the source code or a builder, or that a close relationship exists between the developers and operators.
sentence.187: FOCUSFJORD samples can be configured with up to 13 unique registry values which allow operators to control and organize compromised hosts.
sentence.188: In addition to specifying details related to the loading and persistence mechanisms and C2 communications, there are two keys which allow the operator to add additional context about the victim: Registry key 12 is the “group” name.
sentence.189: When a new FOCUSFJORD sample is first executed and writes its configuration to registry, this value is set to “default” and is later manually changed by the actor, usually to the victim’s domain name or organization name.
sentence.190: Registry key 13 could be interpreted as the “console” name, although we do not fully understand how the identifier is used by the operators.
sentence.191: We have observed the values “galway”, “iceland”, “helen”, and “idapro”.
sentence.192: It is not clear how or if UNC215 uses these configuration parameters to organize and track large numbers of compromised hosts.
sentence.193: We observed different console values within the same network, identical console values using different C2 addresses, and identical console values targeting different countries.
sentence.194: Some FOCUSFJORD samples from 2018 and 2020 use the same console values despite the significant gap in time (See Table 1).
sentence.195: The NCC Group discussed these configurations in a 2018 report and released a decoding tool.
sentence.196: Trendmicro noted changes to supported configurations in FOCUSFJORD, dubbed SysUpdate, in their 2020 and 2021 reports following public disclosures.
sentence.197: This suggests that operators using FOCUSFJORD are sensitive to security vendor reports and will update the code to avoid detection and exposure.

sentence.206: Additionally, on at least three occasions, UNC215 employed a custom tool associated with Iranian actors whose source code was leaked.
sentence.207: In several cases, we identified FOCUSFJORD samples with registry key names in regional languages.
sentence.208: The registry key names are hardcoded into every FOCUSFJORD sample, as the malware needs to read and decrypt those registry key values for proper execution.
sentence.209: FOCUSFJORD samples (MD5: d13311df4e48a47706b4352995d67ab0 and MD5: 26d079e3afb08af0ac4c6d92fd221e71) observed on Israeli and UAE networks, and a memory dump (MD5: d875858dbd84b420a2027ef5d6e3a512) submitted to a public malware repository by a likely Uzbekistan financial organization are configured with registry keys in Farsi.
sentence.210: Linguistic analysis suggests that these terms were auto translated as they are not commonly used by native Farsi speakers.
sentence.211: Another FOCUSFJORD sample uploaded from Uzbekistan (MD5: ac431261b8852286d99673fddba38a50) contains a configuration with registry key names in Hindi.
sentence.212: Notably, this variant also contains an error message string in Arabic ('ضائع' – which translates to: lost or missing).
sentence.213: In April 2019, UNC215 deployed the SEASHARPEE web shell against financial and high-tech organizations in the Middle East and Asia.
sentence.214: The SEASHARPEE web shell was developed and used by Iranian APT actors until the code was leaked online in the telegram channel Lab Dookhtegan a few weeks earlier in March 2019.
sentence.215: Around this time, the Turkish-language file Sosyal Güvenlik Reformu-Not-3.doc "Social Security Reform - Note - 3.doc" (MD5: 6930bd66a11e30dee1ef4f57287b1318) was distributed to a suspected Turkish government entity based on data from an open-source malware repository.
sentence.216: The document contains "C:\Users\Iran" paths that were likely included to obfuscate the source of the activity.
sentence.217: The use of Farsi strings, filepaths containing /Iran/, and web shells publicly associated with Iranian APT groups may have been intended to mislead analysts and suggest an attribution to Iran.
sentence.218: Notably, in 2019 the government of Iran accused APT27 of attacking its government networks and released a detection and removal tool for HYPERBRO malware.
sentence.219: Tradecraft Mistakes While UNC215 prioritizes evading detection within a compromised network, Mandiant identified several examples of code, C2 infrastructure, and certificate reuse indicating that UNC215 operators are less concerned about defenders’ ability to track and detect UNC215 activity.
sentence.220: In several instances, UNC215 used the same exact file against multiple victims and frequently shared infrastructure across victims.
sentence.221: This lack of compartmentalization is not uncommon, but does show that UNC215 is relatively less concerned about the ability for their compromises to be linked to each other.
sentence.222: C2 servers used by UNC215 frequently reuse the same SSL certificate, as described in Team Cymru’s research in 2020.
sentence.223: On one network, between April 2019 and April 2020, an operator repeatedly and infrequently revisited a compromised network whenever an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tool detected or quarantined tools like HYPERBRO and Mimikatz.
sentence.224: After several months of repeated detections, UNC215 deployed an updated version of HYPERBRO and a tool called “anti.exe” to stop Windows Update service and terminate EDR and Antivirus related services.
sentence.225: Attribution Mandiant attributes this campaign to Chinese espionage operators which we track as UNC215 a Chinese espionage operation that has been suspected of targeting organizations around the world since at least 2014.
sentence.226: We have low confidence that UNC215 is associated with APT27.
sentence.227: UNC215 has compromised organizations in the government, technology, telecommunications, defense, finance, entertainment, and health care sectors.
sentence.228: The group targets data and organizations which are of great interest to Beijing's financial, diplomatic, and strategic objectives.
sentence.230: The activity detailed in this post demonstrates China’s consistent strategic interest in the Middle East.
sentence.231: This cyber espionage activity is happening against the backdrop of China’s multi-billion-dollar investments related to the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) and its interest in Israeli’s robust technology sector.
sentence.232: Chinese companies have invested billions of dollars into Israeli technology startups, partnering or acquiring companies in strategic industries like semi-conductors and artificial intelligence.
sentence.233: As China’s BRI moves westward, its most important construction projects in Israel are the railway between Eilat and Ashdod, a private port at Ashdod, and the port of Haifa.
sentence.234: China has conducted numerous intrusion campaigns along the BRI route to monitor potential obstructions—political, economic, and security—and we anticipate that UNC215 will continue targeting governments and organizations involved in these critical infrastructure projects in Israel and the broader Middle East in the near- and mid-term. sentence.263: title: Dark Web Profile: MuddyWater APT Group url: https://socradar.io/dark-web-profile-muddywater-apt-group/ By SOCRadar Research Security concerns grow day by day with the rise of cyberattacks.
sentence.264: Among the threats, cyber espionage is one of the prominent activities.
sentence.265: It can be used to get a hold of sensitive or classified data that may be intellectual property, government, or trade secrets.
sentence.266: The threat actors’ goals might be financial gain, reputational harm, political interests, or cyberwarfare.
sentence.267: Today, we’ll review a high-profile cyber espionage group MuddyWater.
sentence.268: Who is MuddyWater? Stuxnet was a big hit on Iran’s nuclear program in 2010.
sentence.269: Iran took that as a wake-up call and began investing in and improving its cyberwarfare capabilities.
sentence.270: In 2011, Iranian threat actors began to be involved in sophisticated attacks.
sentence.271: One area they focused on is cyber espionage campaigns.
sentence.272: The first major campaign was observed in 2012, called the Madi campaign.
sentence.273: Operation categories of MuddyWater MuddyWater, also known as Static Kitten, UNC3313, or MERCURY, is an Iranian state-sponsored APT group.
sentence.274: According to the FBI and other US and UK-based agencies, they operate as a subordinate element of the Iranian Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).
sentence.275: It is believed that they have been active since late 2017 and have been in close contact with MOIS since 2018.
sentence.276: MuddyWater was observed to be conducting malicious activities across Europe, Asia, Africa, and North America.
sentence.277: However, their main focus primarily resides on the middle east, per other Iranian threat actors.
sentence.278: They are targeting private and government organizations listed below: Defense Education Energy Financial Services Government and administration agencies Healthcare High-Tech International Organizations Media Countries affected by MuddyWater
sentence.279: They are primarily conducting cyber espionage activities and intellectual property (IP) theft attacks, but on some occasions, they have deployed ransomware on the targets.
sentence.280: However, it is believed they deployed ransomware to cover their tracks.
sentence.283: The group exploits various known vulnerabilities and uses a wide range of tools.
sentence.284: For initial access, the group commonly leverages spear-phishing and tries to trick the victims into opening malicious documents hosted in commercial file-sharing services.
sentence.285: After obtaining initial access, they usually drop web shell and gain local administrator access on the infected machine.
sentence.286: On the compromised machine, they use tools such as Mimikatz to dump credentials.
sentence.287: To broaden the compromise, they laterally move by leveraging in-built or deployed tools within the network.
sentence.288: MuddyWater generally uses DNS to communicate with their C2 servers while using tools such as PowerShell, vpnui[.]exe (a unique version of Ligolo), and remote monitoring software such as ScreenConnect, Remote Utilities, and eHorus.
sentence.289: The figure below shows an instance of the MuddyWater attack chain observed by Microsoft.
sentence.291: Which Tools and Vulnerabilities MuddyWater Use? PowGoop DLL Loader: PowGoop malware is a malicious DLL loader.
sentence.292: It disguises itself as a legitimate Google Update executable.
sentence.294: Small Sieve is a simple Python backdoor used to distribute Nullsoft Scriptable Install System (NSIS) installer.
sentence.296: It collects the victim’s username, computer name, and IP address and sends it to the MuddyWater group.
sentence.297: Canopy malware is also known as Starwhale malware.
sentence.298: Mori: Mori is a backdoor that uses Domain Name System tunneling to communicate with the group’s C2 infrastructure.
sentence.300: POWERSTATS is a backdoor that runs PowerShell scripts to maintain persistent access on the victim systems.
sentence.301: MuddyWater-associated tools & vulnerabilities provided by SOCRadar Who Did MuddyWater Target in Their Campaigns? MuddyWater campaign timeline MuddyWater’s targets are mostly the neighbors of Iran in the middle east region.
sentence.302: If we analyze the graphic below, we can see that Turkey, Israel, Iraq, UAE, and Pakistan are among the top targets of MuddyWater.
sentence.303: Observations may show that MuddyWater acts according to the political interests of the Iranian state through the connection of MOIS.
sentence.304: So, countries in which Iran has political interests should be aware of MuddyWater’s cyber espionage campaigns.
sentence.305: Countries targeted by MuddyWater Motivations Behind MuddWater’s Attacks in the Last 2 Years
sentence.306: In September 2020, a series of agreements called the Abraham Accords were signed between Israel, United Arab Emirates, and Bahrain.
sentence.307: These countries signed these agreements intending to normalize diplomatic relations in the region.
sentence.308: The US brokered the agreements, a major diplomatic breakthrough in the Middle East.
sentence.309: The Abraham Accords can be an improvement in the region from a neutral point of view, but some may feel uneasy about these agreements.
sentence.310: In particular, Iran may have felt concerned about the Abraham Accords because they could lead to closer ties between Israel and other countries in the region, potentially undermining Iran’s influence.
sentence.311: With these developments in mind, we may deduce that the cyber-espionage activities carried out by MuddyWater between September 2020 and March 2021 were a reaction to these agreements.
sentence.312: MuddyWater, as far as known, primarily conducted campaigns in the middle east and its neighboring regions in late 2020 and early 2021.
sentence.313: September 2020 – Operation Quicksand – Israel: According to ClearSky, MuddyWater targeted many prominent Israeli organizations.
sentence.314: In this specific campaign, security researchers observed that the threat actor used a variant of Shamoon to encrypt data.
sentence.315: However, it is believed that the intent of using Shamoon was not to deploy ransomware but to disrupt operations.
sentence.316: Operation Quicksand (Source: SOCRadar) March 2021 – Earth Vetala Campaign:
sentence.317: According to Trend Micro, Azerbaijan, Bahrain, Israel, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates were the targets of the campaign.
sentence.318: Government agencies, academia, and tourism were some of the targeted sectors.
sentence.319: Latest Attacks of the Threat Actor In January 2022, cybersecurity researchers reported that MuddyWater targeted Turkish private organizations and governmental agencies.
sentence.320: They used multiple malicious PDFs and MS Office documents during the campaign.
sentence.321: With the spear phishing technique, the threat actors tried to convince the victims that the documents were from the Turkish Health and Internal Affairs Ministries.
sentence.322: Malicious PDF used in Turkey campaign (Source: Cisco Talos)
sentence.323: In another incident on December 2022, Deep Instinct reported that MuddyWater, conducted malicious activities, again using spear phishing through emails.
sentence.324: Israeli insurance companies were the targets of the attacks.
sentence.325: As an evolving threat actor, they added a new tool for remote access, Syncro, to their arsenal.
sentence.326: Email from MuddyWater’s Israel attack (Source: Deep Instinct) Conclusion Observations of MuddyWater’s cyber espionage activities can lead to a conclusion that they act according to Iran’s political strategies through MOIS.
sentence.327: Whether it is because of the political implications, or another reason, Israel and Turkey seem to be significant targets for the MuddyWater.
sentence.328: If you are an organization residing in the middle east, there might be a possibility of being a target of MuddyWater.
sentence.329: What can you do to defend against them?
sentence.330: Excluding the technical mitigations, keeping up with the political climate of the middle east region might give a heads-up if the tension rises.
sentence.331: On the technical side, MuddyWater evolves with each attack they perform, but they still bear similar techniques.
sentence.332: You can apply the following recommendations per your needs.
sentence.333: Security Recommendations Against MuddyWater MuddyWater leverages spear phishing.
sentence.334: Provide necessary training to your employees for security awareness.
sentence.335: Gain visibility into external-facing digital assets with an Attack Surface Management solution.
sentence.336: Regularly apply security patches and software updates.
sentence.337: Apply the least privilege principle across the network, especially to critical systems and services Secure domain controllers (DC) using best practices.
sentence.338: Enable multifactor authentication (MFA) to prevent lateral movement.
sentence.339: Refer to IOCs and take necessary actions toward mitigation.
sentence.340: SOCRadar’s Attack Surface Management provides visibility into external-facing digital assets.
sentence.341: SOCRadar has a predictive, preventive, and proactive approach toward security at its core.
sentence.342: With SOCRadar’s Attack Surface Management, security teams can track which CVEs are present in the environment.
sentence.343: Knowing which CVEs are present in the organization can give the organization an advantage in defending against MuddyWater.
sentence.344: SOCRadar Attack Surface Management Most threat actors specializing in cyber espionage widely leverage spear phishing, just as MuddyWater does.
sentence.345: If you receive any suspicious email, you can use free SOC Tools on SOCRadar Labs to analyze it.

sentence.360: title: Cobalt Strike, a Defender’s Guide – Part 2 url: https://thedfirreport.com/2022/01/24/cobalt-strike-a-defenders-guide-part-2/ Our previous report on Cobalt Strike focused on the most frequently used capabilities that we had observed.
sentence.361: In this report, we will focus on the network traffic it produced, and provide some easy wins defenders can be on the look out for to detect beaconing activity.
sentence.362: We cover topics such as domain fronting, SOCKS proxy, C2 traffic, Sigma rules, JARM, JA3/S, RITA & more.
sentence.363: As with our previous article, we will highlight the common ways we see threat actors using Cobalt Strike.
sentence.364: Big shout-out to @Kostastsale for helping put this Part 2 together!
sentence.365: Also thanks to @svch0st, @pigerlin, and @0xtornado for reviewing this report.
sentence.366: Even though network monitoring and detection capabilities do not come easy for many organizations, they can generally offer a high return on investment if implemented correctly.
sentence.367: Malware has to contact its C2 server if it is to receive further instructions.
sentence.368: This article will demonstrate how to detect this communication before threat actors accomplish their objectives.
sentence.369: There are a couple of factors that we can utilize to fingerprint any suspicious traffic and subsequent infrastructure.
sentence.370: Before we get into that part, we should first discuss what makes Cobalt Strike so versatile.
sentence.371: Cobalt Strike’s versatility comes from the ability to change the indicators with each payload.
sentence.372: This is made possible thanks to Malleable C2 profiles.
sentence.373: Our other post touched on Malleable C2 profiles and how threat actors use them; however, that was just some of their many applications.
sentence.374: Below you can find information related to some of the most important fields that could throw off an analyst while investigating a Cobalt Strike network communication:
sentence.375: The reference profile below is taken from Raphael Mudge’s GitHub repository.
sentence.376: ###Global Options### set sample_name "whatever.profile"; set sleeptime "0"; <================ # Decimal number to indicate the time the beacon will sleep for between communications in milliseconds set jitter "25"; <================ # A number that indicates the percentage of a random sleep time that beacon will introduce to its C2 comm set useragent "<string>"; <================ # Custom user agent of your choice set data_jitter "35"; <================ # Represents the value bytes variable that would instruct Cobalt Strike to send a random string on http-get/post to match the bytes value.
sentence.377: set headers_remove "<header to remove>"; <================ # Specifying headers to be removed in a comma separated manner.
sentence.378: ####### Not much explanation is needed here, you can change the certificate information to your heart's content.
sentence.379: ####### https-certificate { set C "US"; set CN "whatever.com"; set L "California"; set O "whatever LLC.
sentence.380: "; set OU "local.org"; set ST "CA"; set validity "365"; } ###HTTP-Config Block### http-config { set headers "<headers to include>"; <================ # Specifying the headers that you want to include. header "<name of the header(s)>"; <================ # Specifying the name of the header that will store the data that are transmitted to the C2 server set trust_x_forwarded_for "<true OR false>"; <================ # If the C2 server is behind a redirector, this option would allow to forward the traffic to the correct destination set block_useragents "<user agents>"; <================ # User agents that C2 server will block and show a 404 response set allow_useragents "<user agents>" <================ # Opposite of the above } ###HTTP-GET Block.

sentence.383: header "Connection" "close"; ### Metadata corresponds to the information that the beacon is sending to the C2 server about itself.
sentence.384: The operators may choose to enable additional fields that will include data on the C2 communication.
sentence.385: You can mix and match fields below: metadata { #base64; <================ # Base64 encoded string base64url; <================ # URL safe Base64 encoded string #mask; <================ # Encrypting and encoding the data with XOR mask and random key #netbios; <================ # Encoding data as netbios in lower case #netbiosu; <================ # Another variation of netbios encoding #prepend "TEST123"; <================ # Choosing a string to prepend to the transmitted data append ".php"; <================ # Choosing a string to append ### Termination statements: This statement tells Beacon and its server wherein the transaction to store the transformed data.
sentence.386: You may choose one of these termination statement methods.

sentence.390: #print; } parameter "test1" "t We added comments to the profile above to explain the numerous fields operators can change to customize the profile to their needs.
sentence.391: All these different fields provide control and flexibility over the indicators of the C2 channel.
sentence.392: Many free, open-source randomizer scripts exist to create a unique profile such as Random C2 Profile Generator by @joevest, Malleable-C2-Randomizer by @bluscreenofjeff, and C2concealer by @FortyNorthSec.
sentence.393: Below are some of the Cobalt Strike C2 servers that we observed during intrusions.
sentence.394: On the right column, we show the URLs that the Cobalt Strike payloads were configured to query.
sentence.395: A trained eye could spot some of the Malleable profiles that exist on freely available resources such as Raphael Mudge’s list on his GitHub page.
sentence.396: Another example is the “jquery-3.3.1.min.js” which is associated with this malleable C2 profile as we observed in four intrusions.
sentence.403: | +----------------------+-----------------------+ A deep dive into all available fields can be found on this post from @ZephrFish.
sentence.404: He also includes other fields related to post-exploitation beacon configuration along with network communication-related fields.
sentence.405: Another great resource is this article released by SpecterOps.
sentence.406: Domain Fronting Domain fronting is another method for concealing communication between the endpoint and the command and control servers.
sentence.407: The main purpose of domain fronting is to connect to a restricted host while pretending to communicate with an allowed host.
sentence.408: It essentially masks your traffic to a certain website by masquerading it as a different domain.
sentence.409: This technique is possible thanks to Content Delivery Networks (CDNs).
sentence.410: Domain fronting was mostly used by web services to bypass censorship in several countries that restricted traffic (e.g., China).
sentence.411: In recent years, attackers have started using this technique to hide their malicious infrastructure behind legitimate domains.
sentence.412: Because domain fronting is a complicated topic to grasp, below we have included an image from the official Cobalt Strike page that discusses this technique.
sentence.413: Cobalt Strike made domain fronting possible by allowing the operators to configure related settings via the malleable C2 profiles.
sentence.414: The following prerequisites must be met in order for domain fronting to be possible: Own a domain.
sentence.415: (e.g., infosecppl.store) Pick one of the many web services that provide CDN capabilities.
sentence.417: Setup the CDN service to create a new CDN endpoint and redirect traffic to your domain.
sentence.419: Setup a profile to facilitate domain fronting.
sentence.420: Identify a domain that uses the same CDN to ensure that the traffic will be forwarded to the correct resource.
sentence.421: Step five is where things get interesting.
sentence.422: Attackers can use legitimate domains that are registered under the same CDN provider.
sentence.423: As demonstrated in the screenshot above, all they have to do is include their CDN endpoint domain (created in step three) in the host header of the request.
sentence.424: In that way, the legitimate website will forward the traffic through the CDN to the original destination according to the host header.
sentence.425: In the screenshots below, you can see how the malleable C2 profiles are configured to allow domain fronting using the Fastly and AzureEdge CDNs:
sentence.426: This research paper released by academics from the University of California, Berkeley, is a great introduction to domain fronting.
sentence.427: This paper inspired many researchers to expand the possibilities of this unique way of hiding the final destination server on web traffic.
sentence.428: One of those researchers is Vincent who wrote a great article on domain fronting.
sentence.429: He explains in simple terms how it works.
sentence.430: He also published a Python script to identify possible domains that can be leveraged for domain fronting.
sentence.431: Looking into our reporting, we don’t see many instances of domain fronting.
sentence.432: This is most likely due to the complex process of setting up the necessary infrastructure.
sentence.433: Although, based on the data we have collected regarding malicious infrastructure, domain fronting appears to be used by threat actors.
sentence.434: According to our data from early 2021 up to now, Amazon Cloudfront takes the lead on preferable CDN used by threat actors, by a large margin.
sentence.435: The data above is available via our services.
sentence.436: More information on this service and others can be found here.
sentence.437: Reverse Proxy using Cobalt Strike Beacon A technique that we come across often is a reverse proxy.
sentence.438: We see instances where threat actors use their beacon sessions to establish RDP access through a reverse proxy.
sentence.439: Cobalt Strike has the ability to run a SOCKS proxy server on the team server.
sentence.440: This enables the operators to setup a listening port and leverage it to relay traffic to and from the open beacon session.
sentence.441: The screenshot below demonstrates this implementation.
sentence.442: Image credit: cobaltstrike.com Some of the cases we have observed threat actors using reverse proxy are: Diavol Ransomware BazarLoader and the Conti Leaks Snatch Ransomware
sentence.443: In most, of the above cases, the aim of the attackers was to establish a Remote Desktop session.
sentence.444: There are numerous advantages to establishing a RDP session, including the ability to navigate using a graphical environment and easily move laterally once the necessary access has been granted.
sentence.445: Below, we demonstrate how attackers take advantage of this technique using proxychains from the attackers’ kali Linux host.
sentence.446: In the first image, the attackers open a socks listening port, in this case port 8888, on the Cobalt Strike team server.
sentence.448: In this second image, we employ proxychains from the attacker’s Kali Linux host to RDP into our target’s environment via the SOCKS server.
sentence.449: We essentially add the team server’s IP address into the proxychains configuration and connect with xfreerdp.
sentence.450: RDP into the target host using reverse proxy Looking into the generated artifacts, we can see that a 4624 type 3 event is created on the target host.
sentence.451: One interesting aspect that we have also mentioned in similar cases from our reporting is that the victim’s hostname is captured in this logon event as well as the source address being 127.0.0.1. Security Event ID 4624 Type 3 shows the attacker’s hostname Once again, the running Cobalt Strike beacon acts as the intermediary to facilitate the Remote Desktop session via reverse proxy.
sentence.453: C2 Traffic This section will attempt to illustrate how the different malleable C2 profiles can affect network communication.
sentence.454: In some of the examples below, we simulated the malicious C2 channel to show how different malleable profile configurations can change the observed traffic.
sentence.455: After that, we’ll examine network data associated with lateral movement and the various methods employed by Cobalt Strike operators based on our observations.
sentence.457: We will use a slightly modified version of the jquery profile to illustrate how the configuration defines the various fields that make up the C2 connection.
sentence.458: Our previous article presented this jquery profile as one of the most commonly used profiles by threat actors in the intrusions we reported.
sentence.459: As shown above, malleable C2 profiles can generate unique network traffic based on the provided configuration.
sentence.460: A portion of the malleable C2 profile configuration is shown at the bottom half of the screenshot.
sentence.461: At the top half of the screenshot, we show the HTTP communication between the Beacon and the Cobalt Strike server.
sentence.462: The malleable profile determines the content of all parameters used in GET and POST requests.
sentence.463: Because of how simple it is to change these parameters, creating network signatures for proactive defense can be difficult.
sentence.464: Defenders can create signatures for publicly available profiles (see Sigma section below) or profiles extracted and made available thru open-source reporting.
sentence.465: One could search for traffic that matches known patterns (such as jquery or amazon) but the target IP/domain does not match the expected infrastructure.
sentence.466: DNS C2 traffic Cobalt Strike is capable of using DNS as the C2 method.
sentence.467: Operators can choose to configure their server to respond to beacon requests in A, AAAA or TXT records.
sentence.468: This strategy is useful for more covert operations, as the destination host could be a benign DNS server.
sentence.469: Defenders will have to inspect the traffic data and look for suspicious DNS records.
sentence.470: The screenshot below is from the official Cobalt Strike documentation page and shows how DNS communication works between the compromised host and the C2 server.
sentence.471: In the below example, we emulated this technique and configured the Beacon to communicate over DNS and request new tasks using A records.
sentence.472: In the same way, we can configure the Beacon to use TXT or AAAA records for requesting tasks or sending information to the server.
sentence.473: It is worth noting that the default method is the DNS TXT record data channel.
sentence.474: Below is the infrastructure that we used for demonstration purposes: Target Host: 192.168.88.179 Internal DNS server: 192.168.88.2 Cobalt Strike C2 domain: infosecppl.store We instructed the Beacon to execute the command systeminfo on the compromised host.
sentence.475: As you can see from the screenshot below, it took 148 packets containing DNS requests and responses to finish the task and send back the data to the Cobalt Strike Server.
sentence.476: The activity took 5 seconds to complete.
sentence.477: As with HTTP/HTTPS traffic, DNS traffic can be randomized using malleable C2 profiles.
sentence.478: Some of the options that are available to threat actors are as follows:
sentence.479: The above table was taken from Cobalt Strike’s official documentation SMB Beacons Another option for threat actors is to employ SMB beacons, once they have gained access to the network.
sentence.480: SMB beacons open a local port on the target host and listen for incoming communication from a parent beacon.
sentence.481: The communication between the two beacons is possible thanks to named pipes.
sentence.482: The operators can configure the pipename on the client; however, the default pipename starts with “msagent_#” for SMB beacons.
sentence.483: For a list of default pipe names for other services including some custom profiles check out @svch0st’s post here.
sentence.484: SMB beacons are mostly used to make network detection harder and to get access to isolated systems where communication to the internet is prohibited.
sentence.485: Additionally, due to SMB protocol being accessible in most internal networks, it makes for a reliable C2 method.
sentence.486: Operators can also chain beacons and move laterally inside the network.
sentence.487: According to our records, SMB beacons are not frequently used.
sentence.488: However, they’re still a powerful weapon in the hands of skilled operators.
sentence.489: As we do not see SMB beacons used often in our intrusion cases, we took an example case from our lab to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method.
sentence.490: We ran a PowerShell loader on the target host, which loaded a stageless SMB beacon in memory.
sentence.491: In our case, the SMB Beacon is communicating over the network with a parent Beacon using named pipes.
sentence.492: For this example, we chose the named pipe “my_pipes”.
sentence.493: As you can see from the screenshots below, windows event 4688 contains the execution of the PowerShell command.
sentence.494: As explained in our previous Cobalt Strike article, Sysmon events 17 and 18 can log named pipes.
sentence.495: However, Sysmon should be explicitly configured to log named pipes.
sentence.496: A good public Sysmon config that includes named pipes and much more is Olaf‘s Sysmon Moduler.
sentence.497: Below, you can see the named pipe created that we specified on the Cobalt Strike interface when we created the SMB listener.
sentence.498: Furthermore, the SMB Beacon will communicate over port 445 to the main beacon as we described above, which will then send the results to the C2 server.
sentence.499: This is known as chaining beacons.
sentence.500: The below screenshot illustrates the SMB communication between the beacon on the beachhead host and the chained beacon(s).
sentence.501: Another way to describe the communication is a parent/child relationship.
sentence.502: The network traffic shows the target host communicating over SMB with the other compromised host running the parent HTTP Beacon.
sentence.503: Named Pipes are used to facilitate the transition of data.
sentence.504: 192.168.38.102 = SMB Beacon 192.168.38.104 = HTTP Parent Beacon Detecting and Analyzing C2 Traffic Thanks to free, open-source tooling, investigating network traffic has become more accessible.
sentence.505: There are specific tools that we use to analyze suspicious network traffic in our intrusion cases.
sentence.506: We believe that no single tool can provide complete detection coverage, but we can get close by combining them.
sentence.507: In the following section, we will look at these tools that could accelerate analysis for defenders.
sentence.508: Sigma We’ll go through a few Sigma rules that can help us detect Cobalt Strike’s network activity.
sentence.509: Cobalt Strike DNS Beaconing is a rule created by Florian Roth which looks at DNS logs to detect the default DNS C2 behavior based on the dns_stager_subhost, put_output and dns_stager_subhost as seen above.
sentence.510: Below is a more generic rule created by @bareiss_patrick which is a good example of detecting suspicious DNS traffic based on a high amount of queries for a single domain.
sentence.511: Another more generic rule created by Daniil Yugoslavskiy uses dns logs to look for 50 or more TXT records from a single source in one minute: Default Cobalt Strike Certificate is a rule written by Bhabesh Raj that uses Zeek logs to detect the default Cobalt Strike certificate.
sentence.512: RDP over Reverse SSH Tunnel WFP by Samir Bousseaden is a rule that can look for suspicious RDP activity using reverse tunneling.
sentence.513: CobaltStrike Malleable Amazon Browsing Traffic Profile by Markus Neis which looks at proxy logs for the Amazon Malleable profile.
sentence.514: Other malleable profile rules include CobaltStrike Malformed UAs in Malleable Profiles, CobaltStrike Malleable (OCSP) Profile, and CobaltStrike Malleable OneDrive Browsing Traffic Profile.
sentence.515: All Sigma rules here are documented towards the bottom of Part 1. Rita Rita stands for Real Intelligence Threat Analytics (RITA), developed by Active Countermeasures.
sentence.516: Rita is a framework for detecting command and control communication.
sentence.517: It takes Zeek logs data and can, in our experience, accurately detect beaconing activity.
sentence.518: One of the great features of Rita is its ease of use and detailed output information in various forms, including CSV and HTML.
sentence.519: One simply can point Rita to the Zeek logs and wait for the results.
sentence.520: The more available data, the more precise the results will be.
sentence.521: Zeek logs can be generated from the PCAP(s).
sentence.522: The screenshot samples below show the results created by Rita based on the traffic we used in the previous sections to demonstrate the jquery malleable C2 profile.
sentence.523: We left the Beacon running for an hour to simulate an actual infection while several other network-unrelated processes ran in the background.
sentence.524: During this hour, we tasked the Beacon with carrying out several commands.
sentence.525: Rita determined that one hour of network data was adequate for identifying the beacon link and assigning it the highest score.
sentence.526: Although, the more data you have, the more accurate the results will be.
sentence.527: Below, we can see the results from one of our recent cases, BazarLoader and the Conti Leaks.
sentence.528: The first three IP addresses relate to the CS servers with which the Beacon communicated.
sentence.529: Rita accurately identified beaconing activity related to Cobalt Strike C2 communication.
sentence.530: Using Rita, we can identify malicious C2 traffic based on multiple variables, including communication frequency, average bytes sent/received, number of connections etc.
sentence.531: As a result, we can detect Cobalt Strike beaconing regardless of the malleable C2 profile utilized or any additional jitter present.
sentence.532: JA3/JA3S JA3 is an open-source project created by John Althouse, Jeff Atkinson and Josh Atkins.
sentence.533: JA3/JA3S can create SSL fingerprints for communication between clients and servers.
sentence.534: The unique signatures can represent several values collected from fields in the Client
sentence.535: Hello packet: - SSL Version - Accepted Ciphers - List of Extensions - Elliptic Curves - Elliptic Curve Formats For more information on how JA3 works, you can visit the official GitHub repository here: https://github.com/salesforce/ja3.
sentence.536: The JA3 tool is used to generate a signature for the client-side beacon connection with the server.
sentence.537: JA3S, on the other hand, is able to generate a server fingerprint.
sentence.538: The combination of the two can produce the most accurate result.
sentence.539: JA3S can capture the full cryptographic communication and combine the JA3 findings to generate the signature.
sentence.540: The downside of this method is that it can produce inaccurate results if the Cobalt Strike is behind redirectors.
sentence.541: We can find many reports that contain the JA3 value that corresponds to the Cobalt Strike fingerprint.
sentence.542: When it comes to Cobalt Strike infrastructure, the known JA3 and JA3s signatures that we are looking for are: JA3 72a589da586844d7f0818ce684948eea a0e9f5d64349fb13191bc781f81f42e1 JA3s b742b407517bac9536a77a7b0fee28e9 ae4edc6faf64d08308082ad26be60767 By using JA3/S signatures, we can discover various malware C2 servers and not just Cobalt Strike.
sentence.543: Salesforce provides a thorough collection of signatures that belong to many different applications here.
sentence.544: Some other example signatures with well known JA3 fingerprints are: Trickbot: 6734f37431670b3ab4292b8f60f29984 AsyncRat: fc54e0d16d9764783542f0146a98b300 Dridex: 51c64c77e60f3980eea90869b68c58a8 JA3 of Python usually hosting Empire or PoshC2: db42e3017c8b6d160751ef3a04f695e7 TOR client: e7d705a3286e19ea42f587b344ee6865 Another very good website to test the JA3 signature against a large database is ja3er.
sentence.545: JARM Similar to JA3/JA3S, JARM has the ability to fingerprint the TLS values of the remote server.
sentence.546: It does this by interacting with the target server sending 10 TLS Client
sentence.547: Hello packets and recording the specific attributes from the replies.
sentence.548: It will then hash the result values and create the final JARM fingerprint.
sentence.549: Unlike JA3/S, JARM is an active way of fingerprinting remote server applications.
sentence.550: John Althouse has created a medium post that accurately conveys the differences between JA3/S and JARM: “JARM actively scans the server and builds a fingerprint of the server application.
sentence.551: Whereas JA3/S is passive, just listening, not reaching out, JARM is active, actively probing the target.
sentence.552: And is able to build a fingerprint of the server application where JA3S could not.”
sentence.553: According to research and further changes on the JAVA TLS version as mentioned below, the JARM fingerprint that corresponds to a default configuration of the Cobalt Strike is: 07d14d16d21d21d00042d41d00041de5fb3038104f457d92ba02e9311512c2 Cobalt Strike is dependent on Java to run both the client graphical user interface (GUI) and the team server.
sentence.554: When we scan a Cobalt Strike server using JARM, the results we get back are dependent on the Java version that is used.
sentence.555: According to Cobalt Strike’s documentation, OpenJDK 11 is the preferred version that needs to be installed by the operators.
sentence.556: This makes it easier to identify a potential Cobalt Strike server, however, defenders should be aware that this outcome alone is prone to false positives.
sentence.557: This is because many other legitimate servers on the internet use this version of Java to operate their web applications.
sentence.558: On April 20th, 2021 Java Disabled TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 in favor of TLS 1.2 or above.
sentence.559: Following this change, the JARM fingerprint for Cobalt Strike servers changed: From: 07d14d16d21d21d07c42d41d00041d24a458a375eef0c576d23a7bab9a9fb1
sentence.560: To: 07d14d16d21d21d00042d41d00041de5fb3038104f457d92ba02e9311512c2 This change was highlighted by @bodziurity and @WLesicki in a collaborative effort: Cobalt Strike has a post dedicated to JARM that goes into detail on how JARM works and how the specific hash value is created based on the Java version.
sentence.561: Looking into our reporting for this hash value will return four of our cases.
sentence.562: All these cases involve Cobalt Strike as the post-exploitation method.
sentence.563: To generate a JARM fingerprint against a server, you can run the JARM python tool: python3 jarm.py
sentence.565: [port] While JARM’s offer another tool to help reveal adversary infrastructure they are not an indicator that can be used in isolation.
sentence.566: JARM signatures can be masked, Dagmawi Mulugeta presented at HiTB Amsterdam in 2021 a tool that enables red teams or adversaries to mask the JARM signatures of their infrastructure.
sentence.567: Called JARM Randomizer the tool can be configured as a proxy in front of the Cobalt Strike server to serve up false data to potential internet scanners.
sentence.568: Other JARMs can be found at: https://github.com/cedowens/C2-JARM.
sentence.569: Arkime (Moloch) and JA3/S We included Arkime as it integrates with JA3/JA3S and other plugins to enhance network analysis.
sentence.570: Arkime is a tool that we use a lot to investigate network activity and gather indicators.
sentence.571: It can index network traffic and make events easily searchable.
sentence.572: Arkime is simple to set up and excellent for reviewing traffic.
sentence.573: Arkime makes use of additional analysis tools by including them as plugins.
sentence.574: More on this and other tools in the next report.
sentence.575: All for now That wraps up Cobalt Strike, a Defender’s Guide Part 2.
sentence.576: Would you like to see something specific in Part 3?
sentence.577: Contact us here or on Twitter with suggestions.
sentence.578: Thanks for reading and hope this helps!
sentence.579: Please see the bottom of our first report for more detections & rules.
