sentence.1502: title: Xollam, the Latest Face of TargetCompany url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/f/xollam-the-latest-face-of-targetcompany.html Xollam, the Latest Face of TargetCompany This blog talks about the latest TargetCompany ransomware variant, Xollam, and the new initial access technique it uses.
sentence.1503: We also investigate previous variants' behaviors and the ransomware family's extortion scheme.
sentence.1504: By: Earle Maui Earnshaw, Nathaniel Morales, Katherine Casona, Don Ovid Ladores June 06, 2023Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe After first being detected in June 2021, the TargetCompany ransomware family underwent several name changes that signified major updates in the ransomware family, such as modifications in encryption algorithm and different decryptor characteristics.
sentence.1505: The earliest samples of the TargetCompany ransomware appended victims’ files with the extension “.tohnichi,” the name of its victim enterprise at that time, signifying a targeted attack on the organization of the same name.
sentence.1506: As a result, it was initially known as the Tohnichi ransomware.
sentence.1507: Later, the group continued appending encrypted files with names based on its victims, such as “.artis” for the Artis Zoo in Amsterdam.
sentence.1508: Other extensions include “.herrco,” “.brg,” and “.carone.” Industry experts then later identified the ransomware as TargetCompany from the pattern it adopted of appending encrypted files after the company it was targeting.
sentence.1509: The variants Tohnichi (active in 2021), Mallox, and Fargo (both active in 2022) targeted vulnerabilities in Microsoft SQL (MS SQL) Server for initial access.
sentence.1510: We elaborate on the behavior of these variants in our Ransomware Spotlight: TargetCompany.
sentence.1512: The infection chain of the earlier TargetCompany variants Our investigations show that its latest variant, Xollam, now deviates from the gang’s tried-and-tested initial access method.
sentence.1513: In this blog, we discuss this latest development in the TargetCompany ransomware’s behavior and look into its previous infection chains.
sentence.1514: Simultaneously active: Xollam and Mallox variants
sentence.1515: In 2023, Xollam was observed as following a technique similar to the one followed by phishing campaigns: using Microsoft OneNote files as initial access to spread and deliver malware.
sentence.1516: This latest TargetCompany variant executed a spam campaign with malicious OneNote file attachments, a deviation from its roots of targeting vulnerable MS SQL databases.
sentence.1517: Based on our investigations, Xollam uses a pseudo-fileless technique through PowerShell, which executes reflective loading to download its payload.
sentence.1518: As we discuss in later sections, we have also observed this technique in earlier variants of the TargetCompany ransomware.
sentence.1520: The attack flow of the latest TargetCompany variant, Xollam, which uses malicious OneNote files for initial access The latest variant of the ransomware, Xollam, was detected in February this year.
sentence.1521: In the same month, the older Mallox variant was also active, as it claimed the attack on the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
sentence.1522: The gang released 1.28 GB of compressed datasets that included financial balance sheets, employee reimbursement details, bank statements and internet banking credentials, industry audit reports, and documents related to FICCI subcommittees.
sentence.1523: Reflective loading, Mallox, and Fargo variants
sentence.1524: The Mallox variant of the ransomware was first detected in the wild in October 2021.
sentence.1525: Later samples in January of the following year showed that the ransomware group started to employ reflective loading as part of its defense evasion.
sentence.1526: The Mallox variant connects to an IP address to load the encrypted ransomware, with its download URL only available for approximately 24 hours.
sentence.1527: Notably, this made the dynamic analysis of old samples difficult.
sentence.1528: Our investigations revealed that the payload downloaded by the PowerShell script was a .NET downloader, which would subsequently retrieve an encrypted payload from the command-and-control (C&C) server.
sentence.1529: The downloaded file has a random file name and might have different extensions such as “.png,” “.bmp,” and “.jpg,” among others.
sentence.1531: A closer look at the reflective loading technique that TargetCompany threat actors incorporated; the IP address it connects to changes every 24 hours and deploys different payloads The payload would then be decrypted through XOR or inversion and executed in memory.
sentence.1532: The specific payload that is downloaded varies depending on the link on the .NET downloader.
sentence.1534: Both Mallox and Fargo variants use a set of tools via remote desktop for defense evasion.
sentence.1535: It’s important to note that reflective loading enabled the Mallox variant to evade traditional antivirus solutions, making it challenging for organizations to protect themselves against these attacks.
sentence.1536: Meanwhile, the Remcos backdoor payload is executed via WmiPrvSE.exe, and the payload most likely arrives by exploiting public-facing websites and domains.
sentence.1537: Our investigations showed that the gang used different sets of defense evasion and reconnaissance tools such as GMER and Advance Process Termination to manually uninstall antivirus products on the target system.
sentence.1538: We also observed the presence of YDArk.exe (PCHunter64) for performing rootkit behaviors, and that TargetCompany attempts to terminate security-related processes and services by dropping KILLAV.
sentence.1539: In addition, the ransomware drops a batch file named killer.bat that terminates various services and applications, including GPS-related services.
sentence.1540: Afterward, it proceeds to steal system information like machine details and other relevant data.
sentence.1543: The ransomware encrypts the victim's files using the ChaCha20 encryption algorithm and generates the encryption keys using a combination of Curve25519, an example of elliptic curve cryptography, and AES-128.
sentence.1544: In June 2022, the gang targeted other victims with encrypted files appended with the extension “.fargo.”
sentence.1545: We also observed that like Mallox, the Fargo variant employed reflective loading.
sentence.1546: In the last two months of 2022, there was an increase in attacks launched by the TargetCompany ransomware using its Mallox variant.
sentence.1547: Extortion While the Mallox and Fargo variants were operating simultaneously in 2022, TargetCompany initiated its double-extortion scheme by setting up a Telegram channel where it could publish stolen information.
sentence.1548: In August 2022, just two months after the group launched its Fargo variant, Mallox created a Twitter account where it could announce its victims.
sentence.1549: Since this account was eventually suspended, the threat actors created a new one. Figure 6.
sentence.1550: The first Twitter account (eventually suspended) that Mallox created for announcing its victims (top), and the new Twitter account that replaced it (bottom); the new account remains active as of this writing In November of the same year, Mallox launched its data leak site where, as of writing, it has declared only 20 victims.
sentence.1551: However, our telemetry data revealed far more attacks at 269 attempts on Trend Micro customers from March 2022 to April 2023.
sentence.1552: In a January 2023 interview, threat actors behind TargetCompany said that they choose only a small percentage of their victims to publish on their leak site.
sentence.1553: They also limit the amount of leaked data to what they deem particularly interesting and claim to have no intention of publishing everything.
sentence.1554: While the group said that it remains small and closed, the actors behind it mentioned that they are “open to suggestions.”
sentence.1555: Interestingly, a new member of the cybercrime forum RAMP under the name “Mallx” was observed recruiting affiliates for the Mallox ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) affiliate program.
sentence.1556: Our investigations also revealed that the ransomware might have connections with other groups such as the BlueSky ransomware, as well as the threat actors who perform brute-force attacks on MS SQL Servers.
sentence.1557: TargetCompany shares similarities with these groups in terms of threat actor profiles, targets, deployed remote control, and encryption algorithm.
sentence.1558: We discuss other possible affiliations, as well as victim profiles and behaviors in our Spotlight feature on the ransomware group.
sentence.1559: Conclusion The TargetCompany ransomware is making bolder ventures beyond its tried-and-tested techniques by joining the bandwagon of OneNote phishing campaigns, which allows it to cast a wider net for increased profitability.
sentence.1560: Within just two years of activity, the threat actors behind the ransomware are proving their hunger for prolificacy, expanding their business model with a RaaS affiliate program and maintaining several platforms to announce victims and expose stolen data.
sentence.1561: We can expect TargetCompany to make even bigger moves in the future, especially since the threat actors behind it have admitted that they created TargetCompany to move away from the restrictions and inflexibility of their previous groups.
sentence.1562: Now unhindered, the gang will naturally try to maximize profits from its victims.
sentence.1563: To protect systems from ransomware attacks, we recommend that both individual users and organizations implement best practices such as applying data protection and backup and recovery measures to secure data from possible encryption or erasure.
sentence.1564: Conducting regular vulnerability assessments and patching systems in a timely manner can also minimize the damage dealt by ransomware families that abuse exploits.
sentence.1565: We advise users and organizations to update their systems with the latest patches and apply multilayered defense mechanisms.
sentence.1566: End users and enterprises alike can mitigate the risk of infection from new threats like the TargetCompany ransomware by following these security best practices: Enable multifactor authentication (MFA) to prevent attackers from performing lateral movement inside a network.
sentence.1567: Adhere to the 3-2-1 rule when backing up important files.
sentence.1568: This involves creating three backup copies on two different file formats, with one of the copies stored in a separate location.
sentence.1570: It’s important to keep operating systems and applications up to date and maintain patch management protocols that can deter malicious actors from exploiting any software vulnerabilities.
sentence.1571: Authors Earle Maui Earnshaw Threats Analyst Nathaniel Morales Threat Analyst Katherine Casona Threat Analyst Don Ovid Ladores Threats Analyst
sentence.1572: title: Operation Tainted Love | Chinese APTs Target Telcos in New Attacks url: https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/operation-tainted-love-chinese-apts-target-telcos-in-new-attacks/ By Aleksandar Milenkoski, Juan Andres Guerrero-Saade, and Joey Chen, in collaboration with QGroup Executive Summary In Q1 of 2023, SentinelLabs observed initial phases of attacks against telecommunication providers in the Middle East.
sentence.1573: We assess that this activity represents an evolution of tooling associated with Operation Soft Cell.
sentence.1574: While it is highly likely that the threat actor is a Chinese cyberespionage group in the nexus of Gallium and APT41, the exact grouping remains unclear.
sentence.1575: SentinelLabs observed the use of a well-maintained, versioned credential theft capability and a new dropper mechanism indicative of an ongoing development effort by a highly-motivated threat actor with specific tasking requirements.
sentence.1577: In collaboration with QGroup GmbH, SentinelLabs recently observed initial threat activities targeting the telecommunication sector.
sentence.1578: We assess it is highly likely that these attacks were conducted by a Chinese cyberespionage actor related to the Operation Soft Cell campaign.
sentence.1579: The initial attack phase involves infiltrating Internet-facing Microsoft Exchange servers to deploy webshells used for command execution.
sentence.1580: Once a foothold is established, the attackers conduct a variety of reconnaissance, credential theft, lateral movement, and data exfiltration activities.
sentence.1581: The deployment of custom credential theft malware is central to this new campaign.
sentence.1582: The malware implemented a series of Mimikatz modifications on closed-source tooling.
sentence.1583: This post details the multi-component architecture and functionality of a sample, referred to as mim221.
sentence.1584: We assess that mim221 is a recent version of an actively maintained credential theft capability upgraded with new anti-detection features.
sentence.1585: The use of special-purpose modules that implement a range of advanced techniques shows the threat actors’ dedication to advancing its toolset towards maximum stealth.
sentence.1586: These techniques include in-memory mapping of malicious images to evade EDR API hooks and file-based detections surgically terminating Event Log threads instead of the host process to inhibit logging without raising suspicions staging a credential theft capability in the LSASS process itself by abusing native Windows capabilities.
sentence.1587: Version numbers and build timestamps indicate a maintained software project by designated developers.
sentence.1588: Closer analysis reveals an element of pragmatism in that the threat actors use modified publicly available code to achieve their goals.
sentence.1589: In terms of attribution, the tooling suggests an immediate link to the ‘Operation Soft Cell’ campaign but remains slightly vague on the specific threat actor.
sentence.1590: That campaign has been publicly associated with Gallium and possible connections to APT41 have been suggested by the use of a common code signing certificate and tooling that shares code similarities.
sentence.1591: APT41 is also known to target telecommunication providers.
sentence.1592: Given previous target and TTP overlaps, and an evident familiarity with victim environments, we assess with medium-confidence that Gallium is involved.
sentence.1593: However, we also recognize the possibility of closed-source tool-sharing between Chinese state-sponsored threat actors, and the possibility of a shared vendor or digital quartermaster.
sentence.1594: Regardless of clustering specifics, this finding highlights the increased operational tempo of Chinese cyberespionage actors and their consistent investment in advancing their malware arsenal to evade detection.
sentence.1595: Infection Vector and Initial TTPs As initial attack indicators, we observed command execution through webshells on compromised Microsoft Exchange server deployments.
sentence.1596: The threat actors used C:\MS_DATA as their main working directory for storing malware and staging data for exfiltration.
sentence.1597: Noting that the Microsoft TroubleShootingScript toolset (TSSv2) uses C:\MS_DATA for storing log files, we suspect that its use as a working directory is an attempt to make malicious file system activities look legitimate.
sentence.1598: After establishing an initial foothold, the threat actor conducts reconnaissance like querying user and network information using a variety of tools.
sentence.1599: For example, the attackers used dsquery and query to obtain information about Active Directory objects, including user information, and Remote Desktop user sessions.
sentence.1600: They also used the Local Group (LG) tool to enumerate all local groups and members in a domain.
sentence.1603: -attr objectSID sAMAccountName displayName mail memberOf >da.back&cd "cmd" /c cd /d c:\windows\system32\inetsrv\&query user&cd "cmd" /c cd /d
sentence.1606: The attackers then check connectivity with both the Internet and specific local machines of interest.
sentence.1611: [IP ADDRESS/HOSTNAME]&cd They also retrieve networking information, like network adapters, specific machines, and network services like Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP).
sentence.1615: c:\windows\system32\inetsrv\&netstat.exe -nob "cmd" /c cd /d c:\windows\system32\inetsrv\&netstat -aon |find "3389"&cd "cmd" /c cd /d C:\MS_DATA\&netstat -aon |find "[IP ADDRESS]"&cd
sentence.1616: The threat actor made use of the native makecab tool to compress information gathered for exfiltration.
sentence.1617: "cmd" /c cd /d C:\MS_DATA\&makecab da.back d.zip >1.txt&cd For lateral movement, the attackers made use of the PsExec tool and the net use command for accessing shared resources on remote machines.
sentence.1620: In order to steal credentials, the attackers employ custom modified versions of Mimikatz, including an executable named pc.exe.
sentence.1621: Mimikatz publicly available code (top); strings from a Mimikatz modification (bottom)The pc.exe executable stages the execution of three other components that ultimately result in stealing credentials from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process.
sentence.1622: We refer to the four component chain as ‘mim221’ based on the version number that the tool displays (2.2.1).
sentence.1623: We observed the threat actors deploying individual chunks of pc.exe in the working directory and merging these into pc.exe using the type command.
sentence.1624: pc.exe file chunksWe noticed that the attackers ceased their activities after stealing credentials.
sentence.1625: This could indicate a multi-phase attack strategy, where the deployment of backdoors and further persistence mechanisms is carried out separately after credential theft has ensured continued access.
sentence.1626: The intrusions were detected and interrupted before the attackers could carry out further phases, such as deploying backdoors.
sentence.1627: mim221 The architecture of mim221 consists of four components: the pc.exe Windows executable, and the AddSecurityPackage64.dll, pc.dll, and getHashFlsa64.dll DLLs contained therein.
sentence.1628: mim221 execution overviewmim221 Component Size Compilation timestamp pc.exe 502 KBs Thu Jun 09 08:02:12 2022 (UTC) AddSecurityPackage64.dll 119 KB Thu Jun 09 08:01:46 2022 (UTC) pc.dll 297 KB Tue Jun 07 16:55:05 2022 (UTC) getHashFlsa64.dll 216 KB Fri May 27 20:56:26 2022 (UTC) pc.exe The main binary executed by the threat actor is pc.exe.
sentence.1629: It decrypts AddSecurityPackage64.dll and pc.dll, stores pc.dll on the file system, and then loads and executes AddSecurityPackage64.dll by invoking its exported function, pathAddPackage.
sentence.1630: The execution of pc.exe requires a password supplied by the operator (in this case, P2sSW0rd1234!@#$C), which the operator provides through the key command-line parameter.
sentence.1631: pc.exe decrypts AddSecurityPackage64.dll and pc.dll using the AES encryption algorithm, providing the operator-provided execution password as an initialization vector.
sentence.1632: pc.exe loads and executes the decrypted AddSecurityPackage64.dllusing reflective image loading.
sentence.1633: This technique involves first mapping a Windows PE image in memory and then executing the image’s main entry point or an export function.
sentence.1634: Among other activities, the image mapping process includes allocating memory for the image, storing the image headers and sections in the memory, populating the images’ import and delay import tables, adding exception handlers, and executing TLS callback and export routines.
sentence.1635: The Phant0m tool provides a complete implementation of this process.
sentence.1636: While reflective image loading is a known technique at this time, its use was first observed in the DoublePulsar and subsequently the SlingShot frameworks in 2017 and 2018, respectively.
sentence.1637: This technique enables the fully fileless loading and execution of a malicious image without invoking the standard Windows API, such as LoadLibrary.
sentence.1638: This eliminates detection based on API hooking and file artifacts.
sentence.1639: When it is finished executing, pc.exe displays a message indicating a version number and build timestamp: Version 2.2.1 - build on Jun 9 2022 16:02:12.
sentence.1640: AddSecurityPackage64.dll AddSecurityPackage64.dll, which is the original filename of this mim221 component, is responsible for: Obtaining the SeDebugPrivilege and SYSTEM privilege by access token impersonation.
sentence.1641: This allows mim221 to inspect and extract credentials from the LSASS process.
sentence.1642: Disabling Windows event logging in an attempt to evade detection; and Injecting pc.dll into LSASS as a Security Package.
sentence.1643: Security Packages are used to extend the Windows authentication mechanism and can be abused to execute malicious code in the context of LSASS.
sentence.1644: In an attempt to remain undetected, AddSecurityPackage64.dll disables Windows event logging by killing threads of the Windows Event Log service without stopping the execution of the service itself.
sentence.1645: This is achieved by locating the process that hosts the Event Log, enumerating the processes’ threads, identifying the threads assigned to the service by their service tag (eventlog), and terminating them.
sentence.1646: Querying service tag informationAddSecurityPackage64.dll injects pc.dll into LSASS by deploying pc.dll as a Security Package.
sentence.1647: To this end, AddSecurityPackage64.dll issues an RPC call to LSASS – to the ncalrpc:[lsasspirpc] RPC endpoint, providing the file path to pc.dll to LSASS.
sentence.1648: This call instructs LSASS to load and execute pc.dll, which then stages the getHashFlsa64.dll credential theft component.
sentence.1649: getHashFlsa64.dll conducts credential theft in the context of LSASSpc.dll and getHashFlsa64.dll In the context LSASS, pc.dll decrypts, reflectively loads, and executes the code credential theft component getHashFlsa64.dll in a manner similar to pc.exe.
sentence.1650: pc.dll and getHashFlsa64.dll share the same original filename: getHashFlsa64.dll.
sentence.1651: pc.dll is implemented such that its main routine returns FALSE, making LSASS execute pc.dll and then unload it.
sentence.1652: This is a detection evasion technique making LSASS load pc.dll while avoiding appearing as an added (registered) Security Package.
sentence.1653: LSASS normally creates registry entries when adding Security Packages and does not unload them once loaded.
sentence.1654: This provides an opportunity for defenders to detect the loading of malicious Security Packages.
sentence.1655: Previous research provides more detail on this topic.
sentence.1656: getHashFlsa64.dll accesses the memory of its host LSASS process and stores stolen credentials in a Mimikatz log file named pc.log for later exfiltration.
sentence.1657: Example pc.log contentgetHashFlsa64.dll exports a function named GetMyVersion, which displays a version number and build timestamp (Version 2.2.0 - build on May 28 2022 04:56:23), in a format consistent with the output from pc.exe.
sentence.1658: The credential theft functionality of getHashFlsa64.dll is implemented in its export function GetLogonInfo.
sentence.1659: The GetMyVersion functionAdditional Information Error Messages and Public Code Reuse The mim221 components implement error logging.
sentence.1660: The error messages follow a consistent output format.
sentence.1661: Example error messagesIt is important to note that we observed code segments that seem to be modified versions of publicly available code.
sentence.1662: For example, the implementation of AddSecurityPackage64.dll looks like an adaptation of public code that demonstrates injection of a Security Package into LSASS using RPC calls.
sentence.1663: Similarity between publicly available code (top) and AddSecurityPackage64.dll (bottom)Timestamp Information The mim221 components that reflectively load other executables, pc.exe and pc.dll, patch beforehand a string in the loaded executable, which provides further timestamp information: ====A!B@C#0-2022-05-23 16:33:03S. The patching involves replacing the string with configuration information, such as the mim221 execution password and a path to the log file for storing stolen credentials.
sentence.1664: Patched timestamp stringAttribution Analysis We assess it is highly likely the initial attack phases we observed were conducted by Chinese threat actors with cyberespionage motivations.
sentence.1665: Telecommunication providers are frequent targets of espionage activity due to the sensitive data they hold.
sentence.1666: Our analysis identified indicators that point to the operation Soft Cell actors.
sentence.1667: Operation Soft Cell has been associated with the Gallium group based on TTPs and some of the domains the group has been using.
sentence.1668: Active since at least 2012, Gallium is likely a Chinese state-sponsored group that is targeting telecommunication, financial, and government entities in Southeast Asia, Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.
sentence.1669: While the group’s original focus has been on telecommunication providers, recent reports suggest that Gallium has recently expanded targeting across other sectors.
sentence.1670: The initial intrusion vector and the majority of the TTPs we observed closely match those conducted by, or associated with, the Soft Cell actors.
sentence.1671: This includes deploying webshells at Microsoft Exchange servers for establishing an initial foothold, following same file naming conventions, using the LG tool and the net, query, and tasklist Windows built-in tools for gathering user and process information, and the PsExec Windows Sysinternals tool and net for lateral movement and exploration, respectively.
sentence.1672: It is worth noting that the attackers’ activities at one of the targets suggested previous knowledge of the environment.
sentence.1673: We had observed activity at the same target a few months prior, which we attributed to Gallium primarily based on the use of the group’s PingPull backdoor and TTPs.
sentence.1674: By pivoting on the original filename of mim221’s getHashFlsa64.dll, we observed another sample that steals credentials from LSASS.
sentence.1675: This sample has the PDB path of e:\vs_proj\mimkTools\getHashFlsa\getHashFlsa\x64\release\getHashFlsa64.pdb and has been first submitted to VirusTotal from Vietnam on January 04, 2023.
sentence.1676: The path partially overlaps with the PDB path of a Mimikatz Soft Cell executable (E:\vs_proj\simplify_modify\Win32\simplify.pdb) and another Mimikatz executable of a Chinese threat actor thought to be part of the Soft Cell activity group arsenal (E:\vs_proj\mimkTools\dcsync_new\x64\dcsync64.pdb).
sentence.1677: This indicates that mim221 and these binaries may originate from the same source.
sentence.1678: Closer analysis confirms that the sample we pivoted to is a previous, less-advanced version of mim221 – Version 2.2.0 – that does not include some mim221 components, such as AddSecurityPackage64.dll and pc.dll.
sentence.1679: We refer to this sample as mim220.
sentence.1681: Previous research indicates possible connections between the Soft Cell actors and APT41, which is known to conduct Chinese state-sponsored espionage activity as well as financially motivated activity targeting multiple sectors with a broad geographical coverage, including telecommunication providers.
sentence.1682: The connection between the Soft Cell actors and APT41 that most relates to the activities that we observed is based on the Whizzimo, LLC certificate of the Soft Cell binary with a PDB path E:\vs_proj\simplify_modify\Win32\simplify.pdb, a binary that possibly originates from the same source as mim221.
sentence.1683: This certificate has been reported to be used by APT41.
sentence.1684: Pivoting on this certificate reveals further Mimikatz modifications, some with filenames very similar to those we observed.
sentence.1685: Conclusions Chinese cyberespionage threat actors are known to have a strategic interest in the Middle East.
sentence.1686: This is evident from their consistent targeted attacks on various entities including government, finance, entertainment, and telecommunication organizations.
sentence.1687: The recent activities targeting the telecommunication sector this post discusses are some of the latest such attacks.
sentence.1688: Our analysis of mim221 highlights the continuous maintenance and further development of the Chinese espionage malware arsenal.
sentence.1689: These threat actors will almost certainly continue exploring and upgrading their tools with new techniques for evading detection, including integrating and modifying publicly available code.
sentence.1690: SentinelLabs continues to monitor espionage activities and hopes that defenders will leverage the findings presented in this post to bolster their defenses.

sentence.1692: title: Defending Users’ NAS Devices From Evolving Threats url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/22/a/defending-users-NAS-devices-from-evolving-threats.html Defending Users’ NAS Devices From Evolving Threats In our latest research, we analyze the threats targeting well-known brands of network-attached storage (NAS) devices.
sentence.1693: By: Stephen Hilt, Fernando Merces January 20, 2022Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe Threats to the internet of things (IoT) continue to evolve as users and businesses grow increasingly reliant on these tools for constant connectivity, access to information and data, and workflow continuity.
sentence.1694: Cybercriminals have taken notice of this dependence and now regularly update their known tools and routines to include network-attached storage (NAS) devices to their list of targets, knowing full well that users rely on these devices for storing and backing up files in both modern homes and businesses.
sentence.1695: More importantly, cybercriminals are aware that these tools hold valuable information and have only minimal security measures.
sentence.1696: In our latest research paper, “Backing Your Backup: Defending NAS Devices Against Evolving Threats,” we studied the current infrastructure, environment, threats, and recommendations for defending systems against current threats targeting NAS devices.
sentence.1697: To emphasize the importance of mitigating the risks of malware infection and targeted attacks on NAS devices, we analyzed the technical details of two malware families that potentially included NAS devices in their existing business models, the REvil ransomware and StealthWorker botnets.
sentence.1699: While the disappearance of REvil (aka Sodinokibi) in mid-2021 is filled with uncertainty, security researchers have found a Linux version of the REvil ransomware that they have dubbed as Revix.
sentence.1700: After analyzing the samples, we found four different versions of the malware, all of which rely on an embedded JavaScript Observed Notation (JSON)-based configuration to set parameters before encrypting files.
sentence.1702: Revix’s JSON-based configuration While some parameters are ignored by the ransomware, these are most important ones that we observed: pk: A 64-byte key nbody: The ransomware note text-encoded in base64 nname: The ransomware note name ext: The extension added to encrypted files After compromising the system, the malicious actors execute it manually on a NAS device to encrypt files and create a ransom note with a unique key per victim.
sentence.1704: Revix encrypting a QNAP NAS device Figure 3.
sentence.1705: Revix ransom note While the differences between the versions are minor, the group advertised the capability of encrypting NAS devices as early as May 2021 in underground forums.
sentence.1706: Given the vulnerability of NAS devices that are directly connected to the internet, we can expect a new wave of ransomware attacks affecting these gadgets in the future.
sentence.1707: StealthWorker In 2021, security researchers found brute-force attacks launched from the StealthWorker botnet on Synology NAS devices.
sentence.1708: We found multiple samples for this botnet and confirmed that newer versions are capable of brute-forcing and compromising servers running on several products and systems such as WooCommerce and WordPress.
sentence.1709: This botnet is also designed to generally attack any web server using HTTP authentication and other NAS devices like QNAP.
sentence.1710: Valid credentials found during compromise are then uploaded to the command-and-control (C&C) server, usually at port 5028/TCP. Figure 4.
sentence.1711: StealthWorker brute-force function targeting QNAP devices Figure 5.
sentence.1712: Infected Linux device connected to a C&C server How to protect NAS devices Without proper security implemented in NAS devices, users and businesses will continue to be targeted since these tools can be used as entry points for information theft, malware infection, and the disruption of operations, among others.
sentence.1713: Here are some best practices to protect your systems against threats that leverage the gaps in your NAS devices: Avoid connecting a NAS device directly to the internet.
sentence.1714: Regularly change the credentials for accessing an NAS device.
sentence.1715: Never use the preset default credentials that come with the device as these are well-known to malicious actors.
sentence.1716: Enable two-factor authentication (2FA) for additional security.
sentence.1717: Regularly check NAS manufacturers’ online security guides, such as Synology’s recommended best practices and QNAP’s recently released suggestions on how to help defend their devices against additional exposure on the internet.
sentence.1718: To find more technical details, threats, insights, and recommendations in protecting your NAS device, download our research “Backing Your Backup: Defending NAS Devices Against Evolving Threats.” Authors Stephen Hilt Sr. Threat Researcher Fernando Merces Sr. Threat Researcher
sentence.1719: title: Enigma Stealer Targets Cryptocurrency Industry with Fake Jobs url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/b/enigma-stealer-targets-cryptocurrency-industry-with-fake-jobs.html Malware Enigma Stealer Targets Cryptocurrency Industry with Fake Jobs We discovered an active campaign targeting Eastern Europeans in the cryptocurrency industry using fake job lures.
sentence.1720: By: Aliakbar Zahravi, Peter Girnus February 09, 2023Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe We recently found an active campaign that uses a fake employment pretext targeting Eastern Europeans in the cryptocurrency industry to install an information stealer.
sentence.1721: In this campaign, the suspected Russian threat actors, use several highly obfuscated and underdevelopment custom loaders in order to infect those involved in the cryptocurrency industry with Enigma stealer (detected as TrojanSpy.MSIL.ENGIMASTEALER.YXDBC), which is a modified version of the Stealerium information stealer.
sentence.1722: In addition to these loaders, the attacker also exploits CVE-2015-2291, an Intel driver vulnerability, to load a malicious driver designed to reduce the token integrity of Microsoft Defender.
sentence.1723: Stealerium, the original information stealer which serves as the base for Enigma Stealer, is an open-source project written in C# and markets itself as a stealer, clipper, and keylogger with logging capabilities using the Telegram API.
sentence.1724: Security teams and individual users are advised to continuously update the security solutions of their systems and remain vigilant against threat actors who perform social engineering via job opportunity or salary increase-related lures.
sentence.1726: The Attack kill chain used by Enigma Stealer operator (click the image for a larger version) Using fake cryptocurrency interviews to lure victims
sentence.1727: The infection chain starts with a malicious RAR archive — in this instance, contract.rar (SHA256: 658725fb5e75ebbcb03bc46d44f048a0f145367eff66c8a1a9dc84eef777a9cc) — which is distributed to victims via phishing attempts or through social media.
sentence.1728: The archive contains the files, Interview questions.txt, and Interview conditions.word.exe.
sentence.1730: The files found inside the malicious RAR archive These files set up the pretext for a fake cryptocurrency role or job opening.
sentence.1731: One file, Interview questions.txt (SHA256: 3a1eb6fabf45d18869de4ffd773ae82949ef80f89105e5f96505de810653ed73) contains sample interview questions written in Cyrillic.
sentence.1732: This serves to further legitimize the package in the eyes of the victim and draw attention away from the malicious binary. Figure 3.
sentence.1733: A machine translation of Interview questions.txt The other file Interview conditions.word.exe (SHA256: 03b9d7296b01e8f3fb3d12c4d80fe8a1bb0ab2fd76f33c5ce11b40729b75fb23) contains the first stage Enigma loader.
sentence.1734: This file, which also masquerades as a legitimate word document, is designed to lure unsuspecting victims into executing the loader.
sentence.1735: Once executed, the Enigma loader begins the registration and downloading of the second-stage payload.
sentence.1736: Analysis of the Enigma infrastructure Enigma uses two servers in its operation.

sentence.1738: The second server 193[.]56[.]146[.]29 is used for DevOps and logging purposes.

sentence.1740: Since this malware is under continuous development the attacker potentially uses the logging server to improve malware performance.
sentence.1741: We have also identified the Amadey C2 panel on 193[.]56[.]146[.]29 which has only one sample (95b4de74daadf79f0e0eef7735ce80bc) communicating with it. Figure 4.

sentence.1751: The initial stage of Enigma, Interview conditions.word.exe, is a downloader written in C++.
sentence.1752: Its primary objective is to download, deobfuscate, decompress, and launch the secondary stage payload.
sentence.1753: The malware incorporates multiple tactics to avoid detection and complicate reverse engineering, such as API hashing, string encryption, and irrelevant code.
sentence.1754: Before delving into the analysis of "EngimaDownloader_s001," let's first examine how the malware decrypts strings and resolves hashed Windows APIs.
sentence.1755: By understanding this, we can implement an automated system to help us retrieve encrypted data and streamline the analysis process.
sentence.1756: Please be advised that to enhance code legibility, we have substituted all hashes with the corresponding function names.
sentence.1757: EngimaDownloader_s001 API Hashing: API hashing is a technique employed by malware to conceal the utilization of potentially suspicious APIs (functions) from static detection.
sentence.1758: This technique helps the malware disguise its activities and evade detection.
sentence.1759: It involves replacing the human-readable names of functions (such as "CreateMutexW") with a hash value, such as 0x0FD43765A.
sentence.1760: The hash value is then used in the code to call the corresponding API function, rather than using the human-readable name.
sentence.1761: The purpose of this technique is to make the process of understanding the code more time-consuming and difficult.
sentence.1762: For API Hashing the EnigmaDownloader_s001 uses the following custom MurmurHash: Figure 7.
sentence.1763: Custom implementation of murmur hash The malware employs dynamic API resolving to conceal its API imports and make static analysis more difficult.
sentence.1764: This technique involves storing the names or hashes of the APIs needed, then importing them dynamically at runtime.
sentence.1765: The Windows API offers LoadLibrary and GetProcAddress functions to facilitate this.
sentence.1766: LoadLibrary accepts the name of a DLL and returns a handle, which is then passed to GetProcAddress along with a function name to obtain a pointer to that function.
sentence.1767: To further evade detection, the malware author even implemented their own custom version of GetProcAddress to retrieve the address of functions such as LoadLibrary and others.
sentence.1768: The use of standard methods like GetProcAddress and LoadLibrary might raise a red flag, so the custom implementation helps to avoid detection.

sentence.1883: title: Ex-Conti and FIN7 Actors Collaborate with New Domino Backdoor url: https://securityintelligence.com/posts/ex-conti-fin7-actors-collaborate-new-backdoor/ This blog was made possible through contributions from Christopher Caridi.
sentence.1884: IBM Security X-Force recently discovered a new malware family we have called “Domino,” which we assess was created by developers associated with the cybercriminal group that X-Force tracks as ITG14, also known as FIN7.
sentence.1885: Former members of the Trickbot/Conti syndicate which X-Force tracks as ITG23 have been using Domino since at least late February 2023 to deliver either the Project Nemesis information stealer or more capable backdoors such as Cobalt Strike.
sentence.1886: Background This discovery highlights the intricate nature of cooperation among cybercriminal groups and their members: Since late February 2023, Domino Backdoor campaigns have been observed using the Dave Loader, which we have linked to the Trickbot/Conti syndicate and its former members.
sentence.1887: Domino’s code shows overlap with the Lizar (aka Tirion, Diceloader) malware family, leading us to suspect that it was created by current or former ITG14 developers.
sentence.1888: One of Domino’s final payloads is the Project Nemesis infostealer.
sentence.1889: Project Nemesis was first advertised on the dark web in December 2021, though has been rarely used since then.
sentence.1890: Analysis Ex-Conti Members Deploy Domino in Recent Campaigns Former members of ITG23 (aka the Trickbot/Conti syndicate) are likely behind recent campaigns using the Dave Loader to load Domino Backdoor and probably collaborated with current or former ITG14 developers to purchase or use the new malware family.
sentence.1891: X-Force previously assessed that Dave is one of several loaders or crypters developed by members of the Trickbot/Conti group.
sentence.1892: Although the group has fractured, many of its loaders/crypters — including Dave — have been maintained and continue to be used by factions composed of former Trickbot/Conti members, including Quantum, Royal, BlackBasta, and Zeon.
sentence.1893: The Dave Loader has been used recently with several Cobalt Strike samples with the watermark “206546002,” which X-Force and other security researchers — here and here — have associated with groups composed of former members of the Trickbot/Conti syndicate, including Quantum and Royal.
sentence.1894: X-Force observed Dave-loaded Cobalt Strike samples using this watermark in suspected Royal attacks in fall 2022.
sentence.1895: Dave Loader has also been used this year to load IcedID and Emotet, both of which serve as initial access vectors for ransomware attacks from former Trickbot/Conti-affiliated factions.
sentence.1896: Recently observed Dave samples were discovered loading a new malware, which we have named Domino Backdoor.
sentence.1897: This new backdoor gathers basic system information, which it then sends to the C2, and in return receives an AES encrypted payload.
sentence.1898: In most instances, the received payload was a second loader that was found to have code overlap with Domino Backdoor, and as such we have dubbed it Domino Loader.
sentence.1899: This loader contains an encrypted payload within its resources, which it decrypts using AES.
sentence.1900: The decrypted payload is a .NET infostealer, which identifies itself as ‘Nemesis Project.’
sentence.1901: The Domino Backdoor is designed to contact a different C2 address for domain-joined systems, suggesting a more capable backdoor, such as Cobalt Strike, will be downloaded on higher value targets instead of Project Nemesis.
sentence.1902: Domino’s Connections to ITG14 Analysis revealed that both the Domino Backdoor and Loader share code overlap with the Lizar Malware, also known as Tirion and DiceLoader, which is attributed to the threat group ITG14 (FIN7).
sentence.1903: In addition to having similar coding styles and functionality, both Domino and DiceLoader share the same configuration structure and have similar bot ID formats.
sentence.1904: Lizar was reportedly first used in March 2020, when it was originally named Tirion, and has been observed in numerous ITG14 campaigns up to the end of 2022.
sentence.1905: Domino has been active in the wild since at least October 2022, which notably is when Lizar observations began to decrease.
sentence.1906: X-Force researchers found additional evidence connecting Domino Backdoor to ITG14’s Carbanak Backdoor.
sentence.1907: We identified Domino Backdoor samples from December 2022, which used a different loader that we have dubbed NewWorldOrder Loader.
sentence.1908: The samples used the name ThunderboltService.exe and downloaded and loaded the Project Nemesis Stealer.
sentence.1909: Around the same time, we also uncovered NewWorldOrder Loader samples, with the same filename ThunderboltService.exe, used to load the Carbanak Backdoor.
sentence.1910: Carbanak has been used by ITG14 since late 2015.
sentence.1911: Finally, X-Force analysts also observed that two of the Domino Backdoor C2 addresses belonging to MivoCloud: 94.158.247[.]72 and 185.225.17[.]202 are very close to C2 addresses ITG14 has used previously for SSH-based Backdoors such as 94.158.247[.]23 and 185.225.17[.]220.
sentence.1912: While such overlap is insufficient for attribution, it is nonetheless consistent with other evidence linking Domino to an ITG14 developer and may indicate the latter’s preference for MivoCloud for at least some of their C2 addresses.
sentence.1913: MivoCloud has also been used to host Diceloader and Carbanak C2 servers.
sentence.1914: Collaboration between members of ITG14 and former members of ITG23 is not without precedent.
sentence.1915: Other researchers — here and here — observed ITG14 attacks using Ryuk ransomware in 2020, which has been attributed to the Trickbot/Conti cybercrime syndicate, while others have also identified connections between a FIN7 developer and tools used by the BlackBasta group, whose members also have ties to the former Trickbot/Conti syndicate.
sentence.1916: Project Nemesis The Project Nemesis infostealer has been active in the wild since December 2021, when it was offered for sale on several Dark Web forums.
sentence.1917: It can collect data from a range of web browsers, as well as applications including Steam, Telegram, Discord, crypto wallets, and VPN providers.
sentence.1918: Domino has been used to install Project Nemesis since at least October 2022 — prior to its use in late February 2023 by ex-Conti actors.
sentence.1919: This leads us to assess that the ITG14 members responsible for developing Domino probably had a relationship with Project Nemesis and offered Domino and the infostealer to the ex-Conti threat actors as a package.
sentence.1920: The ex-Conti members in turn likely used the Project Nemesis infostealer against lower value targets.
sentence.1921: The use of infostealers by former Trickbot/Conti members and their distributors is not without precedent — other security researchers observed the Vidar infostealer delivered during DEV-0569 Batloader campaigns that also led in some cases to Cobalt Strike and Royal ransomware.
sentence.1922: We assess that infostealers may often be deployed during lower priority infections, e.g., on personal computers or those not belonging to an Active Directory domain, while higher priority infections receive other backdoors such as Cobalt Strike.
sentence.1923: Malware Deep Dive This section contains a deeper look at the Dave Loader, Domino Backdoor, Domino Loader, and Project Nemesis Infostealer malware.
sentence.1924: Dave Loader The sample analysed for the purpose of this report is a 64-bit executable with MD5 hash 2CC79806701F1A6E877C29B93F06F1BB and a reported compile date of 28 February 2023.
sentence.1925: This sample is identified as a variant of Dave Loader, a crypter linked to threat group ITG23 and more commonly observed with payloads such as Emotet.
sentence.1926: This sample has two encrypted resources within a resource directory named “XKLKLCRTE.”
sentence.1927: Dave Loader loads the resources using the API calls LdrFindResource_U and LdrAccessResource, and decrypts them using XOR and the key mh8ZqMlTsaDYBZe7ma\x00.
sentence.1928: The smaller payload, with resource ID 3412, is a shellcode blob that contains code designed to load a PE file.
sentence.1929: The second payload, with resource ID 6732, is a PE file.
sentence.1930: Dave Loader executes the decrypted shellcode and passes the PE payload to it, which the shellcode then loads and executes.
sentence.1931: Domino Backdoor The loaded payload is a 64-bit DLL written in Visual C++, with MD5 hash CDBE0FEB82B1CAF164C7DA42CB9A20BE.
sentence.1932: The payload was found to be a hitherto unknown backdoor, which will be referred to as Domino Backdoor.
sentence.1933: Upon execution, Domino Backdoor starts by generating a Bot ID for the infected system by gathering the username and hostname and creating a hash of the collected data, to which it then appends its current process id.
sentence.1935: This bot ID format is similar to that generated by Lizar, which also used a checksum of system information, combined with the process ID.
sentence.1936: However, Lizar used a CRC algorithm to create its hash, whereas Domino uses a custom algorithm which XOR’s multiple values together.
sentence.1937: Interestingly, Lizar used a similar XOR-based algorithm as part of its encryption mechanisms during communication with the C2. Fig 1 — Domino Backdoor system ID generation The malware then proceeds to decrypt its configuration block, which is stored in the data section of the binary.
sentence.1938: The config is decrypted using XOR and a 16-byte key which is stored immediately before the encrypted config block.
sentence.1939: In this case the key is {03 9B 54 72 17 D3 5E E6 E0 E9 EF E0 DF 36 0D 79}.
sentence.1940: Fig 2 — Domino Backdoor config decryption In the analysed sample the decrypted config contains two pipe-delimited IP addresses, 88.119.175[.]124 and 94.158.247[.]72.
sentence.1942: A second config block, which is decrypted separately, contains an RSA public key.
sentence.1943: The malware generates a random 32-byte key, which it encrypts using the RSA key.
sentence.1944: It then attempts to connect to the C2 via TCP port 443 and send the encrypted key.
sentence.1945: Prior to the C2 connection, the malware checks whether the host system is connected to a domain.
sentence.1946: If the system is detected as being domain joined, then the malware uses the second IP address from the config to connect to the C2, otherwise, it defaults to the first.
sentence.1947: If the initial connection is successful, the malware then proceeds to gather basic system information, including username, computer name, and OS version, which it then encrypts using AES-256-CBC and the generated, shared key (null bytes used for IV).
sentence.1948: An example of the unencrypted data structure, which the malware sends to the C2, can be seen below. 00000000 39 00 00 00 0b 15 61 36 34 38 36 32 38 63 31 33 |9…..
sentence.1951: This structure breaks down as follows: Offset Size (bytes) Contents Description 0x0 4 0x00000039 Size of structure 0x4 1 0x0B Hardcoded value 0xB (11) 0x5 1 0x15 Size of system id string 0x6 21 a648628c13d928dc-4480 System ID string 0x1B 1 0x03 Value indicating presence of domain string 0x1C 1 0x01 Unknown 0x1D 1 0x0A OS Major version (10) 0x1E 1 0x00 OS Minor version 0x1F
sentence.1952: 2 0x0000 Unknown 0x21 4 0x5a290000 OS Build Number (0x295A = 10586) 0x25 1 0x0C Size of computer name string 0x26 12 29FeXskdpL Computer Name 0x32 1 0x0A Size of username string 0x33 10 vnPxSFeoNN Username Scroll to view full table
sentence.1953: The malware first sends 4 bytes to the C2 that contain a XOR-encrypted value, which is the size of the data to follow, and then sends the AES-encrypted system data.
sentence.1954: The malware then begins a loop of checking in with the C2 by first sending a 4-byte encrypted size, followed by a 16-byte AES-encrypted block, which decrypts to the following 5 bytes {01 00 00 00 ff}.
sentence.1955: It continues this every second until it receives a response from the C2.
sentence.1956: When it receives a response, the malware expects the C2 to send 4 bytes containing the payload size, followed by the payload itself.
sentence.1957: The malware then decrypts the received payload using AES and the shared key.
sentence.1958: The decrypted data consists of a 4 byte size, followed by a single byte indicating either a command or the load method that the malware should use for the payload, followed by the payload data itself, if applicable.
sentence.1959: If the command byte is 0x3, then the malware exits.
sentence.1960: If the command byte is 0x7, then the malware enumerates the running processes on the system and compiles a list of process names and IDs.
sentence.1961: This data is then encrypted using AES and returned to the C2.
sentence.1962: Otherwise, the malware proceeds to load and execute the received payload using the method indicated by the load/command byte.
sentence.1964: 0x1 — Copy the payload into allocated memory within the current process and create a new thread to execute an export named ReflectiveLoader within the payload DLL. 0x4 — Save the payload to the %Temp% directory with a filename generated via GetTempFileNameA, and execute the file using CreateProcessA. 0x5, 0x6 — Open process with process id provided with the downloaded data.
sentence.1965: Allocate space within the process and write the payload data to the process memory.
sentence.1966: Then create a new thread in the remote process to execute an export named ReflectiveLoader within the copied payload DLL.
sentence.1967: This method is likely intended to be used following command 0x7.
sentence.1968: In the case of the analysed sample, the received payload contained a DLL binary, and command 0x1 was specified.
sentence.1969: Fig 3 — Domino Backdoor command structure Overlap with Lizar Toolkit Domino Backdoor shares a lot of overlap with malware associated with the Lizar Toolkit, which is attributed to threat group ITG14.
sentence.1970: The Lizar Toolkit consists of a backdoor/loader, a collection of modules/plugins which can be executed by the loader, and C2 client and server applications.
sentence.1971: A detailed report on the Lizar Toolkit can be found here.
sentence.1972: In addition to having similar coding styles and utilising similar API calls, Domino Backdoor uses the same configuration structure as the Lizar Loader.
sentence.1973: In both cases, a configuration block containing a pipe-delimited list of IP addresses is decrypted using XOR and a 16-byte key which is stored immediately before the encrypted config.
sentence.1974: Both malware families also generate system IDs in very similar manners.
sentence.1975: In the case of Domino Backdoor a hash is generated from the system username and hostname and the process ID is appended.
sentence.1976: The hashing algorithm is custom and appears to be based on an encryption algorithm used previously in the Lizar Loader.
sentence.1977: Lizar Loader also generates a system ID which consists of a hash of system data followed by the current process ID, however, it uses a CRC algorithm to create its hash.
sentence.1978: Domino Backdoor also incorporates elements that appear in some of Lizar’s plugins.
sentence.1979: For example, the system information gathered by Domino Backdoor and sent to the C2 matches the reported functionality of Lizar’s Info32/Info64.dll plugin.
sentence.1980: Also, the function within Domino Backdoor to enumerate running processes and send a list of process names and IDs back to the C2 is very similar to the functionality of Lizar’s ListProcesses32/ListProcesses64.dll plugin.
sentence.1981: Finally, Lizar’s Jumper32/Jumper64.dll plugin resembles the code within Domino Backdoor, which is able to load a payload using several different methods, with the required one specified using a command ID number.
sentence.1982: Domino Loader The payload received by the Domino backdoor from the C2 during this analysis was a 64-bit DLL, written in C++, with MD5 hash 2373BE26018075847AEA51636B739F66 and an internal filename of MultiRunDll64.dll.
sentence.1983: The payload was found to be a Loader with similarities to Domino Backdoor, and will be referred to as Domino Loader.
sentence.1984: Domino Loader has one export named ReflectiveLoader that contains code taken from the well-known ReflectiveDLLInjection project.
sentence.1985: When run, this code performs the steps needed to properly load the DLL into memory, and allows for DLL payloads to load themselves directly from memory into a host process.
sentence.1986: Once loaded, Domino Loader starts by loading an encrypted payload from its resources and decrypting it using AES-256-CBC and a hardcoded key.
sentence.1987: The Microsoft WinCrypt library is used for AES encryption and decryption by both Domino Backdoor and Loader.
sentence.1988: The decrypted data consists of 4 bytes containing the payload size, followed by a further 4 bytes containing either the entry point offset for the payload or a value indicating the load method which should be used, followed by the payload itself.
sentence.1989: If the entry point/load field contains a positive value, then the loader allocates memory within the current process space, copies the payload data to it, and then executes it at the specified offset indicated by the field value.
sentence.1990: This option is most likely used for shellcode payloads or further DLLs with ReflectiveLoader exports.
sentence.1991: If the value of the load field is -1 then the loader allocates memory within the current process and then loads the PE payload into it using the full PE loading procedure.
sentence.1992: It copies the headers, maps the individual PE sections, processes any relocations, loads the PE’s imports, and then executes the PE from its internally specified entry point.
sentence.1993: Finally, if the load field is equal to zero or another negative number, the payload is loaded as a .NET assembly.

sentence.2065: title: Analysis on recent wiper attacks: examples and how wiper malware works url: https://cybersecurity.att.com/blogs/labs-research/analysis-on-recent-wiper-attacks-examples-and-how-they-wiper-malware-works Executive summary 2022 has experienced an increase in the number of wiper variants targeting Ukrainian entities.
sentence.2066: This blog post looks to explain how wipers work, what makes them so effective and provides a short overview of the most recent samples that appeared in the eastern Europe geopolitical conflict.
sentence.2068: Wiper’s main objective is to destroy data from any storage device and make the information unavailable (T1485).
sentence.2069: There are two ways of removing files, logical and physical.
sentence.2070: Logical file removal is the most common way of erasing a file, performed by users daily when a file is sent to (and emptied from) the Recycle bin, or when it is removed with the command line or terminal with the commands del/rm.
sentence.2071: This action deletes the pointer to the file but not the file data, making it recoverable with forensic tools as long as the Operative System does not write any other file in the same physical location.
sentence.2072: However, malware wipers aim to make the data irrecoverable, so they tend to remove the data from the physical level of the disk.
sentence.2073: The most effective way to remove the data/file is by overwriting the specific physical location with other data (usually a repeated byte like 0xFF).
sentence.2074: This process usually involves writing to disk several Gigabytes (or Terabytes) of data and can be time consuming.
sentence.2075: For this reason, in addition to destroying the data, many wipers first destroy two special files in the system: The Master Boot Record (MBR), which is used during the boot process to identify where the Operative System is stored in the disk.
sentence.2076: By replacing the MBR, the boot process crashes, making the files inaccessible unless forensic methodologies are used.
sentence.2077: The Master File Table (MFT) is exclusive to NTFS file systems, contains the physical location of files in the drive as well as logical and physical size and any associated metadata.
sentence.2078: If big files need to be stored in the drive, and cannot use consecutive blocks, these files will have to be fragmented in the disk.
sentence.2079: The MFT holds the information of where each fragment is stored.
sentence.2080: Removing the MFT will require the use of forensic tools to recover small files, and basically prevents recovery of fragmented files since the link between fragments is lost.
sentence.2081: The main difference between wipers and ransomware is that it’s impossible to retrieve the impacted information after a wiper attack.
sentence.2082: Attackers using wipers do not usually target financial reward but intend to disrupt the victim’s operations as much as possible.
sentence.2083: Ransomware operators aim to get a payment in exchange for the key to decrypt the user’s data.
sentence.2084: With both wiper and ransomware attacks, the victim depends on their back up system to recover after an attack.
sentence.2085: However, even some wiper attacks carry ransom notes requesting a payment to recover the data.
sentence.2086: It is important that the victim properly identifies the attack they've suffered, or they may pay the ransom without any chance of retrieving the lost data.
sentence.2087: In the last month and a half, since the war started in Eastern Europe, several wipers have been used in parallel with DDoS attacks (T1499) to keep financial institutions and government organizations, mainly Ukrainian, inaccessible for extended periods of time.
sentence.2088: Some of the wipers observed in this timeframe have been: WhisperKill, HermeticWiper, IsaacWiper, CaddyWiper, DoubleZero Wiper and AcidRain.
sentence.2089: Most recent wiper examples WhisperKill On January 14, 2022, the Ukrainian government experienced a coordinated attack on 22 of their government agencies, defacing their websites.
sentence.2090: Almost all the compromised websites were developed by the same Ukranian IT company, Kitsoft, and all of them were built on OctoberCMS.
sentence.2091: Therefore, the attack vector was most probably a supply chain attack on the IT provider, or an exploitation of an OctoberCMS vulnerability, combined with exploitations of Log4Shell vulnerability (T1190).
sentence.2093: Example of defaced Ukrainian government website.
sentence.2094: In addition to the website defacement, Microsoft Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC), identified in a report destructive malware samples targeting Ukrainian organizations with two malware samples.
sentence.2095: Microsoft named the samples WhisperGate, while other security companies labeled the downloader as WhisperGate and WhisperKill as the actual wiper, which was considered a component of WhisperGate.
sentence.2096: The identified files were: Stage1 replaces the Master Boot Record (MBR) with a ransom note when the system is powered down, deeming the machine unbootable after that point.
sentence.2097: When booted up, the system displays Figure 2 on screen.
sentence.2098: Despite the ransom request, the data will not be recoverable since all efforts made by WhisperKill are looking to destroy data, not encrypt it.
sentence.2099: In this case, the wallet is most probably an attempt to decoy attribution efforts.
sentence.2102: Stage 2 attempts to download the next stage malware (T1102.003) from the Discord app, if unsuccessful, it sleeps and tries again.
sentence.2103: The payload downloaded from the messaging app destroys as much data as possible by overwriting certain file types with 0xCC for the first MB of the file.
sentence.2104: Then it modifies the file extension to a random four-byte extension.
sentence.2105: By selecting the file types to be wiped and only writing over the first MB of data, the attackers are optimizing the wiping process.
sentence.2106: This is due to not wasting time on system files and only spending the necessary time to wipe each file, rapidly switching to the next file as soon as the current one is unrecoverable.
sentence.2107: Finally, the malware executes a command to delete itself from the system (T1070.004).
sentence.2108: HermeticWiper A month after, on February 23rd 2022, ESET Research reported a new Wiper being used against hundreds of Ukrainian systems.
sentence.2109: The wiper receives its name from the stolen certificate (T1588.003) it was using to bypass security controls “Hermetica Digital Ltd” (T1588.003).
sentence.2110: According to a Reuters article, the certificate could have also been obtained by impersonating the company and requesting a certificate from scratch.
sentence.2113: The attackers have been seen using several methods to distribute the wiper through the domain, like: domain Group Policy Object (GPO) (T1484.001), Impacket or SMB (T1021.002) and WMI (T1047) with an additional worm component named HermeticWizard.
sentence.2114: The wiper component first installs the payload as a service (T1569.002) under C:\Windows\system32\Drivers\. Afterwards, the service corrupts the first 512 bytes of the MBR of all the Physical Drives, and then enumerates their partitions.
sentence.2115: Before attempting to overwrite as much data as the wiper can it will delete key files in the partition, like MFT, $Bitmap, $LogFile, the NTUSER registry hive (T1112) and the event logs (T1070.001).
sentence.2116: On top of deleting key file system structures, it also performs a drive fragmentation (breaking up files and segregating them in the drive to optimize the system’s performance).
sentence.2117: The combination of the file fragmentation and the deletion of the MFT makes file recovery difficult, since files will be scattered through the drive in small parts - without any guidance as to where each part is located.
sentence.2118: Finally, the malware writes randomized contents into all occupied sectors in the partition in an attempt to remove all potential hope of recovering any data with forensic tools or procedures.
sentence.2119: IsaacWiper A day after the initial destructive attack with HermeticWiper, on February 24th, 2022, a new wiper was used against the Ukrainian government, as reported by ESET, without any significant similarities to the HermaticWiper used the day before.
sentence.2120: IsaacWiper identifies all the physical drives not containing the Operative System and locks their logical partitions by only allowing a single thread to access each of them.
sentence.2121: Then it starts to write random data into the drives in chunks of 64 KB.
sentence.2122: There is a unique thread per volume, making the wiping process very long.
sentence.2123: Once the rest of the physical drives and the logical partitions sharing physical drive with the Operative System’s volume have been wiped, this last volume is wiped by: Erasing the MBR.
sentence.2124: Overwriting all files with 64 KB chunks of random data with one thread.
sentence.2125: Creating a new file under the C drive which will be filled with random data until it takes the maximum space it can from the partition, overwriting the already overwritten existing files.
sentence.2126: This process is performed with a different thread, but it would still take a long time to write the full partition since both concurrent threads are actually attempting to write random data on the full disk. Figure 4.
sentence.2128: When comparing IsaacWiper to WhisperKill, the attackers’ priorities become clear.
sentence.2129: WhisperKill creators prioritized speed and number of affected files over ensuring the full drive is overwritten, since only 1 MB of each file was overwritten.
sentence.2130: On the other hand, IsaacWiper creators gave total priority to deliver the most effective wiper, no matter how long it takes to overwrite the full physical disk.
sentence.2131: AcidRain On the same day IsaacWiper was deployed, another wiper attacked Viasat KA-SAT modems in Ukraine, this time with a different wiper, named AcidRain by SentinelLABS.
sentence.2132: This wiper was particularly aimed at modems, probably to disrupt Internet access from Ukraine.
sentence.2133: This new wiper showed similarities to previously seen botnets targeting modems using VPNFilter.
sentence.2134: It was used in 2018, targeting vulnerabilities in several common router brands:
sentence.2136: Exploiting vulnerabilities allowed the attackers to obtain Initial Access inside all types of networks, where the bot would search for Modbus traffic to identify infected systems with Industrial Control Systems (ICS).
sentence.2137: The wiper used was the ELF MIPS wiper targeting Viasat KA-SAT modems, which aimed to firstly overwrite any file outside of the any common *nix installation: bin, boot, dev, lib, proc, sbin, sys, sur, etc. to then delete data from /dev/. CaddyWiper The first version of CaddyWiper was discovered by ESET researchers on 2022-03-14 when it was used against a Ukrainian bank.
sentence.2138: This new wiper variant does not have any significant code similarities to previous wipers.
sentence.2139: This sample specifically sets an exclusion to avoid infecting Domain Controllers in the infected system.
sentence.2140: Afterwards, it targets C:/Users and any additional attached drive all the way to letter Z:/ and zeroes all the files present in such folders/drives.
sentence.2141: Finally, the extended information of the physical drives is destroyed, including the MBR and partition entries.
sentence.2142: A variant of CaddyWiper was used again on 2022-04-08 14:58 against high-voltage electrical substations in Ukraine.
sentence.2143: This latest version of the wiper was delivered together with Industroyer2, an evolution of Industroyer, which has the main functionn being to communicate with industrial equipment.
sentence.2144: In this case, the wiper was used with the purpose of slowing down the recovery process from the Industroyer2 attack and gaining back control of the ICS consoles, as well as covering the tracks of the attack.
sentence.2145: According to Welivesecurity, who have been cooperating with CERT-UA in this investigation, the Sandworm Team is behind this latest attack.
sentence.2146: In this same attack against the energy station in Ukraine, other wiper samples for Linux and Solaris were observed by WeliveSecurity.
sentence.2147: These wipers leverage the shred command if present, otherwise they use the basic dd or rm commands to wipe the system.
sentence.2148: DoubleZero wiper On March 22, 2022 CERT-UA reported a new wiper used against their infrastructure and enterprises.
sentence.2149: Named DoubleZero, the wiper was distributed as a ZIP file containing an obfuscated .NET program.
sentence.2150: The wiper’s routine sets a hardcoded list of system directories, which are skipped during an initial wiping targeting user files.
sentence.2151: Afterwards, the skipped system directories are targeted and finally the registry hives: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (containing the hives Sam, Security, Software and System), HKEY_CURRENT_USER and HKEY_USERS.
sentence.2152: There are two wiping methods, both of which zero out the selected file.
sentence.2155: Conclusion As we have seen in the examples above, the main objective of the attackers behind wipers is to destroy all possible data and render systems unbootable (if possible), potentially requiring a full system restore if backups aren’t available.
sentence.2156: These malware attacks can be as disruptive as ransomware attacks, but wipers are arguably worse since there is no potential escape door of a payment to recover the data.
sentence.2157: There are plenty of ways to wipe systems.
sentence.2158: We've looked at 6 different wiper samples observed targeting Ukranian entities.
sentence.2159: These samples approach the attack in very different ways, and most of them occur faster than the time required to respond.
sentence.2160: For that reason, it is not effective to employ detection of wiper malware, as once they are in the system as it is already too late.
sentence.2161: The best approach against wipers is to prevent attacks by keeping systems up to date and by increasing cybersecurity awareness.
sentence.2162: In addition, consequences can be ameliorated by having periodic backup copies of key infrastructure available.

sentence.2173: APT41 backdoors, old and new url: https://www.ptsecurity.com/ww-en/analytics/pt-esc-threat-intelligence/higaisa-or-winnti-apt-41-backdoors-old-and-new/ The PT Expert Security Center regularly spots emerging threats to information security, including both previously known and newly discovered malware.
sentence.2174: During such monitoring in May 2020, we detected several samples of new malware that at first glance would seem to belong to the Higaisa group.
sentence.2175: But detailed analysis pointed to the Winnti group (also known as APT41, per FireEye) of Chinese origin.
sentence.2176: Subsequent monitoring led us to discover a number of new malware samples used by the group in recent attacks.
sentence.2177: These include various droppers, loaders, and injectors; Crosswalk, ShadowPad, and PlugX backdoors; and samples of a previously undescribed backdoor that we have dubbed FunnySwitch.
sentence.2178: We can confidently state that some of these attacks were directed at a number of organizations in Russia and Hong Kong.
sentence.2179: In this article, we will share the results of our investigation of these samples and related network infrastructure, as well as overlaps with previously described attacks.
