sentence.2181: Higaisa shortcuts The first attack dates to May 12, 2020.
sentence.2182: At the core of the attack is an archive named Project link and New copyright policy.rar (75cd8d24030a3160b1f49f1b46257f9d6639433214a10564d432b74cc8c4d020).
sentence.2183: The archive contains a bait PDF document (Zeplin Copyright Policy.pdf) plus the folder All tort's projects - Web lnks with two shortcuts: Conversations - iOS - Swipe Icons - Zeplin.lnk Tokbox icon - Odds and Ends - iOS - Zeplin.lnk The structure of malicious shortcuts resembles the sample 20200308-sitrep-48-covid-19.pdf.lnk spread by the Higaisa group in March 2020.
sentence.2185: Comparing command lines in the covid-19 and Zeplin shortcutsThe mechanism for initial infection is fundamentally the same: trying to open either of the shortcuts leads to running a command that extracts a Base64-encoded CAB archive from the body of the LNK file, after which the archive is unpacked to a temporary folder.
sentence.2186: Further actions are performed with the help of an extracted JS script.
sentence.2188: Contents of script 34fDFkfSD32.jsBut here is where the similarity with the sample described in our Higaisa report ends: instead, this script copies the payload to the folder C:\Users\Public\Downloads, achieves persistence by adding itself to the startup folder and adding a scheduler task, and runs the payload.
sentence.2189: The script also sends the output of ipconfig in a POST request to http://zeplin.atwebpages[.]com/inter.php.
sentence.2190: The command run by the shortcut also contains the opening of a URL file extracted from the archive.
sentence.2191: The name of the URL file and the target address depend on which shortcut is opened: Conversations - iOS - Swipe Icons - Zeplin.url goes to: https://app.zeplin.io/project/5b5741802f3131c3a63057a4/screen/5b589f697e44cee37e0e61df Tokbox icon - Odds and Ends - iOS - Zeplin.url goes to: https://app.zeplin.io/project/5c161c03fde4d550a251e20a/screen/5cef98986801a41be35122bb.
sentence.2192: This is the only difference between the two LNK files.
sentence.2193: In both cases, the target page is hosted on Zeplin, a legitimate service for collaboration between designers and developers, and requires logging in to view.
sentence.2194: The payload consists of two files: svchast.exe It functions as a simple local shellcode loader.
sentence.2195: The shellcode read from a fixed path.
sentence.2196: Before starting, the loader checks the current year: 2018, 2019, 2020, or 2021. Figure 3.
sentence.2197: Main function in svchast.exe 3t54dE3r.tmp The shellcode containing the main payload is the Crosswalk backdoor.
sentence.2198: On May 30, 2020, a new malicious archive, CV_Colliers.rar (df999d24bde96decdbb65287ca0986db98f73b4ed477e18c3ef100064bceba6d), was detected.
sentence.2199: It had two shortcuts: Curriculum Vitae_WANG LEI_Hong Kong Polytechnic University.pdf.lnk International English Language Testing System certificate.pdf.lnk Their structure fully matched that of the samples from May 12.
sentence.2200: In this case, the bait consisted of PDF documents with a CV and IELTS certificate.
sentence.2201: Depending on which shortcut was opened, the output of ipconfig was sent to one of two addresses: http://goodhk.azurewebsites[.]net/inter.php or http://sixindent.epizy[.]com/inter.php.
sentence.2202: Note that all three intermediate C2 servers are on third-level domains on a free hosting service.
sentence.2203: When accessed in a browser, each displays a different decoy page: Figure 4.
sentence.2206: Page at sixindent.epizy_comThese servers do not play a major role in the functioning of the malware; their precise purpose remains unknown.
sentence.2207: It may be that the malware authors used this to monitor the success of the initial stages of infection, or else tried to lead security teams "off the scent" by masking the malware as a more minor threat.
sentence.2208: 1.1 Attribution These attacks have been studied in detail by Malwarebytes and Zscaler.
sentence.2209: Based on the similarity of the infection chains, researchers classify them as belonging to the Higaisa group.
sentence.2210: However, detailed analysis of the shellcode demonstrates that the samples actually belong to the Crosswalk malware family.
sentence.2211: Crosswalk appeared no later than 2017 and was mentioned for the first time in a FireEye report on the activities of the APT41 (Winnti) group.
sentence.2214: Fragment of shellcode from 3t54dE3r.tmpThe network infrastructure of the samples overlaps with previously known APT41 infrastructure: at the IP address of one of the C2 servers, we find an SSL certificate with SHA-1 value of b8cff709950cfa86665363d9553532db9922265c, which is also found at IP address 67.229.97[.]229, referenced in a 2018 CrowdStrike report.
sentence.2215: Going further, we can find domains from a Kaspersky report written in 2013.
sentence.2217: Fragment of network infrastructureAll this leads us to conclude that these LNK file attacks were performed by Winnti (APT41), which "borrowed" this shortcut technique from Higaisa.
sentence.2218: 1.2 Crosswalk Crosswalk is a modular backdoor implemented in shellcode.
sentence.2219: The main component connects to a C2 server, collects and sends system information, and contains functionality for installing and running up to 20 additional modules received from the server as shellcode.
sentence.2220: The information collected by the module includes: OS uptime Network adapter IP addresses MAC address of one of the adapters Operating system version and whether it is 32-bit or 64-bit Username Computer name Name of running module PID Shellcode version and whether it is 32-bit or 64-bit (The shellcode supports both 32 and 64 bits.)
sentence.2221: It has two-part version numbers; we found ones including 1.0, 1.10, 1.21, 1.22, 1.25, and 2.0.
sentence.2222: For more detailed analysis of one version of Crosswalk, see the VMware CarbonBlack investigation.
sentence.2223: Based on version 1.25 (8e6945ae06dd849b9db0c2983bca82de1dddbf79afb371aa88da71c19c44c996), which was used in the attacks with LNK files, here we will describe the networking aspects of the malware in more detail.
sentence.2224: Crosswalk has broad capabilities for connecting to C2 servers.
sentence.2225: The network configuration for this particular sample is at the end of the shellcode and is XOR encrypted with a 16-byte key.
sentence.2226: The data structure is as follows: Configuration size (4 bytes)
sentence.2227: Key (16 bytes) Encrypted configuration The configuration, in turn, contains the following fields: 0x0 heartbeat interval (in seconds) 0x4 reconnect interval (in seconds) 0x8 bitmask for days of the week when connections may be made 0xC (inclusive) lower bound for time of day when connections may be made 0x10 (non-inclusive) upper bound for time of day when connections may be made 0x14 proxy port 0x18
sentence.2228: proxy type 0x1C proxy host 0x9C proxy username 0x11C proxy password 0x19C number of C2 servers 0x1A0 array of structures of C2 servers A C2 server structure consists of the following fields: 0x0 connection type 0x4 port 0x8 whether DNS name resolution is necessary (yes/no) 0xC length of hostname 0x10 hostname Before attempting to connect, the backdoor checks whether the current day of the week and time match those allowed in the configuration.
sentence.2229: Then, one after the other, it tries combinations of possible proxy servers (any indicated in the configuration plus system proxies) and C2 servers until it connects successfully.
sentence.2230: The communication protocol used between the backdoor and C2 server can be separated logically into two levels: Application-level protocol Transport-level protocol On the application level, messages consist of the following fields: FakeTLS header consisting of 5 bytes: Entry type and protocol version (3 bytes).
sentence.2231: For the client these always equal 17 03 01; for the server, they have random values.
sentence.2232: Data length, not including header (2 bytes) Message contents: Command ID (4 bytes, little-endian) Command data size (4 bytes, little-endian) Client ID (36 bytes), generated based on the UUID when the backdoor starts operation Command data The first two client–server and server–client messages have command IDs 0x65 and 0x64, respectively.
sentence.2233: They contain the data that will then be used to generate the client and server session keys.
sentence.2234: The key generation algorithm is detailed in a Zscaler report.
sentence.2235: For all subsequent messages, the content (not including the FakeTLS header) is transferred in the corresponding encrypted session key. AES-128 is the encryption algorithm used.
sentence.2236: The transport-level protocol depends on the connection type indicated in the configuration.
sentence.2237: Four protocols are supported: Standard TCP connection Application-level messages are sent unchanged as TCP segments.
sentence.2238: Equivalent to HTTP Long Polling The client creates two TCP connections.
sentence.2239: The first will be used to get packets from the server, and the second to send them.
sentence.2240: During the first connection, a GET request is sent to the C2 server.
sentence.2241: The server replies with headers with code 200 and Content-Length: 524288000.
sentence.2242: The subsequent stream of application-level messages from the server to the client is sent as the body of an HTTP response.
sentence.2244: First HTTP connection with C2After the correct response headers are received, the malware establishes a second connection to the same port, where a POST request is made.
sentence.2245: The header dCy is generated by the client based on the UUID and, it would seem, serves as the session ID that links the two connections.
sentence.2246: After receipt of a response with code 200, subsequent messages from the client to the server are sent using separate POST requests.
sentence.2248: Second HTTP connection with C2 Duplication of socket with TLS connection The client establishes a TCP connection and sends an HTTPS request like the following one: GET /msdn.cpp HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: WinHTTP/1.1 Content-Length: 4294967295 Host:
sentence.2250: The HTTPS connection is not used again.
sentence.2251: Subsequent messages are exchanged in the original TCP connection (without TLS encryption).
sentence.2252: Subsequent communication between the client and server occurs via protocol 1, except for when, at the beginning of the session, the client sends two packets with the FakeTLS header, which starts with the sequence 17 03 01.
sentence.2253: The first packet always has length 0.
sentence.2254: The second has length 0x3A, 0x3C, 0x3E, or 0x40 and contains random bytes.
sentence.2255: We were unable to determine the purpose of these packets.
sentence.2257: Additional packets with FakeTLS header KCP protocol This protocol can be implemented on top of any other protocol (including UDP) to ensure quick and reliable data transfer.
sentence.2258: The Crosswalk client uses KCP on top of a TCP connection: KCP protocol data is added to application-level messages that are then sent as TCP segments.
sentence.2260: Crosswalk message with KCP headers (highlighted in yellow) Note that in the Crosswalk samples we detected, none of the samples used the KCP protocol in practice.
sentence.2261: But the code contains a full-fledged implementation of this protocol, which could be used in other attacks: the developers would simply need to set this connection type in the configuration.
sentence.2262: The diversity of protocols and techniques would seem to protect the backdoor from network traffic inspection.
sentence.2263: 2. Loaders and injectors Investigation of network infrastructure and monitoring of new Crosswalk samples put us onto the scent of other malicious objects containing Crosswalk shellcode as their payload.
sentence.2264: We can categorize these objects into two groups: local shellcode loaders and injectors.
sentence.2265: Some of the samples in both groups are also obfuscated with VMProtect.
sentence.2267: Code for injecting shellcode into a running processThe injectors contain typical code that obtains SeDebugPrivilege, finds the PID of the target process, and injects shellcode into it.
sentence.2268: Depending on the sample, explorer.exe and winlogon.exe are the target processes.
sentence.2269: The samples we found contain one of three payloads: Crosswalk Metasploit stager FunnySwitch (discussed later in this report) Crosswalk and FunnySwitch shellcode is located in the data sections "as-is," while the samples with Metasploit show additional XOR encryption with the key "jj1".
sentence.2270: 2.2 Local shellcode loaders The main function of the malware is to extract shellcode and run it in an active process.
sentence.2271: The malware samples belong to one of two categories, based on the source of shellcode that they use: in the original executable or in an external file in the same directory.
sentence.2272: Most of the loaders start by checking the current year, much like the samples from the LNK file attacks.
sentence.2274: Code of the loader's main functionAfter the malware finds the API functions it needs, it decrypts the string Global\0EluZTRM3Kye4Hv65IGfoaX9sSP7VA with the ChaCha20 algorithm.
sentence.2275: In one older version, to prevent being run twice the loader creates a mutex with the name Global\5hJ4YfUoyHlwVMnS1qZkd2tEmz7GPbB. But in recent samples, the decrypted string is not used in any way.
sentence.2276: Perhaps part of the code was accidentally deleted during the development process.
sentence.2277: Another artifact found in some samples is the unused string CSPELOADKISSYOU.
sentence.2280: String "CSPELOADKISSYOU" in data sectionIn the self-contained loaders, the shellcode is located in a PE file overlay.
sentence.2281: The shellcode is stored in a curious way: data starts from 0x60 bytes of the header, followed by the (encrypted) shellcode.
sentence.2282: The data length is stored at offset –0x24 from the end of the executable.
sentence.2283: The header always starts with the PL signature.
sentence.2284: The other header data is used for decryption: a 32-byte key is located at offset 0x28 and a 12-byte nonce for the ChaCha20 algorithm is at offset 0x50.
sentence.2286: Handling of PL shellcode in the loader body (ChaCha20)The ChaCha20 implementation is not always present: some of the samples use Microsoft CryptoAPI with AES-128-CBC for encryption.
sentence.2287: We can also find key information here in the structure of the PL shellcode: at offset 0x28, there are 32 bytes that are hashed with MD5 to obtain a cryptographic key.
sentence.2289: Handling of PL shellcode in the loader body (AES-128)Older loader versions use Cryptography API:
sentence.2290: Next Generation (BCrypt* functions) in an equivalent way.
sentence.2291: They use AES-128 in CFB mode as the encryption algorithm.
sentence.2292: The loaders that rely on external files have a similar code structure and one of two encryption types: ChaCha20 or AES-128-CBC.
sentence.2293: The file should contain PL shellcode of the same format as in the self-contained loader.
sentence.2294: The name depends on the specific sample and is encrypted with the algorithm used in it.
sentence.2295: It can contain a full file path (although we did not detect any such samples) or a relative path.
sentence.2297: Building the file name with PL shellcodeAmong all the loaders, we encountered three different shellcode payloads: Crosswalk Metasploit stager Cobalt Strike Beacon 2.3 Attack examples 2.3.1 An encrypted resume This malicious file is a RAR archive, electronic_resume.pdf.rar (025e053e329f7e5e930cc5aa8492a76e6bc61d5769aa614ec66088943bf77596), with two files: Figure 20.

sentence.2380: FunnySwitch Among the files signed with the Zealot Digital certificate, we discovered two samples of malware containing a previously unknown backdoor.
sentence.2381: We have called it FunnySwitch, based on the name of the library and one of the key classes.
sentence.2382: The backdoor is written in .NET and can send system information as well as run arbitrary JScript code, with support for six different connection types, including the ability to accept incoming connections.
sentence.2383: One of its distinguishing features is the ability to act as message relay between different copies of the backdoor and a C2 server.
sentence.2384: 5.1 Unpacking The attack in question starts with the SFX archive x32.exe (2063fae36db936de23eb728bcf3f8a5572f83645786c2a0a5529c71d8447a9af).

sentence.2387: The files n3.exe and p3.exe are identical and inject shellcode into the process explorer.exe.
sentence.2388: The only difference between them is the final bytes of the shellcode they inject, which contain the XML configuration.

sentence.2401: assemblyThe assembly is the library Funny.dll with obfuscation by ConfuserEx. 5.2 Funny.dll The backdoor starts by parsing the configuration.
sentence.2402: Its root element may contain the following fields: Debug is the flag for enabling debug logging Group is an arbitrary string sent together with system information.
sentence.2403: Password is the key used to encrypt messages.
sentence.2404: ID identifies the relay (if not present in the configuration, the GUID is used instead).
sentence.2405: StartTime, EndTime, and WeekDays restrict the times and days when the backdoor may function The <Config> element may contain an arbitrary number of elements describing various types of connectors: TcpConnector and TcpBindConnector are classes responsible for connecting over TCP as client and server.
sentence.2406: They have two parameters in common: address and port (by default, 38001).
sentence.2407: TcpConnector also has the parameter interval, which indicates how long to wait before trying to reconnect.
sentence.2408: HttpConnector and HttpBindConnector are HTTP client with support for proxy and HTTP server.
sentence.2409: Supported client parameters: url – address to connect to, interval – same as at TcpConnector, proxy and cred – proxy server address and credentials.
sentence.2410: Server parameters: url – list of prefixes on which it will run and timeout – client timeout.
sentence.2411: The standard classes HttpWebRequest and HttpListener from .NET
sentence.2412: Framework are used for client and server implementations.
sentence.2413: Both HTTP and HTTPS are supported: if no SSL certificate is configured for the port on which the server is running, it will be launched with CN = Environment.
sentence.2415: The client, in turn, ignores certificate validation.
sentence.2416: RPCConnector and RPCBindConnector are classes that allow setting up a connection via a Named Pipe.
sentence.2417: They take a single parameter, name, which is the name of the connection.
sentence.2418: TcpBindConnector and HttpBindConnector support simultaneous connections for multiple clients.
sentence.2419: For the network connectors to work, the backdoor adds an allow rule to Windows Firewall with the name "Core Networking ― IPv4" for its executable module.
sentence.2421: Code for adding Windows Firewall rulesJust like with Crosswalk, there are multiple levels of the protocol: in this case, transport, network, and application.
sentence.2422: 5.2.1 Transport protocols TCP TCP supports three types of messages: PingMessage (0x1), PongMessage (0x2), and DataMessage (0x3).
sentence.2423: The first two monitor the connection and are relevant only at the TcpConnector/TcpBindConnector level.
sentence.2425: Messages consist of a signature (4 bytes), encrypted header (16 bytes), and optional data.
sentence.2426: The signature is three random bytes followed by their sum with modulo 256.
sentence.2427: Incoming messages with an invalid signature are discarded.
sentence.2428: The header contains the data size (4 bytes) and byte indicating the message type (0x1, 0x2, or 0x3).
sentence.2429: It is encrypted with AES-256-CBC; the key and IV are taken from the MD5 of the key string.
sentence.2430: The backdoor uses this encryption method in other cases as well, which is why we refer to it as "standard" in the text that follows.
sentence.2431: The key string in this case is "tcp_encrypted".
sentence.2433: Standard encryption in FunnySwitch HTTP with long polling There are three types of requests: GET "connect", GET "pull", and POST "push".
sentence.2434: To start transferring data, the client must connect by sending a GET request to a URL from the configuration and provide a special cookie value.
sentence.2435: The cookie name is eight random characters.
sentence.2436: The value is an encrypted Base64 string containing the session GUID and operation name ("connect").
sentence.2437: The string is encrypted in the standard way with the key "http".
sentence.2438: The client then constantly sends GET requests with pull operations.
sentence.2439: In response, the server returns the relevant array of messages for the client or, if no new messages have arrived in the last 10 seconds, an empty response.
sentence.2440: Client–server messages are periodically sent as an array as well, for which a POST request with push operation is used.
sentence.2442: FunnySwitch connect and pull requestsThe special class MsgPack class, which implements a custom serialization protocol, unpacks the array and other primitive types.
sentence.2443: RPC (Pipe) Similar to TCP, except for the absence of connection monitoring.
sentence.2445: Function for processing incoming network-level communicationsAll messages at this level are encrypted in the backdoor's standard way, with the key string "commonkey".
sentence.2446: Messages are an array of three or four elements: Message type ("hello_request", "hello_response", "message", "error") Source serialized array Destination serialized array Payload (application-level data)
sentence.2447: The MsgPack class is also used for serialization.
sentence.2448: The Source and Destination arrays contain the IDs of the relays through which the message has already passed and the IDs of the routers through it should be delivered to the recipient.
sentence.2449: The bodies of hello_request and hello_response messages contain information about the sender's system.
sentence.2450: When one of these messages is received, the relay saves data about the sender ID, used connector instance and system data.
sentence.2451: These message types are used to establish a direct connection between relays.
sentence.2452: Messages of the "message" type (ones that are not hello_request, hello_response, or error) can be passed via several relays.
sentence.2453: If its Destination field contains only the ID of the current instance, it will be handled locally; if not, it will be sent to the next relay in the list.
sentence.2454: For connecting to the next instance, it uses the connector that was saved when exchanging hello_request and hello_response messages.
sentence.2455: The backdoor collects the following system information: Values of the registry keys ProductName and CSDVersion from HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion Whether the OS is 32-bit or 64-bit List of IP addresses Computer name Username and workgroup Name of running module PID MAC addresses of network adapters Value of the Group attribute in the XML configuration 5.2.3 Application-level protocol At the application level, data is encrypted in the standard way using the value of the Password attribute from the configuration.
sentence.2456: If no such value exists, the key string is "test".
sentence.2457: Data is compressed with GZip prior to encryption.
sentence.2458: After decryption and decompression, the payload is an array (packed MsgPack) consisting of one or two elements: a string with the name of a command and optional array of bytes (data for the command).
sentence.2459: These elements, in turn, contain another serialized array, which contains a message string ID (which will be used to send the result of the command) plus the data for the command.
sentence.2460: 5.2.4 Supported commands Command Description invoke Run JScript code and get the result.
sentence.2461: Implementation was separated out into a JSCore .NET assembly, which is dynamically loaded from a Base64 constant defined in the main assembly.
sentence.2464: Eval class from the JSCore assemblyCode execution is accomplished with classes from the Microsoft.
sentence.2468: Eval class connect Takes an XML string with connector configuration and creates the corresponding object.
sentence.2469: update Packs a response containing the IDs of relays connected to the current copy, together with their system information.
sentence.2470: query Collects the configuration of active connector instances other than the RPCConnector and RPCBindConnector classes.
sentence.2472: createStream Creates a message queue with the indicated name.
sentence.2473: The queue connects with the sender of the createStream command.
sentence.2474: closeStream Deletes the named message queue.
sentence.2475: sendStream Adds a message (byte array) to the queue with the specified name.
sentence.2476: The result of execution of each command is returned to the sender via the invoke-response command.
sentence.2477: 5.2.5 Unused code By all appearances, the FunnySwitch backdoor is still under development, as shown by the incomplete state of message queue functionality.
sentence.2478: Besides the commands described here already, the code contains the functions PullStream and SendStream, which are not used anywhere.
sentence.2479: The first extracts a message from the queue (by queue name), while the second sends its creator an arbitrary set of bytes with the stream-data command.
sentence.2480: The code also contains several unused classes: an implementation of the KCP protocol, limited-size queue SizeQueue, and string serializer StreamString. Figure 46.
sentence.2481: Fragment of KCP class code5.2.6 FunnySwitch vs. Crosswalk Based on investigation of the two backdoors, we believe that they were written by the same developers.
sentence.2482: Several things point at common authorship: Use of multiple transport protocols Support for specifying a proxy server Identical configuration restrictions on time of day and days of the week Implementation of the KCP protocol Implemented (and disabled by default) logging of debug messages and errors Figure 47.
sentence.2485: ShadowPad During the investigation we also discovered two samples containing ShadowPad malware.
sentence.2486: The first of these is the SFX archive 20200926___Request for wedding reception.exe (03b7b511716c074e9f6ef37318638337fd7449897be999505d4a3219572829b4).

sentence.2490: Bait file wedding.docxThe archive contents are unpacked to the folder c:\programdata, from where (besides the bait file being opened) the payload log.exe is launched.
sentence.2491: Both the executable file and the DLL library are obfuscated with VMProtect, but we also found identical unprotected versions (as shown in the following screenshots).
sentence.2492: An unpacked legitimate component of Bitdefender (386eb7aa33c76ce671d6685f79512597f1fab28ea46c8ec7d89e58340081e2bd) serves as log.exe.
sentence.2493: It dynamically loads the library log.dll.
sentence.2495: Loading log.dll in log.exeThe library, in turn, when loaded checks for whether the current module contains a certain set of bytes at offset 0x2775.
sentence.2496: If the loading module meets its expectations, these bytes change to a call instruction for a DLL function.
sentence.2497: As a result, in log.exe right after log.dll loads, a call is made to the function sub_100010D0.
sentence.2498: The called function is not explicitly exported.
sentence.2500: Check and modification of executable module in log.dllA similar technique has been previously described by ESET in the context of Winnti attacks on universities in Hong Kong.
sentence.2501: ShadowPad malware was used as the payload in these attacks.
sentence.2502: In our case, the code run afterwards had been obfuscated with a new approach: all functions are split into separate instructions that shuffle between each other.
sentence.2503: Jumps between instructions occur by means of calls to a special function (rel_jmp), which emulates the jmp command.
sentence.2504: The offset at which the jump occurs is written immediately after a call instruction (see the following figure).
sentence.2506: Structure of obfuscated codeIn addition, to obfuscate the control flow in the code, conditional jumps that never run are included as well: cmp esp, 3181h jb loc_1000BCA9 The obfuscated code is the loader for the subsequent shellcode, which is encrypted in the file log.dll.dat.
sentence.2507: After decryption, the file is deleted and the shellcode is re-encrypted, saved in the registry, and run.
sentence.2508: When log.exe is launched subsequently, the shellcode will be loaded from the registry.
sentence.2509: The data is stored in a hive with a name resembling the following: (HKLM|HKCU)\Software\Classes\CLSID\{%8.8x-%4.4x-%4.4x-%8.8x%8.8x}, in key %8.8X.
sentence.2510: The values inserted in the formatting strings are generated based on the TimeDateStamp in the PE header of log.dll, and therefore are always identical for any given library copy.
sentence.2511: In our case, they equal {56a36bd2-5e2b-20b0-96f2cb9bb3f43475} and EB5D1182, respectively.
sentence.2512: The payload is ShadowPad shellcode that has been obfuscated with the same rel_jmp and fake-jb techniques.
sentence.2513: The following strings are contained in its encrypted configuration: 6/30/2020 1:25:52 PM ccc %ProgramData%\ msdn.exe log.dll log.dll.dat WMNetworkSvc WMNetworkSvc WMNetworkSvc SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
sentence.2515: UDP://cigy2jft92.kasprsky.info:53 SOCKS4 SOCKS4 SOCKS5 SOCKS5 They include the likely data of module assembly (June 6, 2020), name of the service used by the malware to gain persistence on the system (WMNetworkSvc), names of processes into which shellcode can be injected, and the C2 domain cigy2jft92.kasprsky[.]info.
sentence.2516: As we wrote earlier, the other domain kasprsky[.]info has been used by attackers as a FunnySwitch C2 server.
sentence.2517: Investigation of subdomains and IP addresses yields another second-level domain, livehost[.]live, whose subdomain d89o0gm35t.livehost[.]live is indicated as a C2 server in one copy of Crosswalk (86100e3efa14a6805a33b2ed24234ac73e094c84cf4282426192607fb8810961).

sentence.2541: A similar technique has been used by Winnti in the past: according to Trend Micro, an encoded C2 address was stored in GitHub repositories in 2017.
sentence.2542: 7.1 Paranoid PlugX We were able to detect an additional copy of PlugX that contained shellcode fully identical to that downloaded from Google Docs, except for the encrypted configuration.
sentence.2543: It, too, is an SFX archive (94ea23e7f53cb9111dd61fe1a1cbb79b8bbabd2d37ed6bfa67ba2a437cfd5e92) but with different files inside.
sentence.2545: Contents of the SFX archiveWhen unpacked, the archive runs the script 1.vbs, which in turn passes control to a.bat. Figure 60.
sentence.2546: Contents of a.batThe main payload is in the file image.jpg, which is actually a specially crafted .NET assembly.
sentence.2547: The assembly launches with the help of InstallUtil.exe from .NET Framework, enabling it to bypass application allowlist restrictions.
sentence.2549: Running shellcode in image.jpgThe purpose of image.jpg is to run the same PlugX shellcode with the help of CreateThread.
sentence.2550: Its configuration contains two C2 servers: update.upgradsource[.]com and ns.upgradsource[.]com.
sentence.2551: The domain upgradsource[.]com is mentioned in a Unit42 report on a group of similar samples named "Paranoid PlugX." They received this name due to the presence of a script for wiping traces of malware from the system.
sentence.2552: Comparing the sample we found to those described in that report, we conclude with strong confidence that it belongs to the same group.
sentence.2553: Among other reasons, the structure of the .NET Wrapper module in image.jpg, and much of the cleanup script a.bat, is nearly identical.
sentence.2554: According to Unit42, the main targets of Paranoid PlugX attacks were gaming companies—which are known to be a typical area of interest for Winnti.
sentence.2555: Investigation of the network infrastructure provides yet another piece of confirmation of the relationship between Paranoid PlugX and Winnti.
sentence.2556: As of late 2017, update.upgradsource[.]com resolved to the IP address 121.170.185[.]183.
sentence.2557: Later, update.byeserver[.]com and update.serverbye[.]com resolved to this address as well.
sentence.2558: The second-level domains byeserver[.]com and serverbye[.]com, in turn, are listed by FireEye in its report on APT41. 8.
sentence.2559: Conclusion Winnti has an extensive arsenal of malware, as can be seen from the group's attacks.
sentence.2560: Winnti uses both widely available tools (Metasploit, Cobalt Strike, PlugX) and custom-developed ones, which are constantly increasing in number.
sentence.2561: By May 2020, the group had started to use its new backdoor, FunnySwitch, which possess unusual message relay functionality.
sentence.2562: One distinguishing trait of the group's backdoors is support for multiple transport protocols for connecting to C2 servers, which complicates efforts to detect malicious traffic.
sentence.2563: Malicious files of varying resemblance are used to install the payload, from primitive RAR and SFX-RAR files to reuse of malware from other groups and multistage threats with vulnerability exploits and non-trivial shellcode loaders.
sentence.2564: But the payload may be one and the same in all these cases.
sentence.2565: Most likely, the choice is dictated by the precision (or lack thereof) of an attack: unique infection chains and highly attractive bait are held back for targeted attacks.
sentence.2566: Winnti continues to pursue game developers and publishers in Russia and elsewhere.
sentence.2567: Small studios tend to neglect information security, making them a tempting target.
sentence.2568: Attacks on software developers are especially dangerous for the risk they pose to end users, as already happened in the well-known cases of CCleaner and ASUS.
sentence.2569: By ensuring timely detection and investigation of breaches, companies can avoid becoming victims of such a scenario.

sentence.2598: title: Operation ‘Harvest’: A Deep Dive into a Long-term Campaign url: https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/enterprise/mcafee-enterprise-atr/operation-harvest-a-deep-dive-into-a-long-term-campaign/ A special thanks to our Professional Services’ IR team, ShadowServer, for historical context on C2 domains, and Thomas Roccia/Leandro Velasco for malware analysis support.
sentence.2599: Executive Summary Following a recent Incident Response, McAfee Enterprise‘s Advanced Threat Research (ATR) team worked with its Professional Services IR team to support a case that initially started as a malware incident but ultimately turned out to be a long-term cyber-attack.
sentence.2600: From a cyber-intelligence perspective, one of the biggest challenges is having information on the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) an adversary is using and then keeping them up to date.
sentence.2601: Within ATR we typically monitor many adversaries for years and collect and store data, ranging from indicators of compromise (IOCs) to the TTPs.
sentence.2602: In this report, ATR provides a deep insight into this long-term campaign where we will map out our findings against the Enterprise MITRE ATT&CK model.
sentence.2603: There will be parts that are censored since we respect the confidentiality of the victim.
sentence.2604: We will also zoom in and look at how the translation to the MITRE Techniques, historical context, and evidence artifacts like PlugX and Winnti malware led to a link with another campaign, which we highly trust to be executed by the same adversary.
sentence.2605: IOCs that could be shared are at the end of this document.
sentence.2606: McAfee customers are protected from the malware/tools described in this blog.
sentence.2607: MVISION Insights customers will have the full details, IOCs and TTPs shared via their dashboard.
sentence.2608: MVISION Endpoint, EDR and UCE platforms provide signature and behavior-based prevention and detection capability for many of the techniques used in this attack.
sentence.2609: A more detailed blog with specific recommendations on using the McAfee portfolio and integrated partner solutions to defend against this attack can be found here.
sentence.2610: Technical Analysis Initial Infection Vectors [TA0001] Forensic investigations identified that the actor established initial access by compromising the victim’s web server [T1190].
sentence.2611: On the webserver, software was installed to maintain the presence and storage of tools [T1105] that would be used to gather information about the victim’s network [T1083] and lateral movement/execution of files [T1570] [T1569.002].
sentence.2612: Examples of the tools discovered are PSexec, Procdump, and Mimikatz.
sentence.2614: The adversary has been observed using multiple privilege escalation and persistence techniques during the period of investigation and presence in the network.
sentence.2615: We will highlight a few in each category.
sentence.2616: Besides the use of Mimikatz to dump credentials, the adversaries used two tools for privilege escalations [T1068].
sentence.2618: This is an open-source tool that is used to get a handle to a privileged token, for example, “NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM”, to be able to execute tasks with System rights.
sentence.2619: Example of RottenPotato on elevating these rights: Figure 1 RottenPotato The second tool discovered, “BadPotato”, is another open-source tool that can be used to elevate user rights towards System rights.
sentence.2621: The BadPotato code can be found on GitHub where it is offered as a Visual Studio project.
sentence.2622: We inspected the adversary’s compiled version using DotPeek and hunted for artifacts in the code.
sentence.2623: Inspecting the File (COFF) header, we observed the file’s compilation timestamp:
sentence.2624: TimeDateStamp: 05/12/2020 08:23:47 – Date and time the image was created PlugX Another major and characteristic privilege escalation technique the adversary used in this long-term campaign was the malware PlugX as a backdoor.
sentence.2625: PlugX makes use of the technique “DLL Sideloading” [T1574.002].
sentence.2626: PlugX was observed as usual where a single (RAR) executable contained the three parts: Valid executable.
sentence.2627: Associated DLL with the hook towards the payload.
sentence.2628: Payload file with the config to communicate with Command & Control Server (C2).
sentence.2629: The adversary used either the standalone version or distributed three files on different assets in the network to gain remote control of those assets.
sentence.2630: The samples discovered and analyzed were communicating towards two domains.
sentence.2631: Both domains were registered during the time of the campaign.
sentence.2632: One of the PlugX samples consisted of the following three parts: Filename Hashes HPCustPartic.exe SHA256: 8857232077b4b0f0e4a2c3bb5717fd65079209784f41694f8e1b469e34754cf6 HPCustPartUI.dll SHA256: 0ee5b19ea38bb52d8ba4c7f05fa1ddf95a4f9c2c93b05aa887c5854653248560 HPCustPartic.bin SHA256:
sentence.2633: 008f7b98c2453507c45dacd4a7a7c1b372b5fafc9945db214c622c8d21d29775 The .exe file is a valid and signed executable and, in this case, an executable from HP (HP Customer participation).
sentence.2634: We also observed other valid executables being used, ranging from AV vendors to video software.
sentence.2635: When the executable is run, the DLL next to it is loaded.
sentence.2636: The DLL is valid but contains a small hook towards the payload which, in our case, is the .bin file.
sentence.2637: The DLL loads the PlugX config and injects it into a process.
sentence.2638: We executed the samples in a test setup and dumped the memory of the machine to conduct memory analysis with volatility.
sentence.2639: After the basic forensically sound steps, we ran the malfind plugin to detect possible injected code in a process.
sentence.2640: From the redacted output of the plugin, we observed the following values for the process with possible injected code: Process: svchost.exe Pid: 860 Address: 0xb50000 Process: explorer.exe Pid: 2752 Address: 0x56a000 Process: svchost.exe Pid: 1176
sentence.2641: Address: 0x80000 Process: svchost.exe Pid: 1176 Address: 0x190000 Process: rundll32.exe
sentence.2643: Pid: 3784 Address: 0x220000 One observation is the mention of the SVCHOST process with a ProcessID value of 1176 that is mentioned twice but with different addresses.
sentence.2644: This is similar to the RUNDLL32.exe that is mentioned twice with PID 3785 and different addresses.
sentence.2645: One way to identify what malware may have been used is to dump these processes with the relevant PID using the procdump module, upload them to an online analysis service and wait for the results.
sentence.2646: Since this is a very sensitive case, we took a different approach.
sentence.2647: Using the best of both worlds (volatility and Yara) we used a ruleset that consists of malware patterns observed in memory over time.
sentence.2648: Running this ruleset over the data in the memory dump revealed the following (redacted for the sake of readability) output: Figure 3 Output Yarascan memory dump
sentence.2649: The output of the Yara rule scan (and there was way more output) confirmed the presence of PlugX module code in PID 1176 of the SVCHOST service.
sentence.2650: Also, the rule was triggered on PID 3784, which belonged to RUNDLL32.exe.
sentence.2651: Investigating the dumps after dynamic analysis, we observed two domain names used for C2 traffic: sery.brushupdata.com dnssery.brushupdata.com In particular, we saw the following hardcoded value that might be another payload being downloaded: sery.brushupdata.com/CE1BC21B4340FEC2B8663B69
sentence.2652: The PlugX families we observed used DNS [T1071.001]
sentence.2653: [T1071.004] as the transport channel for C2 traffic, in particular TXT queries.
sentence.2654: Investigating the traffic from our samples, we observed the check-in-signature (“20 2A 2F 2A 0D”) that is typical for PlugX network traffic: 00000000: 47 45 54 20 2F 42 34 42 42 44 43 43 30 32 39 45 00000010:
sentence.2655: 31 31 39 37 31 39 46 30 36 35 36 32 32 20 48 54 00000020: 54 50 2F 31 2E 31 0D 0A 41 63 63 65 70 74 3A 20 00000030: 2A 2F 2A 0D 0A 43 6F 6F 6B 69 65 3A 20 44 36 43 00000040: 57 50 2B 56 5A 47 6D 59 6B 6D 64 6D 64 64 58 55 00000050: 71 58 4D 31 71 31 6A 41 3D 0D 0A 55 73 65 72 2D During our analysis of the different PlugX samples discovered, the domain names as mentioned above stayed the same, though the payload values were different.
sentence.2656: For example: hxxp://sery.brushupdata.com/B4BBDCC029E119719F065622 hxxp://sery.brushupdata.com/07FDB1B97D22EE6AF2482B1B hxxp://sery.brushupdata.com/273CDC0B9C6218BC1187556D Other PlugX samples we observed injected themselves into Windows Media Player and started a connection with the following two domains: center.asmlbigip.com sec.asmlbigip.com
sentence.2657: Hello Winnti Another mechanism observed was to start a program as a service
sentence.2658: [T1543.003] on the Operating System with the acquired System rights by using the *Potato tools.
sentence.2659: The file the adversary was using seemed to be a backdoor that was using the DLL file format (2458562ca2f6fabddae8385cb817c172).
sentence.2660: The DLL is used to create a malicious service and its name is “service.dll”.
sentence.2661: The name of the created service, “SysmainUpdate”, is usurping the name of the legitimate service “SysMain” which is related to the legitimate DLL sysmain.dll and also to the Superfetch service.
sentence.2662: The dll is run using the command “rundll32.exe SuperFrtch.dll, #1”.
sentence.2663: The export function has the name “WwanSvcMain”.
sentence.2664: The model uses the persistence technique utilizing svchost.exe with service.dll to install a rogue service.
sentence.2665: It appears that the dll employs several mechanisms to fingerprint the targeted system and avoid analysis in the sandbox, making analysis more difficult.
sentence.2666: The DLL embeds several obfuscated strings decoded when running.
sentence.2667: Once the fingerprinting has been done, the malware will install the malicious service using the API RegisterServiceHandlerA then SetServiceStatus, and finally CreateEventA.
sentence.2668: A description of the technique can be found here.
sentence.2669: The malware also decrypts and injects the payload in memory.
sentence.2670: The following screenshot shows the decryption routine.
sentence.2671: Figure 4 Decryption routine When we analyzed this unique routine, we discovered similarities and the mention of it in a publication that can be read here.
sentence.2672: The malware described in the article is attributed to the Winnti malware family.
sentence.2673: The operating method and the code used in the DLL described in the article are very similar to our analysis and observations.
sentence.2674: The process dump also revealed further indicators.
sentence.2675: Firstly, it revealed artifacts related to the DLL analyzed, “C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\SuperfRtch\SuperfRtch.dat”.
sentence.2676: We believe that this dat file might be the loaded payload.
sentence.2677: Secondly, while investigating the process dump, we observed activities from the backdoor that are part of the data exfiltration attempts which we will describe in more detail in this analysis report.
sentence.2678: A redacted snippet of the code would look like this: Creating archive ***.rar Adding
sentence.2679: [data from location] 0% OK Another indicator of discovering Winnti malware was the following execution path we discovered in the command line dump of the memory:
sentence.2681: klcsngtgui.exe 1560413F7E <abbreviation-victim>.dat What we observed here was the use of a valid executable, the AES 256 decryption key of the payload (.dat file).
sentence.2682: In this case, the payload file was named using an abbreviation of the victim company’s name.
sentence.2683: Unfortunately, the adversary had removed the payload file from the system.
sentence.2684: File carving did not work since the disk/unallocated space was overwritten.
sentence.2685: However, reconstructing traces from memory revealed that we were dealing with the Winnti 4.0 malware.
sentence.2686: The malware was injected into a SVCHOST process where a driver location pointed to the config file.
sentence.2687: We observed in the process dump the exfiltration of data on the system, such as OS, Processor (architecture), Domain, Username, etc.
sentence.2688: Another clue that helped us was the use of DNS tunneling by Winnti which we discovered traces of in memory.
sentence.2689: The hardcoded 208.67.222.222 resolves to a legitimate OpenDNS DNS server.
sentence.2690: The IP is pushed into the list generated by the malware at runtime.
sentence.2691: At the start of the malware, it populates the list with the system’s DNS, and the OpenDNS server is only used as a backup to ensure that the C2 domain is resolved.
sentence.2692: Another indicator in the process dump was the setup of the C2 connection including the User-Agent that has been observed being used by Winnti 4.0 malware:
sentence.2693: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; WOW64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko)
sentence.2694: Chrome/57.0.2987.133 Safari/537.36 Other Persistence Activities WMI activity [T1546.003] was also observed to execute commands on the systems.
sentence.2695: From a persistence point of view, scheduled tasks [T1053.005] and the use of valid accounts [T1078] acquired through the use of Mimikatz, or creating LSASS dumps, were observed being employed during the length of the campaign.
sentence.2696: Lateral Movement From a lateral movement perspective, the adversary used the obtained credentials to hop from asset to asset.
sentence.2697: In one particular case, we observed a familiar filename: “PsExec.exe”.
sentence.2698: This SysInternals tool is often observed being used in lateral movement by adversaries, however, it can also be used by the sysadmins of the network.
sentence.2699: In our case, the PsExec executable had a file size of 9.6 MB where the original PsExec (depending on 32- or 64-bit version) had a maximum file size of 1.3 MB.
sentence.2700: An initial static inspection of the file resulted in a blob of code that was present in the executable which had a very high entropy score (7.99).
sentence.2701: When running the file from the command line, the following output was observed: Figure 5 PsExec output The error notification and the ‘Impacket’ keyword tipped us off and, after digging around, we found more.
sentence.2702: The fake PsExec is an open-source Python script that is a PsExec alternative with shell/backdoor capability.
sentence.2703: It uses a script from this location: hxxps://github.com/SecureAuthCorp/impacket/blob/master/examples/psexec.pyi.
sentence.2704: The file is large since it incorporates a low-level protocol interaction from Impacket.
sentence.2705: The Python library combined with the script code is compiled with py2exe.
sentence.2706: The file was compiled during the time of the latest attack activities and signed with an expired certificate.
sentence.2707: Data Exfiltration From what we observed
sentence.2708: , the adversary had a long-term intention to stay present in the victim’s network.
sentence.2709: With high confidence, we believe that the adversary was interested in stealing proprietary intelligence that could be used for military or intellectual property/manufacturing purposes.
sentence.2710: The adversary used several techniques to exfiltrate the data.
sentence.2711: In some cases, batch (.bat) scripts were created to gather information from certain network shares/folders and use the ‘rar’ tool to compress them to a certain size [T1020]
sentence.2713: Example of content in a batch script: C:\Windows\web\rar.exe a -[redacted] -r -v50000
sentence.2714: [Target-directory] On other occasions, manual variants of the above command were discovered after using the custom backdoor as described earlier.
sentence.2715: When the data was gathered on a local system using the backdoor, the files were exfiltrated over the backdoor and the rar files were deleted [T1070.004].
sentence.2716: Where external facing assets were used, like a web server, the data was stored in a location in the Internet Information Services (IIS) web server and exfiltrated over HTTP using GET requests towards the exact file paths [T1041] [T1567] [T1071].
sentence.2717: An example of the [redacted] web traffic in the IIS logfiles: Date /Time Request TCP Src port Source IP User-Agent Redacted GET /****/[redacted].rar 80 180.50.
sentence.2719: *.* MINIXL The source IP addresses discovered belonged to two different ISP/VPN providers based in Hong-Kong.
sentence.2720: The User-Agent value is an interesting one, “MINIXL”.
sentence.2721: When we researched that value, we discovered a blog from Dell SecureWorks from 2015 that mentions the same User-Agent, but also a lot of the artifacts mentioned from the blog overlapped with the observations and TTPs of Operation Harvest [link].
sentence.2722: What we could retrieve from open-source databases is that the use of this particular User-Agent is very limited and seems to originate from the APAC region.
sentence.2724: That seems to be the one-million-dollar question to be asked.
sentence.2725: Within McAfee, attribution is not our main focus, protecting our customers is our priority.
sentence.2726: What we do care about is that if we learn about these techniques during an investigation, can we map them out and support our IR team on the ground, or a customer’s IR team, with the knowledge that can help determine which phase of the attack the evidence is pointing to and based on historical data and intelligence, assist in blocking the next phase and discover more evidence?
sentence.2727: We started by mapping out all MITRE ATT&CK Enterprise techniques and sub-techniques, added the tools used, and did a comparison against historical technique data from the industry.
sentence.2728: We ended up with four groups that shared techniques and sub-techniques.
sentence.2729: The Winnti group was added by us since we discovered the unique encryption function in the custom backdoor and indicators of the use of the Winnti malware.
sentence.2730: Figure 6 ATT&CK technique comparison The diagram reflecting our outcome insinuated that APT27 and APT41 are the most likely candidates that overlap with the (sub-)techniques we observed.
sentence.2731: Since all these groups are in a certain time zone, we extracted all timestamps from the forensic investigation with regards to: Registration of domain Compile timestamps of malware (considering deception) Timestamps of command-line activity Timestamps of data exfiltration Timestamps of malware interaction such as creation, deletion, etc.
sentence.2732: When we converted all these timestamps from UTC to the aforementioned groups’ time zones, we ended up with the below scheme on activity: Figure 7 Adversary’s time of operation In this campaign, we observed how the adversary mostly seems to work from Monday to Thursday and typically during office hours, albeit with the occasional exception.
sentence.2733: Correlating ATT&CK (sub-)techniques, timestamps, and tools like PlugX and Mimikatz are not the only evidence indicators that can help to identify a possible adversary.
sentence.2734: Command-line syntax, specific code similarity, actor capability over time versus other groups, and unique identifiers are at the top of the ‘pyramid of pain’ in threat intelligence.
sentence.2735: The bottom part of the pyramid is about hashes, URLs, and domains, areas that are very volatile and easy to change by an adversary.
sentence.2736: Figure 8 Pyramid of Pain Beyond investigating those artifacts, we also took possible geopolitical interests and potential deception into consideration when building our hypothesis.
sentence.2737: When we mapped out all of these, we believed that one of the two previously mentioned groups were responsible for the campaign we investigated.
sentence.2738: Our focus was not about attribution though, but more around where the flow of the attack is, matches against previous attack flows from groups, and what techniques/tools they are using to block next steps, or where to locate them.
sentence.2739: The more details we can gather at the top of ‘the pyramid of pain’, the better we can determine the likely adversary and its TTP’s.
sentence.2742: While correlating the observed (sub-)techniques, the malware families and code, we discovered another targeted attack against a similar target in the same nation with the major motivation of gathering intelligence.
sentence.2743: In the following diagram we conducted a high-level comparison of the tools being used by the adversary: Figure 9 Tools comparison Although some of the tools are unique to each campaign, if taken into consideration over time with when they were used, it makes sense.
sentence.2744: It demonstrates the development of the actor and use of newer tools to conduct lateral movement and to obtain the required level of user rights on systems.
sentence.2745: Overall, we observed the same modus operandi.
sentence.2746: Once an initial foothold was established, the adversary would deploy PlugX initially to create a few backdoors in the victim’s network in case they were discovered early on.
sentence.2747: After that, using Mimikatz and dumping lsass, they were looking to get valid accounts.
sentence.2748: Once valid accounts were acquired, several tools including some of their own tools were used to gain information about the victim’s network.
sentence.2749: From there, several shares/servers were accessed, and information gathered.
sentence.2750: That information was exfiltrated as rar files and placed on an internet-facing server to hide in the ‘normal’ traffic.
sentence.2751: We represent that in the following graphic: Figure 10 Attack flow In the 2019/2020 case we also observed the use of a malware sample that we would classify as part of the Winnti malware family.
sentence.2752: We discovered a couple of files that were executed by the following command: Start Ins64.exe E370AA8DA0 Jumper64.dat
sentence.2753: The Winnti loader ‘Ins64.exe’ uses the value ‘E370AA8DA0’ to decrypt the payload from the .dat file using the AES-256-CTR decryption algorithm and starts to execute.
sentence.2754: After executing this command and analyzing the memory, we observed a process injection in one of the svchost processes whereby one particular file was loaded from the following path: C:\programdata\microsoft\windows\caches\ieupdate.dll Figure 11
sentence.2755: Memory capture The malware started to open up both UDP and TCP ports to connect with a C2 server.
sentence.2756: UDP Port 20502 TCP Port 20501 Figure 12 Network connections to C2 Capturing the traffic from the malware we observed the following as an example: Figure 13 Winnti HTTP traffic to C2 The packet data was customized and sent through a POST request with several headers towards the C2.
sentence.2757: In the above screenshot the numbers after “POST /” were randomly generated.
sentence.2758: The User-Agent is a good network indicator to identify the Winnti malware since it is used in multiple variants: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; WOW64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/50.0.2661.94 Safari/537.36 Indeed, the same User Agent value was discovered in the Winnti sample in Operation Harvest and seems to be typical for this malware family.
sentence.2759: The cookie value consists of four Dword hex values that contain information about the customized packet size using a XOR value.
sentence.2760: We learned more about the packet structure of Winnti from this link.
sentence.2761: Applying what we learned about the handshake, we observed the following in our traffic sample: Dword value 0
sentence.2762: = 52 54 00 36 Dword value 1 = 3e ff 06 b2 Dword value 2 = 99 6d 78 fe Dword value 3 = 08 00
sentence.2763: 45 00 Dword value 4 = 00 34 00 47 Initial handshake order: Based on our cross-correlation with samples and other OSINT resources, we believe with a high confidence that this was a Winnti 4.0 sample that connects with a confirmed Winnti C2 server.
sentence.2764: The identified C2 server was 185.161.211.97 TCP/80.
sentence.2765: Timeline of Events When analyzing the timestamps from this investigation, like we did for operation Harvest, we came to the below overview: Figure 14 Beijing working hours case 2019/2020 Again, we observed that the adversary was operating Monday to Friday during office hours in the Beijing time-zone.
sentence.2766: Conclusion Operation Harvest has been a long-term operation whereby an adversary maintained access for multiple years to exfiltrate data.
sentence.2767: The exfiltrated data would have either been part of an intellectual property theft for economic purposes and/or would have provided insights that would be beneficial in case of military interventions.
sentence.2768: The adversaries made use of techniques very often observed in this kind of attack but also used distinctive new backdoors or variants of existing malware families.
sentence.2769: Combining all forensic artifacts and cross-correlation with historical and geopolitical data, we have high confidence that this operation was executed by an experienced APT actor.
sentence.2770: After mapping out all data, TTP’s etc., we discovered a very strong overlap with a campaign observed in 2019/2020.
sentence.2771: A lot of the (in-depth) technical indicators and techniques match.
sentence.2772: Also putting it into perspective, and over time, it demonstrates the adversary is adapting skills and evolving the tools and techniques being used.
sentence.2773: On a separate note, we observed the use of the Winnti malware.
sentence.2774: We deliberately mention the term ‘malware’ instead of group.
sentence.2775: The Winnti malware is known to be used by several actors.
sentence.2776: Within every nation-state cyber-offensive activity, there will be a department/unit responsible for the creation of the tools/malware, etc.
sentence.2777: We strongly believe that is exactly what we observe here as well.
sentence.2778: PlugX, Winnti and some other custom tools all point to a group that had access to the same tools.
sentence.2779: Whether we put name ‘X’ or ‘Y’ on the adversary, we strongly believe that we are dealing with a Chinese actor whose long-term objectives are persistence in their victims’ networks and the acquisition of the intelligence needed to make political/strategic or manufacturing decisions.
