sentence.3988: title: Nation-state threat actor Mint Sandstorm refines tradecraft to attack high-value targets url: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/04/18/nation-state-threat-actor-mint-sandstorm-refines-tradecraft-to-attack-high-value-targets/ Over the past several months, Microsoft has observed a mature subgroup of Mint Sandstorm, an Iranian nation-state actor previously tracked as PHOSPHORUS, refining its tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
sentence.3989: Specifically, this subset has rapidly weaponized N-day vulnerabilities in common enterprise applications and conducted highly-targeted phishing campaigns to quickly and successfully access environments of interest.
sentence.3990: This Mint Sandstorm subgroup has also continued to develop and use custom tooling in selected targets, notably organizations in the energy and transportation sectors.
sentence.3991: Given this subgroup’s capabilities, the profile of past targets, and the potential for cascading effects, Microsoft is publishing details on known tradecraft alongside corresponding detections and mitigations to help organizations protect against this and similar threats.
sentence.3992: Who is Mint Sandstorm? Mint Sandstorm is Microsoft’s new name for PHOSPHORUS, an Iranian nation-state actor.
sentence.3993: This new name is part of the new threat actor naming taxonomy we announced today, designed to keep pace with the evolving and growing threat landscape.
sentence.3994: Mint Sandstorm is known to pursue targets in both the private and public sectors, including political dissidents, activist leaders, the Defense Industrial Base (DIB), journalists, and employees from multiple government agencies, including individuals protesting oppressive regimes in the Middle East.
sentence.3995: Activity Microsoft tracks as part of the larger Mint Sandstorm group overlaps with public reporting on groups known as APT35, APT42, Charming Kitten, and TA453.
sentence.3996: Mint Sandstorm is a composite name used to describe several subgroups of activity with ties to the same organizational structure.
sentence.3997: Microsoft assesses that Mint Sandstorm is associated with an intelligence arm of Iran’s military, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), an assessment that has been corroborated by multiple credible sources including Mandiant, Proofpoint, and SecureWorks.
sentence.3998: In 2022, the US Department of Treasury sanctioned elements of Mint Sandstorm for past cyberattacks citing sponsorship from the IRGC.
sentence.3999: Today, Microsoft is reporting on a distinct Mint Sandstorm subgroup that specializes in hacking into and stealing sensitive information from high-value targets.
sentence.4000: This Mint Sandstorm subgroup is technically and operationally mature, capable of developing bespoke tooling and quickly weaponizing N-day vulnerabilities, and has demonstrated agility in its operational focus, which appears to align with Iran’s national priorities.
sentence.4001: Microsoft Threat Intelligence consistently tracks threat actor activity, including Mint Sandstorm and its subgroups, and works across Microsoft Security products and services to build detections into our products that improve protection for customers.
sentence.4002: As with any observed nation state actor activity, Microsoft directly notifies customers that have been targeted or compromised, providing them with the information they need to secure their accounts.
sentence.4003: Microsoft is sharing details on these operations to raise awareness on the risks associated with their activity and to empower organizations to harden their attack surfaces against tradecraft commonly used by this Mint Sandstorm subgroup.
sentence.4004: Recent operations From late 2021 to mid-2022, this Mint Sandstorm subgroup moved from reconnaissance to direct targeting of US critical infrastructure including seaports, energy companies, transit systems, and a major US utility and gas entity potentially in support of retaliatory destructive cyberattacks.
sentence.4005: This targeting was likely in response to Iran’s attribution of cyberattacks that halted maritime traffic at a major Iranian seaport in May 2020, delayed Iranian trains in July 2021, and crashed gas station payment systems throughout Iran in late 2021.
sentence.4006: Of note, a senior cybersecurity-focused IRGC official and others close to the Iranian Supreme Leader pinned the attack affecting gas station payment systems on Israel and the United States.
sentence.4007: This targeting also coincided with a broader increase in the pace and the scope of cyberattacks attributed to Iranian threat actors, including another Mint Sandstorm subgroup, that Microsoft observed beginning in September 2021.
sentence.4008: The increased aggression of Iranian threat actors appeared to correlate with other moves by the Iranian regime under a new national security apparatus, suggesting such groups are less bounded in their operations.
sentence.4009: Given the hardline consensus among policymakers in Tehran and sanctions previously levied on Iran’s security organizations, Mint Sandstorm subgroups may be less constrained in carrying out malicious cyber activity.
sentence.4010: Mint Sandstorm tradecraft Microsoft has observed multiple attack chains and various tools in compromises involving this Mint Sandstorm subgroup.
sentence.4011: The TTPs detailed below area sampling of new or otherwise notable tradecraft used by this actor.
sentence.4012: Rapid adoption of publicly disclosed POCs for initial access and persistence Microsoft has increasingly observed this Mint Sandstorm subgroup adopting publicly disclosed proof-of-concept (POC) code shortly after it is released to exploit vulnerabilities in internet-facing applications.
sentence.4013: Until 2023, this subgroup had been slow to adopt exploits for recently-disclosed vulnerabilities with publicly reported POCs, often taking several weeks to successfully weaponize exploits for vulnerabilities like Proxyshell and Log4Shell.
sentence.4014: However, beginning in early 2023, Microsoft observed a notable decrease in the time required for this subgroup to adopt and incorporate public POCs.
sentence.4015: For example, Mint Sandstorm began exploiting CVE-2022-47966 in Zoho ManageEngine on January 19, 2023, the same day the POC became public.
sentence.4016: They later exploited CVE-2022-47986 in Aspera Faspex within five days of the POC being made public on February 2, 2023.
sentence.4017: While this subgroup has demonstrated their ability to rapidly incorporate new public POCs into their playbooks, Microsoft has also observed that Mint Sandstorm continues to use older vulnerabilities, especially Log4Shell, to compromise unpatched devices.
sentence.4018: As this activity is typically opportunistic and indiscriminate, Microsoft recommends that organizations regularly patch vulnerabilities with publicly available POCs, regardless of how long the POC has been available.
sentence.4019: After gaining initial access to an organization by exploiting a vulnerability with a public POC, this Mint Sandstorm subgroup deploys a custom PowerShell script designed for discovery.
sentence.4020: In some cases, the subgroup does not act on the information they collect, possibly because they assess that a victim does not meet any targeting requirements or because the subgroup wishes to wait and focus on more valuable targets.
sentence.4021: In cases where Mint Sandstorm operators continue their pursuit of a given target, Microsoft typically observes one of two possible attack chains.
sentence.4023: The two attack chains used by the Mint Sandstorm subgroup Attack chain 1: The Mint Sandstorm subgroup proceeds using Impacket to move laterally through a compromised organization and relies extensively on PowerShell scripts (rather than custom implants) to enumerate admin accounts and enable RDP connections.
sentence.4024: In this attack chain, the subgroup uses an SSH tunnel for command and control (C2), and the final objective in many cases is theft of the Active Directory database.
sentence.4025: If obtained, the Mint Sandstorm subgroup can use the Active Directory database to access credentials for users’ accounts.
sentence.4026: In cases where users’ credentials are accessed and the target organization has not reset corresponding passwords, the actors can log in with stolen credentials and masquerade as legitimate users, possibly without attracting attention from defenders.
sentence.4027: The actors could also gain access to other systems where individuals may have reused their passwords.
sentence.4028: Attack chain 2: As is the case in attack chain 1, the Mint Sandstorm subgroup uses Impacket to move laterally.
sentence.4029: However, in this progression, the operators use webhook.site for C2 and create scheduled tasks for persistence.
sentence.4030: Finally, in this attack chain, the actors deploy a custom malware variant, such as Drokbk or Soldier.
sentence.4031: These custom malware variants signal an increase in the subgroup’s level of sophistication, as they shift from using publicly available tools and simple scripts to deploying fully custom developed malicious code.
sentence.4032: Use of custom tools to evade detection
sentence.4033: Since 2022,Microsoft has observed this Mint Sandstorm subgroup using two custom implants, detected by Microsoft security products as Drokbk and Soldier, to persist in target environments and deploy additional tools.
sentence.4034: Drobkbk and Soldier both use Mint Sandstorm-controlled GitHub repositories to host a domain rotator containing the operators’ C2 domains.
sentence.4035: This allows Mint Sandstorm to dynamically update their C2 infrastructure, which may help the operators stay a step ahead of defenders using list-based domain blocking.
sentence.4036: Drokbk: Drokbk.exe is a custom .NET implant with two components: an installer, sometimes accessed from a compressed archive on a legitimate file-sharing platform, and a secondary backdoor payload.
sentence.4037: The Drokbk backdoor issues a web request to obtain the contents of a README file on a Mint Sandstorm-controlled GitHub repo.
sentence.4038: The README file contains a list of URLs that direct targets to the C2 infrastructure associated with Drokbk.
sentence.4039: Soldier: Soldier is a multistage .NET backdoor with the ability to download and run additional tools and uninstall itself.
sentence.4040: Like Drokbk, Soldier C2 infrastructure is stored on a domain rotator on a GitHub repository operated by Mint Sandstorm.
sentence.4041: Microsoft Threat Intelligence analysts assess that Soldier is a more sophisticated variant of Drokbk.
sentence.4042: In certain cases, this Mint Sandstorm subgroup has used TTPs outside of these attack chains, notably when they have failed to achieve short-term objectives.
sentence.4043: In one instance, Microsoft also observed the subgroup using TTPs from both attack chains in a single compromised environment.
sentence.4044: However, in most cases, Mint Sandstorm activity displays one of the above discussed attack chains.
sentence.4045: Low-volume phishing campaigns using template injection Microsoft has also observed this Mint Sandstorm subgroup using a distinct attack chain involving low-volume phishing campaigns and a third custom implant.
sentence.4046: In these operations, the group crafts bespoke phishing emails, often purporting to contain information on security policies that affect countries in the Middle East, to deliver weaponized documents to individuals of interest.
sentence.4047: Recipients are typically individuals affiliated with high-profile think tanks or universities in Israel, North America, or Europe with ties to the security and policy communities.
sentence.4048: Unlike their initial exploitation of vulnerable internet-facing applications, which is largely indiscriminate and affects organizations across sectors and geographies, activity associated with this campaign was highly targeted and affected fewer than 10 organizations..
sentence.4049: The initial emails are most commonly lures designed to social engineer recipients into clicking a OneDrive link hosting a PDF spoofed to resemble information on a topic involving security or policy in the Middle East.
sentence.4050: The PDF contains a link to a macro-enabled template file (dotm) hosted on Dropbox.
sentence.4051: This file has been weaponized with macros to perform remote template injection, a technique that allows operators to obtain and launch a payload from a remote C2, often OneDrive.
sentence.4052: Template injection is an attractive option for adversaries looking to execute malicious code without drawing scrutiny from defenders.
sentence.4053: This technique can also be used to persist in a compromised environment if an adversary replaces a default template used by a common application.
sentence.4054: In these attacks, Microsoft has observed the Mint Sandstorm subgroup using CharmPower, a custom implant, in attacks that began with targeted phishing campaigns.
sentence.4055: CharmPower is a modular backdoor written in PowerShell that this subgroup delivers in phishing campaigns that rely on template injection.
sentence.4056: CharmPower can read files, gather information on an infected host, and send details back to the attackers.
sentence.4057: Reporting from Checkpoint indicates that at least one version of CharmPower pulls data from a specific text file that contains a hardcoded victim identifier.
sentence.4059: Template injection technique What’s next Capabilities observed in intrusions attributed to this Mint Sandstorm subgroup are concerning as they allow operators to conceal C2 communication, persist in a compromised system, and deploy a range of post-compromise tools with varying capabilities.
sentence.4060: While effects vary depending on the operators’ post-intrusion activities, even initial access can enable unauthorized access and facilitate further behaviors that may adversely impact the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of an environment.
sentence.4061: A successful intrusion creates liabilities and may harm an organization’s reputation, especially those responsible for delivering services to others such as critical infrastructure providers, which Mint Sandstorm has targeted in the past.
sentence.4062: As these operators increasingly develop and use sophisticated capabilities, organizations must develop corresponding defenses to harden their attack surfaces and raise costs for these operators.
sentence.4063: Microsoft will continue to monitor Mint Sandstorm activity and implement protections for our customers.
sentence.4064: The current detections, advanced detections, and IOCs in place across our security products are detailed below and shared with the broader security community to help detect and prevent further attacks.
sentence.4065: Mitigation and protection guidance The techniques used by this subset of Mint Sandstorm can be mitigated through the following actions:
sentence.4066: Hardening internet-facing assets and understanding your perimeter Organizations must identify and secure perimeter systems that attackers might use to access the network.
sentence.4067: Public scanning interfaces, such as Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management, can be used to improve data.
sentence.4068: Vulnerabilities observed in recent campaigns attributed to this Mint Sandstorm subgroup that defenders can identify and mitigate include: IBM Aspera Faspex affected by CVE-2022-47986: Organizations can remediate CVE-2022-47986 by upgrading to Faspex 4.4.2 Patch Level 2 or using Faspex 5.x which does not contain this vulnerability.
sentence.4069: More details are available in IBM’s security advisory here.
sentence.4071: Organizations using Zoho ManageEngine products vulnerable to CVE-2022-47966 should download and apply upgrades from the official advisory as soon as possible.
sentence.4072: Patching this vulnerability is useful beyond this specific campaign as several adversaries are exploiting CVE-2022-47966 for initial access.
sentence.4073: Apache Log4j2 (aka Log4Shell) (CVE-2021-44228 and CVE-2021-45046): Microsoft’s guidance for organizations using applications vulnerable to Log4Shell exploitation can be found here.
sentence.4074: This guidance is useful for any organization with vulnerable applications and useful beyond this specific campaign, as several adversaries exploit Log4Shell to obtain initial access.
sentence.4075: This Mint Sandstorm subgroup has demonstrated its ability to rapidly adopt newly reported N-day vulnerabilities into its playbooks.
sentence.4076: To further reduce organizational exposure, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint customers can use the threat and vulnerability management capability to discover, prioritize, and remediate vulnerabilities and misconfigurations.
sentence.4077: Reducing the attack surface Microsoft 365 Defender customers can also turn on attack surface reduction rules to harden their environments against techniques used by this Mint Sandstorm subgroup.
sentence.4078: These rules, which can be configured by all Microsoft Defender Antivirus customers and not just those using the EDR solution, offer significant protection against the tradecraft discussed in this report. Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion Block Office applications from creating executable content Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands Additionally, in 2022, Microsoft changed the default behavior of Office applications to block macros in files from the internet, further minimizing the attack surface for operators like this subgroup of Mint Sandstorm.

sentence.4109: Unraveling its Vectored Exception Handler Approach url: https://securitynews.sonicwall.com/xmlpost/guloader-demystified-unraveling-its-vectored-exception-handler-approach/ GuLoader Demystified:
sentence.4110: Unraveling its Vectored Exception Handler Approach May 31, 2023 OVERVIEW SonicWall Capture Labs Research team recently observed a new variant of GuLoader (a.k.a Cloudeye).
sentence.4111: GuLoader is a shellcode-based downloader, known for its numerous anti-analysis techniques and control flow obfuscation.
sentence.4112: In latest variant of GuLoader it introduces new ways to raise exceptions that hamper complete analysis process and its execution under controlled environment.
sentence.4113: In this blog post, we will discuss Unpacking of GuLoader’s shellcodes.
sentence.4114: Understanding a new anti-debug technique deployed by GuLoader.
sentence.4115: Deep dive into GuLoader’s custom Vectored Exception Handler.
sentence.4116: Writing an IDAPython script to deobfuscate the control flow of shellcode and to make GuLoader’s analysis easy and fast.
sentence.4117: INTRODUCTION GuLoader is an advanced downloader first discovered in 2019 and since then it kept evolving, adding new anti-debugging techniques with its every new variant.
sentence.4118: It downloads malicious payload including AgentTesla, Azorult and Ramcos RAT etc.
sentence.4119: Currently GuLoader is spreading through malspam campaign and packed using NSIS installer.
sentence.4120: UNPACKING GULOADER’S SHELLCODE GuLoader’s shellcode is executed after three layers.
sentence.4121: Layer 1: Recent variant of GuLoader is spreading as NSIS Installer consisting of NSIS script, DLL plugin and encrypted shellcode’s file.
sentence.4122: We need NSIS variant of 7-zip to extract the NSIS script, as typical installer of 7-zip is unable to extract the NSIS script.
sentence.4125: File “Hangarer.Man” contains shellcode of Layer 2 and an encrypted shellcode of Layer 3 which is main shellcode of GuLoader.
sentence.4126: System.dll is DLL file which exports multiple functions.
sentence.4127: An Exported function named as “Call” is called by NSIS script.
sentence.4128: This function is responsible to allocate and execute Layer 2 shellcode.
sentence.4130: NSIS script calling Exported function Call.
sentence.4131: Call function allocates memory space and copies content of file Hangarer.
sentence.4132: Man from offset 0x409 till last byte.
sentence.4134: First parameter of CallWindowProcW is lpPrevWndFunc.
sentence.4135: lpPrevWndFunc is callback function, which is set to address of allocated memory space, which results in indirect execution of the Layer 2’s shellcode.
sentence.4136: Layer 2: Malware immediately decrypts the third layer which located at offset 0x1c9 in layer 2 and starts its execution.
sentence.4139: Layer 3: It is the final GuLoader shellcode.
sentence.4140: This shellcode has complex obfuscation, consisting of junk code, indirect function calls, dynamic API resolution, obfuscated arithmetic value calculations, using stack to decrypt strings, fake instructions, anti-debug, anti-vm, anti-analysis, anti-dump, anti-API hook, anti-emulation techniques.
sentence.4141: During analysis of this variant, we have identified a significant enhancement in GuLoader’s one of most effective anti-debug technique that it’s custom Vectored Exception Handler.
sentence.4142: Malware raises exceptions by executing cleverly crafted series of instructions.
sentence.4143: Also it uses same instructions multiple times in shellcode to make it hard for reverser to perform static and dynamic analysis and to consume lot of time.
sentence.4144: Ultimate goal of GuLoader for using this anti-debug technique is to achieve runtime control flow obfuscation.
sentence.4146: Mentioning them below in order in which they are get executed.
sentence.4147: Scan the virtual memory for the strings related to analysis tools.
sentence.4148: Uses Heaven Gate technique to redirect it’s execution under x64 OS.
sentence.4150: Patch DbgBreakPoint and DbgUiRemoteBreakin API used by debuggers.
sentence.4151: Uses EnumWindows API to enumerates windows.
sentence.4157: An Overview of the Payload’s Execution Sequence Create suspended child process of itself.
sentence.4158: In newly created process, it creates a section using genuine file to avoid AVs suspicious scanning.
sentence.4159: In this case it was using mshtml.dll. Injects complete main shellcode in child process.
sentence.4160: Repeats executing the mentioned evasion techniques one more time.
sentence.4161: After successful bypass , it decrypts the c2 URL and download encrypted payload from c2.
sentence.4163: In analyzed sample, key length was 0x303 bytes.
sentence.4164: GuLoader allocates approximately 60MB of memory space for the payload of size few KBs.
sentence.4165: It decrypts an encrypted payload, use process hollowing to inject decrypted payload into child process and resolves its Import Address Table.
sentence.4166: Lastly, it starts payload execution using the ZwCreateThreadEx API. Fig 4.
sentence.4168: All of the above-mentioned evasion techniques and payload execution sequences are already explained in detail in SonicWall Capture Labs Research team’s blog.
sentence.4170: In the below section we will discuss Exception types and implementation.
sentence.4172: Writing IDAPython script to restore deobfuscate control flow.
sentence.4174: This variant of GuLoader has added two new additional exceptions EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION & EXCEPTION_SINGLE_STEP compared to last variant it has only one exception EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT exception.
sentence.4175: We will discuss each exception and understand its pattern to write a script.
sentence.4177: When malware intentionally tries to write to an inaccessible memory address, exception EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION is raised.
sentence.4178: Here, malware constructs zero by series of arithmetic calculations.
sentence.4179: Then it tries to access memory address pointed by it, which raises exception as zero is inaccessible memory address.
sentence.4182: As we can see the constant values and operations (mov, xor, sub) are keeps varying for each exception raised.
sentence.4184: The FLAGS register is the status register that contains the current state of a x86 CPU.
sentence.4185: The trap flag is 8th bit of FLAGS register.
sentence.4186: When the trap flag is set, the system is instructed to single step, it will execute one instruction and then stop.
sentence.4187: Then contents of registers and memory locations can be examined by Vectored Exception Handler; if they are correct, the system can execute the next instruction.
sentence.4188: The x86 processor has no instruction to directly set or reset the trap flag.
sentence.4189: Malware uses combination of (PUSHFD/POPFD) instructions to set trap flag.
sentence.4191: Pushing the flag register on the stack (PUSHFD) .
sentence.4193: Popping the flag register back off the stack (POPFD).
sentence.4194: When malware is running without debugger, when SINGLE_STEP exception is raised and handled by Vectored Exception Handler.
sentence.4197: However while using debugger, no exception can be seen being raised as trap flag is always gets reset after each debugger event is delivered.
sentence.4198: EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT (code 0x80000003) INT3 instruction (0xCC opcode) is used as software breakpoint in debuggers, that’s why when program is running under debugger, control remains to the debugger after it encounter INT3.
sentence.4199: When malware is running without debugger exception EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT is raised, and control is transferred to the Vectored Exception Handler.
sentence.4202: Now we have understood how exceptions are being raised by malware.
sentence.4203: Next will see how malware uses these exceptions to change the control flow at runtime using its custom Vectored Exception Handler. DECODING VECTORED EXCEPTION HANDLER An application can register a function to handle all exceptions for the application.
sentence.4204: Vectored handlers are called in the order that they were added.
sentence.4205: GuLoader call RtlAddVectoredExceptionHandler API to add its custom Vectored Exception Handler. RtlAddVectoredExceptionHandler accepts two parameters.
sentence.4208: As we can see in below image, pointer of structure EXCEPTION_POINTERS is being passed as an argument to Vectored Exception Handler(VEH).
sentence.4209: Using structure EXCEPTION_POINTERS, VEH can access all the information regarding raised exceptions and reading the values of all the registers of processor using structure CONTEXT.
sentence.4211: Pseudocode of Custom Vectored Exception Handler.
sentence.4212: When EXCEPTION_ACCESS_VIOLATION and SINGLE_STEP_EXCEPTION exceptions are raised, handler perform following steps: It checks whether memory address being currently accessed is zero or not.
sentence.4213: If it is not zero, then it returns 0 and ultimately crashes down.
sentence.4214: But how handler gets the address of currently accessed memory location?
sentence.4215: So it uses ExceptionInformantion[1] member of Exception Record to get this additional information about exception.
sentence.4216: Checks if any hardware breakpoints have been set by checking status of the debug registers(DR0 to DR7).
sentence.4217: If found it set the ContextRecord to 0 which leads malware to crash.
sentence.4218: If successfully pass the check, it then transforms the EIP to new address using logic Context->Eip += ByteAt(Eip + 2) ^
sentence.4219: 0x6A where Value 2 depicts size of instruction (mov, jg, jne etc.) where exception is raised.
sentence.4220: 0x6A is byte key to transform EIP.
sentence.4223: When EXCEPTION_BREAKPOINT exception is raised, handler perform following steps:
sentence.4224: Checks whether hardware breakpoints have been set by checking status of the debug registers(DR0 to DR7).
sentence.4225: Scans for applied software breakpoint i.e. CC byte in loop.
sentence.4226: If successfully pass the check, it then transforms the EIP to new address using logic Context->Eip += ByteAt(Eip + 1) ^
sentence.4227: 0x6A where Value 1 depicts size of instruction (CC) where exception is raised.
sentence.4228: 0x6A is byte key to transform EIP.
sentence.4229: WRITING IDA PYTHON SCRIPT IDAPython is an IDA Pro plugin that integrates the python programming language, allowing scripts to run in IDA Pro. IDA provides different modules to work on disassembly of instructions.
sentence.4230: The python script finds instructions pattern that raise an exception and patch them by jump instruction with transformed EIP offset as a target.
sentence.4231: After running the python script in IDA, we get clean, easy to analyze, deobfuscated code of GuLoader’s shellcode.
sentence.4232: Also finds out that GuLoader’s VEH has been called more than 1100 times.
sentence.4234: Obfuscated code(A), deobfuscated code(B), GuLoader’s entire shellcode graph view(C).
sentence.4235: CONCLUSION GuLoader malware introduces new techniques very often which takes much time and efforts of malware analysts to fully analyzed it.
sentence.4236: We have completely analyzed GuLoader’s custom Vectored Exception Handler and understood how it works.
sentence.4237: We have written python script to defeat GuLoader shellcode control flow obfuscation and saving time and efforts of malware analyst.
sentence.4238: We expect further development in GuLoader anti-analysis, anti-debug techniques in upcoming days.

sentence.4242: title: Pack it Secretly: Earth Preta’s Updated Stealthy Strategies url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/c/earth-preta-updated-stealthy-strategies.html APT & Targeted Attacks Pack it Secretly: Earth Preta’s Updated Stealthy Strategies After months of investigation, we found that several undisclosed malware and interesting tools used for exfiltration purposes were being used by Earth Preta.
sentence.4243: We also observed that the threat actors were actively changing their tools, tactics, and procedures (TTPs) to bypass security solutions.
sentence.4244: In this blog entry, we will introduce and analyze the other tools and malware used by the threat actor.
sentence.4245: By: Vickie Su, Nick Dai, Sunny Lu March 23, 2023Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe
sentence.4246: In our previous research, we disclosed and analyzed a new campaign initiated by the threat actor group Earth Preta (aka Mustang Panda).
sentence.4247: In a more recent campaign we’ve been tracking, we discovered Earth Preta delivering lure archives via spear-phishing emails and Google Drive links.
sentence.4248: After months of investigation, we found that several undisclosed malware and interesting tools used for exfiltration purposes were used in this campaign.
sentence.4249: In this blog entry, we will introduce and analyze the other tools and malware used by Earth Preta.
sentence.4250: Infection chain As we previously mentioned in our past blog entry, the entire attack begins with a spear-phishing email.
sentence.4251: After a long-term investigation into the attack routine, we’ve determined that the full infection chain works as follows: Figure 1.
sentence.4252: The full infection chain We categorize the different TTPs into six stages: arrival vectors, discovery, privilege escalation, lateral movement, command and control (C&C) and exfiltration, respectively.
sentence.4253: In our previous research, we covered most of the new TTPs and malware during the first stage, arrival vectors.
sentence.4254: However, we observed that some of TTPs have been changed.
sentence.4255: In the following sections, we focus on the updated arrival vectors and their succeeding stages.
sentence.4256: Arrival vectors We previously summarized the arrival vectors used by Earth Preta by categorizing them into three types (DLL sideloading, shortcut links, and fake file extensions).
sentence.4257: Starting in October and November 2022, we observed that the threat actors began changing their TTPs to deploy the TONEINS, TONESHELL, and PUBLOAD malware, and QMAGENT malware.
sentence.4258: We believe that the threat actors are employing these new techniques to avoid detection.
sentence.4259: Trojan.Win32.TONEINS Based on our earlier observation, the TONEINS and TONESHELL malware were downloaded from the Google Drive link embedded in the body of an email.
sentence.4260: To bypass email-scanning services and email gateway solutions, the Google Drive link has now been embedded in a lure document.
sentence.4261: The document lures users into downloading a malicious password-protected archive with the embedded link.
sentence.4262: The files can then be extracted inside via the password provided in the document.
sentence.4263: By using this technique, the malicious actor behind the attack can successfully bypass scanning services.
sentence.4265: A lure document (allegedly concerning the government-related Myanmar Sustainable Development Plan) embedded with a Google Drive link and a password For the new arrival vector, the whole infection flow has been changed to the procedure shown in Figure 3.
sentence.4267: Infection flow for the new arrival vector File name Detection name Description Letter Head.docx Decoy document with Google Drive link List of terrorist personnel IN border.rar (all entries below are part of this archive) List of terrorist personnel at the border.exe First-stage legitimate executable for DLL sideloading libcef.dll Trojan.Win32.TONEINS First-stage malware ~$Evidence information.docx Second-stage legitimate executable for DLL sideloading ~$List of terrorist personnel at the border.docx Backdoor.Win32.TONESHELL Second-stage malware Internal Letter.docx Decoy document Letter Head.docx Decoy document Table 1.
sentence.4268: Files in the new arrival vector After analyzing the downloaded archive, we discovered it to be a malicious RAR file with the TONEINS malware libcef.dll and the TONESHELL malware ~List of terrorist personnel at the border.docx.
sentence.4269: The infection flow for these is similar to the arrival vector type C in our previous report, with the only difference being that the fake .docx files have XOR-encrypted content to prevent detection.
sentence.4270: For example, ~$Evidence information.docx is a file disguising itself as an Office Open XML document.
sentence.4271: As such, it seems harmless and can even be opened by using decompression software such as 7-Zip.
sentence.4272: We found that the threat actors have hidden a PE file in one of the archive’s ZIPFILERECORD structures.
sentence.4273: The TONEINS malware, libcef.dll, will decrypt this file with a single byte in XOR operations, find the PE header, and drop the payload to the specified path.
sentence.4275: A PE file is revealed after decrypting the frData member in the last ZIPFILECECORD structure.
sentence.4277: The decryption function of TONEINS The succeeding behaviors of the infection flow are generally the same as those in our previous analysis, where we provide more details.
sentence.4278: Trojan.Win32.PUBLOAD In more recent cases, the malware PUBLOAD was also being delivered through Google Drive links embedded in decoy documents.
sentence.4280: The lure document Invitation letter from the US embassy.docx Since October 2022, we have been observing a new variant of PUBLOAD, which uses the spoofed HTTP header to transfer the data, as LAC’s report also discusses.
sentence.4281: In contrast to the previous PUBLOAD variant, it prepends an HTTP header with a legitimate-looking host name to the packets.
sentence.4282: We believe that the threat actors are trying to conceal malicious data among normal traffic.
sentence.4283: The data in the HTTP body is the same as the past variant, which has the same magic bytes 17 03 03 and the encrypted victim information.
sentence.4284: We were able to successfully retrieve the payload from a live C&C server and were therefore able to continue our analysis.
sentence.4286: C&C traffic of the PUBLOAD HTTP variant Once the payload is received, it will check if the first three magic bytes are 17 03 03 and if the following two bytes are the size of payload.
sentence.4287: It will then decrypt the encrypted payload with the predefined RC4 key 78 5A 12 4D 75 14 14 11 6C 02 71 15 5A 73 05 08 70 14 65 3B 64 42 22 23 20 00 00 00 00 00 00 00, which is the same as the one used in the PUBLOAD loader.
sentence.4289: The first payload retrieved from the PUBLOAD HTTP variant After decryption, it then checks if the first byte of the decrypted payload is 0x06.
sentence.4290: The decrypted payload contains another payload that is XOR-encrypted with the bytes 23 BE 84 E1 6C D6 AE 52 90.
sentence.4292: The second payload retrieved from the PUBLOAD HTTP variant After this is decrypted, there is yet another final backdoor payload that supports data upload and command execution.
sentence.4294: The final payload of the PUBLOAD HTTP variant Command Internal string 0x03 - 0x01 - 0x1B UploadBegin error : %d! 0x1D UploadData error : %d! 0x1A - 0x1E CmdStart error : %d! 0x1F CmdWrite error :
sentence.4296: Command codes in the PUBLOAD HTTP variant In addition, we found some interesting debug strings and event names among the PUBLOAD samples.
sentence.4299: Debug string in PUBLOAD In summary, we think that the new TONESHELL and PUBLOAD archives have been evolving and now have something in common.
sentence.4300: For example, both of them are now being placed in decoy documents (such as Google Drive links) in order to bypass antivirus scanning.
sentence.4301: Discovery Once the threat actors obtain access to the victim’s environment, they can start inspecting the environment via the following commands: net user net user <username> net user <username>
sentence.4302: /DOMAIN Privilege escalation In this campaign, we discovered several tools used for UAC bypass in Windows 10.
sentence.4303: We will go into detail for each of them.
sentence.4305: Win 32.ABPASS HackTool.Win32.ABPASS is a tool used to bypass UAC in Windows 10.
sentence.4306: Based on our analysis, it reuses codes from the function ucmShellRegModMethod3, which is from a famous open-source project called UACME.
sentence.4307: A report from Sophos introduces this tool.
sentence.4308: ￼ This tool accepts an argument, and the following data is written into registry: Registry Key Name Value HKEY_USERS\<SID>-1001_Classes\aaabbb32\shell\open\command (Default)
sentence.4311: It also changes how Windows handles the ms-settings protocol — in this case, the string ms-settings is a Programmatic Identifier (ProgID).
sentence.4312: If the CurVer key is set under a ProgID, it will be used for versioning and mapping the current ProgID (ms-settings) to the one specified in the CurVer’s default value.
sentence.4313: In turn, the behavior of ms-settings is redirected to the custom defined ProgID aaabbb32.
sentence.4314: It also sets up a new ProgID aaabbb32 and its shell open command.
sentence.4315: Finally, fodhelper.exe or computerDefaults.exe will be executed to trigger the ms-settings protocol.
sentence.4319: Win32.CCPASS is another tool that is also used for Windows 10 UAC bypass and similarly reuses codes from the function ucmMsStoreProtocolMethod in the project UACME.
sentence.4321: Code similarities in CCPASS and ucmMsStoreProtocolMethod It works in a similar way to ABPASS.

sentence.4400: Exfiltration Based on our telemetry, we found that Earth Preta used multiple approaches to exfiltrate sensitive data from the victims.
sentence.4401: For example, in some cases, we observed that WinRAR and curl (or cURL) were leveraged to collect and transfer data to the threat actor’s server.
sentence.4402: After further investigation, we even found some previously unseen pieces of malware that were used to collect data in a custom-made file format.
sentence.4403: In the following sections, we share the details of the unique exfiltration toolsets developed by Earth Preta.
sentence.4404: WinRAR and curl According to some of our monitoring logs, the threat actors abused the installed WinRAR binary and the uploaded curl executable to exfiltrate the files (Figure 30 shows the executed command).

sentence.4406: All the exfiltrated data was collected and sent back to the threat actor-controlled FTP (File Transfer Protocol) server.
sentence.4408: Exfiltrate data using WinRAR and curl In some cases, we accidentally stumbled on the account and password of the FTP server.
sentence.4409: Upon checking the FTP server, we learned that the threat actors focused on sensitive and confidential documents, most of which were compressed and protected with a password.
sentence.4410: Based on our observations, the documents were organized via the categorization of the victim’s host name and disk drive.

sentence.4413: Win32.NUPAKAGE Apart from well-known legitimate tools, the threat actors also crafted highly customized tools used for exfiltration.

sentence.4415: The NUPAKAGE malware needs a unique passcode to be executed, with the exfiltrated data being wrapped in a custom file format.
sentence.4416: It seems that the threat actors are continuously updating this tool to provide more flexibility and lower the possibility of detection, including adding more command-line arguments and obfuscation mechanisms.

sentence.4460: For instance, it also avoids files with names starting with “$” or “~”.
sentence.4461: In addition, it generates two files, one with a .z extension and another with a .zip extension.
sentence.4462: The file with a .z extension is the exfiltrated data blob and the file with a .zip extension is the logging file.
sentence.4463: In the generated file with a .z extension, the exfiltrated files will be compressed by the zlib algorithm to minimize the file size.
sentence.4464: It also defines a Boolean field “type” for storage, whether a file is compressed or not.
sentence.4465: If a file is compressed and its file size is less than the original one, the type will be 1.
sentence.4466: Otherwise, the type will be set to 0, and the original file content will be chosen instead of the compressed one.
sentence.4467: Regardless of whether the file content is compressed or not, it will be encrypted in XOR operations with a specific string, qwerasdf.

sentence.4511: At first glance, Cobalt Strike was used in a manner similar to this campaign, including the use of DLL sideloading, the use of a Google Drive link for delivery, and the creation of a schedule task.
sentence.4513: A tweet about Cobalt Strike The infection flow is as follows: The archive file is delivered through a Google Drive link, which contains a legitimate EXE file, a malicious DLL file, and a decoy document written in Burmese.

sentence.4538: Exe, found in the Documents.rar archive, is a novel malware that communicates over the MQTT protocol.
sentence.4539: In March 2023, ESET published a detailed technical report on this backdoor, which it named “MQsTTang.”
sentence.4540: Beginning in January, we discovered that MQsTTang was being used as the new arrival vector in some of incidents we encountered, specifically in campaigns targeting individuals involved with government entities.
sentence.4541: This backdoor is unique because it communicates to its C&C servers over the MQTT protocol, which is commonly used in internet-of-things (IoT) devices.
sentence.4542: Malicious actors using this technique can effectively hide the real C&C server behind the protocol.

sentence.4546: The ee repository Conclusion Over the past year, security researchers have been discovering and analyzing Earth Preta’s campaigns and toolsets.
sentence.4547: We were able to attribute some of these to Earth Preta based on similarities among the TTPs, the malware being used, and the timeline of the campaigns.
sentence.4548: Starting October 2022, the threat actors changed the arrival vector of the TONEINS, TONESHELL, and PUBLOAD malware.
sentence.4549: Instead of attaching malicious archives or Google Drive links to an email, they now embed the download link in another decoy document and add a password to the archive.
sentence.4550: Based on our observations, Earth Preta tends to hide malicious payloads in fake files, disguising them as legitimate ones — a technique that has been proven effective for avoiding detection.
sentence.4551: As for privilege escalation, the threat actors tend to reuse codes copied from open-source repositories.
sentence.4552: Meanwhile, they developed customized toolsets designed to collect confidential documents in the exfiltration stage.
sentence.4553: Overall, we believe that Earth Preta is a capable and organized threat actor that is continuously honing its TTPs, strengthening its development capabilities, and building a versatile arsenal of tools and malware.
sentence.4554: To help prevent potential threats such as the one posed by advanced persistent threat (APT) groups, we suggest that organizations conduct phishing awareness training for their employees and partners to stress the importance of caution when opening emails, particularly those messages from unfamiliar senders or with unknown subjects.
sentence.4555: To assist organizations in protecting themselves against sophisticated threats, we recommend adopting a comprehensive security strategy that employs advanced technologies capable of identifying and halting such threats across multiple channels, including endpoints, servers, networks, and email communications.

sentence.4562: title: Malware Reverse Engineering for Beginners – Part 2 url: https://www.intezer.com/blog/incident-response/malware-reverse-engineering-for-beginners-part-2/ In part 1 of this series, we warmed up and aligned with basic computing terminologies.
sentence.4563: We learned the basics of assembly and how to use disassemblers.
sentence.4564: All of these tools and techniques are very important for reversing malware samples.
sentence.4565: Different sorts of malware have different capabilities and implementations.
sentence.4566: As reverse engineers, we need to be familiar with them and be able to identify and understand them.
sentence.4567: Often, malware targeting Windows will be packed and delivered as a second stage.
sentence.4568: There are different ways to “deliver” malware to the endpoint.
sentence.4569: This blog will cover key concepts and examples regarding how malware is packed, obfuscated, delivered, and executed on the endpoint.
sentence.4570: Here’s what we’ll cover: Basic terms that explain how malware is delivered to endpoints.
sentence.4571: A deep dive on packers – what they are, how they work and how to identify packed samples.
sentence.4572: Following the technical information, we will demonstrate two hands-on analyses of packed malware.
sentence.4573: Basic Terminology for Reverse Engineers to Know An executable file can conceal its true code through either encryption or compression.
sentence.4574: When the file is executed, some initial code usually called a stub, decrypts or decompresses the real code so it can be executed.
sentence.4575: These tools, that we will describe in this section, can be used by legitimate vendors that want to protect their software from piracy and copyright violations but threat actors also use these tools to evade detection and make the reversing engineering and analysis process harder.
sentence.4576: Now, let’s look at these four tools: a packer, crypter, protector, and a loader.
sentence.4577: What’s a Packer? Packers are often used to compress the payload so it will take less space on disk.
sentence.4578: While packers can be used for legitimate purposes, malware developers utilize packers to make the malicious payload smaller and avoid detection based on static malware analysis techniques.
sentence.4579: Examples: UPX is an open-source packing algorithm.
sentence.4581: Andromeda is a custom packer that makes reverse-engineering more difficult.
sentence.4583: Some security tools use signatures or keywords to detect malware.
sentence.4584: To avoid detection by these tools, malware developers can use crypters.
sentence.4585: A crypter encrypts the payload, so it will be harder for signature-based and standard anti-viruses to detect the malicious payload.
sentence.4586: Examples: PEUNION EXECryptor What’s a Protector?
sentence.4587: For most threat actors, one of the goals they want to achieve is to evade detection, and if the malware is detected then make the analysis process harder for researchers.
sentence.4588: That’s where protectors come into the picture – they offer many features that can make static and dynamic analysis tedious and time-consuming.
sentence.4589: Having said that, legitimate organizations can use protectors to protect their software from being cracked and manipulated.
sentence.4590: Usually, protectors will encrypt the payload, remove and obfuscate imports, implement anti-debugging and anti-reversing techniques, and much more. Examples: Themida Enigma Protector VMProtect What’s a Loader?
sentence.4591: Packed malware samples are compressed and stored inside the final executable, which will extract and execute the malware.
sentence.4592: On the other hand, there are loaders that serve as the first stage of the attack, the payload of the malware can be part of the loader’s file or it can be downloaded from a remote location (by the loader, also known as a Downloader).
sentence.4593: In addition, loaders can be used to set persistence and additional components needed for the execution of the malware.
sentence.4594: For example, Bazarloader is a sophisticated loader with multiple techniques that is used in attacks against high-profile organizations.
sentence.4595: Bazarloader delivers all sorts of threats, from spam to ransomware like Conti or Ryuk.
sentence.4596: In many cases, malware is delivered by tools that implement some (or all) of the functionalities of packers, crypters, protects, and loaders –- all to make the analysis harder.
sentence.4597: For example, Morphine has its loader and can encrypt the original file.
sentence.4598: Deep Dive Into How Packers Work and Detection
sentence.4599: Now let’s focus on packers, how they work, how to identify packed files, and how to extract the packed payload that can contain malicious code.
sentence.4601: The packed file contains three main components: packed content, a new PE header, and a stub, as seen in the image below: Packed sample view.
sentence.4602: The packers compress (and if it has the functionality of a crypter also encrypts) the original executable, which is saved in one of the sections of the final packed file.
sentence.4603: The entry point of the original file is relocated, and so is the Import Address Table (IAT).
sentence.4604: The stub is a small part of code that implements the decompression (and decryption) of the originally packed file.
sentence.4605: A new PE header is prepended to the packed file or modifies the existing header so it will be a valid executable.
sentence.4607: Static detection When data is being compressed or encrypted, the output is not structured and resembles more random data, resulting in high entropy.
sentence.4608: In information theory, entropy is a measure of disorder/randomness.
sentence.4609: The calculation is done using logarithm with base 2, also known as Shannon entropy, the result is in units of bits, hence the range of entropy level for binary files is 0 to 8.
sentence.4610: We can check the entropy of the file sections, and if one of them has a value of 7 or higher, there is a high probability that the file is packed.
sentence.4611: Packers may change the final payload’s section names, as seen in the screenshot below.
sentence.4612: But in most cases, malware authors will rename the sections to more commonly used names that will not give away the fact that the file is packed.
sentence.4613: Multiple tools can be used to detect indicators of a sample being packed: PEstudio, DiE (Detect it Easy), CFF explorer, and more.
sentence.4614: There are many examples and tutorials that use these tools, so we will show another free tool that can be handy in this and later stages: radare2.
sentence.4615: Viewing the section of a file (see technical analysis on this packer here).
sentence.4616: Packed samples usually have very few imports as they don’t rely on external libraries like other programs.
sentence.4617: When a file has a low number of imports, it strongly indicates that it contains another component that is dropped/loaded.
sentence.4618: However, malware developers can add “dummy” imports to mislead researchers.
sentence.4619: Viewing the imports for a packed file; full analysis results here.
sentence.4620: Reverse Engineering Example: Static Unpacking of UPX Packed Samples
sentence.4621: Standard UPX packed samples can be identified by the section names, as long as they were not modified by the attackers.
sentence.4622: Let’s take a look at a sample with MD5 5598febfbf00839c9f7047d9fe3205e3.
sentence.4623: The section names of the files contain the UPX string, as seen in the screenshot below: We can use the UPX command line utility to extract the packed payload.
sentence.4624: The command to decompress a packed file is as follows: upx -d <packed>
sentence.4626: You can run the command on the sample and verify that the extracted file has MD5 6d13f5d287fd735a9bbc261aafb49006.
sentence.4628: Dynamic detection When we dynamically analyze a packed file, we aim to extract the payload.
sentence.4629: Several functions can be a good place for putting a breakpoint and attempting to fetch the extraction process.
sentence.4630: Let’s look at API calls and debuggers.
sentence.4631: API Calls Essentially, all packers need to perform the following operations: allocate memory, change permissions, read the encrypted/packed chunk of code, decrypt it, load it to the allocated memory space and execute it.
sentence.4632: To make all of these actions, the program must use system calls because these actions require interaction with the kernel.
sentence.4633: The relevant system calls are VirtualAlloc used for allocating memory in the current process.
sentence.4634: The memory is automatically initialized to zero.
sentence.4635: One of the arguments is dwSize – that’s the size in bytes.
sentence.4636: Knowing the size can help identify when a program allocates big memory space, possibly for the unpacked payload.
sentence.4637: VirtualProtect changes the permissions of the given virtual address.
sentence.4638: When malware wants to grant write or execute permissions flNewProtect argument will be set to PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE (0x40) or PAGE_EXECUTE_READ (0x20).
sentence.4641: In the context of malware execution, it can create a new threat with the malicious unpacked payload.
sentence.4642: We can look for these system calls in the list of imported functions.
sentence.4643: However, malware authors usually try to hide these system calls.
sentence.4644: For instance, we will not see them in the imported function list, and they not even be part of the strings in the sample.
sentence.4645: In this case, the function and the corresponding library are dynamically loaded at runtime – also known as explicit linking.
sentence.4646: In this case, dynamic debugging can be very helpful – debuggers like x64dbg let you put a breakpoint on function calls, even if the function is not imported.
sentence.4647: The breakpoint will be triggered if the system call is executed.
sentence.4648: Debugger A debugger is a powerful tool that allows developers and researchers to follow and control the execution of a program.
sentence.4649: When debugging an executable, you can view the registers, stack, and memory and see how each instruction affects the stored data.
sentence.4650: Debugging malware can reveal code executed only in runtime (meaning that you will not see it in standard static analysis).
sentence.4651: Debuggers also allow you to see how strings and payloads are deobfuscated and constructed – making it easier to find the interesting patterns of the malware.
sentence.4652: Different debuggers can be used to debug Windows executables and DLLs: OllyDbg – not maintained anymore Windbg – powerful kernel-mode and user-mode debugger created by Microsoft.
sentence.4655: The main difference between these debuggers is the implementation, which may result in certain behaviors, but for the most part, it’s up to you to choose which debugger you prefer.
sentence.4656: There are more tools for debugging (and analyzing) .NET
sentence.4657: executables and other Windows executables, but that’s not covered in this blog.
sentence.4659: Extracting Packed Locky Payload In this section, we will present a guide on extracting packed malware from 2 popular malware:
sentence.4661: Make sure to run (and debug) the following examples in an isolated Windows virtual machine.
sentence.4662: You can watch the video of the hands-on unpacking process of Cobalt Strike.
sentence.4663: The video shows generation of a Cobalt Strike payload, analysis of the assembly, dynamic execution of the stager to fetch payload, scanning the endpoint for in memory genetic analysis, and parsing the Beacon configuration.
sentence.4664: The analysis of the Locky ransomware is covered in the section below.
sentence.4665: Reverse engineering tools that will be used in these analyses:
sentence.4666: Windows virtual machine x32 debugger Radare2 Command line commands: file, strings, shasum
sentence.4667: In this example, we will inspect a packed sample of Locky ransomware.
sentence.4668: While Intezer automatically identifies that the file is packed and extracts the payload for us, we will show how you can manually extract the payload here.
sentence.4669: Static analysis First, we will check the entropy of the section (as we did in the previous example).
sentence.4671: As seen in the screenshot below, the .rdata section has an entropy level higher than 7, and it’s very unusual for this section to have randomized data.
sentence.4672: We can run the strings command on the sample.
sentence.4673: The output contains lots of strings that look like a random collection of characters.
sentence.4674: At this point, we can assume that the sample is packed, so we will move to dynamic analysis using the x32dbg debugger.
sentence.4675: Dynamic analysis We will use the API calls we covered in the previous section.
sentence.4676: Put breakpoints on VirtualAlloc and VirtualProtect.
sentence.4677: bp VirtualAlloc bp VirtualProtect Now, let’s run the file.
sentence.4678: It will first stop at the entrypoint, we will hit F9 (continue until next breakpoint – BP), and we will get to the first call to VirtualAlloc.
sentence.4679: As seen in the screenshot below, the BP stopped on the call to VirtualAlloc, which is in the Kernel32.dll, and in the stack view (right low corner) we can see the arguments passed to the function.
sentence.4680: We can see that the required allocated space is relatively small, so it’s probably not called by the unpacking routine.
sentence.4681: So we will continue running the program – hit F9 again.
sentence.4682: It might take a few more hits on the call to VirtualAlloc before we get to a call with the size 0xF41D.
sentence.4683: At this point, we want to see where VirtualAlloc was called and what will be stored in the allocated spaces.
sentence.4684: So, as shown below, we will ask x32dbg to run to user mode.
sentence.4685: We will get to the instruction “ret 10” at this point.
sentence.4686: We need to grab the value stored in EAX, which stores the return value of VirtualAlloc.
sentence.4688: We will hit right-click and follow in the dump.
sentence.4690: but if we follow the execution of the code (hitting F8 several times), we will see that the memory contains some values, but they look random.
sentence.4691: We can continue running the program until the next hit on the VirtualAlloc call.
sentence.4692: Continue running the program until VirtualAlloc is called with the size: 0x17400 – which is even bigger than the previously allocated buffer.
sentence.4693: Then again, hit “run to user code,” or “execute till return” and follow EAX in the dump and step through the use code until you see the allocated memory filled with data that looks like this: The dump contains the unpacked executable – we can identify it by the 0x4D5A (MZ) magic.
sentence.4694: In the memory map, right-click the section and hit “Dump memory to file.”
sentence.4695: The MD5 of the extracted payload is e96dad009437ca774035ffd73708bd3e.

sentence.4699: You have successfully extracted the Locky payload.
sentence.4700: Automating Unpacking for Every File Learning the foundations of reverse engineering is important if it is a skill that you are trying to develop in your career.
sentence.4701: But for many security teams, even at large companies, you may not have the time to manually unpack and reverse engineer files on a regular basis.
sentence.4702: If you have automated tools that can unpack files and conduct reverse engineering-level analysis, those can ensure that you’re using your time efficiently to focus on threats that require your attention.
sentence.4703: Since reverse engineering can be time intensive, you’ll want to only use manual methods for tasks like unpacking after you’ve exhausted your other tools and options.
sentence.4704: Don’t have the time or skills for reverse engineering the volume of packed and obfuscated files your SOC team handles?

sentence.4708: title: Supply Chain Risk from Gigabyte App Center Backdoor - Eclypsium | Supply Chain Security for the Modern Enterprise url: https://eclypsium.com/blog/supply-chain-risk-from-gigabyte-app-center-backdoor/ Recently, the Eclypsium platform began detecting suspected backdoor-like behavior within Gigabyte systems in the wild.
sentence.4709: These detections were driven by heuristic detection methods, which play an important role in detecting new, previously-unknown supply chain threats, where legitimate third-party technology products or updates have been compromised.
sentence.4710: Our follow-up analysis discovered that firmware in Gigabyte systems is dropping and executing a Windows native executable during the system startup process, and this executable then downloads and executes additional payloads insecurely.
sentence.4711: It uses the same techniques as other OEM backdoor-like features like Computrace backdoor (a.k.a. LoJack DoubleAgent) abused by threat actors and even firmware implants such as Sednit LoJax, MosaicRegressor, Vector-EDK.
sentence.4712: Subsequent analysis showed that this same code is present in hundreds of models of Gigabyte PCs.
sentence.4713: We are working with Gigabyte to address this insecure implementation of their app center capability.
sentence.4714: In the interest of protecting organizations from malicious actors, we are also publicly disclosing this information and defensive strategies on a more accelerated timeline than a typical vulnerability disclosure.
sentence.4715: This backdoor appears to be implementing intentional functionality and would require a firmware update to completely remove it from affected systems.
sentence.4716: While our ongoing investigation has not confirmed exploitation by a specific threat actor, an active widespread backdoor that is difficult to remove poses a supply chain risk for organizations with Gigabyte systems.
sentence.4717: At a high level, the relevant attack vectors include: Compromise in the supply chain Compromise in the local environment Malware persistence via functionality of this firmware in systems A more detailed analysis of these risks is provided with suggested mitigations below.
sentence.4718: After a more traditional vulnerability disclosure timeline, we plan to publish details about how this works.
sentence.4719: Key Findings There are two important aspects of our findings: Eclypsium automated heuristics detected firmware on Gigabyte systems that drops an executable Windows binary that is executed during the Windows startup process.
sentence.4720: This executable binary insecurely downloads and executes additional payloads from the Internet.
sentence.4721: Since many more issues like this continue to be discovered, Eclypsium is continuously running at-scale analysis of the information technology supply chain.
sentence.4722: Look for additional findings on this blog and the Eclypsium Platform for your organization.
sentence.4724: Firmware dropping OS executable An initial analysis of the affected UEFI firmware identified the following file: 8ccbee6f7858ac6b92ce23594c9e2563ebcef59414b5ac13ebebde0c715971b2.bin
sentence.4725: This is a Windows Native Binary executable embedded inside of UEFI firmware binary in a UEFI firmware volume with the following GUID: AEB1671D-019C-4B3B-BA-00-35-A2-E6-28-04-36.
sentence.4726: This Windows executable is embedded into UEFI firmware and written to disk by firmware as part of the system boot process, a technique commonly used by UEFI implants and backdoors.
sentence.4727: During the Driver Execution Environment (DXE) phase of the UEFI firmware boot process, the “WpbtDxe.efi” firmware module uses the above GUID to load the embedded Windows executable file into memory, installing it into a WPBT ACPI table which will later be loaded and executed by the Windows Session Manager Subsystem (smss.exe) upon Windows startup.
sentence.4728: The “WpbtDxe.efi” module checks if the “APP Center Download & Install” feature has been enabled in the BIOS/UEFI Setup before installing the executable into the WPBT ACPI table.
sentence.4729: Although this setting appears to be disabled by default, it was enabled on the system we examined.
sentence.4730: This executable uses the Windows Native API to write the contents of an embedded executable to the file system at the following location:
sentence.4731: %SystemRoot%\system32\GigabyteUpdateService.exe It then sets registry entries to run this executable as a Windows Service.
sentence.4732: The mechanism described here is similar to the methods used by other UEFI firmware implants such as LoJax, MosiacRegressor, MoonBounce, and Vector-EDK, referenced previously.
sentence.4733: Stage 2: Downloading and running further executables
sentence.4734: The dropped Windows executable is a .NET application.
sentence.4735: It downloads and runs an executable payload from one of the following locations, depending on how it’s been configured: http://mb.download.gigabyte.com/FileList/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 https://mb.download.gigabyte.com/FileList/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 https://software-nas/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 Plain HTTP (the first bullet above) should never be used for updating privileged code as it is easily compromised via Machine-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.
sentence.4736: However, we noticed that even when using the HTTPS-enabled options, remote server certificate validation is not implemented correctly.
sentence.4737: Therefore, MITM is possible in that case also.
sentence.4738: The firmware does not implement any cryptographic digital signature verification or any other validation over the executables.
sentence.4739: The dropped executable and the normally-downloaded Gigabyte tools do have a Gigabyte cryptographic signature that satisfies the code signing requirements of Microsoft Windows, but this does little to offset malicious use, especially if exploited using Living-off-the-Land techniques (like in the recent alert regarding Volt Typhoon attackers).
sentence.4740: As a result, any threat actor can use this to persistently infect vulnerable systems either via MITM or compromised infrastructure. Risks and Impact These issues expose organizations to a wide range of risks and attack scenarios.
sentence.4741: Abuse of an OEM backdoor by threat actors – Previously, threat actors have taken advantage of legitimate but insecure/vulnerable “OEM backdoor” software built into the firmware of PCs.
sentence.4742: Most notably, Sednit group (APT28, FancyBear) exploited Computrace LoJack to masquerade as legitimate laptop anti-theft feature.
sentence.4743: Compromise of the OEM update infrastructure and supply chain – Gigabyte does have documentation on their website for this feature so it may be legitimate, but we cannot confirm what is happening within Gigabyte.
sentence.4744: In August 2021, Gigabyte experienced a breach of critical data by the RansomEXX group and then experienced another breach in October 2021 by the AvosLocker group.
sentence.4745: Persistence using UEFI Rootkits and Implants – UEFI rootkits and implants are some of the stealthiest and most powerful forms of malware in existence.
sentence.4746: They reside in firmware on motherboards or within EFI system partitions of storage media, and execute before the operating system, allowing them to completely subvert the OS and security controls running in higher layers.
sentence.4747: Additionally, since most of the UEFI code exists on the motherboard instead of storage drives, UEFI threats will easily persist even if drives are wiped and the OS is reinstalled.
sentence.4748: The rate of discovery of new UEFI rootkits has accelerated sharply in recent years as seen by the discovery of LoJax (2018), MosaicRegressor (2020), FinSpy (2021) ESPecter (2021), MoonBounce (2022), CosmicStrand (2022), and BlackLotus (2023).
sentence.4749: Most of these were used to enable persistence of other, OS-based malware.
sentence.4750: This Gigabyte firmware images and the persistently dropped Windows executable enable the same attack scenario.
sentence.4751: Often, the above implants made their native Windows executables look like legitimate update tools.
sentence.4752: In the case of MosaicRegressor, the Windows payload was named “IntelUpdater.exe” MITM attacks on firmware and software update features – Additionally, the insecure nature of the update process opens the door to MITM techniques via a compromised router, compromised device on the same network segment, DNS poisoning, or other network manipulation.
sentence.4753: It is also important to note that the third connection option, https://software-nas/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 , is not a fully qualified domain name, but rather, a machine name that would presumably be on the local network.
sentence.4754: This means an attacker on a local subnet could trick the implant into connecting to their system, without the need for DNS spoofing.
sentence.4755: Ongoing risk due to unwanted behavior within official firmware – Backdoors hidden within UEFI or other firmware can be hard to remove.
sentence.4756: Even if the backdoor executable is removed, the firmware will simply drop it again the next time the system boots up.
sentence.4757: This challenge was demonstrated before when trying to remove Computrace LoJack and relates to vulnerabilities in Lenovo Service Engine on notebooks and desktops.
sentence.4758: Recommendations We recommend exercising caution when using Gigabyte systems or systems with affected motherboards.
sentence.4759: Organizations can also take the following actions to minimize the risk: Scan and monitor systems and firmware updates in order to detect affected Gigabyte systems and the backdoor-like tools embedded in firmware.
sentence.4760: Update systems to the latest validated firmware and software in order to address security issues like this one. Inspect and disable the “APP Center Download & Install” feature in UEFI/BIOS Setup on Gigabyte systems and set a BIOS password to deter malicious changes.
sentence.4761: Administrators can also block the following URLs: http://mb.download.gigabyte.com/FileList/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 https://mb.download.gigabyte.com/FileList/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 https://software-nas/Swhttp/LiveUpdate4 Researchers at Eclypsium Labs are continuing to investigate for any signs of malicious activity related to this discovery.
sentence.4762: We will provide additional updates as new information becomes available.
sentence.4763: For more information or assistance contact Eclypsium at [email protected].
sentence.4764: A list of affected models is available here.
sentence.4765: title: Gotta Catch ‘Em All | Understanding the NetSupport RAT Campaigns Hiding Behind Pokemon Lures url: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/gotta-catch-em-all-understanding-the-netsupport-rat-campaigns-hiding-behind-pokemon-lures/ Researchers at ASEC recently reported on a NetSupport RAT campaign that utilizes Pokemon as the social engineering lure.
sentence.4766: Threat actors staged a malicious website, hosting a Pokemon-based NFT game, offering both a fun and financially rewarding experience.
sentence.4767: In reality, those drawn into the site are coerced into downloading the trojanized NetSupport RAT client, allowing attackers full access to their device.
sentence.4768: NetSupport RAT has been observed in numerous attacks on enterprise environments over the years, and Pokemon is just the latest in a long line of creative lures used to distribute and drop NetSupport RAT.
sentence.4769: It is frequently used by cybercriminals as a ‘quick solution’ in lieu of implementing something more bespoke.
sentence.4770: In this post, we provide an overview of NetSupport RAT and discuss the technical details of a recent campaign.
sentence.4771: Background NetSupport RAT is based on NetSupport Manager, a legitimate tool which is frequently used by bad actors for malicious purposes in ways similar to TeamViewer.
sentence.4772: NetSupport Manager, used maliciously or otherwise, provides full and complete control over the target device.
sentence.4773: Once the client has been installed, attackers can access, acquire, and manipulate any data on the device (exfiltrate data, execute additional payloads).
sentence.4774: In addition, the software allows at least the following: Real-time screen monitoring, optimized for monitoring multiple devices Taking control or redirect user screens Capturing screenshots, audio, video Malicious versions are constantly being sold or rented out via underground crime marketplaces.
sentence.4775: NetSupport Manager RAT offered for rental As NetSupport Manager is a legitimate tool that has a long history of development, it is highly attractive to attackers as it can be relied on to work ‘out of the box’.
sentence.4776: Additionally, it is thoroughly documented and actively supported: benefits that are less likely with custom-built malware that provides similar functionality such as Andromeda, Nanocore, CirenegRAT, Dark Comet and others.
sentence.4777: Malicious use of NetSupport Manager (aka NetSupport RAT) has been observed since at least late 2017.
sentence.4778: The use of “legitimate” or COTS (Commercial off the Shelf) tools is highly beneficial to attackers when attempting to achieve the greatest degree of stealth.
sentence.4779: Custom-written malware can often be detected by some layer of protection, such as EPP and EDR tools, so it is often advantageous to utilize a legitimate tool, even if it takes some creativity to deliver the remote software client.
sentence.4780: ASEC reported that the NetSupport RAT droppers were delivered via phishing emails that entice targets to install a “Pokemon card game”.
sentence.4781: On doing so, the victim unknowingly installs the NetSupport RAT, a doctored version of the NetSupport Manager client (client32.exe) that gives the attacker immediate and direct control of the infected device.
sentence.4782: While this specific attack was centered around the Pokemon theme, other phishing lures are known to be used.
sentence.4783: Some recent NetSupport RAT campaigns utilize .ISO
sentence.4785: This allows the attackers to evade certain types of detection.
sentence.4786: This technique has been used by ransomware actors as well such as by both Maze and Ragnar Locker.
sentence.4787: When opened, the ISO files will contain either the NetSupport RAT installer (with configs/support files) or a .LNK file redirecting the victim to said installer.
sentence.4788: Technical Details A typical example of this kind of .ISO file is the sample CLF_security.iso (288603f501926756c236e368a1fdc7d128f4f9a1).
sentence.4789: This particular .ISO contains an embedded .EXE file (CLFSECUR.EXE) which is then utilized to drop and execute the installer for NetSupport RAT.
sentence.4790: Sample 4233ff7941da62b86fc2c2d92be0572c9ab534c8 has been observed in multiple ISO files masquerading as legitimate software, including: CodeTwo Exchange Manager PCFresh 2022 SDK Tools Google Chrome Google Crash Handler Steelray Project Setup BrowserRenew.iso CLFsecurity.
sentence.4791: ISO Cloudflare_security_setup.iso The RAT installation is disguised to look similar to a Google Chrome installation.
sentence.4792: NetSupport RAT installer disguised as Google Chrome setup.
sentence.4793: The sample is obfuscated via the Babadeda crypter.
sentence.4794: When executed, a base64 encoded string is used to specify various parameters including sessionID and other critical values to the NetSupport connection.
sentence.4795: Base64 encoded RAT execution command The command decodes to look similar to the following: NetSupport RAT decoded command Persistence for the RAT is achieved via registry entry, and a shortcut to the installed RAT executable is written to the Startup folder.
sentence.4796: For example: ~\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\NetSupport.url In this case, the shortcut links to \AppData\Roaming\Steelray
sentence.4799: In addition, the sample generates a scheduled task with multiple triggers.
sentence.4800: NetSupport RAT Persistence via Scheduled Task Install directory of NetSupport RAT The RAT performs a number of discovery operations to understand its host environment.
sentence.4801: Network adapter details are pulled via GetAdaptersAddresses.
sentence.4802: Additional data is gleaned via WMI queries such as: SELECT *
sentence.4805: The malware deploys some anti-analysis measures such as attempting to detect the presence of a debugger via IsDebuggerPresent, and all running processes are enumerated and logged via EnumProcesses (32-bit processes).
sentence.4806: Launch behavior, including delays in execution or outgoing connection, can be controlled by the attacker.
sentence.4807: For example, Sleep statements may be used to delay execution by hours in order to trick sandboxes used in malware analysis or simply to disguise the association between the infection and the social engineering event from the user.
sentence.4808: Network requirements vary across different NetSupport Manager configurations and sessions.
sentence.4809: In the analyzed sample, the client opens a port on TCP 50275 to receive network connections.
sentence.4810: NetSupport RAT has the ability to drop and execute additional components.
sentence.4811: In this particular campaign, system/log data and executable code is dropped into %temp%.
sentence.4813: Data files and executables are also written to ~\Program Files (x86) \Google\Temp.
sentence.4814: These files are all self-deleted after launch or full installation of the attacker configuration.
sentence.4815: A large number of legitimate Google Chrome support files are also written to this location.
sentence.4816: These are used by the malware in order to facilitate the fake Google Chrome installation.
sentence.4817: Conclusion NetSupport Manager is a long-standing tool which, like TeamViewer, has unfortunately attracted ample use by cybercriminals.
sentence.4818: NetSupport RAT, once installed, is very robust and powerful, and threat actors are able to masquerade the dropper or installer in any way they see fit.
sentence.4819: In addition, threat actors using this tool are very quick to update their lures and find ways to entice their victims into installing the malicious remote control software.
sentence.4820: SentinelOne Singularity provides protection against malicious behaviors associated with NetSupport RAT.
