sentence.4822: title: Uncommon infection methods—part 2 url: https://securelist.com/crimeware-report-uncommon-infection-methods-2/109522/ Introduction
sentence.4823: Although ransomware is still a hot topic on which we will keep on publishing, we also investigate and publish about other threats.
sentence.4824: Recently we explored the topic of infection methods, including malvertising and malicious downloads.
sentence.4825: In this blog post, we provide excerpts from the recent reports that focus on uncommon infection methods and describe the associated malware.
sentence.4826: For questions or more information on our crimeware reporting service, please contact crimewareintel@kaspersky.com.
sentence.4827: RapperBot: “intelligent brute forcing” RapperBot, based on Mirai (but with a different C2 command protocol), is a worm infecting IoT devices with the ultimate goal to launch DDoS attacks against non-HTTP targets.
sentence.4828: We observed the first sample in June 2022, when it was targeting SSH and not Telnet services.
sentence.4829: The latest version, however, removed the SSH functionality part and now focuses exclusively on Telnet—and with quite some success.
sentence.4830: In Q4 2022, we noticed 112k RapperBot infection attempts coming from over 2k unique IP addresses.
sentence.4831: What sets RapperBot apart from other worms is its “intelligent” way of brute forcing: it checks the prompt and, based on the prompt, it selects the appropriate credentials.
sentence.4832: This method speeds up the brute forcing process significantly because it doesn’t have to go over a huge list of credentials.
sentence.4833: RapperBot then determines the processor architecture and infects the device.
sentence.4834: The downloading of the actual malware is done via a variety of possible commands (for example, wget, curl, tftp and ftpget).
sentence.4835: If for some reason these methods don’t work, then a malware downloader is uploaded to the device via the shell “echo” commands.
sentence.4836: Rhadamanthys: malvertising on websites and in search engines Rhadamanthys is a new information stealer first presented on a Russian-speaking cyber criminal forum in September 2022 and offered as a MaaS platform.
sentence.4837: According to the author, the malware: Is written in C/C++, while the C2 is written in Golang.
sentence.4838: Is able to do a “stealthy” infection.
sentence.4839: Is able to steal/gather information on CPU type, screen resolution, supported wallets, and so on.
sentence.4840: Evades EDR/AV. Has encrypted communication with the C2.
sentence.4841: Despite the malware being advertised already in September 2022, we started to detect the first samples at the beginning of 2023.
sentence.4842: Although Rhadamanthys was using phishing and spam initially as the infection vector, the most recent method is malvertising.
sentence.4843: Online advertising platforms offer advertisers the possibility to bid in order to display brief ads in search engines, such as Google, but also websites, mobile apps and more.
sentence.4844: Both search engine and website-based ad platforms are leveraged by Rhadamanthys.
sentence.4845: The trick they pull is to display ads representing legitimate applications but in fact containing links to phishing websites.
sentence.4846: These phishing websites contain fake installers, luring users into downloading and installing the malware.
sentence.4847: While analyzing Rhadamanthys, we noticed a strong connection with Hidden Bee miner.
sentence.4848: Both samples use images to hide the payload inside and both have similar shellcodes for bootstrapping.
sentence.4849: Additionally, both use “in-memory virtual file systems” and utilize Lua to load plugins and modules. Comparison between Rhandamanthys’s “prepare.bin” and Hidden Bee’s “preload” modules CUEMiner: distribution through BitTorrent and OneDrive In August 2021, a project was started on GitHub called SilentCryptoMiner, hosting the miner consisting of a downloader and the payload, bot source and the compiled builder, as well as additional software, such as a system watcher.
sentence.4850: It has been constantly updated, with the latest update going back to October 31 2022.
sentence.4851: The repository is popular with cybercriminals, as illustrated by the huge number of samples we detected that featured many small changes and were combined with the different URLs and TTPs, making it clear that the malware is used by multiple groups in various ways concurrently.
sentence.4852: During our investigation, we noticed two methods of spreading the malware.
sentence.4853: The first is via trojanized cracked software downloaded via BitTorrent.
sentence.4854: The other method is via trojanized cracked software that is downloaded from OneDrive sharing networks.
sentence.4855: How victims are lured into downloading these cracked packages is speculation, because we couldn’t find any direct links.
sentence.4856: Nevertheless, many crack sites these days do not immediately provide downloads.
sentence.4857: Instead, they point to Discord server channels for further discussion.
sentence.4858: This suggests some form of human interaction and social engineering.
sentence.4859: The downloader is written in .NET and called CUEMiner.
sentence.4860: Despite being written in .NET, it is wrapped by a C++ based dropper and it connects to a set of URLs, which is varying from sample to sample, to download the miner and configuration settings.
sentence.4861: It also performs several checks in order to ensure it is running on bare metal systems, and not on a virtual machine.
sentence.4862: In case all checks are passed, the malware: Reconfigures Windows Defender to exclude the user profile path and the entire system drive from scanning.
sentence.4863: Fetches configuration details from a hardcoded URL and saves it at different places (for example, c:\logs.uce, %localappdata%\logs.uce).
sentence.4864: Creates empty files and subdirectories in %ProgramData%\HostData to make the directory look benign.
sentence.4866: Does a number of other things.
sentence.4867: The full list you can find in our private report.
sentence.4868: The watcher, as the name suggests, monitors the system.
sentence.4869: If it doesn’t detect any processes that consume lots of system power (for example, games), the miner software is launched.
sentence.4870: When a heavy process, such as a game, is started, the miner is stopped and only started again when the aforementioned process stops.
sentence.4871: This is done in order to stay undetected on the system longer.
sentence.4872: Conclusion Open source malware is often used by less skilled cybercriminals.
sentence.4873: They often lack the required skills and contacts to conduct massive campaigns.
sentence.4874: Nevertheless, they can be still quite active and effective, as is shown by the huge number of CUEMiner samples we detected.
sentence.4875: If along their cybercriminal career they gain more skills, such as programming and understanding security better, they often reuse and improve crucial source code parts from open source malware.
sentence.4876: Code reuse and rebranding is also used quite often by cybercriminals.
sentence.4877: There are many ransomware variants that change names over time while mostly containing the same code base.
sentence.4878: In other cases, cybercriminals re-use parts of the code in new campaigns.
sentence.4879: For example, Rhadamantys stealer features some code overlaps with the Hidden Bee malware.
sentence.4880: This suggests involvement of at least one individual in the Rhadamantys campaign who had also been involved in the development of Hidden Bee.
sentence.4881: To protect yourself against these threats, intelligence reports can help.
sentence.4882: If you want to stay up to date on the latest TTPs used by criminals or have questions about our private reports, please contact crimewareintel@kaspersky.com.
sentence.4883: title: German users targeted with Gootkit banker or REvil ransomware url: https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-analysis/2020/11/german-users-targeted-with-gootkit-banker-or-revil-ransomware/ This blog post was authored by Hasherezade and Jérôme Segura
sentence.4884: On November 23, we received an alert from a partner about a resurgence of Gootkit infections in Germany.
sentence.4885: Gootkit is a very capable banking Trojan that has been around since 2014 and possesses a number of functionalities such as keystroke or video recording designed to steal financially-related information.
sentence.4886: In this latest campaign, threat actors are relying on compromised websites to socially engineer users by using a decoy forum template instructing them to download a malicious file.
sentence.4887: While analyzing the complex malware loader we made a surprising discovery.
sentence.4888: Victims receive Gootkit itself or, in some cases, the REvil (Sodinokibi) ransomware.
sentence.4889: The decision to serve one or the other payload happens after a check with the criminal infrastructure.
sentence.4890: Gootkit attacks observed in Germany Security researcher TheAnalyst was the first to publicly identify an active campaign in November using a sophisticated loader that was eventually attributed to Gootkit, a banking Trojan not observed in the wild for some time.
sentence.4891: Germany’s Computer Emergency Response Team CERT-Bund later confirmed that German users were being targeted via compromised websites.
sentence.4892: Around the same time, we started receiving reports from some of our partners and their ISPs about Gootkit-related traffic.
sentence.4893: We were able to confirm Gootkit detections within our telemetry that were all located in Germany.
sentence.4894: Figure 1: Gootkit infections in Germany in the wake of the campaign After a couple of days, we remediated over 600 unique machines that had been compromised.
sentence.4895: Fake forum template on hacked websites The initial loader is spread via hacked websites using an interesting search engine optimization (SEO) technique to customize a fake template that tries to trick users to download a file.
sentence.4896: The template mimics a forum thread where a user asks in German for help about a specific topic and receives an answer which appears to be exactly what they were looking for.
sentence.4897: It’s worth noting that the hacked sites hosting this template are not German (only the template is); they simply happen to be vulnerable and are used as part of the threat actor’s infrastructure.
sentence.4898: Figure 2: Compromised site loads decoy template to trick victims This fake forum posting is conditionally and dynamically created if the correct victim browses the compromised website.
sentence.4899: A script removes the legitimate webpage content from the DOM and adds its own content (the template showing a link to a file to download).
sentence.4900: Figure 3: A view of the HTML code behind the decoy template There is a server-side check prior to each visit to the page to determine if the user has already been served the fake template or not, in which case the webserver will return legitimate content instead.
sentence.4902: The infection process starts once the victim executes a malicious script inside the zip archive they just downloaded.
sentence.4903: Figure 4: Malicious script, heavily obfuscated This script is the first of several stages that leads to the execution of the final payload.
sentence.4904: The following diagram shows a high level overview: Figure 5: Infection flow Stage 1 – The first JavaScript The first JavaScript is the module that has to be manually executed by the victim, and it has been obfuscated in order to hide its real intentions.
sentence.4905: The obfuscation consists of three layers where one decodes content for the next.
sentence.4906: The first stage (a version with cleaned formatting available here) decodes the next element: Figure 6: First stage script The decoded output is a comma-separated array of JavaScript blocks: Figure 7: Decoded comma-separated array of scripts There are four elements in the array that are referenced by their indexes.
sentence.4907: For example, the element with the index 0 means “constructor”, 1 is another block of JavaScript code, 2 is empty, 3 is a wrapper that causes a call to a supplied code.
sentence.4908: Block 1 is responsible for reading/writing registry keys under “HKEY_CURRENT_USER\SOFTWARE\<script-specific name>”.
sentence.4909: It also deobfuscates and runs another block of code: Figure 8: Third JavaScript layer This fragment of code is responsible for connecting to the C2.
sentence.4910: It fetches the domains from the list, and tries them one by one.
sentence.4911: If it gets a response, it runs it further.
sentence.4912: The above downloader script is the first stage of the loading process.
sentence.4913: Functionality-wise it is almost identical in all the dropped files.
sentence.4914: The differentiation between the variants starts in the next part, which is another JavaScript fetched from the C2 server.
sentence.4915: Stage 2 – The second JavaScript (downloaded from the C2)
sentence.4916: The expected response from the server is a decimal string, containing a pseudorandom marker used for validation.
sentence.4917: It needs to be removed before further processing.
sentence.4919: Figure 9: GET request with C2 server After conversion to ASCII, the next JavaScript is revealed, and the code is executed.
sentence.4920: This JavaScript comes with an embedded PE payload which may be either a loader for Gootkit, or for the REvil ransomware.
sentence.4921: There are also some differences in the algorithm used to deobfuscate it.
sentence.4922: Example for the Gootkit variant (commented, full) Figure 10: The downloaded JavaScript The downloaded code chunk is responsible for installing the persistent elements.
sentence.4923: It also runs a Powershell script that reads the storage, decodes it and runs it further.
sentence.4924: Stage 3 – The stored payload and the decoding Powershell
sentence.4925: The authors diversified the method of encoding and storing the payload.
sentence.4926: During our tests we observed two ways of encoding.
sentence.4927: In one of them, the PE is stored as a Base64 encoded string, and in the other as a hexadecimal string, obfuscated by having certain numbers substituted by a pattern.
sentence.4928: The payload is usually stored as a list of registry keys, yet we also observed a variant in which similar content was written into a TXT file.
sentence.4929: Example of the payload stored in a file: Figure 11: Payload as a file on disk The content of the file is an obfuscated Powershell script that runs another Base64 obfuscated layer that finally decodes the .NET payload.
sentence.4930: Example of the Powershell script that runs to deobfuscate the file: "C:\Windows\SysWOW64\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe" -ExecutionPolicy
sentence.4931: Bypass -windowstyle hidden -Command "IEX (([System.IO.File]::ReadAllText('C:\Users\[username]\bkquwxd.txt')).Replace('~',''));" Below we will study two examples of the loader: One that leads to execution of the REvil ransomware, and another that leads to the execution of Gootkit.
sentence.4933: The example below shows the variant in which a PE file was encoded as an obfuscated hexadecimal string.
sentence.4934: In the analyzed case, the whole flow led to execution of REvil ransomware.
sentence.4935: The sandbox analysis presenting this case is available here.
sentence.4936: Execution of the second stage JavaScript leads to the payload being written to the registry, as a list of keys.
sentence.4937: The content is encoded as hexadecimal, and mildly obfuscated.
sentence.4938: Figure 12: Fragment of the payload stored in the registry, encoded as a hexadecimal string obfuscated with a pattern After writing the keys, the JavaScript deploys a PowerShell command that is responsible for decoding and running the stored content.
sentence.4939: Figure 13: The JS component deploys PowerShell with a Base64 encoded script Decoded content of the script: Figure 14: Decoded content It reads the content from the registry keys and deobfuscates it by substituting patterns.
sentence.4940: In the given example, the pattern “!@#” in the hexadecimal string was substituted by “1000”, then the PE was decoded and loaded with the help of .NET
sentence.4942: The next stage PE file (.NET): REvil loader: (0e451125eaebac5760c2f3f24cc8112345013597fb6d1b7b1c167001b17d3f9f)
sentence.4943: The .NET loader comes with a hardcoded string that is the next stage PE: the final malicious payload.
sentence.4944: The Setup function called by the PowerShell script is responsible for decoding and running the next PE: Figure 15: Hardcoded string (PE) Figure 16:
sentence.4945: Deploying the payload The loader runs to the next stage with the help of Process Hollowing – one of the classic methods of PE injection.
sentence.4946: Figure 17: REvil ransom note Example 2 – Loading Gootkit In an other common variant, the payload is saved as Base64.
sentence.4947: The registry keys compose a PowerShell script in the following format: $Command =[System.
sentence.4950: Convert]::FromBase64String("[content]")); Invoke-Expression $Command;Start-Sleep -s 22222; Figure 18: Registry key storing payload After decoding the base64-encoded content, we get another PowerShell script: Figure 19:
sentence.4951: More PowerShell It comes with yet another Base64-encoded piece that is further decompressed and loaded with the help of Reflection Assembly.
sentence.4952: It is the .NET binary, similar to the previous one.
sentence.4954: The script calls a function “Install1” from the .NET module.
sentence.4955: This function loads another PE, that is embedded inside as a base64 encoded buffer: Figure 20: Another buffer Figure 21: Deploying the payload This time the loader uses another method of PE injection, manual loading into the parent process.
sentence.4956: The revealed payload is a Gootkit first stage binary: 60aef1b657e6c701f88fc1af6f56f93727a8f4af2d1001ddfa23e016258e333f.
sentence.4957: This PE is written in Delphi.
sentence.4958: In its resources we can find another PE (327916a876fa7541f8a1aad3c2270c2aec913bc8898273d545dc37a85ef7307f ), obfuscated by XOR with a single byte.
sentence.4959: It is further loaded by the first one.
sentence.4960: Loader like matryoshka dolls with a side of REvil
sentence.4961: The threat actors behind this campaign are using a very clever loader that performs a number of steps to evade detection.
sentence.4962: Given that the payload is stored within the registry under a randomly-named key, many security products will not be able to detect and remove it.
sentence.4963: However, the biggest surprise here is to see this loader serve REvil ransomware in some instances.
sentence.4964: We were able to reproduce this flow in our lab once, but most of the time we saw Gootkit.
sentence.4965: The REvil group has very strict rules for new members who must pass the test and verify as Russian.
sentence.4966: One thing we noticed in the REvil sample we collected is that the ransom note still points to decryptor.top instead of decryptor.cc, indicating that this could be an older sample.
sentence.4967: Banking Trojans represent a vastly different business model than ransomware.
sentence.4968: The latter has really flourished during the past few years and has earned criminals millions of dollars in part thanks to large ransom payments from high profile victims.
sentence.4969: We’ve seen banking malware (i.e. Emotet) turn into loaders for ransomware where different threat actors can specialize in what they do best.
sentence.4970: Time will tell what this return of Gootkit really means and how it might evolve. Detection and protection Malwarebytes prevents, detects and removes Gootkit and REvil via our different protection layers.
sentence.4971: As we collect indicators of compromise we are able to block the distribution sites so that users do not download the initial loader.
sentence.4972: Our behavior-based anti-exploit layer also blocks the malicious loader without any signatures when the JavaScript is opened via an archiving app such as WinRar or 7-Zip. Figure 22: Blocking on script execution If a system is already infected with Gootkit, Malwarebytes can remediate the infection by cleaning up the registry entries where Gootkit hides: Figure 23: Detection of payload hidden in registry Finally, we also detect and stop the REvil (Sodinokibi) ransomware: Figure 24: REvil ransomware blocked heuristically Indicators of Compromise Compromised websites downloading JavaScript loader: docs.anscommerce[.]comellsweb[.]netentrepasteles[.]supercurro.netm-uhde[.]degames.usc[.]edudoedlinger-erdbau[.]at 3rd stage JavaScript C2s: badminton-dillenburg[.]dealona[.]org[.]cyaperosaintmartin[.]com Variant 1 (Gootkit): NET loader

sentence.4978: title: New IcedID variants shift from bank fraud to malware delivery url: https://www.proofpoint.com/us/newsroom/news/new-icedid-variants-shift-bank-fraud-malware-delivery New IcedID variants have been found without the usual online banking fraud functionality and instead focus on installing further malware on compromised systems.
sentence.4979: According to Proofpoint, these new variants have been seen used by three distinct threat actors in seven campaigns since late last year, focusing on further payload delivery, most notably ransomware.
sentence.4980: Proofpoint has identified two new variants of the IcedID loader, namely “Lite” (first seen in November 2022) and “Forked” (first observed in February 2023), both delivering the same IcedID bot with a more narrow-focused feature set.
sentence.4981: Removing unneeded functions on IcedID, which has been deployed in numerous malicious campaigns without many code changes since 2017, makes it stealthier and leaner, which can help the threat actors evade detection.
sentence.4982: Separate clusters of IcedID activity (Proofpoint) New IcedID campaigns Starting in November 2022, the “Lite” variant of the IcedID loader was delivered as a second-stage payload on systems infected by the newly-returned Emotet malware.
sentence.4983: The “Forked” version of the malware loader first appeared in February 2023, distributed directly through thousands of personalized invoice-themed phishing emails.
sentence.4984: These messages used Microsoft OneNote attachments (.one) to execute a malicious HTA file that, in turn, runs a PowerShell command which fetches IcedID from a remote resource.
sentence.4985: At the same time, the victim is served a decoy PDF.
sentence.4986: Malicious OneNote attachment used in recent campaign (Proofpoint)
sentence.4987: At the end of February, Proofpoint’s researchers observed a low-volume campaign distributing IcedID “Forked” via fake notices from the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
sentence.4988: It is important to note that while some threat actors use new variants of the IcedID malware, others still choose to deploy the “Standard” variant, with one of the most recent campaigns dating March 10, 2023.
sentence.4989: The new variants The “Forked” IcedID loader is quite similar to the “Standard” version in terms of its role, sending basic host info to the C2 and then fetching the IcedID bot.
sentence.4990: However, “Forked” uses a different file type (COM Server) and features additional domain and string-decryption code, making the payload 12KB larger than the “Standard” version.
sentence.4991: Domains decryption (Proofpoint) On the other hand, the “Lite” loader variant is lighter, at 20KB, and does not exfiltrate host info to the C2.
sentence.4992: This change makes sense since it was deployed alongside Emotet, which had already profiled the breached system.
sentence.4993: The “Forked” version of the IcedID bot is 64KB smaller than the “Standard” bot, and is basically the same malware minus the web injects system, the AiTM (adversary in the middle) functions, and the backconnect capabilities that give threat actors remote access to infected devices.
sentence.4994: Standard and Forked bot comparison (Proofpoint) IcedID is generally used for initial access by threat actors, so developing new variants is a worrying sign, signifying a shift towards specializing the bot to payload delivery.
sentence.4995: Proofpoint predicts that most threat actors will continue to use the “Standard” variant, but the deployment of new IcedID versions will likely grow, and more variants may pop up later in 2023.
sentence.4996: title: BumbleBee Roasts Its Way to Domain Admin url: https://thedfirreport.com/2022/08/08/bumblebee-roasts-its-way-to-domain-admin/
sentence.4997: In this intrusion from April 2022, the threat actors used BumbleBee as the initial access vector.
sentence.4998: BumbleBee is a malware loader that was first reported by Google Threat Analysis Group in March 2022.
sentence.4999: Google TAG attributes this malware to an initial access broker (IAB) dubbed EXOTIC LILY, working with the cybercrime group FIN12/WIZARD SPIDER/DEV-0193.
sentence.5000: Read more about BumbleBee here, and here.
sentence.5001: During this intrusion, the threat actors gained access using an ISO and LNK file, used several lateral movement techniques, dumped credentials three different ways, kerberoasted a domain admin account and dropped/executed a bespoke tool for discovering privilege escalation paths.
sentence.5002: Case Summary In this intrusion, the threat actors operated in an environment over an 11 day dwell period.
sentence.5003: The intrusion began with a password protected zipped ISO file that we assess with medium to high confidence due to other reports, likely arrived via an email which included a link to download said zip file.
sentence.5004: The execution phase started with that password protected zip, which after extracting would show the user an ISO file that after the user double clicks would mount like a CD or external media device on Windows and present the user with a single file named documents in the directory.
sentence.5005: When the user double clicks or opens the lnk file, they inadvertently starts a hidden file in the directory, a DLL (namr.dll) containing the Bumblebee malware loader.
sentence.5006: From there, the loader reached out to the Bumblebee C2 server.
sentence.5007: At first, things remained fairly quiet, just C2 communications; until around 3 hours later, Bumblebee dropped a Cobalt Strike beacon named wab.exe on the beachhead host.
sentence.5008: This Cobalt Strike beacon was subsequently executed and then proceeded to inject into various other processes on the host (explorer.exe, rundll32.exe).
sentence.5009: From these injected processes, the threat actors began discovery tasks using Windows utilities like ping and tasklist.
sentence.5010: Four hours after initial access, the threat actor started their first lateral movement using RDP to pivot to a server using the local Administrator account.
sentence.5011: The threat actor then deployed Anydesk, which was the only observed persistence mechanism used during the intrusion.
sentence.5012: The threat actor then started Active Directory mapping using Adfind.
sentence.5013: After this activity, the threat actors went silent.
sentence.5014: Then, the next day, they accessed the server via RDP and deployed a bespoke tool, VulnRecon, designed to identify local privilege escalation paths on a Windows host.
sentence.5015: The tool appeared to be still under development as several command options were not yet implemented.
sentence.5016: The next check in from the threat actors, occurred on the 4th day, where the threat actors again ran VulnRecon, but from the beachhead host instead of the server.
sentence.5017: AdFind was used again as well.
sentence.5018: Next, the threat actor transferred Sysinternals tool Procdump over SMB, to the ProgramData folders on multiple hosts in the environment.
sentence.5019: They then used remote services to execute Procdump, which was used to dump lsass.
sentence.5020: At this point, the actors appeared to be searching for more access then they currently had.
sentence.5021: While they were able to move laterally to workstations and at least one server, it seemed that they had not yet taken control of an account that provided them the access they were seeking, likely a Domain Administrator or similarly highly privileged account.
sentence.5022: After that activity, the threat actors then disappeared until the 7th day, at which time they accessed the server via Anydesk.
sentence.5023: Again, they executed VulnRecon and then also executed Seatbelt, a red team tool for preforming various host based discovery.
sentence.5024: On the final day of the intrusion, the 11th day since the initial entry by the threat actor, they appeared to be preparing to act on final objectives.
sentence.5025: The threat actors used PowerShell to download and execute a new Cobalt Strike PowerShell beacon in memory on the beachhead host.
sentence.5026: After injecting into various processes on the host, the threat actors executed the PowerShell script Invoke-Kerberoast.
sentence.5027: Next, they used yet another technique to dump LSASS on the beachhead host, this time using a built in Windows tool comsvcs.dll.
sentence.5028: AdFind was run for a 3rd time in the network, and then two batch scripts were dropped and run.
sentence.5029: These batch scripts’ purposes were to identify all online servers and workstations in the environment, often a precursor to ransomware deployment by creating the target list for that deployment.
sentence.5030: After the scripts ran, a new Cobalt Strike executable beacon was run on the beachhead.
sentence.5031: Next, the threat actors used a service account to execute a Cobalt Strike beacon remotely on a Domain Controller.
sentence.5032: This service account was most likely cracked offline after being kerberoasted earlier in the intrusion.
sentence.5033: The threat actors were then evicted from the environment before any final actions could be taken.
sentence.5034: We assess based on the level of access and discovery activity from the final day the likely final actions would have been a domain wide ransom deployment.
sentence.5035: Services We offer multiple services including a Threat Feed service which tracks Command and Control frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, BumbleBee, Covenant, Metasploit, Empire, PoshC2, etc.
sentence.5036: More information on this service and others can be found here.
sentence.5037: We also have artifacts and IOCs available from this case such as pcaps, memory captures, files, event logs including Sysmon, Kape packages, and more, under our Security Researcher and Organization services.
sentence.5038: Timeline Analysis and reporting completed by @0xtornado and @MetallicHack Initial Access
sentence.5039: The threat actors managed to get access to the beachhead host after the successful execution of a lnk file within an ISO, which are usually distributed through email campaigns.
sentence.5040: The initial payload named BC_invoice_Report_CORP_46.iso, is an ISO image that once mounted, lures the user to open a document.lnk file which will execute the malicious DLL loader using the following command line:
sentence.5041: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe /c start rundll32 namr.dll,IternalJob Running Eric Zimmerman’s tool LECmd revealed additional details related to the threat actors.
sentence.5042: The metadata included TA machine’s hostname, MAC address, and the LNK document creation date: Execution Execution of multiple payloads The successful execution of BumbleBee payload (namr.dll) resulted in the dropping and the execution of several payloads using multiple techniques.

sentence.5048: Persistence AnyDesk and its installation as a service was used in order to persist and create a backdoor to the network.
sentence.5049: Privilege Escalation GetSystem Threat actors made a mistake by launching the getsystem command in the wrong console (shell console rather than the beacon console).
sentence.5050: The parent process of this command was C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k ClipboardSvcGroup -p
sentence.5052: cbdhsvc , a process where Cobalt Strike was injected into: C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /C
sentence.5054: This command is a built-in Cobalt Strike command that is used to get SYSTEM privileges.
sentence.5055: A detailed write-up of this feature is documented in the official Cobalt Strike blog and was also detailed in our Cobalt Strike, a Defender’s Guide blog post. Valid Accounts Threat actors obtained and abused credentials of privilege domain accounts as a means of gaining privilege escalation on the domain.
sentence.5056: A service account, with Domain Administration permissions, was used to create a remote service on a Domain Controller to move laterally.
sentence.5057: Defense Evasion Process Injection The process injection technique was used multiple times to inject into different processes.
sentence.5058: Almost every post-exploitation job was launched from an injected process.
sentence.5059: Right after its execution, the wab.exe process created two remote threads in order to inject code into explorer.exe and rundll32.exe: Threat actors also created a remote thread in svchost.exe: Multiple processes were then spawned by : C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k ClipboardSvcGroup -p

sentence.5083: We can assert with high confidence that the recon stage was not fully automated, and threat actors manually executed commands and made a mistake in one of those.
sentence.5084: AdFind To enumerate Active Directory, the threat actors executed AdFind from the beachhead host, on three different occasions: The source of execution, the initiating parent process, was different on each occasion and the name of AdFind binary and the result files were different on one occasion, which could indicate multiple Threat actors accessing the network.
sentence.5085: Network scanning Threat actors used two scripts named s.bat (for servers) and w.bat (for workstations) to ping the hosts and store the results in two log files: s.bat script: @echo off for /f

sentence.5093: Invoke-ShareFinder Invoke-ShareFinder is a PowerShell module which is part of PowerView. Invoke-ShareFinder – finds (non-standard) shares on hosts in the local domain Threat actors performed share enumeration using Invoke-ShareFinder.

Seatbelt The tool SeatBelt was used by the threat actors on a server in order to discover potential security misconfigurations.
sentence.5096: Seatbelt is a C# project that performs a number of security oriented host-survey “safety checks” relevant from both offensive and defensive security perspectives.
sentence.5097: Threat actors performed a full reconnaissance by specifying the flag -group=all: Seatbelt.exe -group=all -outputfile="C:\ProgramData\seatinfo.txt" VulnRecon Threat actors dropped two binaries named vulnrecon.dll and vulnrecon.exe on two hosts.

sentence.5102: Below are all the command lines run by the adversaries: Lateral Movement Lateral Tool Transfer Using the Cobalt Strike beacon, the threat actors transferred AnyDesk (1).exe file from the beachhead to a server: The threat actors also transferred ProcDump from the beachhead to multiple workstations: Remote Services Remote Desktop Protocol Threat actors used explorer.exe, where they were previously injected into, to initiate a proxied RDP connection to a server: Threat actors performed the first lateral movement from the beachhead to the server using RDP with an Administrator account: This first lateral movement was performed in order to drop and install AnyDesk.
sentence.5103: SMB/Windows Admin Shares Remote Service over RPC Multiple RPC connections were initiated from the rundll32.exe process where wab.exe previously injected into: These RPC connections targeted multiple hosts, including workstations, servers, and DCs.
sentence.5104: As we can see with one server, which was targeted, the win32 function CreateServiceA was used by the malware in order to create a remote service over RPC on the server.
sentence.5105: Cobalt Strike built-in PsExec Threat actors used the built-in Cobalt Strike jump psexec command to move laterally.
sentence.5106: On each usage of this feature, a remote service was created with random alphanumeric characters, service name and service file name, e.g. “<7-alphanumeric-characters>.exe”.

sentence.5139: Named pipes were created in order to establish communication between CS processes: In this particular case, threat actors used default post-exploitation jobs, which have a pattern of postex_[0-9a-f]{4}.
sentence.5140: Below is the full list of all default named pipes spotted during this intrusion: \postex_0dde \postex_3e9b \postex_4008 \postex_4429 \postex_55f8 \postex_8248 \postex_8c73 \postex_972d \postex_fc2e Named piped are commonly used by Cobalt Strike perform various techniques.

sentence.5142: AnyDesk As mentioned before in the lateral tool transfer section, threat actors remotely dropped AnyDesk binary on a server from the beachhead: A new service was created (Event ID 7045) upon the execution of AnyDesk installer:
sentence.5145: %AppData%\AnyDesk\ad.trace, show that it was used during Day 1 and Day 7 of this intrusion, using the Administrator account each time.
sentence.5146: The usage of AnyDesk can be relatively easy to spot if you have the right logs (*.anydesk.com domains, AnyDesk user agent, etc.):
sentence.5147: The usage of AnyDesk also triggered two ET signatures: ET POLICY SSL/TLS Certificate Observed (AnyDesk Remote Desktop Software) ET USER_AGENTS
sentence.5148: AnyDesk Remote Desktop Software User-Agent Again, those are quick wins to add to your detection capabilities to detect the usage of unauthorized remote administration tools, commonly used by ransomware operators AnyDesk configuration file and the network logs revealed that the id used was 159889039 and the source IP was 108.177.235.25 (LeaseWeb USA – Cloud Provider).
sentence.5149: Impact There was no impact (exfiltration, data encryption, or destruction) during this intrusion.
sentence.5150: However, the observed TTPs show common cybercrime threat actors tradecraft which may have lead to domain wide ransomware had the threat actors had enough time.

sentence.5189: Financially Motivated Campaign Leverages CMD-Based Scripts and LOLBaS for Online Banking Theft in Portugal, Peru, and Mexico url: https://blogs.blackberry.com/en/2023/05/cmdstealer-targets-portugal-peru-and-mexico Operation CMDStealer:
sentence.5190: Financially Motivated Campaign Leverages CMD-Based Scripts and LOLBaS for Online Banking Theft in Portugal, Peru, and Mexico An unknown financially motivated threat actor, very likely from Brazil, is targeting Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking victims, with the goal of stealing online banking access.
sentence.5191: The victims are primarily in Portugal, Mexico, and Peru.
sentence.5192: This threat actor employs tactics such as LOLBaS (Living Off the Land Binaries and Scripts), along with CMD-based scripts to carry out its malicious activities.
sentence.5193: The campaign utilizes phishing emails in Portuguese and Spanish, and social engineering tactics to target victims.
sentence.5194: The emails exploit commonly encountered issues, such as transit infractions and taxes, to create a sense of urgency and legitimacy in their phishing messages.
sentence.5195: By posing as authoritative entities or government agencies, the messages are intended to deceive unsuspecting individuals and get them to disclose their online banking credentials.
sentence.5196: Brief MITRE ATT&CK:registered: Information Tactic Technique Initial Access T1566.001 Execution T1204.002, T1059.001, T1059.003, T1047, T1059.005, T1059.007 Defense Evasion T1027, T1140 Command and Control T1001, T1105, T1132.001, T1071.001 Discovery T1069, T1082, T1087 Exfiltration T1041 Credential Access T1555.003 Persistence T1547.009 Weaponization and Technical Overview Weapons CMD files, Autolt scripts Attack Vector Phishing Network Infrastructure Malicious domains Targets Portugal, Mexico, Peru Technical Analysis Context The Latin American threat landscape primarily consists of financially-motivated malware, usually compiled into the final PE payloads.
sentence.5197: While deploying the final payloads, BlackBerry threat researchers saw a variety of techniques, such as abusing VBE scripts, ISO images, and MSI packages.
sentence.5198: In this case, the threat actor behind the campaign used CMD-based scripts, AutoIt scripts, and LOLBaS. LOLBaS and CMD-based scripts help threat actors avoid detection by traditional security measures.
sentence.5199: The scripts leverage built-in Windows:registered: tools and commands, allowing the threat actor to evade endpoint protection platform (EPP) solutions, and bypass security systems.
sentence.5200: By utilizing these techniques, they can gain unauthorized access to victims' systems, extract sensitive information, and ultimately compromise online banking accounts and payment systems.
sentence.5201: The geographical focus of this threat actor centers on Portugal, Mexico, and Peru, where a significant number of Spanish and Portuguese speakers reside.
sentence.5202: Their selection of countries is likely influenced by the prevalence of online banking usage in these regions, making them lucrative targets for financial fraud.
sentence.5203: The first .CMD file set seen to use AutoIt in its execution was discovered at the end of 2021.
sentence.5204: This suggests that the threat actor was beginning its tests, naming these files “demo” or “test,” upon decompiling the AutoIt script into a human-readable script that supports the timeline of this attack campaign.
sentence.5205: Figure 1 – CMDStealer files with a very low detection rate on Virus Total Operation CMDStealer Attack Vector
sentence.5206: The infection chain begins with the user receiving a phishing email.
sentence.5207: These phishing emails are specially crafted to grab victims’ attention.
sentence.5208: In one instance, we observed one of the emails titled “Multa de Trânsito,“ which translates from Portuguese as “traffic infraction ticket.”
sentence.5209: Each email has an HTML attachment.
sentence.5210: Figure 2 – Phishing email contents The email text employs scare tactics, such as evidence of a traffic violation, prompting the user to open the HTML attachment which contains some junk code and data in HEX format.
sentence.5211: Figure 3 – "multa_de_transito_502323.html" attachment content The data blob in HEX decodes to a slightly obfuscated URL address which upon cleanup translates to: hxxps[:]//multa-ansr-pt[.]fun/?hcBViJAi9EZSc3YQwxpEwfmD7xdG0IF34EWGHj6Q. This URL resolves to: 162.0.232[.]115 IP address.
sentence.5212: During the extensive analysis of the “.HTML” files, BlackBerry identified a large list of HEX-encoded URLs, some of which are listed here: hxxps[:]//factura61[.]click/2/?j5szsmo0bk8tOSQSMS4mmp1XtQrmbNYoCB2GBem8 hxxps[:]//factura61[.]click/2/?vzlv9CZ1gnLrNIaWBJBhJNWRCt7IVXDDwVzOQhSs hxxps[:]//sunat-pe[.]fun/?D80gaUJDUfuLG6lodTSEi7qoqciBWk5xE5w81pJO hxxps[:]//factura61[.]click/2/?CTtBmkRN8KPXVTgUn1ArCPGb5WXTXTaT7etdD7TC hxxps[:]//factura61[.]click/2/?yqJl8r7henupax3WsUvITb0PuSw5sn7HyZWGMvDv hxxps[:]//factura61[.]click/2/?GxkVBvEBTFfSDqaFr8Yjw9kyKH01xRseHoF0DNQc hxxps[:]//multa-ansr-pt[.]fun/?UFqQBhFaXulvEfeTbI38FFDKRth1r2DWKOFqUI0Y hxxps[:]//multa-ansr-pt[.]fun/?l4mm0DEhDbJPYd5qAQmwst09TDTjjvYjiG7ByCvx Opening the attached “multa_de_transito_502323.html” file triggers the embedded JavaScript and reaches out to hxxps[:]//multa-ansr-pt[.]fun/?hcBViJAi9EZSc3YQwxpEwfmD7xdG0IF34EWGHj6Q to pull down the next stage which is a compressed archive (RAR) file.
sentence.5213: The archive file is typically titled with one of the naming schemes (a few are listed below): doc-Impuestos_<[0-9]{6}>.rar doc-Impostos_<[0-9]{6}>.rar Documento_Impostos_<[0-9]{6}>.rar Multa_<[0-9]{6}>.rar Impuestos-Documento_<[0-9]{6}>.rar BlackBerry found different campaigns geofenced to each specific country.
sentence.5214: Threat researchers reported similar campaigns in the past targeting Mexico.
sentence.5215: Weaponization The contents of the previously mentioned archive include a single “.CMD” file typically titled from one of the following filenames, (but there are other names): doc-Impuestos.cmd doc-Impostos.cmd Impuestos-Documento.cmd doc_Factura.cmd Documento_Impostos.cmd The “.CMD” file is large, ranging between 1.34 - 1.37MBs, and consists of two base64 encoded data blobs and code instructions for its execution.
sentence.5216: The script is described in the SANS write-up released on 1/06/2023.
sentence.5217: Figure 4 – Code instructions for both base64 data block execution The first base64 data blob is compiled AutoIt script and the second is AutoIt interpreter (a benign file), used to run the first file.
sentence.5218: The purpose of the AutoIt script is to enumerate the host and download a “.VBS” file which then gets executed via the “SHELLEXECUTE”.
sentence.5219: Next, it invokes the “_OUTRECOVERY()” function to steal Outlook data such as server, user, and password from POP3, SMPT, and IMAP registry keys.
sentence.5220: The script is then instructed to call the “_CHROMERECOVERY()” function.
sentence.5221: It proceeds by downloading the “sqlite3.dll” file from “hxxps[:]//www[.]autoitscript[.]com/autoit3/pkgmgr/sqlite/” which will be required later during the Chrome password theft.
sentence.5222: All data is then sent back to the attacker's C2 via the HTTP POST method.
sentence.5223: The C2 is constructed with the victim's enumerated data, where the values are: v1 – OS language (e.g., 1033 – English US) v2 – keyboard layout (e.g., 1033 – English US) v3 – operating system version (Windows 7,8,10,11 or unknown) v4 – is target an admin or user v5 – OS architecture (x86 or x64)
sentence.5224: The URL then becomes: hxxp[:]//publicpressmagazine[.]com/images/swan/do/it[.]php?b1=1&v1=1033&v2=1033&v3=windows%2010&v4=admin&v5=x86 hxxp[:]//websylvania[.]com/psj/do/it[.]php?b1=1&v1=3082&v2=1034&v3=windows%207&v4=user&v5=x64 To gain persistence on the infected system, it relies on the following code: Figure 5 – Persistence in the system Notably, within the decompiled AutoIt scripts that were used to target Mexico, a list of Mexican banks was also specified.
sentence.5225: If found, some of that data was sent back to the attacker.
sentence.5226: Figure 6 – Financial targets in Mexico Based on the URLs of the financial targets in Mexico, the threat actor behind CMDStealer is highly interested in compromising enterprise/business accounts.
sentence.5227: Operation CMDStealer Network Infrastructure The phishing and C2 (command and control) infrastructure are hosted on services with numerous domains associated with a single address, including fast flux services.
sentence.5228: Such services go a long way in obfuscating NetFlow traffic analysis and infrastructure tracking.
sentence.5229: The domains utilized also heavily use redacted “whois” information and obscure registration data.
sentence.5230: Every stage of this stealer uses domains that have redacted information for years.
sentence.5231: Multiple hosts were identified communicating with most of the CMD Stealer’s C2, but communications were not reliable enough to confirm threat actor ownership.
sentence.5232: Campaigns have utilized the same URL path */do/it.php since at least 8/20/2022, making it a reasonable path to alert.
sentence.5233: Targets This attack primarily targets victims in Portugal, Mexico, and Peru.
sentence.5234: Also, based on the configuration used to target victims in Mexico, the threat actor is interested in online business accounts, which usually have a better cash flow.
sentence.5235: Attribution Based on the code and language analysis, research is confident that the threat actor behind this campaign belongs to Latin America, specifically Brazil.
sentence.5236: Conclusions Defending against LOLBaS executions requires a multi-layered strategy.
sentence.5237: First, organizations should implement robust endpoint security solutions to detect and block suspicious behavior and unauthorized execution of LOLBaS. Additionally, organizations should enforce the principle of least privilege, such as zero trust, confirming that users have only the permissions necessary to perform their tasks, thus limiting potential impact of LOLBaS execution.
sentence.5238: Regular security awareness training should be provided to educate employees about the risks associated with social engineering.
sentence.5239: Continuous monitoring and auditing of system logs can also help detect and investigate any suspicious activities related to LOLBaS. sentence.5247: title: AA20-336A: Advanced Persistent Threat Actors Targeting U.S. Think Tanks url: https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-336a Original release date: December 1, 2020SummaryThis Advisory uses the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK:registered:) framework.
sentence.5248: See the ATT&CK for Enterprise for all referenced threat actor tactics and techniques.
sentence.5249: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) have observed persistent continued cyber intrusions by advanced persistent threat (APT) actors targeting U.S. think tanks.
sentence.5250: This malicious activity is often, but not exclusively, directed at individuals and organizations that focus on international affairs or national security policy.[1]
sentence.5251: The following guidance may assist U.S. think tanks in developing network defense procedures to prevent or rapidly detect these attacks.
sentence.5252: APT actors have relied on multiple avenues for initial access.
sentence.5253: These have included low-effort capabilities such as spearphishing emails and third-party message services directed at both corporate and personal accounts, as well as exploiting vulnerable web-facing devices and remote connection capabilities.
sentence.5254: Increased telework during the COVID-19 pandemic has expanded workforce reliance on remote connectivity, affording malicious actors more opportunities to exploit those connections and to blend in with increased traffic.
sentence.5255: Attackers may leverage virtual private networks (VPNs) and other remote work tools to gain initial access or persistence on a victim’s network.
sentence.5256: When successful, these low-effort, high-reward approaches allow threat actors to steal sensitive information, acquire user credentials, and gain persistent access to victim networks.
sentence.5257: Given the importance that think tanks can have in shaping U.S. policy, CISA and FBI urge individuals and organizations in the international affairs and national security sectors to immediately adopt a heightened state of awareness and implement the critical steps listed in the Mitigations section of this Advisory.
sentence.5258: Click here for a PDF version of this report.
sentence.5259: Technical DetailsATT&CK Profile CISA created the following MITRE ATT&CK profile to provide a non-exhaustive list of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) employed by APT actors to break through think tanks’ defenses, conduct reconnaissance in their environments, exfiltrate proprietary or confidential information, and execute effects on targets.
sentence.5260: These TTPs were included based upon closed reporting on APT actors that are known to target think tanks or based upon CISA incident response data.

sentence.5358: [T1561.002] MitigationsCISA and FBI recommend think tank organizations apply the following critical practices to strengthen their security posture.
sentence.5359: Leaders Implement a training program to familiarize users with identifying social engineering techniques and phishing emails.
sentence.5360: Users/Staff Log off remote connections when not in use.
sentence.5361: Be vigilant against tailored spearphishing attacks targeting corporate and personal accounts (including both email and social media accounts).
sentence.5362: Use different passwords for corporate and personal accounts.
sentence.5363: Install antivirus software on personal devices to automatically scan and quarantine suspicious files.
sentence.5364: Employ strong multi-factor authentication for personal accounts, if available.
sentence.5365: Exercise caution when: Opening email attachments, even if the attachment is expected and the sender appears to be known.
sentence.5366: See Using Caution with Email Attachments.
sentence.5367: Using removable media (e.g., USB thumb drives, external drives, CDs).
sentence.5368: IT Staff/Cybersecurity Personnel Segment and segregate networks and functions.
sentence.5369: Change the default username and password of applications and appliances.
sentence.5370: Employ strong multi-factor authentication for corporate accounts.
sentence.5371: Deploy antivirus software on organizational devices to automatically scan and quarantine suspicious files.
sentence.5372: Apply encryption to data at rest and data in transit.
sentence.5373: Use email security appliances to scan and remove malicious email attachments or links. Monitor key internal security tools and identify anomalous behavior.
sentence.5374: Flag any known indicators of compromise or threat actor behaviors for immediate response.
sentence.5375: Organizations can implement mitigations of varying complexity and restrictiveness to reduce the risk posed by threat actors who use Tor (The Onion Router) to carry out malicious activities.
sentence.5376: See the CISA-FBI Joint Cybersecurity Advisory on Defending Against Malicious Cyber Activity Originating from Tor for mitigation options and additional information.
sentence.5377: Prevent exploitation of known software vulnerabilities by routinely applying software patches and upgrades.
sentence.5378: Foreign cyber threat actors continue to exploit publicly known—and often dated—software vulnerabilities against broad target sets, including public and private sector organizations.
sentence.5379: If these vulnerabilities are left unpatched, exploitation often requires few resources and provides threat actors with easy access to victim networks.
sentence.5380: Review CISA and FBI’s Top 10 Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities and other CISA alerts that identify vulnerabilities exploited by foreign attackers.
sentence.5381: Implement an antivirus program and a formalized patch management process.
sentence.5382: Block certain websites and email attachments commonly associated with malware (e.g., .scr, .pif, .cpl, .dll, .exe).
sentence.5383: Block email attachments that cannot be scanned by antivirus software (e.g., .zip files).
sentence.5384: Implement Group Policy Object and firewall rules.
sentence.5385: Implement filters at the email gateway and block suspicious IP addresses at the firewall.
sentence.5386: Routinely audit domain and local accounts as well as their permission levels to look for situations that could allow an adversary to gain wide access by obtaining credentials of a privileged account.
sentence.5387: Follow best practices for design and administration of the network to limit privileged account use across administrative tiers.
sentence.5388: Implement a Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting & Conformance (DMARC) validation system.
sentence.5389: Disable or block unnecessary remote services.
sentence.5390: Limit access to remote services through centrally managed concentrators.
sentence.5391: Deny direct remote access to internal systems or resources by using network proxies, gateways, and firewalls.
sentence.5393: Disable file and printer sharing services.
sentence.5394: If these services are required, use strong passwords or Active Directory authentication.
sentence.5395: Ensure applications do not store sensitive data or credentials insecurely.
sentence.5396: Enable a firewall on agency workstations, configured to deny unsolicited connection requests.
sentence.5397: Disable unnecessary services on agency workstations and servers.
sentence.5398: Scan for and remove suspicious email attachments; ensure any scanned attachment is its "true file type" (i.e., the extension matches the file header).
sentence.5399: Monitor users' web browsing habits; restrict access to suspicious or risky sites.
sentence.5400: Contact law enforcement or CISA immediately regarding any unauthorized network access identified.

sentence.5409: title: Do Not Cross The 'RedLine' Stealer: Detections and Analysis url: https://www.splunk.com/en_us/blog/security/do-not-cross-the-redline-stealer-detections-and-analysis.html RedLine Stealer is a malware strain designed to steal sensitive information from compromised systems.
sentence.5410: It is typically distributed through phishing emails, social engineering tactics, and malicious URL links.
sentence.5411: Since it was released, threat actors and adversaries have leveraged RedLine Stealer because of its availability and flexibility for stealing credentials that can cause financial loss and data leakage.
sentence.5412: In 2020, there was a RedLine campaign that targeted both enterprise and personal devices.
sentence.5413: Many industries received these malicious campaigns, but the most impacted was the Healthcare and manufacturing sectors.
sentence.5414: Recently this year (May 10, 2023), there was a RedLine campaign found by stormshield that used a malicious chrome extension that will download several malware like Smoke Loader and Amadey Trojan.
sentence.5415: Amadey malware is a botnet that is being used now to distribute RedLine malware to steal data such as browser credentials, crypto wallets and even credit card information.
sentence.5416: This malicious software has been in the top malware sample shared for months on anyrun statistics reports as well as in Malware bazaar.
sentence.5417: In this blog post, the Splunk Threat Research Team provides a deep dive analysis of this threat and valuable insights to enable blue teamers to defend and detect this malware variant.
sentence.5418: Blog details include: Analysis of the phishing URLs The RedLine Loader The RedLine Stealer Capabilities Splunk Security Content Spear Phish Link Data The operators behind RedLine Stealer use several techniques to gain initial access to their victims.
sentence.5419: One common initial access technique that this Trojan Stealer uses is a phishing URL link.
sentence.5420: To gain more insight on how this malware executes its campaign, the Splunk Threat Research Team (STRT) collected 90 days of URL data from URLhaus and used Jupyter Notebooks to analyze the dataset to identify trends of the RedLine URL links.
sentence.5421: Figure 1 shows the list of URLs from the data related to RedLine Stealer.
sentence.5422: Based on URL tags, we can see that this Trojan is also bundled, downloaded or dropped by other malware like Amadey or SmokeLoader.
sentence.5423: Figure 1 Using the URLhaus dataset, we can also learn that RedLine Stealer abuses several known legitimate file/code sharing and collaboration platforms for its campaigns.
sentence.5424: Figure 2 shows the top 20 domains that RedLine Stealer used to host its malware.
sentence.5425: Based on the list below, the most commonly abused legitimate file sharing domains are GitHub, Dropbox, Discord, Bitbucket, OneDrive and Google Drive.
sentence.5426: The use of these legitimate platforms allows threat actors or adversaries to evade detections or to blend in its C2 communication with other normal network traffic so security solutions will not raise any red flags or detection alerts.
sentence.5427: Figure 2 In the following section, we explore a recent RedLine Loader used, the defense evasion technique and RedLine Stealer capabilities.
sentence.5428: Self Extractor Loader The Splunk Threat Research Team found an interesting RedLine Stealer Loader that was compiled as Win32 Cabinet self extractor executable (wextract) (1) (2).
sentence.5429: This self-extracting archive is a type of compressed file that contains multiple files and can be executed as a program.
sentence.5430: When a user runs a self-extracting archive, the contents of the archive are extracted to a specified location on the system.
sentence.5431: Figure 3 shows a simple flow diagram of how RedLine Stealer uses a loader in the form of a self-extracting archive (.exe) to initiate its infection.
sentence.5432: This loader then executes two more self-extracting archive executables that are responsible for decrypting a shellcode to load the Amadey Trojan and two instances of the RedLine Stealer malware onto the system.
sentence.5433: Additionally, the loader also executes a .NET executable that is responsible for defense evasion.
sentence.5434: Figure 3 (For a larger resolution of this diagram visit this link) Defense Evasion Component As described in Figure 3, the Redline Loader will also load an executable named it532878.exe, which is a .NET executable that is responsible for defense evasion.
sentence.5435: Figure 4 shows the code snippet of this RedLine component that will do the following: Escalate its privilege as administrator or trustedinstaller Try to disable Windows Defender service “WinDefend” Try to disable Tamper Protection settings of Windows Defender.
sentence.5436: Try to Disable AntiSpyware, Real Time Protection and notification of Windows Defender.
sentence.5437: Disable Windows update services such as (“wuauserv”, “WaaSMedicSvc”, “UsoSvc”)
sentence.5438: Disable Automatic Update and change Windows configurations related to Windows Update Figure 4 RedLine Stealer Deep Dive C2 Connection Check RedLine Stealer is designed to be stealthy and avoid detection by security software.
sentence.5439: Therefore, it typically starts by decrypting its initial configuration data, which is often encoded or encrypted to prevent detection.
sentence.5440: It starts its code by decrypting its initial configuration that the malware needs to connect to its Command and Control (C2) server and receive instructions on how to operate.
sentence.5441: This includes the domain or IP address of the C2 server, as well as the connection IDs and keys that are used to establish a secure connection.
sentence.5442: Figure 5 shows the code of the decryption algorithm used by RedLine Stealer to decrypt its initial configuration data which is a combination of Base64 and XOR functions.
sentence.5443: Figure 5 Once the initial configuration data has been decrypted, it will constantly check its bind connection to its C2 server to download further command arguments or other configuration settings that will dictate what functionality will be enabled for its malicious client file.
sentence.5444: Figure 6 shows the code of RedLine that consistently checks the connection of its client malware to the C2 server.
sentence.5445: If the connection fails, It will break and throw an exception.
sentence.5446: If the C2 server is already down or offline during analysis, this piece of code can be considered an anti-sandbox technique because RedLine will not continue its execution.
sentence.5447: Figure 6 After establishing a connection to its C2, it will fetch another configuration setting data from its C2 server that will fill the ScanningArg() class, which is a data structure of boolean variables that will serve as a switch to RedLine functionality.
sentence.5448: Figure 7 shows the snippet of ScanningArg() class data member of RedLine which accepts either ON or OFF (True or False) values to enable the chosen RedLine settings or functions.
sentence.5449: Figure 7 RedLine Capabilities RedLine Stealer has several features that will be executed depending on the configuration setting it downloaded from its C2 to steal information from the compromised or targeted host.
sentence.5450: Figure 8 is the screenshot showing several function capabilities of RedLine that we renamed during our analysis.
sentence.5451: Figure 8 Gather System Information As stated earlier, RedLine Stealer has the ability to collect or extract various types of system information from a targeted or compromised computer.
sentence.5452: The information that this malware can retrieve may be sensitive and can potentially compromise the security and privacy of the affected system.
sentence.5453: To provide a more detailed explanation, the table summary below shows each of the functions of the RedLine Stealer malware and describes the specific information that each function attempts to gather.
sentence.5454: Function name (renamed) Description func_GetHostSerialNumber() Retrieve the user domain name, username and host serial number (without “-”) and convert it into a MD5 hash func_GetExecutingAssembly() Get the full file path of its running malware sample func_GetLanguageTimeZoneOsVersion() Retrieves system default language, timezone and OS version func_GetUserName() Get the user name of the compromised host func_GetProcessor() Get processor information of the compromised host by executing "SELECT * FROM Win32_Processor" func_GetGraphicCards() Get AdapterRAM and Graphic Card Name and type by executing "root\\CIMV2", "SELECT *
sentence.5455: FROM Win32_VideoController" func_GetBrowsers() Parse browser application and browser version installed in the compromised host by querying "SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\Clients\StartMenuInternet" or "SOFTWARE\Clients\StartMenuInternet" registry func_GetTotalRAM() Get the total RAM size of compromised host by executing "SELECT * FROM Win32_OperatingSystem" and look for "TotalVisibleMemorySize" func_ListPrograms() Parse all installed application in the compromised host by querying 'SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall' registry func_GetFirewalls() Parse firewall and Anti Virus Product install in the compromised host by running "SELECT * FROM ROOT\\SecurityCenter2" "SELECT * FROM ROOT\\SecurityCenter" "SELECT *
sentence.5457: FROM FirewallProduct" "SELECT * FROM AntiSpyWareProduct" func_ListProcesses() Retrieve process list and process information by running 'SELECT *
sentence.5458: FROM Win32_Process' func_AvailableLanguage() Get the install input language Screen Capture Based on one of the RedLine samples we analyzed, we saw that it has a functionality to capture a screenshot of the targeted or compromised host as part of its data collection and exfiltration.
sentence.5459: In Figure 9 above, the function we’ve renamed as func_ScanScreen() is the one responsible for this screen capture capability.
sentence.5462: Function() to transfer a bit block of color data from the screen to the Graphic drawing surface that will be saved in memory stream for data exfiltration.
sentence.5463: Figure 9 Cracking Browser Password One of the powerful capabilities of this Trojan Stealer is cracking browser sensitive information like passwords, cookies, autofill and credit card information saved within the browser application.
sentence.5464: Figure 10 shows a simple diagram of how RedLine Stealer was able to decrypt the password saved in the chrome browser.
sentence.5465: It starts by locating and copying two specific file of Chrome profiles namely as “%userprofile%\Appdata\Local\Google\Chrome\User data\Local State” and “%userprofile%\Appdata\Local\Google\Chrome\User data\Default\Login Data” in the%temp% folder.
sentence.5466: Afterward it will read the copied “Local State” file to grab the encoded and encrypted master key to decrypt the password stored in the “Login Data”.
sentence.5467: The master key is encoded with Base64 and encrypted using Windows CryptProtectData() API.
sentence.5468: Once the master key is decrypted, it will parse the AES IV (Initialization vector) and the encrypted password in the copied “Login Data” database file to decrypt it using AES GCM algorithm.
sentence.5469: The decrypted password will be sent to its C2 Server as part of its data exfiltration.
sentence.5471: This malware can also steal wallet files by scanning Chrome wallet browser extensions.
sentence.5472: Figure 11 shows the RedLine Stealer code and how it enumerates several known Crypto Wallet directories and looks for files related to crypto currencies by looking for files having “wallet” substring on its file name.
sentence.5473: Figure 11 The table below shows some of the targeted Chrome browser extensions that RedLine Stealer tries to parse to look for Crypto Wallets.
sentence.5474: These extensions are popular among cryptocurrency users and are used to manage and store their cryptocurrency wallets' sensitive information.

sentence.5476: Description 5112ff1b75d9c33d10efafcbacdb4e2116280c1f5f3e6b6a64b44279997d96ee Redline stealer 8f45a89978ea72a7c3304c93cc56ac18087663ae33daa9f30f919652ba961175 loader eb8a15b1a42127970e7facc6133131dcc073a201419d8cc88c3c316819d1c2a2 Redline stealer afc48eabd725325d00324625eb9035c450d730c0b07d4d5a7246cbb1a3a443eb lr657198.exe 2a4193dcb95c7307e0a4f5586446c1c4adad17733a102a40d0b9227649191ff9 zifq8846.exe 5f9eff953d7ca49f594a864517dfdf37950a41693e53b79aa3a5c396613031bc kp356066.exe 52a52e958a0fef6aa14f27083f2d8675a20c2148be6456cacbda149411719b92 zigT1406.exe 850cd190aaeebcf1505674d97f51756f325e650320eaf76785d954223a9bee38 it532878.exe 5e82fc65d9dafc6da041e732597719aa9872bc82d8ff52c272277a1a49b8c9aa jr663319.exe Detections The Splunk Threat Research Team has curated relevant detections and tagged them to the RedLine Stealer Analytic Story to help security analysts detect adversaries leveraging the RedLine malware.
sentence.5477: For this release, we used and considered the relevant data endpoint telemetry sources such as: Process Execution & Command Line Logging Windows Security Event ID 4663, Sysmon, or any Common Information Model compliant EDR technology Windows Security Event Log Windows System Event Log Windows PowerShell Script Block Logging
sentence.5478: We maximized the usage of Windows Security EventCode 4663 for this analytic story.
sentence.5479: An event that is logged whenever an attempt is made to access an object (such as files, registry or directories) in the Windows file system.
sentence.5480: This EventCode can be helpful to monitor suspicious processes accessing critical files or folders like browser databases for credential dumping and data collection.
sentence.5481: As an example, we used this event to develop the analytic “Windows Query Registry UnInstall Program List'' that monitors suspicious processes accessing “uninstall registry”.
sentence.5482: This registry is being abused by several malware and APT to list all installed applications in the compromised or targeted host.

sentence.5489: Automated Playbooks All of the detections associated with this analytic story create entries in the Splunk Enterprise Security risk index by default and can be used seamlessly with risk notables and the Risk Notable Playbook Pack.
sentence.5490: Additionally, the Automated Enrichment playbook pack would also work well with the output of any of these analytics.

sentence.5498: This blog enables security analysts, blue teamers and Splunk customers to identify RedLine Stealer malware by helping the community discover RedLine Stealer tactics, techniques and procedures that are being used by several threat actors and adversaries (APT).
sentence.5499: By understanding its behaviors, we were able to generate telemetry and datasets to develop and test Splunk detections designed to defend and respond against this threat.
sentence.5500: Cyber defenders need to design and deploy effective monitoring capabilities that allow them to detect and respond to RedLine Stealer malware attacks.
