sentence.6118: title: Conti Ransomware url: https://thedfirreport.com/2021/05/12/conti-ransomware/ Introduction First seen in May 2020, Conti ransomware has quickly become one of the most common ransomware variants, according to Coveware.
sentence.6119: As per Coveware’s Quarterly Ransomware Report (Q1 2021), Conti has the 2nd highest market share after Sodinokibi, which we wrote about here.
sentence.6120: In April, we saw a threat actor go from an initial IcedID infection to deploying Conti ransomware domain wide in two days and 11 hours.
sentence.6121: The threat actors stayed dormant for most of this time, before jumping into action on an early Saturday morning.
sentence.6122: The hands on keyboard activity lasted for two and a half hours.
sentence.6123: They utilized RDP, PsExec, and Cobalt Strike to move laterally within the environment before executing Conti in memory across all active systems.
sentence.6124: Summary We assess with moderate confidence that the initial vector used by the threat actor was a zip file, which included a malicious JavaScript file, delivered through a phishing campaign.
sentence.6125: The JavaScript file would eventually download and execute the IcedID malware.
sentence.6126: Discovered in 2017, what started as a commodity malware is now currently being deployed as an initial access broker by ransomware threat actors.
sentence.6127: While there was some initial discovery activity from the IcedID malware, it went quiet, just beaconing to command and control but not performing any other activity.
sentence.6128: After being dormant for over two days, a Cobalt Strike Beacon was dropped and executed on the system infected with IcedID.
sentence.6129: The threat actors then ran another round of discovery activity with native windows utilities such as nltest.exe, whoami.exe, and net.exe.
sentence.6130: They then successfully escalated to SYSTEM privileges via Cobalt Strike’s built-in “named pipe impersonation” (GetSystem) functionality.
sentence.6131: The threat actors continued by moving laterally to the domain controllers on the network using SMB to transfer and execute a Cobalt Strike Beacon.
sentence.6132: During that time, we observed port scanning activity from one of the domain controllers, to identify open ports such as SSH, SMB, MSSQL, RDP and WinRM.
sentence.6133: After a brief gap of 15 minutes, the threat actors used PsExec, to copy and execute a Cobalt Strike Beacon DLL on most of the systems in the network.
sentence.6134: Later in the attack, the threat actor was seen establishing RDP connections from the beachhead host to the domain controller and other systems throughout the environment.
sentence.6135: This RDP activity was being proxied through the IcedID process running on that host, to a remote proxy over port 8080.
sentence.6136: To establish persistence, the attackers created a new local user on one of the domain controllers and added it to the Administrators group.
sentence.6137: Additionally, in an effort to evade any detection and prevention mechanisms, they disabled Windows Defender via a group policy modification.
sentence.6138: Within two and a half hours of Cobalt Strike showing up in the environment and just over two days after the initial IcedID infection, the threat actors completed their objective of encrypting all systems.
sentence.6139: Conti was executed in memory with the help of the Cobalt Strike Beacons domain wide.
sentence.6140: The ransomware note left by the infection included a link to their Tor site for further details.
sentence.6141: After further review of the environment (post encryption), we realized multiple systems (including a domain controller) were unable to be accessed and would not have been restorable even if the ransom had been paid.
sentence.6142: Services We offer multiple services including a Threat Feed service which tracks Cobalt Strike, Metasploit, Empire, PoshC2, etc.
sentence.6143: More information on this service and others can be found here.
sentence.6144: We also have artifacts available from this case such as pcaps, memory captures, files, Kape packages, and more, under our Security Researcher and Organization services.
sentence.6145: Timeline Analysis and reporting completed by @pigerlin, @MetallicHack, @yatinwad, and 1 unnamed contributor.
sentence.6146: Reviewed by @kostastsale, @RoxpinTeddy, and @TheDFIRReport MITRE ATT&CK Initial Access The IcedID DLL that we executed was most likely dropped through a zip file, which included a JavaScript file within it.
sentence.6147: Brad had a few posts about these around the time of this intrusion.
sentence.6149: Various attributes including the computer name and the OS version of the compromised system were sent through encoded cookie values.
sentence.6150: IcedID was executed via rundll32.exe and ran command and control over port 443 for the duration of the intrusion.
sentence.6151: rundll32.exe "C:\Users\REDACTED\AppData\Local\Temp\rate_x32.dat",update /i:"LaborBetray\license.dat" Discovery IcedID ran initial discovery after being executed on the beachhead.
sentence.6152: Various commands were executed to gather more information about the compromised environment; including the currently logged on user, domain trusts, groups, etc .
sentence.6156: Additional discovery commands were executed by Cobalt Strike.
sentence.6165: After moving laterally to a domain controller, they began looking for what networks were present in the environment using dsquery.
sentence.6166: cmd.exe /C dsquery subnet -limit 0 Shortly thereafter, port scanning was observed coming from a domain controller looking for common ports (such as SSH, SMB, MSSQL, WinRM and RDP, etc.)
sentence.6167: on systems residing in the same subnet.
sentence.6169: In order to obtain SYSTEM level privileges, Cobalt Strike’s built-in named piped impersonation (GetSystem) was used: Image: “C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe” CommandLine: “C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c
sentence.6170: echo 4d64fbbbf34 > \\. \pipe\b4312c” ParentImage: “C:\Windows\System32\runonce.exe” ParentCommandLine: “C:\Windows\system32\runonce.exe Lateral Movement The threat actor began lateral movement using remote execution of Cobalt Strike Beacon service binaries.
sentence.6171: Image: C:\Windows\system32\services.exe TargetObject: HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\d8d6deb\ImagePath Details: \\HOSTNAME\ADMIN$\d8d6deb.exe After this initial activity, Cobalt Strike was used to enable RDP, and allow it through the firewall, on the domain controllers.
sentence.6175: 0x0 /f cmd.exe /C netsh firewall set service type = remotedesktop mode = enable cmd.exe /C netsh firewall set rule group="remote desktop" new enable=Yes cmd.exe /C netsh advfirewall set rule group="remote desktop" new enable=Yes Following this, the threat actors then copied a Cobalt Strike Beacon DLL to the ADMIN$ share; and then, distributed it throughout the environment using PsExec. cmd.exe /C
sentence.6177: psexec.exe -accepteula -d -s \\<INTERNAL_IP> rundll32.exe C:\windows\192145.dll,StartW From here, RDP connections were established from the beachhead host to systems throughout the environment.
sentence.6178: The connections were proxied through the IcedID process.
sentence.6179: The threat actor used a redirector (38.135.122[.]194:8080) to proxy the RDP traffic being passed through the IcedID process.

sentence.6214: You’ll notice the fake address and fake phone number as well.
sentence.6215: All the domains were registered on 2021-03-30, and according to public data available in VirusTotal, three of them have been associated with Cobalt Strike infrastructure so far; the domain seen in this intrusion, powelin[.]com and awesents[.]com.

sentence.6235: title: Microsoft research uncovers new Zerobot capabilities - Microsoft Security Blog url: http://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/12/21/microsoft-research-uncovers-new-zerobot-capabilities/ Botnet malware operations are a constantly evolving threat to devices and networks.
sentence.6236: Threat actors target Internet of Things (IoT) devices for recruitment into malicious operations as IoT devices’ configurations often leave them exposed, and the number of internet-connected devices continue to grow.
sentence.6237: Recent trends have shown that operators are redeploying malware for a variety of distributions and objectives, modifying existing botnets to scale operations and add as many devices as possible to their infrastructure.
sentence.6238: Zerobot, a Go-based botnet that spreads primarily through IoT and web application vulnerabilities, is an example of an evolving threat, with operators continuously adding new exploits and capabilities to the malware.
sentence.6239: The Microsoft Defender for IoT research team has been monitoring Zerobot (also called ZeroStresser by its operators) for months.
sentence.6240: Zerobot is offered as part of a malware as a service scheme and has been updated several times since Microsoft started to track it.
sentence.6241: One domain with links to Zerobot was among several domains associated with DDoS-for-hire services seized by the FBI in December 2022.
sentence.6242: Microsoft has previously reported on the evolving threat ecosystem.
sentence.6243: The shift toward malware as a service in the cyber economy has industrialized attacks and has made it easier for attackers to purchase and use malware, establish and maintain access to compromised networks, and utilize ready-made tools to perform their attacks.
sentence.6244: We have tracked advertisements for the Zerobot botnet on various social media networks in addition to other announcements regarding the sale and maintenance of the malware, as well as new capabilities in development.
sentence.6245: In this blog post, we present information about the latest version of the malware, Zerobot 1.1, including newly identified capabilities and further context to Fortinet’s recent analysis on the threat.
sentence.6246: Zerobot 1.1 increases its capabilities with the inclusion of new attack methods and new exploits for supported architectures, expanding the malware’s reach to different types of devices.
sentence.6247: In addition to these findings, we’re sharing new indicators of compromise (IOCs) and recommendations to help defenders protect devices and networks against this threat.
sentence.6248: What is Zerobot? Zerobot affects a variety of devices that include firewall devices, routers, and cameras, adding compromised devices to a distributed denial of service (DDoS) botnet.
sentence.6249: Using several modules, the malware can infect vulnerable devices built on diverse architectures and operating systems, find additional devices to infect, achieve persistence, and attack a range of protocols.
sentence.6250: Microsoft tracks this activity as DEV-1061.
sentence.6251: The most recent distribution of Zerobot includes additional capabilities, such as exploiting vulnerabilities in Apache and Apache Spark (CVE-2021-42013 and CVE-2022-33891 respectively), and new DDoS attack capabilities.
sentence.6252: Microsoft uses DEV-#### designations as a temporary name given to an unknown, emerging, or developing cluster of threat activity, allowing Microsoft to track it as a unique set of information until we can reach high confidence about the origin or identity of the actor behind the activity.
sentence.6253: Once it meets defined criteria, a DEV group is converted to a named actor.
sentence.6254: How Zerobot gains and maintains device access IoT devices are often internet-exposed, leaving unpatched and improperly secured devices vulnerable to exploitation by threat actors.
sentence.6255: Zerobot is capable of propagating through brute force attacks on vulnerable devices with insecure configurations that use default or weak credentials.
sentence.6256: The malware may attempt to gain device access by using a combination of eight common usernames and 130 passwords for IoT devices over SSH and telnet on ports 23 and 2323 to spread to devices.
sentence.6257: Microsoft researchers identified numerous SSH and telnet connection attempts on default ports 22 and 23, as well as attempts to open ports and connect to them by port-knocking on ports 80, 8080, 8888, and 2323.
sentence.6258: In addition to brute force attempts on devices, Zerobot exploits dozens of vulnerabilities, which malware operators add on a rolling basis to gain access and inject malicious payloads.
sentence.6259: Zerobot 1.1 includes several new vulnerabilities, such as: VulnerabilityAffected softwareCVE-2017-17105Zivif PR115-204-P-RSCVE-2019-10655GrandstreamCVE-2020-25223WebAdmin of Sophos SG UTMCVE-2021-42013ApacheCVE-2022-31137Roxy-WICVE-2022-33891Apache SparkZSL-2022-5717MiniDVBLinuxSince the release of Zerobot 1.1, the malware operators have removed CVE-2018-12613, a phpMyAdmin vulnerability that could allow threat actors to view or execute files.
sentence.6260: Microsoft researchers have also identified that previous reports have used the vulnerability ID “ZERO-32906” for CVE-2018-20057, “GPON” for CVE-2018-10561, and “DLINK” for CVE-2016-20017; and that CVE-2020-7209 was mislabeled as CVE-2017-17106 and CVE-2022-42013 was mislabeled as CVE-2021-42013.
sentence.6261: Microsoft researchers have also found new evidence that Zerobot propagates by compromising devices with known vulnerabilities that are not included in the malware binary, such as CVE-2022-30023, a command injection vulnerability in Tenda GPON AC1200 routers.
sentence.6262: Upon gaining device access, Zerobot injects a malicious payload, which may be a generic script called zero.sh that downloads and attempts to execute Zerobot, or a script that downloads the Zerobot binary of a specific architecture.
sentence.6263: The bash script that attempts to download different Zerobot binaries tries to identify the architecture by brute-force, attempting to download and execute binaries of various architectures until it succeeds, as IoT devices are based on many computer processing units (CPUs).
sentence.6264: Microsoft has observed scripts targeting various architectures including ARM64, MIPS, and x86_64.
sentence.6265: Depending on the operating system of the device, the malware has different persistence mechanisms.
sentence.6266: Persistence tactics are used by malware operators to obtain and maintain access to devices.
sentence.6267: While Zerobot is unable to spread to Windows machines, we have found several samples that can run on Windows.
sentence.6268: On Windows machines, the malware copies itself to the Startup folder with the file name FireWall.exe
sentence.6270: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detects this malware and related malicious activity on both Windows and Linux devices.
sentence.6272: To achieve persistence on Linux-based devices, Zerobot uses a combination of desktop entry, daemon, and service methods: Desktop entry: Zerobot copies itself to $HOME/.config/ssh.service/sshf then writes a desktop entry file called sshf.desktop to the same directory.
sentence.6273: Older Linux versions use $HOME/.config/autostart instead of $HOME/.config/ssh.service.
sentence.6274: Daemon: Copies itself to /usr/bin/sshf and writes a configuration at /etc/init/sshf.conf.
sentence.6275: Service: Copies itself to /etc/sshf and writes a service configuration at /lib/system/system/sshf.service, then enables the service (to make sure it starts at boot) with two commands: systemctl enable sshf service enable sshf All persistence mechanisms on older Linux versions use my.bin and my.bin.desktop instead of sshf and sshf.desktop.
sentence.6277: In addition to the functions and attacks included in previous versions of the malware, Zerobot 1.1 has additional DDoS attack capabilities.
sentence.6278: These functions allow threat actors to target resources and make them inaccessible.
sentence.6279: Successful DDoS attacks may be used by threat actors to extort ransom payments, distract from other malicious activities, or disrupt operations.
sentence.6280: In almost every attack, the destination port is customizable, and threat actors who purchase the malware can modify the attack according to their target.
sentence.6281: The following are the previously known Zerobot capabilities: Attack methodDescriptionUDP_LEGITSends UDP packets without data.
sentence.6282: MC_PINGMeant for DDoS on Minecraft servers.
sentence.6283: Sends a handshake and status request.
sentence.6285: TCP_SOCKETContinuously sends random payloads on an open TCP socket.
sentence.6287: TLS_SOCKETContinuously sends random payloads on an open TLS socket.
sentence.6288: HTTP_HANDLESends HTTP GET requests using a Golang standard library.
sentence.6289: HTTP_RAWFormats and sends HTTP GET requests.
sentence.6290: HTTP_BYPASSSends HTTP GET requests with spoofed headers.
sentence.6292: headers are each one random byte (not necessarily ascii).Previously undisclosed and new capabilities are the following: Attack methodDescriptionUDP_RAWSends UDP packets where the payload is customizable.
sentence.6293: ICMP_FLOODSupposed to be an ICMP flood, but the packet is built incorrectly.
sentence.6294: TCP_CUSTOMSends TCP packets where the payload and flags are fully customizable.
sentence.6298: TCP_XMASChristmas tree attack (all TCP flags are set).
sentence.6300: How Zerobot spreads After persistence is achieved, Zerobot scans for other internet-exposed devices to infect.
sentence.6301: The malware randomly generates a number between 0 and 255 and scans all IPs starting with this value.
sentence.6302: Using a function called new_botnet_selfRepo_isHoneypot, the malware tries to identify honeypot IP addresses, which are used by network decoys to attract cyberattacks and collect information on threats and attempts to access resources.
sentence.6303: This function includes 61 IP subnets, preventing scanning of these IPs.
sentence.6304: Microsoft researchers also identified a sample that can run on Windows based on a cross-platform (Linux, Windows, macOS) open-source remote administration tool (RAT) with various features such as managing processes, file operations, screenshotting, and running commands.
sentence.6305: This tool was found by investigating the command-and-control (C2) IPs used by the malware.
sentence.6306: The script, which is used to download this RAT, is called impst.sh: Figure 1.
sentence.6307: The impst.sh script used to download the remote administration toolDefending devices and networks against Zerobot The continuous evolution and rapid addition of new capabilities in the latest Zerobot version underscores the urgency of implementing comprehensive security measures.
sentence.6308: Microsoft recommends the following steps to protect devices and networks against the threat of Zerobot: Use security solutions with cross-domain visibility and detection capabilities like Microsoft 365 Defender, which provides integrated defense across endpoints, identities, email, applications, and data.
sentence.6309: Microsoft Defender Antivirus and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detect Zerobot malware variants and malicious behavior related to this threat.
sentence.6310: Adopt a comprehensive IoT security solution such as Microsoft Defender for IoT to allow visibility and monitoring of all IoT and OT devices, threat detection and response, and integration with SIEM/SOAR and XDR platforms such as Microsoft Sentinel and Microsoft 365 Defender.
sentence.6311: Ensure secure configurations for devices: Change the default password to a strong one, and block SSH from external access.
sentence.6312: Maintain device health with updates: Make sure devices are up to date with the latest firmware and patches.
sentence.6313: Use least privileges access: Use a secure virtual private network (VPN) service for remote access and restrict remote access to the device.
sentence.6314: Harden endpoints with a comprehensive Windows security solution:Manage the apps your employees can use through Windows Defender Application Control and for unmanaged solutions, enabling Smart App Control.
sentence.6315: Perform timely cleanup of all unused and stale executables sitting on yours or your organizations’ devices.
sentence.6316: Detections Microsoft Defender for IoT Microsoft Defender for IoT uses detection rules and signatures to identify malicious behavior.
sentence.6317: Microsoft Defender for IoT has alerts for the following vulnerabilities and exploits which may be tied to Zerobot activity: CVE-2014-8361 CVE-2016-20017 CVE-2017-17105 CVE-2017-17215 CVE-2018-10561 CVE-2018-20057 CVE-2019-10655 CVE-2020-7209 CVE-2020-10987 CVE-2020-25506 CVE-2021-35395 CVE-2021-36260 CVE-2021-42013 CVE-2021-46422 CVE-2022-22965 CVE-2022-25075 CVE-2022-26186 CVE-2022-26210 CVE-2022-30023 CVE-2022-30525 CVE-2022-31137 CVE-2022-33891 CVE-2022-34538 CVE-2022-37061 ZERO-36290 ZSL-2022-5717 Microsoft Defender Antivirus Microsoft Defender Antivirus detects the malicious files under the following platforms and threat names:

sentence.6331: title: Just Because It’s Old Doesn’t Mean You Throw It Away (Including Malware!)
sentence.6332: url: https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/just-because-its-old-doesnt-mean-you-throw-it-away-including-malware Art, automobiles, and wine are often associated with things that appreciate in value as they age.
sentence.6333: Malware isn’t usually thought of this way, as most threat actors strive to keep their tools as current as possible with new lures and exploitation techniques.
sentence.6334: However, every once in a while, a campaign appears that turns this paradigm on its head.
sentence.6335: FortiGuard Labs came across one such recent campaign using the MyDoom worm.
sentence.6336: MyDoom (also known as Novarg and Mimail) was first discovered back in 2004.
sentence.6337: And while it has seen some updates and modifications since its introduction, it is an anachronism in the malware world that continues to operate well beyond expectations.
sentence.6338: Affected Platforms: WindowsImpacted Users: Windows usersImpact: Potential to deploy additional malware for additional purposesSeverity Level: Medium Typical phishing e-mail The typical MyDoom phishing e-mail contains subjects referencing a delivery error or testing.
sentence.6339: Email headers contain a rejection reason and a custom “Content-Type”.
sentence.6340: There is also an attachment that may or may not be zipped.
sentence.6341: This attachment (unless zipped) is the MyDoom executable.
sentence.6342: FortiGuard Labs encountered the following message subjects in our recent investigation: Click me baby, one more time RETURNED MAIL: SEE TRANSCRIPT FOR DETAILS Isnydosj anhr ayownizdiitis Delivery failed Test Delivery reports about your e-mail Status Returned mail: Data format error RETURNED MAIL:
sentence.6343: DATA FORMAT ERROR Returned mail: see transcript for details Mail System Error - Returned Mail The following attachment names were also found to be used repeatedly: document.zip transcript.zip letter.zip attachment.zip .zip message.zip message.scr golfasian.com readme.scr mail.zip text.cmd <random number>@7686f6a96.com file.zip attachment.scr Typical attachment The MyDoom executables attached to its phishing e-mails have an extension hidden by default by most Windows deployments (.cmd, .scr, .com, etc.).
sentence.6344: This increases the chances that users won’t identify it as malicious.
sentence.6345: Despite the extension, the file is a 32-bit Windows executable packed using the UPX (Ultimate Packer for Executables) packer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UPX) to compress and make it more difficult to analyze.
sentence.6346: With that being said, UPX has been around for quite some time.
sentence.6347: When used without modification, it is quite easy to decompress the original executable using the tool itself.
sentence.6348: MyDoom Unpacked The packer decompresses and executes the actual MyDoom code.
sentence.6349: Upon execution, an attempt to alter the Windows firewall settings is made.
sentence.6350: A user logged on to the system would see a request to grant access for the executable to communicate out through the Firewall.
sentence.6351: MyDoom next makes a copy of itself, places it in the “Temp” folder (C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp), and changes the name to a known Windows application/process.
sentence.6353: It also creates a file full of garbage text that is not referenced again once created.
sentence.6354: MyDoom communicates over port 1042 to both send and receive.
sentence.6355: It rotates through a number of possible C2 domains in an attempt to locate an active one.
sentence.6356: As part of the legacy of spreading through file-sharing utilities, MyDoom also litters the “C:\Program Files\Common Files\Microsoft
sentence.6357: Shared” folder with multiple versions of itself.
sentence.6358: It renames itself as some now very old and obsolete applications (e.g., Kazaa Lite) with a random name or phrase attached.
sentence.6359: Application names include: Kazaa Lite Harry Potter ICQ 4 Lite WinRAR.v.3.2 Winamp 5.0 (en) Crack Winamp 5.0 (en) Conclusion Despite its advanced age, there are still fresh infections of MyDoom occurring in the wild, along with corresponding phishing events.
sentence.6360: This goes to show that even older malware can still be dangerous no matter their age Fortinet Protections Fortinet customers are already protected from this malware through FortiGuard’s Web Filtering, AntiVirus, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR services: FortiGuard customers are protected against this latest MyDoom campaign, which is blocked by FortiMail.
sentence.6361: The following (AV) signature detects the malware samples mentioned in this blog W32/MyDoom.
sentence.6363: E!tr The FortiGuard AntiVirus service is supported by FortiGate, FortiMail, FortiClient, and FortiEDR.
sentence.6364: Customers running current AntiVirus updates are protected.
sentence.6365: The WebFiltering client blocks all network-based URIs.
sentence.6366: Fortinet has multiple solutions designed to help train users to understand and detect phishing threats, including the FortiPhish Phishing Simulation Service, which uses real-world simulations to help organizations test user awareness and vigilance to phishing threats and to train and reinforce proper practices when users encounter targeted phishing attacks.
sentence.6367: In addition to these protections, we suggest that organizations have their end users undergo our FREE NSE training: NSE 1 – Information Security Awareness.
sentence.6368: It includes a module on Internet threats designed to help end users learn how to identify and protect themselves from various types of phishing attacks.

sentence.6373: title: Carbon Black’s TrueBot Detection url: https://blogs.vmware.com/security/2023/06/carbon-blacks-truebot-detection.html VMware’s Carbon Black Managed Detection and Response (MDR) team began seeing a surge of TrueBot activity in May 2023.
sentence.6375: Downloader has been seen since at least 2017.
sentence.6376: TrueBot is under active development by Silence, with recent versions using a Netwrix vulnerability for delivery.
sentence.6377: In this article, we will break down what we have seen in customers’ environments and how Carbon Black MDR detects and responds to the threat.
sentence.6378: History Just as its name suggests, TrueBot is a downloader trojan botnet that uses command and control servers to collect information on compromised systems and uses that compromised system as a launching point for further attacks, as seen recently with Clop Ransomware.
sentence.6379: TrueBot was known for using malicious emails to drop their malware but was recently seen using a Netwrix vulnerability as their delivery method.
sentence.6380: VMware’s MDR team has seen this vulnerability used firsthand in customer environments, as explored below.
sentence.6381: TrueBot is also using Raspberry Robin (a worm) as a delivery vector.
sentence.6382: While Silence Group is known for targeting banks and financial institutions, TrueBot has also been seen targeting the education sector.
sentence.6383: In the Carbon Black Detection & Notable Attacks section, we break down the sectors that we have seen targeted from our platform.
sentence.6384: Attribution Though a threat actor group called Silence Group is attributed to this malware, Group-IB has linked the group with Russia’s EvilCorp (Indrik Spider) due to the downloaders they use being similar.
sentence.6385: The MDR team has explored this link and has not found substantial evidence to back this claim.
sentence.6386: Researchers thought EvilCorp to be linked to TrueBot due to TrueBot dropping FlawedGrace.
sentence.6387: FlawedGrace is malware that is attributed to EvilCorp.
sentence.6388: Though TrueBot drops this payload, the malware operators could purchase access to this tool directly from EvilCorp.
sentence.6389: Another link explored was TrueBot dropping Clop Ransomware, which was previously used by EvilCorp.
sentence.6390: However, Clop is ransomware-as-a-service, so anyone can purchase access to this tool.
sentence.6391: Lastly, Silence is a Russian-speaking cybercriminal group that uses Russian web hosting services.
sentence.6392: Though EvilCorp is also Russian, this is not strong evidence to link the two, as there are dozens of Russian APTs.
sentence.6393: Due to these findings, we cannot say for sure whether EvilCorp and TrueBot are connected.
sentence.6394: Carbon Black Detection Carbon Black is very effective at detecting TrueBot and its associated activity.
sentence.6395: This section will focus on what Carbon Black detected and the visibility into the attack process.
sentence.6397: The infection appeared to have started with a drive-by-download from Chrome for the executable ‘update.exe’.
sentence.6398: Figure 1.2 Update.exe being downloaded A user had to click on this in order to execute the malware.
sentence.6399: Upon execution, the malware immediately begins to look for EDR and antivirus software.
sentence.6400: Figure 1.3 Looking for EDR/AV Once executed, it connected to 94[.]142.138.61IP, which is a Russian IP address that is known to be attributed to TrueBot.
sentence.6401: At the address, the executable ‘3ujwy2rz7v.exe’ was downloaded and then launched by cmd.exe.
sentence.6402: Figure 1.4 3ujwy2rz7v.exe activity The executable then connected to the C2 domain name ‘dremmfyttrred[.]com’.
sentence.6403: The activity thereafter included dumps of LSASS, exfiltration of data, and system and process enumerations.
sentence.6404: Managed Detection and Response stops this activity through first the detection of the activity and then the implementation of system quarantines, hash banning, policy reviews, and policy modifications.
sentence.6405: Customers are informed of the observed activity and actions taken by the team every step of the way.
sentence.6406: Indicators of Compromise 45.182.189[.]103 Dremmfyttrred.com 94.142.138[.]61 Locations: Russia, Panama Update.exe e8c342845a02608ecd1cca8ad409895bf530f6c2830b8af8b70a3d90e8b8d3da Document_26_apr_2443807.exe fe746402c74ac329231ae1b5dffa8229b509f4c15a0f5085617f14f0c1579040 172.64.155[.]188 104.18.32[.]68 3ujwy2rz7v.exe Summary TrueBot can be a particularly nasty infection for any network.
sentence.6407: When an organization is infected with this malware, it can quickly escalate to become a bigger infection, similar to how ransomware spreads throughout a network.
sentence.6408: Carbon Black is able to quickly detect TrueBot and its associated activity and, with the help of MDR, be able to detect and contain it early in the attack chain before the threat escalates.
sentence.6409: title: ITG10 Likely Targeting South Korean Entities of Interest to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) url: https://securityintelligence.com/posts/itg10-targeting-south-korean-entities/ In late April 2023, IBM Security X-Force uncovered documents that are most likely part of a phishing campaign mimicking credible senders, orchestrated by a group X-Force refers to as ITG10, and aimed at delivering RokRAT malware, similar to what has been observed by others.
sentence.6410: ITG10’s tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) overlap with APT37 and ScarCruft.
sentence.6411: The initial delivery method is conducted via a LNK file, which drops two Windows shortcut files containing obfuscated PowerShell scripts in charge of downloading a second stage RokRAT shellcode.
sentence.6412: RokRAT can execute remote C2 commands, data exfiltration, file download/upload, and keylogging.
sentence.6413: The uncovered lure documents suggest ITG10 may be targeting individuals and organizations involved in foreign policy associated with the Korean peninsula.
sentence.6414: Key Findings: ITG10 likely targeting South Korean government, universities, think tanks, and dissidents Phishing emails spoof legitimate senders to deliver RokRAT via LNK files Email attachments mimic legitimate documents Additional malware samples possibly related to ITG10 RokRAT campaigns Decoy Documents In late April 2023, X-Force uncovered several Zip Archives files hosting multiple lure documents likely sent via phishing campaigns operated by ITG10. X-Force assesses that the documents are likely decoys geared toward various personnel within two subsets of activity: South Korean government, communication, and educational centers; and energy, manufacturing, and supply chain.
sentence.6415: This section provides analysis of the lure documents and potential targets.
sentence.6416: South Korean Government, Communications and Educational Centers
sentence.6417: The first suspected subset of activity revealed Korean-language lure documents.
sentence.6418: The first titled (0722)상임위원회 및 상설특별위원회 위원 명단(최종).zip
sentence.6419: [(0722) List of Standing Committee and Standing Special Committee members (final).zip)], contains charts listing the Standing Committee members and assignments associated with broadcast media in South Korea as of July 2022.
sentence.6420: Examination of the contents suggests that it is a directory of eighteen South Korean parliamentary committee assignments, the number of committee members, their names, and political party affiliation.
sentence.6421: Committees include Education and Judicial, International and Foreign Affairs, Defense, and Intelligence.
sentence.6422: The intended targets for this lure are likely to be parliamentary members seeking information on their committee assignment or reporters covering parliament.
sentence.6424: An additional decoy document titled 계약서내용.pdf (Contract detail.pdf) appears to be associated with a national South Korean broadcaster.
sentence.6425: The contents detail the company’s approach to radio drama production scheduled for broadcast in May 2023.
sentence.6426: North Korean sponsored threat actors have previously been known to create accounts posing as broadcasting scriptwriters to deceive watchers.
sentence.6427: In 2021, North Korean threat actors compromised several email accounts of prominent defectors to send malicious documents to contacts working on DPRK issues.
sentence.6428: ITG10 has also been known to infect news websites with malware likely to spy on readers.
sentence.6429: A third decoy 2023년도 4월 29일 세미나.pdf (April 29, 2023 Seminar.pdf) appears to be an itinerary for an event hosted in April 2023 by a South Korean think tank.
sentence.6430: The event includes multiple seminars on political theory, military history, and a talk on “Intelligence activities and cyber security of the National Intelligence Service.”
sentence.6431: Members of this think tank include professors from multiple universities and South Korean government entities.
sentence.6432: There are two mobile phone numbers and a Zoom link with a password in the decoy document, which can be scraped to launch phishing material over social medial platforms.
sentence.6433: Based on the document’s content, academic and government employees, especially those in intelligence and cybersecurity, are probable targets for phishing emails containing this type of decoy document.
sentence.6434: 2023년도 4월 29일 세미나.pdf Energy, Manufacturing and Supply Chain The second grouping of lure documents features a zip file projects in Libya.zip containing a LNK file Pipelines Profile (Elfeel- Sharara-Mellitah + Wafa – Mellitah).lnk, as well as additional English-language decoy files.
sentence.6435: The decoy files are a Microsoft Word Document and PDF copy of a document titled Proposed MOU GTE Korea.
sentence.6436: The documents appear to be legitimate and establish a written Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) between an authentic privately owned Libyan energy company and a South Korean consulting firm specializing in energy, procurement, construction and finance (EPC&F).
sentence.6437: In addition, the zip contains a second non-malicious lure PDF titled MFZ Executive Summary Korea detailing a feasibility study regarding the development and expansion of the “sea port free zone of Misurata.”
sentence.6438: Based on the decoy content, the likely recipients of this phishing campaign would be organizations or individuals involved with a construction project in the Middle East.
sentence.6439: The Middle East has been a traditional customer for many large-scale construction projects for multiple South Korean companies, and there has been a recent push by the South Korean administration to what’s known as the ‘2nd construction boom’.
sentence.6440: These construction projects are part of the South Korean government’s pivot to the Middle East, deepening ties both militarily and economically.
sentence.6441: Sample Analysis RokRAT has been previously analyzed as having a multi-stage process with two components.
sentence.6442: The first involves tooling, and the second involves the payload, likely to inhibit researchers from analyzing the final payload, while maintaining the ability to stop delivery once a target system is infected.
sentence.6443: RokRAT campaigns typically begin with a phishing email with a ZIP file attachment, containing a LNK file disguised as a Word document.
sentence.6444: When the LNK file is activated, a PowerShell script is executed, opening a decoy document to start the download process of RokRAT which is hosted at OneDrive or similar cloud application.
sentence.6445: In another campaign, ITG10 was observed delivering RokRAT via HWP and Word files containing LNK files.
sentence.6446: In X-Force’s analysis of recent RokRAT-related files, in lieu of a ZIP file, we found Optical Disc Image files (ISO) containing LNK files that had slightly modified PowerShell scripts, and Hangul Word Processor decoy documents (HWP).
sentence.6447: ISO Files The ISO files that X-Force observed contained a LNK file disguised as an exe icon, subsequently containing a HWP file, and a batch file.
sentence.6448: The LNK file contains a PowerShell command, as seen below as an example.
sentence.6449: Once the LNK file is executed, it extracts and drops a decoy file, and a batch file within the user’s %TEMP% folder.
sentence.6450: In this instance, the files were 2023년도 4월 29일 세미나.pdf – decoy file, and 230415.bat.
sentence.6451: icon_location = C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft\Edge\Application\msedge.exe PowerShell Commands: Related Malware?
sentence.6452: While researching the RokRAT-related files, X-Force also uncovered three LNK files that behave differently than expected.
sentence.6453: There is no use of OneDrive or similar cloud applications to host a second-stage payload, and instead of dropping a batch file, these LNK files drop VBS, with the obfuscation technique for the dropped files being hex-encoding vs. string concatenation.
sentence.6454: In addition, the RokRAT LNK files drop batch files and downloads the payload that is decoded using the first byte as a key, then the payload is executed using Windows API functions (VirtualProtect).
sentence.6455: With these additional LNK files, the VBS downloaders do not perform these actions.
sentence.6456: The LNK files analyzed contain an encoded PowerShell, and once the LNK files are executed, the PowerShell script is run, and two files are dropped to the user’s %TEMP% folder.
sentence.6457: In one analyzed sample, the files dropped were a VBS file (tmp<random-9-digit-number>.vbs ), and a Plaintext file with contents asdfgqwert.
sentence.6458: The VBS file will get executed via Wscript.exe: “C:\Windows\System32\WScript.exe” “C:\Users\Usuario\AppData\Local\Temp\tmp<nine-digit-number>.vbs”.
sentence.6459: Wscript.exe is a service Wscript.exe is a service provided by the Windows system with scripting abilities.
sentence.6460: Subsequently, two GET requests are initiated.
sentence.6461: In a third file we analyzed, instead of the LNK file dropping a VBS and a Plaintext file, a VBS file and a JPEG decoy file are dropped to the users %TEMPT% folder.
sentence.6462: In this case, the JPEG decoy file appears to be a correspondence related to the “Proof of Digital Assets”.
sentence.6463: At the time of this analysis, X-Force was unable to retrieve the final payload from the servers as they have been taken down; therefore, it is uncertain whether these additional LNK files are related to ITG10 activity.
sentence.6464: Further research and analysis are needed to determine relevance and attribution.
sentence.6466: Decoded PowerShell: tmp1698268529.vbs GET Requests: Proof of Digital Assets JPEG X-Force Recommendations Multiple lure documents uncovered in this campaign suggest ITG10 continues to target individuals and organizations involved in foreign policy, potentially related to shifts in the geopolitical and security environment on the Korean peninsula.
sentence.6467: IBM X-Force assesses with high confidence that individuals and organizations holding strategic, political, or military information in connection with the Korean peninsula will see elevated threats from the DPRK, given ITG10’s previous and recent activity.
sentence.6468: Organizations that may be at elevated risk of targeting from ITG10 have the potential to decrease the risk to their organization by employing heightened vigilance toward potential phishing emails, warning employees of the phishing email threats, employing and closely monitoring endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, and leveraging behavioral analytics to identify malicious behavior.
sentence.6469: We also recommend that potentially targeted organizations alert on the following indicators of compromise to detect behavior related to this campaign.

sentence.6472: title: Abusing cloud services to fly under the radar url: https://research.nccgroup.com/2021/01/12/abusing-cloud-services-to-fly-under-the-radar/ tl;dr NCC Group and Fox-IT have been tracking a threat group with a wide set of interests, from intellectual property (IP) from victims in the semiconductors industry through to data from the airline industry.
sentence.6473: In their intrusions they regularly abuse cloud services from Google and Microsoft to achieve their goals.
sentence.6474: NCC Group and Fox-IT observed this threat actor during various incident response engagements performed between October 2019 until April 2020.
sentence.6475: Our threat intelligence analysts noticed clear overlap between the various cases in infrastructure and capabilities, and as a result we assess with moderate confidence that one group was carrying out the intrusions across multiple victims operating in Chinese interests.
sentence.6476: In open source this actor is referred to as Chimera by CyCraft.
sentence.6477: NCC Group and Fox-IT have seen this actor remain undetected, their dwell time, for up to three years.
sentence.6478: As such, if you were a victim, they might still be active in your network looking for your most recent crown jewels.
sentence.6479: We contained and eradicated the threat from our client’s networks during incident response whilst our Managed Detection and Response (MDR) clients automatically received detection logic.
sentence.6480: With this publication, NCC Group and Fox-IT aim to provide the wider community with information and intelligence that can be used to hunt for this threat in historic data and improve detections for intrusions by this intrusion set.
sentence.6481: Throughout we use terminology to describe the various phases, tactics, and techniques of the intrusions standardized by MITRE with their ATT&CK framework .
sentence.6482: Near the end of this article all the tactics and techniques used by the adversary are listed with links to the MITRE website with more information.
sentence.6483: From initial access to defense evasion: how it is done In all the intrusions we have observed they are performed in similar ways by the adversary: from initial access all the way to actions on objectives.
sentence.6484: The objective in these cases appear to be stealing sensitive data from the victim’s networks.
sentence.6485: Credential theft and password spraying to Cobalt Strike This adversary starts with obtaining usernames and passwords of their victim from previous breaches.
sentence.6486: These credentials are used in a credential stuffing or password spraying attack against the victim’s remote services, such as webmail or other internet reachable mail services.
sentence.6487: After obtaining a valid account, they use this account to access the victim’s VPN, Citrix or another remote service that allows access to the network of the victim.
sentence.6488: Information regarding these remotes services is taken from the mailbox, cloud drive, or other cloud resources accessible by the compromised account.
sentence.6489: As soon as they have a foothold on a system (also known as patient zero or index case), they check the permissions of the account on that system, and attempt to obtain a list of accounts with administrator privileges.
sentence.6490: With this list of administrator-accounts, the adversary performs another password spraying attack until a valid admin account is compromised.
sentence.6491: With this valid admin account, a Cobalt Strike beacon is loaded into memory of patient zero.
sentence.6492: From here on the adversary stops using the victim’s remote service to access the victim’s network, and starts using the Cobalt Strike beacon for remote access and command and control.
sentence.6494: The adversary continues their discovery of the victim’s network from patient zero.
sentence.6495: Various scans and queries are used to find proxy settings, domain controllers, remote desktop services, Citrix services, and network shares.
sentence.6496: If the obtained valid account is already member of the domain admins group, the first lateral move in the network is usually to a domain controller where the adversary also deploys a Cobalt Strike beacon.
sentence.6497: Otherwise, a jump host or other system likely used by domain admins is found and equipped with a Cobalt Strike beacon.
sentence.6498: After this the adversary dumps the domain admin credentials from the memory of this machine, continues lateral moving through the network, and places Cobalt Strike beacons on servers for increased persistent access into the victim’s network.
sentence.6499: If the victim’s network contains other Windows domains or different network security zones, the adversary scans and finds the trust relationships and jump hosts, attempting to move into the other domains and security zones.
sentence.6500: The adversary is typically able to perform all the steps described above within one day.
sentence.6501: During this process, the adversary identifies data of interest from the network of the victim.
sentence.6502: This can be anything from file and directory-listings, configuration files, manuals, email stores in the guise of OST- and PST-files, file shares with intellectual property (IP), and data scraped from memory.
sentence.6503: If the data is small enough, it is exfiltrated through the command and control channel of the Cobalt Strike beacons.
sentence.6504: However, usually the data is compressed with WinRAR, staged on another system of the victim, and from there copied to a OneDrive-account controlled by the adversary.
sentence.6505: After the adversary completes their initial exfiltration, they return every few weeks to check for new data of interest and user accounts.
sentence.6506: At times they have been observed attempting to perform a degree of anti-forensic activities including clearing event logs, time stomping files, and removing scheduled tasks created for some objectives.
sentence.6507: But this isn’t done consistently across their engagements.
sentence.6508: Framing the adversary’s work in the MITRE ATT&CK framework Credential access (TA0006)
sentence.6509: The earliest and longest lasting intrusion by this threat we observed, was at a company in the semiconductors industry in Europe and started early Q4 2017.
sentence.6510: The more recent intrusions took place in 2019 at companies in the aviation industry.
sentence.6511: The techniques used to achieve access at the companies in the aviation industry closely resembles techniques used at victims in the semiconductors industry.
sentence.6512: The threat used valid accounts against remote services: Cloud-based applications utilizing federated authentication protocols.
sentence.6513: Our incident responders analysed the credentials used by the adversary and the traces of the intrusion in log files.
sentence.6514: They uncovered an obvious overlap in the credentials used by this threat and the presence of those same accounts in previously breached databases.
sentence.6515: Besides that, the traces in log files showed more than usual login attempts with a username formatted as email address, e.g.<username>@<email domain>.
sentence.6516: While usernames for legitimate logins at the victim’s network were generally formatted like <domain>\<username>.
sentence.6517: And attempted logins came from a relative small set of IP-addresses.
sentence.6518: For the investigators at NCC Group and Fox-IT these pieces of evidence supported the hypothesis of the adversary achieving credentials access by brute force, and more specifically by credential stuffing or password spraying.
sentence.6520: In some of the intrusions the adversary used the valid account to directly login to a Citrix environment and continued their work from there.
sentence.6521: In one specific case, the adversary now armed with the valid account, was able to access a document stored in SharePoint Online, part of Microsoft Office 365.
sentence.6522: This specific document described how to access the internet facing company portal and the web-based VPN client into the company network.
sentence.6523: Within an hour after grabbing this document, the adversary accessed the company portal with the valid account.
sentence.6524: From this portal it was possible to launch the web-based VPN.
sentence.6525: The VPN was protected by two-factor authentication (2FA) by sending an SMS with a one-time password (OTP) to the user account’s primary or alternate phone number.
sentence.6526: It was possible to configure an alternate phone number for the logged in user account at the company portal.
sentence.6527: The adversary used this opportunity to configure an alternate phone number controlled by the adversary.
sentence.6528: By performing two-factor authentication interception by receiving the OTP on their own telephone number, they gained access to the company network via the VPN.
sentence.6529: However, they also made a mistake during this process within one incident.
sentence.6530: Our hypothesis is that they tested the 2FA-system first or selected the primary phone number to send a SMS to.
sentence.6531: However the European owner of the account received a text message with Simplified Chinese characters on the primary phone number in the middle of the night Eastern European Time (EET).
sentence.6532: NCC Group and Fox-IT identified that the language in the text-message for 2FA is based on the web browser’s language settings used during the authentication flow.
sentence.6533: Thus the 2FA code was sent with supporting Chinese text.
sentence.6534: Account discovery (T1087) With access into the network of the victim, the adversary finds a way to install a Cobalt Strike beacon on a system of the victim (see Execution).
sentence.6535: But before doing so, we observed the adversary checking the current permissions of the obtained user account with the following commands: net user net user Administrator net user <username>
sentence.6536: /domain net localgroup administrators If the user account doesn’t have local administrative or domain administrative permissions, the adversary attempts to discover which local or domain admin accounts exist, and exfiltrates the admin’s usernames.
sentence.6537: To identify if privileged users are active on remote servers, the adversary makes use of PsLogList from Microsoft Sysinternals to retrieve the Security event logs.
sentence.6538: The built-in Windows quser-command to show logged on users is also heavily used by them.
sentence.6539: If such a privileged user was recently active on a server the adversary executes Cobalt Strike’s built-in Mimikatz to dump its password hashes.
sentence.6541: The adversary started a password spraying attack against those domain admin accounts, and successfully got a valid domain admin account this way.
sentence.6542: In other cases, the adversary moved laterally to another system with a domain admin logged in.
sentence.6543: We observed the use of Mimikatz on this system and saw the hashes of the logged in domain admin account going through the command and control channel of the adversary.
sentence.6544: The adversary used a tool called NtdsAudit to dump the password hashes of domain users as well as we observed the following command: msadcs.exe "NTDS.dit" -s
sentence.6545: "SYSTEM" -p RecordedTV_pdmp.txt --users-csv RecordedTV_users.csv Note: the adversary renamed ntdsaudit.exe to msadcs.exe.
sentence.6546: But we also observed the adversary using the tool ntdsutil to create a copy of the Active Directory database NTDS.dit followed by a repair action with esentutl to fix a possible corrupt NTDS.dit: ntdsutil "ac i ntds" "ifm" "create full C:\Windows\Temp\tmp" q q esentutl /p /o
sentence.6547: ntds.dit Both ntdsutil and esentutl are by default installed on a domain controller.
sentence.6548: A tool used by the adversary which wasn’t installed on the servers by default, was DSInternals.
sentence.6549: DSInternals is a PowerShell module that makes use of internal Active Directory features.
sentence.6550: The files and directories found on various systems of a victim match with DSInternals version 2.16.1.
sentence.6551: We have found traces that indicate DSInternals was executed and at which time, which match with the rest of the traces of the intrusion.
sentence.6552: We haven’t recovered traces of how the adversary used DSInternals, but considering the phase of the intrusion the adversary used the tool, it is likely they used it for either account discovery or privilege escalation, or both.
sentence.6554: The adversary installs a hackers best friend during the intrusion: Cobalt Strike.
sentence.6555: Cobalt Strike is a framework designed for adversary simulation intended for penetration testers and red teams.
sentence.6556: It has been widely adopted by malicious threats as well.
sentence.6557: The Cobalt Strike beacon is installed in memory by using a PowerShell one-liner.
sentence.6558: At least the following three versions of Cobalt Strike have been in use by the adversary: Cobalt Strike v3.8, observed Q2 2017Cobalt Strike v3.12, observed Q3 2018Cobalt Strike v3.14, observed Q2 2019 Fox-IT has been collecting information about Cobalt Strike team servers since January 2015.
sentence.6559: This research project covers the fingerprinting of Cobalt Strike servers and is described in Fox-IT blog “Identifying Cobalt Strike team servers in the wild”.
sentence.6560: The collected information allows Fox-IT to correlate Cobalt Strike team servers, based on various configuration settings.
sentence.6561: Because of this, historic information was available during this investigation.
sentence.6562: Whenever a Cobalt Strike C2 channel was identified, Fox-IT performed lookups into the collection database.
sentence.6563: If a match was found, the configuration of the Cobalt Strike team server was analysed.
sentence.6564: This configuration was then compared against the other Cobalt Strike team servers to check for similarities in for example domain names, version number, URL, and various other settings.
sentence.6565: The adversary heavily relies on scheduled tasks for executing a batch-file (.bat) to perform their tasks.
sentence.6566: An example of the creation of such a scheduled task by the adversary: schtasks /create /ru
sentence.6568: The batch-files appear to be used to load the Cobalt Strike beacon, but also to perform discovery commands on the compromised system.
sentence.6570: The adversary loads the Cobalt Strike beacon in memory, without any persistence mechanisms on the compromised system.
sentence.6571: Once the system is rebooted, the beacon is gone.
sentence.6572: The adversary is still able to have persistent access by installing the beacon on systems with high uptimes, such as server.
sentence.6573: Besides using the Cobalt Strike beacon, the adversary also searches for VPN and firewall configs, possibly to function as a backup access into the network.
sentence.6574: We haven’t seen the adversary use those access methods after the first Cobalt Strike beacons were installed.
sentence.6575: Maybe because it was never necessary.
sentence.6576: After the first bulk of data is exfiltrated, the persistent access into the victim’s network is periodically used by the adversary to check if new data of interest is available.
sentence.6577: They also create a copy of the NTDS.dit and SYSTEM-registry hive file for new credentials to crack. Discovery (TA0007)
sentence.6578: The adversary applied a wide range of discovery tactics.
sentence.6579: In the list below we have highlighted a few specific tools the adversary used for discovery purposes.
sentence.6580: You can find a summary of most of the commands used by the adversary to perform discovery at the end of this article.
sentence.6581: Account discovery tool: PsLogListCommand used: psloglist.exe -accepteula -x security -s
sentence.6584: This command exports a text file with comma separated fields.
sentence.6585: The text files contain the contents of the Security Event log after the specified date.
sentence.6586: Psloglist is part of the Sysinternals toolkit from Mark Russinovich (Microsoft).
sentence.6587: The tool was used by the adversary on various systems to write events from the Windows Security Event Log to a text file.
sentence.6588: A possible intent of the adversary could be to identify if privileged users are active on the systems.
sentence.6589: If such a privileged user was recently active on a server the actor executes Cobalt Strike’s built-in Mimikatz to dump its credentials or password hash.
sentence.6590: Account discovery tool: NtdsAuditCommand used: msadcs.exe
sentence.6593: It imports the specified Active Directory database NTDS.dit and registry file SYSTEM and exports the found password hashes into RecordedTV_pdump.txt and user details in RecordedTV_users.csv.
sentence.6594: The NtdsAudit utility is an auditing tool for Active Directory databases.
sentence.6595: It allows the user to collect useful statistics related to accounts and passwords.
sentence.6596: The utility was found on various systems of a victim and matches the NtdsAudit.exe program file version v2.0.5 published on the GitHub project page.
sentence.6597: Network service scanningCommand used: get -b <start ip> -e <end ip> -p get -b <start ip> -e <end ip> Get.exe appears to be a custom tool used to scan IP-ranges for HTTP service information.
sentence.6598: NCC Group and Fox-IT decompiled the tool for analysis.
sentence.6599: This showed the tool was written in the Python scripting language and packed into a Windows executable file.
sentence.6600: Though Fox-IT didn’t find any direct occurrences of the tool on the internet, the decompiled code showed strong similarities with the source code of a tool named GetHttpsInfo.
sentence.6601: GetHttpsInfo scans the internal network for HTTP & HTTPS services.
sentence.6602: The reconnaissance tool getHttpsInfo is able to discover HTTP servers within the range of a network.
sentence.6603: The tool was shared on a Chinese forum around 2016.
sentence.6604: Figure 1: Example of a download location for GetHttpsInfo.exe Lateral movement (TA0008)
sentence.6605: The adversary used the built-in lateral movement possibilities in Cobalt Strike.
sentence.6606: Cobalt Strike has various methods for deploying its beacons at newly compromised systems.
sentence.6607: We have seen the adversary using SMB, named pipes, PsExec, and WinRM.
sentence.6608: The adversary attempts to move to a domain controller as soon as possible after getting foothold into the victim’s network.
sentence.6609: They continue lateral movement and discovery in an attempt to identify the data of interest.
sentence.6610: This could be a webserver to carve data from memory, or a fileserver to copy IP, as we have both observed.
sentence.6611: At one customer, the data of interest was stored in a separate security zone.
sentence.6612: The adversary was able to find a dual homed system and compromise it.
sentence.6613: From there on they used it as a jump host into the higher security zone and started collecting the intellectual property stored on a file server in that zone.
sentence.6614: In one event we saw the adversary compromise a Linux-system through SSH.
sentence.6615: The user account was possibly compromised on the Linux server by using credential stuffing or password spraying: Logfiles on the Linux-system show traces which can be attributed to a credential stuffing or password spraying attack.
sentence.6617: The adversary is applying living off the land techniques very well by incorporating default Windows tools in its arsenal.
sentence.6618: But not all tools used by the adversary are so called lolbins: As said before, they use Cobalt Strike.
sentence.6619: But they also rely on a custom tool for network scanning (get.exe), carving data from memory, compression of data, and exfiltrating data.
sentence.6620: But first: How did they get the tools on the victim’s systems?
sentence.6621: The adversary copied those tools over SMB from compromised system to compromised system wherever they needed these tools.
sentence.6622: A few examples of commands we observed: copy get.exe \\<ip>\c$\windows\temp\ copy msadc*
sentence.6624: In preparation of exfiltration of the data needed for their objective, the adversary collected the data from various sources within the victim’s network.
sentence.6625: As described before, the adversary collected data from an information repository, Microsoft SharePoint Online in this case.
sentence.6626: This document was exfiltrated and used to continue the intrusion via a company portal and VPN.
sentence.6627: In all cases we’ve seen the adversary copying results of the discovery phase, like file- and directory lists from local systems, network shared drives, and file shares on remote systems.
sentence.6628: But email collection is also important for this adversary: with every intrusion we saw the mailbox of some users being copied, from both local and remote systems: wmic /node:<ip> process call create "cmd /c copy c:\Users\<username>\<path>\backup.pst c:\windows\temp\backup.pst" copy "i:\<path>\<username>\My Documents\<filename>.pst" copy \\<hostname>\c$\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Outlook*.ost Files and folders of interest are collected as well and staged for exfiltration.
sentence.6629: The goal of targeting some victims appears to be to obtain data.
sentence.6630: How this data is obtained likely differs per victim, but we observed the usage of several custom DLL files used to continuously retrieve data from memory of systems where such data is typically processed.
sentence.6631: The DLL’s used were side-loaded in memory on compromised systems.
sentence.6632: After placing the DLL in the appropriate directory, the actor would change the date and time stamps on the DLL files to blend in with the other legitimate files in the directory.
sentence.6633: Adversaries aiming to exfiltrate large amounts of data will often use one or more systems or storage locations for intermittent storage of the collected data.
sentence.6634: This process is called staging and is one of the of the activities that NCC Group and Fox-IT has observed in the analysed C2 traffic.
sentence.6635: We’ve seen the adversary staging data on a remote system or on the local system.
sentence.6636: Most of the times the data is compressed and copied at the same time.
sentence.6637: Only a handful of times the adversary copies the data first before compressing (archive collected data) and exfiltrating it.
sentence.6638: The adversary compresses and encrypts the data by using WinRAR from the command-line.
sentence.6639: The filename of the command-line executable for WinRAR is RAR.exe by default.
sentence.6640: This activity group always uses a renamed version of rar.exe.
sentence.6641: We have observed the following filenames overlapping all intrusions: jucheck.exeRecordedTV.msteredo.tmpupdate.exemsadcs1.exe The adversary typically places the executables in the following folders: C:\Users\Public\Libraries\C:\Users\Public\Videos\C:\Windows\Temp\ The following four different variants of the use of rar.exe as update.exe we have observed: update a -m5 -hp<password> <target_filename> <source> update a -m5 -r -hp<password> <target_filename> <source> update a -m5 -inul -hp<password> <target_filename> <source> update a -m5 -r -inul -hp<password> <target_filename> <source>
sentence.6642: The command lines parameters have the following effect: a = add to archive.m5 = use compression level
sentence.6644: = suppress error messages.hp<password> = encrypt both file data and headers with password.
sentence.6645: The used password, file extensions for the staged data differ per intrusion.
sentence.6646: We’ve seen the use of .css, .rar, .log.txt, and no extension for staged pieces of data.
sentence.6647: After compromising a host with a Linux operating systems, data is also compressed.
sentence.6648: This time the adversary compresses the data as a gzipped tar-file: tar.gz.
sentence.6649: Sometimes no file extension is used, or the file extension is .il.
sentence.6650: Most of the times the files names are prepended with adsDL_ or contain the word “list”.
sentence.6651: The files are staged in the home folder of the compromised user account: /home/<username>/ Command and control (TA0011)
sentence.6652: The adversary uses Cobalt Strike as framework to manage their compromised systems.
sentence.6653: We observed the use of Cobalt Strike’s C2 protocol encapsulated in DNS by the adversary in 2017 and 2018.
sentence.6654: They switched to C2 encapsulated in HTTPS in Q3 2019.
sentence.6655: An interesting observation is they made use of a cracked/patched trial version of Cobalt Strike.
sentence.6656: This is important to note because the functionalities of Cobalt Strike’s trial version are limited.
sentence.6657: More importantly: the trial version doesn’t support encryption of command and control traffic in cases where the protocol itself isn’t encrypted, such as DNS.
sentence.6658: In one intrusion we investigated, the victim had years of logging available of outgoing DNS-requests.
sentence.6660: This means that only the DNS C2 leaving the victim’s network was logged.
sentence.6661: We developed a Python script that decoded and combined most of the logged C2 communication into a human readable format.
sentence.6662: As the adversary used Cobalt Strike with DNS as command & control protocol, we were able to reconstruct more than two years of adversary activity.
sentence.6663: With all this activity data, it was possible for us to create some insight into the ‘office’-hours of this adversary.
sentence.6664: The activity took place six days a week, rarely on Sundays.
sentence.6665: The activity started on average at 02:36 UTC and ended rarely after 13:00 UTC.
sentence.6666: We observed some periods where we expected activity of the adversary, but almost none was observed.
sentence.6667: These periods match with the Chinese Golden Week holiday.
sentence.6669: Times on the X-axis are in UTC.
sentence.6670: The adversary also changed their domains for command & control around the same time they switched C2 protocols.
sentence.6671: They used a subdomain under a regular parent domain with a .com
sentence.6672: TLD in 2017 and 2018, but they started using sub-domains under the parent domain appspot.com and azureedge.net in 2019.
sentence.6673: The parent domain appspot.com is a domain owned by Google, and part of Google’s App Engine platform as a service.
sentence.6674: Azureedge.net is a parent domain owned by Microsoft, and part of Microsoft’s Azure content delivery network.
sentence.6676: The adversary uses the command and control channel to exfiltrate small amounts of data.
sentence.6677: This is usually information containing account details.
sentence.6678: For large amounts of data, such as the mailboxes and network shares with intellectual property, they use something else.
sentence.6679: Once the larger chunks of data are compressed, encrypted, and staged, the data is exfiltrated using a custom built tool.
sentence.6680: This tool exfiltrates specified files to cloud storage web services.
sentence.6681: The following cloud storage web services are supported by the malware: DropboxGoogle DriveOneDrive The actor specifies the following arguments when running the exfiltration tool: Name of the web service to be usedParameters used for the web service, such as a client ID and/or API keyPath of the file to read and exfiltrate to the web service We have observed the exfiltration tool in the following locations: C:\Windows\Temp\msadcs.exeC:\Windows\Temp\OneDrive.exe Hashes of these files are listed at the end of this article.
sentence.6683: The adversary attempts to clean-up some of the traces from their intrusions.
sentence.6684: While we don’t know what was deleted and we were unable to recover, we did see some of their anti-forensics activity: Windows event logs clearing,File deletion,Timestomping An overview of the observed commands can be found in the appendix.
sentence.6685: For indicator removal on host: Timestomp the adversary uses a Windows version of the Linux touch command.
sentence.6686: This tool is included in the UnxUtils repository.
sentence.6687: This makes sure the used tools by the adversary blend in with the other files in the directory when shown in a timeline.
sentence.6688: Creating a timeline is a common thing to do for forensic analysts to get a chronological view of events on a system.
sentence.6690: A number of our intrusions involved tips from an industry partner who was able to correlate some of their upstream activity.
sentence.6691: Our threat intelligence analysts observed clear overlap between the various cases that NCC Group and Fox-IT worked in the threat’s infrastructure and capabilities, and as a result we assess with moderate confidence one activity group was carrying out the intrusions across the different type of victims.
sentence.6692: Some overlap is very generic for a lot for a lot of groups, like the use of Cobalt Strike, or exfiltration to OneDrive.
sentence.6693: But the tool used for exfiltration to OneDrive is very specific for this adversary.
sentence.6694: The use of appspot and azureedge domains as well.
sentence.6695: The naming convention for their subdomains, tools and scripts overlap too.
sentence.6696: In summary: The adversary: Working hours match with GMT+8.
sentence.6697: Infrastructure: appspot.com and azureedge.net for C2 with a strong overlap in naming convention for subdomains and actual overlap in some subdomains between intrusions.
sentence.6701: Use scheduled tasks and batch files for automation.
sentence.6704: Cloud exfil tool and exfil to OneDrive.
sentence.6705: Erasing Windows Event Logs, files and tasks.
sentence.6706: Overlap in filenames for tools, staged data, and folders.
sentence.6708: We considered labelling them as two activity groups, as of the difference in victims between various intrusions.
sentence.6709: But all the other overlap is strong enough for us to consider it as one group right now.
sentence.6710: This group might have gotten a new customer interested in different data which changed the intent and victims of the adversary.
sentence.6711: But most importantly: The largest overlap is in the top half of the pyramid of pain: domain names, host artifacts, tools, and TTPs.
sentence.6712: And these are the hardest for the adversary to change, and most effective for long-lasting detection!
sentence.6713: Figure 3: Pyramid of pain by David J Bianco Fox-IT and NCC Group found some very strong overlap between what we’ve seen in our intrusion, and what Cycraft describes in their APT Group Chimera report and Blackhat presentation.
sentence.6714: The bulk of the victims they describe are in different regions than we observed which is likely caused by field of view bias.
sentence.6715: SentinelOne also describes an attack and shares IOC’s that show strong overlap with the intrusions we investigated.
sentence.6716: Conclusion At this moment we believe based on the evidence observed that the various intrusions were performed by the same group.
sentence.6717: We can only report what we observed: first they stole intellectual property in the high tech sector, later they stole record, both across geographical locations.
sentence.6718: Both types of stolen data are very useful for nation states.
sentence.6719: Answering if this group has an advanced persistent threat (APT) technique, has some sort of state affiliation, or where they come from goes beyond the scope of this write-up.
sentence.6720: The threat intelligence and IOC’s we are sharing are intended to help discover and present intrusions by this and adversaries.
sentence.6721: A word of thanks goes out to all the forensic experts, incident responders, and threat intelligence analysts who helped victims identifying and eradicating the adversary.
sentence.6722: And everybody from NCC Group and Fox-IT (part of NCC Group) for all the contributions to this article.
