sentence.9119: Figure 11 – NoEscape Ransom note Linux Variant The NoEscape Linux variant consists of three files: “script_linux.sh,” “script_esxi.sh” and “164f8295_linux.elf“.
sentence.9120: Each of these files serves specific purposes and contributes to the overall functionality of the Linux variant of the ransomware.
sentence.9121: Ransomware Targeting Linux Machines The “script_linux.sh” script is designed to facilitate the execution of a ransomware payload “164f8295_linux.elf“.
sentence.9122: Its primary purpose is to carry out the encryption process on the victim’s Linux machine by scanning files in a specified or generic path and running the ransomware payload, “164f8295_linux.elf”, on each file it encounters.
sentence.9123: The below figure shows the code snippet “script_linux.sh”.
sentence.9124: Figure 12 – content of script_linux.sh The script “script_linux.sh” executes the following functions: SetLimits() –
sentence.9125: This function is responsible for adjusting the resource limits of the running process.
sentence.9126: Its purpose is to increase the maximum number of open file descriptors and the maximum number of allowed processes.
sentence.9127: By doing so, the function ensures that the script has the capability to handle a larger number of open files and concurrent processes, which is crucial for efficient file encryption in the context of ransomware.
sentence.9128: EmptyTrash() – This function is responsible for deleting all files and directories in the user’s trash folder.
sentence.9129: It clears the trash before the ransomware starts encrypting files.
sentence.9130: This step is taken to ensure that any previously deleted files in the trash cannot be recovered by the victims.
sentence.9131: By emptying the trash, the ransomware eliminates any possibility of file restoration from that location, making the encryption process more effective and irreversible.
sentence.9133: This function executes the ransomware payload file “164f8295_linux.elf”, by passing the file path to be encrypted as an argument.
sentence.9134: ScanPath(): This function scans a specified path by finding all files within the given directory and its subdirectories.
sentence.9135: It then calls ExecPayload() for each file to execute the Ransomware payload, thereby initiating the encryption process.
sentence.9136: WaitPayload(): This function waits until the payload process is no longer running.
sentence.9137: It checks the number of running instances of the payload executable and waits until the count becomes zero.
sentence.9138: The purpose of waiting for the Ransomware process to finish is to ensure that all files have been encrypted before proceeding to the next steps of the ransomware attack.
sentence.9139: Cleanup() – This function performs cleanup operations after encrypting files in the victim’s machine.
sentence.9140: It removes log files and temporary files from the root directory.
sentence.9141: It also deletes the ransomware, script file, and ransom note (index.html), ensuring that no evidence remains on the compromised system.
sentence.9142: Ransomware Targeting Vmware ESXi Servers The “script_esxi.sh” script is designed to automate the execution of ransomware payload “164f8295_linux.elf” on ESXi servers.
sentence.9143: It targets specific paths, including NFS volumes and VM volumes, and encrypts files found within those paths.
sentence.9144: The below figure shows the code snippet “script_esxi.sh”.
sentence.9145: Figure 13 – Content of script_esxi.sh The script “script_esxi.sh” executes the following functions:
sentence.9146: StopVMS(): This function stops running virtual machines (VMs) on an ESXi server.
sentence.9147: It uses the esxcli command to list all VM processes and forcibly kills them.
sentence.9148: It also kills any remaining processes related to VMs.
sentence.9149: ScanNFS(): This function scans NFS (Network File System) volumes on an ESXi server.
sentence.9150: It retrieves the list of NFS volumes using esxcli and then iterates over each volume to find files.
sentence.9151: For each file found, it calls ExecPayload() to execute the ransomware payload.
sentence.9152: ScanVMS() – This function scans VM volumes on an ESXi server.
sentence.9153: It retrieves the list of VM volumes using the esxcli command and then iterates over each volume to search for specific files related to virtual machines.
sentence.9155: For each file found, the function calls the ExecPayload() function to execute the ransomware payload for encrypting them.
sentence.9156: Deface() – This function replaces the “index.html” and “motd” files with ransom notes to ensure the ransom alert is displayed to victims upon login.
sentence.9158: This function modifies system files such as cron tab entries and configuration files to further disrupt the system and prevent recovery.
sentence.9160: The file “164f8295_linux.elf” (Sha256: 21162bbd796ad2bf9954265276bfebea8741596e8fe9d86070245d9b5f9db6da) is responsible for encrypting the files in the victim’s machine.
sentence.9161: Upon execution, the ransomware encrypts files using the chacha20 algorithm.
sentence.9162: The Ransomware incorporates a feature to encrypt larger files in smaller chunks.
sentence.9163: The TA can mention the file size, which is considered as larger, and the size of encryption in the Ransomware panel while building the binary.
sentence.9164: The below figure shows the code used by ransomware for validating and encrypting larger files.
sentence.9165: Figure 14 – Validating and Encrypting Larger Files Finally, the Ransomware drops a ransom note named “HOW_TO_RECOVER_FILES.txt ” which instructs the victims on how to reach out to the TAs to recover their encrypted files and pay a ransom.
sentence.9166: Figure 15- Ransom Note Conclusion NoEscape RaaS is a new ransomware group that aims to entice new affiliates with the promise of profits.
sentence.9167: They are actively seeking affiliates through postings on various dark web forums.
sentence.9168: Our analysis of the Windows and Linux malware executables indicates that the malware poses a threat to organizations of all types.
sentence.9169: As the group is relatively new, it is likely that they will evolve their tools and tactics to target multiple organizations.
sentence.9170: We will maintain our vigilance in monitoring NoEscape RaaS, their tools, tactics, and procedures, in order to provide regular updates to our customers and readers in the future.
sentence.9171: Our Recommendations We have listed some essential cybersecurity best practices that create the first line of control against attackers.
sentence.9172: We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below: Safety Measures Needed to Prevent Ransomware Attacks Conduct regular backup practices and keep those backups offline or in a separate network Turn on the automatic software update feature on your computer, mobile, and other connected devices wherever possible and pragmatic Use a reputed anti-virus and Internet security software package on your connected devices, including PC, laptop, and mobile Refrain from opening untrusted links and email attachments without verifying their authenticity Users Should Take the Following Steps After the Ransomware Attack Detach infected devices on the same network Disconnect external storage devices if connected Inspect system logs for suspicious events Impact of Ransomware Loss of valuable data Loss of the organization’s reputation and integrity Loss of the organization’s sensitive business information Disruption in organization operation Financial loss MITRE ATT&CK:registered: Techniques Tactic Technique ID Technique Name ExecutionT1059 T1204Command and Scripting Interpreter User ExecutionPersistenceT1547.001 Registry Run Keys / Startup FolderDiscoveryT1083File and Directory DiscoveryDefense EvasionT1070 T1562Indicator Removal Impair DefensesImpactT1486 T1490Data encrypted for impact Inhibit System RecoveryIndicators of Compromise (IOCs) Indicators Indicator Type Description 65f35ae4203cf5041a0aaa358dd3d74c ea1f7940271fc80d06b2f222506020b650ad41bc 68e5caa3f0fd4adc595b1163bf0dd30ca621c5d7a6ad0a20dfa1968346daa3c8MD5
sentence.9179: title: Stolen certificates in two waves of ransomware and wiper attacks url: https://securelist.com/ransomware-and-wiper-signed-with-stolen-certificates/108350/ Introduction On July 17, 2022, Albanian news outlets reported a massive cyberattack that affected Albanian government e-services.
sentence.9180: A few weeks later, it was revealed that the cyberattacks were part of a coordinated effort likely intended to cripple the country’s computer systems.
sentence.9181: On September 10, 2022, Albanian local news reported a second wave of cyberattacks targeting Albania’s TIMS, ADAM and MEMEX systems – the latter two systems critical for law enforcement – reportedly using the same attack type and by the same actors.
sentence.9182: Around the same time, we identified ransomware and wiper malware samples resembling those used in the first wave, though with a few interesting modifications that likely allowed evasion of security controls and better attack speeds.
sentence.9183: Chief among those changes are the embedding of a raw disk driver, providing direct hard disk access inside the malware itself, modified metadata, and the use of Nvidia’s leaked code signing certificate to sign the malware.
sentence.9184: So, what’s new in this blogpost?
sentence.9185: We compare the first and second waves of ransomware and wiper malware used to target Albanian entities and detail connections with previously known ROADSWEEP ransomware and ZEROCLEARE variants.
sentence.9186: The threat actors used certificates from Nvidia and Kuwait Telecommunications Company to sign their malware; the former was already leaked, but we’re not sure how they got their hands on the latter.
sentence.9187: We identified potential cooperation between different attack groups speaking different languages, and the possible use of AnyDesk as an initial entry point to start the ransomware/wiper infections.
sentence.9188: The changes implemented to automate and speed up wiping in the second wave of attacks are reminiscent of the notorious Shamoon wiper attacks in the Middle East.
sentence.9189: Wiper and ransomware, comparing wave 1 and wave 2 Below, we compare and discuss the differences between the wave 1 and wave 2 ransomware and wiper malware.
sentence.9190: Initial Infection – traces of cooperation between different attack groups and use of AnyDesk utility
sentence.9191: Although we weren’t able to identify the initial entry point of the threat actor in the analyzed intrusion, a few days after the second wave wiping activities, we noticed underground chatter about someone having access to an AnyDesk account at another non-governmental but significant Albanian entity, and suggestions for Persian-speaking hackers to use it for deploying ransomware or wiper malware.
sentence.9192: This may increase the likelihood that the initial entry point for wave 2 is through legitimate remote access software such as AnyDesk, especially since we know that the wave 2 wiper modifications included automatic execution upon driver installation only – potential need for urgency due to the limited time/access window.
sentence.9193: The attackers and access provider seemed to belong to different attack groups and spoke different languages.
sentence.9194: The ransomware – use of Kuwait Telecommunications Company signing certificate MD5 96eabcc77a6734ea8587599685fbf1b4 SHA1 6a36962709abbfc1f88f87e7fe88a417302bfe43 SHA256 8ad01b028e6aa711d26879d346a7bef82516e372e0f14e8e69db6aef0f25d992 Imphash 653ee44c85bc91d12ec33dfed8056c27 Link time Wed Jul 06 21:30:41 2016 File type 32-bit executable Compiler MinGW-w32 gcc File size 45.48 KB File name PdftoDoc.exe This second wave sample has the same signing certificate parameters as the first wave sample, which is related to Kuwait Telecommunications Company.
sentence.9195: It’s unclear how the threat actor was able to sign its malware using Kuwait Telecommunications Company’s certificate, but we suspect it was stolen.
sentence.9196: As of the date of this publication, the certificate is no longer valid and has been revoked.
sentence.9197: After the initial execution, the wave 2 ransomware checks for any six arguments (or more) supplied by the threat actor, as opposed to the wave 1 sample that checks for five arguments or more – a small modification that assists in defense evasion.
sentence.9198: Nevertheless, the intrusion analysis conducted on one of the affected machines indicates that in wave 2 the threat actor did not use a BAT file to invoke the ransomware while supplying seven digits similar to wave 1, but instead invoked the wave 2 ransomware immediately from the command line using six zeroes: “000000”.
sentence.9199: If ransomware execution fails because the correct arguments are not supplied, the wave 2 sample displays a different message from that of wave 1; the wave 2 message resembles an error message displayed by a PDF to DOC converter.
sentence.9200: Wave 1 sample – messaging after failed execution Wave 2 sample – different messaging after failed execution The wave 2 ransomware sample continues execution and checks for the mutex Screenlimitsdevices#77!;, a value that differs from the wave 1 sample’s mutex:abcdefghijklmnoklmnopqrstuvwxyz01234567890abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz01234567890 Although we call this malware ransomware based on its behavior, the encrypted files are, in fact, unrecoverable.
sentence.9201: When comparing wave 2 ransomware samples to wave 1, we notice that both have the same , and both use CreateFile and WriteFile APIs to overwrite files.
sentence.9202: During the process of execution, wave 2 ransomware attempts to decrypt and execute embedded scripts, malware settings or API function names.
sentence.9203: The encryption algorithm used is RC4 in both wave 1 and wave 2.
sentence.9204: However, the RC4 key for decryption in wave 2 has been changed in another attempt to evade detection.
sentence.9205: Wave 1 RC4 key: 8C E4 B1 6B 22 B5 88 94 AA 86 C4 21 E8 75 9D F3 Wave 2 RC4 key: F0 B4 ED D9 43 F5 C8 43 C9 D0 A2 4F 22 9B BC 3A It’s worth noting that in both waves, the RC4 decryption method uses CryptoAPI (CryptDecrypt) instead of the usual substitution box method.
sentence.9206: The intrusion we analyzed in wave 2 indicates that the ransomware was probably deployed over the internal network, possibly from another compromised machine.
sentence.9207: This is reinforced by the fact that we didn’t see anything else dropped or executed before the ransomware execution, and the ransomware executable name was randomly generated, potentially by the tool the threat actor used to deploy it over the network (e.g., Mellona.exe).
sentence.9208: Despite all the changes made in the wave 2 ransomware, the ransom notes remained the same and included political messaging that reflects the geopolitical tensions between Albania and Iran.
sentence.9209: Ransom note in both wave 1 and wave 2 ransomware The wiper – use of Nvidia signing certificate MD5 64cb923be15ae255b82e7ebcf24ccfc5 SHA1 e1b8b72fbd1e3b9bbf8bebd2e14a3f2e071c6048 SHA256 d8ec8ec8dfa582c44e81b8a7fcc44defc3d2fa658f75fa495124aedc3b0db367 Imphash 81CA8B811412284938148FC4F2A76C09 Link time 0x6319C758 (Thu Sep 08 03:43:36 2022)
sentence.9210: File type PE 64-bit Compiler Microsoft Visual C/C++ File size 174.00 KB File name DiskSnapshot.exe Driver PDB path c:\projects\rawdisk\bin\wnet\fre\amd64\rawdsk3.pdb Driver key B4B615C28CCD059CF8ED1ABF1C71FE03C0354522990AF63ADF3C911E2287A4B906D47D Similar to the wave 2 ransomware sample, the threat actor made several modifications to the wave 2 wiper malware, probably to evade detection.
sentence.9211: The three main changes are: Modified malware signing Embedding of EldoS RawDisk driver inside the wiper malware Automatic wiping after driver installation command Historically, in ZEROCLEARE and DUSTMAN incidents from 2019, the wiper malware and raw disk drivers were not signed and therefore could not directly access the raw disk for speedy data wiping.
sentence.9212: So, the wipers had to use a third-party loader such as TDL – a signed loader for unsigned drivers – to install the unsigned raw disk driver that allows the wiper malware to directly access the raw disk for wiping data using DeviceControl API methods.
sentence.9213: However, in the first attack wave targeting Albania, the threat actor signed the wave 1 wiper using the Kuwait Telecommunications Company certificate, thus removing the need for a third-party loader.
sentence.9214: The speed and automation improvements remind us of previous Shamoon operations in the Middle East.
sentence.9215: Since the wave 1 wipers were exposed in July 2022, and likely to avoid static detections, the threat actor used Nvidia’s leaked signing certificate to sign the wave 2 wiper in September 2022, again eliminating the need for a third-party loader for the raw disk driver.
sentence.9216: In wave 1, the wiper malware expected to find the raw disk driver in the execution directory or in the system directory.
sentence.9217: The driver wasn’t dropped by the wiper, and the threat actor likely dropped it using other means.
sentence.9218: Conversely, in wave 2 the threat actor embedded the signed raw disk driver in the wiper executable, dropped it and then installed it.
sentence.9219: In addition, the driver being used by the threat actor in wave 2 seems to copy metadata and a few functions from Microsoft’s diskdump.sys crash dump driver[1] (version 10.0.19041.1682) as another means to avoid detections.
sentence.9220: The wiping activity starts automatically after the driver installation command; as opposed to the wave 1 wiper, where installation is one step and wiping execution is a second step.
sentence.9221: Finally, for the most part, wave 1 and wave 2 wipers remained the same, including the reliance on the same authentication key to access the raw disk driver, and the use of the same DeviceControl API methods, but with one exception, as shown below.
sentence.9222: It’s worth noting that the method IOCTL_DISK_GET_LENGTH_INFO is exclusive to all Persian-speaking APT wipers.
sentence.9223: Wave 1 wiper DeviceControl API methods: IOCTL_DISK_GET_DRIVE_GEOMETRY_EX IOCTL_DISK_GET_DRIVE_GEOMETRY IOCTL_DISK_GET_LENGTH_INFO Wave 2 wiper DeviceControl API methods: IOCTL_VOLUME_GET_VOLUME_DISK_EXTENTS (new method in wave 2; used in multiple instances) IOCTL_DISK_GET_DRIVE_GEOMETRY IOCTL_DISK_GET_LENGTH_INFO Based on our telemetry, we suspect the infections are associated with law enforcement institutions in Albania.
sentence.9224: This targeting is consistent with the previous wave of cyberattacks affecting the Albanian government during the July 2022 wave of cyberattacks.
sentence.9225: Conclusions In this publication, we discussed the changes made to the second wave of ransomware and wiper samples that targeted Albanian institutions to evade detection and inflict maximum damage.
sentence.9226: Aside from the changes made to evade detection in wave 2, we suspect that the threat actors needed an automated and speedy wiper execution.
sentence.9227: In wave 2, the raw disk driver was embedded inside the malware and the wiping routine started immediately after driver installation, as opposed to the wave 1 procedure.
sentence.9228: This is reminiscent of Shamoon operations in the Middle East.
sentence.9229: Finally, for defenders we can highlight two important elements from the intrusion and malware analysis presented here: Monitor for remote software activities such as AnyDesk for unauthorized use Always hunt and monitor for expired and/or leaked signing certificates as they can be used by threat actors to load and execute malware Threat detection
sentence.9230: The detection logic has been improved in all our solutions to ensure that our customers remain protected.
sentence.9231: We continue to investigate this threat using our Threat Intelligence and we will add additional detection logic once they are available.
sentence.9232: Our products protect against this threat and detect it with the following names:

sentence.9237: title: BlueNoroff introduces new methods bypassing MoTW url: https://securelist.com/bluenoroff-methods-bypass-motw/108383/ BlueNoroff group is a financially motivated threat actor eager to profit from its cyberattack capabilities.
sentence.9238: We have published technical details of how this notorious group steals cryptocurrency before.
sentence.9239: We continue to track the group’s activities and this October we observed the adoption of new malware strains in its arsenal.
sentence.9240: The group usually takes advantage of Word documents and uses shortcut files for the initial intrusion.
sentence.9241: However, it has recently started to adopt new methods of malware delivery.
sentence.9242: The first new method the group adopted is aimed at evading the Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) flag, the security measure whereby Windows displays a warning message when the user tries to open a file downloaded from the internet.
sentence.9243: To do this, optical disk image (.iso extension) and virtual hard disk (.vhd extension) file formats were used.
sentence.9244: This is a common tactic used nowadays to evade MOTW, and BlueNoroff has also adopted it.
sentence.9245: In addition, the group tested different file types to refine malware delivery methods.
sentence.9246: We observed a new Visual Basic Script, a previously unseen Windows Batch file, and a Windows executable.
sentence.9247: It seems the actors behind BlueNoroff are expanding or experimenting with new file types to convey their malware efficiently.
sentence.9248: After researching the infrastructure that was utilized, we discovered more than 70 domains used by this group, meaning they were very active until recently.
sentence.9249: Also, they created numerous fake domains that look like venture capital and bank domains.
sentence.9250: Most of the domains imitate Japanese venture capital companies, indicating that the group has an extensive interest in Japanese financial entities.
sentence.9251: Executive summary BlueNoroff group introduced new file types to evade Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) security measures; BleuNoroff group expanded file types and tweaked infection methods; BlueNoroff created numerous fake domains impersonating venture capital companies and banks.
sentence.9252: Background At the end of September 2022, we observed new BlueNoroff malware in our telemetry.
sentence.9253: After a careful investigation, we confirmed that the actor had adopted new techniques to convey the final payload.
sentence.9254: The actor took advantage of several scripts, including Visual Basic Script and Windows Batch script.
sentence.9255: They also started using disk image file formats, .iso
sentence.9257: For intermediate infection, the actor introduced a downloader to fetch and spawn the next stage payload.
sentence.9258: Although the initial intrusion methods were very different in this campaign, the final payload that we had analyzed previously was used without significant changes.
sentence.9259: Novel infection chain Long-lasting initial infection Based on our telemetry, we observed that one victim in the UAE was attacked using a malicious Word document.
sentence.9260: The victim received a document file named “Shamjit Client Details Form.doc” on September 2, 2022.
sentence.9261: Unfortunately, we couldn’t acquire the document, but it was executed from the following path: C:\Users\[username]\Desktop\SALES
sentence.9264: Client Details Form.doc Judging from the file path, we can assume that the victim was an employee in the sales department responsible for signing contracts.
sentence.9265: Upon launch, the malicious document connects to the remote server and downloads the payload.
sentence.9266: In this particular case, the executable ieinstal.exe was used to bypass UAC.
sentence.9268: %Profile%\cr.dat Spawned command: cmd.exe %Profile%\cr.dat 5pKwgIV5otiKb6JrNddaVJOaLjMkj4zED238vIU= After initial infection, we observed several keyboard hands-on activities by the operator.
sentence.9269: Through the implanted backdoor, they attempted to fingerprint the victim and install additional malware with high privileges.
sentence.9270: Upon infection, the operator executed several Windows commands to gather basic system information.
sentence.9271: They then returned 18 hours later to install further malware with high privileges.
sentence.9272: Post-exploitation Based on our telemetry, when the malicious Word document opens it fetches the next payload from the remote server: Download URL: http://avid.lno-prima[.]lol/VcIf1hLJopY/shU_pJgW2Y/KvSuUJYGoa/sX+Xk4Go/gGhI= The fetched payload is supposed to be saved in %Profile%\update.dll.

sentence.9276: One of the other methods the BlueNoroff group usually uses is a ZIP archive with a shortcut file.
sentence.9277: The archive file we recently discovered contained a password-protected decoy document and a shortcut file named “Password.txt.lnk“.
sentence.9278: This is a classic BlueNoroff strategy to persuade the victim to execute the malicious shortcut file to acquire the decoy document’s password.
sentence.9279: The latest archive file (MD5 1e3df8ee796fc8a13731c6de1aed0818) discovered has a Japanese file name, 新しいボーナススケジュール.zip (Japanese for “New bonus schedule”), indicating they were interested in Japanese targets.

sentence.9286: Updated method #1: Tricks to evade MOTW flag We observed that the actor examined different file types to deliver their malware.
sentence.9287: Recently, many threat actors have adopted image files to avoid MOTW (Mark-of-the-Web).
sentence.9288: In a nutshell, MOTW is a mitigation technique introduced by Microsoft.
sentence.9289: The NTFS file system marks a file downloaded from the internet, and Windows handles the file in a safe way.
sentence.9290: For example, when a Microsoft Office file is fetched from the internet, the OS opens it in Protected View, which restricts the execution of the embedded macro.
sentence.9291: In order to avoid this mitigation technique, more threat actors have started abusing ISO file types.
sentence.9292: The BlueNoroff group likely experimented with ISO image files to deliver their malware.
sentence.9293: Although it’s still under development, we mention this sample as an early warning.
sentence.9294: This ISO image file contains one PowerPoint slide show and one Visual Basic Script.
sentence.9295: Embedded files of ISO image The Microsoft PowerPoint file contains a link.
sentence.9296: When the user clicks the link, it executes the 1.vbs file through the WScript process.
sentence.9297: When we checked the VBS file, it only generated an “ok” message, which suggests BlueNoroff is still experimenting with this method.<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8" standalone="yes"?> <Relationships xmlns="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/package/2006/relationships"><Relationship Id="rId2" Type="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships/hyperlink" Target="wscript%201.vbs" TargetMode="External"/><Relationship Id="rId1" Type="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships/slideLayout" Target="../slideLayouts/slideLayout1.xml"/></Relationships> Based on our other findings, we discovered an in-the-wild sample (MD5 a17e9fc78706431ffc8b3085380fe29f) from VirusTotal.

sentence.9316: If TrendMicro, BitDefender, or Windows Defender products are installed, the malware conducts a classic unhooking DLL trick intended to remove user-mode hooks from the system library.
sentence.9317: This evasion technique overwrites the .text section of the pre-loaded ntdll library with the freshly loaded one so that the hooked API addresses are recovered with the original API address.
sentence.9318: With this trick, the malware can disable the functionalities of EDR/AV products.

sentence.9393: title: Fork in the Ice: The New Era of IcedID url: https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/fork-ice-new-era-icedid ​Key Findings Proofpoint is tracking new variants of IcedID used by at least three threat actors.
sentence.9394: Initial analysis suggests this is a forked version with potentially a separate panel for managing the malware.
sentence.9395: While much of the code base is the same, there are several key differences.
sentence.9396: One key difference is the removal of banking functionality such as web injects and backconnect.
sentence.9397: Proofpoint researchers hypothesize the original operators behind Emotet are using an IcedID variant with different functionality.
sentence.9398: Overview Proofpoint researchers have observed and documented, for the first time, three distinct variants of the malware known as IcedID.
sentence.9399: Proofpoint calls the two new variants recently identified “Forked” and “Lite” IcedID.
sentence.9400: This report details the following variants of IcedID: Standard IcedID Variant – The variant most commonly observed in the threat landscape and used by a variety of threat actors.
sentence.9401: Lite IcedID Variant – New variant observed as a follow-on payload in November Emotet infections that does not exfiltrate host data in the loader checkin and a bot with minimal functionality.
sentence.9402: Forked IcedID Variant – New variant observed by Proofpoint researchers in February 2023 used by a small number of threat actors which also delivers the bot with minimal functionality.
sentence.9403: IcedID is a malware originally classified as a banking malware and was first observed in 2017.
sentence.9404: It also acts as a loader for other malware, including ransomware.
sentence.9405: As previously published, historically there has been just one version of IcedID that has remained constant since 2017.
sentence.9406: The well-known IcedID version consists of an initial loader which contacts a Loader C2 server, downloads the standard DLL Loader, which then delivers the standard IcedID Bot.
sentence.9407: In November 2022, Proofpoint researchers observed the first new variant of IcedID Proofpoint dubbed “IcedID Lite” distributed as a follow-on payload in a TA542 Emotet campaign.
sentence.9408: It was dropped by the Emotet malware soon after the actor returned to the e-crime landscape after a nearly four-month break.
sentence.9409: The IcedID Lite Loader observed in November 2022 contains a static URL to download a “Bot Pack” file with a static name (botpack.dat) which results in the IcedID Lite DLL Loader, and then delivers the Forked version of IcedID Bot, leaving out the webinjects and backconnect functionality that would typically be used for banking fraud.
sentence.9410: Starting in February 2023, Proofpoint observed the new Forked variant of IcedID.
sentence.9411: To date, Proofpoint has uncovered seven campaigns using the Forked IcedID variant.
sentence.9412: This variant was distributed by TA581 and one unattributed threat activity cluster which acted as initial access facilitators.
sentence.9413: The campaigns used a variety of email attachments such as Microsoft OneNote attachments and somewhat rare to see .URL
sentence.9414: attachments, which led to the Forked variant of IcedID.
sentence.9415: The IcedID Forked Loader, first observed in February 2023, is more similar to the Standard IcedID Loader in that it contacts a Loader C2 server to retrieve the DLL loader and bot.
sentence.9416: That DLL loader has similar artifacts to the Lite Loader, and also loads the Forked IcedID Bot.
sentence.9417: The following picture shows the high-level overview of the various IcedID variants Proofpoint researchers have identified.
sentence.9418: Figure 1: Overview of the three IcedID variants.
sentence.9419: Threat Actor Details Proofpoint has identified hundreds of IcedID campaigns from 2022 through 2023, and at least five threat actors were observed directly distributing this malware in campaigns since 2022.
sentence.9420: Nearly all threat actors and unattributed threat activity clusters use the Standard IcedID variant.
sentence.9421: Proofpoint considers most of these threat actors to be initial access brokers that facilitate infections leading to ransomware.
sentence.9422: Proofpoint continues to see all variants of the IcedID malware in campaign data, so researchers assess with high confidence that the changes detailed below are not direct upgrades to the Standard IcedID codebase.
sentence.9423: It is likely a cluster of threat actors is using modified variants to pivot the malware away from typical banking trojan and banking fraud activity to focus on payload delivery, which likely includes prioritizing ransomware delivery.
sentence.9424: Additionally, based on artifacts observed in the codebase, timing and association with Emotet infections, Proofpoint researchers suspect the initial developers of Emotet have partnered with IcedID operators to expand their activities including using the new Lite variant of IcedID that has different, unique functionality and likely testing it via existing Emotet infections.
sentence.9425: The Lite IcedID variant has only been observed following TA542 Emotet infections, but Proofpoint cannot definitively attribute the Lite variant to TA542 as follow-on infections are typically outside of researchers’ visibility.
sentence.9426: The following are threat actors frequently associated with IcedID. TA578 – Proofpoint has observed TA578 deliver IcedID in campaigns since June 2020.
sentence.9427: Typically, this actor uses email themes such as “stolen images” or “copyright violation” to deliver malware.
sentence.9428: In addition to IcedID, TA578 also frequently conducts campaigns delivering Bumblebee malware.
sentence.9429: TA578 uses the Standard IcedID variant.
sentence.9430: TA551 – Proofpoint has observed TA551 deliver IcedID in campaigns since November 2018.
sentence.9431: This actor usually uses thread hijacking to typically deliver attached files including Word documents, PDFs, and recently, OneNote documents.
sentence.9432: TA551 has used multiple malware types, with recent payloads including IcedID, SVCReady, and Ursnif.
sentence.9433: TA551 uses the Standard IcedID variant.
sentence.9434: TA577 – Proofpoint has observed TA577 use IcedID in limited campaigns since February 2021.
sentence.9435: This actor typically uses thread hijacking to deliver malware, with Qbot being TA577’s preferred payload.
sentence.9436: However, Proofpoint has observed IcedID delivered by TA577 in six campaigns since 2022.
sentence.9437: TA577 uses the Standard IcedID variant.
sentence.9438: TA544 – Proofpoint observed TA544 use IcedID in limited campaigns throughout 2022.
sentence.9439: This actor typically targets organizations in Italy and Japan, and typically delivers Ursnif malware.
sentence.9440: TA544 uses the Standard IcedID variant.
sentence.9441: TA581 – TA581 is a newly classified threat actor Proofpoint has tracked as an unattributed activity cluster since mid-2022.
sentence.9442: This actor typically uses business-relevant themes such as payroll, customer information, invoice, and order receipts to deliver a variety of filetypes or URLs.
sentence.9443: TA581 typically delivers IcedID, but has been observed using Bumblebee malware and telephone-oriented attack delivery (TOAD) payloads.
sentence.9444: TA581 uses the Forked IcedID variant.
sentence.9445: Campaign Details Proofpoint has only observed the IcedID Lite Loader variant delivered as a second-stage payload following Emotet infections associated with November 2022 campaigns.
sentence.9446: Below are examples of the Standard and Forked IcedID variants observed as first-stage payloads.
sentence.9447: Example 1: IcedID Standard Campaign Proofpoint observed a campaign with over 2,800 messages on 10 March 2023.
sentence.9448: This campaign began with thread hijacked emails which contained HTML attachments.
sentence.9449: The HTML attachments used HTML Smuggling to drop a password protected, zipped Windows Script File (WSF).
sentence.9450: The password “747” was displayed in the HTML file.
sentence.9451: The WSF ran a VBScript which initiated a PowerShell command to download and execute an intermediate script which then downloaded and executed the Standard IcedID Loader using a non-standard export “init”.
sentence.9452: Figure 2: Sample email using thread hijacking to deliver an HTML attachment.
sentence.9454: HTML Attachment spoofing Office 365. Figure 4: Contents of smuggled ZIP file.
sentence.9457: This pulled the next stage – the Standard IcedID Loader.
sentence.9458: The IcedID loader connected to the C2 server and delivered and executed the IcedID core bot if specific conditions were met.

sentence.9477: Example 3: IcedID Forked Campaign Proofpoint observed a campaign with over 200 messages conducted from 20 February to 23 February 2023.
sentence.9478: This campaign included two different email lures: 1) a recall notice purporting to be from the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act; and 2) a violation purporting to be from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).

sentence.9482: If the recipient clicked to open the .URL file, the recipient's default web browser would access the URL contained in the file.

sentence.9484: The batch file would download and execute an IcedID loader with rundll32 using a non-standard export: "PluginInit".

sentence.9492: guidassembler[.]com CommsCookie: 1 ProjectID: 3971099397 URI: /news/ ] Malware analysis Before comparing the Standard Loader to the Forked Loader, it is worth covering the highlights of the IcedID Lite Loader as there is code overlap and clear similarities when compared with the Forked Loader.
sentence.9493: For an in-depth analysis of the Lite Loader, check out Proofpoint’s previous report here.
sentence.9494: The Lite Loader’s purpose is to download the next stage of the malware from a hardcoded domain and URI path.
sentence.9495: The domain is decrypted from the configuration and the URI path is decrypted within the function that makes the HTTP request.
sentence.9496: Unlike the Standard IcedID Loader, there is no host information being exfiltrated within the request.
sentence.9497: When the Lite Loader was dropped on Emotet infections, that fact made sense, since this version of IcedID was specifically being deployed on already infected machines, and there was no need to check the host information.
sentence.9498: Figure 15: Config decryption within IcedID Lite Loader.
sentence.9499: Figure 16: Decryption of the URI within the IcedID Lite Loader.
sentence.9500: Considering that Proofpoint has not observed a standalone campaign of the Lite Loader in the wild, the remainder of the analysis section will compare the Standard variant to the Forked variant as well as similarities to the Lite Loader.
sentence.9501: Loader Analysis Field Standard Loader Forked Loader Internal name loader_dll_64.dll Loader.dll FileType Standard DLL COM Server Extraneous string Contains “1.bin” Project ID Project ID differs from loader to bot Project ID is the same across loader and bot Rough size ~36KB ~48KB Botpack decryption Decryption is the same across both As far as behavior is concerned, the Forked Loader functions the same as the Standard Loader.
sentence.9502: The goal is to send host info to the loader C2, then to gate the bot download.
sentence.9503: This gating mechanism is to ensure that only truly infected machines get the bot binary vs researchers or malware sandboxes.
sentence.9504: If the checks are passed, the C2 will return the encrypted bot and DLL loader which is where the real capabilities of the botnet emerge.
sentence.9505: The differences come within the binary itself by how the code is/was structured and how they obfuscate the sample.
sentence.9506: Both variants of the loader initiate their malicious code by creating a thread for the malware main.
sentence.9507: Before this happens though, the Forked Loader decrypts and copies strings into global variables where they will be later used to resolve required functions.
sentence.9508: This pattern of decrypting strings for future use will come up later in the analysis of the DLL loader.
sentence.9509: Figure 17: String decryption of the DLL names used within the Forked Loader.
sentence.9510: With the DLL strings decrypted, the malware then decrypts the loader configuration by taking the first 64 bytes and XORing it against the next 64 bytes.
sentence.9511: The first four bytes of the decrypted buffer will contain the project identifier (ID) (a campaign identifier of sorts) and then a singular domain which is used to gate the download of the bot. Figure 18: Decryption of the config buffer in the Forked Loader.
sentence.9512: For whatever reason, there is an extraneous “1.bin” that is appended to a string which isn’t used.
sentence.9513: As far as Proofpoint researchers can tell, this string is not used and serves no purpose.
sentence.9514: With the config decrypted, the malware creates the cookies that contain the host information and sends an HTTP request that will contain the encrypted bot response.
sentence.9515: Figure 19: Raw response from the loader C2 containing the encrypted bot and DLL loader.
sentence.9516: The response gets decrypted with the IcedID decryption routine, then split into the encrypted bot (being “license.dat”) and the custom DLL loader which is generally some randomly generated filename ending in .tmp.
sentence.9517: DLL Loader Analysis Field Standard DLL Loader Forked DLL Loader Extraneous code Contains code to decrypt strings and domains related to the “lite loader” File type Standard DLL COM Server Internal name init_dll_64.dll Init.dll Rough size 20KB 36KB The start of the DLL loader is the same across both versions of the DLL loader, a thread is created that contains the malicious code for custom loading license.dat: Figure 20: Start of the Standard DLL Loader.
sentence.9518: When comparing the StartAddress function, we see the biggest difference across these two samples: Figure 21: Standard DLL Loader thread function.
sentence.9519: The following shows the thread function for the Forked DLL Loader.
sentence.9520: This function decrypts strings that originally just existed in the Lite Loader. Figure 22:
sentence.9522: The rest of this report section focuses on the Forked DLL Loader, as that is where these differences exist.
sentence.9523: Just like the Forked Loader, the Forked DLL Loader decrypts the DLL strings to be used later to resolve handles to the DLLs needed.
sentence.9524: The strings are decrypted in the same algorithm where the data is split into DWORDs and XOR’d against a random key.
sentence.9525: Figure 23: String decryption for the DLL names needed for execution.
sentence.9526: Next, a function is called that decrypts strings that are not used at any point within the binary itself.
sentence.9527: The function starts by creating a structure that is going to be returned at the end of the function.
sentence.9528: This structure contains two domains and various URIs that could potentially be used to get a separate version of the bot. Figure 24: Decryption of “Lite Loader”" domains.
sentence.9529: For all the Forked DLL Loader variants we have seen, there are two domains that are decrypted: “tourdeworldsport[.]com” and “handsinworld[.]com”.
sentence.9530: Neither of these domains are used within the file, and at the time of this report have no relations on VirusTotal.
sentence.9531: Looking into the “handsinworld” domain, passive DNS shows that the domain started resolving to its current IP of “193[.]37[.]69[.]107” on 12 Nov 2022.
sentence.9532: This is also around the time that Emotet dropped the IcedID Lite Loader onto the Epoch 4 and Epoch 5 botnet.
sentence.9533: More information on the Lite Loader and Emotet can be found in our previous report here.
sentence.9534: The other domain “tourdeworldsport”, also started resolving to the IP “5[.]61[.]34[.]46” on 18 Nov 2022.
sentence.9535: With the domain names decrypted, the DLL Loader decrypts 10 strings that should be URIs to be appended to the domains.
sentence.9537: Within this list though, they have typos for botpackn3dat.
sentence.9538: Most likely there should be a period before .dat.
sentence.9539: This is the same URI structure (/botpack.dat) that the Lite Loader used to download the bot and DLL loader from the C2 in November 2022 when it was dropped via Emotet infections.
sentence.9540: After the strings are decrypted, the structure referencing them is never used again.
sentence.9541: This is most likely code that has been copy/pasted from the lite loader.
sentence.9542: If implemented correctly, these strings should appear in the actual loader of IcedID and not within the DLL Loader where it currently resides.
sentence.9543: These commonalities between the Lite Loader and this DLL Loader make it seem as if the same group that dropped IcedID via Emotet is behind these campaigns as well.
sentence.9544: Bot Analysis Field Standard Bot Forked Bot File format Custom PE Format Custom PE Format Rough size 368 KB 304 KB Removed code Removed web injects capability Versioning Currently at version 119 Currently at version 111 Looking at the Forked IcedID Bot variant and the Standard Bot variant in BinDiff, researchers observed that the Standard IcedID bot contains more functionality than the Forked variant.
sentence.9545: Figure 26: Output of BinDiff showing the Standard Bot vs the Forked Bot.
sentence.9546: Combining Hexray’s Lumina and BinDiff shows that the Standard Bot contains functionality relating to web injects, adversary in the middle (AiTM) and backconnect capabilities that do not exist within the Forked variant.
sentence.9547: This could be because banking fraud has become increasingly more difficult over the last couple of years.
sentence.9548: Figure 27: Functions that have been removed within the Forked Bot.
sentence.9549: Within the communications of the bot, there is an authentication header which contains the bot’s project ID, some other details and the version of the bot.
sentence.9550: Authorization: Basic OTk4MDc1MzAwOjA6MTE5OjY1OjM1 998075300:0:119:65:35 Base64 decoding this value gives up the version as the third component of the list.
sentence.9551: For the Standard IcedID Bot, this value is set to 119 as seen above, but for the Forked variant, we get the following base64 decoded header; 998075300:0:111:67:1
sentence.9552: This value contains version 111, which could indicate the fork happened when the Standard Bot was using that version.
sentence.9553: Finally, there seems to be a bug within the Forked variant of the bot where the URIs of specific requests are not constructed properly which causes 404s to occur.
sentence.9554: Figure 28: Network requests made by the Forked Bot.
sentence.9555: In the example above, the request should be “/news/4/2/1” but for whatever reason the bot does not append the initial / for specific commands.
sentence.9557: After analysis of the separate variants was finished, Proofpoint identified a file called “botpackn1.dat” on VirusTotal that seemed related to our Lite Loader.
sentence.9558: Figure 29: VirusTotal page showing the botpack used in the Lite Loader.
sentence.9559: That filename is embedded within the custom Forked DLL Loader mentioned previously.
sentence.9560: This relationship was enough to prompt further analysis.
sentence.9561: In the article where Proofpoint described the IcedID Lite Loader being dropped via Emotet infections, researchers documented the structure of the botpack format and how to decrypt it as well.
sentence.9562: Taking that same script and applying it to this file leads to a valid configuration where researchers can analyze the configuration.
sentence.9563: Figure 30: Commandline output showing the decrypted botpack structure.
sentence.9564: This botpackn1.dat contains the later stages of the infection chain, so with some pivoting on the VirusTotal relationships, researchers land on the distribution URL (VT Link) “http[:]//lepriconloots[.]com/botpackn1.dat”.
sentence.9565: Pivoting again to find files that reach to the URL, we come across the Lite Loader sample itself.
sentence.9566: Looking at the build artifacts of this sample, it seems like the threat actors have removed the PDB path, but the Lite Loader still contains the build name “Loader.dll”.
sentence.9567: Loader.dll was initially used within IcedID to refer to the Lite Loader back when it was dropped via Emotet infections in November, but that same build name is now being used within the Forked DLL Loader.
sentence.9568: This could mean the codebase is similar enough where the threat actors can interchange the loader and the DLL Loader, or that these actors are copy/pasting extraneous code.
sentence.9569: Figure 31: Embedded build name of the DLL Loader.
sentence.9570: Finally, pivoting on where this “c2.dll” (IcedID Lite loader) came from, the distribution URL “http[:]//104[.]156[.]149[.]6/webdav/c2.dll” is observed.
sentence.9571: Similarly, this IP address hosted an IcedID campaign from TA581 that occurred on 21 February 2023.
sentence.9572: The TA581 campaign ended up loading the DLL “host.dll” from that same directory and led to one of the first campaigns of Proofpoint observing the Forked variant.
sentence.9573: At the time when this distribution URL was live the IP was hosting an open directory on /webdav/ that contained various bat files, a forked IcedID loader as well as this lite loader.
sentence.9574: Conclusion IcedID is a popular malware typically used by more advanced cyber criminal threat actors, and its use across the threat landscape has remained relatively consistent until recently.
sentence.9575: Ultimately, there seems to be considerable effort going into the future of IcedID and the malware’s codebase, including the addition of two new variants described in this report.
sentence.9576: While historically IcedID’s main function was a banking trojan, the removal of banking functionality aligns with the overall landscape shift away from banking malware and an increasing focus on being a loader for follow-on infections, including ransomware.
sentence.9577: Proofpoint anticipates that while many threat actors will continue to use the Standard variant, it is likely the new variants will continue to be used to facilitate additional malware attacks.

sentence.9583: title: Kimsuky Strikes Again | New Social Engineering Campaign Aims to Steal Credentials and Gather Strategic Intelligence url: https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/kimsuky-new-social-engineering-campaign-aims-to-steal-credentials-and-gather-strategic-intelligence/ Executive Summary SentinelLabs has been tracking a social engineering campaign by the North Korean APT group Kimsuky targeting experts in North Korean affairs, part of a broader campaign discussed in a recent NSA advisory.
sentence.9584: The campaign has the objective of stealing Google and subscription credentials of a reputable news and analysis service focusing on North Korea, as well as delivering reconnaissance malware.
sentence.9585: Kimsuky engages in extensive email correspondence and uses spoofed URLs, websites imitating legitimate web platforms, and Office documents weaponized with the ReconShark malware.
sentence.9586: This activity indicates Kimsuky’s growing dedication to social engineering and highlights the group’s increasing interest in gathering strategic intelligence.
sentence.9588: In collaboration with NK News, a leading subscription-based service that provides news and analyses about North Korea, SentinelLabs has been tracking a targeted social engineering campaign against experts in North Korean affairs from the non-government sector.
sentence.9589: The campaign focuses on theft of email credentials, delivery of reconnaissance malware, and theft of NK News subscription credentials.
sentence.9590: Based on the used malware, infrastructure, and tactics, we assess with high confidence that the campaign has been orchestrated by the Kimsuky threat actor.
sentence.9591: The social engineering tactics and some infrastructure characteristics closely relate to a Kimsuky activity privately reported by PwC and discussed in an NSA advisory published during the writing of this article.
sentence.9592: We focus on the specific targeting of expert analysts of North Korean affairs by impersonating NK News and stealing NK News credentials, and provide details on used TTPs to support collaborative hunting and detection efforts.
sentence.9593: Kimsuky, a suspected North Korean advanced persistent threat (APT) group whose activities align with the interests of the North Korean government, is known for its global targeting of organizations and individuals.
sentence.9594: Operating since at least 2012, the group often employs targeted phishing and social engineering tactics to gather intelligence and access sensitive information.
sentence.9595: A hallmark of the activity we discuss in this post is Kimsuky’s focus on establishing initial contact and developing a rapport with their targets prior to initiating malicious activities.
sentence.9596: As part of their initial contact strategy, the group impersonated Chad O’Carroll, the founder of NK News and the associated holding company Korea Risk Group, using an attacker-created domain, nknews[.]pro, which closely resembles the legitimate NK News domain nknews.org.
sentence.9597: The initial email requests the review of a draft article analyzing the nuclear threat posed by North Korea.
sentence.9598: If the target engages in the conversation, Kimsuky uses the opportunity to deliver a spoofed URL to a Google document, which redirects to a malicious website specifically crafted to capture Google credentials.
sentence.9599: Kimsuky may also deliver a weaponized Office document that executes the ReconShark reconnaissance malware.
sentence.9600: Further, Kimsuky’s objective extends to the theft of subscription credentials from NK News.
sentence.9601: To achieve this, the group distributes emails that lure targeted individuals to log in on the malicious website nknews[.]pro, which masquerades as the authentic NK News site.
sentence.9602: The login form that is presented to the target is designed to capture entered credentials.
sentence.9603: This Kimsuky activity indicates the group’s growing efforts to establish early communication and foster trust with their targets prior to initiating malicious operations, including the delivery of malware.
sentence.9604: Their approach highlights the group’s commitment to creating a sense of rapport with the individuals they target, potentially increasing the success rate of their subsequent malicious activities.
sentence.9605: By actively targeting high-profile experts in North Korean affairs and stealing subscription credentials from prominent news and analysis outlets focussing on North Korea, Kimsuky demonstrates a heightened curiosity in understanding how the international community perceives developments concerning North Korea, such as the country’s military activities.
sentence.9606: These actions are probably part of their broader objective to gather strategic intelligence, contributing to North Korea’s decision-making processes.
sentence.9607: Google Credential Theft We observed Kimsuky distributing an HTML-formatted phishing email to selected individuals, which requests the review of a draft article analyzing the nuclear threat posed by North Korea.
sentence.9608: The email primarily aims to initiate a subsequent conversation and is intentionally designed to appear benign: It impersonates NK News leadership and lacks any malicious artifacts.
sentence.9609: Initial email If the target engages in the conversation, Kimsuky eventually follows up with an email that contains an URL to a Google document.
sentence.9610: Follow-up email If the target is not responsive, Kimsuky follows up with a reminder email in an attempt to engage the target in conversation.
sentence.9611: Reminder email The URL’s destination is manipulated through the spoofing technique of setting the href HTML property to direct to a website created by Kimsuky.
sentence.9612: This method, commonly employed in phishing attacks, creates a discrepancy between the perceived legitimacy of the link (a genuine Google document) and the actual website visited upon clicking the URL.
sentence.9613: The displayed URL to a Google document points to an actual article hosted on Google Docs, delving into the topic of the North Korean nuclear threat.
sentence.9614: The article contains visible edits to give the impression of a genuine draft article, aligning with Kimsuky’s luring tactic.
sentence.9615: Google document The spoofed destination of the URL redirects the target to an attacker-created website that masquerades as a legitimate Google Docs site for requesting document access, such as https[://]drive-google[.]shanumedia[.]com/pdf/ul/ji78fghJHKtgfLKJIO/s2.php?menu=ZGFu[...]vbQ== The Base-64 encoded segment, that is, the value of the menu URL query parameter, resolves to the target’s email address.
sentence.9616: This serves as a means of transporting the target’s address to the fake Google Docs site, which enables the site to dynamically display the address, creating a personalized and convincing appearance of legitimacy.
sentence.9617: The design and functionality of this site suggest its potential for reuse in targeting different individuals.
sentence.9618: Malicious Google Docs site We were unable to analyze the functionality behind the Request access web element as the group has taken down the site.
sentence.9619: However, given the theme of the site, we suspect that it has been designed to capture entered Google credentials.
sentence.9620: During conversations with targeted individuals, Kimsuky also seizes any available opportunity to distribute password-protected weaponized Office documents that deploy the ReconShark reconnaissance malware.
sentence.9621: ReconShark exfiltrates information relevant for conducting subsequent precision attacks, such as deployed detection mechanisms and hardware information.
sentence.9622: The implementation of the ReconShark variant we observed in this activity remains the same as the one covered in our previous post on Kimsuky activity, with the main distinction being the use of a different C2 server: staradvertiser[.]store.
sentence.9623: This domain resolves to the IP address 162.0.209[.]27, which has hosted domains that have been attributed to Kimsuky in previous research, such as sesorin[.]lol and rfa[.]ink.
sentence.9624: Kimsuky’s use of ReconShark as part of this activity underscores the malware’s central role within the group’s current operational playbook.
sentence.9626: We also observed Kimsuky attempting to steal credentials for the subscription service of NK News, which is known for its comprehensive expert analyses and news reports.
sentence.9627: Gaining access to such reports would provide Kimsuky with valuable insights into how the international community assesses and interprets developments related to North Korea, contributing to their broader strategic intelligence-gathering initiatives.
sentence.9628: In order to accomplish this, Kimsuky distributes an email that lure targeted individuals to log in to a spoofed NK News subscription service.
sentence.9629: The emails prompt the recipients to confirm their NK News accounts under the pretext of recent security updates.
sentence.9630: Phishing Email The fake login site, hosted at https[://]www.nknews[.]pro/ip/register/, features a login form with the standard web elements, such as Sign In, Sign Up, and Forgot Password?
sentence.9632: When clicked, the Sign In button executes the loginAct JavaScript function, whereas the rest of the buttons do not conduct any activities.
sentence.9633: Fake NK News login site The JavaScript code captures entered credentials by issuing an HTTP POST request to https[://]www.nknews[.]pro/ip/register/login[.]php and then redirects the user to the legitimate NK News site.
sentence.9634: JavaScript code The main website hosted at https[://]www.nknews[.]pro redirects to the legitimate NK News site, https://nknews.org, and uses a certificate issued by Sectigo: Thumbprint: a1597d197e9b084a043ada5c7dac1f9b6d7f7af3
sentence.9636: The domain nknews[.]pro, registered through Namecheap, also resolves to the Kimsuky-linked IP address 162.0.209[.]27.
sentence.9637: The URL https[://]www.nknews[.]pro/config[.]php hosts a password-protected remote management site, which is likely an implementation of the b374k tool, based on the implementation of the login site and the presence of the config.php file.
sentence.9638: The Kimsuky group is known to use this tool for remote management of its infrastructure.
sentence.9639: b374k login site Conclusion SentinelLabs remains actively engaged in monitoring the activities conducted by Kimsuky.
sentence.9640: The findings presented in this post highlight the group’s persistent commitment to targeted social engineering attacks and underscore the need for increased awareness and understanding of Kimsuky’s tactics among potential targets.
sentence.9641: Maintaining vigilance and implementing effective security measures are imperative to mitigate the risks posed by this persistent threat actor.

sentence.9645: title: Warning: New attack campaign utilized a new 0-day RCE vulnerability on Microsoft Exchange Server url: https://www.gteltsc.vn/blog/warning-new-attack-campaign-utilized-a-new-0day-rce-vulnerability-on-microsoft-exchange-server-12715.html Circa the beginning of August 2022, while doing security monitoring & incident response services, GTSC SOC team discovered that a critical infrastructure was being attacked, specifically to their Microsoft Exchange application.
sentence.9646: During the investigation, GTSC Blue Team experts determined that the attack utilized an unpublished Exchange security vulnerability, i.e., a 0-day vulnerability, thus immediately came up with a temporary containment plan.
sentence.9647: At the same time, Red Team experts started researching and debugging Exchange de-compiled code to find the vulnerability and exploit code.
sentence.9648: Thanks to experience finding the previous 1-day Exchange exploit, the RedTeam has a great understanding of Exchange’s code flows and processing mechanisms, therefore research time was reduced, and the vulnerability was uncovered quickly.
sentence.9649: The vulnerability turns out to be so critical that it allows the attacker to do RCE on the compromised system.
sentence.9650: GTSC submitted the vulnerability to the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) right away to work with Microsoft so that a patch could be prepared as soon as possible.
sentence.9651: ZDI verified and acknowledged 2 bugs, whose CVSS scores are 8.8 and 6.3, concerning the exploit as follows.
sentence.9652: However up to now, GTSC has seen other customers also experiencing the similar problem.
sentence.9653: After careful testing, we confirmed that those systems were being attacked using this 0-day vulnerability.
sentence.9654: To help the community temporarily stop the attack before an official patch from Microsoft is available, we publish this article aiming to those organizations who are using Microsoft Exchange email system.
sentence.9655: Vulnerability information The exploit process comprises of two parts as follows: - Requests with a similar format to the ProxyShell vulnerability: autodiscover/autodiscover.json?@evil.com/<Exchange-backend-endpoint>&Email=autodiscover/autodiscover.json%3f@evil.com.
sentence.9657: The use of the link above to access a component in the backend where the RCE could be implemented.
sentence.9658: However at this time, we would like NOT to release technical details to implement RCE yet.
sentence.9659: Post-exploit activities After successfully mastering the exploit, we recorded attacks to collect information and create a foothold in the victim's system.
sentence.9660: The attack team also used various techniques to create backdoors on the affected system and perform lateral movements to other servers in the system.
sentence.9662: We detected webshells, mostly obfuscated, being dropped to Exchange servers.
sentence.9663: Using the user-agent, we detected that the attacker uses Antsword, an active Chinese-based opensource cross-platform website administration tool that supports webshell management.
sentence.9673: We suspect that these come from a Chinese attack group because the webshell codepage is 936, which is a Microsoft character encoding for simplified Chinese.
sentence.9674: Another notable feature is that the hacker also changes the content of the file RedirSuiteServiceProxy.aspx to webshell content.
sentence.9675: RedirSuiteServiceProxy.aspx is a legitimate file name available in the Exchange server.

sentence.9728: Recent TZW Campaigns Revealed As Part of GlobeImposter Malware Family url: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/recent-tzw-campaigns-revealed-as-part-of-globeimposter-malware-family/ In recent years, efforts to apprehend threat groups and shrink their operating landscape have gone international.
sentence.9729: As authorities across multiple countries continue to implement sanctions and openly communicate current trends to the public, threat groups increasingly resort to rebranding or creating similar variants under different names to sidestep crackdowns and obfuscate their identities.
sentence.9730: In a February 2023 blog post, Ahnlab described a new ransomware campaign affecting South Korean organizations which deployed a malware they dubbed “TZW” ransomware.
sentence.9731: Our research links TZW ransomware to a known malware family called GlobeImposter (sometimes referred to as LOLNEK or LOLKEK).
sentence.9732: Close inspection of host origins and prominent file similarities used in both TZW and GlobeImposter campaigns suggest that actors behind GlobeImposter are updating their payloads and obfuscating their infrastructure in a manner consistent with a rebrand effort.
sentence.9733: Overview of GlobeImposter & New Variant TZW GlobeImposter has a long and winding history.
sentence.9734: First observed in-the-wild in 2016, the name “GlobeImposter” is based on the ransomware’s mimicry of Globe ransomware payloads.
sentence.9735: Multiple new versions and variations of GlobeImposter have appeared in the years since.
sentence.9736: Frequently, these have been referred to by their extension (e.g., .DREAM, .Nutella, .NARCO, .LEGO).
sentence.9737: However, these are all part of the same umbrella malware family.
sentence.9738: In that same year, Emisoft released a decryption tool for early versions of GlobeImposter.
sentence.9739: Shortly after, the malware authors responded with an updated version for which no decryption tools are available.
sentence.9740: Since 2017, campaigns delivering GlobeImposter have continued to proliferate even though the ransomware has only evolved slightly.
sentence.9741: The ransomware has also been used in conjunction with some well-documented high-end cybercriminal groups.
sentence.9742: For example, in 2017 TA505 (also known as G0092, GOLD TAHOE) began using GlobeImposter in replacement of Jaff, GandCrab, and Snatch to extend the reach and effectiveness of their campaigns.
sentence.9743: GlobeImposter’s Delivery Methods Explained GlobeImposter is most often delivered via phishing email as an attachment or a link to a malicious attachment.
sentence.9744: The payloads are typically distributed via 7zip or traditional zip file archives.
sentence.9745: The archives often include a JavaScript (.js) file that downloads and executes the GlobeImposter payload.
sentence.9746: More recent campaigns from within the past three years still tend to follow this formula.
sentence.9747: GlobeImposter has also been distributed as a later-stage infection within some well-known botnets.
sentence.9748: For example, in 2017 GlobeImposter was distributed via the Necurs botnet.
sentence.9749: This occurred as part of multiple spam campaigns that also included 7zip archives and followed the execution flow previously described.
sentence.9750: Linking TZW Attacks to GlobeImposter AhnLab’s research revealed a ransomware campaign they referred to as “TZW” with victims in South Korea.
sentence.9751: The name is derived from the first 3 characters of the TOR-based victim portal.
sentence.9752: A closer look suggests that “TZW” samples represent a new variant of the GlobeImposter family.
sentence.9753: The pre-TZW GlobeImposter ransom notes follow the same template as the current TZW samples.
sentence.9754: Ransom note similarities are far from reliable, but it’s worth noting their likenesses.
sentence.9755: Example of a GlobeImposter ransom note.
sentence.9756: Example of a TZW variant GlobeImposter ransom note.
sentence.9757: Once a machine is infected, more concrete markers indicate a deeper level of similarity.
sentence.9758: One such marker is the “CRYPTO LOCKER” string appended to the tail of the encrypted files.
sentence.9759: This is a known marker present across GlobeImposter variants.
sentence.9760: Examples of CRYPTO LOCKER markers at EOF (TZW and LOLKEK variants).
sentence.9761: GlobeImposter has the ability to delete volume shadow copies, thereby inhibiting the recovery of data.
sentence.9762: There are clear similarities around the methodology of the VSS removal.
sentence.9764: GlobeImposter vs TZW variant shadow copy removal procedure.
sentence.9765: Code and functionality, by and large, are identical across GlobeImposter payloads pointing to obzuqvr5424kkc4unbq2p2i67ny3zngce3tbdr37nicjqesgqcgomfqd[.] onion and those pointing to the newer tzw7ckhurmxgcpajx6gy57dkrysl2sigfrt6nk4a3rvedfldigtor7ad[.]onion.
sentence.9766: A thorough comparison of the two respective samples shows there are only minor differences.
sentence.9767: Zoomed-out view of GlobeImposter (hex) compared against the TZW variation.
sentence.9768: AhnLab’s research describes artifacts from a specific sample within a specific campaign.
sentence.9769: We have seen the newer TZW variations vary somewhat with regards to file metadata.
sentence.9770: Two TZW payloads, varied file metadata A majority of the TZW variant samples that we have analyzed resemble the version on the left hand side.
sentence.9771: The version on the right was seen in the samples noted by AhnLab.
sentence.9772: Understanding TZW and GlobeImposter’s Shared Infrastructure Previous GlobeImposter payloads directed victims to a TOR-based portal at obzuqvr5424kkc4unbq2p2i67ny3zngce3tbdr37nicjqesgqcgomfqd[.]onion.
sentence.9774: Beginning in late 2022, we start to see victims also being directed to tzw7ckhurmxgcpajx6gy57dkrysl2sigfrt6nk4a3rvedfldigtor7ad[.]onion.
sentence.9775: The interfaces and required steps are identical: GlobeImposter Victim Portal 2 from late 2022 onward.
sentence.9776: At the time of writing, both victim portals remain active.
sentence.9777: In addition, we can confirm the relationship between these via the publicly-viewable Apache Server Status Page.
sentence.9778: This Apache status screen is visible as a result of a misconfiguration on the Apache server, allowing us to see all the active vhosts (virtual hosts) present there.
sentence.9779: Apache Status page – GlobeImposter victim portal.
sentence.9780: Through this view we see that the following vhosts are active on the device.
sentence.9781: obzuqvr5424kkc4unbq2p2i67ny3zngce3tbdr37nicjqesgqcgomfqd[.]onion tzw7ckhurmxgcpajx6gy57dkrysl2sigfrt6nk4a3rvedfldigtor7ad[.]onion linux[.]3bcd0a[.]com Vhosts on GlobeImposter victim portal.
sentence.9782: This evidence of shared infrastructure suggests that the newly rebranded TZW ransomware samples are likely being operated by the same group that was pushing recent waves of GlobeImposter malware.
sentence.9783: How to Protect Against GlobeImposter and TZW Ransomware SentinelOne Singularity protects against malicious behaviors and malware associated with GlobeImposter and TZW.
sentence.9784: With the site policy set to Protect, GlobeImposter ransomware is detected and prevented automatically.
sentence.9785: In Detect-only mode, analysts can observe the malware’s behaviour and file encryption attempts, rolling back the device to a clean state on completion of the test.
sentence.9786: Conclusion Based on our analysis, the TZW ransomware recently documented by AhnLab is yet another example of the threat actors behind GlobeImposter pivoting their TTPs alongside a rebrand, including a new but related Onion address.
sentence.9787: We also show that the old “LOLNEK” Onion address and the Onion address within the TZW variant are hosted on the same server as two vhosts.
sentence.9788: Regardless of the name or brand, GlobeImposter continues to pose a threat to enterprises.
sentence.9789: Ensuring good user hygiene, along with strong, properly-configured, and robust security controls will go a long way to prevent these attacks from affecting your environment.
sentence.9790: SentinelOne Singularity protects against malicious behaviors and malware associated with GlobeImposter and TZW.
