sentence.9793: title: MERCURY and DEV-1084: Destructive attack on hybrid environment url: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/04/07/mercury-and-dev-1084-destructive-attack-on-hybrid-environment/ April 2023 update – Microsoft Threat Intelligence has shifted to a new threat actor naming taxonomy aligned around the theme of weather.
sentence.9794: MERCURY is now tracked as Mango Sandstorm and DEV-1084 is now tracked as Storm-1084.
sentence.9795: To learn more about the new taxonomy represents the origin, unique traits, and impact of threat actors, to get complete mapping of threat actor names, read this blog:
sentence.9796: Microsoft shifts to a new threat actor naming taxonomy.
sentence.9797: Microsoft Threat Intelligence has detected destructive operations enabled by MERCURY, a nation-state actor linked to the Iranian government, that attacked both on-premises and cloud environments.
sentence.9798: While the threat actors attempted to masquerade the activity as a standard ransomware campaign, the unrecoverable actions show destruction and disruption were the ultimate goals of the operation.
sentence.9799: Previous MERCURY attacks have been observed targeting on-premises environments, however, the impact in this case notably also included destruction of cloud resources.
sentence.9800: Microsoft assesses that MERCURY likely worked in partnership with another actor that Microsoft tracks as DEV-1084, who carried out the destructive actions after MERCURY’s successful operations had gained access to the target environment.
sentence.9801: MERCURY likely exploited known vulnerabilities in unpatched applications for initial access before handing off access to DEV-1084 to perform extensive reconnaissance and discovery, establish persistence, and move laterally throughout the network, oftentimes waiting weeks and sometimes months before progressing to the next stage.
sentence.9802: DEV-1084 was then later observed leveraging highly privileged compromised credentials to perform en masse destruction of resources, including server farms, virtual machines, storage accounts, and virtual networks, and send emails to internal and external recipients.
sentence.9803: In this blog post, we detail our analysis of the observed actor activity and related tools.
sentence.9804: We also share information to the community and industry partners on ways to detect these attacks, including detection details of MERCURY and DEV-1084’s tools in Microsoft 365 Defender, Microsoft Defender for Identity, Microsoft Defender for Cloud Applications, Microsoft Defender Antivirus, and Microsoft Defender for Endpoint.
sentence.9805: As with any observed nation-state actor activity, Microsoft has directly notified targeted or compromised customers, providing them with important information needed to secure their environments.
sentence.9806: Microsoft uses DEV-#### designations as a temporary name given to an unknown, emerging, or a developing cluster of threat activity, allowing Microsoft to track it as a unique set of information until we reach high confidence about the origin or identity of the actor behind the activity.
sentence.9808: Microsoft tracks the destructive actions documented in this blog post as DEV-1084.
sentence.9809: DEV-1084 likely worked in partnership with MERCURY—an Iran-based actor that the US Cyber Command has publicly linked to Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS).
sentence.9810: DEV-1084 publicly adopted the DarkBit persona and presented itself as a criminal actor interested in extortion, likely as an attempt to obfuscate Iran’s link to and strategic motivation for the attack.
sentence.9811: The link between the DEV-1084 cluster and MERCURY was established based on the following evidence: DEV-1084 operators were observed sending threatening emails from 146.70.106[.]89, an IP address previously linked to MERCURY.
sentence.9812: DEV-1084 used MULLVAD VPN, the same VPN provider historically used by MERCURY.
sentence.9813: DEV-1084 used Rport and a customized version of Ligolo.
sentence.9814: MERCURY has also been observed using Rport and a similar version of Ligolo in previous attacks.
sentence.9815: DEV-1084 used the vatacloud[.]com domain for command and control (C2) during this incident.
sentence.9816: Microsoft assesses with high-confidence that the vatacloud[.]com domain is controlled by MERCURY operators.
sentence.9817: Microsoft assesses that MERCURY gains access to the targets through remote exploitation of an unpatched internet-facing device.
sentence.9818: MERCURY then handed off access to DEV-1084.
sentence.9819: It is not currently clear if DEV-1084 operates independently of MERCURY and works with other Iranian actors or if DEV-1084 is an ‘effects based’ sub-team of MERCURY that only surfaces when MERCURY operators are instructed to carry out a destructive attack.
sentence.9820: Early activities, related attacker tools and techniques Microsoft assesses with moderate confidence that the threat actors attempted several times and succeeded to perform initial intrusion leveraging exposed vulnerable applications, for example, continuing to exploit Log4j 2 vulnerabilities in unpatched systems in July 2022.
sentence.9821: After gaining access, the threat actors deploy several tools and leverage techniques to maintain persistence, which provide effective and continued access to compromised devices, such as the following:
sentence.9822: Installing web shells Adding a local user account and elevating privileges to local administrator Installing legitimate remote access tools, such as RPort, Ligolo and eHorus Installing a customized PowerShell script backdoor Stealing credentials Once the persistence is established, the threat actors perform extensive discovery leveraging common native Windows tools and commands such as netstat and nltest.
sentence.9823: Such reconnaissance activities were seen leveraged throughout the attack chain.
sentence.9824: The threat actors consistently perform extensive lateral movement actions using the acquired credentials within a targeted environment.
sentence.9825: These actions mainly involved: Remote scheduled tasks to launch their customized PowerShell backdoor Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to launch commands on devices Remote services to run encoded PowerShell commands After infecting the new devices, the threat actors often installed the same persistence mechanisms as described above.
sentence.9826: Interestingly, after each main attack step, the actors did not always immediately continue their operations but would wait weeks and sometimes months before moving to the next step.
sentence.9827: For execution and communication, the threat actors leverage several C2 servers and sometimes deploy tunnelling tools, such as Ligolo and OpenSSH, commonly leveraged to stay under the radar of security teams and solutions.
sentence.9828: On-premises destructive impact In observed activity, the threat actors leveraged highly privileged credentials and access to domain controllers on on-premises destructive operations to prepare for large-scale encryption of targeted devices.
sentence.9829: To do so, they first interfered with security tools using Group Policy Objects (GPO).
sentence.9830: With defenses impaired, the threat actors proceeded to stage the ransomware payload in the NETLOGON shares on several domain controllers.
sentence.9831: GPO was leveraged again to register a scheduled task used to launch the ransomware payload.
sentence.9832: Finally, the ransomware payload encrypted files found on the file system of the targeted devices by changing the file name extension to DARKBIT and dropped ransom notes.
sentence.9834: On-premises attack flow Moving from on-premises to cloud To move from on-premises to the cloud, the threat actors had to first compromise two privileged accounts and leverage them to manipulate the Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Connect agent.
sentence.9835: Two weeks before the ransomware deployment, the threat actors first used a compromised, highly privileged account to access the device where the Azure Active Directory (Azure AD) Connect agent is installed.
sentence.9836: We assess with high confidence that the threat actors then used the AADInternals tool to extract the plaintext credentials of a privileged Azure AD account.
sentence.9837: The threat actors then used these credentials to pivot from the on-premises environment to the Azure AD environment.
sentence.9838: Azure AD Connect is an on-premises application for managing hybrid identities through features like password hash synchronization, pass-through authentication, objects synchronization, and others.
sentence.9839: As part of the express settings installation process, multiple accounts are created both in the on-premises (Windows Server Active Directory) and cloud (Azure AD) environments.
sentence.9840: The first account is the AD DS Connector Account.
sentence.9841: The account name is prefixed with MSOL_
sentence.9842: and it is created with a long complex password.
sentence.9844: Example of AD DS Connector account
sentence.9845: This account’s permissions are set based on features enabled during the service’s installation, but in most common scenarios, the account has permissions to replicate directory changes, modify passwords, modify users, modify groups, and so on (see all the permissions here).
sentence.9846: In addition, during installation, an Azure AD account called the Azure AD Connector Account is also created.
sentence.9847: This account is used by the synchronization service to manage Azure AD objects.
sentence.9848: The account is created with a long complex password as well, and by default (if using the express settings) prefixed with Sync_[ServerName].
sentence.9849: This user is assigned with the Directory Synchronization Accounts role (see detailed permissions of this role here).
sentence.9850: In older versions, this account might be assigned with the Global Administrator role.
sentence.9852: Example of an Azure AD Connector account There are other entities detailed here that are created but are less relevant to this topic.
sentence.9853: Extracting credentials Two weeks before the ransomware deployment, the threat actors were observed using compromised credentials to access the Azure AD Connect device.
sentence.9854: Next, they set up an SSH tunnel to an attacker-controlled device.
sentence.9855: On a separate attacker-controlled compromised device, evidence indicates cloning of the AADInternals tool.
sentence.9856: One of the functions available in this tool’s library is Get-AADIntSyncCredentials, which allows any local administrator on a device where Azure AD Connect is installed to extract the plaintext credentials of both the Azure AD Connector account and the AD DS Connector account.
sentence.9857: Shortly before the ransomware deployment, we observed authentication from a known attacker IP address into the Azure AD Connector cloud account.
sentence.9858: Investigating this sign-in showed that the threat actors were able to access the account on the first attempt without any guessing or modification of the password, indicating that the actors possessed the password for this account.
sentence.9859: The Azure AD Connector account is configured with single-factor authentication, making it easier for the attacker to gain entry and elevate privileges.
sentence.9860: Cloud destructive impact On the day of the ransomware attack, the threat actors executed multiple actions in the cloud using two privileged accounts.
sentence.9861: The first account was the compromised Azure AD Connector account, which had Global Administrator permissions as it was set up for an old solution (DirSync).
sentence.9862: For the second account, which also had Global Administrator permissions, the threat actors leveraged RDP for access into the account.
sentence.9863: Even though this account had MFA in place, the threat actors accessed it through RDP, which is an open session that evades MFA blocking their activities.
sentence.9865: Pivoting to the cloud Mass Azure resource deletion On the same day, a successful sign-in to the Microsoft Azure environment was observed.
sentence.9866: The threat actors claimed the Global Administrator permission through Azure Privileged Identity Management (PIM) and elevated access to get permissions to the target’s management groups and Azure subscriptions.
sentence.9867: The Azure AD Connector account and the compromised administrator account were then used to perform significant destruction of the Azure environment—deleting within a few hours server farms, virtual machines, storage accounts, and virtual networks.
sentence.9868: We assess that the attacker’s goal was to cause data loss and a denial of service (DoS) of the target’s services.
sentence.9869: Exchange Web Server API abuse The actors went on to provide an existing legitimate OAuth application with both the full_access_as_app permission and administrator consent, which granted the threat actors full access to mailboxes through Exchange Web Services. Figure 5.
sentence.9870: Adding access permission to the existing application With the obtained cloud administrator privileges, the threat actors updated the OAuth application with certificates to conduct malicious activities.

sentence.9937: TLDs from Google brought some discussion about attack vectors.
sentence.9938: Most of those attack vectors are not completely new, like using an “@” to split between username and host.
sentence.9939: While playing a little bit around, an unexpected attack chain appeared, involving a .zip
sentence.9940: TLD, Windows Explorer, WebDAV and a jar file.
sentence.9941: Some further reading and research: tl;dr Combining the following minor issues might cause RCE on a client.
sentence.9942: The Windows Explorer location bar, is also a search function If using a TLD, like .zip, the search will be online, if the file does not exist locally on PATH folders Windows Explorer will happily map a WebDAV folder directly .jar files circumvent the execution Blocker (untrusted Location), however a JRE must be installed Take me to the PoC Introduction While playing around with the newly .zip
sentence.9943: domains some behavior from Windows Explorer was found, which might cause some RCE if a Java Runtime Environment (JRE) is installed.
sentence.9945: A jar full of zippers, symbol picture The Chain Windows Explorer The location bar in the Windows Explorer is also a Search Bar and can be used to find and open files.
sentence.9946: If a file is not found on disk and a domain name is used, it will search online.
sentence.9947: It seems, that the file must be in an on PATH folder, to get directly opened.
sentence.9948: With the introduction of the .zip TLDs this is getting quite interesting.
sentence.9949: So if you write the name of a zip file in the bar, it will open the default browser and go to that page.
sentence.9950: In the next procmon screenshot the flow can be seen: Procmon with pasting dbexport.zip in location bar At first the local on path folders are tested and if that fails the WebDAV Client is started and the dll loaded.
sentence.9951: I could never understand, why it should be a good idea to have a local search function doing things via the internet by default…
sentence.9952: And as I know you guys, leave my .zip domain alone ;) WebDAV If we setup a WebDAV server at that specific .zip domain, in that case dbexport.zip , which can be easily set up via wsgidav wsgidav --port=80 --host=0.0.0.0
sentence.9954: =anonymous the Windows Explorer will not spawn a new browser but will map the folder directly.
sentence.9955: an opened WebDAV folder As it can be seen in the screenshot, the URL changes a bit.
sentence.9956: Shown: Network (WORKGROUP) > http://dbexport.zip Resolved: \\dbexport.zip\DavWWWRoot If we click an executable, we get a confirmation dialog, as the location is not trusted.
sentence.9957: an opened WebDAV folder Phew, so we are safe and this is some kind of not ideal behavior, but at least there is dialog with a warning.
sentence.9958: Bypassing execution blocking After playing with some file extensions, it turns out that this protection is not bulletproof.
sentence.9959: mild shock The execution of typical file types like: bat, chm, cmd, com, exe, hta, js, lnk, pif, ps1, vbs, wsh is indeed blocked.
sentence.9960: Note: Those files will still get executed, if the user clicks on run!
sentence.9961: If there are some custom application handlers registered, it seems that those tools do not have the same restriction.
sentence.9962: One example for this is the .jar filetype, meaning it is possible to execute Java code if the user has a JRE installed, which is quite often the case in business environment.
sentence.9963: This was tested by using the first jar file with a GUI found when googling. running a jar from the WebDAV Promising! Java Malware At this point I was afraid, that it might be necessary to write some Java Malware, like a shellcode loader.
sentence.9964: There are some quite old, but still promising approaches like How to Inject Shellcode from Java.
sentence.9965: Luckily, it turned out to be much simpler.
sentence.9966: Some Copy&Pasted code later a minimalistic and very simple approach to execute a binary was ready.

sentence.9972: = null) { System.out.println(line); } errorReader.close(); reader.close(); } catch (IOException e) { e.printStackTrace(); } } } The interesting part is in line 13: String command = "calc.exe"; defining what to execute.
sentence.9973: So this will just pop a calculator under normal conditions.
sentence.9974: However, if a calc.exe is in the same folder, it will execute that binary, thanks Windows Search Path.
sentence.9975: To generate the jar a simple way without needing a manifest is thew following javac .\HelloWorld.java jar cfe app.jar HelloWorld HelloWorld.class PoC By chaining all together, we get a nice simple flow here.

sentence.9979: As for the most attack chains that require user interaction, the story is important.

sentence.9985: Finding a better story is left as an exercise for the reader.
sentence.9986: Further notes Full path to file and hidden files By supplying a full path like dbexport.zip\app.jar to the explorer location bar, the binary will immediately be executed.
sentence.9987: It seems, that it is somehow possible to hide some files in the folder, but this was buggy during my tests. running a jar from the WebDAV
sentence.9988: However regarding the documentation from MS windows should support hidden files via WebDAV.
sentence.9989: Opening a WebDAV folder will also start the WebDAV service, which is quite famous to use for some ActiveDirectory privilege escalation with relaying to LDAP (RBCD).
sentence.9990: mshta You can also run for example hta files from that WebDAV.
sentence.9991: By typing the command in the start menu an hta file will get executed without a warning.

sentence.9993: LSASS Dump A side effect of the WebDAV is, that the Defender is not going to delete files correctly on that shared folder.
sentence.9994: As LSASS dumps are nowadays recognized by the dump file itself this is a nice way to get your hands on the file.

sentence.10003: Meet ScarCruft’s Dolphin url: https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/11/30/whos-swimming-south-korean-waters-meet-scarcrufts-dolphin/ ESET researchers uncover Dolphin, a sophisticated backdoor extending the arsenal of the ScarCruft APT group ESET researchers have analyzed a previously unreported backdoor used by the ScarCruft APT group.
sentence.10004: The backdoor, which we named Dolphin, has a wide range of spying capabilities, including monitoring drives and portable devices and exfiltrating files of interest, keylogging and taking screenshots, and stealing credentials from browsers.
sentence.10005: Its functionality is reserved for selected targets, to which the backdoor is deployed after initial compromise using less advanced malware.
sentence.10006: In line with other ScarCruft tools, Dolphin abuses cloud storage services – specifically Google Drive – for C&C communication.
sentence.10007: During our investigation, we saw continued development of the backdoor and attempts by the malware authors to evade detection.
sentence.10008: A notable feature of earlier Dolphin versions we analyzed is the ability to modify the settings of victims’ signed-in Google and Gmail accounts to lower their security, most likely to maintain access to victims’ email inboxes.
sentence.10009: In this blogpost, we provide a technical analysis of the Dolphin backdoor and explain its connection to previously documented ScarCruft activity.
sentence.10010: We will present our findings about this new addition to ScarCruft’s toolset at the AVAR 2022 conference.
sentence.10011: Key points in this blogpost: ESET researchers analyzed Dolphin, a previously unreported backdoor used by the ScarCruft APT group.
sentence.10012: Dolphin is deployed on selected targets only; it searches the drives of compromised systems for interesting files and exfiltrates them to Google Drive.
sentence.10013: The backdoor was used as the final payload of a multistage attack in early 2021, involving a watering-hole attack on a South Korean online newspaper, an Internet Explorer exploit, and another ScarCruft backdoor, named BLUELIGHT.
sentence.10014: Since the initial discovery of Dolphin in April 2021, ESET researchers have observed multiple versions of the backdoor, in which the threat actors improved the backdoor’s capabilities and made attempts to evade detection.
sentence.10015: A notable feature of earlier Dolphin versions we analyzed is the ability to modify the settings of victims’ signed-in Google and Gmail accounts to lower their security.
sentence.10016: ScarCruft profile ScarCruft, also known as APT37 or Reaper, is an espionage group that has been operating since at least 2012.
sentence.10017: It primarily focuses on South Korea, but other Asian countries also have been targeted.
sentence.10018: ScarCruft seems to be interested mainly in government and military organizations, and companies in various industries linked to the interests of North Korea.
sentence.10019: Dolphin overview In 2021, ScarCruft conducted a watering-hole attack on a South Korean online newspaper focused on North Korea.
sentence.10020: The attack consisted of multiple components, including an Internet Explorer exploit and shellcode leading to a backdoor named BLUELIGHT, reported by Volexity and Kaspersky.
sentence.10021: In those reports, the BLUELIGHT backdoor was described as the attack’s final payload.
sentence.10022: However, when analyzing the attack, we discovered through ESET telemetry a second, more sophisticated backdoor, deployed on selected victims via BLUELIGHT.
sentence.10023: We named this backdoor Dolphin based on a PDB path found in the executable.
sentence.10024: While the BLUELIGHT backdoor performs basic reconnaissance and evaluation of the compromised machine after exploitation, Dolphin is more sophisticated and manually deployed only against selected victims.
sentence.10025: Both backdoors are capable of exfiltrating files from a path specified in a command, but Dolphin also actively searches drives and automatically exfiltrates files with extensions of interest to ScarCruft.
sentence.10026: Figure 1 provides an overview of the attack components leading to the execution of the Dolphin backdoor.
sentence.10028: Overview of the attack components leading to the execution of the Dolphin backdoor Dolphin analysis Analysis of Dolphin’s components and their capabilities is provided in the following section.
sentence.10029: The analysis is based on the first version of the backdoor that we found, 1.9 (based on a string found in the code) with additional information about changes in newer versions.
sentence.10030: A summarized description of the version changes can be found in the Dolphin evolution section.
sentence.10031: Dolphin installer Ensuing sections describe the installer and loader components responsible for the execution of the Dolphin backdoor in the analyzed attack scenario.
sentence.10032: It is worth noting that this installer and the deployed loader are not exclusive to Dolphin, and were previously seen used with other ScarCruft malware.
sentence.10033: The installer shellcode follows these main objectives: Download and deploy a Python interpreter Generate and deploy a loading chain with its payload Ensure persistence of the loading chain
sentence.10034: The installer downloads a CAB file from OneDrive, containing a legitimate Python 2.7 interpreter.
sentence.10035: The CAB is unpacked to %APPDATA%, and depending on architecture, the interpreter ends up in one of the following directories:
sentence.10037: The installer generates two file paths for loading-chain components, <loader_step_1> and <loader_encrypted_step_2>, with the format <base_dir>\<inf_name>\<dll_name>.
sentence.10038: <base_dir> is randomly selected from %PROGRAMDATA% %PUBLIC% %APPDATA%\Microsoft %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows %LOCALAPPDATA% %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows <inf_name> and <dll_name> are randomly selected from existing filenames (without extension) in %windir%\inf\*.inf and %windir%\system32\*.dll.
sentence.10039: To generate Step 1 of Loader, it uses a script template that is filled with randomly generated names (variables, function).
sentence.10040: The template with generated example is shown in Figure 2. Figure 2.
sentence.10042: The script is then written to <loader_step_1>.
sentence.10043: Step 2 (embedded in the installer) containing the rest of the loading chain, including the payload, is encrypted with a one-byte XOR key derived from the current time and written to <loader_encrypted_step_2>.
sentence.10044: In order to persist the start of the loading chain, the installer sets a Run registry value: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\<random_run_name>\”%appdata%\Python27({32|64})\pythonw.exe” “<loader_step_1>” “<loader_encrypted_step_2>” The <random_run_name> is randomly selected from existing filenames matching %WINDIR%\inf\*.inf, discarding the .inf extension.
sentence.10045: To start the loading chain after installation, it creates a one-time scheduled task.
sentence.10046: Dolphin loader The Dolphin loader consists of a Python script and shellcode.
sentence.10047: Step 1, the Python script, reads a specified file, XOR-decrypts its contents, and executes the resulting shellcode.
sentence.10048: Step 2, shellcode, creates a host process (random CLI executable from %WINDIR%\System32\*.exe), XOR-decrypts further shellcode carried within itself, and injects it into the created process.
sentence.10049: Step 3, another shellcode, XOR-decrypts an embedded PE file – the Dolphin backdoor – and loads and executes it using a custom PE loader.
sentence.10050: Dolphin backdoor Dolphin is a backdoor that collects information and executes commands issued by its operators.
sentence.10051: The backdoor is a regular Windows executable, written in C++.
sentence.10052: It communicates with Google Drive cloud storage, which is used as its C&C server.
sentence.10053: We named the backdoor Dolphin based on a PDB path found in the executable: D:\Development\BACKDOOR\Dolphin\x64\Release\Dolphin.pdb Persistence The backdoor periodically checks and creates its own persistence by making sure that Step 1 of the loader is run every time the system is started, via a registry Run value, in the same way as in the installer: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run\<random_run_name>\”%appdata%\Python27({32|64})\pythonw.exe” “<loader_step_1>” “<loader_encrypted_step_2>” Capabilities The following basic information about the computer and the backdoor is collected: Current backdoor configuration Username Computer name Local and external IP address List of installed security products RAM size and usage Result of check for debugger and other inspection tools (such as Wireshark) OS version Current time Malware version Dolphin downloads commands, issued by its operators, from Google Drive storage and executes them.
sentence.10054: After execution, the output of commands is uploaded.
sentence.10055: Most of Dolphin’s capabilities are controlled through commands.
sentence.10056: The most relevant capabilities are described below.
sentence.10057: File exfiltration By default, Dolphin searches all non-fixed drives (USBs), creates directory listings and exfiltrates files by extension.
sentence.10058: This search can be extended to fixed drives (HDDs), via dedicated commands.
sentence.10059: The following file extensions of interest, specific to media, documents, emails, and certificates, are specified in the default configuration: jpg, doc, xls, ppt, hwp, url, csv, pdf, show, cell, eml, odt, rtf, nxl, amr, 3gp, m4a, txt, msg, key, der, cer, docx, xlsx, pptx, pfx, mp3 Besides this automatic search, specific files can be exfiltrated.
sentence.10060: In the newer versions, the default search was extended to fixed drives.
sentence.10061: The command to get specific files was improved, by caching/storing it in the configuration until completion.
sentence.10062: Portable devices Among regular drives, Dolphin also searches portable devices such as smartphones, using the Windows Portable Device (WPD) API.
sentence.10063: It creates directory listings and exfiltrates files.
sentence.10064: This functionality appeared to be under development in the first version we found, for several reasons: Relying on a hardcoded path with a username that likely doesn’t exist on the victim’s computer Missing variable initialization – some variables are assumed to be zero-initialized, or dereferenced as pointers without initialization Missing extension filtering The code is heavily based on Microsoft’s Portable Devices COM API code sample.
sentence.10065: Apart from automatic search, the operators can specify individual files to be exfiltrated from portable devices.
sentence.10066: In newer versions, this capability was finished and improved by adding extension filtering.
sentence.10067: For unknown reasons, the command to retrieve specific files from portable devices was removed.
sentence.10068: Keylogging and screenshots Dolphin logs keystrokes for windows with titles containing substrings specified in its configuration.
sentence.10069: The defaults are chrome and internet explore (sic).
sentence.10070: This is done via the GetAsyncKeyState API, with keystrokes being logged along with the window name and current time.
sentence.10071: Screenshots are also taken at a configurable interval; the default is once every 30 seconds.
sentence.10072: Screenshots and keylogging are enabled by default, and can be toggled via a command.
sentence.10073: Shellcode Dolphin can receive shellcode for execution.
sentence.10074: The shellcode is stored in the registry, under one of the following keys: HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Themes\Classic\<random_number> HKCU\Software\Microsoft\OneDrive\Update\<random_number> HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Internet Settings\HttpsSoftware\Microsoft\Internet Explorer\Zone\<random_number> (two subkeys as one, likely a coding error)
sentence.10075: It can be executed either locally or in a specified separate process that is created and injected.
sentence.10076: In the newer versions, the shellcode is stored in files instead of the registry, and the stored shellcode is loaded and executed on Dolphin’s startup, which was not the case in version 1.9 (the original version we analyzed).
sentence.10077: Shell commands Dolphin can execute shell commands; this is done via the popen API and their output is retrieved.
sentence.10078: Stealing credentials Dolphin can retrieve credentials from browsers in the form of saved passwords and cookies.
sentence.10079: The following browsers are supported: Chrome Edge Internet Explorer In version 2.2, this capability was removed, presumably to avoid detection.
sentence.10080: It was later restored in version 3.0, but in a different form.
sentence.10081: It is now dynamically received from the C&C in the form of shellcode.
sentence.10082: Google account Another one of Dolphin’s commands modifies the settings of the currently logged-in Google account, lowering its security relative to default settings.
sentence.10083: It steals the existing cookie of the logged-in account from the browser and crafts requests that modify the settings.
sentence.10084: First, it enables access to Gmail via the IMAP protocol by sending an HTTP POST request to: https://mail.google.com/mail/u/0/?ik=<GM_ID_KEY>&at=<GM_ACTION_TOKEN>&view=up&act=prefs
sentence.10085: Then it enables “less secure app access” by sending an undocumented RPC request via an HTTP POST to: https://myaccount.google.com/_/AccountSettingsUi/data/batchexecute These modifications are referred to as “thunder access” in the backdoor, likely being a reference to the Thunderbird email client.
sentence.10086: Accessing their victims’ inboxes with a third-party client via IMAP probably helps ScarCruft operators maintain access to the victims’ emails after stealing credentials, which may not be enough on their own, due to Google’s detection of suspicious login attempts.
sentence.10087: This feature was found in versions 1.9 and 2.0 of the backdoor; it is not present in versions 2.2 or 3.0.
sentence.10088: Data staging Dolphin exfiltrates data to Google Drive storage, staging the data in encrypted ZIP archives before upload.
sentence.10089: The backdoor also maintains a list of files in the form of MD5 hashes, in order to avoid uploading the same file multiple times.
sentence.10090: This list can be reset via a dedicated command.
sentence.10091: Configuration The backdoor contains an initial default configuration that is persisted on first run and loaded on subsequent runs.
sentence.10092: It is stored in the file %ProgramData%\<variable_cfg_name>.inf, where <variable_cfg_name> is randomly selected from existing filenames matching %windir%\inf\*.inf.
sentence.10093: The content is encrypted using AES CBC with random 16-byte keys and IVs, which are stored at the file’s beginning.
sentence.10094: The configuration uses JSON format, with hash-like keys.
sentence.10095: An example of a decrypted configuration is shown in Figure 3.
sentence.10097: Dolphin backdoor configuration The configuration can be modified through commands.
sentence.10098: It contains, among others, the following: Encryption keys Credentials for Google Drive API access Window titles to keylog List of file extensions to exfiltrate Dolphin evolution Since the initial discovery of Dolphin in April 2021, we have observed multiple versions of the backdoor, in which the threat actors improved the backdoor’s capabilities and made attempts to evade detection.
sentence.10099: Figure 4 summarizes the versions seen; a more detailed description of the version changes is provided below.
sentence.10101: Dolphin evolution timeline November 2021 – version 2.0 Version 2.0 introduced the following changes to the version found in April 2021:
sentence.10102: Dynamic resolution of suspicious APIs instead of static imports (for example GetAsyncKeyState) added Shellcode capability finished and improved Persisted shellcode stored in files instead of registry Persisted shellcode loaded and executed on Dolphin startup (previously missing) Portable device file exfiltration capability finished and improved Exfiltration by extensions added Recognition of internal memory and SD cards (from device ID) added Command to get files from portable devices effectively a NOP Device/drive detection and file exfiltration improved Dolphin now unconditionally creates directory listings and exfiltrates files by extension every 30 minutes for all drives and devices (fixed drives, removable drives, portable devices).
sentence.10103: Previously, it was just for removable drives; fixed drives were disabled by default and the code used for accessing portable devices was buggy and broken. December 2021 – version 2.2 Changes introduced in version 2.2 focused mainly on detection evasion.
sentence.10104: The credential-stealing capability and commands related to it – the credential stealing and Google account commands – were removed.
sentence.10105: Most strings in this version are base64 encoded.
sentence.10107: In version 3.0, the code was reorganized and classes renamed, with capabilities remaining unchanged.
sentence.10108: The base64-encoded strings were plaintext again in this version.
sentence.10109: We observed the following additional changes: Command to steal credentials restored in a different form; it now executes shellcode from the C&C Command to get files from portable devices completely removed Command to get files from drives is now cached/stored in the configuration until completion.
sentence.10110: If interrupted (for example by computer shutdown), it is done on the next run.
sentence.10111: This is also useful in the case of removable drives that may not be connected when the command is issued.
sentence.10112: Internet connection check added (https://www.microsoft.com); no malicious code is executed if offline The differences between versions 2.2 and 3.0, especially the discrepancy in string encoding, suggest the possibility that the versions were being developed in parallel by different people.
sentence.10113: Conclusion Dolphin is another addition to ScarCruft’s extensive arsenal of backdoors abusing cloud storage services.
sentence.10114: After being deployed on selected targets, it searches the drives of compromised systems for interesting files and exfiltrates them to Google Drive.
sentence.10115: One unusual capability found in prior versions of the backdoor is the ability to modify the settings of victims’ Google and Gmail accounts to lower their security, presumably in order to maintain account access for the threat actors.
sentence.10116: During our analysis of multiple versions of the Dolphin backdoor, we saw continued development and attempts to evade detection.
sentence.10117: For any inquiries about our research published on WeLiveSecurity, please contact us at threatintel@eset.com.

sentence.10160: title: Iron Tiger’s SysUpdate Reappears, Adds Linux Targeting url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/c/iron-tiger-sysupdate-adds-linux-targeting.html APT & Targeted Attacks Iron Tiger’s SysUpdate Reappears, Adds Linux Targeting We detail the update that advanced persistent threat (APT) group Iron Tiger made on the custom malware family SysUpdate.
sentence.10161: In this version, we also found components that enable the malware to compromise Linux systems.
sentence.10162: By: Daniel Lunghi March 01, 2023Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe Iron Tiger is an advanced persistent threat (APT) that has been focused primarily on cyberespionage for more than a decade.
sentence.10163: In 2022, we noticed that they updated SysUpdate, one of their custom malware families, to include new features and add malware infection support for the Linux platform.
sentence.10164: We found the oldest sample of this updated version in July 2022.
sentence.10165: At the time, we attributed the sample to Iron Tiger but had not yet identified the final payload.
sentence.10166: It was only after finding multiple similar payloads in late October 2022 that we looked further and found similarities with the SysUpdate malware family that had also been updated in 2021.
sentence.10167: As with the previous version, Iron Tiger had made the loading logic complex, probably in an attempt to evade security solutions.
sentence.10168: This new version has similar features to the 2021 version, except that the C++ run-time type information (RTTI) classes we previously observed in 2021 had been removed, and that the code structure was changed to use the ASIO C++ asynchronous library.
sentence.10169: Both changes make reverse engineering the samples longer.
sentence.10170: We strongly advise organizations and users in the targeted industries to reinforce their security measures to defend their systems and stored information from this ongoing campaign.
sentence.10171: Campaign development timeline These are the key dates for understanding the chronology of Iron Tiger’s operations: Apr. 2, 2022: Registration of the domain name linked to our oldest Windows sample of SysUpdate May 11, 2022:
sentence.10172: The command and control (C&C) infrastructure was set up.
sentence.10174: While this could have been tampered with, observed compilation date of our oldest Windows sample. July 20, 2022:
sentence.10175: Oldest Windows sample gets uploaded to Virus Total Oct. 24, 2022:
sentence.10176: Oldest Linux sample gets uploaded to Virus Total We observed that the attacker registered the oldest domain name one month before starting the C&C configuration then waited one more month before compiling the malicious sample linked to that domain name.
sentence.10177: We think the gap between the two updates allows the attackers to plan their operations accordingly.
sentence.10178: Loading process We observed the loading process entailing the following steps: The attacker runs rc.exe, a legitimate “Microsoft Resource Compiler” signed file , which is vulnerable to a DLL side-loading vulnerability, and loads a file named rc.dll.
sentence.10179: The malicious rc.dll loads a file named rc.bin in memory.
sentence.10180: The rc.bin file is a Shikata Ga Nai encoded shellcode that decompresses and loads the first stage in memory.
sentence.10181: Depending on the number of command line parameters, different actions are performed: Zero or two parameters: “Installs” the malware in the system, and calls Stage 1 again via process hollowing with four parameters One parameter: Same as previous action but without the “installation” Four parameters: Creates a memory section with the DES-encrypted malware configuration and a second Shikata Ga Nai shellcode decompressing and loading Stage 2.
sentence.10182: It then runs Stage 2 via process hollowing.
sentence.10183: The “installation” step is considered simple wherein the malware moves the files to a hardcoded folder.
sentence.10184: Depending on the privileges of the process, the malware either creates a registry key or a service that launches the moved executable rc.exe with one parameter.
sentence.10185: This ensures that the malware will be launched during the next reboot, skipping the installation part.
sentence.10187: Updated SysUpdate loading process routine We saw different legitimate executables being used, sideloading different DLL names, and multiple binary files names being loaded by those DLLs.
sentence.10188: We identified the executables and sideloaded files as follows:
sentence.10190: SysUpdate’s seemingly legitimate executables and their respective sideloaded files Legitimate application name Certificate signer Side-loaded DLL name Loaded binary file name INISafeWebSSO.exe Initech inicore_v2.3.30.dll inicore_v2.3.30.bin rc.exe Microsoft rcdll.dll rcdll.bin dlpumgr32.exe DESlock DLPPREM32.dll sv.bin GDFInstall.exe UBISOFT ENTERTAINMENT GameuxInstallHelper.DLL sysconfig.bin route-null.exe Wazuh libwazuhshared.dll wazuhext.bin route-null.exe Wazuh libwazuhshared.dll agent-config.bin wazuh-agent.exe Wazuh libwinpthread-1.dll wazuhext.bin We want to highlight that this is the first time we observed a threat actor abusing a sideloading vulnerability in a Wazuh signed executable.
sentence.10191: Wazuh is a free and open source security platform, and we could confirm that one of the victims was using the legitimate Wazuh platform.
sentence.10192: It is highly likely that Iron Tiger specifically looked for this vulnerability to appear legitimate in the victim’s environment.
sentence.10193: We have notified the affected victim of this intrusion but received no feedback.
sentence.10194: Malware features Looking at the features, several of the functions found in the latest update are similar to the previous SysUpdate version: Service manager (lists, starts, stops, and deletes services) Screenshot grab Process manager (browses and terminates processes) Drive information retrieval File manager (finds, deletes, renames, uploads, downloads a file, and browses a directory)
sentence.10195: Command execution Iron Tiger also added a feature that had not been seen before in this malware family:
sentence.10196: C&C communication through DNS TXT requests.
sentence.10197: While DNS is not supposed to be a communication protocol, the attacker abuses this protocol to send and receive information.
sentence.10199: C&C communication with DNS TXT records First, the malware retrieves the configured DNS servers by calling the GetNetworkParams API function and parsing the DnsServerList linked list.
sentence.10200: If this method fails, the malware uses the DNS server operated by Google at IP address 8.8.8.8.
sentence.10201: For the first request, the malware generates a random number of 32 bits and appends 0x2191 to it.
sentence.10202: This results in six bytes — four for the random number, two for 0x2191 — and encodes the result further with Base32 algorithm using the alphabet “abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz012345”.
sentence.10203: Looking at Figure 2, the contacted domain name is after "TXT"; only the first four letters change as the rest of the encoded series is always the same.
sentence.10204: This is because the random number changes every time, but the end is the same “0x2191” result.
sentence.10205: This explains why the first DNS request always ends with “reeaaaaaa.<c&c domain>”.
sentence.10206: If the C&C reply matches the format expected by the malware, it launches multiple threads that handle further commands and sends information about the infected machine.
sentence.10207: Interestingly, the code related to this DNS C&C communication is only present in samples that use it, meaning that the builder is modular and that there might be samples in the wild with unreported features.
sentence.10208: We continue monitoring this group and malware family for updates on possible variations of C&C communication protocols being abused.
sentence.10209: In all versions, the malware retrieves information on the infected machine and sends it to the C&C encrypted with DES.
sentence.10210: Collected machine information includes the following: Randomly generated GUID Hostname Domain name Username User privileges Processor architecture Current process ID Operating system version Current file path Local IP address and port used to send the network packet The configuration is encrypted with a hardcoded DES key and is a few bytes long following the structure enumerated below: Table 2.
sentence.10211: Configuration structure Field content Length (in bytes) Comment Example Header 4
sentence.10212: We only found one value 0x00000001 GUID 38 Follows the Microsoft format {89D0E853-FA08-4f94-A5FE-A90E6869E074} Size of the C&C section 4 0x00000018 Size of the next C&C domain name and port 4 0x00000014 C&C type 1 0x01 = regular C&C 0x05
sentence.10214: = regular C&C 0x01 C&C domain name Variable dev.gitlabs.me Port number 4 0x00000050 Size of next section 4 Next section contains all the hardcoded names (folder, files, registry values) 0x00000034 Name of the hardcoded directory where files are copied Variable The folder is located either in % gtdcfp Name of the executable vulnerable to side loading Variable TextInputHost.exe Name of the malicious side-loaded DLL Variable rc.dll Name of the binary file containing the encoded Stage 1 Variable rc.bin Name of the service or registry key value used for persistence Variable gtdcfp We noted that Stage 2 does not embed the configuration file, which is copied in memory by the previous stage.
sentence.10215: We only saw one case where there was only one stage being decrypted in memory and the configuration was hardcoded.
sentence.10216: Interestingly, all the samples of this “new” version had a domain name as its C&C. In the previous version of SysUpdate, the group used hardcoded IP addresses as C&C. It is possible that this change is a consequence of the new DNS TXT records’ communication feature as it requires a domain name.
sentence.10217: SysUpdate samples for Linux While investigating SysUpdate’s infrastructure, we found some ELF files linked to some C&C servers.
sentence.10218: We analyzed them and concluded that the files were a SysUpdate version made for the Linux platform.
sentence.10219: The ELF samples were also written in C++, made use of the Asio library, shared common network encryption keys, and had many similar features.
sentence.10220: For example, the file handling functions are almost the same.
sentence.10221: It is possible that the developer made use of the Asio library because of its portability across multiple platforms.
sentence.10222: Some parameters can be passed to the binary (note that “Boolean” refers to Boolean data that is sent to the C&C):
sentence.10224: Parameters passed to the binary as observed from Linux SysUpdate samples Parameter Effect -launch Sets persistence, zeroes boolean, and exits -run Zeroes boolean and continues -x Daemonize the process, zeroes boolean, and continues -i Daemonize the process, zeroes boolean, sets persistence, and continues -f <guid> Sets the GUID to <guid> and continues The persistence is ensured by copying a script similarly named as the current filename to the /usr/lib/systemd/system/ directory, and creating a symlink to this file in the /etc/ystem/system/multi-user.target.wants/ directory.
sentence.10225: Thus, this method only works if the current process has root privileges.
sentence.10226: The content of the script is:
sentence.10227: [Unit] Description=xxx [Service] Type=forking ExecStart=<path to current file> -x ExecStop=/usr/bin/id [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target After running the code dependent on the parameters, if the operator has not chosen a GUID with the “-f” parameter, the malware generates a random GUID and writes it to a file similarly named as the current file, with a “d” appended to it.
sentence.10228: Then, the malware retrieves information on the compromised computer and sends it to the C&C. The following information is sent to the C&C, encrypted with a hardcoded key and DES CBC algorithm: GUID Host name Username Local IP address and port used to send the request Current PID Kernel version and machine architecture Current file path Boolean (0 if it was launched with exactly one parameter, 1 otherwise)
sentence.10229: For the DNS C&C communication version, the malware retrieves the configured DNS server by reading the content of the /etc/resolv.conf file, or uses the DNS server operated by Google at IP address 8.8.8.8.
sentence.10230: In 2022, we already noticed that this threat actor was interested in platforms other than Windows, with the rshell malware family running on Linux and Mac OS.
sentence.10231: For these reasons, we would not be surprised to see SysUpdate samples for the Mac OS platform in the future.
sentence.10232: Interestingly, most of the Linux samples we found used the new DNS tunneling feature we detailed in Figure 2, while only one of the Windows’ samples used it.
sentence.10233: Certificate compromise Another interesting part of this campaign is the fact that some of the malicious files are signed with a certificate with the following signer: “Permyakov Ivan Yurievich IP”.
sentence.10234: Looking for that name in search engines brings results from the official VMProtect website.
sentence.10235: The email address linked to the Authenticode certificate also links to that domain name.
sentence.10236: VMProtect is a commercial software intended to make analysis of code extremely difficult by implementing a custom virtual machine with non-standard architecture.
sentence.10237: The software has been used by multiple APT and cybercrime groups in the past to obfuscate their malware.
sentence.10238: When searching on malware repositories for other files signed by the same certificate, we find multiple files named “VMProtectDemo.exe”, “VMProtect.exe”, or “VMProtect_Con.exe”, which suggests that an official demo version of VMProtect is also signed by this certificate.
sentence.10239: It appears that the threat actor managed to retrieve the private key allowing him to sign malicious code.
sentence.10240: As of this writing, the certificate is now revoked.
sentence.10241: Using stolen certificates to sign malicious code is a common practice for this threat actor, as we already highlighted in 2015 and in all our recent investigations.
sentence.10242: Interestingly, the threat actor not only signed some of its malicious executables with the stolen certificate, but also used VMProtect to obfuscate one of them.
sentence.10243: In late January 2023, a Redline stealer sample (detected by Trend Micro as TrojanSpy.Win32.REDLINE.YXDA1Z, SHA256: e24b29a1df287fe947018c33590a0b443d6967944b281b70fba7ea6556d00109) signed by the same certificate was uploaded.
sentence.10244: We do not believe that the stealer is linked to Iron Tiger, considering that the network infrastructure is different, and previous reports document the malware’s goals to be centered on committing cybercrime than data theft.
sentence.10245: This could mean other users managed to extract the same private key from the VMProtect demo version, or it was sold in the underground to different groups, Iron Tiger among them.
sentence.10246: Infection vector We did not find an infection vector.
sentence.10247: However, we noticed that one of the executables packed with VMProtect and signed with the stolen certificate was named “youdu_client_211.9.194.exe”.
sentence.10248: Youdu is the name of a Chinese instant messaging application aimed for use of enterprise customers.
sentence.10249: Its website mentions multiple customers in many industries, some of them in critical sectors such as government, energy, healthcare, or banking.
sentence.10250: But they also have other customers in industries such as gaming, IT, media, construction, and retail, apparently all located inside China.
sentence.10251: The properties of the malicious file also match the usual Youdu version numbering.
sentence.10252: However, the legitimate files are signed with a “Xinda.im” certificate instead of the stolen VMProtect certificate.
sentence.10254: Comparing the properties of the malicious file (left), and properties of the legitimate Youdu installer (right)
sentence.10255: As seen in the product name identified in the malicious file’s properties, we searched for possible products named “i Talk” but did not find any that could be related to this investigation.
sentence.10256: However, we found traces of files from the legitimate Youdu chat application signed by Xinda.im being copied to folders named “i Talk” on one victim’s computer.
sentence.10257: This suggests that some chat application named “i Talk” might be repackaging components from the official Youdu client along with malicious executables.
sentence.10258: It appears that a chat application was used as a lure to entice the victim into opening the malicious file.
sentence.10259: This would be consistent with the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) of two previous Iron Tiger campaigns from 2020 and 2021: a documented compromise of a chat application widely used by the Mongolian government, and a supply chain attack on Mimi chat, a chat application used in parts of South East Asia.
sentence.10260: Post-exploitation tools We found a custom Chrome password and cookie grabber that appeared unfamiliar, and it was compiled and uploaded in September 2022.
sentence.10261: The file was also signed with the VMProtect certificate but it was not obfuscated.
sentence.10262: In general, the features were simple; the malware decrypts the saved passwords to a file named “passwords.txt”, and the cookies to a file named “cookies.txt”.
sentence.10263: Analyzing its details, the malware first parses the “Local State” file to retrieve the AES key used to encrypt the cookies and passwords.
sentence.10264: It then copies the “Login Data” file to a temporary file “chromedb_tmp”, issues an SQL query to extract the URL, login, and password fields from the file, and then decrypts them and appends the result to the “passwords.txt” file.
sentence.10265: It proceeds to copy the “Cookies” file to a temporary file “chromedb_tmp”, extracts multiple fields from it using an SQL query, and then decrypts the content before copying the result to the “cookies.txt” file.
sentence.10266: Some specific cookies related to Google domain names are ignored, probably because they are mostly related to specific Google features or tracking that are considered useless by the threat actor.
sentence.10267: We found two other samples from this stealer: One compilation date indicated an executable built in November 2020, and the other one in December 2021, although those dates could be tampered with.
sentence.10268: We found those samples were uploaded on November 2021 and August 2022, meaning this stealer existed since at least late 2021.
sentence.10269: Targeting We identified one gambling company in the Philippines as compromised by this campaign.
sentence.10270: Interestingly, the threat actor registered a domain name similar to the company name and used it as a C&C.
sentence.10271: This was not surprising as we have noticed this threat actor targeting this industry since 2019 during our Operation DRBControl investigation, and later in 2021 with an update of SysUpdate.
sentence.10272: We also attempted to notify the company of this incident through all their listed channels but have received no feedback.
sentence.10273: As stated in the “Infection Vector” section, we noticed the Youdu chat application was probably used as a lure.
sentence.10274: It is worth mentioning that the customers mentioned in the Youdu official website are all located inside China, which could be an indicator of the threat actor’s interest in targets related to this country.
sentence.10275: Conclusion This investigation confirms that Iron Tiger regularly updates its tools to add new features and probably to ease their portability to other platforms, verifying the interest we found from this threat actor for Linux or Mac OS.
sentence.10276: It also corroborates this threat actor’s interest in the gambling industry and the South East Asia region, as we previously noted in 2020 and 2021.
sentence.10277: This campaign also substantiates the regular usage of chat applications as infection vectors from Iron Tiger.
sentence.10278: We expect to find further updates of these tools in the future to accommodate other platforms and apps.
sentence.10279: As an additional warning, we want to highlight that the targeting can be wider than the samples and targeting we have already observed.
sentence.10280: In 2022, we discussed a campaign targeting Taiwan and the Philippines that made use of HyperBro samples (detected by Trend Micro as Backdoor.
sentence.10281: Win32.HYPERBRO.ENC) signed with a stolen Cheetah certificate.
sentence.10282: The BfV, a German governmental entity, published a report in January 2022 mentioning attacks against German companies with HyperBro samples that were also signed with the same certificate.
sentence.10283: In October 2022, Intrinsec reported an incident in a French company also using HyperBro samples matching the structure we described in our 2021 investigation.
sentence.10284: This shows the threat actor is likely to reuse the tools mentioned here in future campaigns that might target different regions or industries in the short and long term.
sentence.10285: Considering the active campaign and regular developments made on this malware family, organizations are advised to enhance and broaden their current and established security measures, and heighten overall vigilance for possible infection vectors that can be abused by this threat group.

sentence.10289: The DFIR Report url: https://thedfirreport.com/2023/01/09/unwrapping-ursnifs-gifts/ In late August 2022, we investigated an incident involving Ursnif malware, which resulted in Cobalt Strike being deployed.
sentence.10290: This was followed by the threat actors moving laterally throughout the environment using an admin account.
sentence.10291: The Ursnif malware family (also commonly referred to as Gozi or ISFB) is one of the oldest banking trojans still active today.
sentence.10292: It has an extensive past of code forks and evolutions that has lead to several active variants in the last 5 years including Dreambot, IAP, RM2, RM3 and most recently, LDR4.
sentence.10293: For this report, we have referred to the malware as Ursnif for simplicity, however we also recommend reading Mandiant’s article on LDR4.
sentence.10294: Case Summary In this intrusion, a malicious ISO file was delivered to a user which contained Ursnif malware.
sentence.10295: The malware displayed an interesting execution flow, which included using a renamed copy of rundll32.
sentence.10296: Once executed, the malware conducted automatic discovery on the beachhead host, as we have observed with other loaders such as IcedID.
sentence.10297: The malware also established persistence on the host with the creation of a registry run key.
sentence.10298: Approximately 4 days after the initial infection, new activity on the host provided a clear distinction of a threat actor performing manual actions (hands on keyboard).
sentence.10299: The threat actor used a Background Intelligent Transfer Service (BITS) job to download a Cobalt Strike beacon, and then used the beacon for subsequent actions.
sentence.10300: The threat actor first ran some initial discovery on the host using built-in Windows utilities like ipconfig, systeminfo, net, and ping.
sentence.10301: Shortly afterwards, the threat actor injected into various processes and then proceeded to access lsass memory on the host to extract credentials.
sentence.10302: Using the credentials extracted from memory, the threat actors began to move laterally.
sentence.10303: They targeted a domain controller and used Impacket’s wmiexec.py to execute code on the remote host.
sentence.10304: This included executing both a msi installer for the RMM tools Atera and Splashtop, as well as a Cobalt Strike executable beacon.
sentence.10305: These files were transferred to the domain controller over SMB.
sentence.10306: After connecting to the Cobalt Strike beacon on the domain controller, the threat actor executed another round of discovery tasks and dumped lsass memory on the domain controller.
sentence.10307: Finally, they dropped a script named adcomp.bat which executed a PowerShell command to collect data on computers in the Windows domain.
sentence.10308: The following day, there was a short check-in on the beachhead host from a Cobalt Strike beacon, no other activity occurred until near the end of the day.
sentence.10309: At that time, the threat actor became active by initiating a proxied RDP connection via the Cobalt Strike beacon to the domain controller.
sentence.10310: From there, the threat actor began connecting to various hosts across the network.
sentence.10311: One host of interest was one of the backup servers, which was logged into, the state of backups were checked and running processes were reviewed before exiting the session.
sentence.10312: The threat actor was later evicted from the network.

sentence.10315: The Cobalt Strike server in this case was added to our feed on July 18, 2022, over 2 months before it was used in this case.
sentence.10316: We also have artifacts and IOCs available from this case such as pcaps, memory captures, files, and event logs including Sysmon under our Security Researcher and Organization services.

sentence.10318: Initial Access In this case, the Ursnif malware was delivered using a very familiar technique of being contained within an ISO file.
sentence.10319: The DFIR Report has previously reported on several incidents that involved the tactic of delivering malicious flies using ISO files: As we have previously highlighted, the Event Log Microsoft-Windows-VHDMP-Operational.evtx contains high confidence evidence when users mount ISO files.
sentence.10320: We recommend looking for these events (especially Event ID’s 1, 12 & 25) in your environment and checking for anomalies.
sentence.10321: In this case, the user had saved the file 3488164.iso to the their downloads folder and mounted it.
sentence.10322: Once mounted, the new drive contained a LNK file 6570872.lnk and hidden folder “me”.
sentence.10323: If we parse this LNK file with LECmd (by Eric Zimmerman), it highlights the execution path and the icon it appears as: The contents of hidden folder “me”, included several files and folders that were used for the execution of Ursnif.
sentence.10324: Of interest, the folder included a legitimate copy of rundll32.exe (renamed to 123.com).

sentence.10361: Persistence Once the foothold had been achieved, after execution of Ursnif on the beachhead host, persistence was achieved by creating a ‘Run’ key named ManagerText which was configured to execute a LNK file which executed a PowerShell script.
sentence.10362: Credential Access We observed a process created by Cobalt Strike accessing lsass.exe.
sentence.10363: The GrantedAccess code of 0x1010 is a known indicator of such tools as Mimikatz.
sentence.10364: This was observed on both the beachhead host and a domain controller.

sentence.10388: The actor leveraged Impacket’s wmiexec.py to execute commands with a semi-interactive shell, most likely using credentials gathered by the previous LSASS access.
sentence.10389: The commands executed included directory traversal, host discovery, and execution of tools on the DC.
sentence.10390: A breakdown of the parent and child processes invoked: The command can be broken down as follows: ‘Q’ indicates turn off echo – no response.
sentence.10391: ‘C’ indicates to stop after command execution.
sentence.10393: Output is achieved via the parameter ‘2>&1’, to redirect errors and output to one file: This command line closely resembles the code within the wmiexec.py as part of the Impacket tool maintained by Fortra.
sentence.10394: As Impacket interacts with remote endpoints via WMI over TCP via DCERPC, its possible to inspect network level packets: The use of Impacket by threat actors has been recently detailed by the US CERT in alert AA22-277A – Impacket and Exfiltration Tool Used to Steal Sensitive Information from Defense Industrial Base Organization.
sentence.10395: The Impacket process hierarchy in this case can be visualized as: At the network level, commands are issued by DCOM/RPC port 135, with responses by SMB using port 445.
sentence.10396: We can observe a number of WMI requests via DCERPC from one endpoint to a target endpoint based on the ports.
sentence.10397: Correlating the network activity to the host activity confirms that the ‘Powershell.exe’ process initiated the WMI requests.
sentence.10398: The destination port is within the ephemeral port range 49152–65535, which is for short-lived, time based, communications RFC 6335.
sentence.10399: 13Cubed (Richard Davis) also released an amazing resource to investigate Impacket related incidents here: https://www.13cubed.com/downloads/impacket_exec_commands_cheat_sheet_poster.pdf One of the observed commands invoked via WMI was ‘firefox.exe’.
sentence.10400: This was dropped on the DC and spawned a number of processes and invoked a number of hands-on commands.

sentence.10426: title: Qakbot Returns to ISO Delivery (For Now) url: https://www.esentire.com/blog/qakbot-returns-to-iso-delivery-for-now Adversaries don’t work 9-5 and neither do we.
sentence.10427: At eSentire, our 24/7 SOCs are staffed with Elite Threat Hunters and Cyber Analysts who hunt, investigate, contain and respond to threats within minutes.
sentence.10428: We have discovered some of the most dangerous threats and nation state attacks in our space – including the Kaseya MSP breach and the more_eggs malware.
sentence.10429: Our Security Operations Centers are supported with Threat Intelligence, Tactical Threat Response and Advanced Threat Analytics driven by our Threat Response Unit – the TRU team.
sentence.10430: In TRU Positives, eSentire’s Threat Response Unit (TRU) provides a summary of a recent threat investigation.
sentence.10431: We outline how we responded to the confirmed threat and what recommendations we have going forward.
sentence.10432: Here’s the latest from our TRU Team… What did we find?
sentence.10433: In early February 2023, we reported that multiple threat groups were leveraging OneNote files for malware delivery.
sentence.10434: Qakbot was one such threat group and made up the majority of our observations of malicious OneNote files during this period.
sentence.10435: Since mid-February, observations of Qakbot delivery via OneNote has faded in our telemetry while use of ISO image files has returned.
sentence.10436: The absence of OneNote malware in our telemetry suggests the technique is finding less success in circumventing perimeter gateways and content filters.
sentence.10437: The diminished use of OneNote by Qakbot during the week of February 20th is corroborated by public mentions (1, 2, 3) of ISO images in lieu of the aforementioned file type.
sentence.10438: However, it’s unlikely OneNote has been completely abandoned and it remains probable that threat actors will continue to iterate on the technique to extend its shelf life.
sentence.10439: Qakbot’s infection scheme, as observed on February 22, 2023, is summarized below and in Figure 1.
sentence.10440: A victim is sent an email linking to an externally hosted Zip file.
sentence.10441: The Zip contains an ISO image file.
sentence.10442: The victim double clicks the ISO to mount it (1).
sentence.10443: The mounted file contains a hidden folder (4), a 200+MB padded file and a visible shortcut file disguised as a zip.
sentence.10444: The shortcut file (2) executes a CMD file (3) when clicked.
sentence.10445: The CMD file contains commands which use certutil (renamed here as slaughterhouse.exe) to decode Qakbot’s DLL (brainstorms.sql).
sentence.10446: This file is base64 twice, thus requires two rounds of decoding using certutil.
sentence.10447: The decoded DLL is then executed using rundll32 and injects Qakbot into wermgr.exe.
sentence.10448: Figure 1 Summary of Qakbot's infection chain as seen on February 22, 2023.
sentence.10449: How did we find it? MDR for Endpoint identified the ISO shortcut and certutil behavior.
sentence.10451: Our team of 24/7 SOC Cyber Analysts triaged the case, isolated the host and alerted the customer.
sentence.10452: What can you learn from this TRU positive?
sentence.10453: OneNote quickly gained traction and was adopted by several threat groups (including Qakbot) in January and early February 2023.
sentence.10454: As mentioned in our previous TRU Positive, it’s probable detection of this filetype has improved.
sentence.10455: It’s unlikely that the OneNote filetype has been abandoned, and continued vigilance and blocking at perimeter gateways is recommended.
sentence.10456: ISO image files have shown to be a viable vehicle for malware delivery and execution since emerging as a popular alternative to macro-enabled documents in early 2022.
sentence.10457: ISO images can be mounted natively with a click of a button, displaying as a folder to the end user.
sentence.10458: Victims can be lured into clicking executable content including binaries, scripts or shortcut files masquerading as benign filetypes such as PDFs or folders.
sentence.10459: The use of ISO images has seen some iterative improvements throughout the last year by threats such as Qakbot.
sentence.10460: This includes encapsulating the image in one or more filetypes (Zips, PDFs, HTML), padding the contents with benign data or chaining together a series of scripts to decode or unpack the final payload.
sentence.10461: In this case, the Qakbot Zip and ISO image were retrieved by the victim using a link included in an email.
sentence.10462: It included a standalone file padded with over 200MB of blank spaces, likely to impede analysis of the decompressed ISO file.
sentence.10463: Recommendations from our Threat Response Unit (TRU) Team: Audit and consider blocking OneNote (.one), ISO images (.iso), Disk Image Files (.img) and Virtual Hard Disk files (.vhd and .vhdx) on perimeter gateways.
sentence.10464: Protect endpoints against malware by:Ensuring antivirus signatures are up-to-date.
sentence.10465: Using a Next-Gen AV (NGAV) or Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tool to detect and contain threats.
sentence.10466: Train users to identify and report potentially malicious content using an Phishing and Security Awareness Training (PSAT) program.
sentence.10467: Users should specifically be aware of the threat of OneNote documents for malware delivery.
