sentence.11104: Most of the red team’s Phase II actions failed to provoke a response from the people, processes, and technology defending the organization’s network.
sentence.11105: The organization failed to detect lateral movement, persistence, and C2 activity via their intrusion detection or prevention systems, endpoint protection platform, web proxy logs, and Windows event logs.
sentence.11106: Additionally, throughout Phase I, the team received no deconflictions or confirmation that the organization caught their activity.
sentence.11107: Below is a list of some of the higher risk activities conducted by the team that were opportunities for detection: Phishing Lateral movement reuse Generation and use of the golden ticket Anomalous LDAP traffic Anomalous internal share enumeration Unconstrained Delegation server compromise DCSync Anomalous account usage during lateral movement Anomalous outbound network traffic Anomalous outbound SSH connections to the team’s cloud servers from workstations Lack of monitoring on endpoint management systems.
sentence.11108: The team used the organization’s MDM system to gain root access to machines across the organization’s network without being detected.
sentence.11109: Endpoint management systems provide elevated access to thousands of hosts and should be treated as high value assets (HVAs) with additional restrictions and monitoring.
sentence.11111: The Site 1 krbtgt account password had not been updated for over a decade.
sentence.11112: The krbtgt account is a domain default account that acts as a service account for the key distribution center (KDC) service used to encrypt and sign all Kerberos tickets for the domain.
sentence.11113: Compromise of the krbtgt account could provide adversaries with the ability to sign their own TGTs, facilitating domain access years after the date of compromise.
sentence.11114: The red team was able to use the krbtgt account to forge TGTs for multiple accounts throughout Phase I. Excessive permissions to standard users.
sentence.11115: The team discovered several standard user accounts that have local administrator access to critical servers.
sentence.11116: This misconfiguration allowed the team to use the low-level access of a phished user to move laterally to an Unconstrained Delegation host and compromise the entire domain.
sentence.11117: Hosts with Unconstrained Delegation enabled unnecessarily.
sentence.11118: Hosts with Unconstrained Delegation enabled store the Kerberos TGTs of all users that authenticate to that host, enabling actors to steal service tickets or compromise krbtgt accounts and perform golden ticket or “silver ticket” attacks.
sentence.11119: The team performed an NTLM-relay attack to obtain the DC’s TGT, followed by a golden ticket attack on a SharePoint server with Unconstrained Delegation to gain the ability to impersonate any Site 1 AD account. Use of non-secure default configurations.
sentence.11120: The organization used default configurations for hosts with Windows Server 2012 R2.
sentence.11121: The default configuration allows unprivileged users to query group membership of local administrator groups.
sentence.11122: The red team used and identified several standard user accounts with administrative access from a Windows Server 2012 R2 SharePoint server.
sentence.11123: Additional Issues The team noted the following additional issues.
sentence.11125: Some workstations allowed unprivileged accounts to have local administrator access; for example, the red team discovered an ordinary user account in the local admin group for the SharePoint server.
sentence.11126: If a user with administrative access is compromised, an actor can access servers without needing to elevate privileges.
sentence.11127: Administrative and user accounts should be separated, and designated admin accounts should be exclusively used for admin purposes.
sentence.11129: Most servers, including domain controllers, allowed unrestricted egress traffic to the internet.
sentence.11131: The team observed inconsistencies on servers and workstations within the domain, including inconsistent membership in the local administrator group among different servers or workstations.
sentence.11132: For example, some workstations had “Server Admins” or “Domain Admins” as local administrators, and other workstations had neither.
sentence.11134: The team noticed potentially unusual software, including music software, installed on both workstations and servers.
sentence.11135: These extraneous software installations indicate inconsistent host configuration (see above) and increase the attack surfaces for malicious actors to gain initial access or escalate privileges once in the network.
sentence.11137: During the assessment, the team keylogged a user during a mandatory password change and noticed that only the final character of their password was modified.
sentence.11138: This is potentially due to domain passwords being required to be changed every 60 days.
sentence.11139: Smart card use was inconsistent across the domain.
sentence.11140: While the technology was deployed, it was not applied uniformly, and there was a significant portion of users without smartcard protections enabled.
sentence.11141: The team used these unprotected accounts throughout their assessment to move laterally through the domain and gain persistence.
sentence.11142: Noted Strengths The red team noted the following technical controls or defensive measures that prevented or hampered offensive actions: The organization conducts regular, proactive penetration tests and adversarial assessments and invests in hardening their network based on findings.
sentence.11143: The team was unable to discover any easily exploitable services, ports, or web interfaces from more than three million external in-scope IPs.
sentence.11144: This forced the team to resort to phishing to gain initial access to the environment.
sentence.11146: The team was unable to crack any of the hashes obtained from the 610 service accounts pulled.
sentence.11147: This is a critical strength because it slowed the team from moving around the network in the initial parts of the Phase I.
sentence.11148: The team did not discover any useful credentials on open file shares or file servers.
sentence.11149: This slowed the progress of the team from moving around the network.
sentence.11150: MFA was used for some SBSs.
sentence.11151: The team was blocked from moving to SBS 2 by an MFA prompt.
sentence.11152: There were strong security controls and segmentation for SBS systems.
sentence.11153: Direct access to SBS were located in separate networks, and admins of SBS used workstations protected by local firewalls.
sentence.11154: MITIGATIONS CISA recommends organizations implement the recommendations in Table 2 to mitigate the issues listed in the Findings section of this advisory.
sentence.11155: These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs) developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).
sentence.11156: The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement.
sentence.11157: CISA and NIST based the CPGs on existing cybersecurity frameworks and guidance to protect against the most common and impactful threats, tactics, techniques, and procedures.
sentence.11158: See CISA’s Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals for more information on the CPGs, including additional recommended baseline protections.
sentence.11159: Table 2: Recommendations to Mitigate Identified Issues Issue Recommendation Insufficient host and network monitoring Establish a security baseline of normal network traffic and tune network appliances to detect anomalous behavior [CPG 3.1].
sentence.11160: Tune host-based products to detect anomalous binaries, lateral movement, and persistence techniques.
sentence.11161: Create alerts for Windows event log authentication codes, especially for the domain controllers.
sentence.11162: This could help detect some of the pass-the-ticket, DCSync, and other techniques described in this report.
sentence.11163: From a detection standpoint, focus on identity and access management (IAM) rather than just network traffic or static host alerts.
sentence.11164: Consider who is accessing what (what resource), from where (what internal host or external location), and when (what day and time the access occurs).
sentence.11165: Look for access behavior that deviates from expected or is indicative of AD abuse.
sentence.11166: Reduce the attack surface by limiting the use of legitimate administrative pathways and tools such as PowerShell, PSExec, and WMI, which are often used by malicious actors.
sentence.11167: CISA recommends selecting one tool to administer the network, ensuring logging is turned on [CPG 3.1], and disabling the others.
sentence.11168: Consider using “honeypot” service principal names (SPNs) to detect attempts to crack account hashes
sentence.11169: [CPG 1.1]. Conduct regular assessments to ensure processes and procedures are up to date and can be followed by security staff and end users.
sentence.11170: Consider using red team tools, such as SharpHound, for AD enumeration to identify users with excessive privileges and misconfigured hosts (e.g., with Unconstrained Delegation enabled).
sentence.11171: Ensure all commercial tools deployed in your environment are regularly tuned to pick up on relevant activity in your environment.
sentence.11172: Lack of monitoring on endpoint management systems Treat endpoint management systems as HVAs with additional restrictions and monitoring because they provide elevated access to thousands of hosts.
sentence.11173: KRBTGT never changed Change the krbtgt account password on a regular schedule such as every 6 to 12 months or if it becomes compromised.
sentence.11174: Note that this password change must be carefully performed to effectively change the credential without breaking AD functionality.
sentence.11175: The password must be changed twice to effectively invalidate the old credentials.
sentence.11176: However, the required waiting period between resets must be greater than the maximum lifetime period of Kerberos tickets, which is 10 hours by default.
sentence.11177: See Microsoft’s KRBTGT account maintenance considerations guidance for more information.
sentence.11178: Excessive permissions to standard users and ineffective separation of privileged accounts Implement the principle of least privilege: Grant standard user rights for standard user tasks such as email, web browsing, and using line-of-business (LOB) applications.
sentence.11179: Periodically audit standard accounts and minimize where they have privileged access.
sentence.11180: Periodically Audit AD permissions to ensure users do not have excessive permissions and have not been added to admin groups.
sentence.11181: Evaluate which administrative groups should administer which servers/workstations.
sentence.11182: Ensure group members administrative accounts instead of standard accounts.
sentence.11183: Separate administrator accounts from user accounts [CPG 1.5].
sentence.11184: Only allow designated admin accounts to be used for admin purposes.
sentence.11185: If an individual user needs administrative rights over their workstation, use a separate account that does not have administrative access to other hosts, such as servers. Consider using a privileged access management (PAM) solution to manage access to privileged accounts and resources
sentence.11187: PAM solutions can also log and alert usage to detect any unusual activity and may have helped stop the red team from accessing resources with admin accounts.
sentence.11188: Note: password vaults associated with PAM solutions should be treated as HVAs with additional restrictions and monitoring (see below).
sentence.11189: Configure time-based access for accounts set at the admin level and higher.
sentence.11190: For example, the just-in-time (JIT) access method provisions privileged access when needed and can support enforcement of the principle of least privilege, as well as the Zero Trust model.
sentence.11191: This is a process in which a network-wide policy is set in place to automatically disable administrator accounts at the AD level when the account is not in direct need.
sentence.11192: When individual users need the account, they submit their requests through an automated process that enables access to a system but only for a set timeframe to support task completion.
sentence.11193: Hosts with Unconstrained Delegation enabled Remove Unconstrained Delegation from all servers.
sentence.11194: If Unconstrained Delegation functionality is required, upgrade operating systems and applications to leverage other approaches (e.g., constrained delegation) or explore whether systems can be retired or further isolated from the enterprise.
sentence.11195: CISA recommends Windows Server 2019 or greater. Consider disabling or limiting NTLM and WDigest Authentication if possible, including using their use as criteria for prioritizing updates to legacy systems or for segmenting the network.
sentence.11196: Instead use more modern federation protocols (SAML, OIDC) or Kerberos for authentication with AES-256 bit encryption [CPG 3.4].

sentence.11201: If updates cannot be uniformly installed, update insecure configurations to meet updated standards. Lack of server egress control Configure internal firewalls and proxies to restrict internet traffic from hosts that do not require it.
sentence.11202: If a host requires specific outbound traffic, consider creating an allowlist policy of domains.
sentence.11203: Large number of credentials in a shared vault Treat password vaults as HVAs with additional restrictions and monitoring [CPG 3.4]: If on-premise, require MFA for admin and apply network segmentation [CPG 1.3].
sentence.11204: Use solutions with end-to-end encryption where applicable [CPG 3.3].
sentence.11205: If cloud-based, evaluate the provider to ensure use of strong security controls such as MFA and end-to-end encryption
sentence.11206: [CPG 1.3, 3.3]. Inconsistent host configuration Establish a baseline/gold-image for workstations and servers and deploy from that image
sentence.11208: Use standardized groups to administer hosts in the network.
sentence.11209: Potentially unwanted programs Implement software allowlisting to ensure users can only install software from an approved list
sentence.11211: Remove unnecessary, extraneous software from servers and workstations.
sentence.11212: Mandatory password changes enabled Consider only requiring changes for memorized passwords in the event of compromise.
sentence.11213: Regular changing of memorized passwords can lead to predictable patterns, and both CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recommend against changing passwords on regular intervals.
sentence.11214: Additionally, CISA recommends organizations implement the mitigations below to improve their cybersecurity posture: Provide users with regular training and exercises, specifically related to phishing emails
sentence.11216: Phishing accounts for majority of initial access intrusion events.
sentence.11217: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA to the greatest extent possible [CPG 1.3].
sentence.11218: Reduce the risk of credential compromise via the following: Place domain admin accounts in the protected users group to prevent caching of password hashes locally; this also forces Kerberos AES authentication as opposed to weaker RC4 or NTLM.
sentence.11219: Implement Credential Guard for Windows 10 and Server 2016 (Refer to Microsoft: Manage Windows Defender Credential Guard for more information).
sentence.11220: For Windows Server 2012R2, enable Protected Process Light for Local Security Authority (LSA).
sentence.11221: Refrain from storing plaintext credentials in scripts [CPG 3.4].
sentence.11222: The red team discovered a PowerShell script containing plaintext credentials that allowed them to escalate to admin.
sentence.11223: Upgrade to Windows Server 2019 or greater and Windows 10 or greater.
sentence.11224: These versions have security features not included in older operating systems.
sentence.11225: As a long-term effort, CISA recommends organizations prioritize implementing a more modern, Zero Trust network architecture that: Leverages secure cloud services for key enterprise security capabilities (e.g., identity and access management, endpoint detection and response, policy enforcement).
sentence.11226: Upgrades applications and infrastructure to leverage modern identity management and network access practices.
sentence.11227: Centralizes and streamlines access to cybersecurity data to drive analytics for identifying and managing cybersecurity risks.
sentence.11228: Invests in technology and personnel to achieve these goals.
sentence.11229: CISA encourages organizational IT leadership to ask their executive leadership the question: Can the organization accept the business risk of NOT implementing critical security controls such as MFA?
sentence.11230: Risks of that nature should typically be acknowledged and prioritized at the most senior levels of an organization.
sentence.11232: In addition to applying mitigations, CISA recommends exercising, testing, and validating your organization's security program against the threat behaviors mapped to the MITRE ATT&CK for Enterprise framework in this advisory.
sentence.11233: CISA recommends testing your existing security controls inventory to assess how they perform against the ATT&CK techniques described in this advisory.
sentence.11234: To get started: Select an ATT&CK technique described in this advisory (see Table 3).
sentence.11235: Align your security technologies against the technique.
sentence.11236: Test your technologies against the technique.
sentence.11237: Analyze your detection and prevention technologies’ performance.
sentence.11238: Repeat the process for all security technologies to obtain a set of comprehensive performance data.
sentence.11239: Tune your security program, including people, processes, and technologies, based on the data generated by this process.
sentence.11240: CISA recommends continually testing your security program, at scale, in a production environment to ensure optimal performance against the MITRE ATT&CK techniques identified in this advisory.

sentence.11331: title: McAfee Defender’s Blog: NetWalker url: https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/mcafee-defenders-blog-netwalker/ Building Adaptable Security Architecture Against NetWalker NetWalker Overview The NetWalker ransomware, initially known as Mailto, was first detected in August 2019.
sentence.11332: Since then, new variants were discovered throughout 2019 and the beginning of 2020, with a strong uptick noticed in March of this year.
sentence.11333: NetWalker has noticeably evolved to a more stable and robust ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model, and McAfee research suggests that the malware operators are targeting and attracting a broader range of technically advanced and enterprising criminal affiliates.
sentence.11334: McAfee Advanced Threat Research (ATR) discovered a large sum of bitcoins linked to NetWalker which suggest its extortion efforts are effective and that many victims have had no option other than to succumb to its criminal demands.
sentence.11335: For more details on NetWalker, see the McAfee ATR blog here.
sentence.11336: We do not want you to be one of those victims, so this blog is focused on how to build an adaptable security architecture to defeat this threat and, specifically, how McAfee’s portfolio delivers the capability to prevent, detect and respond to NetWalker ransomware.
sentence.11337: Gathering Intelligence on NetWalker As always, building adaptable defensive architecture starts with intelligence.
sentence.11338: In most organizations, the Security Operations team is responsible for threat intelligence analysis, as well as threat and incident response.
sentence.11339: The Preview of McAfee MVISION Insights is a sneak peek of some of MVISION Insights capabilities for the threat intel analyst and threat responder.
sentence.11340: The preview identifies the prevalence and severity of select top emerging threats across the globe which enables the Security Operations Center (SOC) to prioritize threat response actions and gather relevant cyber threat intelligence (CTI) associated with the threat, in this case NetWalker ransomware.
sentence.11341: The CTI is provided in the form of technical Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) as well as MITRE ATT&CK framework tactics and techniques.
sentence.11342: As a threat intel analyst or responder, you can drill down to gather more specific information on NetWalker, such as prevalence and links to other sources of information.
sentence.11343: As a threat intel analyst or responder, you can further drill down to gather more specific actionable intelligence on NetWalker, such as indicators of compromise and tactics/techniques aligned to the MITRE ATT&CK framework.
sentence.11344: From MVISION Insights preview, you can see that NetWalker leverages tactics and techniques common to other ransomware attacks, such as spear phishing attachments for Initial Access, use of PowerShell for deployment, modification of Registry Keys/Startup folder for persistence and encryption of files for impact of course.
sentence.11345: Defensive Architecture Overview Today’s digital enterprise is a hybrid environment of on-premise systems and cloud services with multiple entry points for attacks like NetWalker.
sentence.11346: The work from home operating model forced by COVID-19 has only expanded the attack surface and increased the risk for successful ransomware attack if organizations did not adapt their security posture.
sentence.11347: Mitigating the risk of attacks like NetWalker requires a security architecture with the right controls at the device, on the network and in security operations (sec ops).
sentence.11348: The Center for Internet Security (CIS) Top 20 Cyber Security Controls provides a good guide to build that architecture.
sentence.11349: For ransomware, and NetWalker in particular, the controls must be layered throughout the enterprise.
sentence.11350: The following outlines the key security controls needed at each layer of the architecture to protect your enterprise against ransomware.
sentence.11351: To assess your capability against NetWalker, you must match your existing controls against the attack stages we learned from the Preview of MVISION Insights.
sentence.11352: For detailed analysis on the NetWalker ransomware attack, see McAfee ATR’s blog but, for simplicity, we matched the attack stages to the MITRE ATT&CK Framework below.
sentence.11354: According to Threat Intelligence and Research, the initial access is performed either through vulnerability exploitation or spear phishing attachments.
sentence.11355: The following chart summarizes the controls expected to have the most effect against initial stage techniques and the McAfee solutions to implement those controls where possible.

sentence.11360: As attackers can quickly change spear phishing attachments, it is important to have adaptable defenses that include user awareness training and response procedures, behavior-based malware defenses on email systems, web access and endpoint systems, and finally sec ops playbooks for early detection and response against suspicious email attachments or other phishing techniques.
sentence.11361: For more information on how McAfee can protect against suspicious email attachments, review this additional blog post. Using valid accounts and protocols, such as for Remote Desktop Protocol, is an attack technique we have seen rise during the initial COVID-19 period.
sentence.11362: To further understand how McAfee defends against RDP as an initial access vector, as well as how the attackers are using it to deploy ransomware, please see our previous posts.
sentence.11364: The exploitation stage is where the attacker gains access to the target system.
sentence.11365: Protection at this stage is heavily dependent on system vulnerability management, adaptable anti-malware on both end user devices and servers and security operations tools like endpoint detection and response sensors.
sentence.11366: McAfee Endpoint Security 10.7 provides a defense in depth capability including signatures and threat intelligence to cover known bad indicators or programs.
sentence.11367: Additionally, machine-learning and behavior-based protection reduces the attack surface against NetWalker and detects new exploitation attack techniques.

sentence.11405: title: Technical Analysis: Black Basta Malware Overview url: https://quadrantsec.com/resource/technical-analysis/black-basta-malware-overview INTRODUCTION Quadrant was recently able to aid a client during an organization wide compromise by the Black Basta ransomware group.
sentence.11406: This group is a “Ransomware as a Service” (RaaS) organization known to target medium and large companies.
sentence.11407: The following contains an overview of the compromise as it progressed, as well a technical analysis of the malware and techniques observed, ranging from a successful phishing campaign to the attempted ransomware detonation.
sentence.11408: Although some exact details of the threat actor’s actions are still unknown, the evidence gathered has allowed for inferences into many of the gaps.
sentence.11409: The names of all clients, all accounts, and some files have been modified for client confidentiality.
sentence.11410: Indicators of compromise, including malicious domain names, have not been modified.
sentence.11411: Any log modification has been made to redact client information, break potential links, or for readability.
sentence.11413: The timeline below shows a high-level overview of the incident: INITIAL ACCESS The Threat Actor began this attack by compromising a user account at a third-party vendor (TPV).
sentence.11414: Although little is known to Quadrant about the compromise on the TPV, access allowed for the use of an "info@" account.
sentence.11415: The use of such an account would have allowed the Threat Actor to pose as the compromised user without creating extra "junk" in the user's inbox which could raise suspicion.
sentence.11416: Following initial phishing emails, the threat actor continued to submit additional phishing emails to the client via similar account names from different domains.
sentence.11417: Both samples reached their victims shortly after noon on the 20th of September
sentence.11418: The phishing emails contained what was later determined to be "Qakbot," a sophisticated trojan.
sentence.11419: Following the infection, these hosts began to beacon on out to over 100 IP's using various ports.
sentence.11420: The client’s Cisco “Advanced Malware Protection” (AMP) detected a connection with one of these IP's over TCP port 2222.
sentence.11421: Although this did trigger an alert in AMP, the Quadrant ingestion of these logs was not configured, so this did not generate an alert through the Sagan Solution.
sentence.11422: The Suricata engine did detect these connection attempts, however no alert was raised by the Packet Inspection Engine.
sentence.11423: Quadrant monitors companies' ingress and egress traffic using onsite Packet Inspection Engine (PIE) appliances running the Suricata Detection engine.
sentence.11424: Although many other rulesets are used to screen for malicious activity, Quadrant has custom rules in place to detect SSH over nonstandard ports, such as TCP 2222.
sentence.11425: These rules did not fire due to the absence of an SSH header in the traffic.
sentence.11426: One may assume that traffic over 2222 would be SSH traffic, however further analysis of the traffic generated by the Qakbot Sample in the lab shows that this connection was likely HTTPS in nature.
sentence.11427: Eventually, the malware was able to find an active C2 server.
sentence.11428: It took about 35 minutes between initial infection and the first successful communication between a compromised host and the C2 domain.
sentence.11429: The second stage payload, which was later determined to likely be the penetration testing framework "Brute Ratel," was then downloaded via a connection to an IP from Russia.
sentence.11430: PERSISTENCE AND ESCALATION OF PRIVILEGE Following the compromise of two hosts and gaining a foot hold, lateral movement began.
sentence.11431: The client's full infrastructure is comprised of three domains: Construction, Commerce, and a Subsidiary.
sentence.11432: Both initial compromised hosts were in the Construction environment.
sentence.11433: These domains had shared trust and were connected via VPN tunnels which allowed the threat actor to move freely between domains.
sentence.11434: We believe that multiple methods and tools were leveraged in order to do this.
sentence.11435: At this point, visibility becomes muddled due to the focus of observation and detection is ingress and egress traffic.
sentence.11436: However, following the investigation into the recorded logs and the follow-on detailed analysis of malware samples, we can make educated guesses on some of the missing pieces.
sentence.11437: Initial lateral movement and the lay of the land was likely conducted using Brute Ratel.
sentence.11438: This was determined through a review of files found on one of the initially compromised hosts.
sentence.11439: One file, "zfgufgfvezdnbcvjkzctpvfdj.dll," matches the hash of previously submitted Brute Ratel samples.
sentence.11440: Due to the lack of visibility, we were unable to find the initial connection from the two "Patient Zeros" to the local Domain Controller.
sentence.11441: However, after reaching the local DC, the attacker was able to gain a better lay of the land and observe the presence of the other two domains.
sentence.11442: Initial Command and Control was conducted from "23[.]19[.]58[.]43"[zedorocop[.]com] and "23[.]106[.]160[.]141" [danimos[.]com].
sentence.11443: The IP’s used for C2 and the level of interaction changed over time as the compromise grew.
sentence.11444: For example, mid-stage infections showed calls to "146[.]70[.]86[.]44"[gerhiles[.]com].
sentence.11445: It’s important to note that the FQDN’s that were used as C2 were all registered the same month as the compromise.
sentence.11446: Multiple administrative and system accounts were compromised during this incident.
sentence.11447: One possible explanation for this comes from “Kerberoasting”.
sentence.11448: This technique was observed in the Commerce environment through a sharp incline of Kerberos requests using RC4 encryption.
sentence.11449: We do not believe that this was successful in this environment, due in part to the lack of additional signs of compromise specific to this Domain.
sentence.11450: However, this technique was likely performed on the other two client domains where visibility gaps existed.
sentence.11451: This is further supported by the source and destination of these requests were cross domain: The source of the “Kerberoasting” was based in the Subsidiary environment and the Domain Controller that was attacked was in the Commerce environment.
sentence.11452: Once administrative access had been achieved, the threat actor also added new administrative accounts to the environment.
sentence.11453: PROPAGATION Unknown to everyone but the attacker, multiple files were being transmitted throughout the environment: Two file names were observed during the incident "Client_s.exe" and "Client.exe."
sentence.11454: It is expected that the different naming schemes are related to the different variations of the Black Basta ransomware.
sentence.11455: Although no sample was able to be provided for the Client.exe (which is believed to be the ESXi variant), Quadrant was able to obtain a copy of "Client_s.exe" for Windows hosts.
sentence.11456: Two ".bat" files were sent throughout the organization.
sentence.11457: Both were designed to turn off antivirus and anti-malware software.
sentence.11458: One does not use any obfuscation and just contains the simple command to stop Cisco AMP Orbital.
sentence.11459: This could indicate that it was written hastily in order to get it onto the target environments quickly.
sentence.11460: The other, targeting Windows Defender, required multiple steps in order to view the commands.
sentence.11461: Tox5, which appeared to be a component of Cobalt Strike, as well as Cobalt Strike beacon with the name of "Ticket-5731.xls." These files continued to replicate throughout the organization though the use of Server qMessage Block (SMB), eventually spreading to almost every endpoint and server in two of the three domains.
sentence.11462: The attack on the Commerce domain does not appear to have been effective, outside of one host in a training environment.
sentence.11463: Most hosts in the Commerce environment HAD more restrictions placed on their operating system by default which likely contributed to the lack of success by the threat actors in the Commerce environment.
sentence.11465: Once a file server was identified, an FTP connection was established to an external site.
sentence.11466: This was not used for C2 activities but only for receiving the exfiltrated data.
sentence.11467: Suricata logs show that “RClone” was downloaded on the file servers in order to facilitate exfiltration of the logs.
sentence.11468: RClone is designed to transfer large volumes of data from one host to the cloud with ease.
sentence.11469: This legitimate program was abused by the attacker to steal client data.
sentence.11470: DETECTION AND RESPONSE The most critical asset of the Security Operations Center is the human SOC Analyst.
sentence.11471: A human can look at the totality of a situation and make a judgement call that no AI or automated process can.
sentence.11472: From the analyst's perspective, the only alert that was generated and brought to the SOC was a Suricata FTP rule looking for CVE 1999-0911, related to an overflow using the MKD command.
sentence.11473: This FTP command is defined as "...causes the directory specified in the pathname to be created on the server.
sentence.11474: If the specified directory is a relative directory, it is created in the client's current working directory.
sentence.11475: " Although many old signatures are decommissioned or otherwise suppressed, Quadrant leaves some rules in place as "hunting" rules.
sentence.11476: These are more focused on the overall techniques or "odd" traffic that could be an indicator of compromise.
sentence.11477: In this case, the analyst investigating the alert observed that this was technically a False Positive, as the command was not used in an abnormal fashion.
sentence.11478: However, looking at the destination, which had not been previously observed in the environment, the file names (which were quite varied), and the volume of the files outbound, the analyst decided to call the client to err on the side of caution.
sentence.11479: Had the analyst not conducted their due diligence or had this archaic signature been suppressed, it is highly likely that this compromise would not have been detected until after the encryption process had begun.
sentence.11480: The current list of rules developed following this incident can be found in I The alert was submitted at 18:27 EDT on 9/21/2022.
sentence.11481: Just over 30 hours after the initial infection.
sentence.11482: The client determined it to be out of the ordinary but was unaware of the extent of the compromise.
sentence.11483: However, during the course of the evening, it became apparent that something was greatly amiss.
sentence.11484: The following morning, the client’s CISO contacted the Quadrant team to report that there was indeed an active compromise within their environment.
sentence.11485: The client provided malware samples from the phishing emails and the analysis began.
sentence.11486: Threat hunting was conducted within the logs.
sentence.11487: A dedicated “out of bands” communications channel was established between Quadrant and the clients.
sentence.11488: As more evidence was uncovered, the full threat began to be realized.
sentence.11489: One aspect of the actions taken by the Incident Response team was a live log review.
sentence.11490: The term "look for anything suspicious" is often a nightmare of a request, because how does one truly define suspicious without a base line.
sentence.11491: However, with the amount of knowledge of the situation and years of experience on his side, a member of the I.R. team decided to look at the raw logs in real time to see if anything stood out.
sentence.11492: Windows Event logs and “clipboard” logs are collected using NXLog Enterprise.
sentence.11493: While clipboard logs are not stored on the local host, they are sent to the Sagan Log Analysis Engine for further analysis and retention.
sentence.11494: While examining this data, the I.R. team member became aware of the use of RDP by the Threat Actor by observing RDPClip.exe logging that looked, by definition, incredibly suspicious.
sentence.11495: Among the many “clipboard” logs observed, "Client.exe -bomb," stood out.
sentence.11496: Although the full extent of the command was not realized at the time, due to the implied malice it was decided that now was the time to attempt to purge the threat actor.
sentence.11497: The Clients response team locked out the accounts that were known to be compromised.
sentence.11498: However, the threat actor had complete control over the environment.
sentence.11499: Following the initial attempt to lock out the threat actor, the threat actor retaliated.
sentence.11500: This resulted in a catastrophic lockout of the client's staff and administrators.
sentence.11502: Knowing that there was an ongoing data exfiltration attempt along with a full network compromise with a relatively short “dwell” time, plans had been put into place to restrict all access to the network in order to mitigate and prevent the threat actor from doing more damage.
sentence.11503: The client's staff was simply waiting on the “order” to halt the network.
sentence.11504: After quick conference between Quadrant and the client, all parties agreed and the decision was made: At approximately 8:45pm on September 22, only 56 hours after the initial phishing email had been opened, the physical cables from between the domains as well as their connection to the Internet were pulled.
sentence.11505: Because of the observation, hunting, and superior teamwork between the Quadrant team and the client, only a handful of ESXi servers were encrypted.
sentence.11506: Had the team not taken action to sever the Internet and domain connections, the encryption command would likely have replicated throughout the Construction and Subsidiary environments.
sentence.11507: With the assistance of a third-party incident response firm and constant ongoing contact with the Quadrant team, the client was able to slowly, systematically, and safely bring their servers on-line while purging any remains of the threat actor over the course of the next two weeks.
sentence.11508: Ultimately, this was considered a success in defense of the client.
sentence.11509: But there were many lessons learned.
sentence.11510: Through the later review of the logging and after-action analysis of the event, more detections rules have been created to better alert on what visibility does exist in this, and many other, client environments.
sentence.11511: TECHNICAL ANALYSIS INITIAL ACCESS: QAKBOT INFECTION
sentence.11512: The two phishing samples provided by the client show two different techniques: Email response as part of an Email Chain: "Re: RE: Logistics":
sentence.11513: The phishing email came from a legitimate vendor "stoneworkers".
sentence.11514: The phishing attachment was submitted to the target in a response to an ongoing conversation that was being held between a member of Quadrant’s client and the TPV.
sentence.11515: The attacker submitted the email from "info[@]stoneworkers[.]org" while posing as "jpeterman[@]stoneworkers[.]org".
sentence.11516: The email had applicable context and the email chain contains back and forth to another member of the TPV as well.
sentence.11518: The phishing email came with no pretext from a site not used by the client.
sentence.11519: However, it is important to note that the site seems to be owned by a legitimate venture capital group, which may indicate a compromise of their organization or that the email account was spoofed.
sentence.11520: The attacker submitted the email from "support[@]capitalizedadventures[.]com" while posing as "Jay Peterman".
sentence.11521: From the two phishing emails, both attachments contain similar malware.
sentence.11522: Only changes to the filenames and corresponding commands were observed between the two.
sentence.11523: When downloaded, the initial attachment is a local HTML file.
sentence.11524: The web page claims to be an adobe site and that the attached document is a PDF which is password protected: Using the password "abc888" to unzip the attachment, the user is presented with an ISO file.
sentence.11525: The two samples produced different ISO names: Claim_Copy_1796.iso and Claim_Copy_5898.iso.
sentence.11526: The subdirectories to the fathomed directory, elude, omicron, and shabbily, are all empty as confirmed by navigating to them and running "ls -a" and returning no files.
sentence.11527: This was verified through "du -h" which resulted in 4.0k size, which is consistent of an empty directory.
sentence.11528: When opened in a Windows environment the following is displayed: The ISO mounts as a DVD Drive.
sentence.11529: The "Claim_Copy" shows the icon for windows file explorer.
sentence.11530: Clicking on these calls the corresponding JavaScript file contained within each iso.
sentence.11531: In both cases the JavaScript files set several variables before running the ".cmd" file contained within the ISO.
sentence.11532: This is likely done as a method to avoid detection from Log Analysis Engines, such as the Sagan Engine, as well as other monitoring services such as Microsoft's Defender or Sentinel.
sentence.11533: The command is called with echo off, so that no text will be displayed to the user.
sentence.11534: Ultimately, this CMD file calls the "db" file.
sentence.11535: In both samples, the "db" file is not a database, but is the actual Qakbot trojan.
sentence.11536: Something interesting to note: the "campus.txt" contains an excerpt from "Through the Looking Glass" by Lewis Carol.
sentence.11537: This inclusion may be to add easily changeable padding to the ISO.
sentence.11538: Doing so would allow the easy addition or subtraction of data in order to change the ISO’s hash value without changing any important content of the executables.
sentence.11539: Following detonation of Qakbot, the malware copied itself to "$CURRENTUSER\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Isoaahffo\djkuuhd.dll," as confirmed by the file's hashes shown below, and sets itself to auto run.
sentence.11540: Following this, the malware begins to beacon out to hard coded C2 servers.
sentence.11541: A breakdown of the observed IP’s and their ports can be found in the INDEX A below.
sentence.11542: This contains over 100 IP’s for potential C2 servers.
sentence.11543: During the initial detonation of 5898, the process imbedded itself into wermgr.exe, the Windows Error Reporting Manager (Process ID 6660).
sentence.11544: Further analysis of the registry keys added by the sample were able to be decrypted by leveraging the decryption script found at the link "https://github.com/drole/qakbot-registry-decrypt".
sentence.11545: These show the full path to the dropped file "xjkuuhd.dll" as well as the Qakbot campaign identifier: "obama206."
sentence.11546: As with the case with other Qakbot investigations, multiple potential IP’s were observed during the testing.
sentence.11547: During the incident, the first warning sign of compromise came from the victims Cisco Advanced Malware Protection alerting.
sentence.11548: Cisco AMP detected an attempt to contact "76[.]169[.]76[.]44"[Van Nuys, CA] over TCP port 2222.
sentence.11549: It is interesting to note that other IP’s were attempted to be reached over port TCP 2222, however, this C2 node was the only IP to return any data over TCP port 2222, which may be why this alert triggered.
sentence.11550: According to Suricata logs, this was also the first IP that was reached out to via 2222.
sentence.11551: A later review of the logs revealed that the first attempt to contact the C2 ip’s ("61[.]70[.]29[.]53"[Taiwan]).
sentence.11552: Due to TCP port 2222’s common use as an alternate port for SSH communication, the Malware Analyst recorded a manual SSH connection to the emulated C2 host in order to show the difference between an SSH connection and the connection made by the Malware sample.
sentence.11553: Evidence suggests that the sample does not communicate over SSH and the communication is consistent with HTTP/S traffic.
sentence.11554: The malware analyst attempted to connect via SSH to the emulated C2 host.
sentence.11555: Note the first packet from the experimental machine to the emulated C2 device following the 3-way TCP handshake shows header information containing the OpenSSH client information.
sentence.11556: This was produced manually as an example of an SSH connection while SSH was running on the emulated C2 host on port 2222.
sentence.11557: An overview of the lab setup and tools can be found in INDEX B. While continuing to run the SSH client on the emulated C2 device, the malware was detonated on the VM, we can see that the same packet following the 3-way handshake no longer contains SSH information but is detected as a Client Hello.
sentence.11558: The emulated C2 Server is now running an HTTPS server on TCP port 2222.
sentence.11559: This PCAP above shows the conversation from the 3-way handshake to the resetting of the connection.
sentence.11560: Following observation of the malware samples, we now know that most of the connection attempts to the C2 IP’s are conducted over TCP port 443.
sentence.11561: Because of the common use of this port, and the use of TLS in these connections, both attempts and the successful connections went undetected by Suricata and Cisco AMP.
sentence.11562: Many of the connections over 443 resulted in minimal connections consistent with nothing more than TCP negations.
sentence.11563: However, IP’s "119[.]42[.]124[.]18"[Thailand] and "193[.]3[.]19[.]37"[Russia] showed multiple packets and data transferred, including the exchange of TLS certificates.
sentence.11564: The size and length of connection indicates that the second stage was downloaded from "193[.]3[.]19[.]37"[Russia].
sentence.11565: The largest connection between P0 and the C2 domain.
sentence.11566: Because of the amount of data outbound, this also may indicate some data exfiltration or interaction with the downloaded second stage from the C2.
sentence.11567: POST-EXPLOITATION TECHNIQUES, TACTICS, AND PROCEDURES COMMAND AND CONTROL Initial Command and Control was initially conducted from "23.19.58.43"[zedorocop[.]com] and "23.106.160.141" [danimos[.]com].
sentence.11568: It’s important to note that the FQDN’s that were used as C2 were all registered the same month as the compromise.
sentence.11569: POTENTIAL COBALT STRIKE INSTALLATION - TOX5.EXE Initial static review of the tox5 sample did not reveal much information, indicators show that this may have the ability to clear event logs.
sentence.11570: A dynamic analysis of "Tox5" shows the malware drops itself in a randomly generated name folder under the "ProgramData" directory and adds itself to a scheduled task.
sentence.11571: During the lab testing of the tox5 sample, we observed the sample gain persistence through duplication of the sample.
sentence.11572: This is observed below by comparing the file hashes for "tox5.exe" and "C:\ProgramData\lplshr\basinqt.exe."
sentence.11573: Although no obvious signs of compromise were apparent to the user of the infected host, a review of the network traffic from the host showed the newly installed program reached out to "gerhiles[.]com", which had been observed during the incident as a Command and Control site.
sentence.11574: Following the resolution of gerhiles[.]com, and the activation of "INetSim" to simulate a website, the PCAP above shows connections were attempted over port 4001.
sentence.11575: Leveraging "netstat -a -n -o" revealed the PID of the service connecting on port 4001.
sentence.11576: Task manager was then use to reveal the service running on PID 3488, which was renamed instance of Tox5.
sentence.11577: Because of the beaconing activity, persistence, and apparent ability to wipe event logs, it is likely that tox5 is a component of Cobalt Strike or similar framework.
sentence.11578: LATERAL MOVEMENT: SMB AND RDP Brute Ratel allows for lateral movement leveraging RPC to create SMB traffic.
sentence.11579: Although no direct RPC actions were observed, possibly from lack of logging or the method of RPC use, multiple logs throughout the incident show the transfer of files using SMB.
sentence.11580: Logging shows actions taken by the attacker that were recorded by RDPClip in the form of clipboard logging, indicating the use of Remote Desktop Protocol.[CI1]
sentence.11581: [SD2] After the connection to the internet and shared domains were severed, automated processes continued to propagate malware.
sentence.11582: Files commonly observed transferred via SMB include: Black Basta Ransomware "Client_s.exe" and "Client.exe" Cobalt Strike beacon with the name of "Ticket-5731.xls" ".bat" files designed to disable Cisco AMP / Microsoft Defender Clipboard logging

sentence.11593: Also note the use of "-forcepath" and "-bomb".
sentence.11594: A search of Active Directory for users whose passwords never expire, and the last set date while writing to a file for later exfiltration: Stopping Cisco AMP / Disabling Microsoft Defender, these are the same commands as observed in the ".bat" files: Transfer and use of Ticket-5731.xls

sentence.11597: Command showing the use of "Bitsadmin" to transfer the Black Basta Ransomware: Connection from Client by threat actor: DISABLING ANTIVIRUS/MALWARE SOFTWARE USING ".BAT"
sentence.11599: The two ".bat" files that were sent throughout the organization were both designed to turn off Antivirus and Antimalware software.
sentence.11600: It is interesting to note that “cc.bat” does not use any obfuscation and just contains the simple command to stop AMP Orbital.
sentence.11601: This could indicate that it was written hastefully in order to get it onto the target environment.
sentence.11602: "cc.bat" is a simple script designed to stop Cisco AMP.
sentence.11603: “W.bat”, on the other hand, has some simple but clever obfuscation in place.
sentence.11604: When using "vim” or another text editor, the .bat file appears to contain Chinese characters.
sentence.11605: However, performing "cat" or "strings" reveals the actual data.
sentence.11606: This uses a mixture of disguising the ASCII as UTF-16 via manipulating the start of the file, as well as obfuscating the data using a simple cypher.
sentence.11607: The strings of characters following "set" act as the key.

sentence.11614: Over the past several years, multiple cyber security firms and the FBI have posted increased observation of the use of “RClone” to exfil data.

sentence.11620: Two file names were observed during the incident "Client_s.exe" and "Client.exe."
sentence.11621: It is expected that the different naming schemes are related to the different variations of the ransomware.
sentence.11622: Although no sample was able to be provided for Client.exe (which is believed to be the ESXi variant), Quadrant was able to obtain a copy of "Client_s.exe" for Windows hosts.
sentence.11623: From a static malware analysis review, very little was initially able to be obtained from the sample aside from the ".basta" suffix and a relation to "Fax." Static analysis conducted inside of x32dbg, showing a relation to "FAX" and the potential use of the directory "ProgramData": Upon detonation, running the malware sets itself up as the service "Fax" and enables it to start during safe boot.
sentence.11624: The ransomware then proceeds to restart into safe mode using bcdedit.exe.
sentence.11625: BCDEdit is a command line program in windows which is used to modify the “Boot Configuration Data.”
sentence.11626: While in safe mode, the encryption of files occurs.
sentence.11627: Once the encryption is complete, the system is then restarted into the standard operating mode.
sentence.11628: Using the automated malware analyzer CAPEv2 allowed for the detection and capture of this JSON, which indicates the creation of a Mutex: Using the automated malware analyzer CAPEv2 allowed for the detection and capture of this JSON, which shows the addition of "Fax" to the registry allowing it to start in Safemode: Using the automated malware analyzer CAPEv2 allowed for the detection and capture of this JSON which shows the use of BCDEdit to restart the host into safemode with networking:

sentence.11632: During the end state of the active compromise, two flags were observed in Clipboard logging, "-bomb" and "-forcepath".
sentence.11633: The writeups conducted by "Northwave-Security" and "Deepinstinct" share more light onto these flags.
sentence.11634: These show that "bomb" designates a full detonation of all reachable hosts, and "forcepath" is for a specific instance or directory.
sentence.11635: According to the recent writeups above, this indicates that this is one of the newest renditions of the malware.
sentence.11636: We are attempting to better understand the use of the "-bomb" flag and how it communicates with the other infected machines.
sentence.11637: It is likely that the reason the machine is restarted into safe mode with networking indicates that this communication may occur at this time.

sentence.11641: The lab environment consisted of three Virtual Machines running inside of VMWare Workstation 16 Pro.
sentence.11642: The network was configured not to allow any connection to the internet.
sentence.11644: The analysis host ran the Linux distro "REMnux."
sentence.11645: Upon startup, an iptables setup script was ran containing all the hardcoded C2 IP’s for the Qakbot malware.
sentence.11646: This was done in order to all the malware to communicate with the hard coded IP’s without allowing commination to a C2 host.
sentence.11647: Additional software used during the analysis includes:
sentence.11649: Network packet capture and analysis Inetsim: An "Internet Simulation" tool which creates fake http and other services for malware samples to interact with.
sentence.11650: FakeDNS: A fake DNS service which responds with a predetermined IP.
sentence.11651: Default IP is the host FakeDNS is installed on.
sentence.11652: Readpe.py: Used to read Portable Executable files.
sentence.11654: The experimental host rans Windows 10 build 19041.
sentence.11655: This host was used for detonation of the malware samples provided by the client.
sentence.11656: NXlog is installed on this host.
sentence.11657: Windows logging is forwarded to Host 3.
sentence.11658: Host 1 is configured to be the internet gateway.
sentence.11659: Aside from the logging connection to host 3, all other connections are forced through Host 1.
sentence.11662: Regshot: Captures a "snapshot" of the registry before and after detonation of a sample to observe the changes on the host.
sentence.11664: Qakbot Registry Decryption Tool: Used to decrypt Qakbot registry entries.

sentence.11705: title: Earth Preta’s Cyberespionage Campaign Hits Over 200 url: https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/c/earth-preta-cyberespionage-campaign-hits-over-200.html APT & Targeted Attacks Earth Preta’s Cyberespionage Campaign Hits Over 200
sentence.11706: We present a case study of the cyberespionage efforts by Earth Preta.
sentence.11707: This study on an active campaign delves into the structure, goals, and requirements of the organizations involved, and provides an opportunity to conduct wider intelligence analysis and insights in the development of effective countermeasures.
sentence.11708: By: Trend Micro March 27, 2023Read time: ( words) Save to Folio Subscribe Since 2022, we’ve been following a series of cyberespionage efforts carried out by multiple groups carried from an old campaign.
sentence.11709: It combines the collective activities carried out by subgroups of advanced persistent threat (APT) group Earth Preta (also known as Mustang Panda), representing a comprehensive network of operations for gathering sensitive information from various entities.
sentence.11710: An analysis of their deployments also revealed a level of coordination and collaboration.
sentence.11711: Through extensive analysis and as of this writing, we discovered over 200 victims, leading to a wider intelligence analysis of the groups’ goals, different operation groups, and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs).
sentence.11712: Our study aimed at understanding the different phases and facets involved in this operation, shedding light on the motives and techniques used by Earth Preta to provide valuable insights and aid in the development of effective countermeasures.
sentence.11713: Key findings While not exhaustive of the entire study’s findings due to security and confidentiality concerns, we determined the following findings key to the entire research:
sentence.11715: Earth Preta has a centralized development unit that produces the implants and tools, and disseminates them to other operational groups responsible for penetration and implantation.
sentence.11716: This is evident in the Earth Preta group as it appears that multiple sub-operational groups use the same toolset with different techniques.
sentence.11718: The different operational groups manage their own methods of entry and privilege escalation, demonstrating a high degree of specialization within each group.
sentence.11720: Towards the end of 2022, there were changes in how information was collected.
sentence.11721: The latest active targets were related to maritime, shipping, border control, and immigration agencies.
sentence.11722: Prior to this shift, most of the data collection efforts were aimed at academic institutions, ore and material refineries, specialized fabrication plants, financial institutions, and energy production and distribution.
sentence.11723: These key findings can help intelligence communities and decision-makers in understanding Earth Preta’s capabilities, objectives, and impact on international security and intellectual property.
sentence.11724: With this entry, we hope to emphasize the importance of international cooperation in combating this significant threat.
sentence.11725: Method and findings We found that some operational part of the collective group were focused on stealing intellectual property and sensitive business information, while others targeted government and diplomatic entities.
sentence.11726: We also found the operations having specific geographical regions for which they tailored their collection requirements.
sentence.11728: Earth Preta’s top 10 targeted industries We used a qualitative approach to identify the collection requirements, methods, and objectives of the operational groups and their respective places in the organization.
sentence.11729: We established links between the operational threat groups by grouping overlaps in victimology and identifying core indicators, such as implants or payloads. Figure 2.
sentence.11730: Earth Preta’s targeted regions Case studies Overlaps Throughout our investigation, we observed several instances where victims were compromised by two groups simultaneously, indicating possible overlaps in collection requirements between these groups.
sentence.11731: While there are no indications of overlaps in individual devices, there are strong indications of targets intersecting, suggesting these groups are pursuing similar objectives.
sentence.11732: Additionally, the overlaps among victims indicate a lack in targeting coordination and/or planning within the overall groups' leadership or management.
sentence.11733: These targeting overlaps have been observed in multiple groups, such as Groups 724, 1358, and 5171.
sentence.11734: Since these groups operate across a variety of sectors, it is likely that the overlap in collection requirements is the result of similar objectives rather than coordination between the toolset and collected materials.
sentence.11735: However, we have not been able to identify any evidence of coordination between these groups or a shared toolset.
sentence.11736: Infection and exfiltration vectors Group 5171's exfiltration methods are sophisticated and designed to avoid detection.
sentence.11737: Several victims in key countries, such as Singapore, Vietnam, Netherlands, Ghana, and Myanmar, have indications of files exfiltrated via a dedicated USB mass storage device.
sentence.11738: For instance, in January 2023, a device from Vietnam loaded the Adobe CEF Helper under the path <C:\Users\XXX\AAM
sentence.11740: and exfiltrated documents to drive F:.
sentence.11741: The same device also carried out another collection in December 2022, where data was copied from folder <C\:$RECYCLE.BIN\S-XXXXX$XXXH.pdf>, indicating that the user deleted the collected data.
sentence.11742: Roaming endpoint attacks In contrast to Group 5171, Group 1358’s uses malicious USB mass storage devices as its primary method of compromise.
sentence.11743: Our analysis indicated that toward the end of 2022 and early 2023, all documented intrusions from Group 1358 used USB mass storage devices.
sentence.11744: In addition, there were multiple instances where initial compromise occurred while the assets of the target were roaming abroad through a technique known as the “traveling laptop attack.”
sentence.11746: Small sample of Earth Preta’s traveling laptop attack deployments and victims APT subgroups responsible for attack Victim organization’s industry, country Country where attack was deployed from Group 724 Maritime, Australia Papua New Guinea Group 1358 Construction, France Togo Group 5171 NGOs, Africa N/A This mix of traditional intelligence trade craft and cyber techniques could mean that these groups have access to advanced resources and support from nation states, since such techniques are not typically available to independent hackers.
sentence.11747: Moreover, this approach could signify the growing convergence of cyber- and physical security as cyberattacks continue to move beyond digital systems and into the physical world.
sentence.11748: Operation groups While this is not a comprehensive list, we summarize and attribute the operational functions to specific groups as contributing units to Earth Preta’s cyberespionage activities and deployments.
sentence.11749: As we continue following this campaign and track its activities, these group names will be updated accordingly once analyses and attribution are confirmed.
sentence.11750: Group 724 Group 724 is possibly related to Earth Preta.
sentence.11751: The group utilizes sideloading with Adobe CEF Helper to establish a persistent foothold in the user's home directory, employing a naming convention with one of the following patterns: AcroRD32XXX AAM UpdatesXXX AcrobatXXX Eset Malware ProtectionXXX "XXX" denotes three random letters.
sentence.11752: The group uses a USB drive as an entry point into a target's system, indicating its preference for leveraging physical vectors for intrusion.
sentence.11753: This group is considered one of the most dangerous in the Southeast Asian region and has been known to target a myriad of organizations.
sentence.11754: Group 724 also appears to be focused on compromising targets in specific industries and countries.
sentence.11755: The group has been observed targeting sectors such as finance, government, manufacturing, fabrication, construction, energy, transportation, air traffic, and food production.
sentence.11756: This targeted approach indicates that the group has developed a clear understanding of the vulnerabilities and high-value assets present in these industries.
sentence.11757: The significant level of proliferation suggests that it is well-funded and includes a large team of skilled individuals, likely enabling it to carry out attacks on multiple targets simultaneously.
sentence.11758: The group uses customized USB storage devices tailored to individual targets as part of their intrusion tactics.
sentence.11759: These customized devices appear to be carefully crafted to bypass security measures and appear legitimate to the target.
sentence.11760: With this preference for a physical entry vector, the group can increase the chances of a successful intrusion and maintain its covert operations.
sentence.11761: This technique highlights the level of sophistication and planning that goes into Group 724's attacks.
sentence.11762: Group 1358 Group 1358 is a highly sophisticated threat actor that employs advanced tactics and techniques to infiltrate and compromise a wide range of targets worldwide.
sentence.11763: The group has been observed utilizing Avast’s WSC DLL for sideloading, a technique leveraging the Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service to execute malicious code.
sentence.11764: This group is potentially composed of several operating groups utilizing the same tools and techniques.
sentence.11765: Persistence is established at ProgramData\AvastSvcXXX, where "XXX" represents three random letters.
sentence.11766: The group uses generic USB mass storage devices as an entry point, suggesting that they prioritize ease of access over customization.
sentence.11767: This group’s choice of malware is PlugX, an older and well-known remote access tool.
sentence.11768: Despite its age, PlugX remains an effective tool for threat actors due to its flexibility and evasion capabilities.
sentence.11769: The group's victimology is extensive, targeting organizations across various sectors globally.
sentence.11770: However, recent observations suggest that the group has shifted its collection efforts towards maritime-related information since December 2022.
sentence.11771: Targets have included shipping information, sea vessel movements, border and immigration control, export-related government agencies, food production, and humanitarian groups.
sentence.11772: While some of the targets are related to maritime research and development, most of the information we found as targeted pertain to operational maritime information, even to the extent of compromising specific vessels or tugboat companies.
sentence.11773: Exfiltration methods utilized involve the use of USB sticks that are plugged in, enabling the PlugX tool to copy all collected data into a previously known and expected USB stick.
sentence.11774: This technique allows the group to remain undetected and avoid detection by traditional security measures.
sentence.11775: Group 5171 Group 5171 is a threat actor that utilizes advanced techniques to infiltrate and compromise targets across the Middle East and Europe.
sentence.11776: The group uses DLL sideloading with Adobe CEF Helper and establishes persistence in the RECYCLERS.BIN folder.
sentence.11777: In addition, the group also employs USB-based data exfiltration as part of their tactics.
sentence.11778: Group 5171 differentiates itself from other threat actors with their use of the travelling laptop attack.
sentence.11779: This technique involves infecting a laptop with malicious code in transit.
sentence.11780: Usually, the device will be travelling as part of a routine work travel and upon return to the origin country, a more elaborate exploitation and lateral movement can be initiated.
sentence.11781: This method allows the group to bypass traditional security measures and gain access to their targets undetected.
sentence.11782: Sectoral targets of Group 5171 are spread out, indicating that the group does not focus on specific sectors but rather adopts a more opportunistic approach.
sentence.11783: However, observing victims’ business verticals and sectors indicate that Group 5171’s collection efforts show a high level of interest in research and development related to IT solutions, materials manufacturing and fabrication, energy production and synthetization, air travel, and space.
sentence.11784: Conclusion We deem the findings of this research on Earth Preta’s cyberespionage operations have significant implications for international security and intellectual property.
sentence.11785: There are strong indications of intertwined traditional intelligence tradecraft and cyber collection efforts, indicative of a highly coordinated and sophisticated cyberespionage operation.
sentence.11786: We identified several distinct operational groups, each with unique TTPs and objectives, which reveals a highly specialized and organized cyberespionage operation.
sentence.11787: This study also suggests that Earth Preta’s cyberespionage operations have a broad reach and have the capacity to target high value targets.
sentence.11788: The shift in collection priorities toward intelligence regarding specific areas also indicates that Earth Preta is targeting critical infrastructure and key institutions that can affect national and international relations, economies, and securities.
sentence.11789: Given the scale and sophistication of Earth Preta’s cyberespionage operations, the international community needs to take proactive measures to defend against this significant threat.
sentence.11790: This includes robust cybersecurity measures, effective countermeasures against cyberespionage, and increased international cooperation in combating this threat.
sentence.11791: The international community must raise awareness on the threats posed by Earth Preta’s cyberespionage operations, promote information sharing, and develop effective countermeasures.
sentence.11792: It is essential to have a coordinated response to this threat, with the support of the private sector, academia, and civil society, to ensure the safety and security of critical infrastructure and intellectual property.
sentence.11794: For a list of the IOCs, download the appendix here.

sentence.11796: title: Updated: New Evidence Emerges to Suggest WatchDog Was Behind Crypto Campaign url: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/teamtnt-cryptojacking-watchdog-operations/ This post is also available in: 日本語 (Japanese)Author's Note New evidence has emerged that suggests the group WatchDog was behind a cryptojacking campaign that we attributed to TeamTNT in a blog published on June 8, 2021.
sentence.11797: This updated information changed our view on the evidence initially gathered by Unit 42 researchers.
sentence.11798: Specifically, the domain oracle.zzhreceive[.]top was originally linked to TeamTNT operations due to the usage of the term zzhreceive, which has been witnessed within several TeamTNT operations.
sentence.11799: Given recent developments and the growing analytic visibility within the cloud research community, this domain has now been attributed to the cryptojacking operations associated with the group WatchDog.
sentence.11800: The following is an update of our original blog, more accurately aligned to the current intelligence community information regarding WatchDog’s mimicry of TeamTNT operations.
sentence.11801: Executive Summary The copying and incorporation of cryptomining operational codebase or script functions have become a central behavioral indicator of cryptojacking groups and their operations.
sentence.11802: Unit 42 researchers have identified tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) used by the TeamTNT cryptojacking group being used by the WatchDog cryptojacking group.
sentence.11803: The new scripts from WatchDog are overtly copying TeamTNT infrastructure naming conventions and using a known WatchDog C2 hosting system, 199.199.226[.]117.
sentence.11804: With the identification of these new WatchDog scripts, Unit 42 researchers found that techniques that have been synonymous with the TeamTNT group have gone missing.
sentence.11805: For instance, the new scripts do not: Researchers have also observed that the new WatchDog scripts do not use the exploit-laden GoLang binaries traditionally associated with WatchDog.
sentence.11806: While WatchDog is believed to be the author of these new scripts, several of the scripts were found within TeamTNT-owned public malware repositories.
sentence.11807: It appears that WatchDog may be attempting to expand their cryptojacking operations, while simultaneously masking their operations to appear more like the known cryptojacking operations performed by TeamTNT.
sentence.11808: The stealing, hijacking or incorporation of cryptojacking TTPs within other cryptojacking operations has become a common trend within cryptojacking groups.
sentence.11809: Most notably, TeamTNT was reported to have copied the code used to detect and remove Alibaba Cloud Security from compromised instances from the Kinsing group.
sentence.11810: Also, cryptojacking groups such as “Rocke” began as a forked GitHub repository from the cryptojacking operation created by “The 8220 Mining Group.”
sentence.11811: This operation shares up to 30% of its cryptomining code base with tools developed by the group “Pacha.”
sentence.11812: Pacha and Rocke were subsequently involved in a documented crypto war, which has lasted nearly two years.
sentence.11813: While little research has been written on recent Pacha operations, Rocke is still developing new malware.
sentence.11814: Palo Alto Networks customers running Prisma Cloud are protected from the threats presented in this report through the Runtime Protection feature, Cryptominer Detection feature and the Prisma Cloud Compute Kubernetes Compliance Protection, which alerts on an insufficient Kubernetes configuration and provides secure alternatives.
sentence.11815: Additionally, Palo Alto Networks VM-Series and CN-Series products offer cloud protections that can prevent network connections from cloud instances toward known malicious IP addresses and URLs.
sentence.11816: New WatchDog Malware There are two samples that show the evolution of WatchDog techniques to mimic TeamTNT operations, 36ca9f84864ad022c255b7d91e75997f035716e4df5dc1c90ee2651f092f5d79 and 49366ae4766492d94136ca1f715a37554aa6243686c66bf3c6fbb9da9cb2793d.
sentence.11817: These samples, first witnessed on Dec. 5 and 11, 2020, respectively, show the direct replacement of the known WatchDog C2 infrastructure with new C2 infrastructure.
sentence.11818: As shown in Figure 1, the original WatchDog infrastructure, in the dark blue rectangle, has been commented out of the bash script functionality and replaced with the new infrastructure seen in the light blue rectangle.
sentence.11821: The new script also makes use of the exact URL address directory tree pattern that is present within the known WatchDog operations, with the directories b2f628 (red) and b2f628fff19fda999999999 (orange), as shown in Figure 2. Figure 2. URL directory pattern.
sentence.11822: These two samples contain a hardcoded Monero (XMR) wallet address and an associated mining pool, as shown in Figure 3. Figure 3.

sentence.11824: Mining Pools If these changes are indeed new TeamTNT behaviors, which is highly unlikely, it would represent the first time the TeamTNT cryptojacking operations have used a mining pool outside their traditional Monero mining pool, MoneroOcean[.]stream.
sentence.11825: This cryptojacking operation introduces two new mining pools never before known to be used by TeamTNT actors, but have been witnessed within WatchDog operations.
sentence.11826: These mining pools are nanopool[.]org, shown in Figure 4, and f2pool[.]com, shown in Figure 5.
sentence.11827: The new mining pools are both instructed to use the Monero wallet address, 43Xbgtym2GZWBk87XiYbCpTKGPBTxYZZWi44SWrkqqvzPZV6Pfmjv3UHR6FDwvPgePJyv9N5PepeajfmKp1X71EW7jx4Tpz.

sentence.11854: With the presence of the C2 infrastructure from these new scripts, Figure 9 and Figure 10, both of which use the WatchDog directory, b2f628, there is a clear link to the TeamTNT infrastructure.
sentence.11855: The domain oracle.zzhreceive[.]top resolves to the IP address 199.19.226[.]117, which is also the resolution IP address for the known TeamTNT subdomain zzhrecieve.anondns[.]net.
sentence.11856: The usage of the anondns[.]net domain has been linked to several TeamTNT campaigns across multiple reports including, irc.anondns[.]net, ircbd.anondns[.]net, sampan.anondns[.]net and teamtntisback.anondns[.]net.
sentence.11857: Additionally, the 199.19.226[.]117 system has also been linked to WatchDog operations through the toolkit file 1.0.4.tar.gz, 51de345f677f46595fc3bd747bfb61bc9ff130adcbec48f3401f8057c8702af9, which was hosted on hxxp://global.bitmex[.]com[.]de/cf67355a3333e6/1.0.4.tar.gz and contains C code for the masscan utility, which is the same toolkit used in the TeamTNT operations.

sentence.11860: The malware repository 85.214.149[.]236:443/sugarcrm/themes/default/images/ contains known TeamTNT malware that includes the same files as the known TeamTNT repository hxxp://dockerupdate.anondns[.]net:443/sugarcrm/themes/default/images/, which is linked to TeamTNT via the malware sample 1aaf7bc48ff75e870db4fe6ec0b3ed9d99876d7e2fb3d5c4613cca92bbb95e1b, as shown in Figure 11.
sentence.11863: Of note, some the of malware samples included in this repository were the Kubernetes and Docker-focused malware, ‘kube.jpg’ and ‘tshd’, presented in Unit 42's Black-T blog, but these appear to no longer be used in the new scripts discussed within this blog.
sentence.11864: See the appendix for a full listing of the known TeamTNT malware metadata collected from the malware repository.
sentence.11865: The malware sample 0414946ab4bced2c1c41f4b8a75be672b34bbdee6f29e0a0bf7946b93f7044b1 is of note in this context as it contains the hardcoded IP address, 199.19.226[.]117, as well as the hardcoded Monero wallet address associated with the nanopool and f2pool mining pools, and the mining workers previously discussed (Figures 12 and 13).
sentence.11866: As the previous section mentioned, the IP address 199.19.226[.]117 also resolves to the known TeamTNT domain zzhrecieve.anondns[.]net. Figure 12.
