sentence.12587: title: Too Log; Didn't Read — Unknown Actor Using CLFS Log Files for Stealth url: http://internal-www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2021/09/unknown-actor-using-clfs-log-files-for-stealth.html The Mandiant Advanced Practices team recently discovered a new malware family we have named PRIVATELOG and its installer, STASHLOG.
sentence.12588: In this post, we will share a novel and especially interesting technique the samples use to hide data, along with detailed analysis of both files that was performed with the support of FLARE analysts.
sentence.12589: We will also share sample detection rules, and hunting recommendations to find similar activity in your environment.
sentence.12590: Mandiant has yet to observe PRIVATELOG or STASHLOG in any customer environments or to recover any second-stage payloads launched by PRIVATELOG.
sentence.12591: This may indicate malware that is still in development, the work of a researcher, or targeted activity.
sentence.12592: CLFS and Transaction Files PRIVATELOG and STASHLOG rely on the Common Log File System (CLFS) to hide a second stage payload in registry transaction files.
sentence.12593: CLFS is a log framework that was introduced by Microsoft in Windows Vista and Windows Server 2003 R2 for high performance.
sentence.12594: It provides applications with API functions—available in clfsw32.dll—to create, store and read log data.
sentence.12595: Because the file format is not widely used or documented, there are no available tools that can parse CLFS log files.
sentence.12596: This provides attackers with an opportunity to hide their data as log records in a convenient way, because these are accessible through API functions.
sentence.12597: This is similar in nature to malware which may rely, for example, on the Windows Registry or NTFS Extended Attributes to hide their data, which also provide locations to store and retrieve binary data with the Windows API.
sentence.12598: In Microsoft Windows, CLFS is notably used by the Kernel Transaction Manager (KTM) for both Transactional NTFS (TxF) and Transactional Registry (TxR) operations.
sentence.12599: These allow applications to perform a number of changes on the filesystem or registry, all grouped in a single transaction that can be committed or rolled back.
sentence.12600: For example, to open a registry key in a transaction, the functions RegCreateKeyTransacted(), RegOpenKeyTransacted(), and RegDeleteKeyTransacted() are available.
sentence.12601: Registry transactions are stored in dedicated files with the following naming scheme: <hive><GUID>.TMContainer<number>.regtrans-ms or <hive><GUID>.TxR.<number>.regtrans-ms.
sentence.12602: These are CLFS containers that are referenced in a master .blf
sentence.12603: file that only contains metadata and can be found in various locations including user profile directories.
sentence.12604: Registry transaction forensics were briefly explored in a previous blog post.
sentence.12605: The CLFS master and container file formats are mostly undocumented; however, previous research is available on GitHub.
sentence.12606: Malware Obfuscation As with many malware families, most of the strings used by PRIVATELOG and STASHLOG are obfuscated.
sentence.12607: Yet the technique observed here is uncommon and relies on XOR’ing each byte with a hard-coded byte inline, with no loops.
sentence.12608: Effectively, each string is therefore encrypted with a unique byte stream.
sentence.12609:
Figure 1: Sample string deobfuscation for "PrintNotify" Interestingly, some of the deobfuscated strings from the installer are used for logging error messages and have spelling errors or typos such as: Log index=%d, data border exceed bounday.
 Interal data hash mismatch.
 Log buffer size=%u too small, expect aleast %u bytes.
 Introducing STASHLOG In addition to containing obfuscated strings, the installer’s code is protected using various control flow obfuscation techniques that make static analysis cumbersome.
sentence.12610: Figure 2 is a graph overview of the installer’s main() function demonstrating the effects of the control flow obfuscation.
sentence.12611: Figure 2: Graph view of main() STASHLOG has two different modes of operation: Without any arguments, during which it will prepare the environment With a single argument, which is a file that should be hidden in a CLFS file Preparing the Environment Executed without arguments, the installer prints two values to the console: The GUID returned from the registry value of HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGUID A 56-byte value derived from a randomly generated GUID with CoCreateGUID() Figure 3: Sample console output The 56-byte value is a concatenation of the random GUID, its SHA1 hash, and the SHA1 hash of the previous values.
sentence.12613: The randomly generated GUID is stored as a string in the GlobalAtom table, prefixed with win::.
sentence.12614: This table resides in memory and contains strings with their identifiers available to all applications.
sentence.12615: If a string prefixed with win:: already exists when the installer is executed, then the pre-existing GUID in the GlobalAtom table is reused.
sentence.12616: Effectively, when executed with no arguments, the installer generates and prints out encryption keys that the actor uses to pre-encrypt the payload before it is written to disk.
sentence.12617: Stashing the Payload When launched with an argument, the installer opens and decrypts the contents of the file passed as an argument.
sentence.12618: It verifies that the file is suffixed by its SHA1 hash, and then generates the same 56-byte value using the stored GlobalAtom GUID string in memory.
sentence.12619: The 56-byte value is SHA1 hashed again and the first 16-bytes form the initialization vector (IV), while the key is the 16-byte MachineGUID value from the host’s registry.
sentence.12620: The encryption algorithm is HC-128, which is rarely seen used in malware.
sentence.12621: The expected decrypted file contents have a 40-byte header: struct payloadHeader { DWORD magic; DWORD minWinVer; DWORD maxWinVer; DWORD totalSize; WORD numBlocks; WORD unknown; BYTE sha1sum[20]; } In the analyzed installer, the “magic” value is referred to as a checksum; however, STASHLOG verifies this value matches the hard-coded value 0x00686365.
sentence.12622: The number of blocks, specified at offset 16, must be between 2 and 5.
sentence.12623: The malware also checks that the operating system version is within a lower and upper boundary and that the SHA1 hash of the decrypted data matches the payload header value at offset 20.
sentence.12624: Following the payload header, the malware expects blocks of encrypted data with 8-byte headers.
sentence.12625: Each block header has the following structure: struct blockHeader { DWORD magic; DWORD blockSize; } Once the malware has checked and validated the structure of the payload, it searches for .blf files in the default user’s profile directory and uses the .blf file with the oldest creation date timestamp.
sentence.12626: In practice, the malware should typically find the file used for registry transaction logs: C:\Users\Default\NTUSER.DAT<GUID>.TM.blf If a matching .blf file is indeed found, it is opened with the CreateLogFile() API from clfsw32.dll.
sentence.12627: This function opens CLFS logs and expects a file name in the following format, without the .blf extension: log:<LogName>[::<LogStreamName>] The log file is reset using the CloseAndResetLogFile() function and will be opened again to insert the data.
sentence.12628: Before inserting data into the CLFS log file, the malware decrypts each block using HC-128.
sentence.12629: The key is the 16-byte atom GUID and the IV is the first 16-bytes of the atom GUID SHA1 hash.
sentence.12630: Each block is then re-encrypted with the new key material as follows: The encryption key is the 16-byte GUID from GetVolumeNameForVolumeMountPointW().
sentence.12631: The IV is the first 16-bytes of the SHA1 hash of the concatenated GUIDs from: GetVolumeNameForVolumeMountPointW() The registry value HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGUID The contents are written to the CLFS log file using the clfsw32.dll API function ReserveAndAppendLog().
sentence.12632: The payload header is written to the log file as the first entry, followed by separate entries for each block.
sentence.12633: The data is effectively stored in the first container file for the registry transaction log: C:\Users\Default\NTUSER.DAT<GUID>.TMContainer00000000000000000001.regtrans-ms.
sentence.12634: Onto PRIVATELOG The PRIVATELOG sample recovered by Mandiant is an un-obfuscated 64-bit DLL named prntvpt.dll.
sentence.12635: It contains exports, which mimic those of legitimate prntvpt.dll files, although the exports have no functionality.
sentence.12636: PRIVATELOG expects to be loaded from PrintConfig.dll, which is the main DLL of a service named PrintNotify, via DLL search order hijacking.
sentence.12637: The malicious code is executed at the DLL’s entry point.
sentence.12638: It starts by verifying the command-line arguments of the process it is running in and expects to be running under svchost.exe -k print.
sentence.12639: If this matches, the malware resolves the function address for the ServiceMain export function of PrintConfig.dll, which is the service entry point of the service using this command line.
sentence.12640: This function is patched using Microsoft Detours—a publicly available library used for instrumenting Win32 functions—so that the execution flow appears to happen in the legitimate service DLL.
sentence.12641: The patched ServiceMain function is where PRIVATELOG executes most of its functionality.
sentence.12642: Similarly to STASHLOG, PRIVATELOG starts by enumerating *.blf files in the default user’s profile directory and uses the .blf file with the oldest creation date timestamp.
sentence.12643: If a matching .blf file is found, PRIVATELOG opens it with the clfsw32.dll function CreateLogFile().
sentence.12644: The log file is then marshalled and parsed using other functions specific to CLFS, such as CreateLogMarshallingArea(), ReadLogFile() and ReadNextLogFile().
sentence.12645: The malware expects to find specific entries which match our analysis of the installer.
sentence.12646: PRIVATELOG expects the first log entry to have the following format:
sentence.12647: A size greater than 40 (payload header size)
sentence.12648: A WORD value of 2, 3, 4, or 5 at offset 16 (number of blocks)
sentence.12649: If the first entry matches the aforementioned criteria, then subsequent records are read until one has an 8-byte header with the following: Its first DWORD must equal 2 (assumed magic value)
sentence.12650: Its second DWORD must be less than the entry’s size minus the header.
sentence.12651: This value equals the size of the payload which will be decrypted.
sentence.12652: Once the expected log entry is found, its contents are decrypted using the HC-128 encryption algorithm.
sentence.12653: The decryption key and IV are generated using the same unique host properties that were used by STASHLOG.
sentence.12654: It is worth noting that PRIVATELOG only decrypts the first matching block and that at least 2 to 5 blocks are expected to be inserted by STASHLOG.
sentence.12655: PRIVATELOG finally uses a rarely seen technique to execute the DLL payload, which this time relies on NTFS transactions.
sentence.12656: The injection process is similar to Phantom DLL hollowing and is described as follows: Open a transacted handle to a copied file via the API CreateFileTransactedA()
sentence.12657: In the sample analyzed by Mandiant, the file used for the transaction is a copy of the legitimate binary C:\Windows\System32\dbghelp.dll, which is copied to C:\Windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\dbghelp.dll.
sentence.12658: Overwrite the transacted file with the decrypted payload contents Create a section backed by the transacted file with SEC_IMAGE attributes via the API NtCreateSection() Map a view of the newly created section This implicitly loads the transacted file data to some degree.
sentence.12659: The PE header is validated, and sections mapped into memory; however, it does not fix section permissions or resolve imports.
sentence.12660: Fix the section permissions Resolve the imports in the Import Table Execute the payload's entry point Find and execute the export function named SvcMain Hunting for PRIVATELOG Container Sample Figure 4 shows a fabricated container file representing a sample expected log file created by STASHLOG and loaded by PRIVATELOG.
sentence.12661: Figure 4: Example log file created by STASHLOG YARA Rules Mandiant created YARA rules to hunt for PRIVATELOG and STASHLOG as well as possible variants based on various methodologies and unique strings that they use.
sentence.12662: Rules to detect CLFS containers matching PRIVATELOG structures or containing encrypted data are also provided.
sentence.12663: These rules should be tested thoroughly before they are run in a production environment.

sentence.12686: These would cover cases where PRIVATELOG may resolve imports dynamically with LoadLibrary() and GetProcAddress(), versus static imports in currently known samples.
sentence.12687: Figure 5 identifies key modules loaded by PRIVATELOG that may be used to create hunting queries: ktmw32.dll, dbghelp.dll and clfsw32.dll. Figure 5: Memory view of a running PRIVATELOG process
sentence.12688: Example hunting queries include: Any process writing or loading C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\dbghelp.dll Any process loading both clfsw32.dll and ktmw32.dll svchost.exe -k print loading clfsw32.dll or ktmw32.dll Any svchost.exe process loading clfsw32.dll Concerning svchost.exe, although we have observed many cases of other svchost.exe processes loading ktmw32.dll, we have only rarely observed svchost.exe processes loading clfsw32.dll.
sentence.12689: File writes to .regtrans-ms or .blf files are fairly common, however stacking the process name and file paths may also provide good results.
sentence.12690: For example, file writes to the registry transaction file for the default user are likely to be uncommon.

sentence.12692: title: Ransom Cartel Ransomware: A Possible Connection With REvil url: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/ransom-cartel-ransomware/ This post is also available in: 日本語 (Japanese)Executive Summary Ransom Cartel is ransomware as a service (RaaS) that surfaced in mid-December 2021.
sentence.12693: This ransomware performs double extortion attacks and exhibits several similarities and technical overlaps with REvil ransomware.
sentence.12694: REvil ransomware disappeared just a couple of months before Ransom Cartel surfaced and just one month after 14 of its alleged members were arrested in Russia.
sentence.12695: When Ransom Cartel first appeared, it was unclear whether it was a rebrand of REvil or an unrelated threat actor who reused or mimicked REvil ransomware code.
sentence.12696: In this report, we will provide our analysis of Ransom Cartel ransomware, as well as our assessment of the possible connections between REvil and Ransom Cartel ransomware.
sentence.12697: Palo Alto Networks customers receive help with the detection and prevention of Ransom Cartel ransomware through the following products and services: Cortex XDR and Next-Generation Firewalls (including cloud-delivered security services such as WildFire).
sentence.12698: If you think a cyber incident may have impacted you, the Unit 42 Incident Response team is available 24/7/365.
sentence.12699: You can also take preventative steps by requesting any of our cyber risk management services. Indicators of compromise and Ransom Cartel-associated tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) can be found in the Ransom Cartel ATOM.
sentence.12700: We updated this blog on Oct. 15 based on further analysis, additional evidence and discussion around the complexities of redirects from REvil’s dark web leak site.
sentence.12701: Updated sections include our History of the REvil Disappearance and the Ransom Cartel Overview.
sentence.12702: Table of Contents History of the REvil DisappearanceRansom Cartel OverviewTTPs Observed During Ransom Cartel AttacksRansom NotesRansom Cartel TOR SiteTechnical Details Ransom Cartel and REvil Code ComparisonRansom Cartel Tactics, Techniques and ProceduresMalware, Tools and Exploits UsedConclusionIndicators of Compromise History of the REvil Disappearance In October 2021, REvil operators went quiet.
sentence.12703: REvil’s dark web leak site became unreachable.
sentence.12704: Around mid-April 2022, individual security researchers and cybersecurity media outlets reported a new development with REvil that could signify the gang’s return.
sentence.12705: REvil’s name-and-shame blogs at the dnpscnbaix6nkwvystl3yxglz7nteicqrou3t75tpcc5532cztc46qyd[.]onion and aplebzu47wgazapdqks6vrcv6zcnjppkbxbr6wketf56nf6aq2nmyoyd[.]onion domains started redirecting users to a new name-and-shame blog available at blogxxu75w63ujqarv476otld7cyjkq4yoswzt4ijadkjwvg3vrvd5yd[.]onion/Blog.
sentence.12706: This redirect was documented in our post, “Understanding REvil,” in Bleeping Computer’s post on REvil’s TOR sites redirecting to a new ransomware operation and in a Twitter post from vx-underground.
sentence.12707: Later the same day, the redirect was removed (as noted by vx-underground).
sentence.12708: At the time, it was not possible to make a definitive attribution stating which group was behind the redirect because the new name-and-shame blog did not claim any name or affiliation.
sentence.12709: At the start of the redirect, no breached organizations were listed on the site.
sentence.12710: Over time, the threat actors began adding records that had appeared on “Happy Blog,” mostly from late April to October 2021.
sentence.12711: They also included the old file-sharing links previously used by REvil as proof of compromise.
sentence.12712: The newly established blog listed Tox Chat ID for communication with the ransomware operator.
sentence.12713: The blog hinted at its operators’ connection to REvil with the claim that the newer group offered “the same, yet improved software.”
sentence.12714: Unit 42 initially believed that this blog was linked to Ransom Cartel and that the “improved software” the threat actors referred to was a new Ransom Cartel variant.
sentence.12715: However, after further analysis and seeing more evidence, we believe it is also possible that the name-and-shame blog and Ransom Cartel are two separate operations.
sentence.12716: Whether this blog is operated by Ransom Cartel or a different group, what is clear is that, while REvil may have disappeared, its malicious influence has not.
sentence.12717: The operator of the newly established blog appears to have some type of access to REvil or ties to the group.
sentence.12718: At the same time, our analysis of Ransom Cartel samples (detailed in the sections below) provides strong evidence of ties to REvil as well.
sentence.12719: To read more about REvil, its disappearance and the redirect, please refer to our blog, Understanding REvil.
sentence.12720: Ransom Cartel Overview We first observed Ransom Cartel around mid-January 2022.
sentence.12721: Security researchers at MalwareHunterTeam believe the group to have been active since at least December 2021.
sentence.12722: They observed the first known Ransom Cartel activity and noticed several similarities and technical overlaps with REvil ransomware.
sentence.12723: There are a number of theories about the origins of Ransom Cartel.
sentence.12724: One theory in the community suggests that Ransom Cartel could be the result of multiple groups merging.
sentence.12725: However, researchers at MalwareHunterTeam have put forward that one of the groups believed to have merged has denied any connection with Ransom Cartel.
sentence.12726: Additionally, Unit 42 has seen no connection between these groups and Ransom Cartel other than that many of them have connections to REvil.
sentence.12727: At this time, we believe that Ransom Cartel operators had access to earlier versions of REvil ransomware source code, but not some of the most recent developments (see our Ransom Cartel and REvil Code Comparison for more details).
sentence.12728: This suggests there was a relationship between the groups at some point, though it may not have been recent.
sentence.12729: Unit 42 has also observed Ransom Cartel group breaching organizations, with the first known victims observed by us around January 2022 in the U.S. and France.
sentence.12730: Ransom Cartel has attacked organizations in the following industries: education, manufacturing, and utilities and energy.
sentence.12731: Unit 42 incident responders have also assisted clients with response efforts in several Ransom Cartel cases.
sentence.12732: Like many other ransomware gangs, Ransom Cartel leverages double extortion techniques.
sentence.12733: Unit 42 has observed the group taking an aggressive approach, threatening not only to publish stolen data to their leak site, but also to send it to the victim’s partners, competitors and the news in an effort to inflict reputational damage.
sentence.12734: Ransom Cartel typically gains initial access to an environment via compromised credentials, which is one of the most common vectors for initial access for ransomware operators.
sentence.12735: This includes access credentials for external remote services, remote desktop protocol (RDP), secure shell protocol (SSH) and virtual private networks (VPNs).
sentence.12736: These credentials are widely available in the cyber underground and offer threat actors a reliable means to gain access to victims' corporate networks.
sentence.12737: These credentials can also be obtained through the work of ransomware operators themselves or by purchasing them from an initial access broker.
sentence.12738: Initial access brokers are actors who offer to sell compromised network access.
sentence.12739: Their motivation is not to carry out cyberattacks themselves but rather to sell the access to other threat actors.
sentence.12740: Due to the profitability of ransomware, these brokers likely have working relationships with RaaS groups based on the amount they are willing to pay.
sentence.12741: Unit 42 has seen evidence that Ransom Cartel has relied on this type of service to gain initial access for ransomware deployment.
sentence.12742: Unit 42 has also observed Ransom Cartel encrypting both Windows and Linux VMWare ESXi servers in attacks on corporate networks.
sentence.12743: Tactics, Techniques and Procedures Observed During Ransom Cartel Attacks Unit 42 observed a Ransom Cartel threat actor using a tool called DonPAPI, which has not been observed in past incidents.
sentence.12744: This tool can locate and retrieve Windows Data Protection API (DPAPI) protected credentials, which is known as DPAPI dumping.
sentence.12745: DonPAPI is used to search machines for certain files known to be DPAPI blobs, including Wi-Fi keys, RDP passwords,
sentence.12746: credentials saved in web browsers, etc.
sentence.12747: To avoid the risk of detection by antivirus (AVs) or endpoint detection and response (EDR), the tool downloads the files and decrypts them locally.
sentence.12748: To compromise Linux ESXi devices, Ransom Cartel uses DonPAPI to harvest credentials stored in web browsers used to authenticate to the vCenter web interface.
sentence.12749: We also observed the threat actor using additional tools, including LaZagne to recover credentials stored locally and Mimikatz to steal credentials from host memory.
sentence.12750: In order to establish persistent access to Linux ESXi devices, the threat actor enables SSH after authenticating to vCenter.
sentence.12751: The threat actor will create new accounts and sets the account’s user identifier (UID) to zero.
sentence.12752: For Unix/Linux users, a UID=0 is root.
sentence.12753: This means any security checks are bypassed.
sentence.12754: The threat actor was observed downloading and using a cracked version of a legitimate tool called PDQ Inventory, which is a legitimate system management solution that IT administrators use to scan their network and collect hardware, software and Windows configuration data.
sentence.12755: Ransom Cartel used this as a remote access tool to establish an interactive command and control channel and to scan the compromised network.
sentence.12756: Once a VMware ESXi server is compromised, the threat actor launches the encryptor, which will automatically enumerate the running virtual machines (VMs) and shut them down using the esxcli command.
sentence.12757: Terminating the VM processes ensures that the ransomware can successfully encrypt VMware-related files.
sentence.12758: During encryption, Ransom Cartel specifically seeks out files with the following file extensions: .log, .vmdk, .vmem, .vswp and .vmsn.
sentence.12759: These extensions are associated with ESXi snapshots, log files, swap files, paging files and virtual disks.
sentence.12760: Post-encryption, the following file extensions have been observed: .zmi5z, .nwixz, .ext, .zje2m, .5vm8t and .m4tzt.
sentence.12761: Ransom Notes Unit 42 has observed two different versions of ransom notes sent by Ransom Cartel.
sentence.12762: The first note was first observed around January 2022, and the other one first appeared in August 2022.
sentence.12763: The second version appeared to be completely rewritten, as shown in Figure 1. Figure 1.
sentence.12765: The note on the left was first observed in January 2022; the note on the right was first observed in August 2022.It's interesting to note that the structure of the first ransom note used by Ransom Cartel shares similarities with a ransom note sent by REvil, as shown in Figure 2.
sentence.12766: In addition to the use of similar wording, both notes employed the same format of a 16-byte hexadecimal string for the UID. Figure 2.
sentence.12767: Ransom Cartel ransom note shown on the left, compared to a ransom note sent by REvil shown on the right.
sentence.12768: Ransom Cartel TOR Site Ransom Cartel’s website for communication with victims was available via a TOR link provided in the ransom note.
sentence.12769: We’ve observed multiple TOR URLs belonging to Ransom Cartel, which likely indicates that they had been changing infrastructure and actively developing their website.
sentence.12770: A TOR private key is needed to access the website.
sentence.12771: When the key is entered, the following page is loaded: Figure 3.
sentence.12772: Ransom Cartel TOR site landing page.
sentence.12773: Upon entering the TOR site through the Authorization button, a screen requesting input of the details included in the ransom note is requested.
sentence.12775: Ransom Cartel website, requesting the ID and key provided in the ransom note.
sentence.12776: Once authorization is completed on the TOR site, the page shown in Figure 5 appears.
sentence.12777: The site includes details such as ransom demand, in both US dollars and bitcoin, and the Bitcoin wallet address. Figure 5.
sentence.12779: Technical Details Two Ransom Cartel samples were used during this analysis: File one SHA256: 55e4d509de5b0f1ea888ff87eb0d190c328a559d7cc5653c46947e57c0f01ec5File two SHA256: 2411a74b343bbe51b2243985d5edaaabe2ba70e0c923305353037d1f442a91f5 Both of the samples contained three total exports:
sentence.12780: RathbuigeServiceMainSvchostPushServiceGlobals The samples also contain a DllEntryPoint, should the DLL be executed without specifying an export.
sentence.12781: The DllEntryPoint leads to a function that iterates over a call to the Curve25519 Donna algorithm 24 times.
sentence.12782: Once the iteration ends, the sample will query the system metrics, specifically for the SM_CLEANBOOT value.
sentence.12783: If this value is anything other than 0, the ransomware will proceed to spawn another instance of itself via rundll32.exe, specifying the Rathbuige export.
sentence.12784: SM_CLEANBOOT Values Description 0 Normal Boot 1 Fail-Safe Boot 2 Fail-Safe with Network Boot Table 1.
sentence.12786: The Rathbuige export starts by creating the following mutex: Global\\266ee996-e1ac-4eaa-9bdb-0b639d41b32d Once the mutex is created, the sample begins to decrypt and parse its embedded configuration.
sentence.12787: The configuration is stored as a base64-encoded blob, whereby the first 16 bytes of the base64-encoded blob is the RC4 key used for decrypting the rest of the blob once it has been decoded.
sentence.12790: Once decrypted, the configuration is stored in JSON format and consists of information such as encrypted file extension, the threat actors' public Curve25519-donna key, a base64-encoded ransom note, and a list of processes and services to terminate prior to encryption.
sentence.12792: Example of decrypted Ransom Cartel configuration.
sentence.12793: A breakdown of the keys and their values within the configuration can be seen in Table 2. Configuration Key Value pk Attacker public key dbg Debug mode wht Allow listed items Files to avoid Extensions to avoid prc Processes to terminate svc Services to terminate nname Name of ransom note file nbody Ransom note content ext Encrypted file extension Table 2.

sentence.12801: Following decryption of the configuration, certain system information is gathered, including the username, computer name, domain name, locale and product name.
sentence.12802: This information is then formatted into the following JSON structure: {"ver":%d,"pk":"%s","uid":"%s","sk":"%s","unm":"%s","net":"%s","grp":"%s","lng":"%s","bro":%s,"os":"%s","bit":%d,"dsk":"%s","ext":"%s"} Table 6 describes the purpose of each key within the structure.
sentence.12803: Key Value ver Version of the ransomware, hardcoded.
sentence.12804: In both samples set to 0x65 (101) pk Public key found within the configuration uid Unique identifier calculated via CRC-32 hashing certain machine information sk Encoded session secret unm Username net Computer name grp Computer domain lng Computer locale bro Does keyboard locale match any hardcoded locale value – true/false os Product name bit System architecture dsk Disk information ext Ransomware extension Table 6.
sentence.12805: Hardcoded JSON format keys and values.
sentence.12806: Once the gathered data has been formatted into the JSON structure, it is then encrypted using the same procedure that Ransom Cartel follows to generate session_secret blobs, which will be discussed shortly; put simply, it involves AES encryption, utilizing the SHA3 hash of a Curve25519 shared key for the AES key.
sentence.12807: Once encrypted, it is written to the registry key SOFTWARE\\Google_Authenticator\\b52dKMhj, with the sample first attempting to write to the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE hive, before writing to HKEY_CURRENT_USER if the right permissions are not possessed.
sentence.12808: Once the data has been written to the registry, it is then base64-encoded and embedded within the ransom note, replacing the {KEY} placeholder.
sentence.12809: Once the configuration has been parsed and stored within the registry, the command line provided to the ransomware is parsed.
sentence.12810: There are a total of five possible arguments, as shown in Table 7. Argument Description -nolan Instruct the sample not to attempt any form of network drive encryption -nolocal Prevent the encryption of all local volumes -path Target specific file path to encrypt -silent Appears to instruct the ransomware to avoid terminating running processes and services, and it begins encrypting files immediately -smode Causes the ransomware to use BCEdit in order to enable Safe Boot; check out this article on REvil’s use of “Windows Safe Mode” encryption for a discussion about this particular technique.
sentence.12813: With that, let’s move on to analyzing the session secret generation procedure.
sentence.12814: Ransom Cartel first checks to see if the registry already contains previously generated values; if so, it will read those values into memory.
sentence.12815: Otherwise, it will generate a total of two session secrets at runtime, with each secret containing 88 bytes of data.
sentence.12816: First, a public and private key pair will be generated using the code from this Curve25519 repository (session_public_1 and session_private_1).
sentence.12817: When generating the first session secret, another session key pair is generated, (session_public_2 and session_private_2) and session_private_2 is paired with attacker_cfg_public (the public key embedded within the configuration) to generate a shared key.
sentence.12818: This shared key is then hashed with the SHA3 hashing algorithm.
sentence.12819: The resulting hash is used as an AES key with a random 16-byte initialization vector (IV) for encrypting a data blob consisting of four null bytes followed by session_private_1. Figure 8.
sentence.12820: Diagram of session secret generation procedure.
sentence.12821: From there, the encrypted blob is hashed using CRC-32, and then appended with the values session_public_2, the AES IV, and the calculated CRC-32 hash.
sentence.12823: The second generated session secret follows the exact same procedure; however, instead of using attacker_cfg_public, it utilizes an embedded public key (attacker_embedded_public_1) within the binary to generate the shared key. Figure 9.
sentence.12825: One final embedded public key (attacker_embedded_public_2) is used to encrypt the data formatted into the JSON structure described above.
sentence.12826: This method of generating session secrets was documented by researchers at Amossys back in 2020; however, their analysis focused on an updated version of Sodinokibi/REvil ransomware, indicating a direct overlap between the REvil source code and the latest Ransom Cartel samples.
sentence.12827: Once the session secrets have been generated, they are written to the registry, alongside session_public_1 and attacker_cfg_public.
sentence.12828: Path Name Value SOFTWARE\\Google_Authenticator\\ WRZfsL attacker_cfg_public SOFTWARE\\Google_Authenticator\\ RB4y session_public_1 SOFTWARE\\Google_Authenticator\\ Kbcn0 session_secret_1 SOFTWARE\\Google_Authenticator\\ BSjHn session_secret_2 Table 8.
sentence.12829: Registry paths and values used by Ransom Cartel.
sentence.12830: At this point, all the required information is gathered and generated so that file encryption can begin.
sentence.12831: For each file, a unique file public and private key pair are generated (file_public_1 and file_private_1), once again using Curve25519 Donna.
sentence.12832: file_private_1 and session_public_1 are paired together to generate a shared key, which is hashed using SHA3.
sentence.12833: The generated hash is used as the encryption key for Salsa20 (a symmetric encryption algorithm), and a random eight-byte nonce is generated using CryptGenRandom.
sentence.12834: The CRC-32 hash of file_public_1 is calculated, and then four null bytes are encrypted using the generated Salsa20 matrix.
sentence.12835: Certain elements of the above data are then retained and used as part of the encrypted file footer; each file footer is 232 bytes in length and is made up of the following:
sentence.12839: crc_file_public_1 (four bytes) encryption_type (four bytes) block_spacing (four bytes) encrypted_null (four bytes)
sentence.12840: Similarly to the session_secret generation, this structure is identical to that of the REvil samples analyzed by Amossys, further showing that there have been very few changes to the REvil source code when developing Ransom Cartel samples.
sentence.12843: Ransom Cartel and REvil Code Comparison The Ransom Cartel samples analyzed revealed similarities with REvil ransomware.
sentence.12844: The first notable similarity between Ransom Cartel and REvil is the structure of the configuration.
sentence.12845: Examining a sample of REvil from 2019 (SHA256: 6a2bd52a5d68a7250d1de481dcce91a32f54824c1c540f0a040d05f757220cd3), the resemblance can be seen.
sentence.12846: However, the storage of the encrypted configuration is slightly different, opting to store the configuration in a separate section within the binary (.ycpc19), with an initial 32-byte RC4 key followed by the raw encrypted configuration, whereas with the Ransom Cartel samples, the configuration is stored within the .data section as a base64-encoded blob.
sentence.12849: Once the REvil configuration has decrypted, it utilizes the same JSON format, but contains additional values such as pid, sub, fast, wipe and dmn.
sentence.12850: These values indicate additional functionality within the REvil sample, which could mean that either the Ransom Cartel developers removed certain functionality or they are building off of a much earlier version of REvil.
sentence.12853: As discussed previously, another major overlap is the code reuse across the two samples of Ransom Cartel.
sentence.12854: Both use an identical encryption scheme, generating multiple public/private key pairs, and creating session secrets using the same procedure found within REvil samples. Figure 13.
sentence.12856: Both use Salsa20 and Curve25519 for file encryption, and there are very few differences in the layout of the encryption routine besides the structure of the internal type structs.
sentence.12859: A particularly interesting difference between the two malware families is that REvil opts to obfuscate their ransomware much more heavily than the Ransom Cartel group, utilizing string encryption, API hashing and more, while Ransom Cartel has almost no obfuscation outside of the configuration, hinting that the group may not possess the obfuscation engine used by REvil.
sentence.12860: It is possible that the Ransom Cartel group is an offshoot of the original REvil threat actor group, where the individuals only possess the original source code of the REvil ransomware encryptor/decryptor, but do not have access to the obfuscation engine.

sentence.12925: Conclusion Ransom Cartel is one of many ransomware families that surfaced during 2021.
sentence.12926: While Ransom Cartel uses double extortion and some of the same TTPs we often observe during ransomware attacks, this type of ransomware uses less common tools – DonPAPI for example – that we haven’t observed in any other ransomware attacks.
sentence.12927: Based on the fact that the Ransom Cartel operators clearly have access to the original REvil ransomware source code, yet likely do not possess the obfuscation engine used to encrypt strings and hide API calls, we speculate that the operators of Ransom Cartel had a relationship with the REvil group at one point, before starting their own operation.

sentence.12945: title: Malicious ISO File Leads to Domain Wide Ransomware -
sentence.12946: The DFIR Report url: https://thedfirreport.com/2023/04/03/malicious-iso-file-leads-to-domain-wide-ransomware/ IcedID continues to deliver malspam emails to facilitate a compromise.
sentence.12947: This case covers the activity from a campaign in late September of 2022.
sentence.12948: Post exploitation activities detail some familiar and some new techniques and tooling, which led to domain wide ransomware.
sentence.12949: This case shares similarities of the IcedID campaign detailed by Malware-Traffic-Analysis.net, where the ADGet.exe application was referenced.
sentence.12950: This intrusion began by the execution of IcedID malware contained within an ISO image.
sentence.12951: The ISO file was delivered to the victim as part of a malspam campaign.
sentence.12952: Delivering payloads using an ISO image is a common technique observed in several prior cases.
sentence.12953: This technique has grown in use as threat actors look to evade Mark-of-the-Web controls.
sentence.12954: The ISO image delivered a hidden directory containing a IcedID payload and a batch file.
sentence.12955: After being successfully mounted, the end user only sees a malicious LNK file named documents inside the virtual hard drive.
sentence.12956: Clicking on the LNK file executes the batch file, which copies the IcedID payload to the user’s AppData\Local\Temp folder and loads it using rundll32.
sentence.12957: A scheduled task was created at that time to maintain persistence on this host as well.
sentence.12958: Upon the execution of the IcedID payload, discovery commands using Windows utilities such as net, nltest, and ipconfig were executed to discover domain trusts, domain admins, workstation configuration, etc.
sentence.12959: Around 16 hours after the initial execution, the first Cobalt Strike beacon DLL rapuab1.dll was executed from the IcedID malware.
sentence.12960: This led to another round of discovery using net followed by AdFind.
sentence.12961: The threat actor installed Atera and Splashtop remote access software via an MSI file named hp.msi.
sentence.12962: After that, the threat actors tried a GetSystem privilege escalation technique, which was blocked by antivirus.
sentence.12963: The threat actor then proceeded to exploit CVE-2020-1472, aka ZeroLogon.
sentence.12964: This was followed by a batch script used to perform DNS lookups on hosts across the environment.
sentence.12965: After this, the threat actors began their first lateral movement to a server in the environment by copying their Cobalt Strike DLL over to the host and executing it via a remote service.
sentence.12966: They then repeated the install of the remote access software package.
sentence.12967: Some two hours later, a Cobalt Strike beacon named Nigu.exe was executed.
sentence.12968: With this beacon, the threat actors succeeded in elevating to SYSTEM on the beachhead host and proceeded to dump LSASS memory.
sentence.12969: Another round of activity took place using system tools, batch files, and Adget.
sentence.12970: Several more beacons were also loaded on the host using DLLs and PowerShell.
sentence.12971: At this point, the threat actors had the clear text credentials for one of the domain administrator accounts and began moving lateral to other systems.
sentence.12972: They issued remote commands using WMIC to conduct discovery, as well as distribute and execute Cobalt Strike beacons.
sentence.12973: These actions, however, failed to get a beacon to launch on the domain controller being targeted.
sentence.12974: After an hour or so of failures, the threat actors proceeded to RDP to the domain controller.
sentence.12975: Once there, they then loaded textbin[.]net, a pastebin style site, to download Cobalt Strike PowerShell code to the host in a file named pon.txt. Trying to execute this locally failed as well, and the threat actor moved on to downloading a variety of beacon executables (e.g. lsass.exe, lsasss.exe, etc.).
sentence.12976: These beacons, however, continued to crash and fail to run.
sentence.12977: Around an hour after starting the RDP session, the threat actors executed a PowerShell command to disable Windows Defender Antivirus on the host and reviewed Group Policy Objects for the domain.
sentence.12978: The Cobalt Strike beacons then began to execute successfully on the domain controller.
sentence.12979: Now, with Cobalt Strike beacons on the domain controller, the threat actors continued with discovery actions using Invoke-ShareFinder and other PowerShell and system utilities.
sentence.12980: A few hours later, the threat actors installed the RSAT tools onto the beachhead host.
sentence.12981: However, they appear to have been unfamiliar with the tools and called up the help menu before using Get-ADComputer to collect the details on hosts in the environment.
sentence.12982: Back on the domain controller, ProcDump was used to dump LSASS memory.
sentence.12983: The PowerShell command Get-EventLog was then used to collect logon events on all domain administrators in the network.
sentence.12984: The threat actors went quiet for around seven hours.
sentence.12985: When they returned, several more Cobalt Strike beacons were launched and several different Mimikatz implementations were executed on the domain controller, including a Mimikatz executable and a PowerShell implementation.
sentence.12986: For the next several hours, repeats of previous discovery actions and additional beacons executed using remote WMIC commands, were observed.
sentence.12987: During this time, Windows event logs point to the threat actors completing DCSync activities on one of the domain controllers.
sentence.12988: A new batch file, localdisk.bat, was also executed using remote WMI commands, to collect disk data on hosts around the environment.
sentence.12989: These discovery actions were completed several times again in other various batch files.
sentence.12990: On the start of the fourth day, the threat actors continued to repeat their previous discovery and beacon spreading activity.
sentence.12991: Near the end of the day, the threat actors moved to install AnyDesk on several servers including a backup management host, likely as a further means of persistence or later command and control.
sentence.12992: Next, the threat actor executed PowerShell to pop up an alert message on several hosts, letting the user know that the machine was infected with Cobalt Strike.
sentence.12993: After completing this activity, they used Rclone to exfiltrate copies of the backup files to the Mega.io cloud storage service.
sentence.12994: The threat actors then staged a ransomware binary named locker_64.exe on the backup server but did not immediately execute it.
sentence.12995: Around two hours after dropping the file, it was executed using a command line argument, which included a list of hosts to target.
sentence.12997: The threat actors then proceeded to execute the payload manually in several ways, across various hosts.
sentence.12998: Finally, they connected to a domain controller and dropped three scripts; one to copy the ransomware executable to all hosts, one to reset every users password in the organization, and a final one to execute the staged ransomware payload using PsExec.
sentence.12999: Once executed, the ransomware left the ransom note README_TO_DECRYPT.html, which informs the victim that Quantum ransomware is responsible for the intrusion.
sentence.13000: The time to ransomware was just over 78 hours from the initial IcedID infection.
sentence.13001: All domain joined systems were encrypted with Quantum ransomware.

sentence.13008: This intrusion began by the execution of a malicious LNK embedded in an ISO file (masquerading as a folder).

sentence.13010: Malicious ISO file First, the user clicked on the ISO file, which created a new virtual hard drive disk.
sentence.13011: Such activity can be tracked with Event 12 from Microsoft-Windows-VHDMP/Operational.
sentence.13012: This ISO file contains a LNK named documents and a hidden directory named max containing a cobalt strike DLL beacon and a batch file.
sentence.13013: As we can see below using LECmd from Eric Zimmerman, the file documents.lnk points to max\eyewear.bat. As a consequence, when the victim clicked on the LNK file, it triggered the execution of the batch file eyewear.bat The batch file eyewear.bat then executed two commands: It first moved a DLL file named eyewear.dat, initially located in a hidden folder named max, to the user’s AppData\Local\Temp\ folder : C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c
sentence.13017: Then, DLL was executed using rundll32.exe : C:\Windows\system32\cmd.exe /c

sentence.13019: After beginning to move laterally, the threat actors used many other execution techniques such as PowerShell and executables run from their interactive RDP session in addition to DLLs.
sentence.13020: A number of application crashes were observed across several compromised hosts.
sentence.13021: This activity was a result of the threat actors attempting to execute various dropped tools or beacons on the endpoint, triggering a Windows Error Reporting (WER) fault process.
sentence.13022: Application crashes are recorded in the Windows Application event log under Event ID 1000 and 1001.
sentence.13023: The NSA Cyber Windows Event Monitoring Guidance, has the following statement: Application crashes may warrant investigation to determine if the crash is malicious or benign.

sentence.13042: This is a common technique used by threat actors, and implemented by the GetSystemCobalt Strike command.

sentence.13049: The beacon creates the named pipe (seen in Sysmon EventID 17) and impersonates the NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM account used to connect to the pipe.
sentence.13050: The MITRE Cyber Analytics Repository (CAR) details the Get System elevation, CAR-2021-02-002: Get System Elevation Winlogon Token Impersonation/Theft Multiple access to WinLogon with granted access 0x40
sentence.13052: Such access can be tracked with Sysmon event ID 10 (ProcessAccess).
sentence.13053: As explained in this blog written by Jonathan JOHNSON, opening a handle to WinLogon in order to duplicate the token and call ImpersonateLoggedOnUser is a known Cobalt Strike technique.
sentence.13054: ZeroLogon On the second day of the intrusion, a spike in NetLogon traffic was observed from the beachhead host to a domain controller.
sentence.13055: This traffic then triggered several network signatures for CVE-2020-1472 otherwise known as ZeroLogon.

sentence.13058: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass The threat actors delivered the initial malware as a zip file, with the contents of a ISO file, which contained their payload to gain access to the target environment.
sentence.13059: These packages are designed to evade controls such as Mark-of-the-Web restrictions.

sentence.13157: ADGet : An uncommon tool An Active Directory collection tool called ADGet was dropped into a user’s temp folder and executed with an output filename argument.
sentence.13158: No file meta data is provided.
sentence.13159: Its a simple to use tool, the application is invoked from the command line and passes an output file name to save enumerated AD objects.
sentence.13160: ADGet is an uncommon tool, however, its function is very similar to ADfind–the key difference is that LDAP queries are not passed, they are instead coded into the binary itself.
sentence.13161: The AD objects will be enumerated generating a zip output file containing the following TSV (tab separated files) files if using a default configuration: These files can be viewed with any editor or reader that supports CSV or TSV.

sentence.13264: title: SeroXen RAT for sale url: https://www.cybersecurity-insiders.com/seroxen-rat-for-sale/ This blog was jointly written with Alejandro Prada and Ofer Caspi.
sentence.13265: Executive summary SeroXen is a new Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that showed up in late 2022 and is becoming more popular in 2023.
sentence.13266: Advertised as a legitimate tool that gives access to your computers undetected, it is being sold for only $30 for a monthly license or $60 for a lifetime bundle, making it accessible.
sentence.13267: Key takeaways: SeroXen is a fileless RAT, performing well at evading detections on static and dynamic analysis.
sentence.13268: The malware combines several open-source projects to improve its capabilities.
sentence.13269: It is a combination of Quasar RAT, r77-rootkit and the command line NirCmd.
sentence.13270: Hundreds of samples have shown up since its creation, being most popular in the gaming community.
sentence.13271: It is only a matter of time before it is used to target companies instead of individual users.
sentence.13272: Analysis Quasar RAT is a legitimate open-source remote administration tool.
sentence.13273: It is offered on github page to provide user support or employee monitoring.
sentence.13274: It has been historically associated with malicious activity performed by threat actors, APT groups (like in this Mandiant report from 2017), or government attacks (in this report by Unit42 in 2017).
sentence.13275: It was first released in July 2014 as “xRAT” and renamed to “Quasar” in August 2015.
sentence.13276: Since then, there have been released updates to the code until v1.4.1 in March 2023, which is the most current version.
sentence.13277: As an open-source RAT tool with updates 9 years after its creation, it is no surprise that it continues to be a common tool used by itself or combined with other payloads by threat actors up to this day.
sentence.13278: In a review of the most recent samples, a new Quasar variant was observed by Alien Labs in the wild: SeroXen.
sentence.13279: This new RAT is a modified branch of the open-source version, adding some modifications features to the original RAT.
sentence.13280: They’re selling it for monthly or lifetime fee.
sentence.13281: Figure 1 contains some of the features advertised on their website.
sentence.13283: SeroXen features announced on its website.
sentence.13284: This new RAT first showed up on a Twitter account, established in September 2022.
sentence.13285: The person advertising the RAT appeared to be an English-speaking teenager.
sentence.13286: The same Twitter handle published a review of the RAT on YouTube.
sentence.13287: The video approached the review from an attacking/Red Team point of view, encouraging people to buy the tool because it is worth the money.
sentence.13288: They were claiming to be a reseller of the tool.
sentence.13289: In December 2022, a specific domain was registered to market/sell the tool, seroxen[.]com.
sentence.13290: The RAT was distributed via a monthly license for $30 USD or a lifetime license of $60 USD.
sentence.13291: It was around that time that the malware was first observed in the wild, appearing with 0 detections on VirusTotal.
sentence.13292: After a few months, on the 1st of February, the YouTuber CyberSec Zaado published a video alerting the community about the capabilities of the RAT from a defensive perspective.
sentence.13293: In late February, the RAT was advertised on social media platforms such as TikTok, Twitter, YouTube, and several cracking forums, including hackforums.
sentence.13294: There were some conversations on gaming forums complaining about being infected by malware after downloading some video games.
sentence.13295: The artifacts described by the users matched with SeroXen RAT.
sentence.13296: The threat actor updated the domain name to seroxen[.]net by the end of March.
sentence.13297: This domain name was registered on March 27th, 2023, after seroxen[.]com was decommissioned.
sentence.13298: The threat actor used GoDaddy for registration and Cloudflare for hosting the website.
sentence.13299: These domains are only used for selling and marketing purposes, and not for Command and Control (C&C) communications.
sentence.13300: Figure 2: SeroXen website Based on the packed versions uploaded to VT, it appears that the RAT is being used for targeting video game users.
sentence.13301: Several lure injector cheat files have been observed with names invoking popular videogames such as Fortnite, Valorant, Roblox or Warzone2.
sentence.13302: The threat actor used Discord for the distribution of some of the samples. Figure 3.
sentence.13304: One of the most relevant announced features is that it is a fully undetectable version.
sentence.13305: This is currently true from a static analysis point of view, since the RAT is packaged into an obfuscated PowerShell batch file.
sentence.13306: The file’s size typically ranges between 12-14 megabytes, as we can see in sample 8ace121fae472cc7ce896c91a3f1743d5ccc8a389bc3152578c4782171c69e87 uploaded to VT on May 21.
sentence.13307: Due to its relatively large size, certain antivirus may choose not to analyze it, potentially bypassing detection.
sentence.13308: This sample currently has 0 detections on VT, but some of the crowdsourced Sigma Rules do detect the activity as suspicious.
sentence.13309: As the malware is fileless and executed only in memory after going through several decryptions and decompression routines, it is more difficult to detect by antiviruses.
sentence.13310: In addition, its rootkit loads a fresh copy of ntdll.dll, which makes it harder to detect by Endpoint Detection & Response (EDR) solutions that hook into it to detect process injections.
sentence.13311: Regarding the dynamic analysis, it is worth noting that some sandbox environments might fail to detect the RAT due to its utilization of several techniques to evade virtualization and sandbox detection mechanisms and string encryption subsequent payloads.
sentence.13312: The RAT employs anti-debugging techniques by leveraging Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to identify the system’s manufacturer.
sentence.13313: This enables it to identify virtualization environments such as VMware and abort the execution to delay and make the analysis harder.
sentence.13314: The RAT also checks for the presence of debuggers and uses pings make the threads sleep.
sentence.13315: Currently, most child processes and files dropped during the execution of the RAT have a low detection rate.
sentence.13316: Execution analysis When the malicious payload is delivered to the victim, commonly through a phishing mail or a Discord channel – the victim often receives a ZIP file containing a benign file in plain sight, and the heavily obfuscated batch file is hidden and automatically executed when launched.
sentence.13317: The bat file format is always very similar and looks like the contents of Figure 4, followed by base64 encoded text later in the file.
sentence.13320: During the bat execution, the script extracts two separate binaries from the base64 encoded text, AES decrypts, and GZIP decompresses it to produce two separate byte arrays.
sentence.13321: These byte arrays are then used with .NET reflection to perform an in-memory load of the assembly from its bytes, locate the binary’s entry point, and perform an Invoke on both.
sentence.13322: Throughout the decryption process, the attackers had the need to create a legitimate looking folder to drop an illicit version of the System Configuration Utility msconfig.exe that is required later.
sentence.13323: For this purpose, the script creates the folder “C:Windows System32”, with a space after Windows and deletes it as soon as the utility is running.
sentence.13324: If it wasn’t for this file temporarily dropped into disk, the RAT would be fully fileless.
sentence.13325: The execution of one of the above-mentioned binaries leads to another obfuscated binary carrying an embedded resource.
sentence.13326: This resource is hidden behind anti-sandboxing and debugger techniques, only to lead to more obfuscation and encryption techniques that lead to the final payload.
sentence.13327: This payload has been built using the Github project Costura, which allows SeroXen to pack the code’s dependencies into the .NET assembly so it can run self-contained.
sentence.13330: The extraction of the resources leads to the final payloads.
sentence.13331: This is in the form of two .NET assemblies: CSStub2.InstallStager.exe, and CSStub2.UninstallStager.exe.
sentence.13332: And a Win32 binary called CSStub2.$sxr-nircmd.exe, which corresponds to the unmodified command-line utility NirCmd.
sentence.13333: The payload InstallStager.exe is a compilation of the open-source rootkit named r77-rootkit – a fileless ring 3 rootkit written in .NET.
sentence.13334: This rootkit supports both x32 and x64 Windows processes and has the following features: Fileless persistence: The rootkit is stored as obfuscated data in the registry and is spawned with PowerShell via Task Scheduler to be injected into the winlogon.exe process.
sentence.13336: Option to embed additional malware to be executed with the rootkit – in this case NirCmd and/or Quasar.
sentence.13337: The added malware will be decompressed and decrypted before it is injected into other processes.
sentence.13338: In memory process injection: the rootkit injects itself and additional malware(s) into all processes.
sentence.13339: Injection is done from memory: no files are needed to be stored on disk.
sentence.13340: Hooking: Hooks several functions from ntdll.dll to hide its presence.
sentence.13342: The rootkit can receive a command from any running process.
sentence.13344: The rootkit uses several evasion techniques: AMSI bypass: PowerShell inline script patches “amsi.dll!AmsiScanBuffer” to always return “AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN”.
sentence.13345: DLL unhooking: Removes EDR hooks by loading a fresh copy of “ntdll.dll” from disk to avoid process hollowing detection Hiding entities: Hiding all entities starts with a configurable prefix, which in SeroXen’s case its “$sxr”.
sentence.13346: This prefix hardens the visualization of the attack on the system, but eases attribution of the malware family during the analysis.
sentence.13347: The prefix is used to hide files, directories, NamedPipes, scheduled tasks, processes, registry keys/values, and services.
sentence.13348: R77 technical documentation provides a guideline of where can the prefix be found: Config parameter Details Example HIDE_PREFIX The prefix for name-based hiding (e.g. processes, files, etc…).
sentence.13349: L”$sxr” R77_SERVICE_NAME32 Name for the scheduled task that starts the r77 service for 32-bit processes.
sentence.13350: HIDE_PREFIX L”svc32″ R77_SERVICE_NAME64 Name for the scheduled task that starts the r77 service for 64-bit processes.
sentence.13351: HIDE_PREFIX L”svc64″ CHILD_PROCESS_PIPE_NAME32 Name for the named pipe that notifies the 32-bit r77 service about new child processes.
sentence.13352: L”.pipe” HIDE_PREFIX L”childproc32″ CHILD_PROCESS_PIPE_NAME64 Name for the named pipe that notifies the 64-bit r77 service about new child processes.
sentence.13353: L”.pipe” HIDE_PREFIX L”childproc64″ CONTROL_PIPE_NAME Name for the named pipe that receives commands from external processes.
sentence.13354: L”.pipe” HIDE_PREFIX L”control” The two main components in this project are the InstallStager service and the Rootkit.
sentence.13355: The InstallStager service is responsible for: Creating a registry key to store the malware code and writes it as encrypted data.
sentence.13356: Creating a scheduled task to execute the malware using PowerShell.
sentence.13357: PowerShell will decompress and decrypt the final payload (Service) that will be injected into the winlogon.exe process and executed via dllhost.exe using process hollowing techniques.
sentence.13359: Starting payload after decryption using process hollowing.
sentence.13360: Now the second and main stage of the Rootkit is ready to start.
sentence.13361: The service kicks off the load of the rootkit’s DLL that is embedded as a resource and saves its configuration as a registry key.
sentence.13364: The service creates 3 listener threads: NewProcessListener: Enumerates all running processes and injects the rootkit when new processes are created.
sentence.13365: ChildProcessListener: Injects the rootkit to a newly created process by another process and updates the callee via NamedPipe. Figure 7.
sentence.13367: ControlPipeListener: Creates a NamedPipe to receive commands from any process.
sentence.13368: Supported commands are listed below: Command Details CONTROL_R77_UNINSTALL The control code that uninstalls r77.
sentence.13370: The control code that temporarily pauses injection of new processes.
sentence.13371: CONTROL_R77_RESUME_INJECTION The control code that resumes injection of new processes.
sentence.13372: CONTROL_PROCESSES_INJECT The control code that injects r77 into a specific process, if it is not yet injected. CONTROL_PROCESSES_INJECT_ALL
sentence.13373: The control code that injects r77 into all processes that are not yet injected.
sentence.13374: CONTROL_PROCESSES_DETACH The control code detaches r77 from a specific process.
sentence.13376: The control code detaches r77 from all processes.
sentence.13378: The control code that executes a file using ShellExecute.
sentence.13379: CONTROL_USER_RUNPE The control code that executes an executable using process hollowing.
sentence.13380: CONTROL_SYSTEM_BSOD The control code that triggers a BSOD.
sentence.13381: CONTROL_R77_TERMINATE_SERVICE The control code that terminates the r77 service.

sentence.13387: Since Seroxen is based on QuasarRAT, the C&C server utilizes the same Common Name in their TLS certificate.
sentence.13388: The functionalities offered by the threat actor for the C&C server closely mirror those found in the Quasar Github repository, including support for TCP network streams (both IPv4 and IPv6), efficient network serialization, compression using QuickLZ, and secure communication through TLS encryption. sentence.13390: Conclusion The SeroXen developer has found a formidable combination of free resources to develop a hard to detect in static and dynamic analysis RAT.

sentence.13392: While the combination of NirCMD and r77-rootkit are logical additions to the mix, since they make the tool more elusive and harder to detect.
sentence.13393: The Alien Labs team will continue to monitor the threat landscape for SeroXen samples and infrastructure.
