sentence.13419: title: A lookback under the TA410 umbrella: Its cyberespionage TTPs and activity url: https://www.welivesecurity.com/2022/04/27/lookback-ta410-umbrella-cyberespionage-ttps-activity/ ESET researchers reveal a detailed profile of TA410: we believe this cyberespionage umbrella group consists of three different teams using different toolsets, including a new version of the FlowCloud espionage backdoor discovered by ESET.
sentence.13420: ESET researchers have documented and analyzed TA410 activity going back to 2019.
sentence.13421: TA410 is a cyberespionage umbrella group loosely linked to APT10, known mostly for targeting US-based organizations in the utilities sector, and diplomatic organizations in the Middle East and Africa.
sentence.13422: TA410 has been active since at least 2018 and was first publicly revealed in August 2019 by Proofpoint in its LookBack blogpost.
sentence.13423: A year later, the then-new and very complex malware family called FlowCloud was also attributed to TA410.
sentence.13424: In this blogpost, we provide a detailed profile of this APT group, including its modus operandi and toolset that includes a new version of FlowCloud, discovered by ESET.
sentence.13425: This very complex backdoor contains interesting espionage capabilities.
sentence.13426: ESET will present its latest findings about TA410, including results from ongoing research, during Botconf 2022.
sentence.13427: For YARA and Snort rules, consult ESET’s GitHub account.
sentence.13428: Key points in this blogpost: TA410 is an umbrella group comprised of three teams ESET researchers named FlowingFrog, LookingFrog and JollyFrog, each with its own toolset and targets.
sentence.13429: ESET telemetry shows victims all around the world, mainly in the governmental and education sectors.
sentence.13430: TA410 had access to the most recent known Microsoft Exchange remote code execution vulnerabilities, e.g., ProxyLogon in March 2021 and ProxyShell in August 2021.
sentence.13431: ESET researchers found a new version of FlowCloud, a complex and modular C++ RAT.
sentence.13432: It has several interesting capabilities, including: Controlling connected microphones and triggering recording when sound levels above a specified threshold volume are detected.
sentence.13433: Monitoring clipboard events to steal clipboard content.
sentence.13434: Monitoring file system events to collect new and modified files.
sentence.13435: Controlling attached camera devices to take pictures of the compromised computer’s surroundings.
sentence.13436: FlowCloud deploys a rootkit to hide its activity on the compromised machine.
sentence.13437: The LookBack backdoor utilized by TA410 uses a custom network protocol, which can function over HTTP or raw TCP, for C&C server communications.
sentence.13438: TA410 is one of the users of the Royal Road malicious document builder.
sentence.13439: TA410 teams compromise their targets in various ways, which indicates to us that those victims are targeted specifically, with the attackers choosing which entry method has the best chance of infiltrating the target.
sentence.13440: The first stage of the FlowCloud version identified by ESET researchers can check whether specific security software is installed on the machine it tries to compromise, but this isn’t implemented in the loaders we analyzed.
sentence.13441: However, we found a custom AntivirusCheck class, which can check running processes against a hardcoded list of executable filenames from known security products, including ESET products.
sentence.13442: In case one of these products is detected, FlowCloud goes through its regular loading process and cancels the auto_start_after_install configuration value.
sentence.13443: Even though we believe that this version of FlowCloud is still undergoing development and testing, the cyberespionage capabilities of this version include the ability to collect mouse movements, keyboard activity, and clipboard content along with information about the current foreground window.
sentence.13444: This information can help attackers understand stolen data by contextualizing it.
sentence.13445: FlowCloud can also gather information about things happening around the victim’s computer by taking pictures using connected camera peripherals and recording audio using a computer’s microphone.
sentence.13446: This latter function is triggered by any sound over a threshold of 65 decibels, which is in the upper range of normal conversation volume.
sentence.13447: Attribution ESET researchers believe that TA410 is composed of three different teams, using very similar tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) but different toolsets and exiting from IP addresses located in three different districts.
sentence.13448: These teams, referred to below as FlowingFrog, LookingFrog, and JollyFrog, have overlaps in TTPs, victimology and network infrastructure.
sentence.13449: FlowingFrog uses Royal Road RTF documents, a first-stage implant called Tendyron, and a very complex second-stage backdoor called FlowCloud.
sentence.13450: LookingFrog uses a first-stage backdoor called X4, and LookBack as a second stage.
sentence.13451: JollyFrog uses only generic malware families such as Korplug (aka PlugX) and QuasarRAT.
sentence.13452: Part of the activity of this team was described by Fortinet, who attributed the activity to APT10. ESET researchers, however, believe this activity is different from the operations that APT10 (aka A41APT) has conducted recently.
sentence.13453: FlowingFrog and JollyFrog share network infrastructure – more precisely, the domain ffca.caibi379[.]com, as mentioned by Proofpoint.
sentence.13454: FlowingFrog and LookingFrog ran a phishing campaign at the same time against the same targets, as also mentioned in the same Proofpoint article.
sentence.13455: In ESET telemetry, we do not see any other overlap between these subgroups.
sentence.13456: We believe that these subgroups operate somewhat independently but that they may share intelligence requirements, an access team that runs their spearphishing campaigns, and also the team that deploys network infrastructure.
sentence.13457: Victimology Most TA410 targets are high-profile organizations in the diplomacy and education sectors, but we have also seen victims in the military sector, a manufacturing company in Japan, a mining company in India, and a charity in Israel.
sentence.13458: According to ESET telemetry, the victims are located in Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.
sentence.13459: Interestingly, there is no clear segmentation of the targeting (by sector or geography) among the different teams.
sentence.13460: An element worth mentioning is that TA410 targets foreign individuals in China.
sentence.13461: In ESET telemetry, we have observed this as having happened at least twice: for instance, one victim is a French academic, and another is a member of a diplomatic mission of a South Asian country in China.
sentence.13462: Since 2018, we have seen the following targets, also depicted in Figure 1: FlowingFrog: University, foreign diplomatic mission of a South Asian country in China, mining company LookingFrog: Diplomatic missions, charity, government and industrial manufacturing JollyFrog: Education, church, military, diplomatic mission Figure 1.
sentence.13463: Map of countries and verticals targeted by TA410 Initial compromise and typical TTPs If we exclude the different backdoors, the three teams use a similar modus operandi.
sentence.13464: They compromise their targets either by spearphishing, according to Proofpoint, or, for LookingFrog and JollyFrog, by compromising a web-facing application such as Microsoft Exchange or SharePoint.
sentence.13465: This could indicate that victims are targeted specifically, with the attackers choosing which entry method is the best for a given target.
sentence.13466: The public-facing application compromise approach is what we have seen the most.
sentence.13467: Attackers linked to LookingFrog exploited Microsoft SharePoint servers in 2019 to gain code execution, probably by leveraging CVE-2019-0604.
sentence.13468: They then dropped an ASPX webshell that was used to install other malicious components.
sentence.13469: These were either dropped directly via the webshell or downloaded from a remote server using certutil.exe, a known LOLBin.
sentence.13470: In 2020, we saw further exploitations by JollyFrog, of Microsoft SQL servers and IIS servers running custom applications.
sentence.13471: In August 2021, we observed LookBack being loaded by an IIS worker process on a server belonging to an industrial manufacturing company in Japan.
sentence.13472: This happened following the exploitation of the Exchange ProxyShell vulnerability on that server, as we describe in ESET Threat Report T3 2021.
sentence.13473: This shows that LookingFrog operators closely follow the discovery of RCE vulnerabilities in popular server applications and quickly make use of any available exploit in order to gain control of unpatched servers run by organizations on their target lists.
sentence.13474: In addition to the full-featured backdoors analyzed in the following sections, these attackers use a variety of tools such as vulnerability scanners, exploits from the Equation Group leaks, proxy/tunneling utilities (HTran, LCX, EarthWorm), and lateral movement scripts such as WMIExec. Arsenal TA410 – FlowingFrog FlowingFrog uses a first stage that ESET researchers have named the Tendyron downloader, and a complex second stage named FlowCloud, so named by the developers in its modules’ PDB paths.
sentence.13475: Royal Road and Tendyron downloader Royal Road is a malicious document builder used by several cyberespionage groups (see the analysis by nao_sec).
sentence.13476: Files built with this tool are RTF documents exploiting Equation Editor N-day vulnerabilities such as CVE-2017-11882.
sentence.13477: TA410 operators always use the Royal Road encoding bytes: A9 A4 6E FE, as seen in Figure 2. Figure 2.
sentence.13478: Encoded Royal Road payload On October 13th 2020, we noticed that a new Royal Road RTF document, shown in Figure 3, had been uploaded to VirusTotal.
sentence.13480: Royal Road RTF document found on VirusTotal (SHA‑1: ADD5B4FD9AEA6A38B5A8941286BC9AA4FE23BD20)
sentence.13481: When opened, the document triggers the injection of a custom downloader – a PE executable – into an iexplore.exe process.
sentence.13482: The PE resources 103, 104 and 105 contain the payload URLs, XORed with 0xD3.
sentence.13483: The following files are downloaded and written to disk: http://103.139.2[.]93:1702/tdr.dat written to %localappdata%\Tendyron\Tendyron.exe (SHA-1: 09C76522136B5E9BAB74381FEEE265F7E9B1D550) http://103.139.2[.]93:1702/okt.dat written to %localappdata%\Tendyron\OnKeyToken_KEB.dll (SHA‑1: F359D3C074135BBCA9A4C98A6B6544690EDAE93D) http://103.139.2[.]93:1702/md.dat written to %localappdata%\Tendyron\Tendyron.conf (we were not able to retrieve this file)
sentence.13484: Finally, this process separately downloads http://103.139.2[.]93:1702/t86.dat (resource 101), loads it into memory, and calls its startModule export.
sentence.13485: Unfortunately, we were not able to retrieve this sample.
sentence.13486: Tendyron.exe is a legitimate executable, signed by online-banking security vendor Tendyron Corporation, and that is vulnerable to DLL search-order hijacking.
sentence.13487: Persistence for the downloaded payload is established via the Tendyron value under the Run key HKCU\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run.
sentence.13488: When executed, Tendyron.exe loads the malicious OnKeyToken_KEB.dll.
sentence.13489: The export OnKeyT_ContextInit contains code that decrypts hardcoded shellcode (see Figure 4) and injects it into iexplore.exe using WriteProcessMemory.
sentence.13491: Shellcode decryption loop The next stage, injected into iexplore.exe, is a backdoor written using the Microsoft Foundation Class (MFC) framework.
sentence.13492: It also contains RTTI symbols and thus a few C++ class names: ClientSocket Manager DllManager KernelManager These class names are the same as used in Farfli/Gh0stRAT, a backdoor that has been used for more than 10 years to conduct (mostly) cyberespionage operations.
sentence.13493: Its source code was leaked and is now available on GitHub.
sentence.13494: Thus, we believe that TA410 developers reused code copied from Farfli.
sentence.13495: The C&C server is hardcoded, in cleartext, in the sample; in this specific case, it is set to 114.118.83[.]141.
sentence.13496: On VirusTotal, as shown in Figure 5, we can see one more HTTP request to 103.139.2[.]93 was triggered during the execution of the RTF file.
sentence.13497: The result of the request to http://103.139.2[.]93:1702/SL3716/S8437AEB.DAT was recorded by VirusTotal and the SHA-1 of this encrypted file is 140F81037A76B7B16A00E1D5E0E2CD9F6687F642.
sentence.13498: This URI is typical of those used to download FlowCloud, a complex C++ implant described in the next section.
sentence.13499: Figure 5. URL requests seen by the VirusTotal sandbox during execution of the malicious RTF document
sentence.13500: The identical encrypted file was also downloaded from http://114.55.109[.]199:56022/SL3716/S8437AEB.DAT by a FlowCloud dropper version 4.1.3 (SHA‑1: 014421BDB1EA105A6DF0C27FC114819FF3637704).
sentence.13501: A summary of the compromise chain is provided in Figure 6. Figure 6.
sentence.13502: Compromise chain from the Royal Road document to FlowCloud FlowCloud FlowCloud is a complex implant written in C++.
sentence.13503: It consists of three main components, deployed in a multistage process that uses various obfuscation and encryption techniques to hinder analysis.
sentence.13504: Multiple versions of FlowCloud have been identified since 2020, most notably versions 4.1.3 and 5.0.1 described by Proofpoint.
sentence.13505: In this section, we analyze FlowCloud versions 5.0.2 and 5.0.3.
sentence.13506: Contrary to those previously found, the samples we obtained for version
sentence.13507: 5.0.2 contain verbose error messages and meticulous logging.
sentence.13508: This deployment process is very similar to the one described by Proofpoint for version 5.0.1.
sentence.13509: The three main components are a driver with rootkit functionality, a simple persistence module, and a custom backdoor.
sentence.13510: We describe these in detail in the upcoming sections.
sentence.13512: The first stage is responsible mostly for creating the files and registry keys used by the other stages.
sentence.13513: The values for these executables and configuration data can be found, encrypted, in the loader’s resource section.
sentence.13514: Table 1 contains an overview of these resources and their use.
sentence.13516: Contents of the dropper’s resources Resource IDRoleInternal name 100FlowCloud RAT DLLfcClientDll 10132-bit rootkit driverDriver 10264-bit rootkit driverDriver 103DLL hijacking vulnerable appN/A 104Shellcode loaded by the malicious library in the DLL hijackingSETLANG_dlcore 105Shellcode that loads fcClient (unused)N/A 106Final dropper stagefcClient 10732-bit persistence modulefcClientWD_x86 10864-bit persistence modulefcClientWD_x64 109Legitimate library used for module stompingslam 110DLL used for hijackingXXXModule_dlcore0 1000Protobuf serialized FlowCloud configurationN/A 1001Dropper configurationN/A 2000Used as an alternative or extension to resource 2001N/A 2001Path to the registry key for the PrintProcessor service (used by the driver)N/A 10000Installation configurationN/A In the instances we observed, most resources are written to disk encrypted, and only decrypted in memory when needed.
sentence.13517: In some cases, they are then re-encrypted but with a different key.
sentence.13518: This technique makes it harder to dump the plaintext values from the process’s memory and to analyze exit dumps.
sentence.13519: The paths and registry keys to use, and whether they should be decrypted before being written, are defined in the installation configuration.
sentence.13520: The samples we analyzed all store their files in the %ProgramFiles%\MSBuild\Microsoft\Expression\Blend\msole\ directory; we believe that this is the default value.
sentence.13521: FlowCloud uses filenames that are either similar to those of legitimate Windows files (e.g., rebare.dll which could be mistaken for rebar.dll) or innocuous looking (e.g., AC146142) to avoid suspicion.
sentence.13522: Figure 7 presents a graphical overview of the deployment process and its elements.
sentence.13523: We explain each of the steps in further detail in the upcoming sections.
sentence.13525: FlowCloud deployment process First, the loader decrypts and parses the embedded installation configuration, which uses the Windows INI format.
sentence.13526: This configuration defines the malware’s install path along with the filename or registry key where each embedded resource is to be written.
sentence.13527: The same values are hardcoded in the following stages, which leads us to think that the samples are generated using a builder.
sentence.13528: In a sample we analyzed, this configuration is accompanied with comments explaining the values for some sections.
sentence.13529: Figure 8 shows this installation configuration with the comments translated to English.

sentence.13533: Note that some fields are commented out.
sentence.13534: The configuration can also contain a section defining specific security software to check for, but this isn’t implemented in the loaders we analyzed.
sentence.13535: However, there is a custom AntivirusCheck class, which can check running processes against a hardcoded list of XOR-encrypted executable filenames from known security products: 360 Total Security, Avast, Avira, AVG, Bitdefender, ESET, Jiangmin Technology Antivirus, Kingsoft, McAfee, Micropoint, Norton, Rising Antivirus, and Trend Micro.
sentence.13536: This class is only used if the loader is set to directly start the fcClient module via the auto_start_after_install configuration key.
sentence.13537: Depending on the configuration keys used, the loader can either load the fcClientDll RAT module directly, thus bypassing most of the complex deployment process, or it can create a service or scheduled task.
sentence.13538: In the former case, the task or service attains persistence by being set to start automatically on boot.
sentence.13539: In the samples we observed, the task or service was configured to execute the next step of the installation process by running a legitimate application vulnerable to DLL search-order hijacking.
sentence.13540: The application and the accompanying relevant and malicious DLL were both embedded in the loader’s resources.
sentence.13542: In the samples we analyzed, the vulnerable application was either setlang.exe from Microsoft Office 2003 with a malicious setlangloc.dll or vpreview.exe from Visio Preview 2007 with a malicious vviewres.dll.
sentence.13543: Strings contained in the malicious DLL also point to emedres.dll from Emurasoft’s EmEditor as a possible third target for DLL side-loading.
sentence.13544: This is a real possibility as such vulnerabilities were present in older versions of EmEditor, but we did not see any samples using it.
sentence.13545: In all observed samples, the malicious library is the same and serves to load and execute shellcode from a file that is stored under the same name as the DLL, but with a .dat extension.
sentence.13546: We analyze this shellcode in the next section, but first, we want to look at the notable anti-analysis techniques used in this library.
sentence.13547: Despite its relatively simple goals, the library’s code makes heavy use of anti-debugging tricks and control flow obfuscation to hinder analysis.
sentence.13548: In the function that loads the next file, the useful code is repeatedly interspersed with the same sequence of opcodes to obfuscate the program’s flow.
sentence.13549: As shown in Figure 9, this short snippet is packed full of anti-analysis tricks, but ultimately amounts to an unconditional 16-byte jump.
sentence.13550: This is enough to foil many automatic analyses, including decompilers.
sentence.13552: Annotated disassembly of the control flow obfuscation snippet The above snippet is bookended by calls to two anti-debugging functions, as can be seen in Figure 10.
sentence.13553: The function, which we named crash_if_debugger in the previous screenshot, calls IsDebuggerPresent and checks some commonly hooked library functions for a breakpoint as their first instruction.
sentence.13554: If those checks detect a debugger, the function returns a value that will cause the program to jump to an invalid address and crash.
sentence.13555: The second one raises an exception via the INT 0x2D instruction and exits if it was handled by a debugger. Figure 10.
sentence.13556: Decompiler view showing the obvious pattern of anti-debugging checks.
sentence.13557: Note that we had to remove the aforementioned obfuscation for the decompiler to produce any output.
sentence.13559: When it is first executed, this module sets up persistence and installs the backdoor, rootkit, and persistence modules.
sentence.13560: It then sets specific registry keys and files as guardrails to skip the setup on subsequent runs.
sentence.13561: First, persistence is established by using the ITaskService COM interface to create the \Microsoft\Windows\CertificateServicesClient\NetTask scheduled task.
sentence.13562: If a task with the same name already exists, it is deleted before the new one is created.
sentence.13563: This task will run the DLL hijacking target as SYSTEM at each boot.
sentence.13564: Afterwards, the rootkit module is decrypted and written to the %System%\drivers folder as hidmouse.sys.
sentence.13565: A hidmouse service is then created to run that module and is immediately started.
sentence.13566: The file is then deleted from the disk and replaced by a copy of the legitimate hidusb.sys driver from the same folder.
sentence.13567: Thus, anyone looking at the file on disk rather than the one mapped into memory would see a legitimate, benign file.
sentence.13568: On Windows 10 machines, the system time is briefly changed to make it look like the service was created in January 2013.
sentence.13569: Both this and the use of the legitimate driver directory help the rootkit blend in with other drivers.
sentence.13570: The following files are copied to the %System% directory:
sentence.13571: The backdoor: rescure.dat A decoy DLL: sspisrvui.dat as sspisrvui.dll (timestomped to July 2013)
sentence.13572: The encrypted shellcode: rebare.dat The rebare.dat shellcode is very similar to that used in the self-decrypting DLL, but it loads fcClient directly.
sentence.13573: FlowCloud then starts a suspended process to perform injection on it.
sentence.13574: This process is created via CreateProcessAsUserW using a token retrieved from the explorer.exe or winlogon.exe process in the current session.
sentence.13575: The injected code loads the same backdoor (rescure.dat) into the process’s memory and calls its startModule export to finish the installation.
sentence.13576: Meanwhile, the injection process is terminated.
sentence.13577: At this point, installation of the backdoor is complete.
sentence.13578: All that is left is to execute the backdoor.
sentence.13579: To achieve this, the new process loads the decoy DLL and manually replaces its content in memory with the fcClientDll module (a process known as module stomping or DLL hollowing), before calling its main function.
sentence.13581: This complex module is the main component of the backdoor.
sentence.13582: It provides a wide range of capabilities from full file system access to control of camera peripherals and everything in between.
sentence.13583: Although we did not observe any plug-ins, the backdoor contains code that hints that they can be used to further extend functionality.
sentence.13584: Before diving deeper into the functionalities, we want to highlight some notable characteristics: Configuration information and data for communications with the C&C server are Protobuf-serialized, compressed, and encrypted.
sentence.13585: File exfiltration is done through encrypted, Protobuf-serialized structures and is disguised as HTTP by prepending the data with a hardcoded, fake POST request.
sentence.13586: The Content-Length header is the only variable element, as it is set to the actual size of the data sent.
sentence.13587: This hardcoded request can be seen in Figure 11.
sentence.13588: Multiple functionalities are implemented through the use of COM objects and interfaces.

sentence.13590: Hardcoded, fake HTTP POST request used for FlowCloud C&C communication This component uses an encrypted, Protobuf-serialized configuration that it tries to read from a file on disk or a registry key.
sentence.13591: The configurations we observed were composed of three sections:
sentence.13592: server_config: This section contains information about the C&C servers and identification information about the victim and backdoor.
sentence.13593: policys [sic]: This section defines the behavior of the backdoor’s components and is described in detail in the following paragraphs.
sentence.13594: install_config: As the name indicates, this section defines the installation parameters.
sentence.13595: An example of such a server_config is shown in Figure 12.
sentence.13596: This configuration corresponds to resource 1000 in the initial loader.
sentence.13597: It defines the address and port for both the exfiltration server (file_server) and the C&C server (exchange_server), along with the encryption key to use for communication with each.
sentence.13598: A fallback server can also be defined for each of these.
sentence.13599: The file_key field defines the encryption key to use when storing files that are to be exfiltrated.
sentence.13600: The other entries are used to identify the backdoor and the victimized host:
sentence.13601: product_name: A name for the backdoor in use.
sentence.13602: PCArrowI seems to correspond to FlowCloud.
sentence.13604: id_prefix: This value is prefixed to the generated ID.
sentence.13605: Presumably, used to group victims or campaigns.
sentence.13607: This value uniquely identifies the victim.
sentence.13608: Initially, it is empty; the value is generated on the first execution using the following format: <prefix>_<current timestamp>_<machine hostname> 12345678910111213141516171819202122 server_config { product_name: “PCArrowI" product_version: "v5.0.2" id: "1202_[REDACTED]" root: "" file_server: "47.111.22[.]65" file_server_port: "80" file_server_bak: "" file_server_bak_port: "" exchange_server: "47.111.22[.]65" exchange_server_port: "81" exchange_server_bak: "" exchange_server_bak_port: "" file_server_key: "E\367\016\031<…>" xchg_server_key: "8\335\325$<…>" file_key: "U\267\323\353\<…>"
sentence.13610: server_config section of a decoded FlowCloud configuration FlowCloud’s capabilities are spread out over a series of singleton classes, each of which implements a cohesive set of functionalities related to a specific type of data or action.
sentence.13611: These roughly follow an internal naming convention where classes with names ending with manager_handler perform actions in response to C&C commands, while those whose names end with manager automatically perform actions based on timers or event listeners.
sentence.13612: Each manager stores collected data in its own SQLite database, while data that is collected on demand is returned directly to the C&C server.
sentence.13613: Data is encrypted with the aforementioned file_key before being inserted into the database.
sentence.13614: The location of the SQLite databases is defined by the data_folder install configuration key, with the default value being %ProgramFiles%\MSBuild\Microsoft\Expression\Blend\msole\fcdata.
sentence.13615: The classes are orchestrated by an instance of fc_kernel_manager.
sentence.13616: This object is responsible for initializing other components and handling C&C connections.
sentence.13617: It can also update the local configuration when the corresponding command is received.
sentence.13618: As shown in Figure 13, parameters and frequency of automated actions can be specified and finely tuned through configuration policies.
sentence.13619: Data exfiltration is likewise automated: policies can contain a cache_size or cache_count parameter, which determines how much data can be collected locally by the corresponding class before it is staged for exfiltration.

sentence.13621: The policys [sic] section of a decoded FlowCloud config As we have previously mentioned, this implant uses a lot of classes.
sentence.13622: Rather than documenting each of them individually, we will present an overview of the available functionality by grouping them into three categories: those that interact with the file system, functionalities that collect information about programs and processes, and those that gather real-time information about user activity.
sentence.13623: File system FlowCloud provides interaction with the file system in a variety of ways, most of which can store file metadata and content in their SQLite database.
sentence.13624: One of these is a component that walks through all mapped file systems and collects files that are not excluded by filters in the smfile_search_policy.
sentence.13625: It also creates an invisible window that listens for file creation, modification, or renaming events.
sentence.13626: The corresponding files are collected unless they are excluded by that policy.
sentence.13627: Another component collects information about mapped volumes, including mount point, name, drive type, and disk usage data.
sentence.13628: This same class collects file and directory metadata.
sentence.13629: As a complement to these automated measures, the backdoor implements functions that provide full access and control over the content of mounted drives.
sentence.13630: This includes bidirectional file transfers between the C&C and the compromised machine. Programs and processes FlowCloud is able to automatically obtain a list of installed software through the use of the undocumented IShellAppManager COM interface.
sentence.13631: This functionality can also be invoked via a C&C command.
sentence.13632: Figure 14 shows, after the extraneous code has been removed, how that interface is used.
sentence.13634: Simplified code showing how the IShellAppManager COM interface is used to list installed applications Other commands can be used to retrieve a detailed list of available services and currently running processes.
sentence.13635: Another interesting feature is the near real-time monitoring of process activity.
sentence.13636: To achieve this, FlowCloud runs WMI queries every second to get all process creation and termination events.
sentence.13637: The obtained information is correlated with data from the Win32_Process table for a more detailed view.
sentence.13638: User activity FlowCloud is able collect a miscellany of data that we have decided to group under the “User activity” umbrella.
sentence.13639: It has the ability to monitor the clipboard for changes and save any data it contains.
sentence.13640: As seen in Figure 15, it achieves this by creating an invisible window with a custom class and registering two clipboard formats.
sentence.13641: This window uses AddClipboardFormatListener (on Windows Vista or more recent) or SetClipboardViewer (on Windows XP and prior) to listen for clipboard content changes. Figure 15.
sentence.13642: Set up monitoring of the clipboard Collected clipboard content is stored along with information about the current foreground window.
sentence.13643: This information can help attackers understand the data by contextualizing it.
sentence.13644: FlowCloud can periodically take screenshots and store them with information about the foreground process and time since the last user input.
sentence.13645: To limit the disk space used, images where fewer than 5% of the pixels differ from the most recently stored capture aren’t saved.
sentence.13646: This feature can also be invoked on demand by the server.
sentence.13647: Another of the backdoor’s components records mouse and keyboard activity to a database.
sentence.13648: It does not collect these directly, but instead acts in tandem with the keylogger component of the driver (described in the next section) by reading data from the \\.\pipe\namedpipe_keymousespy_english named pipe.
sentence.13649: Interestingly, FlowCloud can also gather information about things happening around the victim’s computer.
sentence.13650: The first way it does so is through a C&C command that takes a picture using connected camera peripherals.
sentence.13651: This feature is implemented using the CCameraDS class from OpenCV.
sentence.13652: The second way it can collect information about the computer’s surroundings is by recording audio.
sentence.13653: Much like a voice assistant, FlowCloud can use a computer’s microphone to listen to its surroundings, but instead of recording being triggered by a command word, it seems to be triggered by any sound over a threshold defined by the decibel_limit field of the audio_policy.
sentence.13654: The default value is 65 decibels, which is in the upper range of normal conversation volume (commonly defined to be anywhere between 50 and 70 dB by various sources).
sentence.13656: The loaded shellcode is a self-decrypting DLL.
sentence.13657: It first decrypts the embedded DLL using a byte-oriented XOR-and-ADD scheme (shown in Figure 16).
sentence.13658: The shellcode we analyzed used the key 0x7B. Once it has decrypted the embedded DLL, the shellcode manually performs the functions of LoadLibrary and calls the loaded module’s startModule export.
sentence.13659: for (int i=0; i < ciphertext_length; i++) plaintext[i] = ((encrypted[i] ^ key)
sentence.13661: Pseudocode for the DLL decryption routine This newly loaded module uses the same anti-debugging and anti-analysis techniques as the hijacking DLL described above.
sentence.13662: On top of those, it also uses a few tricks of its own: Covers its tracks by overwriting the code previously modified by the malicious library with a useless call to lstrlenW. Base64-encoded strings are used for function imports (via GetProcAddress) and only decoded as needed.
sentence.13663: Exits if the process’s executable is not the expected DLL hijacking target (e.g., setlang.exe).
sentence.13664: The module creates a new process using the same executable and performs process injection on it, redirecting the existing thread to the written code region.
sentence.13665: This code inside the new process launches a thread that decrypts and loads the fcClient module before calling its startModule export.
sentence.13666: That function will perform the final stages of the installation and load the DLL containing the backdoor functionality.
sentence.13667: Driver (hidmouse.sys) FlowCloud’s driver serves a dual purpose: it acts as both a keylogger and a rootkit.
sentence.13668: It accomplishes this mainly by hijacking native drivers’ handler functions for specific I/O control codes and replacing them with its own: Read (IRP_MJ_READ) for the keyboard driver (kbdclass or KeyboardClass0) Read (IRP_MJ_READ) for the mouse driver (mouclass or PointerClass0)
sentence.13669: Device control (IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL) for the network driver (tcpip or nsiproxy)
sentence.13670: The driver also provides kernel-level functionalities to be used by the RAT.
sentence.13671: They can be invoked via IO control codes or by writing to specific registry keys.
sentence.13672: This module is signed with a certificate with the thumbprint 02ED6A578C575C8D9C72398E790354B095BB07BC.
sentence.13673: Issued to Hangzhou Leishite Laser Technology Co. in 2012 by Wosign and revoked in 2014, it seems most likely this certificate was stolen.
sentence.13674: Keylogging In its IRP_MJ_READ handlers for keyboard and mouse events, the driver simply records IO events to lookaside lists before passing them to the legitimate handler.
sentence.13675: This ensures that the driver doesn’t interfere in a way that could be noticeable by the user.
sentence.13676: These events are then parsed to the format used by the backdoor’s keymouse_manager and written to the named pipe \\.\pipe\namedpipe_keymousespy_english.
sentence.13677: Rootkit After hijacking the aforementioned drivers, the rootkit erases the DLL names associated with them from internal structures used to display device drivers.
sentence.13678: The rootkit can prevent processes from being shown by utilities that list running processes, such as Task Manager.
sentence.13679: As shown in Figure 17, it achieves this by removing their entries from the ActiveProcessLinks list of the undocumented KPROCESS kernel structure.
sentence.13680: Since this structure is not part of the public API and can change between releases, the rootkit contains code to match the operating system’s build number to the correct offsets in this structure.
sentence.13681: That code covers all versions from Windows XP to Windows 10 20H1.
sentence.13682: This functionality can be invoked on any process via the IOCTL_HIDE_PROCESS_BY_PROCESSID (0x222028) control code.
sentence.13683: It is also used, on driver startup, to hide the process with the PID contained in the registry key HKLM\HARDWARE\{76BA14B7-AF0C-4dc9-9E9D-2A6970F231D9}.
sentence.13684: This process is further camouflaged by changing its associated executable filename to one of svchost.exe or dllhost.exe in the same kernel structure.
sentence.13686: Function used to prevent a process from being displayed in lists of running processes Through its hijacking of the network driver, the rootkit can also hide a single process’s network traffic from local utilities.
sentence.13687: The process whose traffic is to be hidden is set through the IOCTL_SET_TRAFFICHIDE_PROCESSID (0x222048) control code.
sentence.13688: Some of the rootkit’s functions are used by the fcClientDll module to hide the process in which it is running.
sentence.13689: Control codes to manipulate a process name in various internal structures are also exposed by the driver.
sentence.13691: This module is relatively simple compared to other components.
sentence.13692: The previously mentioned NetTask already accomplishes persistence in most cases, by executing on system startup.
sentence.13693: This module complements that mechanism by ensuring persistence in a very specific edge case where execution of the malware might be interrupted: the user logs out on a system with hibernation and Fastboot enabled.
sentence.13694: On systems where either of those is disabled, this module does nothing.
sentence.13695: FlowCloud v4.1.3 This older version of FlowCloud has already been described in a Proofpoint blogpost and presents similarities to the newer version described in the preceding subsections, so we will only highlight notable differences and new information revealed by our analysis.
sentence.13696: This version runs multiple anti-analysis and anti-detection checks before executing its payload, and terminates if any of those tests detect that the process is being analyzed.
sentence.13697: It checks running processes for executables of several known cybersecurity vendors.
sentence.13698: While most of these names are also present in version 5, this list is not a strict subset of the one v.5 uses.
sentence.13699: This tends to support the proposition that versions 4 and 5 of FlowCloud are maintained in parallel.
sentence.13700: It also embeds a DLL version of the Pafish (aka Paranoid Fish) sandbox and analysis detection tool as one of its encrypted resources.
sentence.13701: This library is loaded in memory and all of the anti-analysis/anti-sandboxing checks it implements are run.
sentence.13702: Interestingly, the driver installed is the same as the one for version 5.0.2.
sentence.13703: Those used by version 5.0.3 provide identical functionality, but differ slightly.
sentence.13704: TA410 – LookingFrog LookingFrog uses two main malware families: X4 and LookBack.
sentence.13705: We have seen both of them on machines belonging to the same victim. X4 X4 is a custom backdoor that is used as a first stage, before LookBack is deployed.
sentence.13706: It is loaded by a VMProtect-ed loader, usually named PortableDeviceApi.dll or WptsExtensions.dll.
sentence.13707: Unfortunately, we were not able to uncover any persistence method.
sentence.13708: The loader injects an orchestrator into memory in a svchost.exe process.
sentence.13709: In turn, the orchestrator injects the network component into memory and communicates with it via a file located at C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Crypto\RSA\MachineKeys\Log\rsa.txt.
sentence.13710: Figure 18 shows a summary of the X4 components.
sentence.13712: Summary of the X4 components The network component is shellcode.
sentence.13713: It is encrypted using the AES algorithm and stored in the Windows registry.
sentence.13714: Table 2 shows the three registry keys used by X4.
sentence.13716: Network shellcode registry keys Registry KeyDescription HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\DRM\X4KeyAES key. HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\DRM\PSKeyName of the process into which the shellcode will be injected (spoolsv.exe). HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\DRM\X4DataEncrypted shellcode.
sentence.13717: The decrypted shellcode looks like it was based on Metasploit and communicates with a hardcoded IP address via HTTP.
sentence.13718: An interesting characteristic is that it uses the fake Host header onedrive.live.com.
sentence.13719: Every second, the orchestrator, which lives in memory only, reads the cleartext rsa.txt file to check whether there are new commands to execute.
sentence.13720: The commands are received from the C&C server, via the network shellcode.
sentence.13721: In the orchestrator, the commands are identified by a numerical identifier that is computed from the command name, as shown in Figure 19. Figure 19.
sentence.13722: Custom hash function seen in X4 The orchestrator handles seven commands, detailed in Table 3.
sentence.13723: Output of these commands is written to C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Crypto\RSA\MachineKeys\Log\output.log.

sentence.13726: It can also modify X4Key and PSKey.

sentence.13733: X4 provides basic functionalities to control the machine remotely, but it lacks more advanced spying capabilities.
sentence.13734: LookBack The LookBack backdoor has previously been described by Proofpoint; we are therefore providing a quick summary and our analysis of the custom network protocol.
sentence.13735: Backdoor In all samples we observed, the LookBack loader is a legitimate version of libcurl.dll with the curl_share_init (ordinal #52) export modified to load the SodomNormal communications module.
sentence.13736: This corroborates the observation by Proofpoint researchers.
sentence.13737: This module is embedded in the library’s resource section and encrypted with an algorithm similar to RC4.
sentence.13738: The encryption/decryption function, shown in Figure 20, always uses the same key. Figure 20.
sentence.13739: Decompiled view of the function used to encrypt and decrypt the embedded module The SodomNormal component tries to read configuration information from a sodom.ini file.
sentence.13740: This configuration file is encrypted using the just-described function and starts with the magic bytes 0xAF1324BC.
sentence.13741: If this file is unavailable or invalid, a hardcoded default configuration is used.
sentence.13742: A unique victim ID is then generated from the victim’s CPUID, username, and IP address.
sentence.13743: This is sent to the server along with the computer’s name and the configuration data.
sentence.13744: The communications module then downloads the main backdoor module, named SodomMain, from the C&C server.
sentence.13745: Unfortunately, we couldn’t obtain this module.
sentence.13746: Communication protocol LookBack can communicate over HTTP or via its “normal protocol”.
sentence.13747: In either case, the data being transferred is the same.
sentence.13748: LookBack’s normal protocol uses raw TCP sockets and a custom message format described in Table 4.
sentence.13749: This message is composed of eight header fields, followed by a body of variable length.
sentence.13750: The message body is encrypted with the function previously described for the SodomNormal resource in the loader (Figure 20).
sentence.13751: The encrypted data is then compressed with the deflate algorithm via the compress function of the statically linked zlib.
sentence.13753: LookBack message format FieldOffset (bytes)Note Magic bytes0x00The constant 0x48AB2EC2.
sentence.13754: Messages that don’t start with this magic value are discarded.
sentence.13755: <Message dependent>0x04 Compressed body size0x08 Uncompressed body size0x0C Checksum0x10CRC32 of the message body.
sentence.13756: Message type0x14Integer value indicating the message’s content and the associated action to be performed.
sentence.13757: We have found code for over 50 message types.
sentence.13758: There seems to be little to no overlap between the values used by the client and the server.
sentence.13759: Table 5 presents the types we have analyzed in more depth.

sentence.13771: The HTTP protocol uses the message format detailed in the previous paragraph, but it adds a few extra steps to disguise its traffic as legitimate HTTP.
sentence.13772: It uses a pair of hardcoded templates, one for client requests and another for server responses.
sentence.13773: The fields required for HTTP, such as content length, address, and port number, are filled in with the correct values; useless data is used for the others.
sentence.13774: For client requests, the messages are encoded with a modified hexadecimal algorithm that uses the encoding alphabet a-p instead of the conventional 0-9a-f.
sentence.13775: This provides some obfuscation and ensures that messages will not contain binary data or be obviously hex encoded, both of which could look suspicious in an application/x-www-form-urlencoded message.
sentence.13776: The request’s body is composed of this encoded value prefixed with the hardcoded string id=1&op=report&status=. Client request and server response templates are shown in Figure 21 and Figure 22 respectively, with the template fields in angle brackets.

sentence.13783: Template used for HTTP server responses TA410 – JollyFrog This third team uses off-the-shelf malware from the known malware families QuasarRAT and Korplug (aka PlugX).
sentence.13784: JollyFrog mostly aligns with what was described by Fortinet as APT10. Korplug Korplug, also known as PlugX, is a backdoor that has been used for years by many different cyberespionage groups.
sentence.13785: Despite being well known, it is still in use and we have observed TA410 using it as recently as in April 2021.
sentence.13786: In the case of TA410, Korplug arrives as a RARSFX archive, generally named m.exe, containing three files: qrt.dll: A custom loader.
sentence.13787: qrtfix.exe: A legitimate signed application from F-Secure, vulnerable to DLL search-order hijacking.
sentence.13790: The loader allocates memory using VirtualAlloc and copies the content of qrt.dll.usb there.
sentence.13791: Then it jumps right into the shellcode that will decompress and load the Korplug payload.
sentence.13792: QuasarRAT QuasarRAT is a full-featured backdoor freely available on GitHub.
sentence.13793: It is used by numerous threat actors who perform cyberespionage or cybercrime.
sentence.13794: TA410 uses a custom downloader and a custom loader written in .NET, which are convenient for identifying their instances of QuasarRAT among all the noise created by other attackers.
sentence.13795: Named sll.exe, this downloader is digitally signed with the certificate seen in Figure 23.
sentence.13796: The certificate is likely stolen and belongs to 北京和赢讯时科技有限公司 (translated: Beijing Heyingxunshi Technology Co., Ltd.) with thumbprint 850821D88A4475F0310F10FBA806353A4113D252.
sentence.13797: Although the certificate has now been revoked, it was still valid when this sample was signed on August 10th, 2020.
sentence.13799: Digital signature of the QuasarRAT downloader This downloader simply downloads the loader and encrypted QuasarRAT payload from the hardcoded C&C server http://ffca.caibi379[.]com, at /rwjh/new/.
sentence.13800: This server was previously linked to FlowCloud (FlowingFrog).
sentence.13801: The loader is named PresentationCache.exe and is protected with DNGuard, a commercial .NET packer.
sentence.13802: It is also signed with the same certificate as the downloader.
sentence.13803: It decrypts and loads the final QuasarRAT payload, which uses cahe.microsofts[.]org as its C&C server.
sentence.13804: Conclusion TA410 is a cyberespionage umbrella targeting high-profile entities such as governments and universities worldwide.
sentence.13805: ESET is revealing its latest findings about this group, including results from ongoing research, during Botconf 2022.
sentence.13806: Initial access to targets is obtained by exploiting vulnerable internet-facing applications such as Microsoft Exchange, or by sending spearphishing emails with malicious attachments such as RTF documents created via the Royal Road builder.
sentence.13807: Even though the JollyFrog team uses generic tools, FlowingFrog and LookingFrog have access to complex implants such as FlowCloud and LookBack.
sentence.13808: YARA and Snort rules for these implants are available in ESET’s GitHub repository.

sentence.13941: title: When byte code bites: Who checks the contents of compiled Python files? url: https://securityboulevard.com/2023/06/when-byte-code-bites-who-checks-the-contents-of-compiled-python-files/ During our continuous threat hunting efforts to find malware in open-source repositories, the ReversingLabs team encountered a novel attack that used compiled Python code to evade detection.
sentence.13942: It may be the first supply chain attack to take advantage of the fact that Python byte code (PYC) files can be directly executed, and it comes amid a spike in malicious submissions to the Python Package Index (PyPI).
sentence.13943: If so, it poses yet another supply chain risk going forward, since this type of attack is likely to be missed by most security tools, which only scan Python source code (PY) files.
sentence.13944: We reported the discovered package, named fshec2, to the PyPI security team on April 17, 2023, and it was removed from the PyPI repository the same day.
sentence.13945: The PyPI security team has also recognized this type of attack as interesting and acknowledged that it had not been previously seen.
sentence.13946: Here’s how my threat research team identified the fshec2 as a suspicious package and the novel method that the attackers employed as they attempted to avoid detection.
sentence.13947: I’ll also tell you what our researchers found when investigating the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by the malware — and provide evidence of successful attacks.
sentence.13949: Unusual behaviors ReversingLabs regularly scans open-source registers such as PyPi, npm, RubyGems, and GitHub looking for suspicious files.
sentence.13950: As the team observed before, these often jump out at us from the millions of legitimate, nonmalicious files hosted on these platforms because they exhibit strange qualities or behaviors that, experience tells us, often signal malicious intent.
sentence.13951: That was the case with fshec2.
sentence.13952: The package initially caught our attention following a scan using the ReversingLabs Software Supply Chain Security platform, which extracted a suspicious combination of behaviors from an fshec2 compiled binary.
sentence.13953: Those suspicious behaviors extracted from the decompiled file included the presence of URLs that reference the host by IP address, as well as the creation of a process and execution of a file.
sentence.13954: A manual review of the fshec2 package followed.
sentence.13955: It revealed that it contains only three files.
sentence.13956: The code inside two of those Python source code files, _init_.py and main.py, appeared benign.
sentence.13957: It was only upon inspection of a decompiled version of the third file, full.pyc, that more interesting behaviors came to light and the true nature of the package emerged.
sentence.13958: Figure 1: Files containing package functionality Unmasking an unusual loader Threat actors are always trying to evade detection from security solutions.
sentence.13959: Obfuscation is one of the most popular methods to achieve this.
sentence.13960: For example, several of our previous research blogs have explored incidents in the npm landscape in which JavaScript obfuscation was used.
sentence.13961: That includes the Material Tailwind and IconBurst campaigns, as well as the more recent campaign we identified distributing Havoc malware.
sentence.13962: Historically, npm has been the unfortunate leader and PyPI an also-ran in the race to see which open-source platform attracts the most attention from malware authors.
sentence.13963: In the last six months, however, ReversingLabs and others have observed a marked increase in the volume of malware published to PyPI.
sentence.13964: In fact, in May, the creation of new user accounts and projects on PyPI were temporarily suspended for a few hours due to a high volume of malicious activity.
sentence.13965: Along with the increase in malicious modules, my team has observed an increase in the use of various obfuscation techniques in malware published to the PyPI repository.
sentence.13966: One of the most popular obfuscation techniques is execution of Base64-encoded malicious code, which was first observed in campaigns related to W4SP authors in November 2022.
sentence.13967: Variations of that attack, in which malicious code is embedded in code but shifted past the edge of default screen borders (thereby hiding it from view), are still seen in the wild.
sentence.13968: Today, however, attackers have more tools at their disposal.
sentence.13969: For example, use of W4SP crew obfuscation tools such as Hyperion and Kramer is on the rise — likely a response to the improving detection capabilities of security companies monitoring PyPI and other public package repositories.
sentence.13970: The fshec2 package uses a significantly different approach that doesn’t rely on obfuscation tools.
sentence.13971: It instead places the malicious functionality into a single file containing compiled Python byte code.
sentence.13972: How Python attacks (usually) work Before I get to the new obfuscation method my team discovered, here’s a look at how malicious attacks using Python typically work.
sentence.13973: There are three types of Python files that may play a role in a malicious campaign: plaintext Python files, which have a /oy extension; compiled Python files, which have a .pyc extension; and Python files that have been compiled into native executables using tools such as py2exe and PyInstaller.
sentence.13974: In most of the malicious campaigns that my team has observed leveraging PyPI packages, the executables are not present in the malicious package but are downloaded and run by the plaintext PY files from external infrastructure.
sentence.13976: Here, we observed a compiled Python file (full.pyc) present inside the PyPI package that contained malicious functionality.
sentence.13977: The entry point of the package was found in the __init__.py file, which imports a function from the other plaintext file, main.py, which contains Python source code responsible for loading of the Python compiled module located in one of the other files, full.pyc.
sentence.13978: This innocent-seeming import of a function triggers a previously unseen loading technique inside the main.py file that avoids using the usual import directive, which is the simplest way to load a Python compiled module (and also something that is likely to get noticed.)
sentence.13979: Instead, Importlib, the implementation of import in Python source code portable to any Python interpreter, is used to avoid detection by security tools.
sentence.13980: (Some explanation: Importlib is typically used in cases where the imported library is dynamically modified upon import.
sentence.13981: However, the library loaded by main.py was unchanged, meaning that the regular import function would have sufficed.
sentence.13982: This tends to support the theory that Importlib is used to avoid detection.)
sentence.13983: Figure 2: Loading of the compiled Python module from main.py After the module is loaded, its get_path method is invoked
sentence.13985: Using ReversingLabs Software Supply Chain Security, my team was able to detect and extract this code from the decompiled PYC file.
sentence.13986: The get_path method, which isn’t found (in readable form) anywhere inside the original fshec2 package, performs some of the common malicious functions observed in other malicious PyPI packages we have analyzed.
sentence.13987: Among other things, it collects usernames, hostnames, and directory listings.
sentence.13988: It also fetches commands that are set for execution using scheduled tasks or cronjob, depending on the host platform.
sentence.13989: Figure 3: The decompiled code extracted from the full.pyc compiled byte code file showing the content of the get_path() method.
sentence.13990: The fetched commands are just another Python script, which is intended to change (see Figure 4).
sentence.13991: In fact, while I have been writing this blog, my team observed it download and execute yet another Python script from the cron_script located on the same host.
sentence.13992: The cron_script contained functionality almost identical to the script found in full.pyc, the compiled Python module shipped with the PyPI package.
sentence.13993: In this way, the fshec2 attack is engineered to be able to evolve.
sentence.13994: The full.pyc file contains functionality to download commands from a remote server identified in the commands path on the C2 server.
sentence.13995: The downloaded commands are a Python file almost identical to full.pyc but with the location for downloading stage 2 commands placed in a cron_script, which periodically downloads new commands.
sentence.13996: This allows the attackers to change the content served at the commands location to make the malware serve new commands.
sentence.13997: Figure 4: Code responsible for downloading cron_script file A misconfigured web host gives up the goods Given the malware’s reliance on remote C2 infrastructure, it made sense to scout out the web host used in the attack to get more information about the malware’s capabilities.
sentence.13998: As it turned out, the web host had plenty to tell us!
sentence.13999: Like regular developers, malware authors often make configuration mistakes when setting up infrastructure.
sentence.14000: Such mistakes can reveal interesting information about the inner workings of malicious software.
sentence.14001: That was the case with the web host that was set up to communicate with compromised systems.
sentence.14002: For example, trying to access an invalid page on the web host did not generate a 404 “page not found” error, as you would expect.
sentence.14003: Instead, visitors were served a page from a Django application listing a variety of commands (see Figure 5).
sentence.14004: Figure 5: Uncovered web locations Fortunately for us, the Django application was configured in debug mode, with error descriptions that gave us a detailed list of reachable host paths.
sentence.14005: Some of those we had already seen in the downloaded scripts used in the attack, but there were new paths that we had not seen, including: admin, uploaded_files, and download.
sentence.14006: Unfortunately, the trail went cold there, because all three of them require authorization to execute page functionality.
sentence.14007: Figure 6: Password-protected file download form Still, some information was exposed by this oversight, even without knowing the password.
sentence.14008: For example, command No. 7 in Figure 5 provides a way to download files by their ID using the command: download/<int:file_id>, where file_id is an integer and the files in question are numbered in sequential order, starting from 1.
sentence.14009: As seen in Figure 6, the filename is also leaked without requiring authorization.
sentence.14010: The sheer number of these mistakes might lead us to the conclusion that this attack was not the work of a state-sponsored actor and not an advanced persistent threat (APT).
sentence.14011: While my team didn’t collect enough evidence to prove that assumption one way or another, harvesting the filenames by incrementing file ID let us determine that the attack was successful in some cases.
sentence.14012: Our researchers still can’t say who or what the targets were.
sentence.14013: However, we can confirm that developers did install the malicious PyPI package and that their machine names, usernames, and directory listings were harvested as a result.
sentence.14014: Using the method described above, our researchers downloaded files with ID Nos. 1-18.
sentence.14015: The resulting filenames show that at least two targets were infected with username and hostname combinations desktop__desktop-7G-Series and Txxxx_Axxxx__LAPTOP-UH9S5HF2 (identifying information removed).
sentence.14016: Some of the filenames suggest that additional malware commands include keylogging functionality.
sentence.14017: Finally, my team can’t exclude the possibility that there were other channels of distribution besides the fshec2 PyPI package that we haven’t encountered. Figure 7: Names of the files that can be downloaded Conclusion Even though this malicious package and the corresponding C2 infrastructure weren’t state of the art, they remind us how easy it is for malware authors to avoid detection based on source-code analysis.
sentence.14018: Loader scripts such as those discovered in the fshec2 package contain a minimal amount of Python code and perform a simple action: loading of a compiled Python module.
sentence.14019: It just happens to be a malicious module.
sentence.14020: Inspector, the default tool provided by the PyPI security team to analyze PyPI packages, doesn’t, at the moment, provide any way of analyzing binary files to spot malicious behaviors.
sentence.14021: Compiled code from the .pyc file needed to be decompiled in order to analyze its content.
sentence.14022: Once that was accomplished, the suspicious and malicious functionality was easy to see.
sentence.14023: Figure 8: Inspector tool provided by PyPI security team
sentence.14024: The discovery of malicious code in the fshec2 package underscores why the ability to detect malicious functions such as get_path is becoming more important for both security and DevSecOps teams.
sentence.14025: Most application security solutions either do not focus on supply chain security or only perform source-code analysis as part of the package security inspection.
sentence.14026: That is why malware hidden inside the Python compiled byte code could slip under the radar of the traditional security solutions.
sentence.14027: ReversingLabs Software Supply Chain Security supports static analysis and unpacking for a wide range of binary file formats, including the kind of compiled Python byte code seen in this attack.
sentence.14028: As seen with fshec2, analyzing this kind of file allows defenders to extract indicators of malicious intent, making security assessment much easier.
sentence.14029: Figure 9: Behavior indicators and networking strings extracted from the decompiled PYC file using ReversingLabs Software Supply Chain Security.
sentence.14030: This includes detection of process creation, file execution, gathering of sensitive information, presence of IP addresses, and much more.
sentence.14031: Simple scanning of source code from open-source packages will miss this type of threat.
sentence.14032: And, as the attackers press their advantage and become more sophisticated, even more advanced tools will be needed to make sure your developed code and software development infrastructure remains protected.

sentence.14037: title: MoonBounce: the dark side of UEFI firmware url: https://securelist.com/moonbounce-the-dark-side-of-uefi-firmware/105468/ What happened?
sentence.14038: At the end of 2021, we were made aware of a UEFI firmware-level compromise through logs from our Firmware Scanner, which has been integrated into Kaspersky products since the beginning of 2019.
sentence.14039: Further analysis has shown that a single component within the inspected firmware’s image was modified by attackers in a way that allowed them to intercept the original execution flow of the machine’s boot sequence and introduce a sophisticated infection chain.
sentence.14040: By examining the components of the rogue firmware and other malicious artefacts from the target’s network, we were able to reach the following conclusions:
sentence.14041: The inspected UEFI firmware was tampered with to embed a malicious code that we dub MoonBounce; Due to its emplacement on SPI flash which is located on the motherboard instead of the hard disk, the implant is capable of persisting in the system across disk formatting or replacement; The purpose of the implant is to facilitate the deployment of user-mode malware that stages execution of further payloads downloaded from the internet; The infection chain itself does not leave any traces on the hard drive, as its components operate in memory only, thus facilitating a fileless attack with a small footprint; We detected other non-UEFI implants in the targeted network that communicated with the same infrastructure which hosted the the stager’s payload; By assessing the combination of the above findings with network infrastructure fingerprints and other TTPs exhibited by the the attackers; to the best of our knowledge the intrusion set in question can be attributed to APT41, a threat actor that’s been widely reported to be Chinese-speaking; In this report we describe in detail how the MoonBounce implant works, how it is connected to APT41, and what other traces of activity related to Chinese-speaking actors we were able to observe in the compromised network that could indicate a connection to this threat actor and the underlying campaign.
sentence.14042: Revisiting the current state of the art in persistent attacks In the last year, there have been several public accounts on the ongoing trend of UEFI threats.
sentence.14043: Notable examples include the UEFI bootkit used as part of the FinSpy surveillance toolset that we reported on, the work of our colleagues from ESET on the ESPectre bootkit, and a little-known threat activity that was discovered within government organisations in the Middle East, using a UEFI bootkit of its own (briefly mentioned in our APT trends report Q3 2021 and covered in more detail in a private APT report delivered to customers of our Threat Intelligence Portal).
sentence.14044: The common denominator of those three cases is the fact that the UEFI components targeted for infection reside on the ESP (EFI System Partition), a storage space designated for some UEFI components, typically based in the computer’s hard drive or SSD.
sentence.14045: The most notable elements of the ESP are the Boot Manager and OS loader, both invoked during the machine’s boot sequence and which also happen to be the subject of tampering in the case of the aforementioned bootkits.
sentence.14046: While all of the above were seen in use by advanced actors, a different class of bootkits raises even higher concern.
sentence.14047: This one is made up of implants found in the UEFI firmware within the SPI flash, a non-volatile storage external to the hard drive.
sentence.14048: Such bootkits are not only stealthier (partially because of limited visibility by security products into this hardware component), but also more difficult to mitigate: flashing a clean firmware image in place of a malicious one can prove to be more difficult than formatting a hard drive and reinstalling an OS, which would typically eliminate ESP level threats.
sentence.14049: MoonBounce is notable for being the third publicly revealed case of an implant from the latter class of firmware-based rootkits.
sentence.14050: Previous cases included LoJax and MosaicRegressor, which we reported on during October 2020.
sentence.14051: In that sense, MoonBounce marks a particular evolution in this group of threats by presenting a more complicated attack flow in comparison to its predecessors and a higher level of technical competence by its authors, who demonstrate a thorough understanding of the finer details involved in the UEFI boot process.
sentence.14052: Our discovery: a sophisticated implant within UEFI firmware The UEFI implant, which was detected in spring 2021 , was found to have been incorporated by the attackers into the CORE_DXE component of the firmware (also known as the DXE Foundation), which is called early on at the DXE (Driver Execution Environment) phase of the UEFI boot sequence.
sentence.14053: Among other things, this component is responsible for initializing essential data structures and function interfaces, one of which is the EFI Boot Services Table – a set of pointers to routines that are part of the CORE_DXE image itself and are callable by other DXE drivers in the boot chain.
sentence.14054: The source of the infection starts with a set of hooks that intercept the execution of several functions in the EFI Boot Services Table, namely AllocatePool, CreateEventEx and ExitBootServices.
sentence.14055: Those hooks are used to divert the flow of these functions to malicious shellcode that is appended by the attackers to the CORE_DXE image, which in turn sets up additional hooks in subsequent components of the boot chain, namely the Windows loader.
sentence.14056: This multistage chain of hooks facilitates the propagation of malicious code from the CORE_DXE image to other boot components during system startup, allowing the introduction of a malicious driver to the memory address space of the Windows kernel.
sentence.14057: This driver, which runs during the initial phases of the kernel’s execution, is in charge of deploying user-mode malware by injecting it into an svchost.exe process, once the operating system is up and running.
sentence.14058: Finally, the user mode malware reaches out to a hardcoded C&C URL (i.e. hxxp://mb.glbaitech[.]com/mboard.dll) and attempts to fetch another stage of the payload to run in memory, which we were not able to retrieve.
sentence.14059: The diagram below contains the outline of the stages taken from the moment the hooked Boot Services are called in the context of the DXE Foundation’s execution until the user-mode malware is deployed and run during the Operating System’s execution.
sentence.14060: The full description of each step in the diagram, along with the analysis of both the MoonBounce driver and user-mode malware can be found in the technical document released alongside this report.
sentence.14061: Flow of MoonBounce execution from boot sequence to malware deployment in user space Note that at the time of writing we lack sufficient evidence to retrace how the UEFI firmware was infected in the first place.
sentence.14062: The infection itself, however, is assumed to have occurred remotely.
sentence.14063: While previous UEFI firmware compromises (i.e. LoJax and MosaicRegressor) manifested as additions of DXE drivers to the overall firmware image on the SPI flash, the current case exhibits a much more subtle and stealthy technique where an existing firmware component is modified to alter its behaviour.
sentence.14064: Notably, particular functions were modified with an inline hook, meaning the replacement of the function prologue with an instruction to divert execution to a function chosen by the attacker.
sentence.14065: This form of binary instrumentation typically requires the attacker to obtain the original image, then parse and change it to introduce malicious logic.
sentence.14066: This would be possible for an attacker having ongoing and remote access to the targeted machine.
sentence.14067: Other pieces of malware on the radar In addition to MoonBounce, we found infections across multiple nodes in the same network by a known user-mode malware dubbed ScrambleCross, also known as SideWalk.
sentence.14068: This is an in-memory implant, implemented as position-independent code, that can communicate to a C2 server in order to exchange information and stage the execution of additional plugins in memory, of which none has been sighted in the wild yet.
sentence.14069: This malware was thoroughly covered by our colleagues at Trend Micro and ESET, so we will refer the reader to their excellent write-ups to understand its internals better.
sentence.14070: The position-independent code constituting ScrambleCross can be loaded in one of two ways, the first being a C++ DLL named StealthVector.
sentence.14071: It obtains the ScrambleCross shellcode by applying a modified ChaCha20 algorithm on an encrypted blob, which may reside as an additional file on disk or be embedded in the loader itself.
sentence.14072: We detected both variants of this loader in the network in question.
sentence.14073: StealthVector gets loaded through the introduction of a modified benign system DLL, in which the import address table is patched to append the malware’s DLL as a dependency.
sentence.14074: In one case, we observed such altered wbemcomn.dll (MD5: C3B153347AED27435A18E789D8B67E0A) file, which originally facilitates the functionality of WMI in Windows and was located in the directory %SYSTEM%\wbem.
sentence.14075: As a consequence, when the WMI service was initiated, the rogue version of this DLL forced the loading of a StealthVector image named wmiwk.dll.
sentence.14076: Appended IAT entry to a rogue wbemcomn.dll file which forces the loading of StealthVector upon initiation of the WMI service The table below specifies all instances of StealthVector that we detected in the targeted network, along with timestamp artefacts that might point to the date of their creation.

sentence.14078: It works by decrypting a shellcode BLOB with AES-256 and injecting it to the address space of another process.

sentence.14113: In addition to the above components, we found other stagers and post-exploitation malware implants during our research, some of which were attributed to or have been used by known Chinese-speaking threat actors: Microcin: a backdoor typically used by the SixLittleMonkeys threat actor, which we have been tracking since 2016.
sentence.14114: It is worth noting that since its inception, the SixLittleMonkeys group has been using Microcin against various targets, partly against high-profile entities based in Russia and Central Asia.
sentence.14115: The implants we observed in this campaign are shipped as DLLs that ought to run in the context of exe, with the primary intent of reading a C2 address from an encrypted configuration file stored in %WINDIR%\debug\netlogon.cfg and reaching out to the server to obtain a further payload.
sentence.14116: Interestingly, the Trojan holds a scheduling algorithm that would skip any work on Saturdays, checking the local time every hour to determine if Saturday has passed.
sentence.14117: Mimikat_ssp: a publicly available post-exploitation tool used to dump credentials and security secrets from exe, also used widely by various Chinese-speaking actors (e.g. GhostEmperor, which we reported on).
sentence.14118: Go implant: a formerly unknown backdoor used to contact a C2 server using a RESTful API, where a combination of a hardcoded IP address and a hypermedia directory path on the underlying server are used for information exchange.
sentence.14119: Both the IP and the server directory path are encrypted with AES-128 using a base64 encoded key stored in the backdoor’s image.
sentence.14120: The IP and directory path tuple are used during execution for: Initialising communications with the server; Sending information from the infected host; Requesting a specific server path containing a command for execution and downloading it;
sentence.14121: Sending back the result of the command’s execution to the C2 server.
sentence.14122: The commands retrieved from the server are also encrypted with AES-128, with the key stored in the command’s file itself.
sentence.14123: Command execution results are then encrypted using the same key.
sentence.14124: We found the following list of supported commands: Get list of drives; Get content list from a specified directory; Download a file from the C2 server; Write text to a given *.bat file and execute it; Run a shell command.
sentence.14125: It is important to note that we could not conclusively tie most of those additional pieces of malware to the intrusion set related to MoonBounce, with the exception of Microcin, where some timeline artefacts coincide with other events related to ScrambleCross, as outlined in the figure below.
sentence.14126: This suggests a low-confidence connection between Microcin and MoonBounce and may indicate usage of shared resources between SixLittleMonkeys and APT41 or involvement of the former’s operators in the MoonBounce activity.
sentence.14127: Timeline of events related to artefacts found in the network containing the MoonBounce-infected machine Who were the targets?
sentence.14128: Currently, our detections indicate a very targeted nature of the attack – the presence of the firmware rootkit was detected in a single case.
sentence.14129: Other affiliated malicious samples (e.g. ScrambleCross and its loaders) were found on multiple other machines in the same network range.
sentence.14130: In addition, we found several other victims of an undetermined nature with the same versions of ScrambleCross reaching out to the same command and control infrastructure.
sentence.14131: One particular target corresponds to an organization in control of several enterprises dealing with transport technology.
sentence.14132: What were the attackers trying to achieve?
sentence.14133: We traced some of the commands executed by the attackers after gaining a foothold in the network, which point to lateral movement and exfiltration of information from particular machines.
sentence.14134: This aligns in profile with some of the previous operations by APT41, wherein intrusions were typically made to intervene in the targeted companies’ supply chain, or to heist sensitive intellectual property and personally identifiable information.
sentence.14135: The usage of the UEFI implant in particular indicates the actor’s aim to establish a longstanding foothold within the network, as would be expected in an ongoing espionage activity.
